I didn't know very much about this game, except that it was one of Grasshopper's fun hack and slash games. I didn't know their work either, except for No More Heroes. When I saw that this game was free on Humble Bundle, I really was happy to have the chance to play one of their games.
And, well, It was a fun moment. I really enjoyed myself on this game, even though it's really, really short. I beat it in only 10 hours. Killer Is Dead doesn't really have gigantic replayability, once you've finished the main story, you only have the Gigolo missions and all that stuff, which, to be honest, didn't really interested me.
About the gameplay, it's REALLY good. I never got tired of it, it's really fun. You have two main weapons, you have your katana, which you'll be using most of the time, and Mondo's right arm. His arm can shoot projectiles that will weaken your enemies, or sometimes even one shot them if you aim for the head. It's a fun mechanic, without a very deep gameplay. The katana though, is really fun and complex. There are some combos, unlockable techniques, and QTEs.
The story, in itself, is kinda hard to talk about. You get in the game without knowing very much, except that you are an hitman named Mondo, and that you are sent in every level because of a bounty placed on someone evil, which, you'll have to kill to complete the level. The levels are pretty long, and short at the same time. The level design isn't very complex, so you'll have to go through a lot of corridors.
The boss fights, though, are very fun. They all have something proper to themselves, and it makes them very unique and fun to replay.
In the end, I had a good time with this game. Definitely not a perfect game, but it's really fun for what it is, and the story might surprise you sometimes, if you actually pay very attention to the plot, just like me.

This is a top-down puzzle game with a little action/shooting in it. I have not played any single player mode at all, but the co-op element is quite good. Co-op partner shares the same screen, so both players cannot wander too far away from each other.
The puzzles are a little too easy for me, but this makes this game a good casual top-down platformer that can be played without stress.
Movement controls aren't very good, a gamepad with analog stick is highly recommended. Because some platforms are diagonal, using keyboard to navigate is very awkward sometimes.
This game do have some awesome moments. There is a stage where you evade obstacles while dodging bullets to get to the other side before a giant monster get to you. Also there are a few awesome boss fights.
Graphics are not bad. Audio is good. Story plot is negligible. There are a few glitches especially when the connection is bad while playing online co-op, but nothing is too game-breaking. Glitches are easily fixed by reloading a checkpoint or replaying the level.
Replayability is limited. You can only replay the stages a few times to earn all the collectibles or challenges. After all that, there is no point to replay anymore.
100% Achievement is moderately easy.
The DLCs adds a little content into the game, but some challenges can be quite frustrating to complete if you aren't very good in the game.
My Score: 8/10

Surprisingly Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light is a fully fledged Tomb Raider game.
I didn't expect the perspective transition from third person to isometric to be this well done.
Do not make the mistake of thinking this is just a casual Diablo-clone spinoff.
Essentially Guardian of Light is closer to an isometric Metroidvania than a Diablo clone. There isn't any loot dropped from enemies, no stats, levels and you do not level your character. Instead you explore tombs and collect power ups for health and ammo while puzzle-platforming.
The game features the same gameplay basics as the triple A positions in the franchise, some things it does even better. The shift to isometric makes navigation and solving environmental puzzles a lot clearer while keeping the challenge on about the same level as the other titles.
Additionally we also have good combat which always felt like an afterthought in the previous Tomb Raider games. The game features a host of weapons and powerups that sufficiently mix it up during these segments.
Of course the game isnt perfect, sometimes it features some strange bugs and level props sometimes obscure the action (there is no see-through effect when Lara is behind something). However i never felt like this diminished the experience and so far did not lead to any frustrations.
It would be truly fantastic if we could get this Tomb Raider concept developed more, made it more open, more Metroidvania.
Sadly instead we got an uninspired 3rd person shooter with a lot of gore and hair physics.

Excellent and beautiful isometric environmental puzzle platformer. As clever and fun and challenging environmental puzzles as Trine 2's.
A very cheesy and cliche storyline with big plotholes, but it barely detracts from the otherwise spectacular experience. It is kind of a bittersweet thing then, that the storyline is barely paid attention to in each level. The story was clearly given much less attention during development, since the cutscenes aren't even animated, but just lazy digital paintings.
There is definite room for replayability, since you can play through the campaign differently either solo or co-op. The puzzles were just the right difficulty - I was able to figure them all out eventually, without walkthroughs. It has a very good and well-structured final boss fight (although that fight is disappointing from a purely logical standpoint).

I absolutely love the action combat of this game because it requires precision and strategic approach to most of the Hero Mode bosses/raids but allows you to just spam click your way through everything else for the fun Hack 'n Slash aspecs of this genre.  Dodging attacks is pretty easy for most classes but some are unlucky in not having any invincibility frames in their dodge when wielding certain weapons but for the most part all mobs/bosses give plenty of tell-tale signs of which kind of attack is coming.
There are many different kinds of weapons that have very different play styles and most of the gender locked classes can wield two types, which are unchangable during missions but can be freely swapped everywhere else.  Many different types of enchantable gear to upgrade your characters with [jewelry, standard armor pieces, costume parts with stat boost, etc] but &^$%, Forge Upgrading your armor/weapons past +6 is aggravating, and forget about +10 and higher unless you're filthy rich.
To be honest though, as much as I love this game, I find it very rage inducing due to these few reasons:  Dodging and attacking, Equipment Random Number Generator and Enchanting.  The dodging and attacking around bosses can be really fun but sometimes a few mistakes will cost you an expensive self rez item, especially if you don't want to wait 24 hours to refight the special/raid boss for a chance of a high valued drop.  Other times you'll find that team mates will kite a bosses incoming attack haphazardly which makes the whole 'unlucky positioning' a regular thing unless you just try to dodge everything, whether aimed at you or not, causing the overall fight to take longer.  The random number generator for upgrading/finding quality gear is standardly unfair unless you spend real-life money to prevent your gear from being destroyed on failed attempts.  The same can be said about finding and using the Enchantment Scrolls which makes having optimally Enchanted-Enhanced Weapons, Armor and Jewelry an annoyingly difficult and arduous task to complete.
Overall though its a game I've enjoyed plenty for extended periods of time and after long breaks as well.  I highly recommend giving it a few plays.

Introduction:
My only prior familiarity with Magic: The Gathering was via my oldest son, who gravitated towards the card game.  Such games follow an effective business model, encouraging individuals to invest large quantities of money into cards to ensure probability is in their favor.  Though the game seemed somewhat interesting from what I had seen, I simply did not want to go down that investment path.
After looking at the Magic: The Gathering - Duels of the PLaneswalkers series, my interest grew as not only did each new version add additional layers, but was also a finite investment, regardless if one purchased all the DLC.  From the standpoint of true Magic: The Gathering fans, I can understand how this would be a complete affront, given it is a trading card game.  Looking through the reviews, I gathered as much.
Summary:
After assessing all the Duels of the Planeswalkers series, I can say without a doubt that my favorites are 2013 and 2015.  Personally, I think 2013 is a great way to get started with the game, moving towards 2015 once one truly is ready to truly get into deck building.  Having stated that, if you are tride and true CTG fan, perhaps something like HEX might be of more interest.  Nevertheless, given Magic Duels is shutting down for good, I caution anyone considering that route as such games can quickly become a money sink.

Its really just another Hearthstone rebrand cash grab but Bethesda has already said they are working on ES6 so no one should be upset whether this is just a hastily prepared card game or not doesnt matter, we have games on the way.

1. Maybe make some of the cards and effects a bit less like hearthstone. This game has several of the same keywords, for example: Charge = Charge,  Guard = Taunt, Lethal = Poisonous, Ward = Divine Shield, Last Gasp = Deathrattle, Shackle = Frozen,  Summon works very similary to Battlecry, Cover works very similary to Stealth, and Drain = Lifesteal but Drain actually came first. Basically, what I'm trying to say, is add more unique key words like Beast Form, Breakthrough, and Prophecy.
2. Add hero powers. I know this one seems contrary to the last one, but I do feel like it's necessary. Hero powers usually guarantee you can do at least something every turn. Maybe make "Racials." You get to pick one of the 10 races to be your avatar, so maybe give each race a special ability that they can use like hero powers. Then people can just change their race to go with the deck they're playing. This might cause some problems because some of the powers would work notably better with certain cards but it shouldn't be game breaking as long as they are all very closely ballanced.
3. Instead of the game having the default two lane system, I think when queuing for a game, you should be able to chose if you want to play a single lane or two lane battle becaue personally, it's too confusing for me. Like I'm not always sure which lane to play cards in at which times. So why not give the players the option to play single lane games? This becomes problematic when looking at cards that have you target a lane or cards that get bonuses if a specific thing is in that lane, but that can be fixed by giving those cards adjusted costs/stats in Single lane battles, or straight up banning them. There are also cards that maybe do something in both lanes, so they'd be worse in single lane battles, but I don't think those cards need to be changed because there's nothing wrong with a few cards that just aren't good. And finally, there are cards that let you move cards to the other lane. This one is a bit more akward. The game has single lane formats outside of the standard play, but I've never tested a move effect in one of those battles so I don't know how those work, but however it's done, I'm sure it's fine how it is.
4. More shouts. These cards were absolutely genius and a great edition to the game. I'd love to see more of them and many more unique cards/effects like those.
Overall, the game is good. Sometimes I find myself thinking, "this is too much like hearthstone," but other times I find myself thinking, "this isn't enough like hearthstone." I don't give this game enough credit but yeah, it's pretty good so if you enjoy The Elder Scrolls or Hearthstone (Or both like me), you'll probably like this game.

I've never played the original Fallout games or Fallout 3, though I have heard much about them, and I have 200+ hours on Fallout 4 on console after buying it on release. Of the few singleplayer games I've experienced, this one is easily the best I've ever played. If you've already played a Fallout game before, this is a must-buy. If you're new to the Fallout franchise and are hesitant to get this game because you think that you'll be overwhelmed by the story or gameplay mechanics, dont be. You can pick up the mechanics easily after a few hours of gameplay, and will be so intrigued by the environment you find yourself in that you'll be eager to uncover much of the lore, of which can be easily accessed both within the game and online. Even by 2010's standards when the game was released, the graphics and combat are pretty outdated. However, much like in an action movie with an interesting world and characters, with not so great action scenes, you'll be far more invested in the combat of this game than in a game with flashy combat and a mediocre story, like a Call of Duty campaign. The lack of graphical fidelity is offset by the amazing artwork natural beauty of the Mojave landscape, and you likely wont even care.
After an opening sequence that introduces you to the world and sends chills down your spine, the game lends itself excellently to the core of Fallout: player freedom. Within five minutes, you have created your character, selected their stats, and are unleashed upon the wastes. If you are unsure of how to build your character, this video helped me immensely:
I personally recommend putting about 6 points in Strength, and investing heavily into Edurance, Intelligence, and Charisma. If you cant think of a backstory, consider being a rogue cowboy wanderer, like The Man With No Name or Mad Max. Ultimately however, only you are truly able to build a character that interests you. The dialogue system is amazing, and there are hundreds of unique NPCs to interact with, each time you are able to let your character shine through with dialogue options that can make you seem like a jerk, kind, or evil. There are even a variety of skill checks within conversations so that characters with different skillsets can display their talents, and so that the Speech skill doesn't seem mandatory. Combat and enemies types are varied, and there are hundreds of weapons and fighting styles to accommodate all kinds of gameplay. Exploration always feels fun and exciting,  and there is always a new dungeon to explore, a new weapon to be found, and a new quest to be completed.
The story centers around the two expansionalist nations: the New California Republic (NCR), and the Legion. They are both vying for control of the Hoover Dam, which as the primary source of power in the region, will allow them to annex the Mojave Wasteland and draw wealth from the lucrative New Vegas Strip. There are also numerous secret underlying factions that are attempting to undermine these powers and seize control for themselves, but these are for you to discover. The majority of locations you find will in some way be related to the two, and while some people may find this to take away from the random and varied locations of the less developed worlds of Fallout 3 and 4, it seems far more believable that 200 years after nuclear armageddon, structured nations would rise. While the NCR is a democracy and the Legion is a dictatorship, the NCR is often criticized for its lack of care for its citizens and high taxes, while the Legion uses methods like subjugation and slave labor to maintain law and order in a world that severely needs it. Throughout your travels, you can find a host of NPC's that you can bring along with you called "companions." These companions can help fight enemies, carry your equipment, and each feel unique and different in their own way, and even have their own questlines to complete which will unlock new and special perks.
The game isn't without its flaws however, though from my understanding of its development, these can be mostly attributed to Bethesda not giving the developers enough time and resources for them to fully realize what they wanted the game to be. As I said earlier, the game suffers from poor graphics and combat, many locations are empty and were obviously meant to be content,  many assets are recycled from Fallout 3, and a host of issues regarding the game feeling incomplete at times. What is finished is seriously fun, and I can only dream of Obsidian getting to remaster this game and add all the elements they never could. That game would truly be a 10/10. The most glaring issue is the crashes, especially with mods. It's hard to immerse myself in the world when I'm worried about the game crashing every 30 minutes. Eventually after I had played it enough, the game seemed to work out what was wrong and then only ended up crashing after about 2 hours of continuous play. All in all, it's the best single player game I have ever played, and I could not more highly recommend buying it, downloading some mods, and creating your own adventure in the Mojave Wasteland. New Vegas awaits!
I would recommend buying the DLC's as well. You can see my thoughts for each of them here.
Dead Money: At first, I didn't like Dead Money, as I found it unfun and too difficult. However, on secondary playthroughs after I was more experienced, it became my favorite DLC. The haunting omnipresence of the Sierra Madre provided a gloomy sense of dread as I creeped around the Villa, always wary of the ghost people. I loved interacting with the new companions, and uncovering their stories through tons of extremely well-written dialogue. Unfortunately, I found there to be too few enemy types, and it began to feel repetitive toward the end. The best part of the expansion is the unsettling backstory of the casino, hidden in terminals and in dialogue for the player to discover.
Honest Hearts: My third favorite, Honest Hearts is a pleasant contained story, but I didn't care much for the factions or their members. It was too short, the quests were few and felt uninteresting in comparison to the main game, but I found the dynamic between Joshua Graham and Daniel to be one of the better parts. Uncovering the bittersweet tale of the Father in the Cave was far better than anything presented in the main questline, and was one of the greatest moments in the whole game.
Old World Blues: I realize that I may recieve hate for saying this, but OLB was the weakest DLC for me. While the cheesy 50's sci fi theme had me busting a gut in some parts, the giant collect-a-thon that was every quest began to wear me out. The opening dialogue sequence drags on for far too long, getting the upgrades for the sonic emitter and stealth suit required replaying the same lab over and over, and the robo-scorpions. The ♥♥♥♥ing robo-scorpions. Finally though, the endless slog payed off in a fantastic ending that completely twisted my perspective of the characters.
Lonesome Road: I have a love/hate relationship with Lonesome Road, my second favorite expansion. Apart from the lack of enemy diversity, it has the best gameplay in the whole game, and the map perfectly complemented the eerie and unknown nature of Ulysses's hatred for the Courier. I loved how alone I felt, and with limited dialogue I could only gaze upon the destruction caused by nuclear fire. The largest problem is how the story makes absolutely no sense. The reason Ulysses hates you is just stupid, and interfered with the backstory of my character, who apparently had a vague and poorly-defined history with Ulysses. Once again though, I'm willing to forgive some of its greater faults, as the ending is phenomenal.

If you are looking for a great open-world first-person shooter, than you should take a look at Far Cry 2 in a Steam summer sale. This game has nothing to do with the first Far Cry game because it is a completely different world and setting.
Main story: The player takes control of a mercenary on a lengthy journey to locate and assassinate "The Jackal", a notorious gun runner. He is the one who is selling weapons to the people and the main reason for the escalation in Africa. To find him you must take missions from two factions during a civil war: the APR and the UFRR.  “The jackal” will finding you, so you have to be like him to gain his attention.
This game takes place in Africa and has a very big area with 50 square kilometers and many different terrain like deserts, savannas and jungles. There is a dynamic weather system that has a day-night cycle and different weather conditions such as storms and strong winds. The time of day also affects the behavior of AI, in terms of enemy alertness and aggressiveness. To travel through the game you can use many vehicles including cars, trucks, quads and boats or you go by foot.
To defeat your enemies you have access to a large arsenal of weapons. Assault rifles, shotguns, sniper rifles, machine guns, explosives and a flamethrower. You have four weapon slots but only three can be chosen, because the first slot is always a machete for melee attacks. You can use hand grenades and Molotov cocktails too. Weapons can become dirty and prone to jamming if you use them to much, so you should change them from time to time.
The realism in Far Cry 2 is very nice. Apart from the weather and the weapon degradation, the player needs to hold a physical map and a handheld navigation system to get around, no minimap in this game. The greatest feature is the fire. For Example, a small fire can become very large in an area like a savanna with strong wind. You are able to burn complete outposts with one Molotov.
If you are not on a main mission you can collect diamonds to buy better gear, take save houses and spy outposts or kill all the enemies in there. Or you take side missions to get more diamonds and take special missions for antimalarial drugs.
You can use many different play styles. Being like Rambo and use LMG’s, shotguns and a flamethrower or being like a ghost with a sniper rifle and kill them silently? Your choice.
A negative point is, that the enemies respawn to fast. If you cleared an outpost and turn around after you drove 50 meters, they are back. That’s annoying.
Far Cry 2 was released in 2008 and looked very beautiful. In 2016 it is still looking very awesome and runs perfectly on newer systems. The Dunia Engine has the best vegetation I’ve ever seen, very realistic and nice. Lights and shadows are also very nice, only the nights are too bright and in 2016 the rain looks a little bit unrealistic if there is no sun, but 90% of the time your eyes will enjoy it.
Far Cry 2 includes multiplayer and an awesome map-editor to create your own maps for the multiplayer with strict rules, that the map is balanced at the end. You can create realistic maps, recreate maps from other games [de_dust2] or just build funny maps like a race map. This is the easiest map-editor and I created a lot maps in 2008. The multiplayer was funny but today I think, no one is still playing that.
Far Cry 2 is a great Ego-Shooter with a large open-world, a realistic and beautiful setting with a weak story bur strong gameplay elements. Most of the time you are a lonely wolf in a big and beautiful world and anyone is your enemy. It is an open-world adventure more like a sandbox game as a theme park title. This is not an action-title like Far Cry 3 or far Cry 4, so if you want that, then don’t buy it. If you loving large open world games and playing with different play styles, go and buy it on sale for less than $5,00. It’s absolutely worth it.

Perhaps one of the best turn based games of all time. Wizardry 8 is, sadly, the last chapter in Sir Tech's long running Wizardry series.
I've played this game since it initially game out back in 2000, and I still regularly play it today which is a tribute to simply how good this game is. The quest resolves around some mysterious artifacts, an evil dark savant, and an awful lot of random encounters. The combat is turn based, with each of the characters in your party been able to perform actions on each round, which can vary from casting one of the many spells, to playing an instrument, or simply hacking away with your sword.
The spell casting system deserves a special mention; rather than simply having a fixed damage for each spell, they can be cast at a variety of power levels, with lower level spells been easier to cast at the higher levels (up to level seven). This help stop even your lowest level spells from becoming redundant for most of the game.
This game is however fairly hard, (through it is perhaps the easiest Wizardry game), and you will most likely have quite a few frustrating moments, save often because you never know what is round the next corner or whenever the rng will go your way.
All in all if you enjoy any type of turn based strategy games, and especially if you enjoy turn based RPG's then trust me but this game because you are missing out.

I actually got it for very cheap duting a steam sale, and getting inspired by some reviews to check it out. It is worth the full price as well.
What is good?
It is actually really fun to play, and easy to get into. The game looks good for what it is and does not demand a power PC. It has good music and style in general - nothing spectacular, but totally fitting. The game is kind of a hack and slash but without the tedious hacking and loot. You can't really compare the games, except for the look.

The bad?
The story is easily forgettable. In fact you really don't care, but does not detract from the game. It could be a story about anyone, it is not better or worse because it is about Lara Croft. The game is not very difficult and not very long, but that did not really detract for me either, but some might have a problem with that.
Controls?
Solid and easy. I prefer with the keyboard, but a controller works fine as well.
Replayable?
Perhaps. I rarely replay games unless they are something special. I don't really have the time either. But I can see the replay value if you want to try different play-styles, and also get all the challenges and bonuses in the game.
Yes, get it.

There may be a good game in there but a lack of polish means you'll have to dig to find out.
Some standard conventions are ignored, which results in unwarranted frustration (especially considering how easy it is to include them).  The game doesn't start in full screen.  At certain points ESC will exit the game rather than the context you're in (like a menu).  Worst of all, the control scheme is arcane and confused despite decades of great examples to draw on.

TL;DR: This game is gorgeous. And free. Just play it.
Well, after playing for the first time i was confused af and i did have to look at the guides. Then it got updated because the cutscenes didn't show up. After playing it again from start to finish i must say it all makes sense now (i do recommend replaying it once you know what happens, to better understand the story).
+++PROS
+Beutiful soundtrack
+Voice-acting (although it isn't in english)
+Thriller feelings
+Amazing presentation of the story through dialogue and cutscenes
+Good graphics
+Minor details have gameplay objectives or story meanings
+Just the right amount of horror
---CONS (the best term would probably be frustating things)
-Unlike most point and click games where you have many "clue-paths" and they converge onto the ending, this game is pretty linear and the clues get "unlocked" for you to get them only after certain points in the story. This is more a warning to change your mentality for this game rather than a con.
-You need to revisit the places you already searched to get clues. If a place doesn't have clues maybe you don't have everything to "unlock" it or maybe it really doesn't have any clues (i haven't found any bug relating this so if you don't find that clue you have missed something. go to the amazing guides if you get too frustated).
-The two mechanics (clue combining and object selection) seem a bit odd until you get used to them but they are extremely important to finish the game. Just as a reminder an object is selected when you have it highlighted at the object selection, if it has a bright border don't hesitate to close the "objects" tab, if they don't work you are missing something or you haven't found the right place to click.
-The hints and the clues in this game are NOT STRAIGHTFORWARD. Most hints have two or three steps that you need to
(/imagine/guess/get inspired from a tiger-shaped cloud that passes by) to get the next clue. Other hints and uses of objects seem a bit odd logic-wise but are always understandable once you do get them. You can spend time thinking and getting a strong feeling of acomplishment or you can look at the amazing guides to fight frustation, it's entirely up to you. Lastly, remember that everything that seems like a hint can surely be a hint later on for something you don't expect.
To sum up, be aware that this is not the typical straightforwad pixelhunting game: the places are hidden but they are easy enough to find, the difficulty is knowing where, when and what exactly you need to to do in order to progress. The game is free and it's totally worth your time (and maybe money). A solid 9/10 for a free game.

Ahh! Space. The final frontier. The place where crap hits the fan at every corner. It really seems like space exploration is doomed from the get-go, right? I mean, there are so many games in space and most of them tell the tale of some poor protagonist who crash lands on a eerie planet and has to create an entire colony to survive, using tools crafted from all kinds of weird materials (I'm still waiting for a hammer made of a stick and a rabbit).
Planet Nomads goes where other games have gone before. Much like Osiris, Empyrion and Subnautica, the player crashes on a planet and needs to craft the hello out of random things to survive. Thankfully, just as in those other games I've mentionned, your guy/gal is a hybrid of McGyver, Einstein and Dr. House (minus the cane). So what sets Planet Nomads apart from all those survival games?
Well, for an early access game, it is amazingly stable. I haven't had one single crash. The graphics are quite gorgeous and the sound is... uh... irritating as hell. What works for Nomads is the survival aspect. It's quite unforgiving. You sadly aren't  armed to the teeth and the wildlife is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to see you stomping around. They even throw rocks at you. More like boulders actually, but you get the idea. The fun truly begins when you start the Nomad part in Planet Nomads. Meaning getting some wheels or hover-thingies under your butt. It seems like the physics aren't yet fully developed so you'll have some glitches turning your vehicle upside-down, fly up in the air where you can't reach it and so on. Fun stuff. Although after deconstructing and rebuilding your vehicle for the 10th time, it can sometimes get a little old. Even then, this is the game's strongest point so far.
As of the writing of this review, the game is still in EA, but updates are coming in regularly and it seems like the devs are on top of things. Planet Nomads is a pretty solid bet for an early access game (even though the pricetag can make you gag a little bit). All in all, I enjoy this game. It still needs work as the flora and fauna is fairly monotone, some other biomes would be nice too, a better way to set a nav point than eye-balling it on the map, and of course, a lot more parts to craft and customization options. You quickly reach a point where all you can do is to build vehicles as the parts for the bases are boring and uniform (bluntly put) and there's no way to add color or anything like that. Also, some NPC's would be nice. Even just a handful to help out and talk to, quest around randomly or whatever.
Bottom line, Planet Nomads is a diamond in the rough and shows massive promises to become a fantastic game.

At first I hated this game and was about to write it off like “No man should grind” but as this was still in alpha, I set aside the many bugs, glitches and fit inspiring combat issues to focus on what the game is going to/could be.
Starting is of course challenging but the easy tutorials bound to the F1-5 keys help to reduce this, the grind is bearable at first and gets better with time and automation (When building conveyors to mining drill, build the conveyor from the storage end first otherwise she’s dead captain).
The mesh collisions when walking over an area you have just mined is quite restricting with the occasional falling through the world, which is easy enough to correct by using your jet pack and not emerging under a building. Again, this is in alpha so you have to expect some issues for the moment.
The food and water situation can be annoying at first but once you have a stasis bed in your base, you have no drama's, I think this has improved with the more recent patches though.
Gathering exotic resources at first is rather difficult (Depending on where you spawn) as you have to building a basic vehicle that makes the game a lot like a 4x4 simulator. The lack of a “flip vehicle” feature does cause issues but when you have a good design down pat and a towrope, you can get out of most jams easy enough, which adds to the adventure.
Once you have advanced to the stage where you can get a flying vehicle, things get far easier to manage, expand and collect. Just be careful to not flip your flying vehicle, unlike the land vehicles it can be tedious to right your orientation or you can deal with camera POV bouncing around in 3rd person constantly as you go about your business. As the Devs mentioned though, mount the propellers on top and it should be easier to manage.
The worst and most annoying glitch I came across was built blocks disappearing, first time was a land vehicle, second time was a base I had literally just finishing. (I looked away for a second then looked back and poof, gone)
As for the logs, I have found quite a few of them now and I’m not bored with finding more yet but a bit of NPC dialogue would be awesome and make the grind a bit more enjoyable if you can listen to the logs while working.
All in all this is one of the better survival alpha’s I have played and hopefully this will get better as the development continues. Allowing the modding community to get involved would be cool as some other reviews have mentioned but understandable if you don’t want to have your game twisted by unwanted elements.
This game is getting better as time goes on as mentioned and you can see some elemets/tech scattered through the sandbox environment that will eventually be introduced to the building tree as time goes on.
The game runs quite well (6700k OC to 4.7ghz  w/ 32gb ram, GTX 1080 on SSD) and I never experienced a game crash the entire time I was playing making for a stable run experience, only FPS drop occurs around the auto save but this is, I suspect, going to be optimised in the future.

-You have to pay to get more plants

Received game for free through Humble store.
But sadly I cannot recommend this product. It has amazing potential but it ruined by two factors: bugs and combat mechanics.
The combat mechanics just don't feel powerful at all and are extremely poorly designed. Being a massive fan of the hack-slash / combo-based combat I thought I would jump right into this game and enjoy it from minute 1.
But alas it was not to be, already from the menu screen I hated the game. How is that possible you may wonder? Bugs and horrendous controls. You use arrow keys to select the menu button, left mouse button to select that menu (enter does not work!) and space bar to go back to previous screen.
You cannot disable v-sync even though there is an option there to do that.
You can only change one setting at a time and have to then use left mouse while still on that setting to apply it, if you are not on that specific setting you want to apply it does not save it when you left click or use space bar to go back to previous menu.
The bugs and design flaws do not end there sadly, on the second boss fight of the game I had to restart from last save point as the boss bugged out and got stuck in a loop, after restarting from save the fight continued as it should and the boss did not get stuck in the bugged loop that prevents you from damaging it.
Then as for combat, it is just not at all what it should be. You have a magical katana - the least you can expect as a player is significant impact of said katana. I am not talking about challenge (so far the combat is not challenging at all, just annoying due to bad design) I am purely talking about how it feels and how it plays.
You are supposed to make combos but your character is slow and unresponsive so making big satisfying combos is not at all possible.
Alternative attack modes are equally disappointing and timing a guard parry is as buggy as the rest of the game.
Do yourself a favour and give this buggy mess a miss.
Shame though, as the story and characters are very unique, this could have been an amazing title if only they had polished it better and done a better job on the combat.

This game is my favorite single-player first-person shooter of all time. I enjoyed Doom back in the 90s, but other than that i am not really a fan of the genre. I find the mechanics somewhat repetitive - you are forced to kill everything, everywhere, spraying bullets around like you're in some kind of direct-to-video action flick. Even acclaimed shooters like Half-Life and Bioshock come across as cartoonish and tedious to me. Counter-Strike changed everything. A game where you only get a rifle and a sidearm, where every shot matters, where a bullet to the head means instant death and spending the next few minutes learning from people far more skilled than you. After playing Counter-Strike, every first-person shooter felt like a mindless kill-fest where stealth or tactics did not matter. The good news is those things do matter in Far Cry 2.
You are still pretty much railroaded into killing everything that moves. It is an FPS, after all. But stealth always feels like a possibility. The tension before the killing ensues, the time you spend crouching motionless in elephant grass, is a highlight of the game.
The enemies in Far Cry 2 are some of the most human i have encountered. It's why killing them takes a toll - they are a lot like you. If you have been seen - if any of your enemies spot you - the whole base goes on alert. Forever. They will lay down suppressive fire in your last known position. They will wall-bang. They will establish search parties. They will freak out and start getting paranoid over the slightest noise. If you are seen - or heard - again, expect to die. One or two shots from an enemy rifle will wipe you out. But stay perfectly still, crouched in the undergrowth, and the enemy may creep past just a few meters away. And, as they widen their net, you may be able to slip through and circle round. Inevitably,♥♥♥♥♥♥will go south. You are spotted and clipped, then running through the jungle, sliding to obscure their line of sight, spinning round to lob a grenade or to spray and pray. Mostly, you will die. It is ♥♥♥♥ing brutal.
I know some reviewers have complained about the mechanics of this game. Respawning bases. Deteriorating weapons. Malaria. I will admit i played with Dylan's realism mod and never tried it any different, but in Dylan's mod it all makes sense. You are sick and scared and stumble into the jungle with a pea shooter. So you see an AK, grab it, but it jams in no seconds flat. You see an unguarded jeep, jump in, then get hit by an RPG half a click down the road. The game teaches you these hard lessons in the first half hour. How are you supposed to survive in Ubisoft's nightmare version of Africa? Don't pick up jury-rigged weapons. Don't jack jeeps. Wait till dusk, get your belly in the mud and proceed to your destination at a crawl. Avoid the roads, avoid the checkpoints, scout your targets and look for a headshot. Value reliability over firepower. Value cover over speed. Value your life.
The story is grim. You play an opportunistic soldier of fortune in the midst of a civil war. Almost everyone is evil and corrupt, and the vast majority attack you on sight. Even if you try to minimize casualties on an assassination or sabotage mission, something will invariably ♥♥♥♥ up and the bodycount will rise. Or your next mission will require you to clean out a whole area anyway. Every time you hear a squeak you expect a technical to pull up and unload 50 cal into your back. Every time the sun falls on a certain pattern of leaves your trigger finger will twitch. And gosh, those hanging vines really do look like bodies sometimes, don't they? I loved Spec Ops: The Line for its simulated PTSD effects, but those were mostly scripted. Far Cry 2 plays it totally straight and your brain still goes there.♥♥♥♥♥♥is ♥♥♥♥ed up, man.
So yeah. The game is punishing. It's bleak. You spend most of your time holding your breath and crouched in the dirt. Every now and then you are awed by a herd of zebra crossing the savannah at sunset, or the majesty of a tropical storm, or the slow rising moon. And then a bullet ricochets off a nearby cliff face and everything turns to♥♥♥♥♥♥again. A lot of games have made an impact on me due to their strong narratives. Far Cry 2 is different. The plot is thin as a potato chip, but its unforgiving sandbox houses an atmosphere thick enough to haunt me offline. Best single-player FPS since Doom? For me, yes. Hands down.

You are dropped in a war-torn african country, you have one mission. Kill the man that has been arming both sides.

It all makes it more difficult to survive, and instead of holding your hand all the time the game lets you approch how you want to. All in all i would say this is one of the best games i have ever played. It is almost 8 years old, but is a though competitor for even the newest games.

Finally time to write my review for Planet Nomads. I truly am beginning to enjoy the game as it's come a long way from it's meager beginning, but more importantly has a lot of future potential. Now I usually don't put stock in "it's gonna be great" type reveiws because I feel a product should be reviewed on it's CURRENT state, not promises of the future (at least not entirely). PN is at a stage now where there is SO much to do and the game is very stable. It's definitely fun, enjoyable, challenging and worth it's price.
I would like to see more content in the type of building arena. Once you've built up to a certain point (which is fairly easy to achieve) there's nothing left and all you have now is exploration (which is a good part of the game). Biome variety is good, I'd like to see some more content in the way of furniture or base personalization which is completely absent. My play style is build a base, explore from there, but make 1 home and then branch out with exploratoin bases for different biomes and there is nothing to make a home with really. I'd also LOVE to see mod support. That's probably they only concern I have at the moment in regard to PN's staying power. Without mod support there's a finite amount of game play avaible.
Bottom line, it's worth the price now if you enjoy good graphics, exploration and a survival style mechanic.

I've had Viridi for years and am just now getting around to reviewing it. The concept is basic: take care of plants and watch them grow, bloom, and thrive. Incredibly relaxing to play because it's a totally safe game (nothing jumping out at you... literally the only non-plant life form is the little snail hanging out on the pot). The music is absolutely delightful. A free plant once per week makes it easy to look forward to playing every so often. I try to check in at least once a week to pull weeds and water my plants.
I highly recommend getting Eidolon, a walking-type game also made by Ice Water Games. As soon as it hits your library, you get a bonus pot in Viridi that is placed in the Grove, a location straight out of Eidolon (with Eidolon music to match!). The Grove is a pleasant reminder of Eidolon for me, and I appreciate the opportunity to have two pots going.
Viridi was there for me in my Steam library while I was going through a time of intense loneliness and sadness. I looked forward to visiting my pot every day and found solace in the beautiful music and simple act of nurturing something when I could barely take care of myself. You can't get that kind of comfort from just any game. This one is special. <3

When I first started out, there was a bug apparently (some cutscenes were missing, and those were important because they contained clues to solve a particular puzzle - so I waited about a month before replaying the game).
I didn't expect the game to be as deep as it turned out to be (at least, from my perspective).
The moment I launched the game and heard the intro music, I wasn't impressed. I found the tune rather derivative and lacking in originality, but I did find it suitable and fitting for this game (which is a crossbreed between a visual novel & point-&-click).
Meaning, it is story-centered (so there's a bit of reading, but most of the story-telling is done thru the gathering and combining of clues & visual scenes - with the latter being typical of the VN genre).
The story touches upon several themes that are portrayed quite well in my opinion. There are references to what I would consider emotional incest (which is rather taboo, but mistifying nonetheless), abandonment (or at the very least, a fear of it), separation & sacrifice.
Especially the former (i.e. emotional incest/enmeshment) is rather difficult to portray without it appearing distasteful, but I have to say the developers really pulled it off graciously.
Project PRICE feels very tender and poetic.
The crew created something that felt very emotional, sentimental, delicate, frail & fragile.
Somewhat twisted & quite tragic as well.
Surprisingly, the game really did speak to my heart (I was very touched by it). And for that I am grateful.
PS I found the drawings to be of very good quality. I wouldn't mind investing in the artwork :)
PPS there is an original twist regarding the title of the game, but I'd rather let any potential players discover this for themselves :)
NB there was one particular puzzle (involving a code - in the first half of the game) that I had difficulty solving - the solution was right in front of me, but I somehow couldn't see it (admittedly, it was a bit cryptic and the wonky narrative confused me a little).
NB2 please bear in mind that the developers are not English native speakers, so there are some erroneously constructed parts of text, but overall the game is comprehensible and the developers do seem to care about using proper spelling and grammar to the best of their abilities (the text was quite literally translated from Chinese to English, so that elucidates why this is the case).
NOTE: the game consists of two parts (in the second part, the music was much more to my liking, and I found it a bit more original than the opening soundtrack)

Probably the best mainstream online card game right now. A ton of detail, accessible story modes, limits to cheesey builds and a focus on balance. At least so far. I know these things tend to change over time and people really figure out the meta. But so far, no "hunters spamming raptors."
Story mode is really well done, with interesting story tidbits between arenas with special rules and novelty enemy deck builds. About half the campaigns are cordoned off by cash shop or grind, but it didn't take me too long to earn my first 1000 gold map. And that map had about an hour of content. Not terrible. Excellent voice acting; some of the best I've seen in a video game in a long time. I'd rather see Bethesda's stories told in this form from now on, personally, and out with left-clicking trolls and acolytes for lifeless fetch quests.
Gotta say, they'd probably be getting a lot more synergy from the Steam Community Store, so that cards have a real word value and time is restricted by how much people like playing the game and think its worth, instead of an arbitrary value set by the developer. As far as I can tell, though, cash shop prices aren't too bad; about 10 cents a card. I  wouldn't buy any though, personally, as I almost never go in on that stuff. The starting decks and rewards for completing the story give enough cards to make diverse builds that are viable in ranked mode. Hopefully nobody gets dollar signs in their eyes and nerfs the first sets, because us "sardines" are the people who play the games regularly and keep them populated for the "whales and dolphins."
There's a 'build a deck arena' mode that's pretty expensive on coins or real life currency. It's $2 for one ticket or $10 for 6. You get three chances to lose, so maybe you won't get stomped immediately, but I'm sure it's entirely possible to lose all three chances in just a few minutes. It's fun to build the deck, though, and they at least give you one free ticket for the vs AI arena; a mode which itself is a fun microstory. Too expensive for the single player mode, though. One entry is the cost of 1/10th an hour long story mode map unlock.
I've found deck building quite fun, but so far I feel a little bit limited in what's possible. At least with the cards I have now, I can mostly make something balanced with a strong hint of theme. I suspect that's what this game is going for in general, though, as you have to fill your deck with 50 cards, a limit of three of the same card, and decks can only contain two of the five principle card types. Up to 70 cards in a deck. Seems like a lot from what I recall of other games.
Lanes are a great subtle edition that I think outdates games like Hearthstone. Available tactics are at least doubled, with the normal lane, and the 'shadow lane' that makes cards immune for a short time. The story mode has some crazier lanes, too, and I think they're available in 'chaos arena', an event that I have yet to see pop up.
I really think it's worth giving a try if you like Hearthstone style card games, deck building, or Elder Scrolls. At the very least I think most fans will like the story mode.

I'm just gonna go ahead and say that FC2 is my favorite game in the series. I found Far Cry 3 to be casualized and easy. There was no challenge from start to finish and it follows the same Ubisoft open world formula from recent Assassin's Creed games. Far Cry 2 is vastly different and I prefer it over Far Cry 3 and 3.1, I mean 4 for a number of reasons.
I mean just the fact I don't have to climb any radio towers to see more of the map or having the map littered with collectable icons are great. The feel and sounds of the guns are also really good for a 2008 game. Every gun in FC2 feels unique and don't feel like a toy compared to FC3 and 4. Guns jam, they have recoil, they show signs of wear and tear, and more. They don't feel like brand new military weapons but rather feel like they fit the African milita setting of the game. Every gun in FC3 and 4 feel like they're brand new and the sound is muddy when shooting them. In my opinion the gunplay in FC2 is some of the best I've played in a first person shooter, and I play quite a few of them (check my Steam game list if you want).
The AI I think is pretty decent for a 2008 title. There are games released today that have far worse AI than this game. In Far Cry 3/4 if you're up on a cliff or a decent distance away and you take an enemy down via sniping then the others in the camp or nearby will always somehow zero in on your location. In FC2 the enemies will try to help their fellow comrades by carrying them to safety and search the immediate area, not instantly know which direction the shot came from like in FC3/4.
As for the malaria it never really inconvenienced me when out and about, and I thought it was a pretty nice touch to the overall setting. I also don't feel it artificially prolonged the game like say having a crap ton of collectables all over the map.
As for the story I'd have to sayit's not the best. In fact I enjoyed Far Cry 3's story more than FC2, but when it comes to the gameplay then FC2 for me wins easily.
I give it an 8/10.
PS. Don't mind the 2.6 hours on record. I played this game to death when it came out on PS3 and bought it on Steam a couple years ago on sale.

The REAL problem: BUGS, i played the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game at 1999~2000, and they managed to create a whole NEW set of bugs. The thing is, there's a lot of remasters and remakes, these days to compare it to, and as such, it is HARD to let it pass, when you played so much better works. GF is a simple game, there is no big physics engines or great details to workaroud, it should be so simple to "remaster" it. The cherry on the top of the ♥♥♥♥ cake: the FU!@#%¨ TANK controller achievement DIDN'T POPUP, d@mn it.

Grim Fandango was considered one of the best games ever made in the 90s. As for today, the gameplay mechanic can be annoying at times, with some vague and nonsensical puzzles from year/act 3 onward. However, Grim Fandago still remains as one of the most original, creative game ever made, a great journey that every gamer should experience.

This little game is not as much fun as people here on Steam make it seem. It's actually the opposite.
Let's see what's good and what's bad.
The story is almost non-existent. Sure, there is some generic uninteresting intro, but that's it. To be honest, I don't mind it as I didn't expect much story from a game of this style (like Alien Swarm which also had very little story)
The graphics is okay. There's nothing that exceptional to mention here. Maybe just that even though the graphics is not that special, it doesn't run as well as I'd expect (on my main computer it's fine, on my laptop it is not).
The sound is average and there's also some music. The soundtrack isn't too memorable but I'm glad it's there. Games tend to get quite "sterile" without music.
What really kills this game is the gameplay. That's a major flaw. Controls are awkward and your character sometimes does whatever he/she likes. It might be better on consoles, but I'm using a PC, so I'm rating that. There are many frustrating and unfair puzzles. Don't get me wrong - the idea behind most puzzles is good, but the execution is weak. Why? Controls. Movement is fine, but jumping is a disaster. You often end up falling to your death and as a consequence lose your valuable points. Which raises the question: Why the hell are you punished for developer's fault? That's ridiculous. There are several moves and tools you can use to get through the levels and puzzles. You've got two tools - a spear and a rope. Both are pretty useful to get to high or distant places. But good luck getting back down. You're forced to use a leap of faith as there is no way to drop while hanging on the edge of platforms. There might aswell be, but it's not in the tips and I haven't found it by myself. Such a thing should be mandatory in Lara Croft games.
There's also a coop mode which I haven't tried yet. If it plays better than singleplayer, this review might change to positive in the future. It's a fat chance though.
To sum it all up, the developers had ideas but clearly didn't know what they were doing. It's a shame because this doesn't look like a bad title. Well, let's hope they learn and don't ♥♥♥♥ up like this with their next game.

It's more modern than its graphics imply - this game isn't just some old-school zombie that was kept alive by fans, it's an RPG that may be slow at at times, and have more than a few quirks that do require research before building your party, but it has a much deeper system than at first appears.
It has true 3d, like an FPS while controlling a full party, and the party is arranged on a grid where "short range" is determined by what quarter of the grid is facing the enemy - attacks to the rear attack your rear line mages first, while your front line fighters cannot reach the enemy.
It has an odd hybrid point-buy combined with train-through-use system, as well - skills are both bought and then trained through use, making player choices not be so much a min-maxxing for what skills are most valuable and worth your points, as much as it is a choice of what skills you can train through use the easiest, and which ones need those level-up skill points to get jump-started.
If anything, Wizardry 8 is a transitional game. It seems clear that Sir-Tech was working hard to modernize their game while still keeping the depth of their old games, and it's a shame they couldn't have gotten past this point to create a Wizardry 9 that would have more fully brought the game into being both a modern RPG as well as the homage to the RPGs of years past. However, this game gives you all you need to see where they were going.

I was introduced to this game via the Night Dive Bundle (Thanks Bundlestars!). I was originally planning to get it simply for Systemshock 2, but this wonderful game came along with it. after doing some research, i found out just how loved it was, so I tried it for myself.
Basic, spoiler free tldr Plotline: Create your party, grab 3 artifacts and stop evil dude from doing the same, whist exploding everyone and everything that stands in your way of saving the world.
The plot is pretty much put to the wayside in my own opinon, but it is interesting enough to be noteable.

At first, It can be a bit daunting for players used to newer RPGs, but everything is very well streamlined when it comes to the User Interface and inventories. That is, once you get used to it.

Combat:
Basic lowdown: up to six PC's and two followers fighting together against enemies, using ranged, melee, or magic, with enemies in a 3d space. Works in a similar way to the older FFs, and is very fun at as well as aggrivating in earlier stages.
The game spices up this style of combat  by applying the strategies of positioning and formations, which are vital for both staying alive and dealing damage. The enemies have a bad tendency to be either mediocore or brutal, crushing your party to a pulp at times. But, the combat remains rather balanced throughout, and exciting.
Characters and Character Progression:
Much like Oblivion or Morrowind, each character has Basic Stats that can only be raised through leveling up, and Skill Stats that can be leveled both through gaining levels or by use in combat. Creating a character that fits his or her role into the party is absolutely esssential, and if not created properly, can permanently cripple the party. To survive basically, you need at least one Melee character in the front, a Ranged in the back, along with a caster to support them. Character classes basically divvy up the general roles into more specifc ones, with some classes unable to use certain weapons, you must choose carefully.
The combinations of both races and classes, and the distribution of stat points allows for immense variety in playstyles, from the practical to the ridiculous.
Probably my favorite thing about the progression is seeing how far my party has come from the beginning. From my caster being barely able to cast basic magic to being a Lord of Death on the battlefield, erasing damage to party members and boosting their stats to ridiculous levels.
Another thing that stands out is the wide variety of Voice packs that each character can posess, and can be changed at any time. From laid back to the edge of sanity, sultry or sneaky, your choice. My favorites are the Male and Female Chaotic voices. These add much needed soul to the game, as well as some laughs.
Graphics:
The game looks "Good Enough" for the modern age of games. Thankfully, with programs included such as Nglide, the game can run on just about anything. Laggy areas can be prevalent, even on modern, top of the line PC's, but usually, it will run at a glorious 60fps. What makes it even better, is that Steam Cloud saving for some odd reason works perfectly with this game, and the game's saves can flawlessly transfer from computer to computer.
Stuff I do not like about this game:
This game is hands down the best of this specifc genre that I have ever played, but it still has its flaws.
-quests and objectives can be rather ambigous, and without the help of online guides, some of these can be very frustrating.
-Crafting recipies are never revealed in game, which can be agrivating unless you have them online.
-Travelling the world can be rather slow, as it is quite expansive, and portal spells can only be unlocked later in the game.
-Saving is a bit awkward, having to go into the options menu every time can get annoying.
-Starting off on the wrong foot party wise can lead to a near impossible playthrough.
Otherwise, I heartily recommeded to those wishing to sink a lot of time into a great, easily scaleble game.

For those of you who did not grow up in the age of PC gaming with single-core, less than 277Mhz CPU/GPU setups, and CRT monitors only up to 15"... have you got a shock in store.
Wizardry 8 is amazing. Simple as that. And not only is it the final game in the Wizardry series, it is also the final of the Dark Savant Trilogy, which consists of Wizardry 6, 7 and 8. We had to wait nine years for 8 after VII, but you know what, it was worth the wait. To some of us anyway. For those of us that played Wizardry Gold, the wait was a little shorter, but still, five years is a long time to wait for the final story of an amazing story arch and series of games.
Depending on how you ended VII, if you did, then you have multiple beginning story archs to be a part of, then again, so to you have multiple endings.
Remember in the beginning of Zelda: OoT, where you have to find the three gems to unlock the Temple of Time? Well, I think that borrowed from this entire story, because that is it. You have to find three gems, but make no mistake... you will not do it as quickly as you'd like. And then the story is just plain weird after you get them, because then you have to become a Templar. And well... that is the funny part, you will see.
This title also takes away from the stepping from spot to spot of the previous two titles and you are able to walk (via first-person perspective) and turn and such in a full 3D environment. And even better, you can see the enemies this time, no random popping of battles. It may not seem like it, but in its day, this was amazing stuff to see. This game is amazing even today, so give it a go, you will enjoy it. It's fluid, it's great, and it will make you laugh with some of the story stuff, but I will not spoil anything.
There are also mods for the game, however I have not tried any yet, as I am still giving it a go in vanilla forme.
The game runs great, has multiple beginning and ending story paths and tells a great story for its time. I recommend this, especially if you enjoy the older RPG titles of PC gaming.

Short version:
If you're a fan of classic cRPGs (especially those that are party-centric with turn-based combat) this game belongs in your library, particularly if you can get it on a discount.
Long-winded version:
Wizardy 8 is a worthy capstone to the long-running series.  It is certainly one of the best cRPGs of its time and, arguably, one of the best of all time.  All of the elements that made up a great game of this genre in the 2000s is here:  robust character creation, flexible party formation, plentiful combat, and addictive character progression.
As might be expected of a game its age, the graphics in Wizardry 8 are dated.  But, importantly, not cripplingly so.  Watching a freshly killed opponent explode and seeing their skull careen across the screen is just...timeless.  Unlike the graphics, the sound is still top notch.  The ambient environmental sounds, whether in a dungeon, jungle, or graveyard, do a very nice job of bringing some immersion to the game.
While RP elements such as open world exploration and NPC interactions are light compared to the standards of today, the character creation and party formation system provides enough variety that you'll develop an affinity for the members of your party as you go along.  Stat and skill prgression is a fairly straightforward affair:  raise the tank's strength and stamina, raise the mage's intelligence, etc.  But what's nice is that it's not just leveling up that provides progress.  Using skills repeatedly also raises their scores.  So, yes, you can develop a mage that's awesome with a bow (given enough practice).  On top of such flexibility, progress actually feels like progress.  You can sense the improvement in your characters as they climb the godly ladder even as they face more difficult opponents.
The story is decent enough but, frankly, isn't likely to be the reason someone keeps playing the game.  That motivation will likely come from character/party development and....
Combat.  This is truly a towering strength of the game.  It's plentiful and it requires adapting tactics to have any sort of long term success.  Fortunately, the game allows you to do just that.  The AI mobs can be surprisingly, and unforgivingly, clever.  Don't just stand in the middle of open ground...get your party's back against a wall to avoid being surrounded.  Guard that mage, because the mob's not going to charge headlong at the lady in plate armor with the big, pointy stick (unless you find a way to give them no alternative).  If the enemy has access to long range attacks, they will use them, so you better not sit back waiting for that fireball to explode in front of you.  There are even going to be situations in which your party is in over its head.  Retreat to fight another time.  Not every combat will provide a challenge, but just enough will to keep you on your toes.
In conclusion, while it has the drawbacks of age, Wizardry 8 still provides a great cRPG experience.  As I said in the short version above, if you like classic games of the genre, give this one a go, particularly if it goes on sale.

"The AI cheats... really my main complaint."
Magic: The Gathering can be a fun trading card game, but for the new guy it can be equally overwhelming. Magic: The Gathering - Duels of the Planeswalkers 2013 can be a reasonable introduction for anyone with interest in Magic without breaking the bank or the rules. In this more "safe" environment you are taught how the game works at your own pace without the criticism of others. Beginner tips really help with understanding the different abilities and how the game plays out, when I started playing this was an invaluable aid.
However, for the more mature Magic audience, this game does cheat, in the sense that AI opponents will always get what they need, and you never get what you need. I was frustrated when my 1 health enemy, running a green deck, pulled their last flyer kill spell when I, running a white deck, could have finished them off with another attack, I had over 40 HP and when it came my turn I drew a plains, the absolute last card I needed at that time, and was squashed the very next turn as she summoned an army of tokens and buffed them all in their final attack. Another gripe is that, no matter how much you press "continue" or the TAB key, you have to wait the annoying few seconds for a phase of a players turn to finish up.
Overall, I'd recommend it for someone starting out, it's cheap, it's helpful, and ultimately fairly harmless. The nice thing is that if you decide Magic isn't your thing, you haven't gone out and spent the hundreds of dollars it could take making even one good deck. Give it a shot at your own expense!

MTG is a card playing game set in a fantasy universe. You play a mage who "casts" the cards and you have one or more opponents who play/cast cards of their own. Each player starts with 20 life and  you must lower the life of your opponents to 0 to kill them.
I would recommend this game for fans of MGT and for people who don't have experience with the trading card game but I would advise you don't pay too much for this game. This game is well suited to teach you Magic: The Gathering's rules. There are a nice selection of decks to choose from and there  are some puzzles you can solve as well as a campaign. The graphics are very slick and smooth, the music is great and the sound effects are good too. I have some negatice criticism about the game too. You cannot create a deck from scratch. As such, if you wanted to play a custom deck and build it all from scratch, well here you can't. The campaign feels very short and be finished in just a few hours (on normal). The decks that you are provided with all begin with just a subset of the full deck. To get the cards that you are missing, you must win battles with that deck. Cards are unlocked one at a time and it feels extremely long to unlock all cards. So to resume, let's say it's a nice magic but very limited in terms of replayability. So my advice is: Buy this game if it's really cheap, say 5$. You'll then get enough entertainment from this game for your 5$. But otherwise, the game will quickly feel like it's missing some features that were deliberatly locked in order to include that content in Downloadable Content (DLC). I have not purchased a single DLC.

I didn't hear about TowerClimb until recently. I wasn't sure if I was going to like it at first. Seem very brutal with only 1 extra life (2 with easy mode). However as I watched others play it I knew I had to get this game.
It's intense.
Once you know how the control works it becomes an incredible journey. You are a man/woman. You want to climb the tower. You are weak but you are resourceful. You never felt so impowered and powerless at the same time. You feel the clinging to the rock as if your life depends on it. There is jumps that you will question because you won't be sure if the distance is close enough to make it. The controls are tight, the music fits perfectly, and I like the art (pixelated, not the weird filter seen in the trailer).

Last, there is a log of all the deaths you encounter with a kill screenshot for each one. It's really cool to see your progress on an interactive graph. There is a challenging game mode aside from the main story that takes everything you learn from the main game and mismatches it all. 20 Minutes With Towerclimb:
Fantastic, suspenseful rogue-lite experience full of thrills and endless content. Earthy, low-resolution pixel art combined with pretty lighting effects oozes atmosphere. Tight, responsive controls. Lots of level variety, fully destructable environments. Sometimes it makes you think slow and carefully, working your way through environmental puzzles while trying to conserve resources. Other times it will push you to your limit, forcing you to work you way up the tower as fast as humanly possible. 6-player local cooperative (fantastic). Supports split-screen or same-screen, but I have yet to test that feature.
Technically primitive. Screen stretching not implemented well, so playing without a black border seems like a no-go (for now). Head-scratching interface choices (Shift-Esc to exit to main menu?), and analog controls that desperately need a dead-zone adjustment. One slip could kill you, you don't want it to be the fault of your controller. The control scheme itself could benefit from few more buttons, as you often find yourself playing twister with your fingers to pull items out, keep them in hand, and use them with care.
Highly recommended for fans of the Rogue-lite genre, specifically fans of Spelunky. This is Spelunky in reverse, but more cerebral, and more suspenseful. What could be more terrifying than dangling over a great abyss, hanging from your fingertips, wondering if your next move could be your last?
Very fun and very difficult. Like many people are saying here, if you're a fan of Spelunky you should definitely give it a try.

I eyed this game for so long. I wasn’t sure if I should pick it up or not for what it is.
I do love plattformers. I do love the roguelike genre so I figured I can’t do wrong.
Yup I was right. The game’s incredibly fun. I can honestly see myself playing it whenever I just want to take my mind off of things.
There’s no real story as far as I know.
All that I know is that you’re one weak human with an iron will and one goal: to reach the top of the tower.
Keyboard or Controller. Pick your poison. I’ve tried both and I’m just more comfortable with a controller as of now but that might change.
The controls are rather simple. You’re able to walk or run, jump and climb walls.
In order to climb up or down you have to cling to it first. That my friends is crucial. That means that you have to press the key/stick against the wall, hold the jump button and hold it while climbing either up or down. As soon as you let go or if you’re not paying enough attention to it you let go and, in most cases, fall to your death. Thankfully there’s an option called invert climb. Basically you don’t have to hold the jump button in order to cling to a wall just press your key/stick against the well.
The same goes for running. You can choose between holding a set key/button in order to run or if you run by default.
Let’s talk about jumping. There are two forms of jumps. Jumps while running and while you’re standing still. While running you’ll jump further and while standing you’ll jump higher. So you’ll see you’ll have to make some precise jumps if you don’t want to take a bath in some
lava.
Now onto the potions. You start off with four kind of potions.
Three blues, three reds, one green and one revive potion.
The blue ones allow you to perform one double jump. The red ones allow you kill enemies and to break blocks. More importantly if you throw such a potion down while jumping it’ll give you small boost which you can use to get higher or further. The last one is a revive potion which will revive you once most of the times. I say most of the times but it depends how you die. If you fall down in lava for example that’s it. If you try to impale yourself on some spikes it’ll revive you.
Next stop: items.
There are different kind of items. So far I’ve found a sword, a boomerang, crates and so on. I’m pretty sure there’s a ton I haven’t found yet. To make it short: You’ll use most of the items to give you a boost in mid air. So it’s best to experiment what the items do and how you can use and abuse them. The witch sells you some items if you have enough berries for her potion of youth. Or whatever she uses those for.
Berries! No need to drool we won’t be eating those.
So far I’ve seen three different kind of berries. Blue, red and yellow.
The blue and red ones work the same as the potions. Yellow on the other hand speeds you up while climbing which is pretty neat.
Then there are golden berries. Those are pretty much the currency in the game and with those you can buy various things from the witch as I said earlier like the potions which you’ll really need if you want to reach the top.
Level design is next up.
Depending on the RNG, and how far you come, you’ll find yourself in different kind of levels.
I’ve had the pleasure to get a lava stage three times in a row. Basically lava will
rise and fill up the level so you’re under some pressure to find and reach the exit. The music isn’t any help to not stress you out.
Another level I’ve successfully died in I had to control some kind of balloons and maneuver one through a bunch of razor sharp fans.

My favorite one so far is the water level. Basically you’re able to
through the stage which is a nice change. You just have to watch out so that no worms or fishes try to eat your face. Fun times.
That’s pretty much it as of now. There might be a lot more but that’s all I’ve seen as of now.
Deactivate depixelize. Please do me that favor even if you hate pixels. The game looks so much better without that option. The game looks gorgeous. It maybe could be a bit more defined here and there and might be a bit rough around the edges but overall I’m more than pleased with the looks of it. The combination of the look, controls and the music … For some reason I enjoy every death.
The music in the game’s just good.
It gives you a sense of mystery while playing, is relaxing in some instances and then it pressures you whenever you’re trying to not bath in some lava.
I especially like the sound effects of the enemies My favorite sound must the hound even though it looks like a dog(e).
The Tower wants you dead. Keep that in mind. Not to mention the RNG can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥but we’re all used to it by now. Well I know that I am and that I don’t mind so called
RNG.
TowerClimb is a really fun game that you can play every now and then either in short bursts or for the whole day. It’s challenging but at the same time rewarding. Just making it to the exit of a level is pure joy … just to find out that the tower decided that you’re not worthy of him and gets you killed in one way or another.

In many ways, I find this is a game you have to experience. Not because of a heavy reliance on story or art, but because the mechanics of the game and every new thing introduced are just that interesting. Each area you see will kill you in new and interesting ways, and there is just something novel about being utterly destroyed time and time again knowing that you could have done better. This game accomplishes that. Thoroughly. Like, seriously, did you have to make it so that the ledge cling mechanic locks you there specifically when it is inconvenient?
Playing towerclimb is like being in a relationship, you'll be up countless nights playing with it. You'll spend countless hours at your job thinking, "I KNOW I can get to the third
area", and you'll spend countless more hours wondering how to do so. You love it yet you want to strangle it. In a romantic kind of way.
