The odds are stacked against the player far too heavily. I love challenging games and rogue-lites like Spelunky, but TowerClimb is more than unfair, which makes it difficult for me to have fun playing it. Others may enjoy the struggle, but I find that it doesn't make me feel like I want to revisit it after an hour or two of gameplay.

There's a certain look and feel that Super Nintendo games had that gets me like no other games do. It's hard to put my finger on exactly, but I think it was a combination of soft-edged sprites and synth woodwind soundtrack that gave a lot of titles a deep, otherworldly feel. TowerClimb somehow manages to evoke that same sense of depth and wonder while relentlessly murdering me again and again in the most delightful ways.
Part of the unique feel of TowerClimb comes from the mysterious, parable-like setup for the game. There are immense stone towers, people keep trying to climb them, and no one knows what's at the top. You control a never-ending series of unfortunates who challenge the tower, mantling up through floor after deadly floor. It plays a lot like a reverse Spelunky, with your character able to run, jump, scale walls, and crawl along ceilings in search of the exit high above. In place of treasure are tools like crates and springs, and golden berries that can be traded for potions that let you double-jump, break blocks, and teleport.
You're going to need every move and tool at your disposal, though, because the levels in TowerClimb are bizarre and merciless. Sometimes you'll enter a level and it'll start filling with lava. Sometimes everything will be coated in acid. Sometimes carnivorous worms burst from the walls. And sometimes there are pleasant, floaty dandelion-things to ride... straight into the jaws of a bloodthirsty hound. Even if the level gimmick isn't out for your hide, the random generation might very well give you an improbable network of tricky jumps to the exit, far worse than anything you may have encountered in the likes of Spelunky. I'm not kidding about the challenge here, and if not for all the neat things to find and entertaining ways to die, it might not be worth overcoming.
But there is indeed a lot to discover in the tower, and the pixellated graphics make experimentation essential to figuring out what you're encountering. Enemies may get the best of you the first time you meet them, in part because they can be very unpredictable but mainly because you might not know what they are at first. You'll run into all manner of plants and animals, NPCs, chests, shortcuts, and more among the randomly-generated floors. Navigating is always challenging given some of the layouts, but your control over your character is very precise and allows for masterful moves once you fully grok the mantling.
It's hard and you're going to die a ton, but TowerClimb makes it look so good you'll hardly mind. The graphics remind me very much of the old SNES Lemmings port, with chunky detail and silky-smooth animations and bizarre, impossible terrains. Sound design is also excellent, with some very detailed effects and a soundtrack reminiscent of ancient titles like Soul Blazer and Super Metroid in parts. The unexpected nostalgia rush definitely colors my view but make no mistake, TowerClimb is a tight, challenging roguelike platformer with plenty of wonders to offer.

I've played many more hours than Steam says, having bought it in beta.

Don't expect Spelunky though. Towerclimb is slower, grittier and even more difficult. You have to be even more careful and it's more about evasion than killing stuff. It's fun cause it's difficult and you die a lot. There are several general level themes in the first part of the game (standard caves, jungle, lava caverns...) and special levels (rising lava, water levels, levels where you fly on giant flying plant ballons and more/weirder). And once you finish that, which will take closer to tens of hours, there's chapter two that has more specific (some could say gimmicky, imo a good thing in a game like this) and even more difficult levels, where the gameplay is a bit different.
The graphics was pixel art before it was cool. It's pretty nice and features some cool shader effects, but I understand people who have enough of that. Also the music is excellent.
Towerclimb has local coop and it is even more fun (and a bit easier, since, unlike spelunky, it's not that easy to harm each other. The biggest problem is that setting up controllers is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥

At this point the engine is a little dated, and if you are expecting the latest in FPS and graphics, you need to be ready to mod. Some issues with crashing to desktop and infinite load screens persist, but are easily solved with a bit of work. Definitely pick this up.

Asymmetric's West of Loathing is closer to Fallout than Fallout 4 will ever be, letting you talk your way out of almost every single fight and providing options other than just shooting everything to death.
In some ways the setting reminds me of New Vegas but actually set during the Wild West and not some grotesque post-apocalyptic version of it. The ending cutscene is also like New Vegas, showing you how the different factions you helped or destroyed fare after the story and storylines of individual characters.
The background of the story is as follows: West of Loathing takes place shortly after an event known as the The Cows having Come Home. As a result of this, the cows have slaughtered many civilians for some unknown reason, but it could be as simple as they were fed up of being food for us humans.
Starting off as a simple man/woman living in a homestead just outside the town of Boring Springs, you're given the choice of setting some backstory for your character as well as their class. I chose to be a witty, gunslinging man who was a Snake Oiler, a sort of thief class that can heal themselves or hurt foes with snake venom harvested from the snakes in their briefcase. Yep, thats a thing.You can also be a fisticuff wielding Cowpuncher or magic using Beanslinger but I have yet to try these.
Boring Springs serves as a tutorial area, once you're done here you can never come back. It teaches you how to fight, buy and sell items, and most importantly, that you can avoid combat almost entirely with the right stats and dialogue choices. Your time here ends after you chase down one of the three unique horses or decide to go for a basic one. I chose the locoweed addicted one myself just for laughs, but the other two choices are a ghost horse and a dark horse.
One more thing to remember before leaving Boring Springs is to choose whether you want a partner to accompany you or to go solo (if you're brave enough to try). Ultimately I ended up with Susie, a sharpshooter traumatised by the recent death of her family by the arrival of the cows and so harbours an immense hatred for them. The other choices are the old man Pete, doc Alice and a secret one that is best to find out for yourself.
Upon finally leaving Boring Springs, the Wild West is yours to explore to your hearts content. After settling in to a room at the starting area of Dirtwater, the game gives you your main objective to strive for (your companion will remind you if asked, thankfully) and thats that, you can do whatever the hell you want until you feel its time to progress the story, no pressure whatsoever.
The overworld of West of Loathing and the various locations that make it up consists of settlements, mountains, mines, forts and more to search through. Then you have more unique places like the circus (complete with demon clowns) and a jelly bean museum, and my personal favourite, the Necromancer tower that can be found if you collect all the tomes and clues relating to its location.
But some of these locations, like the aforementioned Necromancer tower, can't be discovered or entered without a prerequisite item. For example, there's a cave known as the Lost Dutch Oven Mine where you need stench resistance to enter or your character will straight up refuse to go in. Another place like this is the cave place that can only be found by following tracks from another location.
A lot of items and locked doors early on will be inacessible without the required skill or stat, such as safecracking, meaning a lot of backtracking will occur towards the late game. Of course you can ignore these if you so wish but with the short travel time between locations, its not much of a bother to do so. Assuming you don't mind the random encounters on the overworld, but these can be avoided too.
The dialogue between characters is the best part of the game though, cracking jokes at the expense of other games and itself, referencing well known movies and books, or just being outright silly. Apart from the occasional repeated encounter, I never skipped the dialogue because of this.
XP levels up your stats, of course, and can be farmed infinitely at certain locations, some in particular are great for your character or companion. I myself farmed snakes for their venom which I would then sell for extra meat, and for Susie I farmed cows for a good two hours to boost her stats, resulting in her being able to one shot basically every enemy. Combat is simple enough with just the right amount of depth to it if you want to play a more challenging run.
Overall I got a good 16 hours out of West of Loathing (3-4 of those of was just farming XP), for a game that has the look of a flash browser game I didn't expect to sink this much time into it, nor did I expect to laugh so much.

There is a central conflict in gaming that more and more games have addressed: The simple and perplexing problem that traditional narrative becomes less engaging when more interactivity is allowed. The conflict between story and gameplay. Grim Fandango represents that central conflict. It is a game that is aesthetically astonishing, with a sharp and engaging script, that is mostly un-fun to play.
Although the game boasts remarkably striking visuals, a sharp and funny script, and an evocative and original world, the puzzles are constantly, if not nearly always, frustrating and illogical. The nonsensical puzzles do lead to amusing moments of whimsy. However, this does not compensate for boredom and frustration in a game that is clearly smart enough to know better.
Despite this frustration, this game stays with us as a classic, because of its beating heart and dedication to a thoughtful world. Grim Fandango may not be a great game, but it remains a curious and wonderful artifact of a medium struggling against itself.

i am somewhat galled by the misleading bit about how "remastered" it is.  yes, it clearly has been "remastered," but only a little bit (at least visually).  it seems that only certain moving/foreground bits have been "remastered," leaving all the backgrounds in their original very low resolution. the result is pretty ugly looking to be honest. it also makes it clear when important bits and items have been "remastered" drawing more attention to them, as they dont mesh with the background cleanly. this can be pretty annoying at times, especially on a high resolution monitor, and frankly often just looks like shody work.
that said, the game itself is pretty fun (albiet with occasionally infuriating moments as is common with many of the early hunt and click style adventure games), with quite humorous writing and voice acting, so all in all i would recommend this game for those interested in this style of game, or if you want to relive the early days, but do not expect a "remastered" game on the level of games like Day of the Tentacle.

TL;DR: What a treat! Buy it!
I never got to play the original, but as I can see from other reviewers, Youtube videos, and using the "original/remastered" switch in the menu, not much has changed gameplay-wise, and that's good, because it didn't have to. I'm playing with a PS3 controller (and non-"tank" mode, if that means something to someone), and it just works like a peach. It seamlessly shows the mouse/keyboard indicators etc. if I start using them, and they go away immediately when I go back to the controller. It's all so neat!
The story is very compelling. Given the fact that we don't know anything about what happens after we're dead, this game can be considered believable, and so that is the way I have chosen to see the story: a comedic take, on what might actually be on the other side of death.
And it is tragic hilarity, difficulty and absurdity, wrapped in an (almost) flawless gameplay-taco. There are a few quirks here and there. It takes a little while to get used to controlling the *AHEM* "vehicle", and two times I have witnessed items appearing in places they clearly shouldn't be (after retrieving a certain dental protector, and returning to its original place, there it suddenly was, back in its place; and a cigarette kept hovering 3 feet off the ground, as I climbed to the roof). But seriously...that's it.
The puzzles felt appropriately difficult. I never felt stumped for more than 2 minutes, before I "saw the light", unlike e.g. Monkey Island 2 (which I love, but IT IS needlessly intricate at times). The game conveniently shuts "doors" and opens new ones, to keep you from wasting time in places that do not matter to your current mission. If you get stuck, just try looking for something that stands out a tiny bit (graphically or otherwise), and try to think of something that would be funny to do. Try the 4-5 applicable items you have, on anything you can otherwise interact with (it mostly somewhat makes sense). You never have more than 10-12 objects, and of those some will be duplicates, and most will have a very specific use. The pacing, puzzle-solving and humor are all balanced very well, in a way that keeps the story rolling and believable (as much as it can with its setting).
The music and sound effects are more than fantastic! The graphics are quaint, and extremely true to the original. The "lip"-syncing is flawless! Only Glottis freaks out sometimes, but he also did that in the original. The actors are great, and REALLY help sell the whole setting.
Aside from the teeeeny tiiiiny non-game-breaking glitches once in a while, I have nothing to complain about.

I'm just gonna go ahead and say that FC2 is my favorite game in the series. I found Far Cry 3 to be casualized and easy. There was no challenge from start to finish and it follows the same Ubisoft open world formula from recent Assassin's Creed games. Far Cry 2 is vastly different and I prefer it over Far Cry 3 and 3.1, I mean 4 for a number of reasons.
I mean just the fact I don't have to climb any radio towers to see more of the map or having the map littered with collectable icons are great. The feel and sounds of the guns are also really good for a 2008 game. Every gun in FC2 feels unique and don't feel like a toy compared to FC3 and 4. Guns jam, they have recoil, they show signs of wear and tear, and more. They don't feel like brand new military weapons but rather feel like they fit the African milita setting of the game. Every gun in FC3 and 4 feel like they're brand new and the sound is muddy when shooting them. In my opinion the gunplay in FC2 is some of the best I've played in a first person shooter, and I play quite a few of them (check my Steam game list if you want).
The AI I think is pretty decent for a 2008 title. There are games released today that have far worse AI than this game. In Far Cry 3/4 if you're up on a cliff or a decent distance away and you take an enemy down via sniping then the others in the camp or nearby will always somehow zero in on your location. In FC2 the enemies will try to help their fellow comrades by carrying them to safety and search the immediate area, not instantly know which direction the shot came from like in FC3/4.
As for the malaria it never really inconvenienced me when out and about, and I thought it was a pretty nice touch to the overall setting. I also don't feel it artificially prolonged the game like say having a crap ton of collectables all over the map.
As for the story I'd have to sayit's not the best. In fact I enjoyed Far Cry 3's story more than FC2, but when it comes to the gameplay then FC2 for me wins easily.
I give it an 8/10.
PS. Don't mind the 2.6 hours on record. I played this game to death when it came out on PS3 and bought it on Steam a couple years ago on sale.

This is one of those RPG's that you have to play, yeah you can cry that it's old, or it's dated in many respects. Played a fair amount of Skyrim so this game is a blast.
It has similarities to Hearthstone in presentation. That's pretty much where the similarities end.
The main difference is the 2-lane system. You have a board with a divide down the middle, you can play cards that affect 1 or both lanes (although affecting both lanes is less common), and importantly minions can only trade within the lane they are played into. Although abilities can cross between lanes.
So for instance, you can play a minion who has the text [deals 1 damage to a creature] in one lane, while targeting a minion in the other one. This also applies to minions who use targeted buffs.
The next main difference is the rune system, you have 5 runes (yes the storymode only introduces this later on but trust me it's 5), once you break an opponents rune they draw a card. And here's the neat bit, some cards have the unique ability to be played when the rune is broken (prophecy keyword). So you can have your own rune broken, draw a special card (a prophecy) and play that card to screw up your opponents attack/turn planning.
This has the effect of countering aggressive players/decks and offers a comeback mechanism for a player who is behind.
Once you get used to the game you can play around the common prophecies, so there is some skill involved.
Oh and you can heal above the starting 30HP because why the hell wouldn't you.
You can play against a competent AI in storymode, matches against a random AI or an arena which has some little twists on the lanes.
I have seen the AI make the odd error in play order (for buffs and such) but those are few and far between really. (certainly above and beyond anything the derpy AI in hearthstone could muster).
Oh and the AI decks are actually fairly competitive, none of this stupid vanilla minion decks with zero synergies involved.
The game has a casual and ranked system, the ranked system is much better than Hearthstone, because once you gain a rank increase you do not lose it until the season resets. I cannot stress how much this makes the gameplay more natural, and I think it has a healthy impact on the meta as a whole.
There's also arena vs players which has .gasp. Actually good rewards. Seriously, I took my first run 1_3 result which is terrible (aggro is hard) but still got 25 gold, some soul gems and a pack. That's a loss of only 25 gold for performing well below par. Another more recent run I got 5_3,  with 2 packs and 75 gold. That's an in-game reward of 275 gold worth, for a 150 gold entry fee.
Bear in mind a pack in TES legends is 6 cards for the basic in-game currency price of 100 gold.
I would recommend it if you're comfortable with the main gameplay. But beware players are trying their absolute best there so it can get tense.
Oh btw the storymode is awesome, some nice little stories with a narration and characters all keeping you invested in what is going on and of course. It's in the TES lore so if you've played skyrim or oblivion you will see some favourites in-game.
Wabbajack.
Dragons.
Now those are the pros, a few cons are;
_When playing against the AI in arena it will tend to go super aggro on you, which means you learn bad habits when you want to actually draft and play against real players.
_Currently you cannot cancel playing a card once it is put into play (unlike hearthstone where you can undo this).
_The animations in the game are not that impressive outside of a few spells at present. Most legendary entrance animations seem dull after a while. (I like the dragons though)
_Some entrance sound effects are lacking as well, for instance the card "Lydia" was given a different voice from her in-game voice in Skyrim for unknown reasons. This irks me.
_Games are much much longer than some other games (as someone who played a lot of hearthstone, yes this means TES Legends is much slower in pace). So you have to be patient
_You will still run into aggro decks and super slow grindy control decks here. Fortunately with the variety in game modes you can quite easily dip into something else to cool off.
_quest rewards in-game seem quite conservative. going from 40-70 gold, which seems a little underwhelming but bear in mind you can "grind" playing the AI to get a 15 dust reward for each win. So you win some you lose some.
_It is a fremium game. You can play for free but you will eventually want to purchase some cards or an extra storymode or something to get your collection growing faster. . (Oh and the game does have decks you can buy for gold as well, this isn't a con but it's related).
_There are a lot of concepts to understand and get to grips with, if you've played card games before this isn't a problem. But I can see new players being a little swamped with all the mechanics you have to remember.
Overall i've had a lot of fun learning how to play the game. It starts off with a neat story that introduces you to the game concepts without beating you over the head about remembering very basic things like knowing how to breathe.
You can play without spending money, but you will have to be patient (as with all fremium games).
I think the game has potential to be pretty good thanks to the lanes and the fair variety of other mechanics I haven't mentioned here (but I won't spoil you with those), there's some really tough decisions and strategy you want to understand to get good at the game as well.
And of course if you've dipped into the elder scrolls universe you will get some joy from seeing characters you are familiar with.
Recommended for folks who have played card games and/or the elder scrolls games. New card game players will want to take a bit of time to get used to how it all works, I mean if you want to. I'm not your mother.

What I like about the game:
-The writing is clever and hilarious. The game is full of gags, satire, and absurd logic, and it's all executed perfectly. The humor is easily this game's strongest point for me.
-The combat system is fun, and allows for lots of creativity in how you approach battles.
-The art style is simplistic, but pleasing to the eye.
-You are able to decide what kind of character your protagonist is, with the choices the game gives you. Are they a stone-cold, battle-hungry killer, or do they avoid conflict whenever they have the chance?
-There's tons of weaponry, apparel, food, and drink to choose from, to really customize your characters stats and fighting style.
-The music is epic and really enhances the experience.
-If you're stuck on a quest, there's always something else to do that's fun.
-You can fast-travel from anywhere, even from inside buildings and caves.
-You get experience fairly quickly. If you need more experience, there's always places to grind, and battles are so enjoyable in this game that even grinding is a joy.
What I don't like about this game:
-Lockpicking and Safecracking are two very important skills that are difficult to find the skill books for if you made some mistakes in the introductory chapter, leading to a lot of frustration. In addition, the skill books are quite expensive themselves.
-...that's all I got.
I highly recommend this game if you want a good laugh, enjoy strategic and creative grid-based battles, or just feel like killing demonic cows.

I recommend this game, but barely. It's free and it's short; if it weren't either of these things, I would say don't bother.
Depression and non-normative thinking/behaviour manifests itself in what can seem to be the most ordinary people. It's a basic concept, but it's not easy to understand. While
does try to address that, it only succeeds to a middling degree. It's far too short and feels much too hollow to really pack a punch, but maybe it's better thought of as an advertisement for the sentiment instead of a novel or an article. I certainly didn't leave the game feeling significantly affected, or like I had a miraculously more lucid understanding of the inner workings of a man on a morbid mission, but I did leave feeling like I knew that that was what the game was trying to tell me.
At the end of the day,
hits few high marks but also few low marks; it's relatively unremarkable, but it's short, and it's free. So the question isn't exactly "Why?" but instead "Why not?" For better or worse.

Negatives:

Interface is sterile and clunky with mouse, because I guess this game is a money grab of a port. Interface, sound and music is a huge downgrade from the first Duels game. The decks here are less clever and original than in the previous game. Most of the story mode consists of 'encounters' which aren't fights against other Magic decks, but just an AI that casts the same spell infinitely until you find a way to beat it. This has nothing to do with the rules of Magic. The cinematics with the 'animated' comic book panels is beyond outdated for a 2013 game, and do not serve to 'actionize' the superfluous story. (Wizards, please. This is a card game, not a Marvel cartoon.)
There are some hours of entertainment in this title, but you might want to skip the cheesy cinematics and the great amount of forced tutorials and just get the first Duels, which is better and cheaper. The few things in 2013 that work, work a bit better in the 2012 Duels and much better in the 2009 Duels.
If you are playing to learn the rules of Magic, this title might be a tad easier to get in to, but once you're learning, you'll find the encounters boring and the real opponents too few. You might try your hand at playing online, and with luck the servers are faster and more stable than they were at release. Otherwise you're SOL.

- The decks are incredibly well balanced. Almost all decks feels equally powerful. To begin with many of the decks will feel very weak but they get much stronger as you progress and unlock all cards. I have unlocked every single card in the game and I consider the 2013 version to be absolute best Magic game in terms of balancing.
- A lot of different variety of amazing decks to suit your playstyle. All feel great as they get full unlocked and tweaked to perfection.
- Plane Chase (not in the later versions): This game mode is essentially is a regular 2, 3 or 4 player FFA which you battle across a variety of diverse worlds, each with its own unique effect on the game. This makes the game unpredictable as it can quickly turn the tables. This game is pretty fun but does not seem very balanced. For instance if you encounter the plane called Jund, you better prepare to get steamrolled very fast if you are a non-green, non-black, non-red colour player and your enemy is.
- Virtually no one playing the game online. If you want to play against other players online, the 2014 and 2015 is still the best options. 2014 will mostly be Two-Headed Giants mode. 2015 lacks Two-Headed Giants mode but will have better chances of finding FFA games. But the game is absolutely amazing if you have friends playing it.
This version plays slower than the 2014 and 2015 version. It will not play as swift and responsive as the later versions. The longer wait between turns is a little annoying.
BUG: Deck "Peacekeepers" does not seem to unlock cards properly. You can unlock the first 10 cards with a promo code. The rest will unlock as you win games but as soon as you exit the game, the unlocked cards will be lost. This can be fixed if you go to the "Deck Manager" and make a small change before clicking "Back" and then save the changes.

I would definately recommend this game despite it's flaws. I would say I slightly prefer the overall play of 2014 version but this is still one the best Magic: DotP. Better than 2015 and MUCH better than the new free Magic Duels, which is an atrocity to be perfectly honest.
If you are new to Magic Duels of the Planeswalkers and have yet to decide which version to try, I would recommend the 2014 version first for the above reasons. There are not exactly a lot of players playing it, but you can often find Two-Headed Giants games in 2014 version. This does not seem to be the case in this version. A real shame because it has some really kickass decks.

This game has clicked with me. Hard. I love procedurally generated games, especially platformers, and this game offers a challenge unlike most others. It's never unfair, as all of my deaths were my own fault, so it avoids being too frustrating or annoying. What it IS, is satisfying. REALLY satisfying. Getting past just the first room/area was a challenge, and it felt GREAT getting past it.
That's not even the first level, just the first ROOM in the first level, and they're always different. One level had rising lava for no real reason, one other had dogs on every ledge, one was full of wasps, and yet I always had a great time. The graphics are both retro and modern (thanks to amazing lighting effects) and charming as hell, and the music is great. I love roguelikes and I play a lot of them, but I think this is one that will stick with me for a very, very long time.

This game is a real gem hidden amongst the crowd and im glad i've found it.
The premise of the game is simple: Your character, through some sort of sheer bravery, lust for death or perhaps morbid curiosity, decides to enter a tower full of monsters, traps and random layouts to climb to the top (Cause why the hell not?).
There's really nothing else to the game. Im serious! That's
all this game is about! The experience whilst climbing the tower however is unbelievably satisfying and I have to admit i never though i'd see myself replaying this game again.
The game is kept extremely simple. Simple controls, simple UI (I think all there is is that menu on the left that displays your current inventory, items etc) simple shop/npc system (All ive seen so far is some guy asking for stuff and a witch selling you potions/items) and simple goal (Get to the top). In fact, there really is no reason to look at a wiki or guide for this game since everything is so simple to figure out (Or that could just be me).
I think one thing the game does very well is making everything your own doing. I dont know how to put it. If you fall to your death/get mauled by a dog/burn in lava/ dismembered by a trap/ punctured by spikes and all sorts of other things, its
. In retrospect, it is a really does feel like an achievement when you actually do make it out past a level without dying. Very little is left to chances and alot of it is to do with skill. That's something i found enjoyable.
In terms of content however, im not exactly sure. Im not one to look into wikis and guides cause in my extreme minority opinion, looking at a guide or wiki destroys a very large part of playing the game (Figuring out stuff!). With that said, ive only seen very few items variety, 2 special level events (Lava and a worm thing), about 4 to 5 different map biome/layout/type, 2 NPCs and 1 special door (Path of exiles shortcut). I dont know if this was planned to make the game remain as simple as possible or not but it's very likely that im still missing out on a ton of content such as secrets and future levels (I believe I've only made it up until 2.5k feet).
I guess the best way to make a comparison for this game is to say it's upward spelunky with less content and
more skill. Either ways, im pretty sure this game is worth the 30RM/10$ i paid for it. At least im pretty darn sure it's better spent on them then
other games...

I've been following this game for about three years, starting with the Let's Play series done by JSmithOTI, a youtuber who covers many different games. The idea of the game and its unique art style immediately caught my attention. I had been familiar with rogue-likes and different platformers; the original Spelunky is one of my favorite games and I saw a lot of similar aspects in TowerClimb.
I finally made the jump to purchase the game in April of 2015 while the game was still in beta and began playing it religiously. I got a good deal of my own friends into it and they themselves enjoyed the challenge posed by simply Chapter 1. The gameplay feels fluid and reminds me of the classic platformers I grew up loving. Since then, the game has only improved and expanded. It is amazing to look back and see that so many years of work and dedication were put into the making of this game and the same work and dedication that comes from the community.
I am proud to have been a part of TowerClimb in my own little way and hope that it can entertain you just like it has for me.
If I had to summarize what I enjoy about the game, the major points would be a great soundtrack and the mental challenge it gives. At the beginning of a run, you can take it slowly and space out every jump, but as the game gets more hectic and fast-paced, you really feel your mind kicking into overdrive just to make the precise movements and grabs you need to survive. TowerClimb properly has proposed a puzzle that players feel a desire to solve. Learning piece by piece lets you truly experience the game, but an active community and veterans from half a decade ago are available to help out a novice player.
I would reccomend this game to all my friends and everyone who likes a frustrating challenge that reaps a fulfilling reward.

A retro gem worth taking a look at, Wizardry 8 is a single player RPG that allows you to create several party members, choosing from around a dozen races and classes to do so. The game is aging but should appeal to old school gamers who remember the days when video games were about interesting game mechanics and not just having the latest and greatest graphics. The game is turn based, which should appeal to players who enjoy games from the time period the Wizardry series of games originally came out in. Sadly, it seems not many today know or remember Wizardry, but if you enjoy games with a lot of different mechanics you can utilize while not being required to use them to complete the game, and have a special place in your heart for retro games of an amazing caliber, Wizardry 8 has a lot to love.
The battle system is easy to learn but hard to master, yet once you are able to do so, you will feel like a true boss stomping over weaker enemies that gave you trouble before, while still weary and afraid of what new beastie may be lurking around the next corner. As far as the story and dialog goes, Wizardry 8 certainly has no problem seating itself into a more comical niche. At first glance, it may appear some of the  lines and plot are just corny and lame because of Wizardry 8's age, however, if one were to look closer, they may see that the game enjoys being campy, welcoming your eye rolling and snickering.
Embrace the silly dialog and goofy plot! Enjoy the in depth character creation and entertaining battle sequences! And if you find yourself afraid to venture forth to your next objective without going back and leveling some more, don't be ashmed! The world of Wizardry 8 can be rough and heartless, at times, but with your wit and your strength, you may yet complete your adventure!

An old fashioned game for those who appreciate the feel of table top roleplaying, without the hassle that comes with a group of people. The game is deep, and highly complicated throughout, and in the end all players begin to decide what classes and gameplay is 'the best'. The only thing that I have seen as a downside to this game's design is the fact that what you encounter, and the overall difficulty is as much dependant on luck as it is skill. Creatures actively hunt you down, and you can easily end up against odds you cannot possibly overcome, especially if you have decided to try to run from an encounter, instead of putting your back to a wall and fighting it out in hopes of surviving with at least a few members of your party alive. If you are the type who enjoys tabletop games such as D&D or Pathfinder, this game will likely tickle your fancy, but if you are looking for another Fable or even a Final Fantasy, or Skyrim, you may as well move on, as this game will only frustrate you.

Haven't played it much from steam since i already have another highly modded version of it but wanted to support it all the same since i have, in fact, spent countless hours playing it.
Still, hands down the best old-school rpg's of its kind. The character customization, combat, magic system and difficulty set this game apart from most others and it has some pretty solid music tracks to set stage for epic battles. A multitude of races that all have their unique strengths and weaknesses along with a great selection of classes that all rely on seven primary attributes (strength, intelligence, willpower, endurance, dexterity, speed and senses) which somehow all manage to be relevant at least in some way to every class.
One of my favourite things about this game is that you can make up a party of 6 adventurers from scratch and by the time you are done, they all have personality. One thing of note about this game is the amount of lines of voiced dialogue from you party members.In any given battle they will be shouting out about being hurt, landing killing blows or getting poisoned and the like that really immerse the player in what is going on in the battle, all the while doing so in the personality of the voiceset you picked. While this may not seem new, the sheer amount of things they will comment on gives enough variety so it always seems to add to the situation instead of being repetative annoying drivel. MANY games have attempted to give the freedom of character creation and maintain a level of personality and have failed. This game does not, and considering it has some of the most in-depth of its kind that is fairly amusing.
The only thing about this game that hasn't held up well over time is the greatly outdated first gen 3d graphics and a mediocore story (mostly due to limited interactive npcs). This game is BEGGING for a remake/facelift and someone would stand to make a LOT of cash in doing so.

What I like about the game:
-The writing is clever and hilarious. The game is full of gags, satire, and absurd logic, and it's all executed perfectly. The humor is easily this game's strongest point for me.

-You can fast-travel from anywhere, even from inside buildings and caves.
-You get experience fairly quickly. If you need more experience, there's always places to grind, and battles are so enjoyable in this game that even grinding is a joy.
What I don't like about this game:
-Lockpicking and Safecracking are two very important skills that are difficult to find the skill books for if you made some mistakes in the introductory chapter, leading to a lot of frustration. In addition, the skill books are quite expensive themselves.
-...that's all I got.
I highly recommend this game if you want a good laugh, enjoy strategic and creative grid-based battles, or just feel like killing demonic cows.

Overview:
Unlike the other Lara Croft games, this one goes for a top down approach.  The levels progress linearly but provide enough open space, variety, and alternate paths to keep the game engaging.  There is a good mix of player freedom and player direction.  The game can be played solo or coop.
Pros:
Level design.  Each level is fairly unique and provides a varied array of puzzles to solve.  There are lots of envirornment hazards and challenges to over come as well as plenty of enemies.  There is a good variety of enemies in each level.  Some levels are quite large and include a lot of puzzles.
Puzzles.  The puzzles in this game are actually really good.  Some are quite involved and stretch over the course of the entire playing field.  Some puzzles require thought to solve, while others are tests of skill and reaction.
Cons:
Controls.  You can play this game with the keyboard and mouse, but I did run into some instances where the controls just wouldn't work right.  Bottom line, this game should be played with a controller.
Conclusion:
This is a good pick up and play for 30 minutes game and each level doesn't last longer than that.  The game isn't all that long, but for the price it is well worth it.  The puzzles are satisfying and the combat is great arcade style fun.  Beyond that, there isn't much.  The story gets the job done, but isn't fantastic.  There is little to none character progress and the hidden collectables throughout the levels do not add anything to the game.  Still, this is a good addition to the Lara Croft franchise.
Score: 8.4 / 10

Run, run, jump, throw a spear, jump onto spear, jump and fire a hook to the closest ring, swing left and right to gain speed, jump to the platform, get to the rock, roll it through four monsters that just spawned, keep rolling to the nearby platform. The gate opens. You step in. Ok, the easy part is done. Now... go and get the artifact and keep pushing forward to reach Xolotl and finally stop him!
There's no need for any introduction when it comes to Lara Croft and Tomb Raider games. The difference between this game and all the other Tomb Raider titles is the pace of action and camera view (fixed isometric), as well as a multiplayer option (two player co-opeative hot-seat or via internet). Lara is still equipped with her dual pistols, remote bombs and grappling hook but she can expand her arsenal during this adventure with dozens of weapons (although you will most probably stick to 3 or max 4 of them).
The story. Is it really important? Alright, here's the short version: Lara was hunting an ancient mirror that entrapped a creature of darkness for centuries inside a Mayan temple. A band of mercenaries got there before her and released the spirit. Now it's up to Lara and Totec, an ancient guardian, to hunt him down and stop his evil plans of world domination. Honestly, it's completely unimportant and unimaginative and the real value of this game is in its gameplay.
This is still the same, good old Tomb Raider game. It's just a little bit faster and the levels are shorter. Your goal is always the same: reach the level exit until you can finally face Xolotl and be done with this adventure. The puzzles are pretty simple and will only require you to control your character with some skill to be done. The real challenge are... challenges! Each level has a number of them, including speed runs (beat the clock) and some item collecting (each level has 10 red skulls that need to be found). Honestly, I really loved completing challenges and I kept repeating each level until all were done. I would usually try and beat the score challenge on my first run, as well as collecting the skulls and power-ups, then come back and try the speed run. Some challenges on some levels are real easy and you won't even notice you completed them (meaning that you will be surprised when the "challenge complete" text flashed out) while some require strong effort. For example, the very first level has a "Disable Xolotl's fire trap in under 00:30" and that took me more than 30 minutes to complete. Fortunately, dying in game is not really punishable (you lose 5000 points which is ok if you are not doing the score challenge) so you can commit suicide and just try again from the save point. Another great thing is that you can collect weapons, artifacts and other power-ups in any order - once you collect them, they are saved. You can even quit the game right after picking up an item and it's ok, you will never have to do it again. You can even pick up a grenade launcher on level 7 and go play level 1 with it in your inventory, possibly making some puzzles easier with it. Cool, eh?
Now the real fun is the multiplayer mode. Unfortunately, I never tried it (nobody wants to play with me!) but I've seen videos and I loved it. In multiplayer, two players control Lara and Totec, while some puzzles (and solutions) are different than in a single player game. The game requires true co-operation and seems to be very fun to play.
Overall, this game provides a lot of joy. It takes about 8 to 10 hours to complete the single player game and probably another 15 to complete all the challenges. There are 12 achievements in the game and 11 are really easy, while the last one asks you to complete all the challenges. It's far from hard, but it takes time to complete. I know I will do it, I really enjoyed completing time runs and I am not really a kind of gamer who likes speed runs in any games. This one is somehow different.
Love the game, definitely recommending it to everyone. Especially if you can play this with someone in co-op that's even better! :)

It’s a shame they didn’t take notes from Guardian of Light when developing the most recent reboot of Tomb Raider. While Lara croft in the most recent core entry in the Tomb Raider series is trying her best to shed all the enjoyable puzzles and adventuring that made the series famous to instead become the new quick time event action movie star and dethrone Drake from Uncharted, Lara Croft in the Guardians of Light offers everything that made Tomb Raider great.
The game is centered on fast paced action combat, exploration, and completing various interesting and sometimes challenging puzzles.  Unlike the core entries in the franchise, Guardians of Light takes the approach of having players control the game from an isometric view point, this type of view point allows for a very enjoyable seamless co-op mode experience.
As far as visuals go there’s nothing in this game that will overwhelm you, but for an isometric view game from 2010 it holds up very well. The level design on the other hand is absolutely brilliant, offering a wide variety of puzzles ranging from one room dungeons to entire expansive multi-tomb map sized puzzles. The puzzles are normally completed through various interactions between Lara and her co-op companion Totec, the Guardian of Light. Each character plays slightly different from one another, each with their own pros and cons, Totec is bulkier and has a shield so he fits more into the role of a tank, he also uses throwing spears as his primary weapon that can also be used to make platforms for the much lighter and more nimble and agile Lara Croft. Totec can also raise his shield above his head to use as a platform and then Lara can use her grappling hook to pull up Totec or make rope bridges for him to climb up. There are many instances in the game where you are put into a situation where you have to act very quickly and rely heavily on your partner to either lift you into the right position or to carry you to safety before you are either crushed, mauled, or mutilated, and in these intense, fast paced, high pressure situations is where the game shines.
The combat handles just the way you’d expect it to for an isometric view arcade shooter. There aren’t really any complaints as long as you aren’t the guy who gets stuck as player 2 using a gamepad controller, because you’ll be SoL and instead of a crosshair you will get stuck with the tiniest little light that shines on the wall in the direction you are facing as your point of reference for the general area in which you’ll be firing. This honestly wouldn’t be that bad, when you see the light it works really well, but the problem is that it’s constantly being hidden behind objects in the foreground and you have to blindly fire at enemies while you franticly search for your little light. The game does offer a fairly extensive variety of weapons to choose from, from pistols to assault rifles to flame throwers, they’re all present and accounted for.  Each character has their own primary weapon; Lara’s being her pistols and Teco’s being his throwing spears, both of which have unlimited ammunition, all of the other weapons are useable by both characters and their ammunition is monitored by a depleting ammo bar below your health bar that is replenished by the abundant ammo drops located on the map and from enemy drops.
The game tries to shake things up and keep the gameplay from feeling stale by adding various challenges for each level such as reach the end of the level by “X” amount of time, or blow up a certain number of random objects placed throughout the map. Completion of these challenges result in acquiring a unique perk or item that can be applied to your character to greatly aid you in your adventures.  An example of the most beneficial perk I came across during my adventures was a perk that became activated if I managed to chain together a large enough kill streak without being injured by any enemies, my gun would then switch over to rapid triple shot mode and allow me to plow through hordes of enemies like a true bonafide bad♥♥♥♥♥ The best part is that all the perks and items you acquire are useable on both characters, so you don’t have to worry about your partner hording the juicy loot.
Overall Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light provides an excellent experience that becomes even that much more enjoyable when played with a friend in co-op. The fast paced action combat is thrilling and there is an abundance of quality puzzles that keeps you engaged and entertained. With the only complaint being minor control issues for player 2, the Guardian of Light is truly a game worth buying and enjoying alongside a friend.

Can you say 'underrated?'
Yea, you'd better believe it, Far Cry 2 is the best title in the series, for me. Perfect? No, but neither is the rest of the series. Totally satisfying? No, but neither is the rest of the series. Dropping with atmosphere like the knifed fresh corpse of a wilderbeast drips that essential red elixir? You
believe it. And this is a quality that evades the rest of the series entirely.
You are [I can't remember I've played too many similar games], a face into which a video game camera has been thrust, itself belonging to a body which has been thrust right into the meatgrinder of a central african (I wanna say 'kinda Kenya but more sandy' though this may be entirely incorrect) civil war, complete with savage flora, savage fauna and savage hearts. You begin the game staring wonderously at the bump map'd face of a taxi driver as he drives you deeper and deeper into a threatening looking square of hell - dissapointingly scaled to accomodate the xbox 360 I believe, but certainly impactful - where he drops at a hotel. You get out, get to your room, get to bed and wake up with infected with Malaria and dodging bullets as fighting has broken out in the town.
You escape. You have no idea where you are. The landscape is alien and scary, the locals seem more like human big cats with AKs and a thirst for blood than video game villains, the roars of labouring car engines spark off immediate "
" sprints for cover, trees flex in the breeze, bushes rustle, a hot sun beats down on you like a express post migraine, and you eventually make it to a safe house where a bunch of uncaring locals welcome you to their collective deathwarrant and start giving you orders. You net some pills for the Malaria - things which will always stick with you and occasionally give you cause to run errands for the missionaries who supply them - and a rusty assault rifle and you're loose - free to do what you will, if you dare.
The quality of this game is in the oppressive environment which has been really wonderfull captured. Occasional townships light up real nice in dusty battles, blood diamonds litter the map in padded suitcases, militia held checkpoints stare down at you from every hilltop or intersection.
Difficult, yes. Challenging, yes. But inaccesible? No. The completionist in me loved this game - finding diamonds is just so easy, though finding them all would be a very lengthy mission indeed. Discovering every portion of the map, likewise a treat in itself. Ticking off enemy base camps and noting down the location of weapons stashes for future reference, all of these tasks are seamless and require one to go out of one's way only very rarely. The sandbox gameplay is so dense and rewarding infact that the campaign is almost a saddle on it - a key final mission of the opening zone became markedly less imposing for me when I realized that it was set in a clifftop fortress which I had comprehensively massacred on my first day in country.
Complete that story, those missions, though, because they will eventually open up new areas for you to explore, new people for you to meet (interactable characters are rare but convincing) and new atmosphere to soak up.
This game is a simulator, a simulator of that gritty, horrifying mode of hot Central African civil war that movies like Blood Diamond and co just about hinted at. It is not the best game ever made, and it is no the best game available on these pages, but it is a good one, and I would recommend it ahead of the next two games in the series. Or the third one at least, which completely failed to live up to the achievements of this title.

Let me start off this review by saying, that the game currently has very little to offer in terms of gameplay if you are not much of a creative person, but if you are, then be prepared to a big grind fest early on in the game until you get the ability to construct auto miners, after that prepare yourself to the next gameplay phase - driving simulator, because resources are scattered across multiple biomes and while driving at max speed from 30-50kmph, it takes a while to get you around the map.
The graphics aren't that great to be honest and most people with high end computers can't even run the game at medium to max settings. The player built and derelict found structures (same building blocks) look very bland. The material textures feel like they are made out of plastic and all player built things look very fake and lego-like.
Wildlife in this game is pathetic, AI is horrible. You have only a handful of species on the planet and they all spawn near their "nests". Each nest has its own unique model and spawns 1 specific creature type. They don't sleep at night, they don't attack each other, they just wander around near their nests and "guard" it.
One of the most annoying creatures is the gorilla like creature, that once aggroed starts to rush in on you and throw boulders at you. The problem with this creature is that you get hit by the boulder no matter if it actually hits you or not. Even if you are in the vicinity of the boulder impact 2+ meters away, you still get hit and it's almost impossible to avoid the boulders, when they start throwing them at you.
From the surface the physics look alright, but when you start to dive in and make some more complicated builds, you start to notice the imperfections of its implementation. Suspensions, hinges, rotating blocks feel very rubbery and the connections don't feel solid between moving parts and stationary parts of your builds. All the creations feel like lego and very toy like. The vehicles bounce a lot and the mass of them feels very off. They are too light and bouncy. Wheel traction is too week and your vehicle is all over the place when you try to climb a hill or drive on uneven terrain.
Worst part of physics is when you collide with your vehicles and creatures, where creatures can and might send your vehicle into the air, flip it over or do all kinds of crazy shenanigans. As said before, I don't feel the mass of the vehicle while driving, it's too toy like, artificial and fake.
There is no water dynamics in the game. Water sits at a certain map height and once you dig deep enough you will encounter water across the whole planet, therefore underground bases can only be made in mountains. Water doesn't have any flow mechanics or anything like that, it's basically static.
You have quite a wide variety of basic primitive blocks and prefabs, that you can use to create your buildings, vehicles and other objects, such as floating bases on water. In the current version of the game being reviewed there is no option to build flying vehicles without exploiting wheel physics and using wheels to propel contraptions into the air by making wheels friction against the vehicles itself (google up on youtube, plenty of videos about this).
Also game has issues regarding complicated things. I've experienced a few times, when reloading a save game, discovering that my vehicles, when parked next to my base, just vanished and couldn't be found anywhere.
One of the games selling point entering early access on Steam and on Kickstarter was that the game eventually will feature multiplayer. Recently in 2017 the developers changed their minds and there will be no co-op or multiplayer for this game. It was the main reason why I bought this game, to check it out and if its good, share it with my friends so that we could play it together when multiplayer would be released, sadly it will never happen.
I did have some really high hopes for this game to succeed and was hoping that it might challenge similar games like Planet Explorers, Empyrion: Galactic Survival or Space Engineers, but nope. Without any form of co-op/multiplayer play I don't see this happening.
As one reviewer said, it might have been a marketing strategy, because if they would have launched into early access as a single player game without any multiplayer options, it's doubtful that it would have as much attention, because currently what you get in early access isn't that much.
I am fully aware on how early access works and I also am aware how early access can be done the proper way. Take for example The Fun Pimps, makers of 7 days to die. They didn't abandon features, that were announced in their kickstarter of the game. Ideas got shifted here and there during the early access period, but the always stood by what were the main kickstarter goals, most of which are already fulfilled.
The only excuses from the developers regarding this issue was that it would take them too long and it would be hard.
Game feels very grindy once you get the grasp of most of the game features and have managed to unlock all there is to unlock, survival aspect end game is a non issue and you barely worry about food or water, because you can replenish that by just sleeping in the stasis pod.
That said about single player, if we want video games to be better in the future, it's important to not let developers take our money and do whatever they want, but let us vote with our wallet. When I bought the game, it was supposed to have multiplayer eventually, so that the grind wouldn't feel that grindy, because it's always more fun to do stuff together with someone unless you are the kind of a person, that really wants to be just by themselves all the time.

[Early Access Review]  Fantastic gameplay experience.
I've played many similar games all reaching for that certain "something" about solo exploration of an alien planet.  All of them have their strengths and weaknesses, but ultimately leave me still wanting more.
Planet Nomads has succeeded in hitting that sweet spot for me.  It's very light on the combat, heavier on the survival.  But it's not a terror-fest the whole time.  There are long periods of peace, calm and building.  You can build up bases, of course, but in this game the key vehicle is a rover.  Finally, this game moves away from hovercraft and small space ships.  Rovers are a blast!
Survival mode is tough but not too much so.  The game is really in it for the long haul.  Yes, eventually you may exhaust the resources in your immediate area, so you can pack up materials and drive someplace else.  Hence "Planet Nomads."
There are some subdued story elements here and there... traces of other, similar shipwrecked crew, abandoned bases...you'll find them.  They add to the feel of the game without forcing the direction of gameplay.
Also, amusingly, there are occasional (actually rare) physics glitches that can make things more fun, in a Kerbal Space Program kind of way.
In summary:  Just what I've always wanted.  Most fun I've had gaming in years.  Here's hoping they stay on this path while they strive for their 1.0 release.

Gamers take on the role of an astronaut who has crash-landed on a strange extraterrestrial planet far from home. You must survive by building your own shelters, vehicles and other equipment by using your various skills and talents.
The gameplay is centered around the exploration of the planet and the multiple biomes located across its surface. However, surviving isn't easy, and players must test their instincts against the planet's alien wildlife, extreme weather and deadly radiation.
Making your way across the procedurally generated, voxel-based world, players will find new challenges and species to explore. Upon crashing, gamers soon start to wonder how they will survive and what will happen to them. The different biomes on each planet offers new opportunities and downfalls for gamers to figure out. Your main objectives are to eat, drink and rest. With each new day comes new challenges, and learning the basics like how to craft a shelter or life-saving antidotes, will determine rather you survive the day or not.
Using your XJB-600 particle-manipulating Multi-Tool, players can mine resources and cut down trees to build the necessities they need. You can also craft vehicles to make it easier to explore and build a greenhouse for a steady source of food. No matter how you decide to craft your adventure, it is up to you on how you will journey across the forbidden planet. In the end, Planet Nomads is a fun adventure where crafting your survival is key.

Planet Nomads hits a lot of my buttons right off, and in the best way.  The survival needs make sense and resource gathering is enjoyable.  Once you get a few mining machines set up building becomes something you can enjoy fully without losing half an evening searching for minerals.  Although the machine gathering rate is a bit excessive but I expect this to get tuned down some after alpha.
The world you land on is absolutely stunning with a good if basic variety of flora and fauna.  I'm looking forward to more variety in the future.  Birds and fish especially.
Vehicle and base building are smooth and fun with a few exceptions:  block linking could use some work as it's a bit particular.  There needs to be a intermediate power source for hover vehicles since the nuclear generator is required but very heavy and leads to having your ride flip over being a common problem.
Exploring is fun. Plenty of variation in biomes and the changes in scenery due to heading north or south feel very natural.  There are a lot of little touches that remind me of Star Wars Galaxies  (without the xp grind) which for me is a big plus.
The developers are very responsive to the community including bug reports and weekly updates.
Can't wait to see what the future holds for Planet Nomads.
One last thing: This title is not yet optimised.  The roadmap indicates plans to do an optimization pass towards November so I hope they come through on that.  Otherwise, even if you meet the recommending requirements don't expect constant 60fps.  More like average 30ish with some skips and short freezes and a bit of render lag.  This should get better after the opt. pass.
Great game so far and truly worth the entry fee.  If you love survival and sci-fi you'll enjoy Planet Nomads.

It costs 10 euros but really it costs 19euros (which still isn't a lot) because it's hard not to buy the expansion and the six additionnal decks, all the more so as the expansion is included in the interface of the game and simply not available when not bought and as the ten decks of the normal version are only unicolored decks.
Anyway, it's a real pleasure to play through the different modes available and to unlock the cards of the numerous decks (you shouldn't forget to go get the 10 bonus cards for the ten normal decks). Planeswalkers, 2vs2 or free-for-all modes are particularly nice. And again unlocking overpowered cards and trying to understand the numerous playstyle is quite enjoyable.
I was annoyed by some details though, like the loading times which are long for a game of that type. It seems quite irrelevent at first but tend to get annoying really. The interface of the different menus is horrible. Going through the cards that compose your decks and adding some or removing some is a pain.
The sounds are ok, but some of them are a bit annoying and as you hear them constantly it can become very tiring.
And last but not least, mana flood and mana starvation are intolerably frequent ! It's just as if your player didn't know how to shuffle his library. Of course, things shouldn't go perfectly each time, but truly, we are really near to "If you keep a hand with only one land, it means you're going to have a game with very few lands" and "if you accept a hand with five lands, well, you're going to draw a lot of lands just after that" I've lost too many games because of land starvation or flood and it is all the more annoying when your opponents never seem to encounter these problems.
Also very strangely, the game seems to always forget the last card you've unlocked before quitting which makes every first game you play useless from that point of view as it unlocks the last card you had unlocked the previous time you played. It's VERY annoying as winning 40 times with a deck to unlock all its cards is already A LOT.
Anyway, I totally recommand the game. It's really enjoyable on the whole. I might even buy the 2012 edition or 2014 once I've unlocked all the cards of that one.

Despite the market being saturated, I love strategic card games. I play every single one of them, albeit sometimes only for a few hours. 50 hours in and I’m still playing Elder Scrolls: Legends. However, I do feel that there’s an almost arbitrary choice between a lot of the new generation CCGs and a lot of it may come down to personal preference based heavily on the lore of the universe and your connection to it.
I have a deep love for the Elder Scrolls universe, so I immediately liked the dark magic / fantasy setting and appreciate the gritty characters and graphics more so than the cartoonized CCGs. I enjoy the lane mechanic, which can really spice things up (usually in crazy PvE) fights and bring something new to the game. Talking of PvE, this game has it in great abundance, and the only real money I've spent so far has been on the Brotherhood campaign which I thoroughly enjoyed. I spend a lot of time in the PvE arena and I think it's a great way to farm vs the AI and an effective gold spender for getting more than a pack worth of rewards.
The runes and prophecy mechanic (you draw a card when you lose a rune at 5 health down and if that card is a prophecy, you play it for free) gives some scope for a comeback. This means even if you think you're dead next turn, a well timed prophecy draw can result in a turn around. It adds an extra element to deck building, too.
The game doesn't feel grindy - a combination of flexible quests that are fun to complete, Twitch drops and generous rewards for both PvE and PvP doesn't make me feel like I'm falling behind on cards or that I need to spend real money to have a good time.
Finally, it's a good package. An intuitive, sleek UI, beautiful graphics, easy mechanics with some unique features, customizable profiles and titles, short matches and an array of content all add up to a good package. Not a genre defining one, not that innovative perhaps, but fun enough to have drawn me in for 50 hours and hopefully many more in the future.

I have spent many hours playing this game and I have tried really hard to like it. I used to play Magic the Gathering competitively and am generally fond of card games that require planning and strategy. Elder Scrolls Legends is not well designed or well balanced. There are a few big creatures and cards that have mechanics that are heads and shoulders above everything else without any real counters to it. A quick glance at the top decks in the meta all share basically the same strategy, stall and slow the game down (either with prophecy cards, board clearers, shackle or guards) before playing big creatures. Simply put, there is no real aggro or combo in the game.
To new players in this game, the first 100 hours or so will be spent collecting cards that are "viable" in the meta. At the time of this review, that will be a lot of blue cards, and a few other colors. After that, the player will likely start entering into tournaments with prizes centered around getting more cards to build other decks.
But here's the thing, the top meta decks play so similiarly right now that there is often no real point in building others. A few cards are simply overpowered. It doesn't matter if it's blue/green, blue/white, blue/ purple or purple/green. The meta decks all play the same and it is boring.
The Interface of the program is fine, but the card design, balance and strategic depth is not. It is one reason why I suspect the wait times for matches has gotten longer and popularity poor despite the fact that Elder Scrolls is a big franchise. Please fix the mechanics of the game so there is actual balance between the colors and create variety in the meta so that each game doesn't desolve into stall until 8 or 9 mana, play big creatures, win.

Also, the enemies are quite interesting anf bursting with personality when facing them. Although the pixel art can be somewhat overdone nowadays it does have it's own style and flair with it's interesting colors. And I cannot forget when climbing these mountains you literally have this sense of urgency to NOT look down.. I literally felt like I was on top of a mountain and was about to fall off of it and funny how it's just a simple 2D game. This game is truly a masterpiece and needs more love than it currently deserves. Only thing I ask for is daily runs or something this is a very addicting game and probably better than Spelunky in some ways. I recommend this as a buy if you're an indie game enthusiast.

||| My experience with the game:
One of the best roguelites I've played to date. I entered into the beta long before this game had a steam release, and being inexperienced with difficult platformers at the time, I was unable to make any real progress through the first chapter (the only 'finished' part of the game at that point). The game managed to keep me going despite my failures, as each death felt fair to me and reminded me that I just needed to get better. Eventually I put the game down, not out of frustration, but out of anticipation for its full release and the day I'd be able to come back with a little more skill. When I heard this game got a steam release, I was beyond excited. While waiting for my steam key from the devs, I dived into the game once more to prepare myself for the new hazards the game would throw at me. After many losses, I finally did it. I beat chapter 1 and finished the beta. I was dumb and thought that meant I had a pretty good handle on how to play the game.
Then I got my full copy and got to play Chapter 2. It makes Chapter 1 look like a big tutorial.
My god, the game is so much harder on Chpt. 2. You have to plan every movement you make and know how to move quickly yet carefully. Every new area I reached made me ecstatic. It was such a rewarding experience to triumph over a stage that looked unbeatable before. As long as I've played this game (probably quadruple my time on steam) I have not beat this game as of the time I write this review, but I've gotten very close. And I won't stop until I do.
||| Opinion of the game:
This game is a ton of fun and a fantastic example of a platformer roguelike. As it stands right now, it's got a ton of content, challenge, and replayability. With many items to find and manage and a new crafting system, there's a lot of incentive to explore the stage a bit and maybe even risk your hide to open that chest that lava is about to overtake. Even for those who beat Chpt. 1 + 2 (Considered the story), there's the centurial trials, 100 floors of mixed and matched biomes and enemies to provide an extreme challenge for those who are looking for it. This being said, the game DID and STILL DOES have some issues that need to be ironed out. The options menu, while previously non-existent, is still a little lacking. It provides basic resolution options & fullscreen, splitscreen toggle for multiplayer, a fast scaling toggle, toggles for shaders and an ugly (IMO) filter that's on by default, as well as a controls menu. I can't find any sort of options for audio, which is fairly annoying considering how simple it would probably be to add them. It's still not a huge deal given you can just use your audio mixer.
The controls are also something to get used to. A lot of people will prefer controller to keyboard with how many binds the keyboard demands you use (and most of the time, very quickly) but until the most recent patch, the d-pad on the controller didn't really work with the game. That's been fixed, though. Still, be aware that the controls will probably be harsh to you for a short while, but they're far from unusable.
The visuals are going to probably turn a lot of people off of playing the game, and I wouldn't say that's entirely unfair. Most of the pixel art is extremely low res, your character being about 30 pixels total. Some people are going to find the graphics pretty appealing for low-res pixel art, it's really all down to your preferences. The shaders and particle visuals are pretty as well.
The game is extremely difficult, but the game is very much fair and does a good job of making you feel like everything that went wrong with your climb was your fault or preventable. RNG not playing a huge factor means your experience and skill that you develop while playing will stick with you and are the main factor in deciding the distance you climb. RNG only really comes into play when you reach chapter 2.

A tough as nails but surprisingly fair and rewarding platformer that expects you to plan & execute your moves carefully.

This game can be difficult to pick up at first, as it's complex stat/skill system can be a little overwhelming, especially if you don't know what you're doing. But overall, once you get used to things, this game is extremely enjoyable. (Assuming the outdated graphics don't bother you)
The class system is pretty extensive, several to chose from, with the ability to multi class in addition to that. Luckily there are a few hybrid classes to begin with (Lord and Samurai for example) so you may not have to multiclass to get the build you want. The combat in slow but satisfying, with enemies exploding as you defeat them.
Leveling get's pretty slow as you go along but the skills you have develop as you use them (Sword skill increases as you attack with a sword, Wizardry skill increases as you cast spells, etc.) and how fast they increase is dependent on your stats. (Sword skill is dependent on Strength and Dexterity, magic element skills are dependent on Intelligence/Piety etc.) This system of skills increasing is one thing that makes this game unique and makes very slow leveling much, much, more bearable.

The thing that really makes this game unique is the magic system. Your casters don't have just one magic meter, they have a magic meter for each and every element, and the amount of magic they each have is mostly dependent on your caster's skill level with magic (other factors being character level, piety stat, etc.). Normally I prefer hybrids over pure casters but this game's magic system makes classes that only cast spells appear much more appealing.
You get a good amount of character portraits and voices mix and match to create characters that are just right for you. Plus you can change them at any time so if one voice or portrait get's tedious you can always try a new one without having to reset the character completely. (The only thing you can't change is the character's gender)
NPC interaction is also extensive, to the point where it's kind of tedious, and you can even recruit a few NPCs into your party, and develop them the same way you would develop your own characters.

Speaking of development, the way you can develop your characters any way you want in terms of stats and skills, which you can increase as you level, is what makes this game really great. (Though it can be very unforgiving if you develop them poorly)
However, the game can be very unforgiving as well. Unlike most RPGs, monsters get stronger as time goes by so if you start struggling with tough monsters you can't go back to fight weaker monsters as those monsters will be stronger as well. The complexity of stats and skills is great, but it may be to the point where you need to look up a walkthrough on how to build your characters before you can even make a party that doesn't get killed easily.

Overall, this is an amazing game, if you can handle the complexity and the outdated graphics and difficult gameplay.
Pros:
+ Character development is deep, especially for a party-based RPG
+Open world gameplay gives you several story choices, even if you aren't aware of them.
+Graphics are outdated but are still pretty well-made
+Did I mention deep character development?
Cons:
- Very difficult and unforgiving, even on Novice difficulty
- May require a character building guide
- Several things in this game may slip by you without a walkthrough
- Combat is slow, with encounters lasting an average of 5-10 minutes (Some are faster, some are slower)
