Disclaimer: At the time of this writing I am 6 hours into the game; this review is written from a very nub perspective.
My first impression of this game from the trailers was, "This could be what a Mechwarrior/Battletech MMO could have been..."  Well, it turns out, not exactly; while the game view is notably more like Mech Commander than anything else I've played, the rest of the game play is very reminiscent of EVE, complete with things that sound hard to do, until you do them.  Once.  That's all it takes.
The tutorial is very detailed (and for good reason) but moves quickly as you go step-by-step through learning the interface, which is largely accessible by visible buttons on the UI.  The mech bay view (where you get your missions, store your unused-but-not-sold items, store materials you will eventually sell/use for crafting, research, skillgain, buy/sell, and configure your mechs [called robots in the game, since your pilot is remote rather than within]) is fairly easy to adapt to, and is one of the reasons I mention EVE.  Cargo is nearly identical in terms of access, repairs, movement between bays, and unit configuration, and market access and use it all but the same as I recall it (from about 4 years ago), but skill gains are different, almost opposite.  Where in EVE you would select a skill and a timer would start and count down to completion of study, this game accrues skill points daily at a set rate (which can be increased with ingame functions); when you login you get your allotment of points, then for the next 2 days you gain points again, whether you login or not.  If you don't login after the third day though your skillpoint gain stops, and will begin again when you login next.  Said points are then spent for an immediate gain of a skill on a scale from 1-10, with difficulty/complexity ratings that modify skill gain (again, same as EVE did) to cost more points the more complex the skill is rated.
Combat is fairly straightforward.  The one thing that I do not like is that there seems to be no 'shooting from the hip' at all, ever; you wait until your guns lock on, even if you're at point blank range, then engage them and they fire on a timer, automatically quitting when the primary target is out of range or destroyed.
You can loot containers while fighting.  You can lock several targets at once, provided they are in range of your gear/skill.  You can reload guns in combat.
There are non-combat focused missions as well as combat missions, and you can toggle PVP on/off.
In base areas there are tiles placed to speed movement; very helpful.
The chat community seems friendly so far, and is knowledgeable and helpful when asked clear questions.
Completing the tutorial was an area of boredom, until I realized that I actually did need to know 'all this crap.'  DO the tutorials, but don't stick around trying to farm easy loot from drones, or using your materials to gain research, or anything else; you all but full reset once you join the real world via choosing a faction.
That's LONG, and don't be in doubt, it can be done much faster, but use this time to learn the game as far as you can, given no true baptism by fire.
This is a serious game for serious gamers, but can be enjoyed by teens on up to graybeards.  There is some number crunching, and I have yet to PVP, but so far... so good.
Bottom line: I reckon I can get a couple hundred hours out of this game in its current state.
8/10 would buy game on sale again.  For the time I expect to put in, paying full price would still be a good deal.

I've been itching to get into this game for quite some time. but there were two major issues at that time:
1. Price: 30$ may not seem like alot. but it's alot when the reported playerbase is quite small. no one wants to pay 30$ to test the waters and find a dead world.
2. Playerbase: the reported levels of activity have been low. really low.
After the Winter sale, Perpetuum went through a price restucture. NOT a price drop, a restructure. if you pay 30$ now, you will get the same starting bonuses, premium currency, as would have before. but now the barrier of entry is much lower. want to get into a game as deep as Eve online mechanically, but aren't too sure about it? getting in is a mere 10$ usd, plenty low for me to jump in and check things out.
I'm an old eve player, so there is some bias there. if you've never played eve, then BOY OH BOY LEARNING CURVE OF DEATH.
If you have played eve, but left due to the pricey subscription, and was annoyed with the skill system, then this game is for you. the user interface is a carbon copy. down to the market system, character profiles, man even character creation looks like pre 2011 eve online.  that may not be for everyone, it's a little more noob friendly than eve, but the nostalgia factor is strong. the gameplay, and combat system is pretty much exxactly eve online.
But neo! these aren't space ships! how can they be so similar?
you target enemies the same way.
you cycle weapons (and reload them), the same way.
you loot the same sorts of things.
you use the same module systems, power grids, power management.
this game is essentially mechwarrior and eve had a secret affair and this is the result. you may hate it for the learning curve and pace of gameplay. or you may absolutely LOVE IT TO DEATH for it's deep, intricate gameplay mechanics.
it's as deep and rewardingly intelligent as EVE online. It's also just as brutal, can be just as tedious, and just as fustrating.
if you left EVE online for good, but reminisce about old friendships, corporate antics, political upheavals, and personal stories, then you NEED to give Perpetuum a chance. it feels just like home, at a fraction of the price.
the only major flaw is the size of the playerbase, and that's both the fault of the gaming community at large, and lack of advertisement by the developers.
for players who don't even know what EVE online is; this game has an hour long tutorial, and you'll need to absorb every last bit of it. skip it and you WILL have a bad experience. this game is not for casual players, but it can casual be at times if you want it to be. it's a very, VERY deeply crafted system with industrial mechanics, mining, marketing (at a low point atm only because the player base is small), and excellent pvp.
If you don't want to risk 10 USD to give the game a try, then watch plenty of videos on starting out on EVE online. it may look totally different, but all the core mechanics and ingame menu's, as well as ship equipment systems are identical. if you don't see yourself playing eve online, then this isn't probably for you. if you're interested in EVE online but balk at the price tag, give this baby a try, and you'll know whether you'll like eve online.
FINAL SCORE (scored higher due to personal bias and experience in EVE online):

assuming playerbase doubles or triples, or amount of players a non issue:  9/10 Old eve farts welcome any time.

Even though I only have 25 hours of play time so far in Perpetuum, I can say it feels like the game I have been looking for for a long time. It has it all, pvp, pve, crafting, a player controlled market, a very good community feel, and a wonderful look to the graphics. If you have played EVE you will get a feel for how this game works straight away, but being a bittervet is NOT a requirement to enjoy Perpetuum! There is crafting, a deep and complex system I have not even scratched the surface of, and resource gathering is interactive and absorbing. The combat is also something I am only just getting into - I have been focussing so far on gathering - but it feels and looks rewarding and fun. The "levelling" here is aka EVE too, you assign points to "Extensions" to boost various attributes or parts of your robot (did I say you are a consciousness controlling a robot via a miniature wormhole? Very cool premise to this game!), but in this game you accrue Extension Points daily, and assign as you want. This is a pvp sandbox, so combat in certain zones is inevitable if not mandatory, but I am looking forward to it:) This game has a lot of similarities to EVE, but it is not EVE, it is it's only animal and stands apart from its more well known Icelandic relative. The dev team here seem friendly, and the small but dedicated fan base certainly are friendly and helpful. You do not need to buy the upgrades, but it will give you a leg up in terms of EPs, however due to the nature of EP accrual, new players will catch up with veterans soon enough. This is a game where the long view of things is needed, but honestly that is a good thing in this day of "rush to the end game and move on" gaming. I really do urge you to get this game - B2P and worth it even if you miss one of the frequent sales. Hope to see you soon on Nia!

For fans of Elder Scrolls and card battle games, Elder Scrolls: Legends is a
!  Even if you don't play Elder Scrolls but love card battle games, you'll love this. I don't play World of Warcraft but I still enjoy Hearthstone. This game has similarities and influences of
and
but it doesn't play exactly like either one.  It does follow one common rule: attack the enemy until their health runs out.  Similar to Magic and Hearthstone, ESL seems to have more RPG elements.  It's a card game but truly feels like a RPG at the same time.  Depending on the character you select may have an effect on your cards, you can level up, earn new name titles, daily quests, a nice story mode with cut scenes, and sometimes there might be a set of extra rules for the match.  ESL uses the characters, lore and vocals you're familiar with in the Elder Scrolls games.
Now for the part I'm sure some of you are wondering.  Is it a money hog?  So far, I think no. Keep in mind it is a FREE game and free games need income. I've found that the card pricing is very similar to Hearthstone except ESL has more options for buying cards with gold.  Naturally the most dedicated players will buy cards like crazy but the game gives you tons of cards at the beginning and as you play through the story.  Also, if you've already got a Bethesda account the game gives you extra free card packs.  The game is very enjoyable without buying cards with real money.  You can earn gold in the game to buy cards too.  If you're more of a casual gamer with games like these you'll still have fun.
The verdict: Is it better than Hearthstone or Magic? In all honesty this will come down to preference. It's like comparing Poker, Texas Hold 'Em, and Rummy.  At the end of the day it's still a card game.  My
is that ESL is better than the other two.  That's because I'm an Elder Scrolls fan and I love how this game is developed.  It's a very well made game and I encourage you to try it.

A massive, dense series of time, score, and other challenges, utilizing the classic mechanics of Pac-Man, coupled with exponentially greater speed, route selection emphasis, a few gameplay tweaks, and much higher enemy count for racking up huge score combos.
Anyone who loves Pac-Man, but is looking to have their skills tested to the utmost.
Anyone who loves Pac-Man, but always wanted a faster, more intense experience.
Anyone who loves fast paced, twitch-heavy action that increases in speed and challenge the better you perform.
Anyone who doesn't mind repetition of a basic premise, honed to the nth degree.
Anyone who dislikes the basic mechanical design of Pac-Man, naturally.
Anyone who wants the classic Pac-Man experience (that is not to be found here.)
Anyone who wants great variety in gameplay or map design.
Anyone who tires of repetition and skill drills.
Anyone who can't enjoy the simple impetus of "can I beat my best score/time?" and demands more payoff than that.
If you've played Pac-Man - and if you're a gamer at all interested in the history of this industry, it's unconscionable if you haven't... go and find an actual cabinet somewhere in your town and play it before coming back to this - then you know that at higher scores/levels, the game can get pretty frenetic and intense.
Championship Edition DX+ takes those high level Pac-Man dynamics to their absolute extreme. It needs to be made clear: this is not the classic Pac-Man in a new graphical package with some optional modes. This is an entirely different, highly specialized Pac-Man experience, dedicated to speed, score, and precision.
The game consists of progressively challenging score attacks and time trials, challenging players to find the fastest and most efficient route to achieving specific goals. Goals include eating as many ghosts as possible, eating a certain number of fruits within a time limit, or simply surviving for a set amount of time as the game's speed ramps up with each ghost eaten and each dot sequence completed.
To that end, eschewing the classic Pac-Man design and instead amplifying it, the number of ghosts and the rate at which the game pace intensifies and escalates, have been increased dramatically. You are given a limited number of bombs as emergency countermeasures when in a particularly sticky spot, and eventually the pace becomes so frantic that only the most skilled players will be able to change direction quickly enough to follow the ideal paths for score and enemy avoidance (or consumption.)
There are a number of unlockable maps, each with its own specific challenges. As you complete challenges, more maps and likewise more challenges (including in maps you've already unlocked) appear. The result is what feels like an endless (though, there is a finite number) of time and score trials, each forcing you to master the given map and advance your skills accordingly.
There are a number of different visual styles available both for Pac-Man and his enemies, and for the maps themselves, which can be freely mixed and matched. There is also a large DLC suite available for the game which adds yet more content.
Familiar Pac-Man fun anyone can pick up and play.
Skill ceiling that goes extremely high for those who want it to.
Clever map designs that force forethought and quick reflexes.
Extremely gratifying, cathartic, and viscerally pleasing to chow down on endless rows of ghosts
Plenty of visual customization (for a Pac-Man game,) and a fun mix of classic game inspired contemporary jams to listen to while you chomp.
Leaderboards, achievements, and medals for those who want them.
Facebook integration for those who want it. (I don't, but... options never hurt anyone.)
Leaderboards commonly dominated by cheats.
May feel highly repetitive to some players.
No classic arcade version mode (which may be especially disappointing given the barebones and problematic Pac-Man Museum port on PC.)
No option for strictly classic music mode, which would have been nice in my opinion.
Lots of visual customization options, but no way to save them so that every map automatically starts with your favorite settings (some maps default to their own style and must be changed every time manually.)
I owned this game for years on Xbox 360 before finally buying it for PC as well. If you love Pac-Man but are craving more challenge, speed, and intensity, this is definitely the game for you. It's a smörgåsbord of seemingly endless Pac-Man trials.
This is a game that can be played fairly casually if one wishes to do so, but if you want to climb the leaderboards (although on Steam, they are unfortunately dominated by hacks/cheats much of the time,) you will be forced to achieve a level of skill with Pac-Man that makes the game worthy of the "Championship" moniker.
In either extreme, and everything in between, the simple, elegant gameplay of Pac-Man is just as fun as ever, and reaches its arguable apotheosis here.

If you are reading this now and wondering if you should spend money on this game, please don't. For the whole duration of my playthrough I was either bored to death by the unnecessarily long drives and dull combat, or kept wondering how such a fundamentaly flawed game was released by a experienced company as Ubisoft.
The graphics are technically decent if compared to other games from when Far Cry 2 was released, but they did not age well. The map is huge but you can hardly tell any difference from the places you go apart from the 3 basic biomes (desert, savanna and jungle). Everything is bleached by a clear brown fog, even the jungles are a dull brownish color.  Almost every building on the map looks like it's part of a shanty town and the very few urban settings are minuscle and lame.
Sound is mostly mediocre, with a few very annoying sounds playing all the time like some metal banging from the regular cars, or a weird tire screeching sound that's played every other time you get shot (!). The few musics are unremarkable at best. The voice-over dialogues are terrible, the actors seem to have been rushed into reading their lines as fast as possible.
The story is terrible and almost non-existent, wasting an excelent opportunity to delve deep in such an important and completely overlooked theme that are the civil wars happening in Africa. The player character is despicable and so are almost everyone you get to interact with throughout the game and you suspension of disbelief is constantly broken by the lack of sense on the assignments given to your character. In a few moments the game seems to give options to the player, but soon after you learn that your choices mean nothing and the story follows it's pre defined path.
But the worst of all is the gameplay. 70% of the time spent playing Far Cry 2 involves driving, a few times even walking large distances devoid of anything but the infamous ever respawning enemy guard posts present at every other road crossing. The main missions are very repetitive and are limited to driving to a certain spot, killing someone/taking or giving an item/destroying something and then going somewhere else to repeat this pattern until the mission is completed. The side missions are utterly repetitive and often send you all the way across the map. And to add insult to injury, every now and then you need to drop everything you are doing to go fetch some malarial pills, which is probably one of the dumbest repeteable side quest ever on the history of videogames.
Bottom line is, if you have money to spend on a game, there are many other better options on Steam, so do yourself a favour and skip this one.

Far Cry 2 heavily expands the appealing, basic formula established in Far Cry 1. I would call it the first modern Far Cry game since most of the hallmark Far Cry features come into their own in this title. The core of a Far Cry/Crysis game is fast paced, streamlined, semi-realistic, immersive first person military shooter in large open environments where the player is free to explore multiple approaches (stealth, close range assault, sniping, explosives, vehicles, turrets, or any combination thereof) to overcoming enemies.
Far Cry 2 also introduces a large open-world, non-linear mission system with multiple factions, weapon and equipment unlocks, safe houses and buddy companion-system. The central african environments are breathtaking and the game takes great pains to immerse the player in the environment. The HUD is incredibly minimal with most actions and situations being context sensitive and told through actual interaction with the environment. For example, rather than healing being simply invisible (the health bar just refills), you'll see your character inject a syrette in his/her forearm, reset a broken limb, or pull a bullet from a gaping wound in their leg. The map just doesn't appear on the HUD, you actually pull a physical map and GPS out. When your character suffers the affects of malaria, you're vision will blur and turn green and you'll have to pull out a pill bottle and swallow a pill to counter-act the effects. All these things effectively serve to immerse the player in the world, but don't inhibit gameplay. The enemy AI is also very sophisticated and will communicate with one another, actively hunt for you and attempt to surround you (or where they think you are), or even get scared and take cover or run. My primary grievance is that random encounters when traveling can be a bit to frequent and bypassing frequent road blocks and guard posts can get to be a grinding chore in traveling around the map.
The mission system that unveils the story is fun and engrossing. The story is not just handed to you, but the player will have to really pay attention if they want to figure out what is really going on. The interplay of the factions, the player, and their buddies is fascinating and keeps the game fresh from start to finish. The side missions do get a bit redundant though, which include destroy arm shipments, and assassinations. Luckily, the core Far Cry gun play is solid and doesn't get old quickly. It is fun when a situation goes from you getting a jump on a bunch of enemies to reinforcements showing up and surrounding you as you run short on ammo and having to fight for your life to break the encirclement and make a run for it. Which brings me to the buddy system which is rich and unrivaled in any FPS/RPG that I have seen. The system is rather organic and you really seem to build a relationship and history with your buddies who are fellow mercenaries try to profit in this little civil war.
All in all, there are few games I can safely recommend as must plays for anyone, but this is definitely one of them.

I don't usually go for Early Access games as they vary in level of completion. However, I was intrigued by the building and exploration gameplay shown in the videos/screenshots with the beautiful alien environments (rather than dystopian crime-ridden cityscape). As of present, the game is still very much a work in progress but still fun to explore and build. There are plenty of expensive polished AAA games out there but all I can find it shooter, shooter shooter, COD clone, COD clone, which is not really to my taste (I'm bad at PVP).
Although there is some optional combat with dangerous animals in the game (or run away!), it's optional and only later on as the player starts with very little and has to gradually build their way up by searching for an harvesting raw materials to turn into composite materials which are turned into the final items using '3D printers'. Base-building is thus a major feature along with the possibility of making a mobile vehicle base to live, well, like a nomad.
As you construct machines, walls etc. you can unlock others which give you an interesting challenge. As with Minecraft, I like the freedom of choosing what to build and how to design it and hoping they will be adding a greater range of (are they called blocks?) to build with. As of recent, I built a medium size vehicle complete with it own stasis chamber (bed) and certain utility machines and have been exploring the procedurally-generated world looking for new biomes and rare materials whilst keeping an eye out for unexpected holes in the ground and obstacles. To a fair extent, it's very much a case of 'play your way'.
From a player perspective, the advantage of joining at this early point is that you may be able to influence and assist the future development of the game along with supporting it and there definitely feels like great potential.
Unfortunately, in my case I'm getting performance issues due to my limited computer hardware though the gameplay is attractive enough to keep me glued.

Don't be fooled by the name: this game is not an RPG. It is first and foremost a puzzle game. The title isn't misleading though: DROD has become synonymous with excellency in puzzle games, and RPG means it will appeal to every fan of min-maxing or theorycrafting one can usually find in RPGs.
This is a numbers game wrapped in a pleasant interface, an original soundtrack and a deep backstory sprinkled over all the DROD games. This game is story heavy for a puzzle game, but story light for an RPG: there is no complex story to read or numerous anecdotes and side-quests. The story elements are delivered through voice acting and will make you love Tendry for is panache !
The game is best enjoyed with at least two playthroughs. Saving often and backtracking is an inherent part of the gameplay. You have to strike a balance between going forth to gain knowledge of level layout and going back to better optimize your road.
The DROD series is user content friendly and DROD RPG is no exception: if you liked the game, you can get more !
I highly suggests you visit the official website caravelgames for additional content... including FREE games !

DROD RPG is basically a fancy version of the classic Magic Tower game.  It's a great thinking-man's RPG that revolves around resource management and route planning.  The player has to navigate various floors of dungeon environments in which color-coded keys needs to be obtained and used in an optimal fasion in order to reach the exit with the greatest amount of keys and HP remaining.   Along the way you can find various attack and defensive upgrades that will play a big role in how the games turn-based auto combat plays out.
The game rewards careful planning and good decision making because over the length of the game, bad decisions and poor management compounds into situations in later floors where the player could find themselves low on resources to push through.  The game is pretty lengthy for what it is and there are multiple endings, the harder of which will only be able to be obtained by those who really master optimizing their playthroughs.  As a fan of the Magic Tower type genre, I loved the games interpretation of this format and would recommend it, even if the voice acting is hilariously bad (so bad I can't tell if it was intentional).

[ I've played through the game when it was first released, back in 2008 ]
DROD RPG is a min/maxing puzzle dungeon crawler that focuses on decision making which enemies to kill, which items/keys to take and use and has a steady progresion in hero power that's really satisfying. You'll upgrade your weapon and shield and find items that take you to secret paths with lots of goodies. There's a lot of backtracking to scavenge for health potions, power ups and secrets but it doesn't feel tedious as the level design keeps that in mind and has a lot of shortcut paths or teleports.
Expect 20+ hours if it's your first playthrough. I struggled back than and got myself in situations where I couldn't progress without dieing to the next enemy. This may be frustrating for some, as it involves restarting the game and playing again with the new gained knowledge. Took me around 3 restarts till I got the hang of it, then you'll progress more wisely and in doing that the game will be much more enjoyable. It has this type of progression that I personally miss a lot in games, progression not only through the player character but through the knowledge of players. Think of games like Doom where you struggle if you ignore all secrets or games like Dark Souls. Knowledge is key and the game definately rewards this.
It's not for everyone, but Caravel Games is on of the last developers who releases more than 5 minute demos so you can really see for yourself if you like it.
I also want to mention how funny this game is sometimes. Tendry talks a lot and his quirky analogies and reactions are hilarious. The voice acting is not AAA but it's still good.

The DROD (Deadly Rooms of Death) series, a hidden gem long revered by discerning puzzle connoisseurs, finally makes its Steam debut with DROD RPG: Tendry's Tale, complete with Steam Cloud, Achievements and Leaderboards!
DROD RPG is quite different from the main DROD series, which will also appear on Steam (hopefully) very soon. DROD first appeared in 1996 and has been kept up, reworked, and extended by just a few talented, dedicated developers and an active player/modder community.
(NOTE: when I refer to DROD RPG as opposed to Tendry's Tale, I refer to the engine and imply the possibility of there being further official DROD RPG titles)
While there are many similarities, the core gameplay mechanic in DROD is solving individual "rooms", while DROD RPG is about optimizing choices throughout an entire run through the game. Both games are laid out as a set of floors consisting of interconnected rooms. Floors are connected by stairs. Generally it's possible to backtrack just about anywhere at any point in (each half of) the game.
Tendry's Tale has about 400 rooms total, including 40 secret ones. The game is split into two halves with independent stats/progression.
DROD RPG, like DROD is a turn-based game. The basic movement commands are the same as DROD - 8 directional movement, and sword rotation. DROD RPG borrows mechanics from the main series such as door orbs, trapdoors, and bombs. Many of the enemies and characters will also be familiar.
Unlike DROD, DROD RPG has stats: HP, ATK, DEF, GR (gold), and items - weapons, shields, usable accessories, and keys. Unlike DROD, enemies do not move in DROD RPG. Instead of combat being purely a question of who strikes first, combat plays out based on stats (yours and your enemy).
Thus, the optimization gameplay is making decisions about when to and when not to fight, use keys, pick up items and stat boosting powerups, and determining a good order to do these actions in (e.g. pick up power ups before engaging in fights to save HP).
But, to make smart decisions, you must first explore and learn the world. This means you will need to save and restore often, which the game openly encourages.
The game is easy to start but very difficult to complete, especially if going for the secret/true endings (though perhaps not as difficult as some other titles in the DROD series). Luckily, there is lots of spoiler-free tips from fellow players available on the community forums at
. Also, the second, harder half of the game has a secret option to make the game somewhat easier at the cost of scores and achievements. This might be a good choice for initial exploration.
The gameplay experience is further enhanced by an excellent soundtrack and an entertaining story that ties into the greater lore of the DROD world. It's absolutely not necessary to have played previous DROD games to appreciate Tendry's Tale, but it does help to understand some of the references.
If you finish the game and still want more, you can play the many community made "holds".
So, I highly recommend Tendry's Tale to puzzle enthusiasts (although I recommend the main DROD series even more highly!). I've bought most of the DROD games at their original full price of $20 with absolutely no regrets.

DROD RPG is a terrific and unique puzzle game revolves around the management of health, attack, keys, special one-use items, and more. Choices are obvious at first (fight a roach and take five damage or a wraith and take twenty? hmmm), but options widen with each new encounter and room, leading to a truly staggering number of choices and routes throughout the game. Each route has its advantages and disadvantage, but only a few will leave you with enough health to complete the final challenges and hardest bosses.
It can be frustrating in early stages as you learn the game's "language", that is to say the nature of tradeoffs from each decision and what it truly costs in terms of health or keys to pick up an item or leave it behind, but once you get into the swing of things it makes for an extremely intense and satisfying puzzle experience.
The base game is also split into two halves, with the first half serving partially as a tutorial but also having a completely distinct design style, resulting in both halves of the game being uniquely challenging. On top of this, there are many officially approved expansions freely available from the Caravel Games forums, some of which have even more sadistically precise challenges than the main campaign.

This is a game where you have to use your noggin' to make choices.
If you enjoy using judgement and logic to conserve resources effectively, this is a game you will enjoy.
If you enjoy optimizing mathematical puzzles under the veil of stat-based RPG, this is a game you will enjoy.
This game is like a grid based dungeon crawler, not totally unlike Desktop Dungeons (except not random at all), or Legend of Grimrock (except completely turn-based, with no reflexes required).  It's obvious inspiration is Tower of the Sorcerer.  You find stuff, stab baddies like goblins and evil brains with a big pointy sword,  get stronger, and try to make to the end alive.  It's brimming with secrets and you are generally rewarded for not acting rashly, despite the personality of the protagonist.
If you have heard of DROD before, be warned that this game is utterly unlike most entires into the DROD franchise.  It's a puzzle game of a different sort, but that's not a bad thing.  Less pure logic and more judicial logic.  It's a slow burner, but a good game, and it's pretty cheap for how long it'll take you to make it to the end alive.  Give it a shot!

As someone who's been playing DROD RPG outside of Steam for a few years now, I thought I'd describe exactly what playing this game is like and why I enjoy it. Please note that the gameplay is not like your typical RPG, nor is it all that similar to the other DROD games, although it is still a turn based game that requires a lot of thinking.
DROD RPG is a resource management optimisation game. The optimisation is not just about choosing what resources to spend, but WHEN to spend those resources to ensure you make the most out of them. Fighting monsters is automatic and costs you Hit Points based on your Attack and Defense stats, the higher they are, the less HP you lose. You also have keys and money that can open doors. There are also accessories with various additional effects, such as destroying walls, letting you jump over pits and doubling money gains.
The gameplay involves figuring out in what order to fight monsters, gain stats, kill bosses, collect resources and spend keys to ensure that you don't waste enough resources in the long-term that you're able to reach the end of the game without getting stuck in an unwinnable position. The game quite happily lets you get stuck, but you can (and should) save the game at any time because you will be restoring to previous saves quite a lot. This is by design, you're expected to do this.
There is zero randomness in the game. Fighting the same monster with the same stats will always produce the same result, and the level layouts never change. It's one big manually crafted puzzle.
Along the way you will reach numerous scorepoints that award you a score based on the resources you have. An important part of the appeal of the game is to try and maximise your scores to beat or match other people's scores on the leaderboard. There's a lot of replay value in this, as maximising a scorepoint early in the game will often require a different set of actions than if you're trying to maximise one in the late game. I personally find it a lot of fun to try and figure out e.g. how the person in the #1 spot on the leaderboard managed to beat me by 20 points, and it's an awesome feeling when you finally work it out.
The game has an easy to use level editor built-in to it, and there are a number of level sets available for download from the offical forums if you're looking for more. There's a huge amount of content available at a range of difficulty levels to sink your teeth into if you enjoy the game. The offical level set, Tendry's Tale, is split into two entirely separate halves, and the second half is quite difficult.
Ultimately DROD RPG is a game that you'll either love or you'll hate but you should definitely give it a try. The game will allow you to get a lot out of it if you're willing to invest the time in it, and is a pretty unique experience. I really enjoy it myself and it's kept me consistently entertained for an enormous amount of time.

Even though this is a spin-off and not a main Tomb Raider entry, this game is pretty Tomb Raider-tastic.
Lara hunts down an artifact no one should wield and sets off apocalyptic events that only she can stop? YEP.
Plenty of shooting of natural and supernatural enemies in well-paced fight encounters? YEP.
Lots and lots of booby traps to avoid, disarm, or survive? YEP.
Puzzles that usually involve timing, platforming and typical Lara acrobatics? YEP.
Smartass one-liners and quips from Lara almost everytime she opens her mouth? Yep.
Well-placed and often hidden collectibles? Yep.
MANY, MANY GUNS? YEP.
Tomb raiding? You bet!
The controls are snappy and responsive, the puzzles and platforming are very satisfying, and ultimately pretty much everything about the gameplay is rewarding in some way. Every level has a handful of optional objectives you can try to complete for even more rewards -- such as artifacts or relics that boost your stats or combat ability in various ways. The game's visuals and audio both are actually a hell of a lot better than I expected, and I often found myself gleefully looking around to admire the level design or dancing around a boss in time with the boss stage's music.
Bonus: You can play this with a friend, and the game even redesigns much of the levels' puzzles to accomodate 2 players. The second player character, Totec, CANNOT be played on his own, i.e. if you're playing on your own, Lara is your only option. But, well, she's the far cooler option anyway. :P
A tip: Use a controller. The game only fully recognizes Xbox 360 type controllers but you can very easily fool it into accepting others by using a controller emulator (x360ce). Mouse and keyboard controls have much more precise aiming for shooting, but I found they just were too clunky for me for -everything- else.

After seeing many reviews praising Viva Kebabs, I thought it would be best to try a HSP from there for myself so here's my review. (I got a lamb HSP with cheese and the holy trinity)
Signage: 10/10. The Halal certification was on the front of the store. A bit small but noticeable enough. There were neon lights on the side which were still fairly noticeable during the day.
Greeting: 10/10. As usual, Viva Kebabs is pretty busy but the guys there are nice. Don't remember the exact words but I remember hearing 'brother' which is always welcoming.
Packaging: Styro/10.
Chips: 10/10. They were cooked fresh, nice and crispy with a slight crunch. Defs worth the wait.
Sauce: 10/10. The amount of sauce was very generous, some even dripped onto the floor. I forgot what other sauce went on the holy trinity besides barbecue and garlic (Blanked out lmao) but the guy knew what I wanted straight away.
Cheese: 10/10. A good amount of cheese that melted with the heat of the meat. The cheese was covered in sauce as well so it didn't taste plain.
Meat: 10/10. A great ratio between the meat and chip serving size. The meat didn't taste bland at all, my tastebuds must have jumped with joy when they experienced the taste of the overall HSP. The meat was stacked like a mountain, heaps of meat there.
Price: 9/10. It was $15 which is a fair price considering the top notch quality, and you get to choose a drink.
Overall rating: A solid 10/10. Everything is cooked fresh and tastes splendid. The serving size is pretty big, I struggled to finish it by myself so it'll definitely fill you up. This stick figure RPG hides a lot of fun behind its sticky facade!
Before I get to the basics of the gameplay, let me say the writing is great and it's what hooked me from start to finish.  The dialog and descriptions of objects are funny without being groan-worthy or memey.   The game for me soon became more about reading everything I could because I really enjoyed the (sometimes self aware) humor throughout the game.
For the RPG side of it, you get to choose from  melee, ranged or magic user choices; the magic user is called a beanslinger so I went with that one.  You use the world map to travel around from location to location and you'll get random encounters during your travels a lot of the time.   As you gain exp (often not from combat but through dialog or skillful use of your , well skills) you use the exp gained to level up various skills that you get at the start, or gain throughout the game from looted/found skill books.
I did not find the combat very challenging, and that was perfectly ok because I was playing the game entirely for the story/writing by the time I realized it was easy.   There are several places in the game where you can create an infinite number of combat encounters for yourself so you can make it as easy or hard on yourself by choosing or not choosing to grind up a little.   (edit: a hard mode exists, I wasn't aware, but it's a spoilery kinda thing so search at your peril)
I played from start to finish and completed almost every side quest, afked a little, and it took me about 15 hours of playtime.  I did not hurry in any sense, I took my time and enjoyed the narratives and descriptions along the way.
Few pros:
-excellent writing
-good humor that doesn't insult the player, not a collection of memes to be 'funny'
-plenty to do lots of side quests and interesting random encounters
-can be played almost entirely using just the mouse, you'll need the keyboard sometimes though
-appropriate music for the setting, though I admit it got a little repetitive after 15 hours
-lots of non-combat skills that affect a lot of things throughout the game, I didn't feel cheated spending exp on these skills
-for a stick figure game the animations and art really conveyed a lot, well done game creators!
-stupid walk mode!
A few cons:
-not a con for me, but the combat can be quite easy if you grind up a little exp and spend it on combat skills (EDIT: i was informed that a hard mode exists, so look into that if you want!)
-the game is in black and white until a little ways into the game where you can unlock a sorta sepia toned background, I found it to be hard on my eyes until I had the more tan colored option unlocked
-I personally found it a little difficult to remember where certain NPCs or items were again when I had to backtrack or returned to the game after a day or two break; finding this information to help me on the internet was easy but ingame could have used a little more direction, or maybe if I could have put notes on the map I could have helped myself but that wasn't an option
Recommended if you like RPGs that are witty and humorous with a lot of well written dialog and descriptions.

17 August 2017 : Labyrinth is currently in Early Access. I played it in EA.
Labyrinth is a tactical deck game, similar in play style to games such as Duelyst. There isn't much to work with since it's in Early Access. Sadly, random tactical deck games like Duelyst have shown little or no long-term promise and have collapsed under a deluge of RNG criticisms and money-grabbing moves. As of now, there is only 1 stage of campaign and it's the tutorial. Perhaps, Free Range Games have given up on Labyrinth?
Gameplaywise, for Casual Raids and Adventures, you choose and control 3 heroes who each have their own deck and unique abilities. There is a Warrior (Aggro) deck, Healer deck, Thief deck and Mage Deck. You have to edit each of their decks separately. It's overtly complex. The game is based on a turn timer with each unit on the map having a place on the turn timer. Taking actions with Tick cost will cause your unit to move further back on the turn timer. On your hero's turn, you get to move your hero up to 3 spaces, draw 1 card and play your hand. Each card has a Tick cost which affects the turn order of play. Using a high cost card will move your hero's turn further down the turn timer causing him to act later. Cards that have a Tick cost of 0 are casted for free and do not move your hero further down the turn timer. Think of the initiative track in Heroes of Might and Magic, Gunbound or Horus Heresy (if any of this is familiar).
The general idea is that you will have 3 heroes and 1 big bad boss which you have to kill, kill him and you win.
Conclusion, it's not ready for show yet but it might show more promise in the future. In its current state, it's only good for a demo. Also, Pay To Win.
Note: Labyrinth is made by Free Range Games. Founder is Chris Scholz. It is located in Sausalito, California. Labyrinth is also being made in collaboration with former Magic: The Gathering US National Champion and founder of Stone Blade Entertainment, Justin Gary, and his team. Stone Blade Entertainment made Sol Forge and Ascension.
1. Unique Systems
Thief uses Amp
Warrior uses Rage
Healer uses Faith
1. Pay To Win
You still to pony up that cash to buy packs. It's 100 gold for 1 pack. Don't forget to buy the heroes too.
2. Overtly Complex
In one match, you have to edit 3 decks for 3 heroes. How do you expect to scale up with such complexity? My guess is that there will be a need to simplify.
3. Ugly 3D models
E
.. Seriously, your 3D modeller needs to improve by leaps and bounds.
4. Core Mechanic Sales
Even heroes and bosses are up for sale for a price.
1. Multiple Campaigns
You have multiple heroes, separate them all into their own individual campaigns, then combine them together. Since you only have 1 campaign stage at the moment, splitting it up into multiple campaigns will give you time to build backstory and creates opportunity to add more stages and more content.

Labyrinth has a lot of potential. This game takes a pretty cool idea and is executing it decently so far. It is still in its very early stages but very playable. Heroes have some interesting design behind them, but there's definitely some balance issues to work out.
The time system has some cool aspects but there's room for improvement. At present, some combinations of boss abilities can cause heroes to become stun-locked, which isn't that fun.
The story seems okay. The writing itself is pretty weak. I like the character design.
All in all, I'd say this game is really coming along, keep an eye out for it, it might be worth your time if you like tactics games and a CCGs.

I feel that I've played enough of the game over the last few days to be able to write a review.
Don't let the "RPG" and "card" mechanics fool you--this is a turn-by-turn tactics game, with minimal story outside of the tutorial, with the option to set up an AI Boss defense to protect, well, whatever it is that you're trying to protect. Honor maybe?
If you like Final Fantasy Tactics for the gameplay, then this should be something up your alley. If you played The Mighty Quest for Epic Loot, then this is definitely up your alley as it is one of the closest niche games out there that lets you customize a defense and watch replays of enemy heroes getting rekt by your clever designs.
So, even though I am giving this a thumbs up, it is worth mentioning that this game is in alpha (for whatever reason I'm not sure--this launched from a Kickstarter well over a year ago). This means it's not perfectly butter-smooth and you'll likely encounter a few hiccups. But most of the mechanical bugs feel like they've been ironed out, so normal gameplay isn't riddled with them or anything.
But since it is in alpha, and because it is a niche title of sorts, the playerbase is rather limited. What this means to you, as a potential new player, is that the game is horribly imbalanced against you. In less than a day I went from playing against low-leveled player bosses all the way to fighting the players who are in the top of the veteran pool--all while only being able to use a glorified starter deck. It will feel like an MMO that has a training island where you're absolutely slaying rabbits for quests, and then in less than a day you're dropped into end-game raids while still wearing your lvl1 gear. Basically a few hours after you finish the tutorial, you're expected to compete with established players who have every card they need, while you're horribly far behind. The gold awarded per match is terrible so you may spend hours of losing before you finally score enough offensive wins to purchase a single card pack. Like Hearthstone, you can "dust" your unwanted cards at a loss to pick specific cards for your decks, and successful defenses award you a wee bit of dust, but don't expect to have nearly enough to do anything with for a long while.
If there were more new players like myself, however, this wouldn't be an issue. The new player experience has been voiced by several others here in the reviews as mostly negative, and I've left my input for them as well, so now it is only a matter of time before we see how responsive they are.
In all, the game is really fun if you can get past the fact that you will lose, a lot, because of your inferior card pool and your inability to win consistently enough to get better cards. Ignore people when they suggest that "eventually" you can earn your cards, because nobody wants to play a game for 2 months just to get to the point where they can finally compete with the same enemies they've been dealing with since day 2. But do know that every successful defense replay will remind you why the game is a blast, and try and stick with it so that development can make it a better experience for everyone.

So, I now have played some Labyrinth, enough to get a feel for the game, and I have real difficulty giving it a rating. So please note that this rating is only temporary.
I chose to recommend this game (as of yet), because of several reasons, which I will list below. I will also weigh what the game has going for it, but let me at least say that the game has enormous potential.
PROS: The game has a nice mix of genres. It somehow mixes tactical, unit overview with the card gameplay of Hearthstone and Magic. Games are short, so yo won't need much time to play the game. The atmosphere of the game is great, with pretty music, well-designed battlefields, and great effects when playing the game. It has a strong D&D feel going, which is solid. It requires you to make sure you have three decks that are perfectly tuned to each other.
CONS: The game suffers from the same illness as most early access games: it is simply not finished yet. The tutorial does not cover all the terms being used in game, there is no "Controls" menu, and after the two tutorials, you are kind of left on your own. Two classes are not explained, and some mechanics are really vague in how they work. On top of that, there is very little content. The game is intended to be played versus other players, but since there are only 4-6 different bosses available as of yet, the game can get quite boring quite fast. For the game to be successful, the developers will have to add more content. The interface and controls are quite clunky (turns have no end turn button, which can be a real pain, card dragging is inaccurate and sometimes messes up what you were doing).
THINGS-I-JUST-KINDA-FELT-LIKE-NEEDED-NOTICING: The game has a lot of potential. I have said it before, but it feels great, and the idea is fantastic. Some reviews here complain about the game being hard to start with, because you will need to grind relentlessly to get some good cards. I have so far not encountered that problem, although I managed to get all of my Heroes to max level. The game has some technical difficulties, and will need some serious polishing, but I love the challenge it poses  and the content it provides.
If you are not sure, then please, just wait, and see how the game improves over time. The devs are still taking commentary, so the game might change drastically over the coming years.

This game deserves a better rating, good graphics, mechanics and survival elements. I think some reviewers have been motivated by other things than their impression of the actual game. So what does this game offer?
Well first there are survival aspects, food, water, stamina(sleep), and things like temperature, illness and one or two others. Its a bit more demanding than most building heavy survival games, but not very demanding either in the temperate zone you start in. I like that you can basically choose between foraging and a technical solution, for example you can go and collect vegetably things, or you can built a greenhouse and grow them yourself. Again, nothing crazy like 40 different sorts of lettuce, just a basic vegetable thingy, or herbs. The former gets made into food, the latter into medical items.
Secondly base building. This also ties into your progression, you "advance" your character in the game by getting better gear(better spacesuit, jetpack, weapon and collector/mining thingy), you aquire this gear by building it from progressively harder to acquire materials(mostly by increasing the distance to the raw resources from your starting zone). What you also need to built the gear is machinery though, and every time you built a new piece of something it unlocks related items. For example a wall piece might unlock a ceiling piece and a door piece. Items are tiered, MK 1 spacesuit, MK 2 and so on. A MK 2 something would need a MK 2 machinery piece.
Most machinery pieces come in two kinds besides their MK tier level, a compact version which seems to be always MK 1, and versions beyond that which sport conveyor ports. Yes this is a similar concept as what SE uses, i say similar because its more basic. For example a fabricator may pull automatically from one or several storage boxes, but you can't make a dumping box that gets automatically pulled out and sorted in different storage boxes by the conveyor system. Also no way to dock vehicles to a base that i have seen.
Which brings us to vehicles, very remiscent again from Space Engineers small planet based vehicles. You have suspension, wheels, batteries etc. Again simplified, but working out of the box. No flying or space vehicles atm, no gun turrets either.
Lastly critters. Thats about the only combat around, big burly gorilla like things that throw rocks and bash you, and more skittish creatures that fight back at times and flee at others. Very basic, but loads less annoying than those dogs SE has.
This game has potential, and the devteam seems dedicated. There is still lots of stuff to add, but the building is already quite decent and the survival nice. Its a bit between planet based SE and ARK. More physics than ark (winches, pistons, freestyle build vehicles), but less action. From SE it takes the building, conveyor and ore system, but adds some more combat and survival aspects. Its a fairly polished games aswell, lacking in building blocks and some more variety but what it does have is well fleshed out.
If you are ok with early access and checking out new features now and again, like building heavy games with survival aspect and good graphics I'd recommend the game. If you are looking for you new main game and want to sink 10 hours a day into this I'd tell you to hold your horses.

DROD is a long-running franchise of puzzle games, sadly very underrated, but in 2008 Caravel Games decided to try something a little bit differnt. Still set in the same universe as the other games, DROD RPG takes a few steps away from regular puzzlers.
Your task is to guide Tendry, a brave soldier through several levels (12 plus a secret stage, each consisting of about 20-30 rooms or more). It's still very much a puzzle game but apart from collecting keys (different kinds open different doors, so you'll have to think twice before using them) you'll also need to fight all sorts of enemies (humans and monsters alike), collect money (by fighting said enemies) and get more powerful to be able to survive.
While still not an RPG, despite its title, the game now has objects you can use (some only once, some more than once) and you can raise (or level, if you wanna stick to RPG terms) your HP, armor and defense to make things easier.
The top-down perspective and the mini-map makes it easy to get an overview of the levels and think up a grand strategy, but sometimes you'll need to try different approaches to certain problems. No matter how tempting it is to kill everything as soon as you see them, it's a bad idea. Wait till you get stronger/more powerful, and in the meantime, try to think of alternate solutions, like bypassing doors, going round enemies without initiating a fight (which is turn-based, by the way), and so on.
Be sure to save as often as possible, though, because it's easy to run into dead ends sometimes. Normally this would make me irritated, and admittedly this game had the same effect on me initially, but after I realized my mistakes (not using items/keys optimally, starting fights with monsters left and right, since 'Hey, there's a health potion right there, why should I care?', not looking for secret areas, etc.) I started over and had a much more fulfilling experience. And despite it being a long game (relatively speaking, but when you think it's over after a few hours, it turns out it's only the end of the first half), replaying certain areas with a more thought-out strategy doesn't take very long at all.
The game is a huge amount of fun, very easy to pick up and pretty hard to put down. Just one more room... (It also has some references to other titles in the series but you'll be fine playing it without any prior knowledge.)
Pros:
- Takes a while to complete (~8 hours or more)
- Save anywhere (you'll need it!)
- Active community on the game's website
- Replayability (try for a higher score, look for secret areas or alternate solutions, download user-made levels, etc.)
Cons:
- A little bit on the trial-and-error side, and sometimes the error part only becomes evident later, so save often
- The voice acting is pretty poor, though after a while I found at least the main charcter's voice more funny than annoying
It's like a game written by someone trying to be deep about life and death but it plays like a clunky point and click from 2003.

Grim Fandango remains one of the best point and click adventure titles to date in it's new remaster. The comedy, characters, theme and setting are all brilliantly displayed as you solve puzzles across 4 different years in the life of Manny Calvera. If you are expecting a major overhaul though, you may be left a little dissapointed. It is just the original game with some refreshed control and graphic options. But that's nothing to be too upset about.
The charm of the game is what shines through the most, with the 2nd Year being the highlight of the game. The Noir style and witty dialogue add so much extra to the experience. Puzzles tend to be more on the abstract side for both better and worse in different scenarios. Some will leave you feeling very accomplished but others end up becoming "guess what the developer was thinking". For the most part though, these are minor issues.
It's a short game of only about 10-15 hours for a first playthrough and achievements help reward multiple playthroughs or a very thorough single one. It's highly recommended as long as you're into this sort of thing.

Some of the puzzles can be difficult to figure out, and sometimes just don't make sense, but the game has an absolutely amazing story and fantastic characters to carry it through some of the weak gameplay.

A true classic, and a LucasArts game that really made a mark when it was first launched. That was ages ago, I think something like 20 years ago(?), but it's really something else.
This is the remastered version, so instead of having a game with pixels being 5cm squares, you get good graphics, and also re-worked sound as well. The result is a game that in visuals and sound holds up well to current standards in my opinion, considering the limitations that comes with remastering the base game.
Controls though are somewhat clunky compared to what at least I am used to today, but this game doesn't rely on quick reflexes or fast responses, so that's not a game breaker.
Despite the age, this game holds up really well. It is a story driven game though, so it is very linear, but it's the puzzles that makes this game what it is. What takes you from one part of the game to the next is solving all those riddles, problems and obstacles that come in your way. This is where the game really shines, since there's few hints and the problems really require some good thinking to figure out. As such it will be a very neat challenge for anyone interested in solving problems.
Coming back to it it took me less than 10 hours, but that was because I still remembered most of the problems facing the protagonist from last time I played it. If you're completely new to this game, my guess is it will provide lots of hours of gaming, in a very unique enviroment. On top of that the developers managed to add a really good sense of humour to this game, not of the same kind but pretty much just as funny as the stuff in Secret of the Monkey Island.
All in all, if you're interested in solving problems and don't mind a linear story driven game, this is definetly something to pick up, it's worth the money. If it's on discount, anyone slightly curious should try it out.

Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light is genuinely fun.
It's different than your average Tomb Raider in a sense that it's in a fixed isometric view but it's Tomb Raider by heart with all the action, platforming and puzzles you would come to expect.
I like the style of this game they made use of the isometric view real well like in stages with different elevations you could see the different levels from above or below so it feels connected even though you reach checkpoints and load another area. Immersion secured.
The puzzles are tough but do-able and gives a sense of accomplishment when you complete it. The feeling like "hey awesome I just figured it out". And the game doesn't make you forget because often times these tricky puzzles contain rewards in the form of powerups or items to boost your stats.  And some puzzles are right just there in your face teasing you. "Look an ammo upgrade 20 feet away from me but I can't walk/run/jump to it. What should I do?" IMO is a good game design since it makes the game one giant puzzle/reward fest.
But it's not all about puzzles, there's action too. The enemies are pretty predictable but will definitely test your reflexes avoiding their attacks and projectiles. There's an incentive in doing good at combat too for if you do well you activate your 'power' which disappears IF YOU GET HIT so it makes combat pretty hectic but pretty fun.
Overall good game. I can't wait for the upcoming sequel.

Although no where near as diverse as the actual table top trading card game, where you can use ANY cards you have in a much more social setting, this is a great electronic verson of the Magic the Gathering. For only $10 (not counting optional DLC), you can play with several decks of every colour in a campaign, in custom games against A.I., or with friends in several game types. The DLC offer allows anyone to purchase extra decks too, again for a fairly low price (especially during steam sales. :D).
The deck building is pretty basic too. You have a set series of cards for every deck and the mana is automatically added for you. Although this can be a pain at times to those who (like me) have been playing for years and like to play around with little things like that, it is perfect for new players who only wanna focus on getting "the best cards" into their deck.
The only REAL complaint I have is the game timer. While this does make sense for being a PC game, the timer is too long in some moments and too short in others, making the game speed and attention to detail needed very out of flux at times. But as long as you have nothing else to look at you can work with it fairly easily.
Overall while this game is more of a plan B for when you can't meet your friends on Friday night it is still a good alternative for a few short games evry now and then, and it is a GREAT game to help those who are new to the game to learn both gameplay and deck building. Just keep an eye on that timer.

It's Magic: The Gathering.....
Okay I'll give a serious review, for those of you who don't know Magic is a card game outside of the game series. If you don't know about the game I would wait until a sale or I wouldn't buy it, the game will teach you how to play but if you don't know if you will like it what's the point. I do play the card game a lot and I can only review the game on it's hardest difficulty. I'm going to split the review into different portions
Campaign- The game has a single player campaign that's seperate from the custom matches, don't expect a super great plot but it's enjoyable. The campaign in my oppinion as an experienced player was to easy even on the hardest difficulty aside from a few challenges, at least until you face Nicol Bolas the final "Boss", although by using Jace's deck he is super easy. I did think it was fun though and will get you through if you feel like playing magic and nobody else you know does.
Decks-The game features a bunch of decks unlocked through the campaign mode, for those new to the series you cannot create your own deck but by defeating oppenents with a deck you unlock specific cards that can be added or removed to that deck and only that deck. You also cannot modify lands, which is a huge bummer. Playing through the campaign I noticed the decks don't really seem to be balanced, the game is much easier using certain decks.
Multiplayer- I can't say to much I don't play online to often, I hear there are a lot of cheaters but I can't say for certain that there are.
Custom matches- Not only are there normal matches ranging from 2-4 players but the game has a planeschase option, it definitely adds a lot of fun to the game. Some frustation too.
I reccomend this game to anyone who plays Magic, in all honesty I enjoyed this one more than Duels of the Planeswalkers 2013

Don't let the screenshots fool you - playing Wacky Wheels can't be good for your eyes. When you actually start driving, those crisp stills turn into a colony of scurrying ants that are running around the screen as pixels shift and change colors. Unlike the platformers and the shooters of old that generally age well and still look just as good decades later, games like Wacky Wheels don't. No amount of nostalgia can fix the headache inducing graphics or the tiny tracks that take all but 5 seconds to circumnavigate. Twenty years later we have a lot of better kart racers to choose from...

NOTE: I played this a lot offline due to some issues not related to the game, so my play time is more like 5-6 hours,
Mario Kart has made quite the impact on gaming. From when it came out on the snes to the present day with Mario Kart 8, it's made people who don't even like racing games enjoy it with it's crazy weapons and a ton of personality. Wacky Wheels was an earlier attempt to give DOS users a kart game. And it does this...and not much else.
I will start with the pros. This game has a good amount of content with 30 race tracks(15 orignal and 15 bonus) and a battle mode where you hit targets to build points, with 12 tracks in this mode(6 orignal and 6 bonus) as well as a time attack, all this is enough to keep you busy. It also has two player split screen and online which is cool. The graphics are nice and colorful, the characters are all animals and are cute. They come with a lot of animations for the time. The sound design is good with nice sound tracks and plenty of the said tracks.
I must say as good as the animation and graphics are, it has problems. It's a little jittery. I can't describe it but it's almost like it's loading scenes as you drive. This isn't so bad that it breaks the game. But I did have to get used to it.
This game also suffers from limited weapons. You have porcupines as a main projectile(as we all know how dangerous they are if fired out of a gun) They are scattered all over the tracks and carry over the races. The less common ones...aren't all that interesting to me. Heck, half of them are planted on the ground and stand out on the road limiting their usefulness.
My biggest issue is the tracks don't have much personality. I can't tell you my favorite stage...because they all feel the same to me. The tracks have diffrent aesthetics(although only 3-4 diffrent ones) but none of them feel diffrent to play.
At the end of the day I don't think this is the worst kart game ever. But if you have better ones as an option I say go for that, as I can't see the need to go back to this game now that i'm finished with it. But if you like kart games then I recommend it, just don't expect anything mindblowing.

Adding some sort of buffer for newer players where they only face level apropriate bosses (perhaps even pre-gen) would go along way towards solving this. Alternatively just adding a small reward for losing matches you play to the end would really take the sting out of losing.
Even with this in mind I still consider this a must play for anyone who likes TCGs, though I would hessitate to sugest it to someone who isn't.
[Edit2] There seems to be changes in the near future to help new players get started and I can personally attest now that without spending a single dollar I have become stable with 3 solid hero decks and 1 solid boss after 22 hours of play. During that time I had a lot of ups and downs in terms of how hard it was to garner wins but it was overall manageable. Don't be discouraged by a few early losses, it does gets easier for F2Players fairly quickly once your heroes start hitting lvl 15.
I will say that I do not feel safe in terms of balance changes as a hit to the viability of the one boss I've been able to work up would ruin my defense for several days at least. Even so I have now at least proven that it is quite possible to go F2P and compete in this game without devoting your life to it.

So I'm an idiot. After re-downloading, and waiting an hour for the game to install whatever it needed, it did finally load.
The game is really well put together, and I've just gone through its Story mode thing. I don't play many card games, but this one was fun, and reminds me of hearthstone, what little I did play of that.
The only gripe I have with the game is that I frequently draw cards too high to play, and usually sit for many turns in the beginning, dying. Though, that can probably be solved by a learning how to make a better deck. I hope. If I draw well, I have fun, even if it's a close defeat. If I draw poor, it's like fighting centurion in For Honor.
EDIT: I've played the game a bit, on my phone not on steam so my hours haven't changed, but I feel the last point of my review is pretty much why I've changed my recommendation. I want to like this game. It's good, it can be very good! But I seem to be on a losing streak, as I only draw high cost cards at the start, and low cost cards near the end.
I built decks with lots of low cost cards to circumvent this, but still sit through the first 3 turns waiting for cost 1-3 cards as I only draw my 3-5 cost cards. I've even tried not putting cost 5+ cards in my deck, but that hampers late game play. I don't want to build towards finishing it really quick, or drawing it out with lots of guard cards, but those seem to be the optimal strategies. It doesn't seem like you can make decks that work throughout the whole game.
A problem with only high cost cards is surviving to use them. A problem with lower cost cards is that spells, and higher cost cards, churn through your dudes like a gambler through money, leaving you royally boned for later. I can't seem to find a good balance, and the only thing that slightly works is less than 60 cards, with a lot of 2-4, with 3>2>4 cost cards, and then having a small pool of 5-6 cost guards because if they aren't guards they usually die as 2-3 cost guards are poopy.
On a tangent, I've tried things like the profiteer and armorers to buff the cards I play, and if they are drawn it seems to work a little bit, but if I can't draw guards and the buffer early enough, then they don't really work out. The idea was that guards protect the buffer, and the buffer buffs cards with charge, my expendables, and whatever I want alive so that they all do their jobs better.
A new point, is stronger cards. Some people have cards that are plain upgrades of the ones I have. For example, I play a 3 cost 2/3 or some hypothetical card. Then my opponent does the same 3 cost, but its a 3/3 with guard or lethal or something from the same card color type. IF I had that card I would put that in my deck, but I don't and so my opponent straight up just did better than me.
TLDR: Bad early draws and failure to get the proper cost cards for the turn you're at really sucks, but when that doesn't happen the game is amazing! Also despite the fact that some cards can be earned by playing long enough, it still sucks to go against them when you can't have them, especially if it's just plain better than your own.
I will continue to play the game form time to time, and try and find a deck that works for me, (I like trying to build around charge, and those nords that summon the 1/1s with charge. Or the imperial might, I like to just have lots of expendables to throw out. I do try out other stuff though.)
If someone has a link to a good deck, or some advice that solves my issues with this game, I'd gladly change this review back to YES over NO.

The latest update has its pros and cons. While they definitely made the game a lot more smooth, they took out some features that made the game more challenging and fun. They have removed hard mode from battles, so now you can only choose between normal mode or hero mode (which is now only accessible to lvl 95 characters). Normal mode has made the game far too easy, and with raid battles now obsolete, missions such as defeating the titan is like a walk in the park - it's so easy, it feels like a slap to the face. Now for the pros...I'm liking that they changed up the dungeons, especially in early game. I started on a new character just to get the whole feel for everything new - dungeons, dialogue, character prologue, etc. Even the missionary training site had been updated, so instead of fighting wood figures, you're fighting gnolls. Enchanting items can now be done from your inventory, you can access
quests from any dock of you're choosing, skills have been updated...the list goes on, and it's all pretty impressive. Of course, my only gripe is with how easy they've made the game. So for those of you that like a challenge and aren't max lvl yet to access hero mode, you'll probably be...disappointed. I love this game and I believe it still has a lot of potential, they just need a push in the right direction.
Let me just start by saying this is my favorite mmo. I've been playing Vindictus for almost 2 years and, despite having left a few times to try out other mmos (including the newer ones), I still can't find anything else like it.
Out of all the other mmos I've played, I'd say Vindictus has the most entertaining and gratifying gameplay there is. Although it's not open world, it's easy enough to enter dungeons and raids via the dock without having to wait too long for other players to join. On the battlefield, you can dish out some pretty devastating combos, which look just as cool as they are powerful. Each class plays differently, so I'd recommend trying them out to get a feel for which one suits you best. Also, there isn't a trade system; if you want to trade with someone, you'll have to organize the details with them and send it through the mail. There's a marketplace too, if "trading" sounds like too much of a hassle, but some items may be way overpriced depending on if they're in high demand.
There are a total of 11 classes right now: 5 males and 6 females (yes, they are gender locked). Lately, it seems like they've been adding classes more frequently, so I think it's safe to say that we'll be expecting to see more in the future.
This is probably the best community I've been a part of in
game. The majority of people are quite friendly and willing to assist; I've met some pretty cool people there just by doing missions. In town, depending on what channel you're on, you may see a group of players dancing in their undies - that's normal. Basically, everyone just wants to have fun :)
I see the question "Is Vindictus dead?" being asked a lot, and I'd say it's far from it. Sure, the community has gotten smaller because some players decided to play the newer mmos, but there's still quite a good amount of people left in Vindictus. With all of the events and updates going on, it seems like Vindictus has really been stepping up their game against the competition lately. I believe that in doing so, it'll bring more people back to the game, as well as attract new players. To be honest, there have been a handful of times that I "quit" the game for long periods, but there's always something that brings me back; in this case, it was the Delia update (she's awesome, by the way), so I'll probably be addicted to this game for a while...again.

The story is this... I had been playing the game casually for awhile and had just finished it a few days before my discovery. My neighbor had recently been a victim of some rather odious domestic violence, so my wife and I were doing whatever we could to help her out. Her BF had turned her lovely home into a hoarders den and gathered mountains of junk everywhere. Clothes that jung from chandeliers; random tools; a 6 foot tall nested stack of gallon ice cream tubs (washed out); lots of exercise equipment (new and old); tons of rotten food in the fridge that I disposed of (8 bags or more);stolen bikes and the rack that they were chained to; a bunch of computers with hard drives taken out and stacked up; random trash just piled up everywhere. Anyway, you've seen the show. We're typically perceptive people and feel so ashamed that this happened under our noses. We're doing what we can now to help out, as she deserves it.
We were told by her fam to take whatever we wanted from his unholy stash, which is swell, but we're selling most things to cover the cost of a dumpster to clean the place out well enough for her to come home. Anyway, I'd been rooting around a box of ancient pc junk and was glancing at the games. There were old Myst rip-offs, bulls**t cheap titles of whatever. Nothing worth anything, as you'd imagine. And then I picked up the next box and I was staring straight at Manny Calavera. My eyes went wide as legs. Could it really be in there? Yes it was. Complete with the Prima guide and original gatefold CD case. How could this be? A little worse for wear, but no matter. Of all the games that have come out in the last 20 years, here it was, this thing that had brought me so much joy over the last few weeks.
I took it home, turned on my monitor and the remastered game was on the screen. I'd paused it while I went to clean up and rummage through the junk. Wish I could share the pic I took of the box and pause screen together. What a coincidence. Lovely.
My neighbor is going to recover and is with family now. though she has little family left. We'll do what we can to help. I hope folks that see this might take a look at their own neighborhood and check in to the neighbors you might be worried about. Perhaps these fences we put up between us don't make for good neighborhoods after all. Look out from that screen of yours every now and then to check in on folks. They might need you.
