Ok... this one is kind of tricky.
I really just wanted a slightly old school linear game with unlockables and stylish hack and slashing, which was EXACTLY what I got!
I also got some extras: extremely weird, sometimes (purposefully) nonsensical, story and characters. The creepiest 'dating' sub game you have EVER played. That's my personal promise right there. A early steep difficulty curve that got much easier after a few hours when you learn the systems (note: get the healing skills first). A much bigger variety of difficulty levels, secrets, bonus missions and unlocks than I expected. A surprisingly small variety of enemies but a surprisingly large variety of unique set pieces, ideas and cut scenes - which added up to it almost never feeling like a grind, rare these days.
In terms of what I was looking for, I got exactly what I wanted and more. The dating sub game was enjoyed by me and my girlfriend in a "haha look at this super dumb piece of sh*t" way. The cringey story, dialogue and voice overs that others hated was also exactly what I wanted and expected from this studio, and it certainly delivered. I wasn't expecting to have to learn and remember as many moves and strategies but it ended up delivering a much deeper experience than I thought it would after I stuck with it - I'm pretty keen to try out the harder difficulties after finishing!
But you need to look at the feedback and make your decisions based off all the reviews. The reviews saying the game is bad because of the story and slightly tricky early gameplay aren't wrong, it just happens to be something I could stomach at the time. If there's any elements you think might not be for you, don't bother, because this game doubles down on all of them. If you think you'll like them, same thing!!

If I had to make a complaint it would be that the combat was so easy as to be basically trivial - I lost only three fights throughout the whole game, and even those I only lost because I had got so used to winning every battle in one or two turns that I no longer bothered checking enemy stats before piling in.  The game was still great fun, but it could have been even more fun (and even more of a time sink) had I had to think and strategise even a little during combat.
There's a way of making the game harder by finding a "hard hat" which is only available at the very start and then only if you very luckily follow the exact right steps, or (more likely) Google how to find it.  That's another small gripe - I wished I had a chance of finding it on my first playthrough so as to be able to make the game more challenging.  But clearly it's only intended to be used on second or subsequent playthroughs, and I can't criticise them too much for that.  And indeed, despite how deeply I already investigated the game on my first playthrough, I may well start a second game soon.
Those are my only small niggles in what is undoubtedly a fantastic game from start the finish, and clearly the result of a huge amount of loving work.  Thoroughly enjoyable, entertaining and amusing, and at this price it must be one of the best-value new games around.

There is a lot to like about this game. Some interesting puzzles, isometric 3D (which you don't see a lot of nowadays), it is quick paced and generally a lot of fun. There are some downsides - the default key mappings are odd for example (Delete to open inventory, Tab to target, Caps Lock to drop a bomb etc). The biggest downside though is its biggest drawcard - the isometric 3D view. The main issue with it is that it is forced - that is, you cannot rotate your view to get a better look at an area. Frustrating when you are looking for a specific item (at one point in the game you have an option to destroy some pillars, and you can run around the area for ages randomly looking for the last pillar because you can't rotate the view yourself and try and locate it the easy way). As well as not being able to rotate, the forced view makes some parts un-necessarily hard - jumping from pillar to pillar or trying to move a ball into a specific spot for example).
Still, despite those downsides, it is worth the price, and the sequel - Temple of Osiris - launches in December, so there is more on the way, which isn't a bad thing.

West of Loathing is a delightful rpg experience with great writing and amazing darkish humor. Don't let the aesthetic fool you into thinking this is a spoof game - it's surpriginly complex, and a single run (around 100% completion) took me 12 hours.
There are multiple ways to approach the main problems, and there are plenty of secrets to discover. The game is not linear, and although it is broken into three chapters, you are never locked out of returning to previous areas (save for the tutorial area). In fact, many longer quests rely on back and forth between locations.
Has no traditional quest log, you get reminders of quests at hand but you will have to remember progress within the quest yourself for the most parts. It is possible to miss stuff entirely, or miss a different solution to a problem. Going back to old areas is often profitable due to increase in off-combat skills, like lockipicking and safecracking, which open up new opportunities for loot.
If you don't enjoy reading and usually skip any lore/book items in games, this game is probably not for you. Most of the game world is built through words, not through visuals. All the ingame writing is great, varying between genuinely funny and somewhat horrifying in tone. This includes things like item descriptions.
Heartily recommended to the fans of the rpg genre - this game is pure joy.

A nice little puzzle game with a disturbing hint to it. It does horror in more of a classical sense, avoiding jumpscares almost entirely (there is one, but it's not that bad) and instead builds an atmosphere of tension. You can tell something is wrong, but you don't quite know what. By solving the puzzles you slowly learn what happened and piece it together yourself, leading to a fairly satisfying conclusion. The puzzles are logical for the most part, although the fact that objects have multiple points of interaction makes it sometimes difficult to tell if you've done everything there is to do. The first part is a little rough because of this, but the second part avoids this issue almost entirely.
The game has one track that plays on repeat, but it doesn't bother me that much because it's a nice tune (reminds me of Lilium from Elfen Lied) and the game is only about an hour long if you take your time, so you won't hear it for overlong.
EDIT: The codec issues have been fixed now, and the game can be fully enjoyed as it was intended to be.

The game for short:
+ Big map that is separated into two regions connected by a stripe of desert
+ very good sound not only for guns but also other things (superior to FC3)
+ good AI (will flank you, try to drive over you with cars, mortar shell you from a distance, ...)
+ Much to do
(with anonymous murder contracts, two warrying factions that both are your contractors as well as enemies, ...)
+ road blocks and military posts make sure you'll be occupied when travelling between places
+ Unusual story
+ public transport as the only way to fast travel (and structured in a way that makes you value it)
+ "buddies" offer alternative ways to complete missions
+ kinda good collectables (like very rare golden AK-47, interview recordings with your main villain, ...)
+ Guns realistic with old guns jamming and breaking often, ...
+ Very good (fire-) physics and dynamic things (at least three times everything FC3 and 4 did / achieved...)
- map is cluttered in a way that often seems to artificially, unneccessarily stretch routes so it takes longer to get from one point of the map to the other
- missions and targets are often placed literary as far away from you as possible (like: you very often have to travel from one corner of the map to the other...)
- there are sounds for animals that are not actually in the game as entities (you'll be hearing lions and so on but only encounter zebras and gnus...)
- AI trying to drive you over can be very annoying if you haven't saved in a while (it also sometimes makes some sounds cars make glitch out)
- some guns and some enemies are configured in a way that makes late-game enemies bullet sponges which will fall to the ground but then continue to 'last stand' against you with a pistol.
- Main Story takes an incredibly long breather between beginning and end, distracting you with the sub-story of the two warrying factions; also takes a rogue turn during the last mission / with the last mission.
------------------------------------------------------------
Das Spiel in Kürze:
+ Grosse Karte die in zwei Regionen unterteilt ist, die durch einen streifen Wüste verbunden sind
+ Sehr gute Geräusche nicht nur bei den Waffen aber auch anderswo (besser als bei FC3)
+ Gute KI (Flankiert einen, versucht dich mit Autos zu überfahren, bombardiert einen mit Mörserbeschuss von weitem, ...)
+ Es gibt viel zu tun (mit anonymen Mordaufträgen, zwei kriegstreibende Fraktionen die beide sowohl Auftraggeber als auch Gegner sind, ...)
+ Strassenblockadenund militärposten stellen sicher, dass man während dem Reisen beschäftigt bleibt
+ Unübliche Geschichte
+ Öffentliche Verkehrsmittel / ÖV ist der einzige Schnellreise Weg (und so aufgebaut, dass man es wertschätzt)
+ "Komparsen" bieten alternative Wege Missionen zu machen
+ Gute Sammelgegenstände (wie sehr rare goldene Ak-47, interview Tonbänder mit dem Bösewicht, ...)
+ Waffen realistisch indem alte / gebrauchte Waffen schneller klemmen und verschleissen, ...
+ Sehr gute (Feuer-) Physik und dynamische Dinge (mind. dreimal mehr als was FC3 oder 4 erreicht...)
- Karte ist so vollgestopft, dass es einem so vorkommt als seien Wege künstlich, unnötig in die Länge gezogen worden
- Missionen und Missionsziele sind meistens so weit von einender Weg wie möglich plaziert (man muss oft von einem Kartenecken in den gegenüberliegenden...)
- Viele Tiere die man als Geräusch hören kann sind nicht wirklich im Game (Man hört etwa Löwen, trifft aber nur Zebras und Gnu's an...)
- Dass die KI einen immer überfahren will kann bei längerem nicht-speichern nerven (und sorgt ebenfalls dafür, dass die Fahrzeug Geräusche glitchen)
- Einige Waffen und Gegner sind so Konfigueriert, dass sie im Endspiel Kugelschwämme werden welche zu Boden fallen und dann noch mit der Pistole weiterkämpfen
- Hauptgeschichte nimmt sich eine sehr lange Auszeit zwischen Anfang und Ende des Games und man wird mit der Geschichte zwischen den beiden Fraktionen abgelenkt; Die Hauptgeschichte nimmt in, mit bzw. bei der Letzten Mission reisaus...

Firstly this game is awesome. Now you most likely want to know why, well I'm going to tell you.
Perpetuum gets referred to as being like "Eve Online" alot. Well there are similarities but It's not quite the same deal. In Perpetuum you get to costomize the fit of your robot or mech and run around the world doing as you please. Literally you can do whatever you want. You are going to be making the most fun for yourself, there's nothing that guides you through areas like a quest line.
Secondly it's a sandbox so having a goal in mind is a good idea although the missions and npc fights are fun. The bread and butter is the pvp which is a high risk/reward system.  There is somewhat of a learning curve but It's not that bad. The amount of freedom and choices you get for customization is enough to keep you interested especially if you like robots and mechs. It's fun experimenting to see what works and doesn't.
Next is the Industrial options. I think everything in this game can be made by the players. It's quite in depth and I had to read into it a little but after getting the hang of it, industry is alot of fun. I'm having fun with industry even though I primarily pvp. Gathering materials and kernels to make items, robots and mechs is the simpliest description of industry I can make.  The Market is player driven. Which also gives players options to "Buy low and sell high" if you're into making NIC that way. NIC is the in game money.
Lastly the community is great and willing to help, just make sure you join the general chat as well as the help! chat. I've already learned alot from the community and there's quite a few corps currently recruiting.  If you like games with depth and appear to be "more than meets the eye" this game could be for you. This review has hardly scratched the surface of Perpetuum.

More of a first impressions than a review. Havn't had a chance to suss out the community, so we'll talk mechanics. In no particular order.
The GUI is...functional. It's something I think would benefit from a once over. Little things like displaying the hotkeys in tooltips would go a long way towards its usability.
The tutorial is just...bad. If I were the devs, this is something I would focus on post-haste. Coming from EVE, nothing was confusing, but it was definitely far from engaging. The first few hours of any game are absolutely vital to getting a player hooked, and I imagine anyone who came in here not knowing what to expect may have gotten turned off pretty quick.
Combat isn't bad, but I think the 'feel' of it could probably use some refinement. As well, the game isn't forthcoming with various hotkeys, which makes it a bit frustrating to rapid-click around until you look them up. If the process of targeting and selection could be streamlined, that'd help the combat portion of the game a great deal.
The gameplay systems are similar to EVE in a lot of ways. I believe another reviewer described it as being Sam's Cola to EVE's coke, and I'll second that. Still, it's fun in its own right, if you can look past  some of the rough edges. I've spent my time in game so far mining, and that at least is a little more engaging than it is in similar games. It does a lot of things so closely to its inspiration as to be near identical in many. I'd hope as they go forward, the developers try to accentuate the differences in their systems more.
All in all I'd recommend Perpetuum for someone looking for an open-world, EVE-like fix. Especially with a group I can see how it'd become quite enjoyable. Still, I'd recommend the Devs look into low-level usability concerns, like the UI and tutorial. An EVE-like game is inherently complex, and if they can maange to ease new players into that complexity well, and engage them in the process, they might have a winning combination.

I can really recommend the single player even to players who have played Hearthstone before, since there are some new elements to be learned, and the single player does a great job at introducing them to you, while also having a mediocre story which is most likely to keep you playing, since it's rewarding, and interests while statisfies the player at the same time. I think it's simply respectible, that they put some effort into a single player mode of a game not even focused on single player, and also being a free to play game.

Think about it. The game's outcome is ultimately determined by chance. To increase that chance, by getting better cards, you have to pay money for a chance to get those betters cards in random packs. 7/10. I recommend this game, but with some reservations. It is aesthetically pleasing, but the game play is clunky.
I enjoyed the setting, the characters, the art style, the music, and the dialogue. The plot is somewhat disjointed and rambling, but that didn't ruin the game for me. It has charm, humor, and wit.
This game is often considered to be the gold standard of the retro point-and-click adventure genre, and perhaps deservedly so, but that doesn't stop it from suffering many of the same problems that plague similar games. The tedious walking back and forth, the pixel hunts for tiny inconspicuous items, the main character who constantly says "I don't want to do that," etc.
The puzzle difficulty is all over the map. Some are so easy that the game is basically telling you what to do, while some are just inscrutable, even after you know the solution. That's not to say they're all bad. In fact, I'd say a majority are fine. But honestly, some of them are the kind of thing you only figure out after trying every possible thing, long after you've run out of ideas that actually make any sense.
So, if you like this style of game and haven't played Grim Fandango, give it a try...but keep a walkthrough on hand. Most of the game will be more fun without it, but I can just about guarantee that there will come a time when you will get stuck. It's just too easy to overlook some little thing, and you won't be able to progress without it.

However, where it shines is... well, darn near everything else. . Why can't this just be a standard feature in most video games?

West of Loathing is a delightful rpg experience with great writing and amazing darkish humor. Don't let the aesthetic fool you into thinking this is a spoof game - it's surpriginly complex, and a single run (around 100% completion) took me 12 hours.
There are multiple ways to approach the main problems, and there are plenty of secrets to discover. The game is not linear, and although it is broken into three chapters, you are never locked out of returning to previous areas (save for the tutorial area). In fact, many longer quests rely on back and forth between locations.
Has no traditional quest log, you get reminders of quests at hand but you will have to remember progress within the quest yourself for the most parts. It is possible to miss stuff entirely, or miss a different solution to a problem. Going back to old areas is often profitable due to increase in off-combat skills, like lockipicking and safecracking, which open up new opportunities for loot.
If you don't enjoy reading and usually skip any lore/book items in games, this game is probably not for you. Most of the game world is built through words, not through visuals. All the ingame writing is great, varying between genuinely funny and somewhat horrifying in tone. This includes things like item descriptions.
Heartily recommended to the fans of the rpg genre - this game is pure joy.

Magic: The gathering – Duels of the Planewalkers2013 is a fun competitive card game to play with friends. Especially when there are four players in the game as it makes it a whole lot more dynamic and you won’t necessary loose just because you got badly RNG’d from the start.
The game consists of a Champaign that works pretty well where you will fight each deck to unlock them. There are also encounters such as fighting the hydra. Each encounter has a different touch to them, such as the hydra it gains attack/health for each turn.
When you have beaten the game you unlock the revenge campaign that upper the difficulty if you found the first campaign too easy.
There is also a challenge mod (that actually is challenging!) where you are presented by different scenarios and have to win the game within a set number of rounds.
There are a few modes to play such as Two headed giant that is basically 2vs2. A classic free for all mode. Last a mode called plane chase that have a extra set of cards where these cards may turn the whole situation upside down by giving all creatures to given player flying or extra creatures.
Oh, and you don’t need to buy card packs in this game as you will unlock cards as you play. You can also unlock everything for a set price if you want, but it is not necessary.
Last! Don’t buy this game if you don’t have any friends that play the 2013 edition as there is just a few to none players online.
Pros:
- Fun with friends
- Challanging
- Don’t need buy cards
Cons:
- Prepare to get RNG’d
- Short campaign
- Few players online

Because of my own curiosity I came back to this game after a year; and to my surprise I was able to rescue my poor plants. I also forgot about sounds - music is amazing, is calming, is relaxing. (+ my childish side likes a farting sound when you pick up a snail. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ )

Viridi is incredibly soothing. The gentle music alone is enough to unwind with. Even the most negligent people can recover plants by watering and zooming in to "sing". Zoom and wait until music bars appear and fill with notes. According to some players, this will help the most abused plants catch up in their growth.
At first glance, you might think the colors are too washed out, but zooming in allows you to see more concentrated hues in the shadows. There are also subtle textures to make the succulents more unique from each other in addition to shape. The weekly randomized free succulent species means you just have to wait for the ones you want; getting species you've had before isn't so bad since there can be color variation. The pet snail is also a nice touch.
This game is a rare gem for relaxation.

Viridi is a game for those who love succulents, but can't grow them if your life depended on it. This game has super relaxing music and calm game play. It features all different types of succulents and starting sets to build up your garden of succulents. The game runs in real time and you have to water your succulents once everyday. You can put the game in vacation mode (Unlike real succulents) if you know you are going to be away for along time so that your plants don't shrivle up from not being watered. Your plants can also get over watered if you spray them two or more times, and the game tells you if they're over watered (thankfully), but is very forgiving with it (unlike real succulents). All critique I have for this game is that there are so many "pay as you play" perks, such as buying other plants. They cost real money since there is no in game currency. Because of that little flaw, you could probably spend up to (or more than) $10 playing this game and getting the plants that you want, also unlocking the garden where you put all of the mature plants. At least you can get a free mystery seed once a week, which is not much but saves you the urge of pulling out your credit card when you get bored of your already matured plants.
~PROS~
-relaxing music
-forgiving gameplay
-vacation mode
-isn't ridculously impossible to grow (unlike real life)
-simple but charming
~CONS~
-gets expensive quickly if you want to pay
-can get boring if you don't want to pay extra
Overall, the game would be a lot better if you could pay to play initially and then all the other plants come as extra, and not the other way around. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys succulents but don't have a green thumb with them (such as myself). If you're looking for a relaxing and calming game, this is the game for you!

Extremely peaceful and quiet. I, myself, would love to attend to my own potted plant; but alas, I cannot. I yearn to have a garden, because it keeps my inner zen. I love this game dearly.
The game exhibits the feeling of having a pot of plants, grouped together. Raising them, accompanied by the mystical and life-envoking soundtrack, will help you release your inner zen. After a hard day's work, falling back on this will make your entire day better. If you're devoted, you can buy plants with real money, but I prefer not to. Viridi for me is checking in every time I feel sad or tired, and when I do, there's almost always something to soothe me with.
There's also other things. For example, clicking on one of your plants, maybe the one you like the most, and zooming in on it (mousewheel or just using two fingers on the trackpad), will make your "in-game character" sing to the plant. By releasing carbon dioxide, the plant basically uses it as food, and thus slightly grows. It may not seem to impact the plant, but by the next day, it'll surely have grown much larger than if you had not sung to it.
Overall, the game is a spot on 10/10 to me. It helps me become peaceful and harmless. It helps me after work. It's like an online medicinal product. I recommend this to anyone and everyone. Whether you like fast-paced shooters or slow-paced puzzle games, or any in between, anyone will surely like this game for peace.

After playing this game for almost 300 hrs now I guess you could say I like this game.
The fact is I adore this game, let me explain a few things I luv about PN.
!. The landscape is beath-taking, so beautiful, colourful and almost life-like.
2. Movement is great, 1st person or 3rd person - 360 degrees.
3. Animals are different and I luv em - even Rocky the Gorilla lol
4. Scavaging & mining which you need to do to survive and build. A fav past-time of mine
5. Building - A base(s) and vehicles with a real sense of suspension - wow Build whatever design you like 4 wheels to 24 wheels - your choice.
6. Flying - well just hovering at the moment with a jet pack, which you can upgrade. Also upgrade your suit and multi-gun
7. Multitool is a well designed piece of kit - use it to mine, build, destroy or reclaim parts to rebuild with.
8. Biomes - there are different biomes covering the entire planet. Hot in the desert, freezing at the poles, with snow too.
9. Minerals are found in each biome and some biomes have the rarer materials that you need to find. So travel is neccesary.
10. Weather systems. Expect rain in the starting biome, Snow in the north and south poles.
I could go on but I think you get the drift of what I am trying to say.
This game has everything I desire in a survival game and theres more to come too. The devs are so active it is amazing what they do. Updates are frequent, which is great for all players.
PN is by far the best type of game in this genre and with supporting devs, we can all expect this great game to flourish.
I hope this helps you when making your decision - to buy or not to buy.
If you like this genre then I'm sure you wont be disaapointed just remember this is still in Early Access so a lot more content to come.
Also if you have any suggestions you feel would be great for PN then please let the Devs know. They like to hear from us.
I have no problem recommending this game to anyone who likes this genre.

I picked this up as part of a Humble Bundle. I'd always heard good things, but I was never interested enough to lay down cash.  This remastered version tweaks the graphics, but from what I understand it is the same game underneath.  The story is great and I enjoyed most of the characters.  I'm not a fan of being loud as humor, though, so Glottis got on my nerves very quickly.  I played the game using the steam controller, which worked fairly well.  You don't get overt clues that you can interact with something, but if you pay attention you will notice that Manny's head will swivel to look at things he can interact with. Even with that tipoff, some of the puzzles were frustrating. I spent entirely too much time running between scenes to try each item in my inventory against each interaction point.  In some cases I had the right idea, but because I didn't line up correctly I missed solving the puzzle (looking at you, draining the vault).  Where the controls really fall down is in controlling the vehicles.  Regardless of what direction the vehicle is oriented, up is forward, back is reverse, left and right turn on the dial in those directions.  It made for frustrating piloting.
I think overall the game has aged well, but the remastering appears to only be cosmetic.  The underlying control problems are still present, and some of the puzzles are incredibly obtuse. Of course, you can play it with a mouse to eliminate some of the control issues.
The problems were such that I feel like I have to recommend against it.  If you are a fan of the game already, sure, go ahead and get it, but you don't need my recommendation for that.  As I moved into year four I was getting more and more eager to be done so I could move on to something else.

UPDATE: Below is my old review, but after the latest update reset my levels (meaning I must grind for boss access), I've become more critical of the clumsy interface and unplayable bosses/no PvP. I can only recommend this game still because it's F2P.
Despite being in alpha, Labyrinth has a good start to put it above many other CCGs, though this may be largely owing to the limited importance of its CCG factor.
In Labyrinth, there are no "Early" and "Late-game" cards; every card is a special ability (offered in addition to a character's basic ability and a passive move which, by default, adds damage reduction), only requiring a variable turn delay to play. This means that A) You're always capable of some action without cards, and B) With the exception of 0-cost cards, you can only use one per turn, making cost management about who you want to move before.
This system is appealing because it heavily impedes any kind of playstyle meta; you're forced to strategize around each character's strengths. In addition, characters' position on the board is important enough to make the game more TRPG than CCG when directly playing.
Another unique element of Labyrinth is the idle side of playing, in which players simply assign and equip bosses (which, to be fair, are the only levels so far) for others to challenge. There are no bitterness-inspiring penalties for having a boss lose, only rewards for winning.
As mentioned, the game is in alpha as of this review, but it still sports some faults:
-The UI is a bit janky, particularly when it comes to inspecting units in-game (you must use the turn order bar's tabs*) and clarity of spell/target selection.
-There is no way to directly battle other players. Bosses are set-and-forget passives, and RNG decides if they get to fight and accrue XP.
-This boss system, instead of bosses being an alternate playstyle with which to challenge defending Hero parties, discourages trying more than one boss. It's hard to level one, and you miss out on rewards if your boss loses, so you have little incentive to stop using your strongest.
-There are no levels to design, a la Mighty Quest for Epic Loot (a game comparable, but inferior due to its p2w inclination)
-The tutorial is fairly long, and somewhat lacking for helping distinguish the various card attributes.
-Characters can only have 20 cards in their deck (plus perks), which is a bit restrictive.
-The Warlord Spirit seems to be the strongest boss by a wide margin.
-It's unclear if only real-money packs will be reimbursed after the release resets the game, or all earned ones.*
Hopefully, all of these problems will see improvement further in the game's development.
*EDITS:
-Apparently, double-clicking a unit also shows its attributes. Don't be discouraged by the lack of response to single or right-clicking.
-It's developer-confirmed, right in the comments, that ALL acquired packs will be reimbursed. Basically, the longer you've played for, the larger your pack-opening spree will be after release.

"Getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked has never been so much fun or rewarding."
Extended review on this game. My impression is overall, very positive. I'll explain why. This review will not cover the specifics of the game itself, aside from my experiences with various aspects of it that I feel was noteworthy.
Prior Experiences and Expectations
- Paying member of Solforge, Hearthstone, Cabals TCG (dropped hundreds of bucks over the years on these. No regrets).
- Play alot of hobby board games across a wide range of genres.
- Banner Saga: Factions. Enjoys tactics game that have a simple core design and are not RPGs. Hate RPGs actually. As little management as possible is best.
- Injustice Mobile (you'll see why this actually becomes relevent).
What drew me to Labyrinth
- Diehard need to scratch the "miniatures wargaming" itch. And I mean, small scale, tactical battles that is NOT JRPG, anime-ish or Warhammer. What I really wanted was the D&D miniatures wargame. Something I admired, but never played.
- Labyrinth, visually and mechnically, resonated with this desire and need.
- Progress reports. You can tell right away that the developers are very market-oriented and open to the public at large. They keep us up to date, they respond to our questions- and they have an Early Access Game that is SOLID.
The Mechanics
-Still learning new things even though I've must have played over 10+ casual battles by now. The mechanics becomes clearer and clearer and I am astounded at how well designed it is. Initially I ignored the ticks entirely, feeling that it's extraneous, but now I am starting to pay attention once I figured out the relationship between "how many cards I can play in a turn is dependent on whether I get moved behind another unit in tick, or I stay ahead of the enemy in ticks- which pretty much determines both initiative and resource usage." Mindblown, I mean, technically, there is no such thing as a turn. The elegance is astounding. I love how the mechanics show you clearly what everything does- I don't find myself needing to look for additional information, through inference, I am understanding the depth of the game.
-Once you've built a Boss Deck or Two, you start grasping the underlying principles of how the Bosses work and you could then build better Heroes.
-The way they choose to present the information is very functional. The ring of health around each unit, and the TCG nature of utilizing keywords are useful. If you've played any kind of TCG/CCGs before, it's simple. And that's one of the things that set this apart. Alot of "tactics" games are badly disguised RPGs with alot of random chance and too MUCH STATS. Labyrinth has none of this problem. There is little to no RNG (and if there was, the cards tell you clearly), everything is clearly labeled, and you juggle with 3-4 stat types at most, with keywords.
The Multiplayer
- Raids are addictive. You just want to keep fighting. And when you're heroes died one turn away from total victory, you feel burning vengeance but also shame because it was entirely your own fault. So far, I always lose because I made a tactical error or I suddenly realize my Hero decks wasn't appropriately geared for fighting that specific Boss strategy. This game is not easy actually, and I wouldn't want it any other way. It teaches me better tactical awareness- and the fact I am aware exactly why I lost is very humbling and makes defeats have value, rather than feeling arbitrary. If you are after winning, you won't enjoy this game as much. But if you want tactics, this game oozes with it.
-I had thought the whole "passive defence multiplayer" thing might be sketchy and wouldn't draw me in (even though I play Injustice Mobile. And Dungeon Keeper Mobile, which has exactly this kind of multiplayer), just like I had assumed that the tick system wouldn't click with me (pun intended), but they actually did it pretty well. The main joy is from devising a good Boss Deck to stomp Heroes when you're offline- since multiplayer is automated for the defender. The key I think, is synergy between the Boss's passive and the deck, but each boss has a Dual Nature, so you can access deck types of other bosses, in addition to unique ones.
-So far, I have a ramp Boss (some freaky Mayan death goddess, can't spell her name) that gets stronger the more turns has passed. So her entire deck is freezing the enemy until you ramp to godhood.
-The other bossI have set up (the giantess) is a "everytime you play a non-attack card, you deal your attack to all enemies within 3 spaces" (paraphrase), so her entire deck is amping her base attack and drawing enemies closer. And just for kicks, I made her generate ludicrous amounts of minions as well.
-As a final note, asyncrhonous multiplayer makes it easy to drop in and drop out. No pressure. No waiting for people to take their turn. Quite casual and addictive. Like a crunchier Injustice Mobile (and we all know how addictive that is.)
The Store
-No premium currency. You get 10 gold per (casual) battle. Quests rewards 100 golds. 100 gold buys you a pack.
-Again, like everything else, I thought I wouldn't be interested or care very much about the cards. Other CCGs have unique creatures and spells that are rich in lore and theme- those draw me in. But cards for attacks and spells for a couple of heroes and bosses? Bah? Boooring, right? BOY, Was I wrong. I actually care what cards I do get now. All cards can be crafted or disenchanted for crafting currency (forgot the name atm), so that's nice.
-Booster packs (keys) are priced nicely, and are consistently priced. Unlike other games that encourage you to buy more for more discounts, this game straight up has a 1:1 exchange rate in terms of packs per buck. This is actually really nice, as I don't have to constantly juggle with "delaying gratification" problems. I get 100 gold, I buy a pack right away. This isn't strictly true if you're paying money directly for the packs, as it is slighly cheaper (by about 0.32 per pack).
-I have dropped something like $25CAD on this game. Both for the original early access price before it went F2P and for 10 packs just the night prior. Because it was worth it and I wanted to support the game. At no point did I feel that I was pressured to get "good cards", indeed, for a vast majority of my heroes, I feel the low-cost or basic cards are the strongest. Hearthstone feels like a grind for example. This game? Not so much. Having only 4 hero classes (so far) and multiple heroes that share those classes with overlapping cards reduces the grinding or "I lack essential cards" feeling that other games produces. This is a huge plus and makes collecting cards an option-expanding activity rather than a chore.
Conclusion:
Overall, it has a minimalistic design philosophy that I really appreciate, both from the mechanics, and the economy. It fulfills a specific kind of niches for a specific type of gamer. It doesn't cheapen its brand by choosing to copy what everyone else is doing, but choosing to put thier own aesthetics and value on it. Of course, this may change as marketability changes, but for now I applaud their willingness to try something different. I look forward to what else this game has in store.

Update March 8th, 2017
I am changing my review from negative to positive despite the weaknesses of the game. Reviewing raids from some opponents provides important input not only on what changes you have to do to your Boss decks, but also how to play properly build and play your hero decks. Of course, this does not mean the problems the game had have suddenly vanished.
- The matchmaking system is still broken, but you can always concede the match and search for another opponent. My suggestion is to keep skipping opponents until you find someone you think you can beat, instead of wasting time fighting lost matches. After I started doing that, the game became much more enjoyable.
- The starting cards can only get you so far in the game and you will quickly hit a wall. This is partly the fault of the matchmaking system which keeps giving you opponents with extremely more advanced decks.
- Progression is kinda slow, however since you only need 2 copies of most cards (and only 1 copy of the perk cards), it is difficult to compare the progression in Labyrinth with other ccgs.

Original review
The game is certainly interesting when you first look at the mechanics. Unfortunately the excitement doesn't last long. Maybe 1-2 days and then the problems it has become painfully obvious. One of the most glaring problems is the matchmaking system which is completely broken. I take my two 6 level heroes for a spin (accompanied by a 12 lv Lavella) and I stumble upon a lair with a 50 health boss and a ton of minions. Yeah, good luck with that.
The other thing I don't like is the absolute reliance on drawing specific cards, at the right time, to win the game. You basically have to keep top decking turn after turn. Do you play against many small enemies? You need AOE attacks. Do you fight against enemies with extremely high armor. You absolutely need those Piercing attacks. Drawing the 2-4 cards from your deck that are the answer to the very specific problem you are facing is completely insane. And after 2 turns you need to draw the same card again because the enemy is spamming minions with ridiculously low casting times, or because his armor is suddenly through the roof. It feels like the game would benefit from a system similar to the one used in Mage Wars, with the RNG elements moved to dice rolls instead of the card draw, rather than having this rock/paper/scissors theme.
Most of the time the raids feel like a coin flip. Why not do that and save the 10-20 minutes I'll drop in a game? Of course if someone spends $100 in the game, to get the "good stuff", his experience may differ. Overall, a neat idea, but with severe problems that will probably prevent it from being something I'll play for a long time. If they fix the matchmaking system and they nerf some heroes (like Radaghar who is instant retreat for me as he is just not worth my time) then maybe I'll give the game another try.

Self-starter type of game.  If a player is looking for green arrows to tell them where to go and what to do, this isn't the game for them; however, if they like to research or theory crafting, setting goals, running basic missions, and near infinite customization of the bots you'll be piloting, then it will be challenging and rewarding.
Time-based skill leveling (regardless of logging in) rewards long-time players and has a tendency to off-put new players.  The development team off-sets this by giving new players a cache of skill points to use to get started.  Resetting the points require cash-shop credits, so one should research what they want to do in-game first.  The tutorial gives a great range of options of what a player can do.
Official information sites need to be solidified: the official wiki is broken
, the twitter page wasn't updated for the last hot patch, server status page wasn't updated for the last update or hot
.  The best place to find information is the official forums where Dev_Zoom tries to keep people updated.
Many of the information sites and tools on this game are now broken links or outdated from updates/patches.  A greater player-base would help with hobby sites containing information, e.g. Perpetuum planner or Profit Reloaded.
One last FYI, a large part of this game is based around PVP and the population typically isn't forthcoming with "trade secrets" like robot builds, money makers, etc.  A more healthy Alpha island population, with little interest in Beta/Gamma island politics, would help players get started on successful assignment completion.

Perpetuum is a game which has evolved nicely over the years. It is alot like EvE online in many ways, with the diverse areas of gameplay like PVE missions, fitting, time based progression, industry, trading, mining, warfare, politics, base building, research, PVP, clans etc. The graphical features and game engine are a bit dated but the art is still good and does a good job of making the world feel extra-terrestrial. The music is also unique and fits well with this game. The robots and mechs are pretty cool and have modules in a similar fashion to eve such as lasers,  ballistics, kinematics, magneto-statics, and missiles. The world has been going through a pretty major overhaul over the past year with random missions assignments, roaming mobs, localized combat stations and a lot more I can't name off the top of my head.
In some way this game is better than EvE for new players, as it has not had over a decade of expansions roll out and such a massive disparity in progression. The biggest problem Perpetuum has is playerbase, right now the game is suffering from a low population, however that means it is a good time to get out there and take advantage the situation.
You got to look at a game like this as a long term endeavor. It will take years to get high level skills and master multiple modes of play. It does not require constant attention either, so if you are like me and play dozens of games you can get sidetracked and come back after a few weeks and have a ton of skill points to blow.
Lastly I would comment on the monetization. The game is B2P and totally playable without a subscription boost, you just need to log in for at least a  few seconds every three days to refresh your skill point generation. The sub system works from subtracting game credits and it works out to less than $10 per month. There is also a Plex type system(ICE) that you can use for the booster or to trade for NIC(credits). Compared to most MMO's your dollars will go alot farther if you choose to spend.
I recommend this game for anyone looking for a game that has some depth and complexity to it and is more tactical than tactile. It is less top heavy than EvE but is modelled after some of the same design aspects. This game is ripe for new players to come in. At its core Perpetuum is a game about robotic gun platforms on a distant alien world some of which are alien(NPC) and some which are controlled remotely by human players(you).

I started playing Asymmetric's first big game, Kingdom of Loathing, nearly ten years ago. KoL features the same caliber of writing and puzzles, but it's limited in many ways to keep you playing over time- a restricted amount of playable turns per day, content exclusive to calendar holidays, that sort of stuff.
With that in mind, and having played KoL for so long, I feel confident in saying that West of Loathing is everything I ever wanted out of an Asymmetric title. Core to any "of Loathing" experience is the writing, and the writing in WoL is some of the most lovingly crafted that I've ever seen in a game. In a lot of game reviews where writing features heavily, now would be the time to invoke certain old, text-heavy titles like Planescape: Torment or the original Fallout, but they don't represent what I mean when I call the writing "lovingly crafted." There's something about West of Loathing that feels personal and warm, as if all the jokes in the writing are jokes being told to you by an old friend during a long-awaited hangout session.
The combat, let's be real, is a little rudimentary. It's Paper Mario without the fun and flashy combos. There's a sense of strategy starting out with regard to what companion joins you on your journey, and acquisition of skills ends fairly quickly, leaving you with a reliable pool of abilities to get through most any encounter- but that's about it. Each class does rely on gear entirely differently, which is at least good for replay value- and that's something this game does in fact encourage.
Go into the journey West with the expectation that you will botch a number of things the first time through. The game allows you to fail on more than one occasion- I myself was permanently banned from the circus on my first playthrough, and on that very same playthrough did irreversible damage to equipment that would have provided my party with a pretty exciting upgrade. But sometimes missing the mark can actually create even more gameplay- showing up to one of the game's later areas without a requisite item will actually unlock an entire, lengthy quest sequence you'd otherwise miss!
If I had to sum up West of Loathing in one word, I'd call it "charming." Its art style doesn't leave anything to be desired, despite the characters being represented as stick figures. The animations are lively, varied, and exceptionally smooth. It much more faithfully calls to mind imagery of being bored in class and doodling in a notebook than any number of games that have deliberately sought out that aesthetic.
If you're a thorough explorer, you'll see all that WoL has to offer in slightly shorter order than some large open-world games, but you can expect to see much greater variation from place to place than those games tend to offer. The West in West of Loathing is full of landmarks and secrets, and I didn't find even one of them to be a disappointment. There's always something for your time, which caters very nicely to treasure hunters like me.
I don't really like giving ratings out of ten, but maybe I can give WoL a letter grade. It feels like an A to me- missing the mark of an A+ due almost entirely due to how rudimentary the combat can be. Maybe the upcoming DLC can add enough content to gloss over that- or if we're really lucky, improve it. Who knows?

West of Loathing
West of Loathing is an indie satyrical RPG focused on exploration. Choosing between 3 quirky classes you set out to the west with barely anything to your name as you explore a plethora of interesting places for hours on end.
Although the graphics may at best be charming and at worst can turn off some gamers and the combat gameplay is nothing ground breaking. The places are definitely well-designed. There is rarely any negative possibility space. You feel as though each location you visit has meaning or at least something interesti ng. This game made you want to explore the world and it's well designed levels and puzzles.
But where this game shines brightest is its narrative and story-telling. This game thrives on its ability to present its story in a satyrical and humorous way without it seeming too cheesy. It is becoming increasingly less common nowadays for games to emphasize a well-written script that this becomes a breath of fresh air from other games that have emphasized graphics and gameplay (not that there is anything wrong with those games).
Who do I recommend it to?
Anyone who is a fan of satyrical and self-referential humor will definitely have hours to burn here.
Anyone who loves exploring interesting locations.
Anyone who wants a good laugh.
Puzzle and RPG fans.
People who love to explore a large open world.

Upon loading Far Cry 2 for the first time I had no idea what to expect ; I went into the game blind and on hard difficulty setting . I simply had no idea what a gem of a game awaited me for the next 100 hours of gameplay.
As I entered Africa I found myself in a cab taking in the spectacular landscaps Africa offered . I listened intently as the driver told me stories of oppressed citizens who are fleeing from bloodthristy warlords who control the state . It wasnt long before I started to feel nauseous and dizzy , soon my world faded to black and I awoke in a hotel room with a man rummaging through my belongings . He began to taunt me with machete and a pistol . I soon realized that this was the man  I am seeking The Jackal because I am a merc and this is my story.
Far Cry 2 is an open world FPS game that gives you the player the freedom to play however you see fit. If you want to travel by vehicle you can . Far Cry 2 gives you a variety of vehicles to choose from . Cars , Buggies , Jeeps , cargo trucks , and assault trucks with either a M249 M2 or an Mk 19 mounted on the top . If you prefer to travel by water Far Cry 2 allows you to this as well with the choice of a swamp boat or a fishing boat also with a handy M249 M2 or a MK 19 mounted on the bow of the boat. You can even swim if thats what you want to do . Sometimes its a better life choice to take to the bush to avoid detection or simply to lose your attackers . In certain situations you can take to the air in hang glider and take in sprawling landscapes . The choice is yours how you want to travel . Far Cry 2 also gives you five fast travel stations that will help you  avoid many dangerous gaurd posts that are scattered accross the map.
Unlike most FPS games that give you easy map navigation via a mini map and quest markers , Far Cry 2 makes you look at an actual map for navigation . On the map you will need to unlock gaurdposts that each have a a supply crate that you may need . After you kill the gaurds and search the camp you will unlock either ammo , Molotov , explosives , or a health crate . But be warned if you return to any post in need of its supplies the gaurds manning the post will have respawned . I very much liked this feature as it made the game more challenging to play . Mercs will occupy vehicles as well in an attempt chase and kill you. In In Far Cry 2 you will learn very quickly that their are very few friendlies in the game.

You will encounter a few friendlies in the game in the form of "buddies" . Buddies will offer you missions throughout the game that that will increase your overall rep or upgrade the safe houses you have liberated. Sometimes buddies will be involved in the quest and if they are KIA during a mission a new buddy will replace them. Every time you encounter a safehouse for the first time you will need to destroy the mercs gaurding it. After you take out the mercs the house is unlocked and you can save at it. Your safe house can be upgraded by completing buddy missions. Potential upgrades consist of Jeep with weapon mount, medkits , ammo crate , molotov crate , and explosive crate. It is very advisable to prioritize safehouses early in the game. Unlike gaurd posts mercs will never return to a house once it has been liberated it.
Like its predecessor Far Cry 2 gives you 4 weapon slots , plus two throwing weapons in the form of gernades and molotovs. But unlike its predecessor Far Cry 2 categorizes in three forms. The first form is your primary weapon slot and it consits of shotguns , assault rifles , sniper rifles , and the powerful MGL 140 gernade launcher. Your shotgun classes are the Homeland 37 , SPAS - 12 , and the deadly USAS - 12 . Your assault rifles consists of G3 - KA4 , AK - 47 , Silent MP - 5 , FAL Paratrooper , and the AR - 16. Sniper rifles consist of the M1903 , Dragunov SVD , and the AS50. You should try to familiarize yourself with each weapon because this will give you far more flexibility on how you plan an attack.
Your secondary weapons consist of pistols , submachineguns , flare gun , IED , and the M - 79 gernade launcher. Your pistols are the Makarov , Star .45 , Silent Makarov 6P9 , and the Eagle .50 . Submachincegun choices are MAC - 10 and the Uzi. Again familiarize yourself with all secondaries serves to give you more flexibility and can save your *** in a tight situation. The final weapon slot is called the special.
Firstly you have the choice of a PKM , RPG - 7 Rocket Launcher , LPO - 50 , Dart Rifle , M - 249 SAW , Type 63 Mortar and the Carl G Rocket Launcher . Your final slot will always be taken up with a machete . By mixing and matching weapon synerigies gives you the most options options on how you choose to play FarCry2 , thus allowing you to keep a fresh perspective while playing. You can only carry one weapon of each class so choose wisly as a wrong weapon synergy will end in another brutal death at the hands of the mercs.
All weapons will be unlocked by purchasing them from the weapons dealer. The only currency he accepts are diamonds. And said diamonds can only be obtained by missions or by finding them hidden throughout the map. Accepting Dealer quests is vitol because completing them will result in you getting a new set of weapon unlocks. Be warned powering through all the dealers quests will result in all secondary quests dissapearing ,  leaving you with only main story quests during that phase of the game. So stagger them out if you want to complete all side quests for 100% completion.
Early on in the campaign you learn that you have contracted Malaria. This creates some very intense situations as you can have an attack during a firefight. To counter the attack you will need Malaria pills , and in this part of the world medications are in short supply. Throughout the game you will be given missions to help the people of this wartorn state. Upon completion of the quests you will be given your medicine. Staying healthy is a priority if you want to kill the Jackal.
Finally play the game as you like by going in guns blazing or stealth your way to fame and fortune . Buy weapon and vehicle upgrades to increase your chance at survival . Kill as many warlords as you can to increase your rep so that the mercs will fear you . Make sure you keep up on your supply of Maleria pills as failure to do so will cause you to to get dizzy and shake uncontroltrollaly at the most inopportune time . Far Cry 2 will kill you in many ways until you learn how to be adaptable , do not get frustrated with this as the game was intended to be difficult . Far Cry exceeded my expectations of it . I would highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys a challenge in an FPS game.
Now that's what I call a huge improvement on a sequel!

Never had much use for watering my own plants, but surprisingly this little game snuck into my weekly routine and has shown me a little of what it must be like for real life plant waterers! I cannot deny the simple, quietly satisfying appeal.
It started out as a laugh; I tried this out as something to show off to my lady. She always gives the snail a spray of water. His name is Jacques. Yes, you can name every plant and your snail, too. Jacques needs that sweet, sustaining hydration to keep pumping out that snail juice (or whatever he excretes) in what appears to be his attempt at the Guinness World Record for longest continuous lap around the rim of a plant pot.
Plants turn a slightly darker, muted shade when they need watering. Eventually you'll be able to identify this by eye. There's nothing to it, just click a plant and click the spray bottle icon. You can get one free plant per week from the in-game store. If one freebie a week isn't enough, there are all manner of plants for sale in the store too. For a very modest fee, some cutesy backgrounds can be purchased that I think go a long way, given the base game is free.
Your plants will grow thirsty and wither in real time if you don't water them, but enabling the very convenient pause feature (Vacation Mode) allows you to safely ignore the game over any amount of time and perfectly preserve your selection of succulents.
The soundtrack has very similar sounding tunes but they're all pleasant and fit the game perfectly. The soundtrack is posted to Steam for sale.
Hats off to
for
. Such a neat little app, unexpectedly comforting and meditative. Now I'm curious to check out their other title,
. Thumbs up review, recommended to any who could use another de-stress technique in their life.
TIP: You can remove the snail and it will safely return to your pot the next time you log on (so rest easy if you accidentally chucked him into the extra-planter-bowl abyss).
EDIT: Nominated for the Steam Awards 2017 category: The “The World Is Grim Enough Let's Just All Get Along” Award. If it's about a peaceful reprieve rather than combat or conflict, this game takes the cake for me!

is a casual/ adventure/ point- and-click game inspired by R.L. Stine, the original creator of the
series. You play as either a boy or a girl, you are given the choice and you travel through three areas to uncover the mystery surrounding strange happenings in your neighborhood. Upon impulse, you press on until you see a two-story mansion that has replaced your old house that you grew up in with your older brother, Chad if playing as the male in the game. You then come across three ghost children that remain in the house until you can solve their problem, usually centered around a particular object of comfort in order for them to vanish in thin air and for you to be able to access later stages in the game (i.e., the basement in the house, master bedroom).

Ready to be in middle school again (if you are out of middle school)? Even being the age where I could have children in middle school (I don't) I still had a lot of fun with this game. I was obsessed with R.L. Stine- goosebumps and fear street when I was in middle school, so I have the experience and background despite being ancient.
Art: 8/10 - The art holds nicely to the style of book covers, which is nice and reminiscent. It's not beautiful but correctly stylized for this kind of game, complete with lovely toxic green ooze. Also they didn't skimp on the backgrounds, I like that.
Story: 8/10 – I traveled back to tweenhood in a good way. R.L. Stein has not lost his knack for writing correctly for his audience. I loved one of the lines that said something along the lines of stickers on lockers are the only thing more permanent than tattoos, sounds like something I would believe in middle school (even now that it sounds so silly) The only thing I had a problem with is the end, it was kind a little too silly even for the goosebumps world if you ask me.
Game Mechanics: 9/10 – There is two mechanics in this game that I have always wanted in adventure games in this one. First you can pick up so much useless junk. I always want to do this, when I take a yellow cotton candy, why can't I take all of the colors? I don't like not being able to have variety even if the majority of it is stuff I won't use. You never know when you need a voodoo head or a blue rose from your neighbor’s yard or maybe even a crumpled up note on the school hallway floor. The other thing I liked is how you can die a lot. I mean not blood and gore dying but I like how you can make dumb choices that lead to untimely death. What would a goosebumps game be without ulitimate doom waiting at the end of some choices?
Positive: The whole feel of the game, great for a goosebumps fan!
Negative: Music, it was pretty unremarkable as I already forgot every track except for Chad's theme (because it was funny). I didn't even bother to rate it. I also felt it was a bit short but I am biased to longer stories (also I am not a middle schooler and I have a much longer attention span.
TLDR (Or if you are in middle school) You like goosebumps? Play this game.

This game is an interesting premise; sandbox/resource-centric game featuring robots.  Unfortunately, I cannot recommend it.
Pros
- Persistent, open, sandbox, malleable world.
- PvE and PvP with distinct and separate areas for each.
- Player controlled economy
- Player created/maintained corporations (guilds).
- Extensive crafting system.
- Complex time-based skill system
- Good number of robots to choose from each with pros and cons.
Cons
- Not newbie friendly (Overly long and tedious tutorial)
- Clunky UI (Not suited for people that have trouble with small/fine print)
- Few, large, old, player empire corporations
- Silent in-game community.  Overly helpful with too much information for a question asked then quiet the rest of the time.  May also overwhelm new players with 'gifts' of in-game money for no reason.
- Extremely low population for an MMO.
- Boring combat with limited cover mechanic (target, press button, watch auto-combat, rinse, repeat)
- Crafting system is a long, drawn-out process that can take several hours or days to complete an item.
This game could be so much more and does have elements to it that can make it interesting.  The background story also has merit but hasn't been expanded upon at all since its initial inception.
If you played this game before and wish to return to see what's changed, some things have but the biggest change is the sheer lack of people.
If you're new, this game will test your patience and you're likely to walk away bored or frustrated (or both).

This game is basically just a lower quality EvE with a stronger emphasis on mining. However, in this game, mining is much more of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Instead of just going to a location and mining stuff, you have to play a mini-game.
For the mini-game, you have to equip and use a geo-locator of sorts, then load it with the specific type of mining locating charge that you want. The charge will find that type of material and that type of material ONLY, no other types, just that one, and it'll only show you the nearest one, and tells you nothing about it, other than in what direction it is away from you. Not a distance, just a direction, and there's a fair bit of error in it too, so you can't fully depend on it. Then, after you find where the deposit is, you have to equip another type of charge to scan the tiles around you to determine which tiles contain how much of the material in your immediate area. So that's two different types of charges you need for mining only ONE type of material. But wait, there's more. In order to mine the material, you need a THIRD type of mining charge for your mining laser, and again, this charge will only mine one specific type of material, no others. So if you're looking for a few different types of materials, you have to have 3 different charges for each one whereever you go, and they're not exactly cheap nor small, they take up quite a bit of cargo space.
All of this is kind of a nice change of pace from EvE's point and click adventure in mining, but it gets tedious VERY quickly. I'd love to recommend EvE, but that game might be worse...

With the success of Super Mario Kart on the SNES, many other companies wanted a piece of the cartoony cart racing pie. Wacky Wheels is one of those, and among PC-gamers, it's one of the more famous ones.
Before I get going with the review, I should point out that I had this game as a kid. I also had an SNES with Super Mario Kart. I did not play this game much.
Wacky Wheels is a DOS game from 1994, and it looks the part. The sprites are big and colourful, but not very detailed, nor well animated. Still, it's not a bad looking game, all things considered. The different characters display a good amount of personality in their sprites, and this is really the strong point of the games looks.
The sound is simple. There's nothing wrong with it, but apart from the main menu music, I'm struggling to remember anything about what the game sounded like, and that means that the sound design did its job, but not much more.
Wacky Wheels is an arcadey kart racer, and it has a lot in common with Super Mario Kart. You drive around a series of tracks, with the goal of getting to the finish line before anyone else. Like other kart racers, there are power-ups scattered along the track. You can always tell what it is that you're about to pick up, be it bombs, fireballs, oil patches or hedgehogs. Actually, the hedgehogs are what sets this game apart from its contemporary competitors. When you don't have any other weapon (all are single-use), using the fire button fires a hedgehog in a straight line, and if it hits an opponent, it makes them spin out. The hedgehogs are weaker than the other weapons, though as you can carry a lot of them, they become the main offense power. And you keep them between levels.
There are some simple terrain hazards, like water, sand, and things placed in the track that forces you to be on your guard when you race, though these are generally not all that hard to avoid.
The track design is a bit repetitive. While the game has 42 different tracks, they end up feeling quite similar after a little while, and none of them are particularly memorable.
Much like any good Kart racer, this game offers a 2-player mode, and this is where it's at its best. Split screen racing can be good fun, if you can find someone else to play with. Racing against the AI is a passable experience, but the AI feels very rigid in how it acts (much like other kart racers from the era).
But there's one big elephant in the room. The framerate. This has nothing to do with sloppy dosbox settings (which is often the case with DOS games on steam), the game really ran this poorly back in the days. It's supposed to run like this. And this sadly kills most of the fun, as the game feels sluggish and unresponsive.
Wacky Wheels is a cart racer that tried to go up against Super Mario Kart back in the days. If you did not have SNES with Super Mario Kart, it was not a terrible game to spend your time with, in particular if you could invite a friend over to play with you. These days I don't see much of a reason to play it though, outside of nostalgia, the game feels sluggish and unresponsive, and there are better kart racing games out there.

Wacky Wheels was a racing game from 3D Realms, the same company that brought us the Duke Nukem franchise. The first thing that would come to mind that this game is very similar to Super Mario Kart in many ways except the racers are all zoo animals. The game unfornately suffers from difficulty in both the tracks and hazards. There's various tracks with very sharp turns and I kept ramming myself into barriers or hazards. Due to the landscapes being flat it's hard to notice if I am on the track or about to collide against something without realizing it. The most annoying issue is that the kart you drive in can take damage if you keep ramming into hazards or walls. When that happens the racer flies out of the kart and crashes into the screen leaving a crack to create a fourth wall humor. And then you are force to start the race all over again. With enough practice I probably could get better at this game, but there's tons of better racing games out there. Wacky Wheels just never got the same popularity as Mario Kart did.

1-3/2016 Original Review:
Picture Dead Island.  Now, take away all the zombies, skill trees, interesting characters, and set the game in Africa.  Hey look, you've got Far Cry 2, a game with a meaningless protagonist who loves doing people's chores!  I get why people could enjoy this game, but I really didn't.  I have yet to finish the game and I'm dreading having to press on.  Here's some pros and cons to help you understand why:
Pros:
-Absolutely beautiful atmosphere/map.  Looking out over a desert, lake, or bayou at sunset is amazing.
-This game's multiplayer was my childhood, and the custom maps feature is awesome.  Playing escape maps with friends online holds some great memories for me.  Unfortunately, online play for this game is near dead now, but if you can get a chance to play some custom maps with friends they're fun.
Cons:  Oh god, where do I start.
-Gameplay wise, get ready for some repetition.  Talk to an NPC, get a quest, drive to the other side of the damn map (or use the poorly implemented quick travel system), shoot people or blow something up, rinse & repeat.  It feels like a sin for a game with such a vast environment to feel so slow, dry, and outright boring.
-This game is literally driving Simulator 2009 edition.  You have to drive so much, only to be interrupted halfway to your destination which feels 35253 miles away by some random mercenary who thought it'd be tactical to literally ram the hell into you.  This occurs WAY too often and gets extremely annoying.
-The game is divided into two acts.  The problem with this, is by the end of act one the game feels like it's ready to end.  But it doesn't.  It goes into act two.  This literally made my jaw drop.  I was so ready to be done with this driving simulator.
-If you're looking for a good story, don't come here.  In the beginning of the game, your character gets an idea in their mind of what they want to do.  Without spoiling anything, I'll say that at literally
opportunity they get to carry out their objective, they're hindered physically (in pain, can't move, etc etc).  Total bs.  If this was the main goal of the game, I'd go to think they'd lift a finger a little more.  I think at the point in the game I'm currently at I can see why the protagonist might be changing their mind about
but since our character doesn't talk we have no way of knowing their intentions.
Overall if you're a fan of the Far Cry series give this a whirl.  Otherwise stay away, stay far away.

While initially likeable, the game quickly turns into a series of frustrations and non-sensical events.
There'd be a lot to like if the game didn't have so many problems.  It's fairly long, plenty of entertaining dialogue and some interesting characters.
The biggest problem the game suffers from is that many of the puzzles are so obscure that there is almost no conceivable way to complete the game on your own.  You will need to use a walkthrough, many times, to figure out what you're supposed to be doing.  Good friggin' luck figuring out the combination lock solution.  It's one thing to look up a solution and feel like an idiot for not thinking of doing something.  In this game, every time you have to look something up, you'll feel like you've been cheated.  Some of them I can't even imagine anyone figuring out except by complete accident.  A quick example:   When you get to the high rollers club, you're supposed to lock the waiter into a cabinet in the kitchen.  There's no way to make him go into the kitchen though, so you'll run around trying to figure out how you're supposed to make that happen.  The solution:  Simply stand in the kitchen for 10-20 seconds and he'll walk in the kitchen and into the cabinet.  There's absolutely no indication or any way for you to know this is the solution, and there's no reason you'd ever stand around in that room for that long anyway by that point.
The inventory system is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥  Instead of having everything showing up in one area, you have to click an arrow to get to the next inventory item, watch an animation of him putting away the current item and pulling out the next one, and repeat until you finally get to the item you want.  Also, the scythe is a solution to several puzzles throughout the game, so you'll have to pull it out occasionally when you're trying to guess your way to a non-sensical answer.  Every time you pull this damn thing out, you have to watch a 5 second animation of him unfolding it.  Then when you put it away, you have to watch another 5 second animation of him folding it back up.  It gets old quickly.
The story doesn't really make any sense.  Pretty much everything he does from year 2 onwards is for the love of a woman that you've very briefly met and talked to during year 1.  There's no real indication or interaction with her that would lead you to believe he's in love with her.  At some point, he just randomly says it.
The game also has several game breaking bugs, so if you do decide to play, make sure you do a hard save every 15-30 minutes.  I had one occur on the elevator at the High Rollers Club.  Drove the forklift into the proper spot and had it hook in.  Then I drove it backwards and hopped out.  Game wouldn't let me get back in so I was forever trapped in the elevator.  Fortunately, I did have a hard save close by.
The game is also occasionally inconsistent which can lead to frustration.  Some examples:  I knew I was supposed to hop into a container in the kitchen, but there was no pointer mark there indicating I could do so, so I was stuck and had to look up the solution.  Solution:  Walk up a nearby ladder and while up on the shelf, the indicator now appears for you to hop in.  Now, pretty much every other climbable object in the game has an indicator that you can climb it, yet the ladder has no indicator for it, you simply click up above it and you walk up it.  There's no way to know you can do this and no reason that you would think you should be able to.  It's also frustrating that it requires climbing the ladder for the mark to show up on the container since there's no actual screen transition.  Another solution to a puzzle requires you to drink something with metal pieces in it.  Well, it doesn't matter if you've drunk the liquid 20 different times outside of that specific room, you have to do it in that room only.  No reason to think that drinking outside of the room shouldn't give you the same result, but it does.
I also found the walking speed to be an annoyance.  If you double click, you can make him run.  The instant you tell him to do something on a mark though, he walks at an intolerably slow speed.  So you have to constantly be double clicking near something to get him to run there and then use the marks.  Seems like making him run everywhere would've been a pretty simple design choice.
Enjoyed at first, but as the game went on, I found it more and more frustrating and having to look up solutions that made me feel cheated didn't help.

Loved Kingdom of Loathing, love West of Loathing. Lots of little things to do, and you can take as little or as much time as you want to finish it.

As a fan of Kingdom of Loathing, I can safely say that West of Loathing is an equally hilarious and involving game about stickfigures getting drunk and beating up goblins. In contrast with its predecessor, West of Loathing immerses you in a kinda-sorta-real (but definitely, definitely not real at all) wild west environment that is loaded with lore and references from its namesake, including food related magic, goblins with terrible grammar, and various other callbacks to KoL.
The Good:
-Excellent writing, on just about every level. West of Loathing will probably make you laugh (to tears, if you're like me) while its vivid descriptions of various happenstance apart from comedy will make you feel all sorts of things from disgust, to fear, to incredulity.
-Easy to understand combat. An RPG though it may be, West of Loathing has at least part of a dedication to accessibility, and accomodates players of all levels. It will challenge you and punish you, but never terribly or unfairly. More over, some well placed buff stacking can often help you overcome challenges, just like in KoL.
-Much like a classic adventure game, West of Loathing give you a great deal of freedom to do whatever you like in whatever order you'd like to do it. The way you're dropped into the world and made to "figure it out" makes for a compelling, organic experience.
-Stupid Walking.
The Less Good:
-Game lacks a truly effective quest log. It's not that I don't necessarily respect the decision to not include it, but the rate at which you can become bogged down with things to do, especially in a text based game, can become quite staggering. Without a better quest log, it gets a little mind boggling.
-The same sort of organic and non-linear gameplay used in WoL can sometimes cause you to miss out on content without ever realizing it, or locking yourself out of certain things without knowing it. (I like this about the game, personally, but I could see why others wouldn't.)
Altogether, this is a very good, and surprisingly large RPG. If you played or still play Kingdom of Loathing, don't miss this. Even if you didn't, it's a solid, well written, and extremely funny experience for only eleven dollars.

(So far at least.) Art and graphic style is pleasing but also doesn't take you out of the feel of Goosebumps. I've run into plenty of identifiable objects/mysteries so far (though haven't solved or used a bunch of them... yet!). But if you're not familiar with them, I don't think you really lose much either. Anything you would is usually just a "welp, that's a death" scenario where the start over can correct your error.
The enjoyment of the game definitely comes from the game itself, not just its throw backs, and so far I am having a blast.
