There is a staggering amount of things to do in this game. It does have much in common with EVE in that it is highly windowed, but it also has some nice features that EVE is lacking, such as the ability to actually control combat (use cover, etc) and the ability to make changes to the world itself. The learning curve is steep, like EVE, but if you enjoyed that game, and have ever wondered how cool it would have been to have gotten in on the ground floor of a game like that before everyone else had an account 10 years older than yours, then come play this one. While it is early access, it's already 50 times more polished than EVE was when it was much older than this.

I will say this first: If you played EVE Online for at least a few months, there is a much less steep learning curve. Though changes are slot to come out and can be buggy as all hell, they respond to the tickets they get about the bugs with a small patch. Usually within 24 hours. This is a game that has been around for quite some time and could use a asthetic facelift,
The positive side to things is that if you get in with the right corp, you can get access to Beta Islands (Open PvP with outposts, all but 1 of which a corp can take over and control), and out to the Gamma Islands that have been added back (Open PvP with no outposts other than the ones that players build). Certain materials/plants can only be gathered on Beta or Gamma islands.
The negative side is that there are only two major corporate alliances. that control all the Beta and Gamma islands. They tend to shoot you first and never question you about your intent on their island. So you've got to be weary of that.
Find out which corporate alliance is which and what they have to offer and how they'll treat you. One is overrun with players who've been playing for so long that they have the best robots and best modules, more NIC than they know what to do with, and several backups of the best robots and best modules all over the islands.
I do like that it's open-ended, though. If you were to ask what the end-game is some would say that it's PvP, some would say that it's getting into a corp with a Beta Outpost, some would say it's getting into a corp with a Gamma Outpost, and others would say that it's whatever you want it to be. Specialize in combat and do PvE and PvP. Mining minerals or harvesting plants can pay very well, depending on the buy orders in various Alpha islands.
I am in a corp that ended up allying with the wrong group. They were demanding, arrogant, and treated our leadership like they were just a figurehead in a dummy corp. It fell apart, but a few months later, it reformed and we have a Beta Outpost and a Gamma Base built. Our people are friendly and offer advice or front you bots/modules/NIC to get you started. We never ask for anything in return other than you being willing to help out new people like you were helped out.
Speaking of joining a chat channel, that segues into the tutorial. It's very informative but it's a lot of information that you won't really appreciate or fully grasp right out of the gate. That's really not something that can be helped. It would be nice if you could skip the tutorial, because I have more than one account, but I've done it often enough I know where everything is and can speed through it.
You can see what corporations a character has been part of in the past and for how long, but all they have to do is start a new character on their account and use it to spy. That's probably one of the biggest issues. "All is fair in love and war" but the ease of how a spy can slip a dummy character into a corporation and there be no way to tell, is a bit ridiculous, really. Putting the names of what characters created on that account and what corporation they've been in or are in they've had in the past would cut down on the easy way to set a spy in with another corp. If it's going to be possible to create a spy character then it should at least time some sort of skill to do it.
Extensions (skills) are increased over time with 1 point per minute every 24 hours (1440 minutes in a day = 1440 EP/day).
I've been around since it launched on Steam (about 1.75 years ago) and I still enjoy it. I enjoy mining. It relaxes me. Do I do things on PvP islands? Heck yeah! I spend a good deal of my time on Beta and Gamma islands and I'm not into PvP. I've lost a few bots to other plays and to NPCs. But, it's just a game. So after a few hours break most people have calmed down enough to just accept that it's happened and move on.
They've recently redone the Alpha 1 and Alpha 2 islands, both in looks and a different way of doing missions (for NIC and sometimes a module or bot upgrade and tokens to purchase the racial "PvP ammo" or Beacons, you'll learn about those if you pay).
The pathing script needs work because your bot will take the shortest overland route without regard to speed boosts from Accelerator Srips (aka "Highways") and Teleporters. Also, the NPC behavior is in many ways quite boring and predictable but can be very frustrating and evil (in a good way). You get zerged if you don't kill them fast enough or run away (Alpha 1 islands) , you don't aggro the whole group when you kill one (Alpha 2 & Beta Islands), or they do hit and run waves of skirmish tactics (Gamma islands).
Summary:
Is it pefect? No, but they are working on it.
Is it fun? That depends on what you find fun but I still love it.
Is it worth the price for 1 account to play it and see if you like it? Yeah. Some people play it for a few days or a few weeks and then just stop playing. Others stick around and get things going themselves.
I would recommend that you at least give it a chance. You won't learn everything on the first day. Be patient and choose who's company you keep carefully.

Perpetuum is the one and only alternative to EVE Online. Whether you like to play industrial non combat character or a beefed up Terminator mech, this game lets you play the way you want. It is a sandbox game with a 100% player driven economy that relies on the players to make their own story and fun. Unfortunately that is also where it stumbles, since the population is nowhere near what you need for a thriving sandbox game. Unlike EVE where a corporation that has 16 members is considered small, in Perpetuum you're talking about one of the bigger corps. Despite this, the game is in a solid shape and is worth recommending.
The game features a variety of small spider like bots and mechs you can pilot that you can fit different types of modules with, ranging from simple weapons  and armor to electronic warfare and battery rechargers.
Sound and music is great, I enjoyed the simple soundtrack and the combat/movement felt impactful and heavy.
Graphics wise, the game isn't spectacular. The textures look terrible, lighting is okayish, the mech variety is nice, but the landscapes all look the same. And when you look at the sharp edges and sudden terraforming walls on the advanced islands, it stabs you in the eye and destroys any sense of world immersion.
However, that is not where the game shines - this game is all about multiplayer and PvP. Ganging up and fighting it out with other players! The combat is strategic and requires more awareness than EVE does, because there are obstacles that block your shots and people can hide behind them. You will want to join a corp as soon as possible and do group content, since you not only get more money, but also more fun that way.
Devs are active and update the game regularly, so you don't have to worry about it being abandoned.
Thumbs up!

Quite simply one of the most immersive and lovely games Iv'e ever played.
Planet Nomads encourages creativity and creative problem solving all against the backdrop of a beautiful planetscape.
(Writing a new review in light of the updates which have added so much to Planet Nomads recently).
Considering this game has only been out for 6 months it has come a long, LONG, way. There have been some very big changes and more are to arrive very soon. Craneballs, the developers, have worked so hard updating the game on a weekly basis, and listened to the comments and suggestions on the forums from the playerbase regularly.
There is still much to be done, and still bugs that need fixing....all that would be expected form a game still in early access, but right now there is now is a game that is very unique, enjoyable, and very much worth playing for lots of reasons.
The new Planetary Options allow for a lot of customisation to make the kind of planet you want to visit.
First off..the planet you crash land on is a *globe* so you can journey right round it and eventually come back to where you started from!  The Custom variation in size means it can be so huge it will take you many hours to traverse (recommended!) There are many diverse biomes to explore: hot deserts, mountainous ranges, deep oceans, bleak icy poles, dense leafy tropics, lakes, swamps, all extremely beautiful in their own unique way. There are also diverse wildlife to encounter on the way; some friendly and cute, others that are best avoided! :D My favourites are the blue speckled salamander types that snarl with big toothy grins if you get too close. Other planetary options allow you to customise the amount of water, how mountainous or how flat you want it, day/night cycle length, the density of the wildlife and the weather. It would be good to see more options develop here.
The most engaging feature of the game has to it's encouragement of experimentation with the building blocks. At present it is limited, the general philosophy seeming to be that *less is more* and it works in the most part! There is so much you can do already with the blocks available. One of the best new recent additions was the hoverpads, which can be used in many different creative ways; not just for a myriad of inventive propulsion methods, but for making wierd and wonderful machines of all sorts! Again...more needs to be added for sure, but what there is presently will keep a creative mind active for many 100's of hours.
A game with a very bright future that is really going places thanks to the unique vision of Craneballs! I personally look forward to many more 100's of hours of gameplay.

Labyrinth is going to be a very exciting game when all is said and done. Of this I am one hundred percent certain. Imagine a card game such as Hearthstone or Magic The Gathering in a turn-based strategy combat game. It’s as exciting as it sounds and the combat comes hard and fast with the main form of strategy coming in the form of having a great understanding of the cards in your possession and the manner in which the enemies, especially the bosses, maneuver and how to combat that.
Unfortunately at this very early stage of development there isn’t very much content to get through and you can complete what is there in half an hour – more if you’re not as skilled at this type of game. However, do keep in mind that the game is early access and what you do get to experience already is a bite sized piece of what the developers are constantly working and striving towards. As such there isn’t very much to discuss gameplay wise other than to say that I enjoyed my time going through the three different combatants that I got to face in my time with the game (thus far that is all that there is).
I played with three characters throughout my experience all of which come with their own unique card decks which means that you’ll have to learn not only one set of cards but however many different classes are in your party. At this stage there is a tank (warfare hero), a healer (faith hero) and a pyromancer (wizardry hero). There is also a rogue (skulduggery hero). Each of the classes that I got to play with behave exactly as you would imagine the class to in this type of game which is already a very strong advantage for the game.
The only thing holding it back at this stage of development is its lack of content but it is coming. Labyrinthe has the potential to be an outstanding collectible card game which is something that I very much look forward to sinking time into and to drag me away from Hearthstone.

Grim Fandango, the once forgotten LucasArts masterpiece has arrived on Steam.  Now this is a remaster I was really excited for.  There's simply something about the game that makes it so unique.  To start off, the story is pure genius; taking on the role of Manny, a travel agent in the Land of the Dead who chases after a lost client after the business becomes crooked!  That's the bare basic, If I were to tell why this story truly shines I'd spoil it.  What I can say is that it has one of the best cast of characters in all of video games and happens to be the first game to make me laugh out loud.  The humor is spot on and the art is beautiful.  Now before I go on praising this game a little too much (which isn't a problem), I must mention:  It truly is story based...  In the sense that the gameplay is hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥  While the remaster is great for those who grew up around it, this game is in no way designed for this generation of gamers.  I won't blame you if you use a walkthrough through the entire game.  The game focuses around puzzles which require you to think way outside of the box.  I find most games easy because you can say:  "Oh I won't try doing that, it's just a video game, It can't have that many complex options..."  Not in this case, you need to be extremely specific.  Also, there's only one solution to the puzzle that usually has you running around doing the most illogical things possible!  But enough about that, I only bought the game back then for it's story; I knew what I was getting into.  Onto the real question; should you buy it?  Absolutely!  Buy it now!  It's an incredible journey.  Not only for Manny and friends but most importantly for you!  You'll laugh, you'll think, you'll slap yourself in the face a few times and scream "WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥?!?!"  But in the end it's all worth it.  It has easily one of the best story and characters in gaming and is an experience I never forgot.

My favorite and only card game I'm playing right now. Just amazing level of strategies that can be introduced, huge variety of playstyles and deck builds. Just to give you a basic idea of how easy it is to make a viable deck, I made a deck specifically to fulfill two of the daily challenges, I call this deck Lethal-Breakthrough because I made it heavy with "Lethal" (Kills any card on attack) and "Breakthrough" (Deal surplus damage to opponent) and I've won most of my matches with it because you can make just about any combination of strategies viable once you understand the game mechanics. My favorite deck is probably Aela's Companions, because they turn into werewolves when you deal enough damage to remove an opponent's rune (every 5 dmg you lose a rune, draw a card, and play the card during your opponent's turn if it has the "Prophecy" keyword).
My favorite part about this game is that the rune system means you will have some amazing upsets, like I've been at less than 10 dmg and my opponent gets cocky and forgets I have a couple cards that will turn into werewolves when they lose a rune and BAM my werewolves now has "Drain" and I start clawing back up to full health and suddenly they're losing when they were just beating me badly by more than 10hp. You really have to watch everything and be ready for anything, I've lost a couple matches when I was winning by a landslide because when you break all your opponent's runes you've just given them 5 more cards than you!
Definetely worth a try, very easy to understand and huge complexity of options, playstyles and strategies.
Oh and everything can be purchased with in-game currency if you play long enough, only PTW perk is time.

Going to try to leave reviews of games now... and I've recently been playing a lot of West of Loathing, so!
West of Loathing is a western RPG, mostly carrying itself in the writing department. And this isn't a bad thing at all; the amount of depth and choice you're given in this game, sometimes even for the simple reward of more dialogue, is highly enoyable and I find this an incredibly easy game to recommend. I didn't know about Kingdom of Loathing prior to this game, so rest assured you don't need to have any knowledge of it prior to this game. I'm not sure how to keep going so I'll just do a pros and cons list.
PROS:
- Writing; it's humorous but provides a lot of depth to the world. Actions feel like they all have consequences and ignoring major sidequests can and will affect your ending. I loved going around to every little object just to read the text.
- Music: There aren't too too many tracks but I never got tired of them. I'll probably buy the soundtrack now that it's available, it's very enjoyable.
- Gameplay: It's simple buy fun and easy to understand. You have three base classes that determine you're main skills, and from there you're free to screw up your character as you wish. The game also has autolevels if you find that intimidating. I plan to do more playthroughs to experience other classes.
- Graphics: Yes, they're simple and resemble a newgrounds title, but I like it and think they work quite well. Every hat and weapon appears and your character which is cute.
- PRICE: This game is CHEAP. One playthrough took me about 9 hours and I plan on playing more. I would pay more for this game.
CONS:
- No real way to work with saves: the game basically runs on autosaves which I like, but if you mess up you can't turn back. I believe this is intentional, but I do wish it was slightly more forgiving for when you make mistakes in the beginning (such as putting on the hard mode hat, without any prior knowledge of the games difficulty)
- UI: The UI works for the most part, but there's some clunkiness to it. You can't tell what items have an interaction without clicking on them in your invetory and that fills up fast. I like the silly names of items, but organizing them can be a drag. Like for example, I may be looking for a quest item, but I don't know what category of item it would possibly be, and the name of the item might be like "that darn cryptic message," when my brain is thinking "I'm looking for that note that I picked up earlier". The game does attempt to provide some rudimentary ways to organize your inventory which work slightly but I definitely had some headaches looking for items. Icons for the organization aren't always clear what is what. (I know some have mentioned the lack of a quest log, but I don't mind your partner filling that role, personally)
- Graphics: I know I praised the graphics earlier, but the style does lend itself to some problems in the busier environments of the game (like Buffalo Hill). It can occasionally be hard to tell what you can interact with.
- Accessibility: I didn't see a controller option for this game, but I feel it could easily work with one. Controllers tire out my hands less, so I hope in the future this is included.

I don't understand why people hate on this game so much, I think its pretty good.
For starters, I really enjoyed the amount of time I spent at the loading screen. It really built suspense for the game and heightened my excitement. Too many games nowadays just blaze through the load screen and it just kills the game for me.
I found the tutorial to be very helpful and necessary. Other computer games I play use a similar WASD configuration, but it feels *really* different for some reason on this game and was very worthy of explanation. It was also really important that the tutorial told us that the space key was jump - it would have taken me forever to figure that out. No other game that I've ever played uses the space key for jumping for some reason, even though it is a very large and very hittable key and it just feels really intuitive, so I hope other game developers take note.
Several times during the tutorial, I found myself being randomly disconnected on the server. This is by far the best feature in the game. Other games, like Team Fortress 2, waste several seconds waiting and determining if you are disconnected from the server. The problem though is I'm not a patient gamer - if there is even a nanosecond when I am not actually connected to the server, I want to know about it, and I want to be kicked off immediately. I don't want to give the enemy the satisfaction of being able to shoot me while I can't get away. Better yet, while in the tutorial, a disconnect from server meant re-starting the whole game. Who doesn't like starting fresh?

Came across this game in the steam sale. It is EvE with robots... its a little bit simpler than EvE, and the tutorial system is very helpful to really give a feel for the game and lead you through all aspects of the game necessary. It is obviously lower budget / update iterations than EvE as its main comparison.
The biggest difference though is terrain.. there is a lot of terrain which makes the battlefield a lot more dynamic which is an interesting addition.
I have found the community to be very helpful and found a corporation which has fully outfitted and looked out for me. I have spent my EP well and can fit quite a few things out of the gate.. although not terribly well :P
The biggest minus to this game is that the economy is very immature, in that there is little demand on the market, and little selling due to the low population. Bigger population would be the fix for that, or maybe centralising the market into 1 market to stimulate as a temporary fix.
With no economy there is no real need to mine/sell/haul except that it is the only realistic way to keep yourself robotted up, but if you are in a corp then they probably have resources to look after all that... so it seems like once you have skills to play a role in PvP / PvE, then you can support the corp and have no real need for your own in game wallet.

Succulent Plant Simulator 2015
This is a calm daily check-in kind of game.  Low-commitment.

You know the nice thing about plants?  They're real things that you can see or touch or even smell — maybe even taste, depending — without running a game to access them.  You can learn valuable skills both from and for tending plants.  You can propagate them by seed or by cutting, show them off, share them.  They have
, and in that you can find some sense of pride and accomplishment.
Viridi... not so much.
Making this game operate on a real-time scale puts it in direct competition with one of humanity's most venerable arts, but in a form which lacks most of the payoff.  Add to this a triad of game development crimes:
-Controls like a lubricated walrus on a skating rink
-Mystery meat navigation
-Redefining "free" with obsession-oriented microtransactions
Viridi is a lovely little screen saver... if only it moved, and if CRT monitors were still a thing.  Other than that, it's not really worth the price.

This is one of the best shooters I've ever played, better than the games afterwards. The open world activities are structured in a very simplistic way, but achieving your objectives is anything but simple. You constantly feel like you're under threat of being attacked when you're outside, and you have to spend about 15 minutes preparing for each mission. Picking and replacing your weapons and maybe even getting new Malaria pills. There's a lot to contend with, you have to take cover and buy yourself time to heal yourself, you need to make sure your weapons don't jam, and you need to defend the buddies you bring with you because they absolutely can die, leaving them gone for the rest of the game. All of this means that pulling off the missions feels INCREDIBLY rewarding.
Honestly I've never played a shooter as immersive as this, and yes the malria and guard post respawn issue is annoying, but not enough to break the game entirely. It's dynamic, it's dark and the world actually feels hostile to you rather than an open world playground. If you're willing to put up with its quirks, you'll find one of the most rewarding shooters of last gen here. They don't make 'em like this anymore.

'The Static Speaks my Name' is a great and rather unusual quick 10 minute game. There honestly is little to nothing to say about this game, as it is very short, and I'll have to add a spoiler alert to add content to this review. I'd recommend this game, it only takes about 10 minutes to play. However, be warned, this game does contain some rather dark and depressing topics.
The story is of a man so obsessed with a painting, a palm tree on a small desert island, most likely in the middle of an ocean. You play as the man's last night alive. The game itself is very short, and quite unusual, with simplistic tasks such as 'Using the bathroom' and 'Cleaning the microwave', then 'Deciding what to do with the man in the cage'.
I'll have to add a spoiler alert to these next parargraphs, as I'll tell the story, as some players didn't seem to understand it. You play as a rather odd man who's obsessed with a painting. Your tasks at the beginning require you to use the bathroom and get breakfast. However, there is nothing to eat, so the man resorts to eating 2 of his pet shrimps. The only room that you are not required to use is filled with the same painting all over the walls. Your character seems to have studied and cracked down on everything this simplistic palm tree painting has to offer; it'd also seem likely that your character has made some crazy conspiricies and observations.
One of your last taks is to decide what to do with the man in your cage. Before this, you have no understanding of this man in a cage. You're forced to pick up your keys (hung up next to your coat on a rack) and use them to open a bookcase that reveals a safe, in which a man, most likely the artist of your obsessed painting, is locked in a cage. You unlock the cage and then 'put yourself to rest', in which you open a door in your room which previously would've said 'not yet..' when you tried to interact with it. Vindictus a game I've played in the past and continue to return in hopes of its improvement, only to be upset time and time again.

I have participated in some endgame content such as dragon raids, which I found to be fun even though I died a lot, but I will not be covering that in this review.
Combat
++ Physics
++ Classic Hack and Slash
+ "Greater" Raids offer unique gameplay not seen as much in the Story
+- Fun w/ killing your friends via the environment
+- Spear Throw friend/foe (does no damage to friend)
+- Fluid and seamless depending on your specs, server, settings
- "Greater" Raids require 16 players to start
- Repetitive use of Skills
- Becomes more repetitive the higher your level
Gameplay
++ Limitless amount of AP (skill points) to spec every skill
+ Gold is an easily obtainable resource
+ Quests sometimes chain through completion (Doing one dungeon sometimes completes two quests)
- Storage is Limited unless you pay and a lot of resources are necessary for quests/crafting
- Linear Environment/Dungeons
- Linear Quest Line
- Linear Way to Kill Bosses - 1 Strategy is usually the most effective and used above all other strategies
- Bosses an enemies do not vary much every 10 levels
- Repeating the same dungeon more than twice - becomes more repetitve at higher levels
- As you level drop rates on items for quests become lower
- Upgrading is high risk or extremely expensive (RNG)
UI
+ Titles
- Cannot View channel location of friends via friend list
- Cannot View location of friends on the minimap
- Cannot Search for Unadded Friends in Friend Menu
- Emotes are hidden need to be googled
- Marketplace/Guild Search appear to be quite slow and may be using Internet Explorer
- Inactive Guilds die, leadership is not transferred
Cash Shop
+ Some of the greatest quality and entertaining costumes and goodies excessible in the RPG world
+- Nexon makes money primarily from costumes and so it appears to have become the focus of the game
+- Almost every second patch has a new costume
+- Wealth of a player shines, people will take their time to oggle you
- Players more interested in costumes than the actual gameplay
- Overpriced AND Restricted relative to other RPGs (common in many Nexon games)
- A bum is still a bum if they enter this game, the costumes and cash shop content are promoted so much that many active players end up buying it and new players or those that cannot afford it feel pressured or distaste.
Other
+ Controls are fair, supporting 3 modes
+- You use the same armor/weapon for most of the game
- Bugs take years to fix
- Sound quality is average
- Music is repetitive
- Monster cries, screams repetitive
Last thoughts:
This is a game you want to play with friends, preferrably join a guild or create one for the exp boost when you party together. This game a lot of perks to group play, but is not as rewarding to solo players.

This is a tricky one to recommend.
Firstly, this game is clearly not ready to buy for the gameplay. It is very unfinished. But I still recommend it as an early access game. A lot of early access games are very buggy, and you have to question whether the developers know what they are doing. If the developers aren't any good, the game won't meet anyones expectations.
But Planet Nomads has proven that they do have solid developers. The game runs well. What features are implemented are quite polished.
My only worry is that this turns into a hollow crafting game with no purpose or long term goals. I haven't done my research, so I don't know what is planned for the game. So far it's just your standard survive, explore, craft and build game.
I hope to eventually see NPCs, missions, storylines, random events, and things like that. As far as I can tell, nothing like this is implemented yet.
So I recommend this game for the traditional reason of wanting to see it become more than it currently is. If you are wanting to buy this game to play it, DON'T. Only buy it to support it.
Pros:
1. VISUALS - Great looking planet, plants, trees, wildlife. It's not just carbon copies of the same asset throughout the entire planet like in No Man's Sky.
2. CRAFTING - Manufacturing parts is pretty much spot-on. Not too many intermediate parts that make recipes confusing.
3. MACHINES/WIRING - Often crafting games completely avoid systems for machines. This game has an interface to configure machines, and wire up those which require electricity. Though the functions are basic now, it has a lot of potential for factorio-style production systems.
4. INTERFACE - Already this game shows great visuals for the interface, and has a straightforward help menu under F1-F5 keys. They are categorized well as Gameplay / Survival / Crafting / etc.
Cons:
1. CONTENT - Aside from a basic land vehicle and essential two tiers of buildings, there doesn't seem to be much to do. There are creatures who can become hostile, although the AI is basic.
2. INTERFACE - Interface was also one of my pro's, but a few features of the interface need improvement. You might end up like I did, being poisoned, radiated, and a few other issues. There doesn't seem to be a way to see what these debuffs are, what they do, or how to get rid of them. But I assume user experience and interface improvements will come, maybe the tutorial system will apply when you get poisoned for the first time, for example.

This will be updated as the game progresses through Early Access.
I got to play the brand-new Early Access version of the game last night (have been playing the Alpha all along), and it continues to show steady improvement with each release, and I think it is worth the money currently, for SOME of the potential buyers.
Of course, pricing an Early Access game is hard. Do you ask a low price, and then when you've got the game fully finished, you've already sold to 80% of your potential customers at that low price? Or do you charge the target price and continue development with people buying in as you add in your promised features?
Planet Nomads is taking the latter option, so then you would not necessarily find the game in it's current state to be worth the current price, depending on your expectations. BUT if you love a pretty, procedurally generated, multi-biome planet to explore, filled with weird, alien life, with survival, various elements of danger, mining/gathering/hunting, and crafting, including bases and ground vehicles, THEN the game is worth the current price. IF you also believe that these dedicated, hard-working, and proven developers will carry forward with adding the currently-promised features that will include air craft, space craft, building in orbit, and travel to additional planets, then it may also be worth it to you to buy. Otherwise, follow the development and see how it goes.
As far as the game goes, Craneballs is taking the opposite approach to that of Keen and their Space Engineers. Instead of developing from building in space toward the goal of landing and 'surviving' on planets, Planet Nomads is being developed from the point of surviving on a planet (after crash-landing in a pod with very little to sustain you), toward the goal of building a ship to launch into orbit and eventually reach other planets.
The Early Access phase marks the beginning of a fairly fleshed out planetary survival, exploring and building sandbox. We know there is much more to come, but the short term goals will be announced in about a week from now, according to their public development information. What is likely to come in the near-term is to add another species, extra species diversity, especially based on biome, fuel-use added to generators, additional block textures, 1st steps toward interplanetary travel, new biomes, alien structure spawning, along with the longer term goals that have originally been mentioned. The longer-term goals may include free-flight through space, building in orbit, additional planets, logical systems and/or automated systems, and other staples of sand-box building games. The planet's generation and advanced Level-of-detail representation is a crafted system meant to permit seemless surface to orbit flight. And at the top of the list of future features is multi-player.
Whether you like the current features, or find some of the promised features to be worth the chance, this game may be worth the current price. I backed the Kickstarter, so I've been playing some since the closed Alpha began, and obviously made the bet long ago that the final game would be worth what I paid. So far, it is looking like it will.

Planet Nomads seemed like a promising new Space Engineers, but after only a few hours, I had just about experienced everything I could. Quick reminder, Early Access doesn't excuse a game of critisism.
One of the best things in game is definitely the ambiance. It's very well done. The graphics are beautiful, and the music really helps add to the immersion of being lost and hopeless on an unknown world.
There are, however, a lot of issues. Textures pop all the time, leading to trees sometimes appearing between your vehicle's wheels, causing it to get stuck. Other times, a rock can appear below you and launch you into the air.
You will also find many times textures being completely warped as you explore further out, which worsens the performance issues.
Placing blocks is extremely frustrating when it shouldn't be as it is the core feature of any sandbox game.
There's also generally nothing to do. You can just build small rovers that will always look all the same due to the lack of building blocks available, and buildings, which had lots of nice decorative blocks, but they locked those behind a deluxe edition preorder. Driving around a planet is only fun for the first few minutes.
And there's no multiplayer. Playing with friends to make the experience better is impossible.
In a nutshell, wait for the devs to add more content before buying. It simply isn't worth the price.

I heard the game was good so I decided to give it a chance but what I got felt a bit awkward, accidentally screwing yourself over made sense but there were a few times where it was too sudden and with no real checkpoints  (other than being able to just completely skip to 'Chapter 2') and no ability to skip what you've already read it almost immediately becomes boring. This isn't even factoring in the complete lack of audio/music in the game. There were also some design choices I wasn't very sure about.
Firstly despite being a text adventure you got forward by essentially clicking hyperlinks and not writing anything yourself which ultimately takes away any feel of actually exploring the place yourself or using any effort to do anything and nearly all the text is describing your surroundings.
Secondly from what I could tell at least 1 choice was randomized (there's a hole in the wall near the start of the game where I found a switch/lever one time and got bitten by insects the second try) , while they could say it helps replayability the idea that you'll probably never be able to learn what definitely will not kill you really bugs me.
Thirdly the text can feel extremely slow and probably still would even if you could skip as it seems to want you to read some stuff 1 line at a time and it ends up dragging on, it actually seems weird that they wouldn't include a speed option like in Visual Novels or something (since slow is not creepy).
Fourthly (?) if you got through the game without any of the death seeming a bit bs the forced fights will definitely make you feel that. There is literally no player input in them unless you count continuously clicking the hyperlinks as you either scratch ot miss each other and hope you aren't the one that ends up dying. While a lot of adventure books randomized stuff like fights via dice rolls in that case it actually felt like your fault if you got a bad roll while this jjust feels cheap.
Overall it had potential including the story itself but it feels like too many corners were cut in its creation and it ultimately just doesn't appeal to me. Perhaps its worth a try while on sale but definitely not at its normal price of £4.

First order of business is that Perptuum is only Early Access as a Steam title. It has existed since late 2010, and as such, will be reviewed fully on the merit of what it has presented to me during my brief playtime, with its four and a half years worth of content.
Good
+ DEV Zoom seems to mingle with the players quite often, both on the forums, as well as ingame. Most games have the developers stay just out of reach of players, but this game always has this one team member accessible for a good portion of the day by day, which I applaud for a show of passion.
+ Newbie Island is a thing here in Perp. I'm going to list this also as a con later on, since I feel the training section is a bit mishandled, but they place new accounts in a "training simulation" which is basically a confined zone of modest size, where you start with all skills at halfway, and they force you to progress through all manners of content, to allow the player to become familiar with how it works. You can skill up as you wish here, with no harm done to your account once you leave this area, so it allows players a chance to tinker and get a feel of the skill system, as well as how it impacts elements of the gameplay, which I personally feel EVE fails at outside of a cold lockout for new players that join New Eden.
+ The game overhauled its mission system to be far more accessible, which as a new player, I found as a great boon. While EVE would try to sugarcoat their quests with flavor text and other vanity, Perp has reworked their system to be more streamlined, allowing players to focus on their personal interests such as mining / combat, go out into the world and accomplish the goal, and return to a mission terminal in record time to collect their reward.
Bad
- Horrible UI. In EVE, you have your toolbar that you can move around as you wish from side to side, yet in Perp, it is always at the top of the screen. You can move the various HUD elements around as you wish, but you cannot resize beyond certain points.
- Unable to change resoulution. Due to some wonky design choices from the dev team, the screensize is either locked to your full resolution, or a screen size befitting 2004. When you go to a larger resolution, it merely pins items spread out, but does not adjust the font sizing on these items, as one of the devs stated in the game that their engine treats the UI as 3D elements or something or the other, and that is why the dev team cannot readily make changes to the endless barrage of players requesting this feature to be overhauled.
- Lack of shortcuts. Again with EVE, you have your toolbar and it lists various keyboard shortcuts for you to utilize to access any element, as well as even having the option to close all screen clutter with CTRL + ALT + W.
Perp? Next to nothing seems to flow the same as you would expect coming from EVE, and your toolbar does not say what any of these hotkeys are. You have to dig deep into the options to find them on your own accord, and it just should not be this way. Information is ammunition, so having it all readily available at your fingertips is somthing that should have readily been copied from EVE's toolbar, not merely left to an options menu. This style of gameplay is the type where more info = better, and taking excess time to click icons manually or assigning things serves to merely drag the experience onward, instead of propelling the player through aspects of the game.
- Training is pretty bad. Compared to EVE's approach of Aura acting as a questline agent to advance you through various elements of training you desire, Perpetuum forces you to advance through all the training before you are allowed into the "real" game. On average, this takes about two hours or so for most players advance through, which is both a blessing and a curse. It is a harsh reminder of just how complex EVE and Perp are in their game systems, but EVE allows players the chance to completely skip the training and take a "feel it out" approach, while Perp does not allow this freedom. Making an alt to play the game differently? Too bad, hope you like getting stuck doing training.
- Overly convoluted gathering system. To gather in EVE, you merely need skill training for the tech, and of course a mining laser / gas harvester. With additional training, you can have mining crystals for certain loadouts to increase your mining yield.
Gathering in Perp? Oh boy, you better get ready to yell at how needlessly involved they have crafted it by comparison. First, you need to equip a mining attachment, or a gathering attachment. From there, you need ammo per cycle, and it gets more aggrivating with mining. Gathering has a universal ammo that you can obtain rather cheap, mining is nowhere near as easy on the user.
To mine, you need your scanner setup with two ammo types. One is a "range finder", the other shows you the density of an area after you've played Marco Polo with the system and wasted enough ammo charges to find the location on the map of where items are set. From here, you need the right mining ammo charges set to mine it. Looking for something low class like Titanium? You need specific Titanium charges to mine it. They can ONLY be used to mine Titanium. This means that if you're not mining for a mission, but rather for yourself, you must waste precious cargo space with various ammo types, which might not be an issue anyways, as you need specific scanner ammos to seek out any mining.
In EVE terms, this would mean having to equip a scanner with Veldspar locator ammo to find the location of a belt, then using another type of Veldspar scanner ammo to actually be able to lock onto it, then you need to cycle your ammo if you have not done so to equip Veldspar mining ammo, so you can actually mine it. This is very horrible design in my opinion, and does not add depth to the game, only tedium to an already arguably tedious playstyle.
- Launcher is unoptimized garbage. A recent update that overhauled the mission structure was implemented with a 1.6 MB download on Steam for the game, which then led to having to load the Perp launcher and sit through updates. The update was a mere 16.06 MB in size, but it took about 15 minutes for my PC to download it, which I haven't seen done in any MMO since FFXI and its 56kbs speed cap.
- Pop is severely low. Usually sub 50 players listed in chat channels, with over 100ish logging in daily to keep their skill points churning in. I see it as each player holding more meaning to the game overall, but others will see this as a dead game walking.
- P2W. In EVE, all choices are final with your skills, unless CCP nukes a set somehow. In Perp? You can pay real money to reset points and have them to spend on whatever you want. Recent balance changes before I joined severely nerfed many loadouts for PvP and other aspects of gameplay people spent months or more training into. Solution? Just open your wallet if you want to and get SP back to invest into the new meta, or lament having skills wasted by wanton dev decisions and train normally into the new meta. EVE works it so new can compete with old by specialized training, while Perp lets the old stay on top by wallet or ingame ICE (PLEX) use.
All in all, I found Perp as the offbrand cola for my desire for a namebrand fix. Sam's Cola is not quite the same as Pepsi, nor is Perp really EVE, but I found myself enjoying it despite its many shortcomings, and appreciating it for what it offers. I can easily recommend EVE for those seeking quality, but at the same time, Perp exists as a cheap pay to own option to EVE's fees.

Level individual stats, or raise your favorite skill up way early. You can't "ruin" your character and the cost to raise the neglected stats does NOT go up from leveling other things. 2: Grinding is easy and non-mandatory. You can progress through the plot quickly if you desire, or wander aimlessly and grind, loot, and explore. Plenty of side places to visit with funny side quests, and a "Wander" button that basically means "feed me a random fight or loot please". I love it.
3: Grinding applicable to your class is available. Various areas have "spawners". If you see it say "Bigger fight" in the menu, that's a "start group battle" button. From spawning Skeletons to level your doctor friend, or spawning cow-monoliths to level your gunslinger friend, if you need a particular type of resource, chances are there's somewhere to farm it.

After reading GaoKao.Love.100Days, I've grown a soft spot for Chinese works. PRICE just so happened to be free, so I decided to check out what it was about.
I found it pretty hard to figure out what sort of game it was initially. The screenshots on the store page didn't help much, but PRICE is essentially an atmospheric horror point-and-click adventure game. Note that I said atmospheric, because while this game has very little in terms of scares, it makes up for it in its ominous atmosphere and a tad of shock value. PRICE actually does more of an effort to make you care for the main characters than it does to scare you, which I can praise.
As a point-and-click adventure, it's decent. The puzzles are fairly challenging, although I had to briefly look up a walkthrough twice in order to finish the game. One thing I do like is that when checking some objects, you can find clues that tell you about what exactly is going on between the protagonist and his sister. You combine these clues together to form an assessment of the situation, which I think is a clever idea to tell the story.
The game's artwork goes for this sort of gothic-anime hybrid. Combined with the fact that the game seems to take place in some Germanic residence, it makes for a very interesting style. The cutscenes are nice as well, although sometimes the video gets glitchy and choppy for some odd reason. There are only three songs in the entire game, and the one you'll be hearing for nearly the entire game is Requiem. It's not a bad song, but hearing it over and over again as I try to solve the puzzle grates my ears. They try to vary things up by adding instrument layers to the song as you progress, which is a neat idea in concept, but it's all you hear, and you'll be wanting to turn down the volume to avoid going insane.
Overall, PRICE is a decent game. It's forgivingly short and not terribly difficult, but it has some flaws that may hurt the quality of the experience. I suggest giving it a try, if only to see if you like it. If not, then I don't blame you.

I am one of the alpha backers for Planet Nomads. I've also been pretty active on the forums even before the alpha was released. 30 hours of my playtime has gone into creative mode (before survival)  while 18 has gone into survival. This game is really all about how you use your imagination to make it a positive experience. You can build just about anything in this game with the blocks you get in creative mode. I've had a blast so far with survival. The game has been a vast improvement and the devs have been working hard trying to release a stable game for players. However, I do have some critcisms of my own about the game that I believe people should be aware of.
pros:
+Devs are transparent, you can watch the progress of the game on trello and see what's going on in the forums. You'd think this should be expected but unfortunately not these days.
+Performance has improved immensely since the alpha and while it still needs some work, I believe runs very well for day one Early Access
+You can build almost anything you want, make things function the way you want etc.
+you can build your own vehicles, test them out, etc.
+UI is pretty decent, fair amount of graphical options that you can tweak
+massive planet
+realistic biomes with creatures dispersed across the planet. Feels like an actual planet.
+diverse flora
+survival provides a decent challenge.
+colorful envornments, world looks beautiful and full of life
+helpful tutorial with the option to turn it off if you want
+communication between devs and players is frequent and positive
+consistent updates
+you can destroy terrrain without spamming your inventory full of dirt and unecessary items
cons:
-no custom keybinding
-fauna is not as diverse as it should be for the size of the planet.
-enemy AI can be buggy, sometimes they attack you, but after a bit they will just stand there and take a beating
-(personal opinion) having an advanced bio suit should prevent you from being hungry and thirsty so quickly, especially when you need to rest, i feel like  hunger and thirst should deplete slower
-should be able to change graphics options within the game
-lack of aquatic flora and fauna
-after a while, you will eventually turn off the music

You start off after your pod lands on an unexplored planet, with only your space suit and tool. From there you start harvesting resources to build a base, and survive. There are two game modes you can play in: survival mode and creative mode.
In the creative mode, you can build as much as you want without needing to worry about gathering resources, or dying. In survival mode, you’ll need to harvest resources to build structures to help you survive. The survival aspects that you’ll need to manage are your hunger, thirst, stamina, and health. If your hunger, thirst, or stamina reach zero, then your health drains until you either die, or eat/drink/sleep replenish it. The survival aspects are pretty manageable - you can find food and water in the wild, and either consume it raw, or refine it to provide even more of a bonus, and avoid any negative side effects like radiation poisoning. You can also sleep in the outdoors using a sleeping bag, but one of the times I went to sleep outside, I died, but have no idea why. Dying isn’t too bad though. You drop all your loot where you died, but it becomes a marked on your compass so you can follow it to retrieve everything.
You’ll have to gather a whole lot of resources and use a 3D printer to produce various crafting components. Resource gathering is very slow without using batteries. The batteries are consumed and need to be crafted frequently using different components. Crafting components are also used to build more structures, such as walls, ground vehicles, and greenhouses. Some structures require power to function, and you need to use generators to provide them with enough energy.
You can upgrade your suit, tool, and jetpack as you unlock new recipes. They are very helpful to increase your mining and exploring efficiency. However, it feels like I’m farming to become better at farming, and it’s not all that satisfying - actually it’s kind of boring after the first hour or two. I travelled for 32,000km to see if there was anything new or different from my spawning location. I encountered a few enemy types, but none of them were very interesting or felt all that engaging. It’s a shame to see such a massive world to explore, but have it feel so empty. I came across some snowy mountains and barren land, but as for flora and fauna, there wasn’t anything new to see. I would love to see more content to discover, not just new biomes, plants, or animals, but maybe some ruins or cool landmarks too.
In order to unlock new crafting recipes, you have to build the earlier recipes that are already unlocked. The way they unlock is fine, and it’s probably good that everything is slowly introduced. In addition to building structures, you can also dig through the terrain. Affecting the world around you is a great feature, however, without a way to rebuild it, or smooth it out, it becomes more of an annoyance when you accidentally put a hole near your base. I hope they add more functionality for terrain morphing in the near future.
I’ve played for about 4 hours in both survival and creative mode. The game has some potential for replay value for those who really, really enjoy base-building and exploration, but I don’t think that it’s at that point yet. I would love to see more content added, as well as multiplayer to the game.
Planet Nomads is off to an okay start, but right now there isn’t a whole lot to do or see. The game has a very long way to go before it even comes close to what the developers envision for it. Until then, it might be better just to keep your eye on its development.

Solid story, good music, charming characters, excellent voice over. You will love it if you are a fan of adventure games. Some thoughts down below.
The game has very well designed retro art style background and characters, the art style keeps its consistency even in the scenery layout, which you don't see a lot around. However from a gameplay point of view, I don't know if this is all that good an idea. The way scenes change from cut to cut don't go alone with the point n click way of control at all.
Now consider the game originally plays on keyboard only, that really not a problem then, but they didn't figure out a better way to do it in the remastered version, which resulted in a lot of difficulties in finding your way around the map. This happened several times during my gameplay, when I just wiggle the mouse all around the screen to find if there's some arrow somewhere I missed. And the puzzle designs are not that great either, although the dialogs are very well written, they failed to deliver the idea, (I think) in favor of keeping the style of the plot together, too many WTF moments when I think only a psychopath can put links between the given hints(or you can just call me stupid, but whatever).
During the gameplay I always have a feeling that the developers are trying to make an animated film but then found out that they were working in a game company, so they try to combine elements of the two together. You can feel this tendency all around the plot, especially on the relationship development between the main characters, and the hero's attitude towards different thing in the game, and the way how time passes in the game has to reflect the plot at the beginning of the game, etc (I don't want to spoil the story, if you've played it I think you'll know what I mean). All these inconsistency in the developer's mind of what game is influenced negatively on the rhythm of how the story is rolling out in front of you, especially in the second half of the game, considering how highly people think of its story, I can't bypass its flaws easily. I couldn't help but thinking what if Lucasfilm made this plot into an animation rather than a game by Lucasarts, all the humor, the noir, the retro style scenery, but sadly it will never happen.
On the whole, as small adventure game it stands its ground as one of the best as may claimed, it's not perfect, but it's really good.

What a concept! A mexican/spanish noir set in the land of the dead, where you play as a travel agent who discovers the corruption within the business, while making friends and enemies along the way. A favourite aspect of mine is the concept of 'sprouting', which is, in the land of the dead, plants consume bone whilst growing, leading to individuals deaths. In turn, those who were once florists in their previous lifes are starkly conflicted in this one. As you will see, characters, location, plot and narrative as well as dialogue are altered by this one small nuance.
After finishing the game, I listened to a few segments of the developers commentary and looked at all the artwork available. My god. It never occured to me how much thought, effort and large of a design process it must have took. And atop that, how much soul was injected into the game via not only developers, but artists, voice actors and the community surrounding its release.
Sure, the puzzles are a little outdated and in some cases clunky. Infact, a few times, without a guide, I'd not have a clue what to do (eg; that damned vault door). But they are certainly interesting! Alot of the puzzles, as I heard in the directors commentary, make the player 'think backwards'. For the vault door, its broken into and closed, in order to be opened. The keno board shows the answers to the guards questions only after they've been answered. To get the metal detector, you need to find it without a metal detector. The list goes on, and I think its an ingenious way to intriuged players.
And the dialogue? It progresses with the game. You go from making silly little puns at small, trivial things in an office; to making rather depthy and character building statements.
There is so much I could say about this game. It is worth the $15 USD in my opinion. But to recap:
>Born too late to crusade
>Born too early to explore space
>Born just in time to play Grim Fandango Remastered

Riding on the success of DotP 2012's improvements, the 2013 release introduces revamped decks, a new unlock system, and a new game mode. While 2013 has less decks available (16 versus last year's 19), they are overall more accessible for quick play because of the 10 promo unlocks provided post-release. The decks are also more balanced in power overall because you aren't locked out of the best cards anymore. However, this is a double-edged sword; While you can unlock a total of 40 cards per deck, many of them are dups and you can only unlock one at a time. To put this into perspective, beating the first campaign (the longest in the game) will unlock 26 cards.
While I enjoyed the difficult challenges (the hardest challenges of the DotP games in my opinion), this game is riddled with issues that will never get fixed or improved since the devs have moved onto their next yearly release. Locking out all but two decks at the start is a terrible way to introduce new players to MTG, especially considering the target market for these games. The one new game mode, Planechase, is only worth playing with friends; The AI is terrible at it, seeming to attack and roll the planar die randomly. Despite being marketed towards new and casual players, this game can only be recommended for experienced MTG players because of the unlock systems and frustration with non-human Planechase.

Magic 2013 was... underwhelming. While I appreciate all the new cards that were added, the experience as a whole felt less interesting than Magic 2012

Given the sheer number of decks, they really should have awarded at least two cards per battle. 30 battles per deck is just a horrible time sink, especially when it's not as fun as it used to be. I'm also starting to wish they had an option to turn off ALL animations. If I'm going to be grinding a long♥♥♥♥♥game, I don't want to see every card taking 5-10 seconds to play.
Sadly Archenemy mode is gone, and 2-headed giant only exists in custom games. I actually found both of those fun. In its place is Planechase mode which... *shudder*. Every round you wait for 3 CPUs to take their turns and they spin that atrocious dice over and over again. It's just... kill me now. Every time.
To the game's credit, decks felt more balanced overall. There's some strategy involved where some decks fare much better versus others, instead of a one-size-fits-all deck, but I kind of miss the feeling of overpoweredness from the previous game. The puzzles are still fun too.
Overall it's a distinctly inferior game compared to 2012. On its own, only average. I'll rate it 6/10. It makes me wish I was playing the last one.

Game with great promise! The game system, using time ticks, is reminiscent of the World of Warcraft Miniature game, which was a great game and sadly got pulled because of company politics. I'm very happy to see it being used again!
The way Defense decks work is a cool variation on asynchronous pvp in that you have a lot of knobs to turn: you choose which boss will guard your halls, what spells and attacks it can use, what kind of perks it will have to boost specific spells or stats, and which creatures will be joining in at the start of the fight. You can choose 5 spells, 5 perks and 5 creatures, and the value of those 15 cards together can't exceed a threshold of 45 stars, making it really fun to try and get that perfect defense deck together - augmented by replays you can see of other players trying (in vain, naturally) to beat down your setup. Consequentially, it makes it really fun to make your own assault teams since there are a lot of things you need to consider in order to be able to beat opposing bosses! It's a pretty tough game difficulty-wise at the moment and I think that's great.
The game of course isn't perfect (yet) by any means, but that brings me to why I really recommend trying or at least following this game: the developers. They are highly responsive to feedback, and I've had several nice chats with the devs on the steam chat, for instance. If you have questions or criticisms, I can recommend bringing it to their attention because in my experience they will listen carefully.
The game is still incomplete at the moment, but is already a lot of fun and I recommend trying it out!

I found Viridi through playing another of this developer's games called Eidolon.
I'm honestly so glad I did.
Viridi is a simple game about watering succulents. I actually meant to type "gardening" there, but it kind of slipped out; you will spend much of your time in this game (nearly all of it, really) clicking on and watering virtual plants. You can also pull weeds -- or leave them, it's your choice, really. There's also a snail. You can name the snail, in addition to each and every one of your plants and the actual planter itself, and on top of all of that you can sing to everything in your garden.
Including the snail.
Viridi is a light and simple game, but somehow, it seems to pack everything you need to keep playing it. I'm honestly impressed by this game's ability to reel me back in time and time again to make sure my plants don't dessicate. (But fear not, those who spend long times away from games -- Viridi comes with a sort of "vacation mode" that you can toggle on for extended absences!) It really is the perfect game for even the most casual and easygoing players, as it only takes a few minutes to pop in and water your garden. As long as the concept appeals to you, you will probably enjoy this title (with the caveat that those anticipating a more robust simulation of actual gardening may be disappointed.)
There's something rewarding about watching your tiny plants quickly grow up and eventually flower under your care.
This is a free-to-play game, and therefore, you know what's coming. Mechanics-wise, you start with a single planter (though Eidolon players get two, which was a lovely surprise!) and an assortment of pre-chosen plants to start your garden off with (and you can choose which arrangement of plants you want, too, in addition to the design and shape of the pot itself!) After that, you're given one free plant per week to do with what you will, chosen at random.  As one would expect, there is also the option to purchase additional planters and plants (for a fairly reasonable price, all things considered.) Basically every plant costs pennies on the dollar, so I really can't complain about pricing here. Planters run a bit more, but nothing in this game is going to break the bank.
(Full disclosure: I have a vehement dislike towards microtransactions in all their forms... but Viridi is inoffensive and charming enough that it's disarmed me. Here, they don't offend me. I think they're tolerable here, and that's about as high of praise as I'll ever give microtransactions.
I've never felt forced to fork over funds to keep playing, and I deeply appreciate that about the game.)
At the end of the day, Viridi is a simple game with a surprising amount of charm. The game's simple visuals, relaxed playstyle, and soothing, interesting music all work together to create a really quite pleasant package, and for once the microtransactions don't take away from it. If you think you'd enjoy this game -- you've really nothing to lose for trying it, it is literally a free game, and you might be pleasantly surprised! I've managed to sink-- somehow, 14 hours into this game over the last year or so, and I've genuinely had a lot of fun with it. I have taken so many screenshots of my planters... Viridi is a really solid experience overall, and I think just about anyone could find something to enjoy about it as long as the concept itself interests them.
And if nothing else, I've learned to recognize some plants IRL because of this game, and that's something I'll always appreciate!

For the past ten years, I've been an on-and-off-again player of the developers' first game, Kingdom of Loathing, and this shares a ton of similarities with it. If you're not familiar with KoL, it's free to play and in your browser right now, so go ahead and try it out if a funny, turn-based stick figure RPG is appealing to you and you're not ready to drop $11.
If you liked the writing and/or gameplay in KoL this is the best of that and actually a 'real game' too. KoL can be a little frustrating to play with the daily turn limits and such, and of course there's nothing like that here.
WoL is paced well and doesn't overstay its welcome - about 10 hours long, 6 if you were just doing mainline stuff.
A minor sticking point for me is the first 30 minutes are basically a point-and-click adventure (go here, pick up KEY_ITEM, go there, use KEY_ITEM, unlock next 'puzzle') but once you're out of that area it's got an overworld with lots of sidequests and such and it doesn't feel so constricted, and future playthroughs let you skip that.
The devs learned a lot from making KoL and you can tell from some of the design decisions about how combat works, stats, skill levels ups, etc. It's fun to play and very funny. I hope you play it!

Perpetuum seems to be one of the 'successors' to Eve Online. It is a game of Robots instead of ships, and the familiarity will be a bonus to people who have played Eve Online with a few exceptions. For one, skills are no longer time based, but point based. Meaning you don't have to wait around endlessly while a skill is being trained. In the same vein, however, your points are daily. Meaning that you only get a limited number of points per day to which to spend on 'extensions' or skills in Eve.
The biggest plus for me, at any rate, is the fact there is a PvP flag. Meaning that you can't be killed as you wander the islands randomly. There are probably spots where the PvP is automatically set to PvP, but I can live with that. I don't have to worry about my beginning mech being blown to pieces because a higher skilled player got a bee in their bonnet and decided my little inventory scraps are worth killing over.

Considering this game? Everything basic that you should know:
-As of this review, all characters are arguably more balanced than they've ever been. Choose anyone you want.
-You can't "screw up" a build in this game. Ability points are infinite and are acquired through dungeon completion.
-Everything prior to level 60 is one long, extended tutorial that forces you to learn your character.
-Level 59 and below is pretty boring, but leveling is VERY fast in this game, and the game really picks up with 8 man raids in the level 60-90 zone.
Gameplay:
-Real time action. Hot keys are not required to do combos. They're mostly used for potions, ultimate skills, and stimulants.
-The game makes HUGE use of invulnerability frames. If you time it right, you can literally dodge roll straight into someone's attack and "eat it" entirely. It's one of those games.
-Very polished battle mechanics and animations. Completely blows C9, RaiderZ, Blade and Soul, Tera, and Dragon Nest out of the water in this respect. Unfortunately, aside from core gameplay, these games outdo Vindictus in pretty much everything else, which I will cover:
Graphics:
-Can be beautiful. It's a nice looking game, no doubt.
-POORLY OPTIMIZED. You will need an inordinately powerful CPU to run the game at 60 fps, if you're that kind of guy.
-The network is handled through p2p. The host usually has no issues with lag, but the rest of the party is at the whims of the host's network strength.
Cash Shop:
-Wide array of cosmetics you can buy, like hairstyles, makeup, skin color/body type, "inner armor" (bikinis and♥♥♥♥♥♥, and pets.
-You cannot effectively maximize your potential in this game without spending cash. "Runes" (to protect your equipment from breaking during enhancement) are only available in the cash shop (save a few exceptions, such as event giveaways) and are required to min-max your crap at endgame.
-The only workaround from spending cash is to save a crapton of gold and farm valuable items to simply purchase pre-enchanted/enhanced armor. The RNG in this game is not as bad as it used to be, but it's still pretty bad.
Despite these weaknesses, Vindictus is still a good game, provided you have a wallet and friends to play with.
Definitely give this a try.

Far Cry 2 is a great adventure/sandbox FPS. It features stunning scenery, a large amount of weapons to choose from and allows the player to either spray 'n pray or o for a more stealthy approach. It constantly keeps you on your toes, as an enemy may appear every moment. The storyline is pretty poor however, especially the ending is a major WTF?!?! moment.

Well, it's hard to say for sure, but I do like the combat, and many things in the environment can be used as weapons. Destructable landscape is a nice touch, so is being able to pick up a recently slain enemy's corpse and beating another enemy with it. Extremely gratifying to the raging sociopath in us all. ;)
The quest system...well..it could use some improvment. An empty room/building screen with some thumbnails of NPCs gives you a quest. If you pick the right NPC. Not game-breaking, but a little awkward in my opinion, and the journal system seems lacking.
The skill system seems a little confusing. For example, there is no obvious way to undo points once you've alotted them. I actually buggered up an early quest that was supposed to teach me how to use the skill system because I inadvertantly put the points into the wrong skill, and could find no way to undo it. So now I can't seem to advance past that quest, short of going out and grinding out some more kills to get more points. However that doesn't seem terribly easy to do, at least as a solo player, since as near as I can tell, everything is instanced. I could be wrong about that, since I got terribly frustrated with that scenario and logged off. I will go back and look into that, and if I am wrong I will change my review accordingly.  Failing that I may start over, and try again.  Simply because the combat is worth a second chance, despite my own ineptitude.
Overall my first impression is that it is a decent game, with extremely fun and visceral combat. I would like to see more character customization,(that isn't hidden behind a microtrans) but that is a complaint in many, many games for me; microtransactions or not.  I have always disliked age and gender-locks, but it is an action game with RPG elements, not a straight-up RPG.  Gender-lock bothers me more in RPGs, as some games go overboard with 'sexy girls with ridiculous physics and sloot-boots'. I want a female warrior, not a pole-dancer.
But anyway, I digress, as I am wont to do. Yes, I would recommend this game if only for the great combat. Perhaps it would be more enjoyable if I weren't a die-hard soloer, but it is not a bad game.

This is a fantastic game with one of the best environments and gameplay I have ever experienced. Despite this, I have heard so many complaints and gripes about this fine title. Many jump into this open world game expecting the many side missons of FC3, or the hand holding of many modern FPS games, and complain when FC2 does not accomidate them. Many also whine when the story does not cater to their ideals and makes them make hard, immoral, decisions. "The story is crap," they say "The ending made me feel bad." I've also heard many complain that playing as an often heartless merc made them feel uncomfortable. How can that be bad? If a game can provoke an emotional response like that, then it has done a fine job. I have heard people, in the same breath, complain about the fast respawn time for enemy outposts breaking immersion, then say that the method of quick travel (finding a bus to take you to another bus stop after a loading screem) isn't easy enough to access and traveling is a pain. I say false to both statements, especially since they contradict each other. Having a world full of hostile entities makes you prepare for such encouters, and also refills the world with more enemies to fight, something that I feel FC3 lacked after you cleared out outposts. As for having to drive for awhile for any mission, I never could go more than a minute without something exploding, cathcing fire, or shooting at me.
With all of this being said, I do acknowledge that this game is not for everyone. Since it does NOT hold your hand in, and instead is fairly abrasive, be it via malaria attack, a lucky mortar strike, or a jamming gun, it likely doesn't appeal to anyone who is looking for some mindless fun/action a la Metal Gear Rising or FC3. This game is rough, and can be frusterating at times, but because of these same qualities, I love this game for not being afraid of trying something different. As a result, I have never played another FPS that has gotten my heart rate up so much everytime an enemy appeared.
Play it, try it, but DON'T expect FC2 to hand you anything.

Good game, if a bit frustrating at times. I'd say a 7.9 out of 10. Maybe.
[EDIT: Chinese version deserves a 8.7 out of 10 due to clarification from cutscenes oddly missing in the English version.]
Good points:
Like the art style, and the simple and sweet item/clue system. Pretty intuitive. Enjoyed how Ivry actually crouches down or reaches up to examine things. Nice, creepy art in cutscenes. Good soundtrack. Liked the story too; liked how vague and disoriented it felt, helps relate to Ivry in his quest to find the terrible truth. The puzzle themselves were pretty straightforward once you find them, and it isn't hard to piece the story together, but the fact that the story itself was vague anyways (what with the protagonist searching for the past, with the only clues being remnants of that past being found in the present) gives lots of room for imagination to wiggle in and conjure up all sorts of scenarios. I liked that a lot. (The urge to fanfiction is strong.)
Bad points:
That said, there are quite a few things I did not enjoy about this game. From what I've seen of the discussions there are quite a few cutscenes missing in the English version of the game? Not sure what's going on there, but I'm gonna play the simp. Chinese version and see if that's any better. Takes out chunks of the story, which is one of the most important things to me in a game, so yeah. :L Became a bit TOO vague.
(EDIT: Played the Chinese version, and yeah there were more cutscenes. Makes more sense now. Also makes the entire puzzle easier to solve.)
The soundtrack also does get repetitive, especially when you're taking a long time, and the constant high pitch does get somewhat grating, especially if you're starting to get annoyed at the lack of progress. Which brings me to my next point, which is that the clues are sometimes not that intuitive and are slightly hard to figure out (one instance was when I didn't realize two object were actually separate, since the clickable areas were put so close together hovering the cursor between them didn't change to indicate they were in fact separate).
Also didn't like the voice acting. Ivry's was okay, if a bit bland (understandable), the Magician's was fine, but the Cat's... I just couldn't accept. That was a pedo voice. (怪蜀黍的声音啊！) Also some grammatical mistakes in the English translation, which wasn't that clear or 'fancy' at times, which took away from the setting slightly. Ivry didn't think like the well-educated high-class heir he appears to be.
Font choice is also a bit funky. I could not understand the top tab (that probably said 'CLUE' but took me a while to figure out from context), though the rest is more fine. Also please please please add a trad. Chinese version? And the discrepancy between the fancy font and cartoonish font in the menus in the simp. Chinese version is slightly off-putting.
The 'thought boxes' also weirdly double as action descriptors. Not sure what's up with that.
Welp I've managed to make myself sound like a nitpicker who sees no good in this game but honestly I think this game IS great, albeit with a few small issues to work out. Also, it's free! :D
