A great core game clogged up by glitches and poorly designed filler.
PROS:
+ Guns are FANTASTIC! (Before entering real combat, that is.) Large variety. Animation's decent, sound effects are excellent, and they tear up landscape pretty good. Poorly maintained guns jam and misfire in varying ways. Firing guns in this game leaves me with a headache and ringing ears... in a good way.
+ Certain aspects are very immersive. You're stuck in Africa. You haven't much to rely on beyond your non-pausing map, health syringes, and safe havens. Ammo and health can burn quickly. Keep moving and stay alive.
+ Asthetically, the map is good. Feels like Africa based on the five or six Nationa Geographic shots I've seen.
+ As many have said, fire is fun. Tall grass and foliage burn up quickly and in large quantities.
+ Visuals haven't aged too poorly. Very serviceable considering the years this game has on it.
+ Some neat dynamic enemy behavior. They talk between each other during combat appropriate to what just happened. They'll sling their wounded buddies over their shoulder and run for cover.
+ The malaria pill fetching reminded me of Zombrex in Dead Rising 2... which was a better game I'd been reminded I could be playing.
CONS:
- Enemy AI sporadically changes between dirt dumb and brilliant. Enemies can miss shots within three feet of you, but nail you in your moving vehicle a hundred yards away. Enemies can not detect you when you crouch right next to them, but discover you crouched in tall grass from a hundred yards away. Weapons they nail you with across the map are pitifully inaccurate when you pick them up and use them youself. They can even detect you THROUGH COVER, often shooting through thinner walls nailing you perfectly.
- Not all guns do not behave predictably. Multiple close quarters headshots with 7.62 ammunition can serve to just stun an enemy. An entire pistol magezine loaded into an enemy's body still has him up and about shooting.
- The map is littered with enemy holdouts. Not a problem in Far Cry 3. When you invade these incampments in FC3, you can clear them out, permanently. In this game, killing everyone in the outpost means: They all respawn! Not even ten real life minutes later! Over sixty of these ♥♥♥♥ing things are upon every major road and water way. If you want to drive for more than two minutes, you'll run into one of these encampments. Your best bet is to floor it through them, and even that doesn't work well. Enemies chip away at your health every time you drive past. Often they'll scramble a vehicle to follow you. No firing weapons in vehicles, your best defense is to bail out, shoot your persuers, repair your car for the umptenth time, and keep moving.
- As many have said, Malaria is an arbitrary difficulty complication. Another example of where this game favors "realism" over "immersion". Every 30 real life minutes you suffer an incurable malaria attack. To not pass out and restart at a safehouse, you need to take Malaria pills. You CAN NOT acquire these pills willingly! You need to progress through the story to get them! Should you decide you want to do the side content for a couple hours, get used to passing out and restarting every once in a while.
- Not much to do outside of the main story. Side missions pretty much always consist of killing everyone in an enemy camp or blowing up a vehicle.
- Story's thread bare. That doesn't matter too much. What DOES matter pretty much every character is horridly voice acted. The actors sound like text-to-speech machines; monotone and rarely giving appropriate inflections. For some strange reason, the game often speeds up their lines as well. They talk as if commas and periods don't exist.
- Random bugs. I've encountered bugs where unpausing causes you to automatically throw a grenade, one where switching to my primary weapon caused my character to start walking to the right for some reason, bugs where vehicles would automatically reverse when I entered them. They all fixed themselves when I restarted the game, but it was rather odd and annoying that they were there in the first place.
I wanted to enjoy this game. I was told "Far Cry 3 without the handholding." At its core, this game is solid. Little design flaws like braindead AI and the constant attacks from guard outposts every five minutes become incredibly bothersome when the game is littered with them. Stealth is almost nonfunctional. Loud combat is buggy but sometimes servicable.
"Immersion" in this game boils down to something like a Grand Theft Auto game where cops won't come after you for murder but will give you a speeding ticket without fail. The unfun components (malaria, cars frequently breaking down, enemies tracking you) compromise the often-breaking components of fun.
My only consolation is I bought this for $2.49. Buy this game on sale if you like unpredictable non-stop hordes of dumb enemies and tearing up the African desert in a boastfully product-placed Jeep.

Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light is a fixed-camera isometric 3D platform game and unlike previous games in the series, puts a heavy emphasis on cooperative gameplay.
You play either as Lara Croft or a 2000 year old Mayan warrior named Totec who team up together to defeat an ancient evil god. Standard cliche save-the-world storyline that does its job well enough.
Each character has their own specialities in navigating obstacles. For example: Lara is much more agile and can dispatch grappling hooks while Totec has a nice shield that can block things and a spear which can be used as a temporary platform for Lara to jump onto.
Play control is very smooth and fluid but the main highlight is the manner in which the cleverly designed puzzles are solved cooperatively and they sometimes have more then 1 solution. Although you can complete the campaign solo, (in which you are given all the tools needed to solve all puzzles) The game shines alot better when played co-op. Skills are split up between the 2 characters. You can tell that they put alot of thought into the designs of the puzzles.
Downsides, the game is rather short at only about 6 hours for the main campaign although it is alot of fun. I have also encountered some random network disconnections while playing co-op online. Keyboard controls feel fiddly and a gamepad is highly recommended although some configuration is required if you're not using a native Xbox360 PC controller. Its also a pity that the game is not designed to be moddable (no mod tools were ever released for it AFAIK) as it feels very well suited for modding.
The 3 mission DLCs which consists of 4 short missions each, making it a total of 12 missions are just more puzzles and have absolutely no additional story to add on to the main campaign. It will probably take an additional hour or 2 depending on your playstyle to finish them all. You can play them solo, or co-op and are meant more for players who have completed the main game and just wants more puzzles to solve.
The additional character DLCs are also quite interesting in that they are not just re-skins, but are actually done with all new voicework. It basically re-tells the main story campaign but from a new perspective. So if you've already completed the game, and wanna replay it, these character DLCs can be worth to buy just to experience another run-thru again. Its quite funny to see Raziel and Kain again in a completely different environment.
In closing, this is a really fun but short co-op game with fluid controls and brilliant puzzles. Although very different from the usual style of the Tomb Raider series, I hope they make a sequel for it, as it is really very good.
Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10

I knew this game was E.V.E.-like. I bought it anyways because some of the gameplay looked fun. It honestly does look, and sound, fun. It's just executed so poorly.
The tutorial takes about an hour, there is way too much to learn at the beginning, It's overwhelming, and that turns off a lot of players, including myself. The UI is bad. It's like playing Tetris, not with your inventory like Diablo, but with all the windows you have to manage. Not 2D tetris, either. 3D Tetris, so you have to know what window is behind what. The fighting is simple and boring, though LOOKS interesting in gameplay videos. You just click on a gun, and that weapon fires. Or, press Space to fire all weapons.
The animations and textures are one of the more disappointing things about this game. It looks like a game that my Grandma could play on her 5 year old store-bought PC. Unfortunately, it runs like Crysis 2 would, on said store-bought, 5 year-old PC. The animations are poor. Watching a robot walk around makes me cringe, because they don't step... They slide. Their feet might make the motion of stepping, but they just slide across the floor...
The movement is worse than anything else. You don't FEEL like a robot. You can go from facing right to facing left INSTANTLY. No side-stepping, no turn animation, you just snap to that direction and go. It's horrible! I want to feel like I'm a powerful robot, or a nimble robot, or a big, heavy mining robot. But, no. You just snap directions, and go about your day. No matter what design you have, the robot's movement is poorly animated and feels way to fast to turn directions.
Overall, I'd give this game like a 3/10. It seems like it would be fun, if things were executed a bit differently. A game like HAWKEN got the movement for mechs right. The stomping, the independent movement of the torso, etc... I just think this game needs more work.

(NOTE: This game was NOT reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher, it was a game I purchased for my own account)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Neat (but very dark) little CYOA and the price is right! 3/5 and worth about $5
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
This little game is quite interesting and is a little fun too. Some positives on this one include a great storyline, some graphics (which is more than some CYOA's) and some interesting battles and encounters. Fans of the RPG-Style of CYOA's will enjoy this quite a bit. Be forewarned however, some of the subject material is extremely dark and graphic. The level of despair in this game is pretty high. Some drawbacks to this game include the somewhat repetitve nature of having to replay certain areas of the game, the lack of audio and it is somewhat predictable after a while. It is also a bit pricey at over $5. However, if you can pick this up on sale and are not bothered by dark subject matter, you'll enjoy this. The enemies are quite Lovecraftian and the story is pretty much on par.
Happy Gaming!

Extremely disappointed with this one. Among many many wrong things with this particular title, there's one unforgivable mistake: there's a pattern in the cards dealt. Yeah; no random factor. If the card you need does not come in your current play, it will, WITH ABSOLUTE CERTAINTY, in the next one.
That's it! Forgotten Tales: Day of the Dead is a card game where difficulty is almost non-existent, and even like this, it becomes annoying.

Forgotten Tales Day of the Dead is a solitaire game golf type: click higher or lower cards until you empty out the field. Surprisingly there’s a story and a theme: Mexican lore of the undead / Los Muertos! Your wife was kidnapped by a mean spirit and you will go through the land of the dead to rescue her. You will gather items and meet colorful characters. The tutorial is well done, there are a lot of achievements to do and levels to complete, plus the levels have several goals to meet. The graphics are stylized and very colorful (a chameleon would have a seizure if left out in front of the game for too long!); the drawings, background and card backs are really beautiful and the music is nice.
The cons are that it’s very repetitive: all the levels feel the same. Also it is VERY easy, I didn’t manage to fail any level. That’s because the cards you draw are not random - this is the first game where I see that! It means that if you’re left with, say a 6 on the board then you know that within the next 2 cards you’ll draw will be a 7 or a 5. We’re far from Fairway Solitaire which drives you nut with its difficulty but therefore lacks the satisfaction of finishing a level or getting an awesome score!
I cannot recommend it, unless it gets patched or something. It’s too bad because the whole game design is top notch, it feels like all those efforts were ruined with this non random draw gameplay mechanics. Only buy this game is you want a very easy game to relax and don’t expect a challenge.

An excellent little puzzle game. While the backgrounds vary, and a few additional mechanics are added by the environment, the options at your disposal are very limited from beginning to end. However, Obulis takes its one trick and manages to deliver a challenging but rewarding experience. I found it relatively easy to work out how I was 'supposed to' complete a mission (or, often, a different way I strongly suspected would work), the difficulty comes in executing your plan correctly. Personally, I would have preferred the balance to have been set the other way round - make it harder to work out a solution, but then easier to deliver. Still, I really enjoyed it overall. As a guide to how much you should consider paying / waiting for it to come up in a sale, though, as always, YMMV, it took me a little over 10 hours to fully complete.

Physic based 2D platform puzzler. Gave me rage, not happy feels

Obulis is a puzzle game that utilizes physics in order for you to solve the puzzles.  You have multicolored balls that must reach a given pocket or hole.  In order to do so you'll have to figure out the proper order and timing on when to release them from their dangling/swinging chain, or when you need to move them with the click of a mouse.  I really liked this game, it was very simple to play, but at times very complex to solve.  That's what I want to see out of any puzzle game, the difficulty being in the puzzle itself, not trying to figure out how to get the game to work for you.  Simple graphics, forgettable music, but it all fits perfectly because of the fabulous gameplay and physics that this game offer.  Highly recommended for any puzzle genre fan.

The game is fairly simple and relaxing, yet requires patience and follow-through. You get a free seedling each week, which you can plant in your pot. The plants grow slowly (but not *too* realistically) and require water every once in a while. Checking in about once a day is usually par-for-the-course. You get a snail buddy. You can sing to the snail too.
You get an achievement for growing the plant to maturity, and for certain plants you also get an achievement for flowering them (which takes even longer and more patience.) You grow to like your plants, you can name them, you become attached to them. Once you're finished with them, you can release them into the garden- never to be seen again. You feel a sense of reward and completion.
If you enjoy plants and slow, simple, relaxing sim games- this is definitely for you. I like to load up the game, water my plants, sing to them, and pin the game to the front of my screen while I go about my daily business doing other things (checking E-mail, reddit, looking at the news, etc.) The music is very calming and good.

I'm no aficionado when it comes to these types of card games, but I'll give my 2 cents anyways, because I enjoyed this game, at first. I can't really compare it to other games since I lack experience with those, but I can at least give my little experience here.
The biggest part that I love about this game is how so many cards can play off one another and stack up to a massive army all to be toppled in an instant when the one card it's all built upon is destroyed. A game can fluctuate immensely and it always has me on my guard or looking for a way to knock everything over with a well timed attack.
The card variety is much larger than I expected when I started and I only got a real idea of how much there was when I looked to my stats and saw how low my % of each level card I had.
The downsides I've run into are as follows;
1: You can buy packs with real money and that always leads to "pay to win" mentalities in alot of players. Sure there are ways to get packs without paying, but using real money gets you much more much quicker. Then there's the "RNG" that tells you what you get. I use the  " " because after opening all of my packs for nothing but duplicates of♥♥♥♥♥♥ I can't help but assume it is predetermined what I get and I just have to grin and bare. My money says it's to try and choke money out of you.
2: I ran into this glitch that skipped a large chunk of my turn. After ending one turn, my opponent did all they could and for some reason, it never said it was my turn again. It just became my turn again without any indication. I was able to play cards when I noticed it was my turn with my hand shimmering with what I could play, but I couldn't attack. It wasn't for lack of time, it's just that none of my cards were available to attack. I looked over everything played and in discard to see if I was mass shackled somehow, but that wasn't it. Either I ran into a cheater or a bug. On the bright side though, it only happened once.
3: This is the biggest one and it's what makes me consider this game an abomination. Through the game stacking my deck in every match I have, I am completely unable to play. No matter what I put into my decks, I'm always given the highest cards I have first and even when I
re-draw, I get them again. I've tried making low level decks so I can play at all, but then I will never draw a creature card, only equipment. I dwindle down my deck more and I'm left with not enough cards to even make a deck because the packs I've gotten give me either more equipment or things far too strong to play early on. Normally I'd chalk this up to bad luck, but when the same exact cards come up time and time and time again endlessly, the odds start to change. At this point it should be near impossible for me to not get something usable, but the game finds a way.
In short, if you want to even be able to play whatsoever, you have to fork over your life savings.
I get that devs need to make money, fair enough. But why not charge a small fee for the game? There are plenty of people willing to buy the game.
I'm sure even more people would want to play if it was FAIR!
By the way, if someone can tell me about that quick chat thing, I'd appreciate it. I've looked all over but the keywords bring up unrelated stuff each time in searches and i can't find anything in the game itself telling me what to press. It's like a closely guarded secret and I've been banging my head on my keyboard to find out how to do it.

Cant write enough about this game. Definitely a hidden gem that only lacks a bit of investment by those seeking an amazing futuristic scifi sandbox mmo. If you enjoyed EvE you will enjoy Perpetuum. My only issues with the game after 650 hours of play time is the poor UI. If there was a better elevation depiction on the Radar for pvp and also a sort of Tactical overlay like what EvE has I would be completely content giving it a 10/10. Main reasons for the lack of said fixes? No one seems to know about this game :P
I played EvE for over 6 years and got fed up with the subscriptions and lack of pvp mechanics to support small scale combat as well as large scale combat without becoming the "death blob" where any monkey who can listen to an FC call targets and hit F1 can be a pvper. In Perpetuum there are mechanics such as interference and AoE damage when robots explode. 100 man drake fleets would not want to orbit the fc at 500m in Perpetuum because if one or two die in close proximity to the rest of the fleet it would be a beautiful cascade of exploding drakes. I have been on the winning and losing side of those cascades and it gets me every time. PvP in perpetuum is the reason I remain here instead of returning to EvE. Every individual needs to be aware of their strengths/weaknesses/surroundings to avoid being a hindrance to a group let alone being effective.
I also spent my first two years in EvE doing industry. As far as crafting goes in EvE it is usually straight forward until you get to t2/t3 manufacturing. All of the crafting in Perpetuum is like t3 and t2 where you must first unlock what you wish to create by gathering kernals and then spending said kernals. After an item is unlocked (there are two trees, one for personal research and one for corporation research. Having an item unlocked for the corp as well as the individual will give bonuses) you can then prototype it. A prototype is much more expensive than the module/robot you wish to produce. It also requires some additional resources that are gathered from destroyed npc's. Once the protoype is done it can be Reverse Engineered into a CT or Calibration Template. The CT is like the BPC in EvE. There are no BPO's, you must continually prototype and reverse engineer what you wish to produce as your CT's get worn-out. As the CT gets used it becomes less and less efficient also. To get the materials needed to actually do the manufacturing side of things it will require components made of a combination of plants, liquids, and ores from various islands to make a finished product.
I know these are fat blocks of text but every detail is needed for this game. The pvp system far exceeds EvE online and the Crafting system has such a depth to it that eve will never reach simply because the sinks for resources and currency are so high. It requires a very hardcore gamer to truly understand this game and it requires an equally hardcore community to utilize all the picks and shovels in this sandbox.

Grim Fandango, or "the last original thought anyone has had even within earshot of LucasArts" is one of the best point & click games I have played.
I just love everything about it; the story, the characters (I hate the bad guys though, but that's how it's supposed to be), the setting, the retro look, the fine details in design and animation, the truly amazing soundtrack, the puzzles, the overall tone and the humour. The game is capable of going from dead serious (no pun intended) and epic, to hilarious, seamlessly.
The only problems I have with it are some technical ones, and how some of the puzzles aren't that satisfying.
I've had very few technical issues; just one crash and I got stuck once, unable to move and therefore had to restart. Sometimes, the Steam Overlay wouldn't work, causing me to miss out on some achievements, even though I completed what needs to be done in order to get them. Restaring Steam a few times did make the Overlay work again. Now I just have to go back and get the achievements, eh...
The puzzles are great. The majority of them are really challenging, interesting and feel rewarding when you finally solve them. Unfortunately, some of them feel confusing and you're not quite sure what you're supposed to do, which resulted in not feeling as accomplished after doing them.
Also, the game has a fixed camera that changes as you move from area to area, which would sometimes obscure something you need to solve a puzzle, or the path to another area. This is because the visual cues that should notify you of them aren't always easy to see.
There's no autosave system, so you'll need to save manually if you don't want to lose your progress. It's a bit of a nuisance, but I haven't lost more than 30 minutes of gameplay total.
Overall, it's an excellent game, one of the best I have played. I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone interested in it. You can wait for a sale, but I think that you'll get your money's worth even for 15€.
I rate this spooky, puzzle-solving skeleton a 9/10.

If you're wondering what kind of game this is, there's two clues in the title.  Firstly, it's a text-based adventure, with minimalistic graphics and a LOT of reading.  So if that doesn't sound like you, SKIP THIS STORE PAGE NOW.  Secondly, it's kind of an old-school "dungeon" explorer, complete with some nice pixel-y maps, but completely lacking in any stats or other regular "RPG" elements apart from an inventory.  Combat consists of nothing more than choosing to fight something, then you keep clicking on text messages until you or it dies.  THAT'S IT.  No stats, no combat tactics, JUST STORY.  Again, if this doesn't sound like something you can live with, LEAVE THIS STORE PAGE NOW.
Phew.  Glad that's over.  Are they gone?!  Good.

Now that it's just me and you, curious one, let me say straight up that whatever else this "game" is, it's extremely well-written and has a fascinating story.  This Nathan Meunier person could probably write books for a living.  And highly Lovecraftian books they would in all probability be.  Yep, he's one of those...but a very GOOD one of those.  The depth this game goes into about rituals and demon summoning and what-not suggests a first-class crackpot who either reads too many "esoteric" texts, or has a spiffingly good imagination.  This Book Is A Dungeon is short, but intriguing, and I certainly look forward to anything Mr Meunier gets up to in the future.
A few suggestions to the dev/author for next time:  The price is a tad on the silly side (one or two dollars would be far more realistic); how about some MUSIC to further invoke that Eldritchean atmosphere; and thirdly, how about some save/checkpoints next time, as redoing bits over and over and over again does get a bit tiresome (especially when the text is so moodily staggered and can't be skipped, and so many bits of the game are so ruthlessly trial-and-error)?

Fantastic first effort, though.  Keep up the good work, sir.

Verdict: 8/10.

(PS Some advice to budding players: Be sure to keep a pen and paper close at hand.  The game might keep a map for you, but you're gonna need to make plenty of notes, just the same!!!)

There are lots of other flaws with the game that I will not list since I've already listed way too much. I bought this game when it was 10% off and I really wished I would have waited until it was $3, since thats all I wouldve wanted to pay for this game, or forgotten about the game and saved my $10 for a better game.

I read more dialogue to only find the same bland humor (it might just be me that doesn't find it funny) as always. Completed most of the side quests I could find which were pretty decent. Still wouldn't have paid $10 if I hadn't already.

A surprisingly overlooked gem in the Lara Croft franchise, Guardian of Light brings a refreshing perspective on the heroine: namely - the iso-metric co-op action shooter.
Seeing Lara from this new perspective gives the game an old-school Prince of Persia feel, giving you the kind of spatial awareness which I felt was always missing from the series.
The single player is an enjoyable balance between frantic shoot outs and challenging (but not impossible) puzzles. Where the game excels is in co-op, where the game neatly divides all the special abilities available in single player between two, adding new combos into the mix. Learning to use the new abilities as a team, while pulling off some neat tricks is a pleasure, as is shooting bad guys for two.
This is a cheap, fun and engaging experience to be shared with friends. Don't overlook it.

This game is absolutely bonkers, in a good way though.
is like normal PAC-MAN, only the map is rotated 90 degrees, there are
of ghosts instead of just 4, and it's a race to eat as many dots, food and ghosts as possible before the timer runs out.
The game is split into several boards with different structures, dot and ghost positioning, and paths to follow. None of them really feel any harder than the others, but they're all difficult in their own way. The DLC boards are a fun addition, but I wouldn't recommend you buy them separately from the game, since it's cheaper to buy the full
pack and just get all of it at once.
Gameplay wise, it's actually a lot more complicated than basic PAC-MAN. Pac controls as you'd expect him to, and the basic premise is still there, but given a twist. Dots appear in simple paths for Pac-Man to follow, and once they've all been eaten, a piece of fruit spawns for him to eat, which creates the next path for him to follow. Power pellets work the same as every other version of PAC-MAN. Eat one and all the ghosts become edible...all 40 of them.
The ghosts in this game are much more numerous than any other version. They generally chase you in lines which get longer and longer as you pass by more sleeping ghosts, and there are usually one or two ghosts roaming around independently to try and throw you off. Often you'll be scarfing down 40 or more ghosts in one go after consuming a power pellet and racking up a ton of points. Some ghosts even hold power pellets so yo can keep yourself going. And if you're afraid you'll run out of juice at a bad time, have no fear. They added a meter on the top of the screen showing how long until the pellet wears off. And even if you do run out at an inopportune moment or are trapped between ghosts with no way out, you have another way to deal with them, bombs.
Bombs are another thing ghosts can carry, and are essentially a screen nuke for all the ghosts chasing you and any other ghosts who Pac is about to collide with. Bombs can be the difference between getting a higher score and getting killed (which doesn't stop the timer, but I'll get to that in a bit), and should be used sparingly, because the ghosts can trap you even more easily if you aren't careful after using a bomb, and the cycle just repeats itself until you run out.
The biggest change to gameplay is the actual objective. Instead of just eating all the dots, this game is a score attack, you want to get as many points as possible in a set amount of time, usually five minutes. Once the timer starts, it does not stop until it runs out, which means dying has a serious impact on your score. This is because respawning takes about 3 seconds, and it slows the game speed meter on the bottom of the screen down to the nearest multiple of 5, slowing you down even more. Using bombs and even going near ghosts can also slow you down. Using a bomb freezes Pac in place for half a second, and going near a ghost slows the game down and briefly zooms in on Pac to let you know to dodge or use a bomb.
And to be entirely honest, I actually really like these changes. It makes the game very fast paced and requires very quick thinking and reflexes to get that high score, making this game a real good challenge and quite addicting to play. I could totally see this in an arcade if they were still as prevalent as they were in the 80s, and I would glady drop a few quarters if I came across it.
A fun spin on a classic title for a perfectly reasonable price, and an absolute steal when on sale. If you like arcade style madness, this is a great time and I highly recommend it.

Far Cry 2, although it's not even really a sequel to Far Cry, is an amazing game. Why did they call it Far Cry 2? I don't know. The only similarities between the two titles involve the driving mechanics and the shooting mechanics. Otherwise, they have nothing in common.
However, in my opinion, Far Cry 2 is the better game. While Far Cry had a more involving story, Far Cry 2 had a more interesting setting. The open world, fictional, war torn, central African country that your mercenary character arrives in is immersive and glorious. From savanahs, to jungles, to deserts and sand dunes, to valleys, Ubisoft Montreal packed everything you might find in a central African country into this 16 square mile playground. The towns are small and sparse, but the wildlife you find in between will capture your bewilderment. This, simply put, is a fully realized environment. And it's absolutely stunning.
On the story side of things, the only thing I have to say about it is that it could have been more inspired. Basically, you choose a mercenary at the beginning of the game, and you play as that mercenary. The rest of the mercs on this list end up being your "buddies". Anyway, the story of the game is that you, an assassin for hire, was sent to this fictional country to kill "The Jackal", an international arms dealer who is supplying both factions that are fighting for power. Well, as soon as you get to this country, your malaria kicks in and "The Jackal" ends up saving you. "The Jackal" is, hands down, the most interesting character in the game. His philosophy about the current state of the country and his knowledge of politics invoke that he has no personal interest in whoever wins, but he is moralistic in that he does care about the civilians. After he leaves you for dead with a gun and machete, you escape and are saved by one of the faction generals who will task you with saving your first buddy. This is where the game gets repetitive, at least it seems to.
Eventually, you'll save every buddy traversing through each area, doing missions for both faction leaders, doing missions for gun runners, doing missions for a mysterious contracter (assassinations). And, without going into details, these missions aren't that interesting. The only interesting moments honestly involve the few cutscenes you have with "The Jackal". But that doesn't mean the story is bad. It's just fleshed out with mercenary work as you are, after all, an assassin for hire. Eventually, you'll travel south to another part of the country where the remainder of the game takes place and more of the same is done. You find more buddies, you do more missions for the APR and the UFLL, and the, endgame.
In terms of gameplay, this game is amazing. The hyper realism (except for car repairs which are the opposite of realistic) is splendid. Your gun will wear down and jam, you have to perform quick self surgeries if near death, branches and shrubs sway out of the way, the HUD is completely off when driving or running around, you have to take malaria pills to fight the malaria. The other interesting aspect is the use of diamonds as a form of currency. This is certainly much in line with how some African countries are due to a lack of a formal government.
To summarize, brilliant FPS despite the weak story. And it's not even a weak story, it's just that the story was so sparse. The Jackal is such a great character, though, that he ends up saving the story.

Disclaimer: I am reviewing this game as someone who has no prior experience with games produced by suda51, hence this review is pieced together purely from experience gained from this game.
Killer is dead is a fast paced hack and slash game set not too far into future, in a world that combines elements of fantasy, cyberpunk and set in modern era. The player controls a character named Mondo Zappa, an amnesiac hitman working for a government agency tasked with neutralizing high risk individuals that have somehow wronged the state, who can vary from higly dangerous murderers, rogue assasins, all kinds of monsters and combination of thereof.
The whole game boils down to twelve episodes, with each episode's objective being getting to a set target, and eliminating them. For the elimination itself you have several tools, your trusty katana Gekkou, a prosthetic arm called Musselback that is able to morph into several weapons such as giant drill, a machine gun or a cannon, to name a few. The combat itself is what you would expect from a hack and slash game, you move around in third person perspective, cutting your enemies apart with your sword or shooting them from afar, depending on what approach you prefer and whether or not do you have blood (which you gain from attacking your enemies) to power your weapons. You can also block or dodge their attack, with dodging at the perfect time and pressing the left mouse button rewarding you with slowmo sequence where you can indiscriminately hack away at your enemy for a short period of time the faster your press the LMB.
Your enemies in most cases (dubbed Wires) come in multitude of variations, ranging from footsoldiers with blunt weapons, rifles, samurai, large beasts with claws and more. This fodder precludes a boss fight, which more often than not boils down to reducing the boss's health to a certain degree, then performing an execution (you can also use this execution on lesser enemies to eliminate them immediatelly, as long as certain conditions are met and you have enough blood to do so) to weaken them. You repeat this once or several times, before a cutscene ensues, after which you get a prompt to execute your enemy in a cinematic fashion.
The story itself to be honest, is pretty weak. At best it's weird, at it's worst it's an incomprehensible mess of poorly written characters and plot which often lacks the necesary explanations and aswers to hold the entire thing together. Half of the characters, I know nothing about. Why is the Boss half cyborg, why does Viviene (his assistant) have 16 arms at several points in the game (usually to randomly assist you in some episodes) and how did she actually became the member of the agency?
Your own assistant, Mika Tanekawa, serves no other purpose but to ressurect you in exchange for tickets you buy from the gift shop where you can spend the money from the episodes and side missions, This shop also serves another purpose. To get mundo laid.
''What?'' You might ask?
Well, the entire economy, apart from purchasing resources for upgrades, consumeables and tickets for ressurection, also contains gifts that you can purchase for use in the Giggolo missions (holy crap this is cringy), where your objective is to bed one of the ''beauties'' by, and I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not, staring at her face when she is looking at you, and shamelessly ogling her when she is not, to build up the guts meter, at which point you can give her a present depending on your decisions (A tiger fan for example, is ought to be a good gift for a Japanese lady). This was probably done to give the game more depth aside from it's premise of being a government executor/assasin, but it comes off as so simplistic, juvenile and crass that it will sooner cause you to become annoyed, especially since you need to complete several of these missions to obtain all the subweapons for the Musselback. There is absolutely no charcter to these women, who repeat the same few lines over and over and ocassionally perform some kind of activity depending on who they are.
The giggolo mode just plain sucks, but enough about it. I think It's about time to wrap it up.
So what will you get for 20 euros, or in the case as it is now for several more hours, for free? A decently fun game in the style of devil may cry with confusing or downright nonsensical plot at some times, mostly crappy characters, and a godawful ''dating'' system that makes rapelay look like epitome of romance in comparison.
Nevertheless, I will still recommend it, maybe it will suit your tastes more.
Final verdict 7/10 (it would be 6/10 if I actually paid for this mind you).

I'm gonna be honest, I never intended to try this. I'm not a huge fan of TES, but I do love the series and it's atmosphere. I was convinced this was simply another Heartstone ripoff, aimed to steal the audience. I imagined it as a cheap clone, because honestly, that's what it seemed like.
I couldn't be more wrong. From games like MTG and Pokemon, where mechanics almost never change, to YGO, where a new one is introduced every other year (and it forces half the players to quit, because it gets worse and worse), to HS - the ultimate softcore TCG, I couldn't believe how TES: Legends achieved so much in inovation and freshness with just a few simple, but well placed mechanics. It really has to be tried to be understood.
From the fact that it offers somewhat of a story mode, with actual content and choices, which reflect on your collection and individual cards, to the battlefield with two lanes, each offering different strategic options, via modifiers or simply via controlling the two lanes so you can manipulate your oponent into reacting in a manner that suits your intents, there is clearly a great amount of thought and design put into this TCG.
And honestly, as someone who's always fallen for TCG games, this is one of the best I've played and the only one that actually takes advantage of being digital in way, that enchances gameplay - it's a feature that I've wanted to see in a digital TCG forever!
In conclusion: if you are a TES or TCG fan, you deffinetely need to give this a spin. There is always a possibility of it not being up your alley, but beyond that (and certain meta/balance complaints that are always a given in TCGs), there is absolutely no reason for this game to be NOT recommended. It's an absolute gem.

If you know me at all, you know I LOVE solitaire.  I’ve been playing it ever since I was a wee lass, but golf solitaire has recently become my favorite version of the game.  Imagine my delight when yet another title released featuring the enjoyable gameplay I’ve come to love.  Forgotten Tales: Day of the Dead had SO much promise: beautiful artwork, a fantastic theme, and interesting new power-ups and board goals I hadn’t seen done in other games — and yet against all odds it failed.  As a lover of solitaire and supporter of indie game developers everywhere, it pains me greatly to have to write this review, but it is my sworn duty to tell the whole truth and nothing but the truth, so help me Dios.
Let’s start with what this game does well, its presentation.  Everything about the way Forgotten Tales looks and sounds is an absolute joy.  I love the Day of the Dead theme, especially the story snippets with cultural references that lovingly incorporate the mythology behind this Mexican day of celebration.  The artwork is beautiful, colorful and uniquely stylized.   And there’s the soundtrack, all royalty-free licensed pieces, but the compositions are wonderful, reminding me of several movie scores I hold dear.  I simply cannot express enough how much I enjoyed the look and feel of this game.  Then we come to the gameplay.
Forgotten Tales uses the golf rule set, which involves playing cards in ascending or descending order until all have been removed from the board. There's a bit more to it than that, but it's a very easy version of the game.  One might wonder how you can possibly mess that up, and I’ll tell you how; you make the draw pile NOT random.  Just let that sink in for a second.  A solitaire game that does not have a random draw deck.  This one point, this fatal flaw, is what ruined the gameplay for me.  Luck of the draw has ALWAYS been a part of solitaire no matter what version you’re playing, and finding ways to overcome it with strategic gameplay and the smart use of power-ups and wild cards is what makes the game so engaging.  But when a useable card is drawn at least 75% of the time, it does NOT feel OR play right.
Looking at things objectively, I understand why this design choice was made.  With the way the game is laid out with each level having 3 rounds (tableaus) to clear on only one deck of cards, too much randomness in the draw would make the later levels practically impossible to complete unless you got super lucky. However, this could have been avoided by splitting the three rounds into their own levels, thus making a random draw deck less punishing.  Doing so would even out the value of the bonus cards, which heavily skew towards the “Joker” and “+5 to Draw Pile” cards, and would also add more focus to the unique board goals. Had these issues been addressed, I am confident Forgotten Tales would have been a near perfect iteration of the game I so love.  Sadly, it is not to be.
So, it is with a heavy heart that I give you this news.  I wanted to love Forgotten Tales: Day of the Day with every fiber of my being, but I simply cannot look past its sole flaw, and that is preventing me from recommending it to solitaire fans everywhere.  Perhaps with a sufficient discount it may be worth it if only to experience the beautiful art and music.  However, if you’re looking for the next great solitaire game along the lines of
and
, you’ll want to keep looking.
Bottom Line: Not Recommended.

Forgotten Tales: Day of the Dead.  Forgotten?  Someone remembered.  Enough to tell the tale in this game anyway.
What we have here is the higher/lower type of solitaire you'll find in several other games such as Regency Solitaire, Chef Solitaire, Faerie Solitaire, Legends of Solitaire, Goat Solitaire, and FarCry 4.  As always, I want to know one thing.  What does this particular solitaire game do to distinguish itself?  From the other solitaire game I mean.  Not like distinguish itself from the field of presidential candidates or anything.  Having written jokingly about that before, and seeing what we have wound up with as the choice for the next president, I'm not going anywhere near that subject.
Considering that what we are playing is the same as many times before, Forgotten Tales spices things up with a story about a guy trying to get his wife back from the land of the dead, which really resonates with me because it reminds me of making love to my ex.  What really makes Forgotten Tales stand out for me though are the variety of power-ups and special cards.
There are several special powers you can use, from revealing hidden cards, to crushing your enemies. Seeing them driven before you. Hearing the lamentations of their women. This is what is best in life.  There are also cards that act as bombs, or rockets destroying everything in their path.  Sometimes it's not so much solitaire as global thermonuclear war.  Shall we play a game?  No fighting though.  Gentlemen, you can't fight in here! This is the War Room! Horror has a face... and you must make a friend of horror. Horror and moral terror are your friends.
Ok, that's a lot of movies so getting back to the game at hand, if you like solitaire games, and I know you do, Forgotten Tales will help fill that dark void in your soul that yearns to devour the world.  At least for a little while.  Ia ia Cthulhu fhtagn!

Who doesn't love a clone of one of the more beloved arcade games? 1942 and its bottom-up schmup ilk are easy to pick-up and play, and require no need to learn complex button presses or tactics. Hold the button down and blast away everything in sight. I was hoping Razor2 would scratch that itch - a 10 minute pick-up and play game. How wrong could the game go? Pretty wrong in fact.
First of all, for a game that was released in 2010 this game doesn't run well. My computer isn't a monster, but it should be able to run something like this. Judging by the screen tearing, rapid drop in frame-rate, and dodgy animation, maybe I'm wrong. Bear in mind the game doesn't run at full resolution, it vertically blocks either side of the screen to squash the image. This is a poor show, even with all these solutions the game runs badly.
The gameplay isn't any great shakes, but after playing the first boss for 10 minutes and not getting anywhere, I decided I was done with this game. The most frustrating thing is there was no feedback whether I was hitting the right part of the boss. The small enemies line up like pawns in a chess game taking all the hits and doing nothing but make the game more frustrating. If a game can't tell the player whether what they are doing is right or wrong - as in you hit the enemy and it turns red - then how does the player know whether their actions are effective or not?
I'm done with this game. It takes something of a certain quality to not even make it through the first level. This is one such game.

Razor 2: Hidden Skies tries gallantly to emulate the shmups of yore, but falls flat not for want of creativity (though it could certainly use a bit more), but inexcusable♥♥♥♥♥♥ups on the game mechanics themselves.
The game attempts, in some places, to be a bullet hell game but the hitbox of your ship is extremely large and does not even match the graphic - it awkwardly extends out an uncertain distance to both sides, but does not seem to include the nose of the fighter. Furthermore, the areas extend visually farther than your actual range of motion, but this is impossible to tell without running right into an invisible wall. In several areas, enemies park right on this wall, giving the illusion that you can zip around them to avoid fire and take them out, right up until you crash into them headlong making the attempt. This is made even more unweildly by the boss fights that zoom the camera out, supposedly to impress you with how big the boss is. Sadly the net result is that now you can see even more but have the same narrow movement lane, exacerbating the problem even more.
Two subweapons are heat-seeking with auto targetting, but there is no mechanic to choose what you'd like to target - the game seems to completely arbitrarily choose for you, and even if the lock-on happens to be a priority target, anything flying in the path of your slow-traveling relativistic missiles will intercept them and explode instead. (Which prompts the question of how does a missile travelling at relativistic speeds even work, and if it does why are they so bloody slow?) The bosses are all recycled variants of each other - fight three tanks, then fight three spinning satellite things, then... etc.
Unfortunately the problems do not stop there. Movement is imprecise and jerky. Combine this with the awkard hitboxes and you've committed a cardinal sin in the shmup genre - dodging is effectively impossible in places, though this doesn't matter a terrible lot since to cover for this the game slathers you in multiple shields which partially refresh upon each pick-up. Despite that fact, you still take a lot of hits simply because your hitbox isn't where you think it is, and it's nigh impossible to guage where its limits are precisely, since it extends well beyond the ship graphic. Unfortunately, the pickups themselves don't make a terrible lot of sense. One of the most common is Energy, which restores a pip on your Energy meter. Which is grand, only the game never quite explains what Energy is for or why you want it, despite being able to upgrade your ship batteries to have more of it. Oh well, free shields I guess!
In general the game is horridly unpolished. The translation is riddled with grammatical errors, word misuse, and typos (I'm not sure what a Gravity Riffle is). Each mission has a cheesy low-quality text-to-speech mission introduction voiceover, only it gets a few words into it before the explosions start and the rest is completely drowned out. Oops. Hope it wasn't important. Soon after starting the second mission, the primary fire input became stuck and I was essentially on autofire for the rest of the game. Which isn't all bad I suppose, except with the input stuck, I became unable to read mission briefings (not a tremendous loss since they're an exercise in bad English and misspelled words) and upon finishing and going to the main menu it would spam me right into a new game on Easy Mode, not allowing me to change settings or even exit the game. I had to alt-tab and manually kill it.
In short, I can't recommend this game at all, even to die-hard shmup fans, unless you seriously need a fix and simply cannot find something else to scratch the itch.

Grim Fandago is about one of the grim reaper salemen, Manuel, who needs to repay off his Earthly sins by selling good travel packets to those passing to the next world. But wait, there seems to be something suspicious going on that stops Manuel from acheiving his goals. He investigates with some friends to find out what is happening with his job, and those behind it.
A unique and comedic point and click game, added with the main character "Manny" and his saracastic humor really makes for a good storyline and play. The side characters are just as amusing and add flavor to the setting. I would say some of the puzzles in this game were moderate to difficult. I've played quite a bit of point and click games and this is on the more difficult end of the spectrum. One good thing is I would say it is mostly kid friendly if you have younger players wanting to try this. There's a few euphemisms in there, but the more adult tones are very subtle.
Overall, its a fun point and click with a nice storyline.

Visually this is a beautiful game that uses The Day of The Dead as an inspiration for the world. It has a unique look with lots of attention to detail. You really get a sense of the entire "universe" and culture of the Underworld.
The dialogue is witty, sarcastic perfection.
As for the gameplay, it is part exploration, part point-and-click, part "oh my god I'm going to lose my mind because I can't figure out what this ONE THING is for."  For me it wasn't easy by any means, and I have to admit I cheated a bit and used a walk-through when I really got stuck. La cosa assurda e grottesca nella storia è che il protagonista Manny, dopo il trapasso, non trova la meritata pace, ma si ritrova in un mondo simile alla realtà, dove è costretto a lavorare con persone senza scrupoli, tra lunghe burocrazie, corruzioni, sfruttamento e ingiustizie, con il timore della morte pur avendola già provata.
Nell’insieme devo dire che pur essendo quattro lunghi capitoli, non si cade mai nella noia o monotonia, perché Manny pur affrontando i suoi compiti con serietà, non manca certo di sparare i suoi  commenti sarcastici e non si vergogna di buttarsi a fare le cose più strane creando così situazioni comiche, mentre i personaggi che incontrerà, alcuni bizzarri altri simpatici, ci faranno sicuramente sorridere.
Godibile la colonna sonora, che con il suo Swing accompagna bene questo stile Noir, con tipiche atmosfere da Gangster; mentre il doppiaggio è veramente ottimo, ben azzeccato, specialmente la voce del protagonista è straordinaria perché dà forza e carattere al personaggio.
Tranquilli, c'è anche spazio per i sentimenti, una bellissima amicizia che si consoliderà durante la storia e che alla fine farà commuovere.
Un consiglio: le cose da fare sono molte, ma non mancate di parlare con tutti, ed esaurite bene tutti i dialoghi, altrimenti rischiate di non sbloccare delle azioni essenziali.
Lo consiglio a tutti Fandango perché è uno di quei giochi che ti rimane impresso anche a distanza di tempo, le sue battute e citazioni hanno fatto storia tra chi l’ha giocato.

Note: I won a free copy of the game through a contest held by the creator (I believe).
Overall, this is an enjoyable and unique game. The story was fun, the writing was good, and it had a creepy atmosphere throughout. I especially liked the crude pixelart drawings and scenery that would pop up every so often, it really added to the text.
A lot of people are describing this game as a "choose your own adventure", but I would disagree. This is a puzzle game that just happens to be text-based. While there are choices, in my playthrough I didn't find they had a long-lasting impact like they would in a choose-your-own adventure book. They mostly altered the short-term, gave clues to puzzles, or were cosmetic (with the exception of the ending, which seemed to come out of nowhere which was a bit disappointing).
Some things that may turn some people off from this game:
- It's very short. I beat it with a friend in just under two hours even though I had to redo a section about three or four times. There are about five "chapters" to the book and it ends rather abruptly.
- There's no real "save" feature, just one or two major milestones you can restart at. This was a bit frustrating because death can be very punishing when you're caught unaware. The first time I died I was set back two chapters (about 30 minutes worth of game). A save feature or at least chapter checkpoints would be nice.
- The game is surprisingly easy. Maybe I just got lucky, but there were only two parts I "lost" at. There were also no points in the game I got "stuck" not knowing what to do.
- A few sections of the game had a very crude combat system that amounted to nothing more than luck and clicking "attack" over and over until the fight ended. There weren't many of these fights (only one or two depending on your choices) but I felt they detracted from the game. I'm all for a combat system, but the way it's currently implemented isn't fun since there's absolutely no strategy that I could discern.
- While the writing is great the story is a bit weak. Things happen but there's no real reason for them. The game doesn't need to explain everything that exists in its world, but considering it sells itself as a book it would've been nice for the story to be a bit more fleshed out.
Ultimately, this was a fun game that harkens back to old horror/text based adventure games (and does it better than I've seen in recent years). Should you buy it? Well, if text-based horror is your thing then this is a very nice title. For me personally the price does seem a bit high considering the amount of content in the game but if even a couple more chapters were added and some of the issues I described above were improved then this could be a real gem.

Honestly, simplicity is bliss and this game definitely has simplicity in mind when it comes to graphics. The pots have cute designs, but they're definitely not over complicated, the plants are unique and all have detail. Even the little snail that happily chugs his (or her) way around your pot looks adorable! This game has a cute factor that's actually mind blowing, it's the ultimate stress reliever, even in the graphics department.
This is a game that's all about patience. You can't go into Viridi with a mentality such as an action or adventure game, this game requires patience because your plants will grow in real-time. Yes, real-time. You water your plants once a day (even your snail if you like, but he's pretty good on his own so I wouldn't bother the lil guy). You watch the background change in real-time, it follows your system clock so if it's night time outside, it'll be dark in the game, same with day time. Viridi has a simple mechanic for gameplay, you water your plants, you listen to the calming music, and you enter your happy place.
Completely nonexistent. You make your own story out of your plants and your little snail friend, that's the bottom line.
As far as I know, this is also nonexistent.
So what are you getting with a game like this? Well, this is your happy place. you go to this game from time to time so you can relax from the natural stress in your daily life. The gameplay is simplistic, the visuals are beautiful and you will absolutely love this game if these things sound appealing to you. Also, there's achievements available, they take time to accomplish because of the real-time aspect of the game, but they're rewarding once you achieve them!
Do I recommend this game? Highly, especially if you're craving some stress relief. This is the ultimate test of patience, and there's a little gift every week for your patience as well. An extra seed to grow a new plant!

There are some aspects to Farcry 2 that i actually like more than 3.
The gameplay of Farcry 2 is pretty much standard like an FPS would be albeit with some addons and differences. You are able to use a primary, a secondary, and melee weapon along with a special weapon including grenades and molotovs. It is a big open world and your main means of travel is by various types of vehicles. To add a bit of realism, guns will jam and explode after awhile of prolonged use.
Unlike its predecessor you can have buddies that protect you and help you on missions. You can pick which character you want to be, though it doesnt really change the outcome. Also unlike its predecessor the setting is completely different as it takes place in Africa and not on tropical islands out on the pacific ocean. While alot of people showed disdain for this setting change, i actually liked the setting and enviroment.
The story of Farcry 2 is gathered via information when you accept missions or when you find cassette tapes left behind by the games main Antagonist "The Jackal". Essentially the lore of this game is in the background and you have to research it and pay attention to understand whats going on.
Farcry 2 still holds up well in its Graphics Department for a game from 2008. The Dunia Engine makes use of fire elements burning the enviroments grass and trees, as well as showcasing a day and night cycle and weather effects not present in the previous game. As for the sound design the explosions, guns etc are all top notch while the voiceacting is pretty decent. A few music tracks caught my attention in this game; i really enjoy the calm music transition to the fast battle paced ones when a firefight is happening.
My only minor gripes with Farcry 2 are having to constantly get Malaria pills, and the long drives it kinda takes to get to some areas. Other that that i recommend playing Farcry 2.

Far Cry 2 is tedious, but if you value immersion above being fast-paced then you'd be hard pressed to find a better game.
The empowerment you feel from playing the game comes from you persevering through mechanics that have been made more difficult than it is in typical FPS games by integrating real-world aspects, sometimes to unrealistic extremes. Playing through the campaign at max difficulty (makes you about as squishy as every NPC mook) with the music turned off (when you're on a far hill quietly picking off enemies one by one, hearing intense combat music play definitely throws you out of the moment).
-Your "reputation" acts as your EXP level in the game, and generic NPC's react accordingly. Guards will tell you to f*ck off and frequently threaten you at the beginning of the game, but as you level up their dialogue will descend into professional respect and then to superstitious fear.
-The HUD is very intentionally limited; the only onscreen effects are your health and ammo and they quickly fade when not in use. The map and compass have to be brought up like a weapon, and simulate a real paper map with pages of different scales. Sometime's it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to be at the very bottom of a map section and not be able to see a decent area around you, but it's frustration with something that would be in real life, not frustration with some contrived immersion-breaking game mechanic so it only adds to the immersion.
-You have to drive everywhere on the map but destinations are often close together and the geocaching side-quests, constant threat of ambush, and the detail put into making the "HUD" map feel real keep transportation from being boring. It's a rush to be looking down at your map, hear a close gunshot, and jolt back to the road to see a patrol that just came around the corner.
-Guns start to jam around after you fire your very limited ammo capacity, but it forces you to plan ahead like a true professional and make full use of your 3 weapons slots. Necessity is the mother of invention, and the situations where you're completely surrounded with everything but your pistol broken because you weren't efficient with your shots make the game memorable. Likewise, the feeling of satisfaction when an outpost hit comes together perfectly because you stored the right backup loadout in your safehouse really seals the deal that you're a true professional and an unstoppable force.
-Despite the game's difficulty, it's very feasible to beat the game without dying. The PC's that you didn't choose to play as can be encountered in-game and and turned into allies, and will rescue you if your health drops to 0. They're not invincible though, and they needed to be protected then met in a safehouse if you want to be rescued again by them.
Far Cry 2 quickly became one of my favorite games because of how it sucked me in, made me feel weak, and then let me slowly adapt to it until I truly felt like the hardcore motherf*cker that I was supposed to be playing. 10/10, would recommend to anyone who wants to get absolutely submerged in a game.

You get to choose 1 out of the 9 starting characters each with different backgrounds. You start off with the intro (which you should enjoy because it's the only time you don't get shot at while at a guard post) and then you somehow all of sudden get Malaria, pass out, and meet FACE to FACE with the guy you were originally supposed to stop named "The Jackal"who then insults you and leaves. A random shoot out happens outside and then you pass out AGAIN and wake up to learn you got saved by some guy but not for free so you get sent to do some missions for him aka the tutorial. By time you finish with the tutorial you will most likely have already thought it's one of the most immersive and realistic shooter game you've ever played due to things like the real time map that you get to hold in your hand and how the guns you've used jammed after using it for a while like in real life. If you never played a realistic shooter game or haven't played one in a while this game will put the pressure on you and remind you real quick the skill you need to survive but enough with the basic explaination now let me get to the Pros and Cons so I can move on from this game.
Before I begin I want you to shout out if you want Pros or Cons first I'll wait.........Ok Cons first it is
+Very nice realistic graphics that really set the mood for the atmosphere even to todays standards
+Decent soundtrack that really convinces you that you're in Africa
+Good selection of realistic weapons that do a good job of matching it's real world copy
+Fun combat for the most part
+Real time realistic map that really makes you really feel there while your character is holding it
+Nice realistic physics
+Plenty of things and enemies to shoot
+Realistic animations for the most part (lol as long as you don't stay in the water until you get low health)
Wait!! You probably realized that you're choice on whether you wanted Pros or Cons first didn't affect this review but I hope that prepared you because your choices and actions barely affect the game's world in any way but let's get to that in CONS
-Your choices and actions barely affect the game's world in any way. You can kill a whole bunch of "APR" and "UFLL" soldiers around their headquarters and then kill 30 people in the town and they will still give you missions and act friendly the next time you come back.
-One of the WORST problems with this game is the high respawn time but let me give you an example and keep in mind that I'm NOT exaggerating....You spend 10 minutes shooting at enemies until fires cover half of the enemy base so then after you think on whether to leave the on fire enemy base in one of those nice cars or on foot you decide to leave on foot instead but after have left the area for about 30 seconds you change your mind and decide to go back to that supposed still on fire enemy base to get that nice car only to see the enemy base back to normal and ALL those enemies you spent ALL that time killing somehow back alive right back to shooting at you and it's gonna be like that the WHOLE game for EVERY place you visit and that goes back to when I said your actions don't affect the world.
-The main realism elements like having to eat food, drink water, sleep weren't added in the game at all so it's hard to look at the minor realistic things like gun jamming and Malaria attack as something other than annoying things that mess up gameplay when a game that's supposed to be so much about survival and realism doesn't add the key elements even when it could have been added seeing as there's plenty of wild animals to eat, water bottles to drink and safe houses to sleep at
-Forced to work for both rival factions and don't get the option to only work for one

This game is good. Very good, even. Resisting the urge to gush, I can honestly say that I had fun all the way throughout this game, and that is VERY rare for me these days.
It was a rather bold step of Crystal Dynamics to make a Tomb Raider game in this vein, rather than how all other Tomb Raiders have been, but I'm really glad they did. It's still very much a Tomb Raider game, in that there are platforming puzzles, lots of enemies to kill, and plenty of treasure to find.
This bird's-eye perspective, however, allows the action to be a lot faster paced. Enemies can (and will) swarm from all around you, while floor tiles ignite on fire, and arrow traps shoot out from the walls. It can get very hectic, but it never gets overwhelming.
One area in particular where this game succeeds, and many others get wrong, is in the area of specialized skills. Many games will have so many that it gets overwhelming, or just one major one, giving the puzzles an arbitrary feel.
I never felt that way with this game, though. Playing single player, you get all of Lara's skills, plus all of Totec's (he's the Guardian of Light). Figuring out which ones to use in which situation felt very organic. In fact, it felt like the solution I used to solve several puzzles was not the one the developers intended, and I LOVE when you're allowed to do that. Too many games put too much importance on HOW you achieve the goal, rather than on the fact that you DID achieve it.
This is designed for co-op, no doubt about it, but it is an extremely solid single player experience. Never did I feel "oh man, I could really use a second player here," which is a testament to fantastic game design.
The graphics are quite good, the music and sound effects fit, and the voice acting is top notch.
It's a fairly quick game (I beat it in around 6 hours), but it's one I would have no problem going back to to collect more trophies. If a friend bought it and wanted to play co-op, I would absolutely say "yes."

A few days ago, I crafted a Steam badge. In the resulting level-up, I was rewarded with a 90% off coupon for a game called Obulis. Checking the store page, I figured the game looked interesting enough, and because the coupon cut the total price down to a meager €0.50, I saw no pain in buying it, especially with all the other games I bought and have yet to even touch. It's a purchase I do not regret.
If you like puzzles, there's no reason why you shouldn't pass this game up. Even at its full price, it's fairly reasonable. Perhaps my only big gripes with this game are the occasionally obstructive foregrounds (such as in the Windmill area in Chapter 1) and the over-reliance on perfect timing rather than logic. Far too many times did I have to reset the level because I cut the chain/rope/pole a split-second too early or too late, making the marble in question completely miss its mark. This is especially bad in levels that require a lot of steps to complete. It's frustrating in that you can't solve the level despite knowing the solution.
But aside from that, everything else about the game is highly addicting and I strongly recommend that you try it if you're a fan of puzzle games. Just keep one thing in mind if you're a completionist: If you can't solve a level, DO NOT LET THE GAME SHOW YOU THE SOLUTION. Otherwise you'll forever forfeit the stars you would have obtained from clearing it. I learned this the hard way.

I haven't been playing Perpetuum nearly as long as some other reviewers, but having a first impression review may be useful to someone out there.
After you complete the training missions, you can hop right into action and start blowing stuff up if you want.  There are industrial missions as well if you are into harvesting.  The stat grind is endless, so completionists will get their money worth from this game.  The faction leveling is slow, and the starting missions are very easy, but involve running around a lot.  I am hoping that once I get to level 2 missions there is less running around and more faction gain, but it's not that big of deal and typical of most MMOs.  The loot I am getting from NPCs I blow up at the start of the game is vendor trash for the most part, but rarely I get some item I can use which can feel rewarding.
Resource gathering is unique, and interesting.  Unlike other MMOs that have nodes everywhere, Perpetuum makes you search for the node by using scanners or giving you a general location via mission updates.  The first scanner you get isn't 100% accurate, so you have to use it a few times to get a bearing on where to head.  When you get close you use a different type of ammo in the scanner to indicate where exactly to dig.  I really like this feature compared with other MMOs.
I haven't played any PVP yet, but the ping I am getting on the US west coast is very low.  Especially now that they have relocated the server and optimized it.  Looking forward to loosing my first mech!
The online community seems accepting to new players, and I have had all my questions answered without a gang of trolls chasing me around on chat and forums.  From what I have read Perpetuum has been in development for a considerable amount of time, and it really shows in the lack of bugs and quantity of hard core helpful players.  Great work!

What I liked:
-Classic arcade-style shooting
-Ability to upgrade ship in between battles
-Decent number of affordable upgrades for ship
-Shields can make your ship tolerate more punishment than some other similar shooters
What I did not like:
-No tutorial or explanation of item pickups
-No saving even between missions (play all at once or lose your score)
-Default controls unintuitive; controls could be remapped but some are hardcoded and these are not identified anywhere
-For example, Space = swap secondary weapon. You can map Space to something else, but it will then do both (annoying)
-Sounds were not well balanced, so voices were always too quiet in contrast with background music even after adjustments
-Level backgrounds did not feel very dynamic, more like a scrolling wallpaper than your ship actually flying through a zone.
Completely mechanical gameplay with absolutely no feeling. Feels as if the developers has never played a shmup before. Avoid at all cost.

I waited to finish the game before writing my review in the hopes that it would change my negative output on it...But it didn't.
When I first played the game (at this point,a minor peeve).I was already put off by the voice acting,which was flatter than a 180 degree angle.Some of the characters spoke as if commas and periods were never invented.Thankfully however,not all.
Next was I was shocked over the level of graphics and physics.Despite being released in 2008,I'd mistaken it for a game that was released in 2005 or 2006.The water in the game seemed as if there was no effort put into the animation as a whole.
But most appallingly of all,as a person who considers himself a ditz for a good story,was the lack of a good narrative. Characterization was endangered if almost non-existant and events unfolded for the sake of formality it would seem. Things seemed to happen just cause.Other things seemed to happen just so there would be an excuse for another thing to happen without any true relevance to the plot or character development.
The potential for the story,as I've said,is depressingly wasted,unexplored and unexpounded despite innumerable opportunities.Generic guards and soldiers disabled any potential for flavor in this so-called civil war.Similarly,the missions were repetitive regardess of who you side with in the game.Any difference is purely aesthetic in nature.The most I could get in major difference were tiny morsels of gossip about the faction's background and the war itself.There was no true point in choosing a side in the world's factions.
Furthermore,events that would seem major to me would happen suddenly without any rising action,falling action or any form of hype whatsoever.Couple this with repetitive gameplay and mission objectives and you end up with dull,wasted surprises for the player.
I want to emphasize the lack of characterization among nearly all characters.They would either just do as they would be told despite being major characters or they would suddenly commit acts that would seem weighty if not for the lack of hype around it.The only thing separating them from the random mooks was the unique character models and the names.I could find more autonomy in a ballpen.Events were almost always too sudden for me to appreciate the deep potential in the story.
All in all,it was a pain for me to play this game.Every hour spent on this game was agonizingly dull and every tidbit of potential in the story I could find was like a droplet of water to a weary desert traveler.Never before has "get it over with" been my objective to play a video game.And again,my main issue was the poor narrative and the unexpounded story.If not for that,then all else could be forgiven.
Despite the negativity in my review,there are 3 aspects that I enjoyed.
~I loved the ability to choose a player character.
~The buddy system allowed variety.If ever I (somehow) get the urge to play this again,it would be because of this.
~The reputation system and how it affected the AI in relation to a firefight with you.
The buddy system offers some tint of retribution and the African Landscape is beautiful if lonely and littered with the occasional random dead body.

I'm genuinely impressed by how much I enjoyed this game. This fast paced twist on the original Pac-Man is very addicting and very fun to figure out. Most modes will start out slow (maybe even slower than the original), then slowly works it's way up to being one of the fastest, most mentally demanding games I've ever played. Every bit of focus is required to survive and get an enormous score. Turning around after collecting a power pellet to devour the 40+ ghosts that have been gathering behind me is so satisfying. This game is a staple what a good reboot/tribute game should be like. Enough to feel like it's still part of the same franchise, but with enough variety and new concepts that it's still a totally new and enjoyable experience. I give this game a solid 9/10. I would have given it a 10, but I found that the replays are super buggy and don't work correctly. Besides that, it's a great game. Deffinitely worth the $10 (or $15 if you bought it with all the DLCs like I did).
