Viridi Is a very simplistic game, a relaxing game that keeps you occupied without giving you a rushed feel. Although there will be in-game purchases you do get a lot out of the free experience.
You create a plant pot, each one has its own design and the ability to name it. Every pot comes with its own snail which you can sing to and water just like the plants (I don't really know why you'd water a snail unless snails can get dried up, which I guess they could? You wouldn't want a crusty snail.) Once a week you get one free seedling. These free seedlings are 100% random and give that little feeling of excitement every time you open one.
Like most free games, In-Game purchases are a large part in the overall game. Besides the once weekly seedling the only way to get new plants would be to purchase them with (I assume this goes this goes w/o saying) real money. This has not bothered me too much as you can still get the relaxing part of the game down, although it can get rather bothersome to know every individual plant would come out of your paycheck. If you reall get into the game, I'm sure you wouldn't regret purchasing some plants or new areas.
One thing that really keeps you on your toes is the wait for your seedlings to up and have ther little spurts of growth. The growth of your succulent brings out the ultimate reward in Viridi. Although patience is key, it does not come w/o its hardships and rewards, which I think Viridi expresses perfectly.
I'm personally very attached to succulents and have friends who do enjoy plants just as much as I, and because of that I would recommend this game. Viridi is a good game, one that I'd love to see others enjoy and although this game is not without its flaws I liked Viridi and I'm sure many others do aswell.

Great game. Enemies are always a danger so you don't want to lower your guard, there's a lot of land on the map which makes it to bypass most (but not all, depending on where you're trying to go) guard posts, you can use stealth and silenced weapons if you want and the weather, terrain, grass height, and time of day has a strong effect on how easy or not easy stealth is, you can upgrade your safe houses until they're practically mini-armories by subverting missions with your best buddy, your second best buddy can save your life once if you get into trouble (you'll need to rest in a safe house afterwards in order for him to become rescue-ready and able to save you again), and weapons can degrade so you want to keep an eye on how rusty your weapons are looking like and want to refresh your weapons at the gun store frequently (for better or for worse, it's not worth picking up used weapons from dead enemies).
Weapons have a nice variety, for example, regarding sniper rifles the SVD Dragunov has a large clip so you can shoot several enemies in quick succession while the AS50 has a smaller clip but fires rounds that are powerful enough to go through most man-made obstacles and kill the enemy trying to take cover behind them. While starting weapons are admittedly basic, the weapons you unlock either later in the game or by complete supply convoy missions available at the gun stores are much better with benefits and weaknesses...which of the later weapons you like will be more determined by your tastes and playstyle as the weapons aren't clearly better or worse than each other, just different.
As far as length of the game goes, it's again determined largely by your playstyle. You can either play slowly, subvert every mission for your best buddy, scout out the map for diamonds and check guard posts (the ones that store ammo or health are very useful and I find myself going to those posts rather than the gun stores to re-supply) or stick to the storyline and only complete your objectives. I'd recommend trying to take it slow though since, while the story isn't bad I wouldn't rate it above Far Cry 3's, IMO, this is a game that's best enjoyed for its gameplay rather than story. Also, Far Cry 3 players should keep in mind that enemies at guard posts respawn.
There's also a rare bug that's still not fixed where, when getting a mission from one of the factions, the door to the room of the mission giver won't open. I remember reading that if you go on another mission (buddy, underground, assassination, or supply convoy) then the problem will fix itself. Or, if you don't have any missions available you can go rest in a safe house for 3-4 days and the door will open afterwards. It is rare though, you'll probably have to play multiple times to see it and if you keep multiple saves then you can load a different save as well (as long as the save took place in a different map area).

This game does more to undermine XENOVERSE than it does to improve on it.
While I do enjoy DRAGON BALL XENOVERSE 2, after playing XENOVERSE 1, I was left stunned at the drop in quality in the new iteration. The campaign in XENOVERSE 2 is pieced together with cutscene and story remnants of XENOVERSE 1. They alter the campaign of XENOVERSE 2 from the earlier game by adding jarring cuts to the story missions which include the newly added villians, Bardock, Turles, and Lord Slug. These characters, apart from Bardock, get no character development and hurt the game rather than add to it. The campaign is simply bad, so do not expect much from it.
The best part of the XENOVERSE campaign are the short sections in which you play as Gohan and Bardock, which are an insane leap in quality from the rest of the story. These sections only constitute a single fight respectively and are not enough to make up for the bad quality of the rest of the campaign.
Super Saiyan is also ridiculously overpowered in this game, with little to no downsides. You can maintain Super Saiyan 1 or 2 that allow you to teleport behind enemy players and hit them with a super attack. This, although fun, ruins the game, making combat unchallenging, and hurting the replayability of the game.
Another ridiculously broken awoken powerup is the earthling "Power Pole Master Mode," which has hilariously awful hit detection and a massive 360 degree hitscan attack. Needless to say, it is not fun to play against people who knowingly abuse this mode.
DRAGON BALL XENOVERSE 2 is a solid game for any DragonBall fan. There is a vast assortment of players and the ability to 1v1 people online and in real life. This makes this game a MUST for anyone trying to relive the days of inviting a friend over for some Budokai 1v1s.
The Hub world is gorgeous, and is an excellent improvement from the first game. Traversing it with flight is a lot of fun and the early in game restriction from flight helps put into perspective the love that was put into crafting it. The previous installment of XENOVERSE had a very condensed hub world split into load sections which was unimmersive.
The graphics are slightly better when it comes to lighting and textures, but it is not extremely noticeable.
Getting awoken skills such as Super Saiyan, Kaioken, Potential Unleashed, and others is far more streamlined. In XENOVERSE 1, getting these awoken skills was by grinding parallel quests that had a CHANCE to drop the skill.
Training is also far better in XENOVERSE 2. You are not tied to one trainer, which makes progressing between trainers easier and less frustrating. You can also train whenever YOU want and not when the trainer wants, although to unlock more of their lessons, you need to take Advancement Tests, which really add to the game and give you a sense of satisfaction upon their completion.
Still a classic, must-have game for adventure game lovers.

A timeless classic, and an amazing example of the kind of world-building and attention to detail that went into the old Lucasfilm adventure games. As a Lucasfilm game, you should expect it to be heavy on exposition and puzzles, with an incredibly well-crafted and well-told story.
It's the afterlife, but you won't be getting a harp or angel wings just yet. You're stuck in the Land of the Dead, a sort of purgatory, filled with travel agents, lawyers, mobsters, corrupt cops, and freedom fighters. Playing as Manny Calavera, you can eventually earn your way to the Land of Eternal Rest, working as a sort of social worker/travel agent to pay off a karmic debt, helping recently departed souls make their way to their rightful rest. But not all is as it seems in this colorful, 30's art deco, Aztec/Mayan-themed world...
A must-play if you have any appreciation at all for story-centric gaming. The only possible downside is that, as an old-school adventure game, it's extremely linear, so there isn't a whole lot of replay value.

I went into this one really wanting to like it.  I have a tendency to go for the kind of seemingly-misogynist garbage that comes out of Japan from time to time just for the sheer heck of it.  I'm a big fan of Conception 2, for instance, and I usually actually really like dating sims.  The aesthetic on offer here is really something to behold.  The cell-shaded noir look really stands out, and the combat is fun and stylish, if a bit shallow compared to the genre it's imitating.
I was willing, at the outset, to forgive a lot on the part of one of my favorite developers, here, but in the end I just can't see myself spending a whole lot of time with this one.  The disingenuously-named "Gigolo" missions are just far too distasteful in execution to be worthwhile.  Basically, I want to cringe myself into a black hole after having completed the first one.  We're talking about a game wherein the explicit goal is to ogle a woman's breasts and crotch *while she's not looking* in order to fill a "guts meter" which allows you to give her a present.  You do this enough times, Mondo gives the camera a thumbs up and takes the polygons off screen (presumably, to ♥♥♥♥ her), and she'll give you some sort of phallic weapon.  The first one you get is a giant drill.  If she catches you looking, her mood meter decreases, but you can fill it up again by averting your eyes for like 2 seconds.
Now, some of you might find this sort of thing hilarious, and hey, good for you.  Personally, I'm not really sure where to begin untangling the Gordian knot of SUDA51's apparent issues with women, here.  The misogyny in the game is actually layered so thickly, it makes me feel as though I'm being tricked into outrage or something, which in turn makes me want to roll my eyes at how juvenile that is, as a development goal for a video game studio.  So, you win, SUDA, if you were trying to troll me, cool.  You succeeded.  But the game is such artless trash that it doesn't really inspire outrage so much as it does pity in me for the bundle of neuroses that must be crouched in some dark corner of the mind of the person who would deliberately make such a game and release it into the wild as-is.
I'm all for depictions of sex and sexuality in video games; I think it's a subject that should be explored more often and more in depth.  It's an important part of being a human.  But what's depicted in Killer is Dead isn't sex.  It's masturbation.  It's what teenage virgins think sex is like, complete with the total absence of depiction of any actual sex.
I made it about as far as the crazy woman in a great deal of pain repeatedly shouting that "it hurts" as she transforms into a giant bug (which you then dismember a leg at a time in a Zelda sort of boss format) before calling it quits.  You win, Killer Is Dead.  Have a good one.  Glad I got you for free; saves me the time requesting a refund.

Razor2: Hidden Skies is a sci-fi "bullet hell" game made by the Brazilian studio responsible for Bad Rats - Invent 4 Entertainment.  The numeral "2" appended to the name of the game begs the question as to the whereabouts of the original game. There was no Razor 1 listed on Invent 4's website which leads me to believe this is the only publicly available game in this series. Unable to find any mention of an original game, it leads me to speculate that the developers artificially appended the title with a "2" to make it seem like a more successful franchise than it actually is.
Razor2 seems to make strides in being as mediocre as possible. Much of each level seems to insult the value of your time by presenting you with repetitive and uninteresting fill content. Most attacks simply vanish into the enemies and offer little to no indication that you're actually doing damage which both makes you wonder if you're using the right weapon and leaves up unsatisfied in the shoot 'em up experience.
To the game's merit many of the enemies have a very appealing design albeit a bit generic. The game's soundtrack is very orchestral that made the game feel a bit like a movie. The boss fights offered a fair challenge but enduring the levels of mediocrity to get to them failed to make the endeavor worthwhile.
The game offers you three lives and a single continue. Once these are depleted you are forced to start the game from the beginning.
The game does support USB controllers but only in game as navigating the menu seemed to require the mouse at some point.
Score: 4.5/10

Razor2's biggest fault is the lack of level structure and enemy variety.  Stages consist of the same formation of enemies, that only have one flight pattern and one bullet pattern, and just repeats over and over.  Fifteen seconds into any stage, and you've already seen everything there is to see for the next few minutes.
Powering up your weapons works in reverse.  That is, leveling up your weapons only lets you keep up with increasing enemy hit points in the next stage.  Whichever weapon you choose not to upgrade becomes completely unusable.
I also had some issues with controller support, which others noted in the forums as well.  However the game is playable on keyboard, so there are workarounds available to those who seek them out.

Pros:
WIthout a doubt the best combat system I've ever seen in a fantasy MMO. Not that I've played many, but once you've played one, you've played pretty much all of them. Click an enemy, wait for it to die. Stats do all of the work.
Not here. You can't win like that. You need to time a dodge for invulnerability frames, or block with a shield, or just plain get out of the way. You need to utilize your character's moveset. There ARE the oh-so-worn-out quickslot skills, but they're minimal and you can only use them once in a while, leaving you to fight with grit and skill.
The crafting system is simple and effective. Gather materials, take it to the right NPC, pay a small gold fee, boom, new weapon, accessory, or armor piece. You also have the option of building up a crafting skill ("expertise" in-game), which can get you items of a higher quality with better stats. It's a little harsh on your character's coin purse but it's a more than worthy investment in the long run.
Story is actually interesting and presented in a way that you don't instinctively ignore. The game opens with a voice-acted, fully-animated prologue. That's unusual for MMO's. Not only that, but the NPC informational onslaughts are easier to pay attention to because of the interface. Large font, short lines, no paragraphs.
The source engine. Need I say more? No, but I will anyway. Physics are everywhere. You can pick up boxes, barrels, pumpkins, etc. and huck 'em around for fun. Very effective way to stun bosses in early levels, too. All of that, and the source engine somehow manages to keep the game looking great without much frame loss. I have to use medium or low textures on this dinosaur of a computer with most games, but Vindictus allows me to use the highest textures in the game no sweat.
Cons:
RNG. Significantly less painful than it used to be, as rare materials are actually attainable now, but the enhancement and enchantment systems are absolute torture. Higher-level bosses have insane defense and you need a damn good luck streak to be able to reach those levels of attack power. The materials for enhancements are easy enough to find, but succeeding an enhancement is another story. +1 to +5 are no problem, but with 680 hours put into the game, not once have I ever succeeded going +6 to +7 without the help of a cash item or an event. When it comes to enchantments, the decent scrolls are rare and difficult to obtain and success rates are unfair.
The grind. I'll be totally honest, level 1-60 goes by in a flash. Almost too easy. 60-70 is a little more of an effort, but enjoyable. Rewarding. 70 and up is where it gets a little tedious.
Underpopulated. When there isn't an event or new contend, it's a ghost town. I reccomend finding an active guild early on so you can build your friendship with them and ask for help down the road when certain quests are Dark Souls difficult. The management is pushing a lot of people away, too. See next point.
Management. The guys at Nexon America HQ take no pride in their work and had I said that on their official forums, the post would be deleted for "spreading FUD." Thay don't listen to the community and they can't take criticism.
The game recently had a change made to it where launching directly was not an option. It was possible, but they didn't tell us how to do it. We figured out how to do it. We asked whether or not the method used was breaking ToU or not. By definition, it should not have broken any rules whatsoever. It didn't involve changing files, didn't involve any third-party software, etc. It was just an alteration to the command line to the desktop shortcut. They said nothing about it for several days until a user submitted a proper ticket detailing the method. The response from a GM confirmed that it was okay to do. Should have ended there.
It didn't. Another GM came out of nowhere and stated that "any means to bypass the intended launch method are prohibited." Yet, go to any other game hosted by the same Nexon America that had the same change made to it, not only is launching directly allowed, they have TUTORIALS on the announcement pages. The Vindictus team does not know what they're doing and they flat-out don't care to hear it. None of this would have been an issue if not for the gaping security hole in the Nexon Launcher. I don't know a whole lot about computers but basically your login information is stored in an unencrypted text file on your hard-drive. Easy to find, too.
All in all, I think the pros outweight the cons if you use Steam instead of Nexon's poor excuse for a launcher.

Please note I recently downloaded the steam version and my play hours are not accurate to that of the time I actually spent on this game.
First off, I would like to say that this game is fun and enjoyable if you have large amounts of time to spare. With that being said, this review is coming from a guy who often has time on his hands, so I hope people will understand that I will be reviewing this game based on my many hours of experience, that is, my review is completely subjective but comes from a perspective of wisdom.
Now, let's move on to the review!
GAMEPLAY
The most important part of any MMO, I believe. The combat that Vindictus presents is truly unique and immersive, giving each class their own personality and style. The animations for each attack feels smooth and natural, something I feel lots of MMOs struggle with. Though sometimes lackluster, the AI feels alive and adds to the game's immersion. You can especially feel this when you are fighting bosses, as they are strong and menacing. Vindictus is one of the more harder MMOs I've played, but in my opnion, that makes it all the more immersive.
STORY
One of Vindictus' weaker points. You will often find yourself skipping through most of the dialouge to complete your quest and to move on to the next one. There is an amazing introduction to the game's universe that far too many people skip, but even that is not enough to get a player invested in the story. Currently, there are three seasons, each one containing a set of main story quests to complete. At this point, I would have explained what the story is about, but honestly, I couldn't care less. Overall, not the big highlight of this game.
MECHANICS
You might be asking 'What does he mean by "mechanics"?" Well basically, how the game works, grinding, leveling, and everything else that makes up Vindictus. This topic will take a bit more explaining, so sit with me here.
-Leveling: Currently, the max level cap is set at 90; a fairly high level if you ask me. When you first start you will level very quickly, but don't let that fool you. Levels 1-60 are easy in both leveling and difficulty, but around the end of season 1 (You should be around level 60 by then) there is a huge difficulty spike and you'll start to notice that it's taking longer and longer to level up. At this point, you should stop to consider if you want to truly be invested in this game, for this is the point where the actual game starts to play out. Overall, the difficulty and slow leveling does increase the longevity of the game, whether you like it or not.
-Grinding: This is what you'll be doing late game, like, a lot. It is very difficult to acquire level 80 gear because the materials are very rare and place a heafty price on the community market, meaning that the gear itself is also expensive. Luckily, the materials for level 90 gear is far less rare and expensive, but the struggle from level 80-90 is still real. This is one of the biggest problems I have with the game because it relies so much on RNG to get good stats and is unfair to people who may not have the money to buy it. Of course, there is always NX.
-NX: Is Vindictus a pay to win game? My answer: No? I say this inquisitively because technically you can pay for stats, but again, it relies on RNG so you're not garunteed a stat boost. I heavily advise against doing this for obvious reasons, but if you have money to spare, I won't stop you. There are also outfits you can buy with NX that give a small stat boost and a few other minor advantages, but nothing that is unfair to people without it. Most people buy outfits (as well as inner armor and hair styles) just to customize their character, nothing more.
-Expertise: Expertise is one of the few things I dislike about the game. There are different things you can expertise in such as goldsmithing, weaponsmithing, armorsmithing, etc. To me, it's such a pointless activity in the game because you can just buy the items you want to craft from the market instead of buying materials that are more expensive than the actual item to craft it. Even if the item you want is not on the market, one of the NPCs can probably craft it for you for an additional price. Don't get too involved with expertise, it's a waste of time and money; but if you do, go all out because you will only start getting benefits until you can craft late game armor and weapons.
-Peer to Peer: You are able to join parties with other player and do battle quests together. While there nothing wrong with this concept, Nexon executed it in a way that screws everybody over; through a peer to peer system. For small battle quests this is fine, though lag is still present; but on 8 man raids? You would a high end PC to be able to host a party of that size, leading to people not wanting to host raids, therefore lowering the activity of Vindictus' community, which is something I will cover a bit further down. The only servers that Nexon hosts are the 24 man raids, but even then they are still laggy.
-Enhancing/Enchanting: I wont go into full detail, but basically it's all RNG. There are some NX items that allow for a higher chance of success, but again I wouldn't try it.
Are you still with me? Great, lets move on from this topic now.
VISUALS/OPTIMIZATION
For a game that came out in 2010 and uses the source engine, it looks absolutely amazing. Vindictus takes a sort of anime style when it comes to character customization and has unique armor and weapons that fit right in to the fantasy world this game offers. Like I mentioned earlier, Vindictus runs on the source engine which is widely known for being able to run on many computers. The only problem is that there are lots destructable things in the enviroment which require a good cpu to process well (That may just be my computer though)
COMMUNITY
The last thing I wanted to talk about. Ever since the release of Vindictus, it's community has slowly been dying. There are few people left nowadays that you'll be lucky to get in a 24 man raid that's not Elchulus. The people who still play are the people that are at the level cap or people who have started new characters that have already met the level cap in other characters. There are no new players anymore, as far as I've seen. Anyways, besides talking about the people who aren't there, I'll talk about the ones who are. Overall, the community is nice and friendly, but there are a few elitists out there. The elitists are the ones who like to put an ATT requirement boat on late game raids so that they can finish the raids quickly, which is something I completely understand, but ATT is everything though.
Overall, the game is immersive and enjoyable if you have time to spare and can handle the grind Vindictus asks of you. I would recommend this game up to level 60, then decide for yourself if you are willing to invest in it.
EDIT: When I wrote this review, I completely ignored season three, which I now feel deserves the attention.
SEASON 3
I've noticed that after each season there is a huge difficulty spike, but unlike the transition from season one to season two, armor and weapon prices for season three (lvl 90 gear) are much cheaper if you don't mind the relatively low stats. Despite the easily required gear, the missions are ridiculously hard. It's very difficult for someone to solo missions in season three (at least for me anyways) and this in turn hurts the game because there aren't that many people who want to join your party. Missions are somewhat longer and its areas are too dense with enemies, making attacking seem like a less viable option when constantly blocking/evading. The Bosses are extremely buffed and have unfair advantages over the player such as unblockable attacks and an unavoidable curse that takes away large amounts of HP during the boss fight.
There's more I wanted to talk about, but I'm running out of characters. I would still recommend tho.

Viridi Is a very simplistic game, a relaxing game that keeps you occupied without giving you a rushed feel. Although there will be in-game purchases you do get a lot out of the free experience.
You create a plant pot, each one has its own design and the ability to name it. Every pot comes with its own snail which you can sing to and water just like the plants (I don't really know why you'd water a snail unless snails can get dried up, which I guess they could? You wouldn't want a crusty snail.) Once a week you get one free seedling. These free seedlings are 100% random and give that little feeling of excitement every time you open one.
Like most free games, In-Game purchases are a large part in the overall game. Besides the once weekly seedling the only way to get new plants would be to purchase them with (I assume this goes this goes w/o saying) real money. This has not bothered me too much as you can still get the relaxing part of the game down, although it can get rather bothersome to know every individual plant would come out of your paycheck. If you reall get into the game, I'm sure you wouldn't regret purchasing some plants or new areas.
One thing that really keeps you on your toes is the wait for your seedlings to up and have ther little spurts of growth. The growth of your succulent brings out the ultimate reward in Viridi. Although patience is key, it does not come w/o its hardships and rewards, which I think Viridi expresses perfectly.
I'm personally very attached to succulents and have friends who do enjoy plants just as much as I, and because of that I would recommend this game. Viridi is a good game, one that I'd love to see others enjoy and although this game is not without its flaws I liked Viridi and I'm sure many others do aswell.

I really think the Adventure genre just isn't for me. To me, the game gets in the way of the adventure.
I almost never walk away from these games and think, "I'm glad that wasn't a movie or a book!"
Games are the wrong medium for this form of expression. The art is incredible, the animations fantastic, but it really should be a ten minute, short animated film showcasing this style, not an arduous "adventure."
Adventure games are movies where you have to make strange guesses and push buttons in order to move the story along... Waiting for animations, exploring the same room multiple times. This adventure does not have the latter problem, but that's because it just involves continuously pushing buttons, and not much in the way of true puzzle solving. Why not make an animated film, people? You might be nominated for an oscar with this art...
I guess I like my adventures far more on the "puzzle" side than the "story" side. Waiting for animations and characters is so boring, compared to working with puzzles and quickly clicking around to jump from one place to another.

Background: Purchased as part of a Bundle Stars Bundle.
Impressions:
Wow.. it's a quick download and a quick deletion. I played up to the first boss and then quit out.
Basically it's a bullet-hell game like '1942' with futuristic 3D ships and a horribly restricted field of view.
It's something you've seen a million times before and does nothing to improve on the formula. The shooting just requires you hold down 2 fire buttons and let them auto fire as you try to dodge the incoming while nabbing the upgrades as they drop down.
The Good:
*Looks pretty decent.
*Controls work well.
*Sound is ok.
The Bad:
*Lack of impact and satisfying enemy destruction.
*Field of view is too close in a tight downward angle.
*Boring enemy attack patterns.
*Cheap enemy tactics, attack from behind, really suck.
*Weapon pickups have no discernible impact on your killing power.
*Just holding down the 2 fire buttons and moving is not fun.
Recommended for:
Fans looking for an updated '1942' type game.. but even then it's a hard sell.
Conclusion.
2/10. Really weak all round and lacking anything original to keep you interested.

I have a soft spot for all old-school 2d platform action games like this.  So when this was on a special, I was really excited. Firstly, this is an indie title, so mentioning anything about graphics is really quite daft.  So I will only mention the gameplay control elements.
And with that, the game is honestly very dull.  The boss fights are tedious and frustrating.  You dont get any sense of achievement during a boss fight as you dont notice if you have destroyed a part of it or not, and you dont really get to focus on the boss as the devs decided to add spawns of continious non-bosses in the boss fights.  So yes, the boss fights are "incredible", but not in a good way.
The collision detection is also really awful, most of the time I dont know whether a bullet actually hit me or not, even though I could swear that it should have hit me.  This is also true in shooting enemy planes, I shot down enemy planes where I could swear I shouldnt have been able to.  Then there is also the fact that enemies just spawn randomly all over the place and that they just hammer and spam attacks in every direction that all you really do at the end of the day is focus on is trying to dodge while just jamming the attack button while you have your homing laser equipped.  The entire combat system thus feels like dumb luck and an exercise of chance and pointlessness.
The controls are also unitiative and silly.  There isnt a brief tutorial to familiarise you with the keys, so it forces you to look up the key config. Sure, it might be better on a controller, but to be honest, I am not going to bother with a controller if there is only partial controller support because I really cannot be bothered to fiddle with a keyboard+mouse AND a controller while playing a game.  Though, this complaint generally stems from my complete disinterest in the title, and I guess if you really manage to get into it, this isnt really an Issue, but I couldnt, so it was an issue for me.
One of the large draws of these action games is a sense of excitement, achievement and skill, and this game does not provide any of it.  There are too many games on the market, and while this would have been worth a go a few years ago, there really are just better alternatives, as it has been done better multitudes of times, and I can therefore not recommend this game.
The controls are awful.  The gameplay is loose and deeply unsatisfying.  Avoid.

Marbles and puzzles.
Obulis is a game of both marbles and puzzles. The  aim is to get the marbles into the same coloured containers. In order to do so you need to manipulate chains, which drop the marbles, to make sure the marbles bump into each other to allow the coloured marble to get to the right container. There is a bit of physics involved in this game as you need to calculate the correct time to release the marble to win. As you win each level you collect stars (which don't do anything except track your wins)
There is no story in this game, just a series of puzzles to complete. The game should last you a while since there are more than 150 levels, depending on whether you choose to play them all that is. The music is nice and calm which helps you think in these puzzle games.
Tghe main problem I have with the game is that there is no sense of progression in this game. Collecting stars isn't a good enough motivator to keep me interested in this game.
I can only recommend this game hardcore puzzle fans otherwise, it's best to spend your money elsewhere.

2D puzzle game with decent music, mechanics and graphics.
I's all about getting the orbs of different colors into a basket of matching color by activating small mechanics in the surrounding, so no direct contact is allowed and it's all placed with just the mouse.
The difficulty increase level by level, and will required better timing and cognitive thinking, but mainly just timing. This makes it very addictive though, since it trigger a nice sense of achievement when you finally succeed some of the trickier levels.
For me it felt like it was all mainly about relaxing and work on my patience, since some levels demanded a few tries to get the timing right.

What can I say about West of Loathing? Stick figures, dad jokes, engaging gameplay, and humor oozing out of every aspect of the game, it is an absolute jjoy to play. With 3 playable classes, decisions that encourage player choice, this game does not limit you to an on-rails experience. Per my First Impressions video, this game is an almost certainty for my top 10 games of 2017!

I remember listening to a podcast this developer did (Video Games Hot Dog, it's really neat) while this game was in development, and they (jokingly, maybe?) referred to it as Skyrim with stick figures. While this is a pretty accurate comparison, it is also a lot more than that.
If you've ever played Kingdom of Loathing (it's free, dork) than you have a good idea what to expect. Well, minus the multiplayer anyway. Jick's hand drawn art comprise the graphics, Hotstuff put some ridiculously over the top puzzles in here, and Riff wrote a lot of corny yet effective jokes.
If you don't know what Loathing is all a bout, this is a turn-based western themed rpg, with a large helping of humor. You have your standard Fighter / Mage / Thief gameplay, but they aren't called what you expect. Stats and items also go out of their way to not be cookie cutter rpg tropes.
The game is very player friendly, and greatly respects your time. You can speed up combat so it plays out super fast, you don't waste a turn when you use items, health is restored after each fight, and the vast majority of fights can be bypassed with skill checks without losing out on the rewards.
This can all make the combat feel pretty easy, but combat difficulty isn't what this series is about and it probably isn't why you are here. The puzzles you will come across range from simple ones you will trip over as you go, to super difficult obscure ones that you might not even notice.
I don't want to talk about the plot for risk of spoilers, but I was laughing right from the start.
Also, I shoveled horse dookie for experience and dug around in spittoons for loot while the game scolded me for doing so. Money well spent.

Going foward it looks like you will be able to earn at least 30 free packs of the latest expansion via a daily quest rewarding 3 packs each day following the launch of an expansion.
You can directly grind dust. Gold and cards can be earned every three wins.
Two free random legendaries just for leveling up.
A card upgrage system when you level that turns your starter meh cards into superior and useable versions.
Obviously anyone who spends money is going to have an advantage over f2p players, that is just a given fact with ccgs.
This does not however mean you cannot slowly grow your collection and provided you are good at ccgs and deck building  can easily utilize your limited collection to create a deck capable of wining most games (at least in casual mode)
One of the biggest problems with the game is the dispersion of cards through the different tiers of rarity.
With out spending any money on the game I very quickly ammased 94% of all the common cards in the base set and 92% of all the commons in the skyrim expansion.
This means most of my packs are just dust/soul gems for crafting. No one is excited to recieve dust and this took alot of the fun out of the pack opening.
The rare slot is fine but the epic slot not only has a great deal of staple cards but also costs the same as a legendary to craft a playset just one of those cards.
The legendary slot is even worse than that, the recent expansion featured 30 legendary cards, more than the epic slot by far! Again very powerful, potentially game winning cards that costweeks of grininding to craft for your average casual player.
As if that wasn't bad enough there are unique and non-unique legendaries, the difference you ask?
Unique legendaries are one per deck while the non-uniques allow a full play set of three per deck..
(and they cost the same amount to craft)
So you want a playset of arguable the best 1 mana card in the game? (Descendant of Alkosh) or one of the best cards in the game atm, Blood Dragons.
That will be 3600 soul gems thank you very much.
Now consider you can only get 15 soulgems per win against the expert ai (up to 300 per day) meaning you arn't earning gold or cards in this time and that a pack which can take as many as 21 wins to earn a pack.
(Not games. Wins. Assuming a 50% win rate, closer to 42 game)
Imagine you get all duplicates, 5 commons, 1 rare. Great you just earned 45 dust.
YES! It's free, you have nothing but your time spend enjoying it too lose so if you like either ccgs in general or the elder scrolls series then give it a shot at least. If you like both those things then why haven't you already downloaded this god dam game to try it out already?!
If your mindset is you want to get all the best cards and go hard on ranked mode without spending any money then just walk away now.
The game is most enjoyable when you are just logging in each day to enjoy playing and can appreciate your collection slowly growing over time. Once you get a specific goal in mind (a legend or playset of a card) and focus entirely on that, the fun is sucked from the game and it will feel like a chore, a job to play and thats never a good thing.
So if you only plan to take it easy, play at your pace and enjoy the dam thing then once again. Stop reading and go install the sucker already! ^-^

There's a lot about this game that is truly
, not just the art style. The game seems to be cobbled together without much care for the player's experience, and the result was that I was frustrated with gameplay, felt like I was fighting the game to play it, and felt like the game did not respect my time. (The ~7hours I've logged in it are only because I'm an unrelenting achievement ♥♥♥♥♥.) This made it difficult to enjoy the game, and so I don't recommend Incarnation 1 -- though I am hoping the dev might tweak things for later chapters, and am eager to see where all this goes.
A few examples of why I found Incarnation 1 a chore to play:
1) Within the first ~10-15 mins of gameplay *after* the intro, you'll encounter a truly frenetic and bewildering sequence of load screens (!?) and short vignettes where there is little meaningful gameplay.
It's exceptionally difficult to start feeling at home in the world of Karma when, right at the start, gameplay is constantly being interrupted.
2) You've got an inventory that displays items you've collected. However, you have no ability select items from your inventory to do anything with them. You can look at them in your inventory, but you learn nothing new by looking at them, and clicking anything in the inventory is not in any way a direct route to interaction in the game. If you've got the right item in your inventory, then when you approach the place where it can be used, the game will just tell you to use the item. And you then use it without actually accessing the inventory at all. This turns the familiar presence of an inventory into a distraction with no relevance to gameplay, and sends mixed signals to the player about how they are supposed to accomplish anything in the game.
3) Using Astral Sight appears to be just a gimmick for introducing (more) psychedelic art. There's very little going on in the spirit world that seems to matter for gameplay. Moreover, Astral Sight helps bring out some weird design decisions about the mechanics. Normally (without Astral Sight) you can pan around the whole screen and see what's going on far away from you. But Astral Sight only works for a small window around your character, so your world shrinks a bit when you use it (presumably the exact opposite of the experience it was supposed to provide of transcending a more mundane plane of existence or whatever). And yet, it's not quite so jarring, because...
4) The world you can see (without Astral Sight) is decoupled from the world you can interact with, nearly all the time. You can always pan around a screen and see what's far away from you, but you've typically got no option to interact with anything until you walk right up to an object.
When you are close to objects, the game simply tells you how you interact with them. As a result, being able to look around the whole screen at any time is basically meaningless for gameplay, since you only get information about which parts of the world are relevant once you've walked up to them.
5) Many of the hand-drawn animations become more irritating than charming, real quick.
The same animation plays every time you perform an action, and just eats up time: cute the first time, maddening the 30th time. Also anytime you are traveling to the left and click to interact with anything to your left, your character will pause, turn to the right, then turn back to the left and do what you wanted. This just seems like lazy programming.

If you’re a Dragon Ball fan, this is a must-have game.
A sequel to its predecessor, Dragon Ball Xenoverse, this game is everything a Dragon Ball fan would want. There’s a huge campaign, going through every major part of the Dragon Ball series (although most of it is the same from the first game), the ability to create and fully customize your own unique character from a few classes, such as a Saiyan or a Majin, online/offline 1v1 battles, quests, raids, online events, and a whole lot more features that make this game the best Dragon Ball game in my opinion.
The campaign, although mostly recycled from the first game, is really long, offering a good amount of time to be spent on this game. I didn’t have a chance to play the first game so that wasn’t an issue, but if you have, that’s something to take in mind. I very much loved the campaign, which there being quite a few funny scenes in the game, with a notable one being the scene with Beerus getting excited for pudding and then getting mad at it being disgusting, leading to you having to fight him 1v1.
One of the main reasons to play this game is to become the strongest warrior in the game, which is a lot of fun and adds to making you seem like you’re actually apart of the Dragon Ball series. You can train with all kinds of iconic characters, which means yes, Goku is one of them. There are many different moves as well as amazing Awoken Skills such as the ability to become SSJ, SSJ2, and SSJ3 depending on how much Ki you have in a battle. There is so many things to do in this game up until that point, and even once you hit max level, you can make many new characters, adding to the replayability that this game has.
I managed to snag this game for $20 during a sale, but even then, I would have bought this game at full price after seeing how amazing of a game this is to Dragon Ball fans. If you have the time and the money, you must buy this game.

Ok I am %62 done with this game and I can give you some details about it.
First off I think my mistake is that I played FarCry first which was great, and then FarCry 3 which was awesome.
I was expecting the same awesomeness with FarCry 2 but I find it more difficult and I am less tolerant with it.
You see, fast travel kind of sucks in this game and missions are most of the time at the total opposite ends of the map. So if you are in the bottom left corner to accept a mission, expect to go back way to the top of the map.
Unlike FC3 when you liberate a post, it is not the scenario here. There is always bad guys. You can't get from point A to B quickly and quietly, unless you go offroad, and even then, it takes longer.
When you come into the game, I was not exactly sure what my objectives were. I had to go on the internet to give myself an idea. It was later after wasting time with side missions that don't really matter (Radio Tower missions) that I eventually learned that I have to get missions from the town and buddies (not real people or your online friends) that you encounter during the game.
Then it started getting interesting. But still the fact that fast travel is not great and posts are always fill with bad guys, makes it redundant and a bit frustrating.
Now I am not saying the game sucks. I am saying my mistake is that I was thinking of FC3 benefits and how I wished FS2 had it. I am even more sure that if I played them in order, I would be enjoying FC2 a lot better than I am now
Given that. I do not fault the game. It is what it is and I am sure that anyone playing it will have a lot of fun.
But don't do my mistake. Play FarCry 2 before you play FarCry 3.

A very fun physics based puzzle game. You simply break a few chains, setting a series of events in motion, and using gravity and inertia to get the marbles to their color coded destinations.

Obulis is a puzzle game that relies on physics, momentum and gravity. There are colored balls hanging in chains and using various items obtained in the map, the player has to guide those balls to the respective colored pots.
It is a great game, beginning with simple levels and gradually progressing on to harder and complex levels as the game progresses.
Some levels are actually easier than the others, even though they award higher stars of completion than other tougher levels. But this is just me, difficulty actually will vary from player to player. Some levels are constrained by your timing - it just has to be perfect or you lose. You definitely will be wanting to tear your head off at some of the tougher levels.
Obulis being one of the oldest games in genre, may seem lacking in advanced features but nowhere will the gameplay dull out. All levels occur at different locations, each with its' own set of objects that can be utilized to help the player accomplish his goal.
All being said, this is a great game, containing upto 10 hours of fun gameplay.

My hours played on this game aren't 100% accurate, as I was playing this game before it hit steam, and in that time, a lot has changed.
The game itself can be fun, but crawling through dungeon after dungeon can get very repetitive and stagnant very quick.
The biggest gripe i have is the sub-par dedication to NA servers, which has been an issue since the game launched. This game can be played with other people, but because of the aforementioned problem, playing in a group is going to cause some stuttering and lag, which is why it is popular to solo dungeons. Which is not a big problem because dungeons can be easy to tackle if you know how to play your class, which also isn't that hard to learn.
Speaking of classes, they're gender-locked-- it's a Korean mmo, what did you expect?
so if you want to play as a magic-user, you have three options, Arisha, the generic anime milf, evie, the token female anime mage, or the newly-added Cyrus, the pretty boy trap.
So any hopes you had about playing a Gandalf-esque character are thrown out the window because the character is basically made for you.
If you want to learn more about the classes in the game, here's a wiki:
Note: at the time of this review, the wiki has not been updated to contain information about the class known as "Cyrus".
On the same token, character customisation is very limited. Facial features can only be slightly changed, and certain features like beauty marks, tattoos, and hair have premium selections that can only be accessed through microtransactions.
Did i mention this game has microtransactions? there are certain items that can be bought from the in-game store, such as elixirs and potions that will increase your damage dealt, and exp gained for a certain duration of time. You can also dye your armor, but you don't get to choose the color you want, instead, the game uses some RNG bull to pick a color for you. If you want to choose what colors you want, you gotta fork over that money.
Leveling is nice and smooth at first, but it slows down real fast. This is done on purpose to coerce you into buying exp elixirs to make leveling up faster in order to play newer content.
An okay game that is otherwise ruined by terrible business practices that Nexon is known for.
Play at your own risk.

Anyone that knows me knows just how over the top and passionate I can be about sports. I’ve always been that way. I was raised by a sports crazed mother who you could hear shouting from one end of the street to the other whenever her beloved Carlton Football Team were playing. In many ways I have become just like her as an adult. We follow the same Aussie Rules team and I have been known to go ballistic whenever my team is scoring or if they’re getting the rough end of the stick from the umpires. Some might say think as bad as my team has been since we won our last premiership (1995) that I think that we only ever lose games due to the umpiring and not because we just flat out suck (I know we do!) Whenever I get an opportunity to get my hands on a sports game I’m generally extremely excited to the point where it can be argued that one of my weaknesses as a game writer or reviewer is the inability to critique a sports game too harshly.
This is the first game by Dancing Developers on Steam. The game is also on iOS. It suits both platforms. It suits Steam because you can play multiplayer games either live or in a play by mail method. What this means is that if you and a friend or challenger live on the other side of the world or in different cities or just have different schedules that dictate that you wouldn’t normally get an opportunity to play against them you can do so. You can play a turn and then you can wait for your opponent to play their turn whether that takes a few hours or a few days. You can finish a game at your leisure. That’s even better for those who don’t have that long to play. Log in before breakfast and make a move and you’re done within a couple of minutes. A great concept and one that has been tried and true since even before Steam’s existence and done outside of video games but a really good one for a soccer game.
For those who do get to experience the live play you will have a timer. It begins relatively slow but I am promised that as you level up and become more battle hardened that the time speeds up. I’m guessing that if you are playing a lower leveled friend that you’ll be expected to play at the lower level’s speed but I haven’t gotten to that point yet. There’s a lot of strategy that you will have to consider within the allotted time as well. It’s not as simple as get ball and kick goal. You need to factor in the same things that make football one of the most strategic sports on the planet. What will your opponent do and how will you outsmart him. In many ways the in game use of strategy is far more important here than in setting default settings and changing on the fly in Football Manager.
The presentation of the game is relatively simple. It doesn’t need to be anything especially great. It delivers just what you need. However, you will need to play the tutorial first because the overlay of the game can be especially frustrating and confusing for a beginner. Thankfully once you play the tutorial you’ll understand the presentation overlay and UI. However, I would like to have seen a better explanation of all of the starting power ups. Learning them on their own was more guess work than what most will ever put in the effort to find out.
At $4.99 TableTop Soccer is fair value for money if you have a friend or can find opponents to challenge you. Beating the computer AI only rewards you with a quarter of the experience you would otherwise generate playing against a real person so those who find it difficult to get into a match will have a difficult time leveling up at the same rate as their equally skilled counterparts.

Before starting this review, I would just like to point out: I was given this game as a gift about 2 years ago when it had a price. Unfortunately, since then Dead Shark Triplepunch has been dissolved (around about June last year I believe). This means that the game is dead, there are no updates for it and it will never change from its current state. It also means that the game is completely free so price is no problem whatsoever.
Epigenesis is a crazy combination, it's very like Grifball but has some aspects of tower defence which doesn't make sense at all but it does make the game a bit livelier. You pick up the ball, double jump over a couple platforms, throw the ball in the hoop and spawn with a seed that has a variety of different towers you can plant. The game keeps going until the timer runs out or one team has planted enough seeds (I have honestly forgotten if this is a thing).
The game is a quick bit of fun that can fill a small gap in your day, however, it gets boring very quickly because the only thing worse than the AI is the player base. The AI do not challenge you whatsoever, they're spectators in a game where teammates and opponents matter which usually means you end games with a stupid score like 10-0. Don't bother trying to find a multiplayer game because everyone's hopped on the train and evacuated from this game.
Overall, I'd say the game had great potential but never fulfilled it on the other hand though, the game is free and I could see people getting at least 20 minutes of fun out of this game maybe even more. If there was a maybe option on Steam I would've given it that but I'm going to recommend it because it's free and it's worth a try.

I rate the game Far Cry 2 3.5/5. Pretty Good.
Pretty good but highly repetitive and full of minor (and often hilarious) graphical bugs. Disappointingly, unlike in Far Cry 3, when you take over an enemy encampment or checkpoint the enemies will return and no ground is actually taken, which means that this far cry from paradise can never, ever be turned back into the quasi paradise it should be and your actions end up feeling like they have very limited permanent effect on the world (as is true in most games). The enemies return to the checkpoint (often within only a few minutes of you having been gone). This results in extremely repetitive gameplay as you are often forced to take over (because you had to drive through or past) the same checkpoints over and over again and to make matters worse these little enemy bases are all over the place and usually almost impossible to avoid. This does give a greater feeling of being in an ongoing warzone but not a truly dynamic one. All too often, Far cry 2 depicts a war that isn't going anywhere and nothing you do seems to matter. This is also true of the ethical dilemmas the game has throughout. Your character (no matter which character you choose probably) could ultimately be best described as some sort of super-soldier sociopath given the near total amorality of the missions you end up doing for one side or another (it makes no difference which side because they are each pretty much the same). Having a character who was supposedly sick with malaria throughout the game was an interesting plot gimmick but was never actually more than a minor inconvenience. The numerous choices you make throughout the game matter not a bit to how the ending of the story comes out. As with most games out there, single choice made at the very end of the game determines your character's fate and hence the ending of the game.

Killer Is Dead includes such technology as lunar tourism and cybernetic enhancements. The main character is an executioner named Mondo Zappa (voiced by Ryotaro Okiayu in the Japanese version and Patrick Seitz in the English version) who receives jobs from the Bryan Execution Firm. This firm, run by a cyborg named Bryan Roses, tasks Mondo with killing dangerous criminals and assassins from around the world. Mondo wields a sword with his right hand but his cybernetic left arm can be converted into many different weapons, including guns, drills, and other objects. Although Mondo travels the world as part of the game, Suda calls it a "personal story" of "a man who doesn't show himself much in the public world but still worms his way into society and mercilessly eliminates the evil dispersed in it". "Love and execution" and "how far can you protect someone" are also central themes of the story.
The game begins following a deranged former executioner named Tokio who has kidnapped a girl and is being hunted by a katana-wielding man who looks like Mondo. Tokio calls him "the darkness" right before he is killed. It then flashes forward two years to the modern day where Mondo is accepted into Bryan's execution agency following his assassination of the former executioner in his place, who had also been taken over by a dark force and was deemed unfit for his job. This man, Damon, warns Mondo about the perils of the job and that he may also fall to the dark side.
Mondo then kills many strange, monstrous beings known as Wires, eventually killing a woman named Alice who was transformed into a grotesque crustacean-like monster following her trip to the Moon. She blames a strange man named David for causing her to become a monster. Subsequently, they are visited by a woman named Moon River, who asks them to assassinate David. Mondo agrees and travels to David's moon palace on the dark side of the moon, though he is unable to kill the ostentatious and eccentric David despite a pitched battle.
While a strange dark force from the moon starts turning people and even inanimate objects into monsters, Mondo learns that Moon River was once the ruler of the Moon, until she was overthrown by David and her race transformed into Wires by the Dark Matter. David has gained control of the moon's Dark Matter and is using it to take over the world, creating Wires as his minions. Meanwhile, Mondo exhibits intense pain from his artificial arm every time he kills a monster.
Eventually, Dolly, a psychic who serves David, attempts to enter the mind of Mondo's assistant Mika to kill him. Mondo uses a sleeping drug to fight her, but in the process dredges up all his memories. He realizes that David is his brother and he lost his arm due to David's attempt to kill him. David was also a former assassin working for Bryan, and after rescuing Mika, the kidnapped girl in the first mission, he brainwashed her and used her to spy on Mondo before going rogue. Bryan gave Mondo his artificial arm in order for him to fight David, though its capability to absorb Dark Matter means that Mondo is vulnerable to becoming corrupted like Tokio and Damon. He decides to head to the Moon yet again to settle the score and stop David's evil rampage.
Mondo fights David in his castle yet again, but during the battle both of them are changed by the Dark Matter into super-powered Wires, after which they fight as equals in their assassin's garb. In the end, Mondo is able to defeat David and stop him from harnessing the full power of Dark Matter. However, Mondo himself is then possessed by the darkness and rebuilds David's castle. Moon River requests that he be assassinated as well, much to the surprise of the Bryan Execution Firm. The game's ending is open-ended, but suggests that Mondo has become the ruler of the moon in David's place.

I'm going to write an unbiased review as possible, this is coming from a person who has played many, many games, across many genres.
The good and bad in no particular order:
1.Now as it stands, the UI is atrocious, especially for a game where so much attention is needed to information on the screen for you to get around and do things, anyone with even slightly poor eyesight will probably be annoyed and have a hard time reading the font size that is unchangeable (as far as I could tell) on the UI, I know I was annoyed and my eyesight isn't bad enough to warrant glasses or contact lenses. (bad)
2. The World does seem to be alive, with things going on around you, though when I played there hadn't been that many people on, but I found some nonetheless, and the possibilities for exploration are very, very great. (good)
3.  The Tutorial is very, very well put together, you learn everything you need to, to get started in the game. Though the tutorial check list seems a bit daunting at first, its pretty easy to follow (with the exception of the horrible font size), and at the end of it all you get some free stuff after completing it that helps you out when you finally get to the game world proper (if you skip the tutorial you don't, good incentive, not to mention you'll be completely lost if you aren't already coming from a game like EVE online). (good)
4. One of the bad parts about the game is that after the tutorial (and chosing the faction you want) you aren't really prompted to do anything, you kinda just spawn at the beginners base of said faction and nothing comes up to tell you what to do. The Quests (Assignments) are very repetitive, mostly go to "A" attack "B" get "Item" from "B"'s wreckage deliver "Item" to "C", or go to area "A" scan for "certain mineral/Artifact" locate "mineral/artifact" mine/retrieve "mineral/artifact" and deliver to "B" or some variation there of, the only difference is that the more in good standing you are with the faction you chose at the end of the tutorial increasingly difficult assignments are unlocked for you to complete, but they never stray far from this template. The game feels very grindy for a game with time-based progression, you have to log in once a day to get certain points to level up skills of your choosing, and you need to level up certain skills to be able to use more powerful mechs, so even if you have the money, you can't use the mech till you level up the skills to use it. (bad)
5. The graphics are atrocious for 2014, or even 2011 or 2010 when the game launched beta or alpha. Maybe for 2003 or 2004 they were good, but damn they ungly now. The mechs don't feel like mechs... look kinda flimsy, even the ones you get to try out during the tutorial which take some time to acquire, (not that they are bad in combat, they just don't look it is all). The sounds for the mechs are also bad, too low when they shoudn't be and cut in and out constantly, the "thump, thump" that you would expect a heavy bipedal mech to have as it walks isn't there, the sounds for the weapons are also bad, except for the missle, which I'd say is alright all around. (bad)
6. Combat is in the vein of Mech warrior online, just with longer locking target times, and point and click targeting/firing, and chance based hitting depending on the weapon used, not as exciting as mech warrior online, but still fun, if you manage to get into a battle that'll make you sweat a bit (that probably won't happen early on), may be too many variables to take into consideration for some people though. Mechs of the same class from the 3 different factions balance each other out well. (good)
7. Crafting in the game is also very, very grindy, you must acquire research points by the hundreds by looting "kernels" from wreckage of mechs you destroyed. Only one kernel amounts to one research point, and you get anywhere from atleast 1 (most of the time, rarely none) to 10 kernels from a mech you destroyed (though i only played the beginning and therefore they may drop more kernels the harder the enemies get), and you need from what I saw in the research panel thousands of them, and you need 2 types of kernels for some 3 research trees with atleast 1 different type of kernel required for each tree. Honestly though you can start making money after your first investment in any one of the trees (you can pursue all of the them, choosing one doesn't exclude you from the rest), by building that first item (which requires you to scan, locate and mine for minerals/metal), and selling it on the market, which gets you a good amount of money from what I saw. Making money seems to be very easy in the game, but money doesn't give you everything, because skill trees and research points must be advanced/unlocked/gained first which is good, but the hard grind you have to commit to isn't. (bad)
These aspects are the ones I chose to review the game from, there are a few more but they don't matter as much to someone just starting out in the game, because it takes a lot of grinding to get to those aspects. Time is something someone who plays this game is going to want to have alot of to get anywhere in it. EVE players wouldn't mind maybe, but not all players are are people who've played EVE and thats why I've written this, because most people who reviewed the game don't seem to review it from an unbiased point of view. But don't take my word for it try it out yourselves if you have the money to spare, its great in some aspects and poor in others, I'd give it a no on the recommendation rating, but I dont speak for everyone.

While not intuitive at first, it gets more and more fun as time goes on, especially after you customize your players in their names and in their gender and in their clothes. The game can be fully played Solo or online either in real-time or with turns, so that you can keep playing multiple matches at once.
The AI gets progressively more challenging as time goes on, with better strategies and clearer goals (no pun intended). Thankfully, it never gets too frustrating or too easy: it stays in a very good balance of fun and challenge.
Pretty weak soundtrack and sound effects. I turned on Spotify and listened to my own playlist while playing.
Limitless: play with many players and improve your players' stats to create the ultimate team.
Overall, I have to say that this game was a lot of fun: interesting gameplay, good customization and great multiplayer component make this an enjoyable casual game that you should check out if you like the concept. Easily the second best soccer game for non-sports fan, right after
.

I'll keep this short and sweet...kind of like this game.
I really enjoyed this point-and-click adventure. Making a bold assumption based upon the credits, it looks like most of the team was Russian (with perhaps some other Eastern-bloc ethnicities thrown in for good measure), and I'm pleased to say that they've broken the Steam stereotype of the churn-and-move-on pattern we've seen all too often from that geography. That's a good start, right there.
The game's art style is very interesting, and matches well with the simple mechanics (which literally involves left-clicking to do anything that you need to, and perhaps hitting the space bar to toggle your astral view, although that can be done via mouse too, if you prefer). Animations are entertaining, both in terms of your protagonist character and all of the NPCs and background critters.
The dev team avoided language and translation issues by simply not using language...everything is conveyed via on-screen cues and fairly obvious, universal symbols. Now, figuring out what the game is about may be a bit more confusing for many at the beginning...this is very much a spirit-world, Eastern-religion-based game (although very cartoony and not to be taken seriously) -- the name is "Karma," after all -- but despite the opening sequence, I found my mission (and why I started as a white glowing, floaty critter, but was a black-colored, ground-based critter when gameplay began) a little obtuse. But, it was easy enough to start putting together the pieces once I played for a few minutes, and it all began to make sense.
Your little critter has the capability of astral view (to see beyond the veil of the readily visible world, or whatever), and understanding this capability took a few moments, as well as understanding WHY I needed to bother with it. For the most part, it aids in uncovering hints as to what you should do in various areas, and every once in a while, it's actually required to manipulate something. It can be toggled at will. Once I was used to it, though, it became second nature to check this fairly often to ensure that I wasn't missing something.
Navigation was easy, and I enjoyed the many environments as well as figuring out how to activate the functions of the "spaceship" (you'll see why I have that in quotes when you play). Puzzles are interesting, of middling difficulty, and seldom frustrating (ok, the leaf maze was a little annoying, but it wasn't that bad). Your little critter moves a little slowly, but you usually don't have that far to go, so that wasn't a big issue, either.
Game was stable, no bugs to speak of, although playing in ultrawide mode could create a couple of funky visuals if you zoom out too far in your view. There weren't in-game graphics options, but really this wasn't a problem the way that it is in many games...overall, things scaled well without the need for tweaking.
The game is short, but thoroughly enjoyable (my play time is inflated due to idling for cards). Some people might complain that $2.99 is too high for a short game, but I think that all too often people don't realize how much work goes into making a game, especially one that feels as polished as this one (it has a fairly good-sized crew working on it for an indie point-and-click). Three bucks really isn't much to ask (you pay more for fancy coffee and enjoy it for less time and don't complain), and I personally feel that Karma is priced appropriately. I was fortunate enough to get it in a bundle, but when subsequent episodes are released, I plan to buy and play them to support the authors. This is a quality game, and they deserve the support.
Long story short, if you like casual point-and-click adventures with a strong cartoon art style, you could do a lot worse. I fully recommend Karma for that audience.

TL;DR - Recommended with reservations (Great visuals, sound, and story - Irritating gameplay and bugs - Check bug reports and comments before making a purchase decision)
Pros:
+ Wonderful visual presence and atmosphere
+ Nice music
+ Good voices
+ Very interesting story
Cons:
- Puzzles can be obtuse
- Some puzzles require precise timing and can be frustrating
- Pretty much requires a walkthrough as far as I'm concerned
- Some irritating bugs
I have fond memories of playing this game when it first came out, so I jumped at the chance to play it again. The opening sequence is one of the best I've seen for an adventure game. I quite enjoyed playing Year 1; however, once I got to the Petrified Forest, the gameplay kind of went downhill. The puzzles became obtuse enough that I had to start referring to walkthroughs. I hit two bugs in the Petrified Forest - one having to do with the flaming beavers, the other happened when I tried to use the wheelbarrow. Fortunately, I was able to get past these by doing reloads.
Year 2 in Rubacave was pretty interesting, but, even though I usually knew what my goals were and what I needed to do, I often had no idea how to go about it. I don't have the patience these days to "try everything on everything", so I looked to walkthroughs again.
Once Manny leaves Rubacava, the game really goes on the rails in the sense that there are fewer puzzles to solve and more cutscenes. The entire Coral Factory section is really boring. Moving into Year 4, I had a problem with Manny getting stuck in the doorway of the boobytrapped garage. The only way to proceed with the game was to switch to Tank Controls to get out of the room. I was referring to walkthroughs pretty heavily just to get to the end of the game.
On the positive side, I really love the characters, the environment, and the story. The game is really fun to experience, but not all parts of it are fun to play. If you love adventure games and have either a lot of patience or the kind of puzzle mind required for this game, then you should definitely get Grim Fandango. If, however, you are easily frustrated by obtuse puzzles and dislike using walkthroughs, then I suggest watching YouTube videos of playthroughs. You'll miss some of the non-required funny dialogue, but I think the game is definitely worth watching as a movie.
Note that according to the global achievements list, only 29% of players make it to the end of Year 1, 19% to the end of Year 2, 16% to the end of Year 3, and 15% to the end of Year 4.

The controls are tight feeling (none of that perpetual lag feeling some mmos have like a constant, bitter after-taste).  Devs are active and there is almost always one online. Community is small, but growing, and diverse in spite of it's size. Its a pay once, play forever model currently, but no pay to win mechanics either (though a equivalent $10/mo sub will give 50% more passive skill points per day). Pros
- Very fair f2p/p2w model. The intructory story/tutorial is alright, just about what you should expect from a free game from a company with as much money as bethesda, but the game deserves praise for giving you access to  a generous number of 50 cards decks with very little overlap with each other from the start (or at least, after finishing the tutorial). You can also get two more themed decks with the most recent cards from the heroes of skyrim expansion with in-game currency,  In less than 30 hours of gameplay I was able to buy two of these decks for 1000 coins, which you get just by playing against other people and playing through the tutorial/story.
-Great art, TES designs at their best. Each and every card is vibrant and nice to look at, and they all come with accompanying sound effects and/or voice over.
- The game's rng is one hell of an important factor in winning games. There's a big overlap between what a common card can do when RNG favors it and what a Legendary card can do when RNG is not in its favor. What this means is that you absolutely do NOT need to spend money on the game to be able to enjoy it. Good cards give you an edge, but good deck synergy and rng still reign supreme.
-Great card/deck identity. The game really benefit from the TES theme, each card and deck built around it oozes personality, and each combination of different races (or lack of) yields a solid, recognizable theme, different from all others. Recognizing and preparing for the strengths of each race and attribute becomes second nature as you play the game. This ties into the game's balance: learn to pace your decisions. Every  deck has a certain "rhythm" to it dictated by its attributes and the races it contains. Learn them to make the most of each deck.
Cons
- Way, way, way too many rng mechanics. Yes, this is a pro if you are just starting to play the game, but you'll eventually be on the receiving end of the RNG beating. Numerous cards have effects such as "summoning a random creature". No, not a random creature from your deck, ANY random creature from the entire game. You WILL get screwed over by a Hail Mary at some point, you need to learn to accept that. This also ties into the next con:
- Built in comeback mechanic. As you burn through your opponent's "life points", you'll break a total of 5 runes. Each time you break a rune, your oponent draws a card. If your opponents card is a "prophecy" card, they'll be able to play it immediately with no cost. This can turn the tides of battle in their favor unexpectedly, so most of the game's meta revolves around trying to be as prepared for this possible random comeback at all times. You are never entirely safe.
Overall, I recommend the game to all fans of TCG games. If you ever played a TCG game, you know luck of the draw and pay to win are just inherent flaws of the game by its very definition, and the game has plenty of things to offer to make up for it, and you don't have to pay a price of entry just to see if it's going to appeal to you.

TES: Legends is a competent and fun CCG; taking part of the smoothness and visual action from Hearthstone and part of the complexity and dynamics from Magic: The Gathering.
Where Hearthstone is quite fixed in its deckcomposition to accommodate an easy grasp of the breath and Magic is overwhelming in its rules that have been hard to translate to a digital form.
The games in Legends are wildly dynamic with the ability to swing from near losses to roaring victories due the ‘rune breaking’ system that challenges rushing players and allows for defensive decks to bide their time while at the same time having the possibility to speed up the game. All this without disrupting the games pace like (counter)interrupts tend to do.
Fun effects, beautiful art, great theming options and wonderful single player campaings. All of this using the TES world I love makes for a very compelling game.
The recent Skyrim update has added great new depths promising good things for the future.
