This could be a long one. This is the game I started with since I didn't want to work backwards at all and I had no interest in FarCry 1. It looked pretty good I'd say since it's an older game. It control well except for maybe the boats which get stuck on tiny pieces of land and are a ♥♥♥♥♥ to get around. The games atmosphere is pretty great too with jungles and desert filled with shotty roads and even worse structures made out of scrap metal. I like some bits and pieces like using rough uncut diamonds as currency since paper money would be very unreliable in a wartorn country. Also though unrealistic fact that you buy a gun once and have unlimited access to it from the shop is also nice. The gun degredation was a good touch and a gun jam can make you worry about the condition your weapons are in, though I will say that it happened too fast with some guns (The dart gun seemed to degrade to the point of malfunctioning after about 20ish shots).
The main complaints I have for this game are things I hate when any game does and it just happens to be very annoying in this one. The first one is it plays like you're the only enemy. This bothers the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me in games like this, this country filled with two factions that supposedly hate each others guts will both open fire on you any time they like. You will NEVER see the two factions fight each other outside of scripted events which happen when the ceasefire breaks. And when you break the cease-fire yourself the two so called enemies have no issue joining forces to attack you. You can be driving in the distance very far away and watch as another vehicle suddenly breaks to turn around and chase you even though there's no way in hell they knew who you were. It all ends up being so annoying, it ends up playing like this country was 100% at peace until your♥♥♥♥♥showed up and they suddenly had to purge you from existance. Also when getting faction missions they constantly remind you that they're not telling any of their soldiers that you're not an enemy, how does this make sense? The sheer amount of their army I killed because the idiots attacked me while I was doing missions for their warlord would be reason enough to let them know.
The second issue I have is that the enemies just respawn way too fast. With outposts set up at random areas thoughout the road it makes driving everywhere a freaking chore. You clear out an outpost to get to a mission, then have to clear out the same outpost on your way back out. It looses it's luster pretty fast when you've cleared the same place out for the 30th time just so you can get to a gunshop or the bus. They really seem to respawn the very instant they're out of your range, I've cleared an outpost but gotten turned around, realized I was going the wrong way and had to clear the same place again, annoying as ♥♥♥♥.
As I said I find these two issues tedius in every game that has them but this game is pretty good in spite of them. It'd be nice if the weapon upgrade system was a bit more robust, and I'd have loved the opportunity to buy a flashlight since stealth is so much better at night time but searching buildings isn't so once you're done with the shooty part looking around becomes an issue. The diamond cases were a nice idea but since they only gave you like 1-3 diamonds hunting them down seemed unrewarding.
Lastly, the buddies. Buddy must be an african word for worthless annoyance. They give you an alternative way to finish a task which is a good idea. The issue is doing it their way tends to take loads more travel which because of the respawn and aggression make it super tedius. They're mostly self serving too, they offer to help you but it ends up being because it benifits them. You only really earn history with that buddy as well which is worthless as far as I can tell, you also earn upgrades for your safe houses occationally but they're usually just ammo crates or something that weren't terribly important to me. And the biggest pain of all is helping the buddy out ALWAYS ends with them surrounded by enemies somewhere remote and you having to save their♥♥♥♥♥ Had they made it so the buddies would help you in combat if you had good history, or if they'd giving you access to something you otherwise wouldn't have, this system would've been great; however, as it is now I'd recommend ignoring the buddy calls unless you want to extend your gameplay. They don't even make the missions any easier most of the time.
That's alot of text but they're very specific issues I had and the game itself was definitely good and worth a buy play.

This game reminds me of Just Cause 2, minus the cool explosions, grapple hook, cool vehicles, or basically anything else.  The "story" is so convoluted and weak, you'll stop caring or paying attention in no time.

Every mission starts with the same voice giving the same instructions. The "pay" rarely varies. Stealth is nearly useless, as your enemies will spot you 200 yards away, crouched in the weeds... and of course they'll hit you with every shot, despite their supposedly inferior weapons. The graphics are pretty bland (even for 2008) without a mod installed.
Overall, if you're into getting achievements (like find all the diamonds, etc) and just like to hunt and gather, you MIGHT like it. But there are no boss fights; side missions and main missions look and feel the same, and the upgrade system isn't very rewarding.

The message here is fitting the title--one of static. It does not condone or condemn the behaviour you see, and really just leaves the player in the pain of a potentially powerfull experience. There is simply no redeeming value.
Here's what I'd like to see: the author of this work using just a little more effort to tell a story that gives us a message, teaches us something in return for our time. What made the character this way? What's the meaning? Is there any hope, and what form does it take? And are there others in real life experiencing this? This could really teach us something about depression, suicide and ourselves. It could be a ray of hope to those living in this dark place.
Deep pain can be used to communicate messages and relate with people. If we want people to start seeing video games as more than just toys, we need to do the extra work needed to craft something like this into the powerful experience it so easily could be. But instead we are left with a crude webchat and white noise powered by Unity.

Viridi is one of those games where you play it for a multiude of personal reasons. Maybe it helps you with stress or anxiety. Perhaps it was recommended for you by a friend. It could be you were looking for something with a nice soundtrack. For all I know maybe you enjoy the idea of taking care of virtual plants. Personally I play this game because it's a nice change of pace for me. The soundtrack is relaxing. Heck I've fallen asleep to it a few times. When I'm stressed out or just need a break from more high intensity games (i.e. Overwatch, 7 Days to Die, Crpyt of the Necrodancer, etc.) this is what I turn to to help reset my mood.
Now this game isn't for everyone and I was skeptical at first when I was debating downloading the game. A few key points to note is the following:
- This is a game that you will need to revisit every couple of days to see your work pay off. Like real plants, the virtual succulents take time to grow. Which means you need to water them every couple of days.
- If you want more seedlings for your pot you have two options: Get a free one once a week or pay less than a dollar for 1 seedling. The decision is ultimately yours of course. Though I've found that the weekly seedling has served me well and I have a lovely pot to look at every time I come here to check on my succulents.
- The controls are simple enough to manipulate. Unless something changed at the time of this review, I've used nothing but my mouse to rotate, plant, water, and otherwise navigate throughout the game.
- The symbols in the game don't blatantly tell you what they are. You have to look at the top right corner of the screen to read the text to see what it is you're hovering over. It may be hard to see since the text color is white, but this is really a minor inconvenience at best. That and basic intuition will give you an idea what the symbols mean. For example the spray  bottle symbol allows you to water the succulent you have selected.
I personally recommend this game for anyone who is looking for a leisure game that requires little thought at what you're actually doing. Really the most thought you are likely to put into the game is where you plant the succulents in the pot and ensuring they are all watered from time to time. This game is great for many reasons like I stated above in the first paragraph. For whatever that reason may be for you, I urge you to try this game for yourself. And heck if you don't like it nobody is stopping you from uninstalling the game.

There are a lot of these online card games around now, probably the most popular being the online version of Magic: The Gathering and Hearthstone, which is set in the Warcraft universe. The Elder Scrolls: Legends is a new take on the idea, borrowing heavily from Hearthstone, but with enough of its own innovations to be a worthy contender.
I won't bother with detailing the rules of the game, I'll just say that it's fun, challenging, and innovative. The single player story mode gives you a solid introduction to the game's tactics while providing new players with a good base of cards, enough to be competitive at least through the first couple of tiers, as well as against the computer decks in single-player practice mode. If you enjoy deck-building and combat-based card games, and especially if you are a fan of The Elder Scrolls setting, I highly recommend you give TES:L a try.

At the price of a Mr. Accessory I feel that I easily got my moneys worth out of it already.

As a Kingdom of Loathing fan and as a guy who bought this game just yesterday, I really can't endorse it enough to communicate what a pleasant and fun experience it is to play.
West of Loathing is made of fun, inoffensive jokes that lean heavily on absurdity and don't give you that gross feeling you sometimes get when you catch yourself laughing at a dead baby joke, or a picture of Donald Trump's head photoshopped onto a Cheezit. Every joke is a strong 8/10 that surprises you just enough to get a chuckle, but this is where the importance of that sort of implementation of humor comes in.
There are a lot of jokes. A lot.
As in, every item description. Every skill description. Almost every interactable, and the game has a bunch of those.
Every conversation is dripping with humorous dialogue, often jumping in an even rhythm between droll observations and wordplay ("Your horses are flying out the door? I'm glad business is going well!", to which someone responds, "No, like they're running out of the door every day. I haven't had a sale in weeks."), to sudden backwards steps in logic that force anywhere between a chuckle and a guffaw of laughter out of you based upon how surprised you are (That same man then gives you a bag of homing oats to feed his horses, which are special pigeon-infused oats that will compel them to go home).
The combat's a bit eeeeehhhhhh but it's very inoffensive at worst, and it's quick and very rarely difficult at all. It's meant to be there to facilitate gameplay, not waste your time. A lot of the animations are absolute gold as well - the Rattlesnake in Thousand Snakes Gulch, instead of slithering, bounces up and down like a pogo stick on its way to attack you.
Plus, dude, there's this skill called Stupid Walking, and it just replaces your walk cycle with one of a dozen different animations that range from swimming on the ground, to step-dancing, to tucking yourself into a ball and rolling across the ground. Each one of those animations even has its own sound effects, because the joke works so much better when you hear the translation from face-sliding to Frankenstein-walking happen.
KoL has an absolutely charming and timeless style of humor that applies to pretty much everyone, and the same is true of WoL. However, this humor all belies something else as well:
West of Loathing is a fantastic point n' click style, "Items are your friends and the only way to solve this quest chain" adventure game as well. Almost every quest has either multiple solutions or hidden paths involved; half of the best loot and skills in the game come from interacting with the environment, not leveling up or solving a quest chain.
In the first area alone, you can miss two party members, four pretty decent items, three horses, three snake skins, a magic ring, and a turnip by either taking hasty solutions to problems or skipping environmental interaction. This game wants you to do everything, and is very open to the notion that you in-fact should if you want the full experience.
The game doesn't punish you for playing like a jackass, and it doesn't rely upon specific builds or character classes to engage in a lot of the environmental gameplay (The Foragin', Dickerin', and Lockpickin' skills, each of which open up specific environmental interactions and dialogue choices, are chosen outside of your class).
It's a fun, open game that doesn't lose its charm no matter how much of it you play. It's not Skyrim, it won't go on for 400 hours of mildly-satisfying gameplay - but the 60 or so hours you can get out of it, you'll probably enjoy a lot more.
So yeah, West of Loathing. I strongly endorse it. For ten bucks, it's a dramatically better decision than you'd expect.﻿

I don't even like the original PAC-MAN that much, but I enjoyed PAC-MAN Champion Edition DX+.  The gameplay has been revised (for the better, I think), and it offers a bunch of short time trials and a handful of new maps.
In this version of the game, ghosts will begin chasing you once they spot you.  A trailing train of ghosts will eventually form, creating an element of gameplay reminiscent of Snake.  Sleeping ghosts dot the map, which will awaken and join this train if you pass by.  Once you collect all the pellets on one side of the map, a collectable (such as a fruit) will appear, and once you collect that, the completed side of the map will refresh with new pellets, sleeping ghosts, and possibly even a new map layout.
The game speeds up so long as you perform well, which is where much of the challenge comes from.  That said, it will enter slow motion mode if you are about to run into a ghost, giving you time to change your direction.  You also have a limited number of bombs that you can use to blast nearby ghosts back to the center of the map.  Since using these penalizes you just like if you were to die, I felt the bomb mechanic was redundant.  Overall, the game is not as difficult as it should be because you accumulate plenty of bombs and extra lives as you play.  I can't confirm it, but I also doubt the ghosts have their distinct AIs that they had in the original PAC-MAN; I felt like the ghosts who had not spotted you yet would almost never choose a path that would pen you in.
I wish there was a simultaneous multiplayer mode, and I didn't appreciate being asked to connect a Facebook account to get all the achievements.  The DLC model for this game is also pretty ridiculous.  Most of the map skins are a pleasure to play on, but a few of them are atrocious.
Worth picking up when it's on sale!

Shadowrun: Dragonfall is good RPG with tactical turn-based combat. Story, dialogue choices and characters are very interesting, but combat itself - not so much. It's repetitive and a bit too easy, also team movement between locations in long fights is very clunky.

The Shadowrun series has always been a favorite on my list of games. The story is well-written, dialogue is interesting and often witty, the characters are interesting and three dimensional, and the world is incredible. Although the plot is pretty linear, you can still influence some missions and make decisions as to how they end or unfold. I love the gameplay and the combat style is highly intuitive and easy to learn.
On the flip side, there are quite a lot of bugs that I encountered during this game, and when I looked up solutions, there are bugs that have been there for years and gone unresolved. Most of them are easily worked around, but they can be a little annoying. Also, be prepared to miss quite a lot, especially if you play on a difficult setting. Some characters miss most of the time and need constant accuracy buffs.

I had high hopes for Far Cry 2. I saw the great reviews it got. But only 5 hours into it I had to stop playing. It was a combination of complete boredom, frustration and knowing I’ve already experienced all the game would have to offer.
Far Cry 2 is a very open world game. After the first guided mission you are free to go wherever you want, which is nice. Except…
Here is the formula for every Far Cry 2 mission I encountered in 5 hours
+Drive to a place that has a mission available
+Drive to the waypoint on your map for that mission. Which is always far away.
+Get shot at driving through areas you’ve already cleared.
+Repair your vehicle.
+Take down a random vehicle with a turret.
+Repair your vehicle.
+Complete mission.
That’s it…that’s how it was for 5 hours before I knew that was all the game had to offer and show me.
I might have been able to push through if the missions were close to one another. But, there’s SO much driving in this game. I didn’t mind that in itself. The fact that it’s not even enjoyable really killed it for me. I thought after clearing a checkpoint it would be good from then on out…WRONG. Enemies always respawn everywhere. Which means you get in constant battles when you just want to drive through an area you already cleared. It makes me feel like I’m not accomplishing anything and gives me no incentive to kill enemies. I just resorted to flying through the checkpoints and killing any vehicles that gave chase to me.
Far Cry 2, in my opinion, commits several cardinal sins in video games.
+Respawning enemies
+Enemies that can hit you from a mile away, consistently. Even with a shotgun?!
+Enemies that can instantly hit you each time you break from cover
+Enemies that know your exact location
+Open world style of gameplay
+Graphics
+Good shooter at its core
+Capturing the African environment and culture
+Music
+Respawning enemies
+Extremely repetitive gameplay
+Too much driving around
+Enemy AI
+Didn't feel rewarded for doing anything
+Strange run on sentences with the voice acting
Below average
Far Cry 2 really does have some good mechanics and systems it employs. But the negative things I mentioned above far outweigh the positives. I couldn’t continue playing and therefore can only recommend if it’s on a big sale and you’re really curious. Otherwise, stay away.

At first glance, Kombine doesn't appear to offer much of a challenge. 40 levels, and the ability to “time trial” each bracket of 10 looks like it could be easily accomplished in a matter of hours.
And that is how this little game gets you.
Kombine doesn't have a tutorial, and deciphering how the game operates is perhaps part of the charm. If you can't work it out by puzzle 4, then the game is probably not really aimed for your entertainment. The concept is simple – activate a colour by clicking on it, then try to ‘combine’ tiles you create into removing that colour's target from the board. Do this with 1, 2 or 3 colours per board and you are onto the next.
Kombine eases you into a false sense of security within levels 1-10, but by level 18 you are seeing how the game taunts you with deceptively simple looking arrangements. By the time you have clicked restart on a single board for the 7th time though, you realise just how clever the game is. You are now trapped, and determined to finish the bracket, or at the very least the board you are stuck on.
There really isn ‘t much to complain about with a game like this. It is designed to appeal to puzzle enthusiasts and gives you the least amount of visual fuss in graphics. There is music you can turn off, and the colours are bold, bright and nonthreatening to the senses. The boards get progressively harder, and there is a definite sense of accomplishment when you trigger an achievement, or finish a board. The game saves at your current opened board, so there isn’t any unnecessary frustration at having to complete each one over again.
Kombine brings a nice challenge to those looking for something to fill in some time on a commute, or during a boring meeting. It will tax the brains, sometimes the nerves, but not the wallet. It is a steal on sale or at retail.

Vindictus is a really fun game starting out. I've played several hours both on and off Steam, and I recommend the game for most of its enjoyable aspects, and if you don't mind grinding later on, then its suitable for you. At first, there's a lot going on and your quests and missions are generally enough to help you level up, as usual in an MMO. I've hit a stagnant period at about level 40. Personally, after that point, its been mostly grinding for level ups. Quests do so much, and are definitely fun, but the grinding has made me bored, and quickly, too. Too much grinding and little quests seems tedious and adds a kind of unbalance to the gameplay. I enjoy the game still, but I guess I would appreciate more balance and more going on in the world and with quests compared to boarding a boat 20 times and still not getting the pay off of a level up.
However, the combat is stunning and smooth and the graphics are great. If you can run this at its full capability, I recommend doing so. There are also jiggly breasts, which probably appeals to a lot of people. Even if you don't enjoy the game, or don't think you'll like grinding to reach your full potential, I think its worth trying out. Don't be fooled by all the clothing packs and pretty outfits. You'll get dragged in before its too late and probably never return from the abyss.

Box Out! Isn't going to turn heads, but is a solid platformer that shows me a developer with real potential: As a lot of the design decisions regarding natural player progression, level design, and basic gameplay shows a lot of good design elements and smart decision making. While the game does seemingly lack content over the long haul, the two based action gameplay regarding switching between forms is the highlight here, and while the art and collision detection fails at points, it was an enjoyable experience in the end. I'd pick it up on sale when you have the chance.
+:
-Good Elements of Level Design here, leading to teaching the player the rules of its world naturally, rather then through a tutorial.
-Switching between elements is probably the most action packed it gets and can be rewarding
-Different objectives leads to different paths in the world to go through and try a level differently.
-Controls are what you would want for game like this and give you the freedom that you need
-Some designs of the actions are rather nice, despite the 8 bit nature of them.
-:
-Art sometimes ends up being misleading as a spike end for example is deadly, but the base of the spike is.
-Can lack oompf. Doesn't stand out at any point, hitting the solid point and nothing more.
-Music can wear on you after a while.
-Extra Modes seem derivative of the main mode.

So, about 1000 internet years ago, a browser game called Kingdom of Loathing happened. Basically, it was the game I'd probably come up with if you told me to make an RPG - a big vehicle to house billions of stupid puns and goofs, without nearly as much thought given to gameplay or art or etc.
West of Loathing is basically the same thing.
You'll probably start off looking at the store page, and assume that it's gotten mostly positive reviews as a joke. The screenshots make it look rudimentary in design and visual style. And, certainly, this game takes a certain kind of person to really enjoy. If, for example, you can't derive massive amounts of enjoyment from the fact that Necromancy is referred to in-game as "Nex-Mex", this probably isn't your bag.
Me? I chuckled again just THINKING about that. So, you probably know by now I'm going to recommend this.
But here's the gist of the game anyway. It's a wild-west RPG that works ideas from the American Southwest into the framework of a more traditional turn-based game. It actually reminds me a bit of Fallout in terms of its execution - heavily skills and consumables-focused. It's surprisingly deep for a game that's effectively a joke storage facility. I recommend speeding up the combat (there's an option for it), because the animations do get tiresome.
There is a suprisingly large amount of content in the game - I'd estimate at least 10 hours' worth based on my current progress. I wouldn't be shocked if this game features the largest number of jokes in a game to date, and somehow most of them land. The visual style is much more richly detailed than it first appears - everything is crudely hand-drawn, but the environments have layers, and the game actually looks pretty good.
The sound design is similarly surprisingly good. I was shocked to find this game has directional audio AT ALL - yet it does.
Overall, West of Loathing is full of little surprises. For $11 (clever in-joke there), you really can't go wrong. It's a solid 10+ hours of amusing quests.
And also I fed my horse spooky oats, for she is a ghost, and ghosts only eat spooky food.

First thing's first: it's a shallow game. It could have been better in many ways. They could have made the world more lively. They could have tried a bit harder with the missions. They could have made a better story. They could have (done much more), but they didn't. I haven't looked into it, so consider this anecdotal in the purest form, but I would wager that it was rushed for release or held back by being designed for consoles.
One thing you'll notice is that the game is still beautiful 7 years down the road, and despite being a game made for consoles first. The shadows, while not as fine as modern games, are still extremely efficient for how good looking they are, which is what mostly contributes to the beauty of the game.
You can play on highest settings and still get very good performance on any semi-modern PC. One of the ways they get such great performance out of good shadows is the clever way they hide the level of detail scaling. If you pay attention during the opening cutscene when the trucks pass in front of you -on ultra- you'll notice how the shadows under them disappear very quickly. In regular play, this is almost entirely hidden by clever level design with high usage of obfuscation; that is to say, very compartmentalized to a big wide open area with a limited amount of "dynamic" shadow objects like cars and characters, supplemented with great-looking grass everywhere and clever usage of trees.
The grass and trees, which move and react semi-dynamically to random wind patterns, produce seemingly dynamic shadows (don't know exactly if they are dynamic or static; if it's dynamic, it's extremely efficient on resources; if it's static, they look very dynamic) that react particularly well with the pretty lighting method the game uses.
Remember: It was made first and foremost for the limited hardware of the Xbox 360.
They deload all rendering of areas you are no longer in while keeping the areas still loaded in memory so there is no loading time, keeping the game openworld. All of the system load in the game is due to graphical fidelity, very low CPU usage is observed due to the mechanics of the game, which works perfectly for consoles which have subpar CPUs but usually good GPUs to keep down prices.
You'll notice that console games are rarely complex for CPU-based actions like lots of pathfinding enemies; just an observation I wanted to point out, totally unrelated to this review.
The game is "atmospheric" and "immersive", since I'm tired and don't know a more clever way to describe it. It pulls you in and really makes you feel like you're in Africa. It really "feels" hot and dry. You can "feel" the heat applied by the light on your character's arm. The sound design is incredibly detailed, and the beauty of the world never strains your suspension of disbelief.
The gameplay is shallow and underrealized. As the Steam review of the game, by the user Koltraiin had said, "No elephants, Lions, Cheetahs, Snakes, Crocodiles." This is indicative of the shallowness of the game; they could have given it more, but it simply wasn't there.
With all this in mind, I find the game fun to play. It's a unique experience for a unique game, and despite being shallow in gameplay it's a great deal for 10 dollars and it goes on sale fairly often. The biggest downside to the game is being a Ubisoft title, and requiring a Ubisoft account to play online.

Gameplay is very technical and not terribly well explained, so expect a steep learning curve. Set in the free state of Berlin, after the dragon Firewing awakened and attacked it you play a Shadowrunner who is contacted by a old colleague to perform a job. Like all good games this run goes bottom up pretty quickly and sets the stage for you to investigate who commissioned your job, why it went bottom up and what you need to do to end the threat (if you want to).
The characters in Dragonfall are great- each has a personality, their own problems and thoughts, from the tough as nails Eiger to the emotionally dead Glory. Talking to them between missions can open up new quests (each with their own outcome- you can fail these) to revealing a little more about their character. The plot twists and turns constantly- nothing is straight forward in this game, and my revenge plan quickly disappeared as I had to thing of the greater picture in the end. There are a whole range of options that will sway the ending, not just what you advise your comrades to do but what you do during missions will count as well. Some of the missions contain great moral choices, which can be a tough choice between what might be the right thing (a loose term for ethics in a dog eat dog world) and cold hard cash.
You have more options in missions this time around, and while you are a still limited to which ones you can select at major points in the game (it’s usually 2-3 missions per major story mission), the city hub gives you a lot more things to do and characters to talk to. There are a few faces back from the first game, and there are enough references from the events in the first game to make the world connected (there is a great cameo from one of the characters in the third game). Customising your character is easy and straight forward, with missions allowing you to pick who you want (there are a few instances of forced companions). The missions contain a lot more options in them now, hacking and Etiquette options are used more often now, which make more viable character builds.
The city hub does allow you to do more things, but it’s still limited in scope- this would be my biggest (and only) gripe. I did like having a bomb shelter named after me though.
if you are chasing 100% achievements for this game, then its easily done, but you will likely need a few saves.

I tried for hours, searching the internet, for fixes to a never ending series of problems with this game.  From glitches with characters and the environment all the way to a persistent buzzing I would hear over my speakers...there were far too many to fix and I eventually gave up.  This game is unplayable...  The most game breaking glitch was having characters who, once talked to, would move and thus ruin the speech script.  Ever have a character say one line, move and thus reset itself?  Thereby saying that one line over and over and over and over until you found that one exact sweet spot for it to finish the sentence and start the next sentence, only to have the character move its arm or turn it head and thus repeat the same problem?  That is what happened to me...over and over and over again...  Ugh...  I applied fix after fix to encounter more and more problems.  The opening scene where you are driven around in the taxi was the first problem.  The NPCs would get in front of the car (while literally BOUNCING around the screen) and thus stop the entire sequence.  Only several reloads and pure luck got me through that.  Add in all the glitches with that persistent buzzing I would hear over the speakers (read around, it is a common problem) and the game went from frustrating to ANNOYINGLY frustrating.  All in all, if you luck out and get the game to work for you...you are fortunate.  As for me, I am truly and greatly disappointed with this game.

I've been playing this game for like four years now, and it's still one of my favorite Free-to-Play games on Steam. It's one of the few games out that lets you play through the entire game without paying a cent. It's becoming kind of a shame more people aren't playing it, because it could use the love.
This game plays pretty much like a "hack and slash" game. The combat is probably the greatest thing about this game, it smooth and it just works. I'm surprised there isn't a whole lot of other MMOs that use combat like this. There is ten characters right now, nexon releases a new one every year, all of them have there own little play styles that's fun in one aspect or another.
The game essentially plays like this: You run missions through a linear dungeon, fight enemys, and there's a boss at the end. A lot of the emphasize in this game is the Bosses. I like to compare some aspects of the boss fights to the "Monster Hunter" games since there is a lot of dodging and attacking if you don't know how the boss is going to move. At first though your probably just going to beat the heck out of the early bosses and leave. The game doesn't really ramp-up difficulty that much til around level 50 or 60ish, which really doesn't take that long to get a character to level 60 if your enjoying the game.
The people who still play the game mostly seem to focus on higher level raids, which you can still find a party decently if you need one. We could really use more players though, but I suppose since this game is five years old you can only expect it to die off a little. Most of the major problems with the game is from the occasional bug nexon doesn't seems to know how to fix, or the lack of players when you want to specfic raid.
Here's the fast version:
PROs:
+Great hack and slash combat
+Unique characters that all have different interesting play styles
+You can play all the content of the game without paying a cent
+Pretty fun bosses
+Lots of good replayable raids
+Has a pretty good story if you bother to read the dialogue.
+Level progression is pretty fast until around level 70ish
+Pretty decent looking armor and weapons
+Great character customization if you bother to put the time or money into it.
CONs:
-Somewhat of a lack of people for raids at times
-The occasional bug shows up every once in a while (since Nexon doesn't seems to be able fix stuff very often).
-After you finish all the missions there really isn't a whole lot to do except repay raids, and other missions.
-Can be repeatitive at times if you don't like re-runing missions
-A lot of the people who do the main high level raids sometimes have ridiculous attack requirements, which can be a bummer for people who don't want to put a lot of time at the end-game phase.
-If you want anything customizable outside of what they give you, your probably going to have to pay for it.
-Nexon "seems" to care about the community, but doesn't really seem to do a whole lot. They at least keep the game working alright.
-Some of the weapon/armor enhancing, and enchantment scolls can become kind of stupid at higher ranks cus you can break your gear, which at high levels can cost you a lot of gold if your not prepared.

If you're looking for a game you can sit and play for a good long while, this is not the game for you, but if you want something you can just quickly check in on once or twice a day for a couple minutes at a time, then Viridi is perfect.
There are lots of different varieties of plants and you get a free seedling every week. Being able to name all your plants (and your snail) is a nice touch. So is singing to your plants. The plants grow at a slow but steady pace so it's extra satisfying when a new plant reaches maturity or blooms for the first time.
A lot of people say it's a great anxiety and stress reliever, with its soothing music and everything. I think this would be true if you could spend more than two or three minutes at a time on it because playing is very relaxing, but since all you really do is spray some water on your plants, pluck some weeds and leave, you're not really in the game long enough to be truly mellowed out by it.
On that note, I'd love it if there was more to do to justify playing for a longer stretch of time. Maybe introduce fertilizers and plant quality, garden pests, different weather conditions you need to prepare for because they'll affect the growth of your plants in different ways. Maybe introduce in-game currency and some kind of market where you sell your mature plants you don't need anymore. Perhaps a multiplayer aspect with festivals where you can show off your plants to your friends or see who has the most diverse or the highest quality plants. There's all kinds of stuff that could be added to this game to suck people into it for longer stretches of time.
I still recommend this game anyway. It's a nice way to spend a few minutes each day on a free game and like I said, I enjoy the delayed gratification of slowly watching my seedlings mature and bloom over several weeks of daily waterings and weedings.

In an age where DLCs are frivolous, borderline exploitative measures to games, it’s hard to believe an expansion of Shadowrun Returns would not only become better than the actual game it was built from but also be worthy being its sequel. The Director’s Cut is more like an official release as unrelated sequel that amazes me to this day from the jump in quality, not so much from its narrative as much as its development as an RPG. As much fondness as I have for the original, Dragonfall is a masterpiece beyond comparison to the first game, and it is without a doubt one of the most choice-based, non-linear RPGs I’ve ever played since Tyranny. While I would not recommend passing up the merits of the original or the third game, if you only have the time or money for one Shadowrun game if your life, you can do no wrong choosing to start with Dragonfall.
If there is one quality that truly sets apart Dragonfall from other well-regarded RPGs is the fact that this is one of the most non-linear, not open-world, games ever created. This is such a well-executed feat that it baffles me more games, especially RPGs, do not utilize the simple framework of Dragonfall.
Many RPGs, old and new, have tried to incorporate means to incentivize players to go off the beaten track to enhance the storytelling through player choice. Mass Effect/Dragon Age: Origins offered three branching pathways of scripted, choice-based areas to blend linearity with open-world designs. Baldur’s Gate/Pillars of Eternity offered massive maps that allowed exploration to guide the player with a sense of freedom. Bethesda’s games allowed open-worlds with linear questlines to give a false sense of non-linearity, of choices without long-term consequences, whereas New Vegas capitalized on them. All of these games have tested the limitations of linearity versus open-worlds, yet none have truly offered a non-linear experience, a player-driven narrative that shapes the order of events like a linear experience. The only closest comparison I can think of are the Civilization games that make a narrative built from the accumulation of decisions, and Dragonfall makes all those decisions story-related.
Despite being an uncommon experience, the actual framework for Dragonfall is a deceptively simple one for an RPG, you need to make cash to pull off the finale mission. It still has the prologue section, the finale and instances in the middle to give the game some amount of structure, yet the order of events (or their absence) is entirely left up to the player. What makes this system genius is how they use monetary rewards as a simple objective; it can be the basis for many complex moral decisions given the Shadowrun universe of megacorporations and underground networks vying for power. The absolute value of these decisions is not only impactful in the moment, but they can have knockdown effects like restocking supplies after a bad run or being just shy of a new upgrade because you went soft on the run that made the employer question you. There are even rewards during the companion missions and additional paths/conversations to reward exploring players with extra profits, and the net total will always be plentiful not to make players reach a point where they cannot continue. This framework is not only thematically appropriate given the dystopian world, but as an RPG, it really does make every decision you make fundamental to the core experience as a role-playing game.
 
Between the two games, a lot of changes under the hood are also made to make these two experiences more distinct to play. Combat feels more punishing than the first game’s leeway for two-thirds of the game whereas critical hits, positioning and other stats feel like they’ve gotten buffs to make fights more taxing. Environments, not only benefiting from greater freedom of choice to explore them, also have more opportunities for skills to be more impactful on the experience. There is no greater sense of reward than being a master Decker who hacks and talks his way through the whole gig without being ousted into combat. Quite frankly, Deckers feel like the game was tailored made for them especially whereas magic users feel like they got the shortened end of the drek, which makes sense in a cyberpunk world; however, there are many magic-related rewards and conversations only accessible to them that this minor complaint is addressed simply as what is common to RPGs.
Having praised these changes, there is one drawback with many knockdown effects on the whole experience. The emphasis on building relationships with your Shadowrun crew, while a novel idea and executed well with their companion quests, makes the other runners worthless. Scratch that comment; these other shadowrunners are worth more than they should be because your companions are free and these nobodies will bite into your budget. Not only do these runners offer less dialogue, but they also do not benefit from the additional perks given to the main five companions, and it’s the only instance where the linearity of game harms the experience. Even the first game only allowed one or two essential characters on some missions whereas these characters all feel essential from their benefits. Thankfully, every companion can be shaped by player’s decisions, so they do retain some replay value as well as offering enough party diversity to work with different builds.
Everything else about the gameplay systems is largely the same as the original, which is great because the other role-playing and combat mechanics were fine. Even the ending, which ends as ambiguous as the original, establishes enough finality of your choices to make it not feel anticlimactic because the whole player-driven journey was the reward. As a result, Dragonfall feels like the series’ first footstep into setting a new bar for RPGs by fleshing out their old problems and creating tons and tons of improvements on the established Shadowrun CRPG formula.
When it comes between Shadowrun Returns and Dragonfall, both games remain highly enjoyable for different reasons. Returns was my first foray into CRPGs; Dragonfall was my return to the Shadowrun universe to see it done its justice as a CRPG. Both games stories, which I have intentionally avoided mentioning any spoilers as the whole development of Dragonfall is a sublime treat, are finely crafted pulpy adventures of its cyberpunk/fantasy. These games can only benefit the active modding scene to bring this underground tabletop classic and CRPGs to modern audiences. Each game holds a candle in my heart for igniting some amount of passion behind role-playing in RPGs, but only one has the scorching flames and corporate grin of a dragon to offer me a deal to redo everything over again to experience it anew. That decision is always the easiest compared to ones made in its future.

It is hard to tell with this game. Is the question "do I recommend it" or "is it good"?
If the former, the answer is most definitely yes... But only because there is enough interesting to make the 10 minutes it takes to play worthwhile. I may be in the minority here but I do think there is quite a bit of this game that simply doesn't function on the level it attempts to. Is it trying to be a serious, realistic, and emotionally effecting look into the life of this person or an unnerving psychological horror that plays the insanity card to get scares? As of now, neither one works as a direct result of the the other.
It's worth noting that you should play this as blind as you possibly can. Once you've had the game's two big surprises spoiled, you've practically already played it. Don't read any descriptions, don't read any reviews, and don't explore anywhere in the game outside of what it tells you to do. If you're reading this chances are it's too late for you regardless.
My previous statement brings me to an important point though. This game is too open to exploration for the story it wants to tell. If you play games like me, you like to explore everything you have before you advance. The game has secrets that reveal themselves in due time, or even not at all to some players who weren't looking hard enough. Many of them are build up to the ending of the game, like a good horror film. Unfortunately my curiosity had me explore and unlock doors right off the bat that should not have been seen. What should have been a slow progression, gradually getting more and more tense, wound up being a few slightly disturbing things that just spring up and leave you, with no context or meaning. And it's the game that allowed me to play it this way.
Good Game Design requires boundaries to be placed to tell its story without making it obvious how these boundaries are limiting you. "the static speaks my name" chose to eliminate some of these boundaries altogether and as a result almost feels like a broken experience. Playing the game out of order like it allowed me to do even caused me to make assumptions regarding details that weren't accurate because I had seen them under different circumstances, further muddling the intentions of the experience. The game gives you choices later regarding these things that mean nothing and have no impact on the way everything else unfolds. It makes the game as a whole and your decisions feel empty and pointless. Ultimately, the game is a bunch of open doors to ruining it's own build up, and shallow options I didn't even realize were there.
Even with this discrepancy aside, the game's intentions feel unclear. It starts like realistic look at a very real and startling issue in this person's life. While I thought this was the point of the game (I even took some of the more startling things I passed as metaphors, visualization a of the character's feelings), I quickly realized this was not the case. The game instead chooses an exaggerated psychological horror route that instantly undermines any emotional impact or deep thought this game could have spawned in me. Its as if the creator started with something effective, thought-provoking, and legitimately startling (by dealing with an issue that hits close to home for me), but then gave up half way and started making a weird outlandish horror out of his fine, real concept. Then the very ending diverts back to this realistic take on life as if it still means anything anymore.
Finally, the game's humor fails. Dealing with something that is never pleasant under any circumstances should lead to some at least decent dark chuckles if your are creative enough and not too mean spirited, right? First of all, attempting to pull off humor in a game of this nature is impossible, and would take some skill to pull off. Honestly I wouldn't try it myself, just to let the game's dread continue to build. But this game tries and fails miserably on multiple occasions. The first comes early, when the game asks you to use the bathroom. Back when this game had me interested in where it would go, I thought this was an allusion of things to come. Looking back now, it's a pointless joke. The man grabbed some stock pee sounds and played then while you sit on a toilet. Another is on a computer, and is arguably the worst offender. It's just awkward and not amusing in the slightest. Good job for trying, but unfortunately those of us who find strange pointless sex and pee jokes funny are probably too immature to be playing this anyways.
"the static speaks my name" shoots itself in the foot less than half way through, which is a shame, because this easily could have been a brief but life-changing and truly unnerving experience had it kept up what it feels like it set out to do. And there's a lot of good here too. Some of the imagery is creepy and the music is impressively atmospheric. In other words, for ten minutes of your time, I do recommend this game. A lot of others seem to like it. For me though, it delves into some pointless excess for a game trying to say what it is intending to, and ultimately lacks the facts or insight to portray it's subject matter correctly.

This is an excellent game that still holds up well even now. The atmosphere of the game is excellent, making you feel like a real badass merc while still retaining enough difficulty, especially at higher settings, to be challenging.
The game is set in a fictional African country where you play a mrecenary tasked with a single mission: find and kil 'The Jackal', a ruthless arms dealer exploiting tensions in the region for his own gain.
To do this, you will have to work closely with two warring factions and various other people, all of whom have their own agenda.
One of the games greatest strengths is that it lets you approach your objective however and whenever you want with no handholding.
You will be given an objective to complete and full authority of how you go about it, what tactics you will use and what weapons you will utilise.
The lack of way points and reliance on checking your map is a nice change from most shooters that have a marker on screen at all times pointing to your objective.
While your postion is always marked on your map as is your objective location, you do have to manually check your map to find out where to go. The fact that your character actually takes out his map in game, instead of you going into a menu, is an excellent touch and helps immerse you in the game.
At the start of the game you will be given a choice of characters with different nationalities and backgrounds. While your choice has no impact on gameplay, as far as i can tell, the characters you don't choose show up in game as 'buddies'.
During a mission you will also recieve a call from one of the many buddies you will meet throught the game who will give you an optional way to complete the mission.
This may be to further their own ends and may cause you to betray the people who originally gave you the mission, however your ultimate goal is to do whatever it takes to get close to and stop the Jackal, an arms dealer, who is playing two opposing factions off against each other while selling arms to them both.
Opting to complete your buddies objective will increase your standing with them which will benefit you in a variety of ways.
You will have two main buddies. Your best buddy will be the one calling you with optional ways to complete a mission while your other buddy will rescue you if you go down in a firefight, drag you to relative safety and thereby give you a fighting chance to survive the engagment.
This works both ways however and you will at times be asked to help out your friends should they run into trouble of their own. Weather you do or not is up to you...
This mechanic alone gives the game some unique elements over other games in the FPS genre and helps keep things interesting.
One of the most touted parts of this game is the effects of fire. Being in a jungle enviroment fire can become very dangerous as it will not just burn in place but will spread to other flammable surfaces and set those ablaze. If you are not careful you can find yourself in a really bad postion with flames all around.
On the other hand you could use the fire mechanic to your advantage and set parts of the world ablaze to flush out enemies and funnel them into your killzone.
Enemies won't just sit and burn, they will run from the fire to try and save themselves and call out warnings to friends.
They will also attempt to help each other when they are in trouble which is really cool to see in game.
The gunplay in the game is excellent with very responsive controls and overall tight mechanics. Guns can degrade in quality with a lot of use and weapons picked up from enemies will always be of lesser quality than ones purchased from a weapon store.
The more degraded a weapon is, the more likely it is to jam, possibly leaving you vulnerable at the worst possible moment.
While clearing jams is easy enough, just a few presses of the reload button, it does get the adrenaline going when you are in an intense fire fight and you weapon suddenly jams just as you came face to face with an enemy!
Weapons can also be upgraded in ways such as accuracy and available ammo by purchasing them at gun store found throughout the world.
The currency is diamonds which you will receive when taking on a mission, rather than after it is completed, allowing you to stock up on what you will need before hand, which i thought was a nice touch.
Diamonds can also be found in cases out in the world by using a gps locator which are then added to your total amount.
Shop owners can also give you missions that if completed will enable them to sell more weapons and upgrades, so it is advised to do them as soon as possible to unlock all the available weapons.
There are a good variety of weapons in the game, ranging from pistols, rifles, RPG's, grenade launchers and even crossbows.
All of the weapons fit the theme of the game and help with immersion as none of them stick out as too high tech or over powered for the setting of the game.
The health system in the game is also interesting. It works as part med pack, part regeneration based. You also have to contend with the fact that your character has Malaria. This results in you having to take medication every now and again to stave off the effects.
If you start to feel ill and have run out of meds, you will collapse unconcious to the ground and may need rescued by a buddy, which could obviously impact whatever mission your are trying to complete.
Meds can only be obtained by doing mission for a local priest whose aim is to help the locals anyway he can. If you help him, he will help you.
Many people didn't really like this mechanic, i did. It is not as intrusive as many people make out and adds some flavour to the game.
Your health bar is split into multiple sections. If you are hit and a section is partially depleted, then it will regen to full on its own. If it is fully depleted then it will require a 'Stimpack' to refill it. Stims are found in first aid lockers throughout the world.
If you get down to your last health bar segment and recieve damage, but are out of stimpacks, then your character will try his best to tend to his wounds when you press the use stim button.
This will result in a short but grusome animation where your character will do things like pull his dislocated thumb back into place, dig a bullet out of a wound and various other things which will result in regaining two segments of health.
This is another cool addition to the game that draws you in.
Overall this is an excellent game that still compares favorably with later entries in the series and has its own unique feel.
I highly recommend this game to anyone with an interest in FPS games or those who have played later installments of the series.

The core mechanics are (for the most part solid), but there are WAY too many bugs, inconsistencies, cheap moves that only the AI can use and delay between attacks. In a fighting game, control is essential, but often control is taken away from the player, or the camera is shifted to make the scene look dramatic, even though you can no longer see what you are targeting.
Dimps really dropped the ball on the first Xenoverse, and they didn't much better here. Stamina is extremely easy to break and once it is broken you lose all ability to recover, dodge, move fast or even GUARD. In a fighting game, it is possible to take all control away from the player because of stamina, at which point, just drop the controller and walk away, because until you have stamina there is a grand total of nothing that can be done. You are just a ragdoll.
Missions range from patherically easy to actually impossible (because of bugs or just general bad design) without consistency. Certain enemies are straight up immune to basic attacks (not super armour which prevents hitstun, but actually does not take damage).
But the worst part of all of this....the sheer amount of grinding, well beyond the point that the game is fun simply because things like Expert Mission 15 exists, even though there is more content beyond it.
It works and is functional (so I have to recommend it), but for the price tag....just please buy something else. You will be a LOT happier. There are a ton of Youtube channels if you want to know the story or whatever.

Memorable and complex. Storywise, it felt very much like playing through a tabletop campaign led by a smart and creative GM. The combat is for the most part fluid and tactical, with a number of smart interface choices over its precedessor, Shadowrun Returns.
PROs: The writing. It strikes a smart balance between detailed world-building and directness, and dives straight into interesting moral choices. That said, I rarely felt forced into a dialogue branch that didn't feel natural, or which forces the player to betray or compromise earlier choices - rare for a game like this! Side missions give the game some amount of nonlinearity, but this is not without its problems (see below). The aformentioned interface is also relatively accessible for a new player, which is good because the game prefers not to hold your hand.
CONs: Occasional balance issues. Compared to Shadowrun Returns, the karma awards are extremely light, so the pressure to min/max is very high. Being that gameplay favors combat, it's difficult to justify dropping a few extra points into roleplay perks. I also noticed that the difficulty curve is spotty (likely an unintended result of some nonlinearity), and perhaps a bit too high at the very beginning. Lastly, it feels oddly short, even though objectively it's a pretty reasonable length. This may be because some of the later missions feel "padded" with large-scale battles and few choices until the very end.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game for table RPG fans, especially if you're the least bit interested in the unique blend of cyberpunk, noir, and fantasy genres elegantly mashed up here. 8.75/10.

Introduction:
Shadowrun: Dragonfall is the second installation in the Shadowrun game series. It was originally released as a DLC but later turn into a standalone title known as Shadowrun: Dragonfall Director’s Cut. Like the original Shadowrun game, Shadowrun: Dragonfall is a turn-based strategy game where your decision in the game will affect the ending and how well others perceive you.
Rating (1-5 Scale)
(3 Stars) Gameplay: Gameplay is similar to the first game (Shadowrun: Return) and not much has to change beside some UI and balancing patches. The missions are still level base and there is still some level of environmental inspection as before. Overall not much has changed, from the first game. Some issues persist like in the first game such as the lack of exploration. An example of this is areas are still level base and there is no ability to return to an area that you have already completed. Missions are quite linear with some minor choices to approach a problem. There also a lack of environmental interaction aside from some *inspection*. Some other issues that persist are certain classes are still heavily favor for smoother sailing while other classes have limited application (same with etiquettes).  Lastly, there is a bug that can be annoying to game breaking (depending on your luck) where you are frozen in combat. After some researching this for a bit, you either open debug mode (alt ~) and hit cheat and then the kill button and hope it goes away or wait for ages and hope it goes away.
(5 stars) Character: In this edition of Shadowrun, you now have a team that you are running with. In addition to this, you can explore and interact with your teammate's past. Thanks to this addition it does not feel like you are running along with a group of strangers and gives a better immersion experience. Aside from that aspect, the game lack dialogue choices that * make a difference* in how you perceive except for a few encounters. Overall the dialogue choices and conversations give a pretty good insight into the characters around you.
(4 Stars) Storyline: The storyline takes a lot of twists and turn and keeps you engaged and immerse in the Shadowrun universe. The first half of the game is tedious as you must grind your way to get to the next transition of the story. However, the second half of the game becomes more exciting as your decision gets emphasize and you can decide the outcome of the story.
(1 or 2 stars) Replay Value: There is not much replay value in this game as you can hit most of the ending if not all the ending right before you do your final run by quick saving and reloading. The only reason you might want to play again is for nostalgia or hunting for achievements.
(5 stars) Steam achievement: Most of the achievement can be acquired through a normal Shadowrun game run, albeit some minor one that may require you to replay the game again due to how tedious it is to set them up.  Overall the achievement is fair just tedious to get them all.
(4 or 5 Stars) Pricing: The amount of value you get for this game is amazing. The storyline is great and you have quite a few missions to get through and if you are finished with those you can always get some fan-made creation storyline from the community. I suggest getting it on sale when it goes to around 3-5 USD.
(4 stars) Overall: This is a terrific addition to your collection of Shadowrun games. While it does not add much new gameplay mechanic to the game, it will, however, provide you with a good 30-40 hours of immersive storyline to dive through.
TL:DR: Good bang for your nuyen. Don’t be a chummer and skip this out for some BTL.

I'll start this review by saying what I wish someone said to me: this game is essentially a CRPG like Baldur's Gate, except the combat is almost identical to X-Com and, obviously, it revolves more around sci-fi than fantasy.
I must admit, the storyline of the game didn't really grip me until I was about an hour away from the end. The story was good up until then, however it only became truly exceptional at that point.
That said, the last hour of this game was such an emotional rollercoaster for me that I absolutely must recommend it to any CRPG fans, especially those who value games where your choices matter. I cannot remember the last time any game made me so anxious about the choices I'd have to make and I consider this to be one of the game's strongest positives. Choosing whether someone lives or dies, choosing whether or not to trust someone or betray them, genuinely made my heart pound with nervousness as to what the consequences may be.
The game also allows for a pretty good amount of pluralism in how you approach tasks - one can get past very many sections by talking, shooting your way through, bartering, and hacking. Be nice if the game had some stealth, but nonetheless I'm happy with the variety of options the player has.

Basically, to save you time the short version is: Buy when on sale. Recommended with caveats.
The long version is:
This game achieves something in terms of role-play. It has well fleshed out character with interesting story lines. The world is unique and goes an extra mile in maturity, despite the fact that you're dealing with classical fantasy races in sort of steam/cyber punk, sci-fi futuristic setting. I think the blend of genres is handled superbly, and all those various races could have easily all been humans with different personalities. Still, what you're dealing with here are, in fact, elves, dwarves, orcs and trolls with smgs, pistols, cyber enhancements and magic. Weird on paper, but it works surprisingly well. The writing of the game is especially good and fortifies the mature feel. You will come across grey morality and choices/consequences which will give you pause because there are some stakes at hand. Story line is solid, with good variety of side quests, all helping to draw you in and uncover a bit more about what the world of Shadowrun is like. You can be a newcomer to the series and will be perfectly fine. The game explains things promptly and clearly, and you will neither get lost, nor feel like you don't have enough info on the lore. Your companions are original and posses personalities that stay consistent throughout the game; it was a pleasure for me to read everything I could uncover about them, either through conversation or whatever other limited information you get through their side quests. Their stories also involve you deeper with lore of the world itself, and that produces a surprisingly good immersion.
Where the game falls short is in the technical department.
There is definitely not enough player choice in this. I stopped playing at the Atzechology run, because it is literally impossible for my party to go stealth. I don't like that. It really kills my role-play. I understand it sounds incredibly snobby and entitled, but whereas so far my character felt like a pro shadow runner, with some of their lines really standing out in the tense situations they found themselves in, suddenly, I get some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥conversation lines at the same time that I am dressed up in hired guard uniforms of an organisation that is supposed to protect the facility in question. And to top it all off, that happens after a mission where I was getting stealth checks based on combat stats to knock personnel off in a quiet matter. Very badly handled, if you ask me.
The erratic rng of combat does not help, but I wasn't playing this game for the combat to begin with. It's well paced, for one, and you will not be trolled with significant road blocks on the way, more like, spend some more time in combat if you happen to miss your attacks(which does happen a lot). You have got some solid consumables to play with, and those really can turn you into a wrecking ball, if used accordingly, and you only get a limited choice of those per run, so you have to be conservative. Additionally, there is no loot or exp from enemies, so you are really incentivised to be a SHADOW runner...unfortunately, where this games fails so badly, is that it turns most of your SHADOW runs into MASS-MASSACRE runs...it's a very odd dev choice, to say the least.
Take it for what it is. The writing of this game is superb, the world is mature and well crafted, the music is appropriate and atmospheric, and it's a shame that it has so averagely handled combat and non-existent stealth.
Thus, buy on sale. 50 or more % off.

Then  there is the UI - it is cumbersome and glitchy - in fact how often you will get stuck in menus is a trap of its own, and in game FPS is pretty choppy with a lot of lag.
The gameplay itself quickly devolves into a game of learn the correct path the developer intends you take, as there is often no warning that the door/switch etc you are about to use is certain death. You can die about five times then its game over and you are forced to play the lottery of trying to get the game to reload.
Really this is one to avoid unless its part of a bundle package.

Oh boy, where to start with this one... well, Call to 10 is a game that is supposed to be inspired by the Saw film series. You wake up in a room with nothing but a camera attached to you, and you must figure out how to escape. Starting this task would be a whole lot easier if the game would actually load instead of crash. Even if you do decide to attempt the one crash fix that the developer mentioned in a single thread in the Steam community hub, which is to delete a .png file from the install directory, the gameplay itself just isn't worth it.
At the beginning, you find yourself in a room with a locked door and a keypad, after a while you will click on an air duct on the floor only to believe nothing happened, but then you find yourself transported to another room; turns out clicking that duct worked, but there's no animation or even transition screen to indicate that it did. You get the keypad combination, leave, enter it, open the door, and find yourself with a series of more doors. If you happen to click on a door that's locked, your character becomes stuck for whatever reason, but it's easily fixed by clicking again... found that one out through trial and error.
The rest is just proceeding through doorways and dying; these are not "traps" as the store page indicates, Call to 10 is just a flat out death simulator. Walk near a pipe? Die from steam. Open the wrong door? Something that looks like a mouse flies out at you and you die. Open the wrong circuit panel? You die. This "game" is nothing more than directionless trial and error, which wouldn't be so awful if you didn't have to start back at the keypad and enter the combination every single time that you screw up. What's even worse is that sometimes, for some unknown reason, instead of tossing you back to the keypad the game just puts you back to the title screen, where you may or may not be able to resume gameplay due to the CRASHING ISSUE THAT THE DEVELOPER WON'T FIX.
Having only spent 7 minutes in total on Call to 10, even I'm surprised that I have so much to say about it. Needless to say, it's another shoddy indie horror "masterpiece" made in FPS Creator that has zero developer support. It should be noted that this game is by the same guy who made Whispers, Krampus, Case #8, and Jackal. A word to the developer: maybe you should stop shoveling garbage onto Steam without first fixing your previous titles. People catch on, and horror connoisseurs will be sure to avoid your "work" in the future. If this game is inspired by Saw, it's when Amanda was in charge of the traps. Unless it's on sale for $0.10, avoid.

The game's main strengths are in its writing and storytelling. The combination of magic and sci-fi has been done well before, but Dragonfall puts a new spin on the melding of two genres. The story moves along at a good pace, and while the missions can be a little bit repetitive by the end, it wraps everything up with a bang.
Deeper reading of the dialogues and plot can lead to interesting perspectives on social issues like poverty, racism, war, and government. A superficial playthrough can easily miss out on a lot of excellent dialogue and nuanced ethical decisions. In the end, however, it is simply a video game, so don't lose sleep over the decisions you make.
Gameplay seems well balanced, although ranged attackers will have many more options for weapons than melee fighters (as my character was). Even so, melee fighters and deckers are able to hold their own.
Overall, an enjoyable title.

Haven't really played a whole lot of CRPGs. But somehow, the world of Shadowrun has always drawn me in. Like some combination of Blade Runner and Dungeons and Dragons. Where the dystopian idea of corporate takeover mixed with magic and dragons. Where the legendary sword might be an experimental gun, and your elven mage might sling some spells while picking off enemies with a rifle.
Shadowrun: Dragonfall mastered this atmosphere perfectly. I feel a sense of dread from the story, as something both mechanical and magical is trying to kill me, but not directly through the world. It is an interesting mystery, feeling like old noir novels rather than some hero with a legendary sword and the power of gods behind him.
The story and atmosphere draw you in, and there are still choices to make. What kind of runner are you? Do you make the right decisions in getting everyone out alive? Did you kill someone you didn't need to? Let someone go that might help you or hinder you on a future run? Even the choice of your class might change the story you experience. Do you know all there is about the matrix, and therefore become the tech expert of your group? Or did you go mage, and all the astral secrets give themselves up to you?
Gameplay is pretty good. You make use of cover, pick off important targets with various skills, position yourself and your team properly. Magic is more about buffs and debuffs, although you might make use of areas out of cover to enhance your own spells. Deckers might make use of more debuffs, but get their own special minigame when you need eyes on a camera, a turret under your control, or procure special data to sell to others.
I did not play much of the Director's Cut, although I have gotten through quite a ways into Hong Kong. I do like the ability to customize my team, for the most part. You have a pretty diverse group that will cover all your bases. And their own backstories are grim and enlightening. They're good people at heart; they just kill people for a living for someone else. The developers made sure all classes had a purpose during combat.
Overall, cyberpunk mixed with magic makes for a very interesting world. It's a lot different than most other CRPGs, as most seem to be fantasy based.
Also, obligatory don't make a deal with a dragon. Trust me.

A couple suggestions to further improve this already 10/10 game:
1) Create another Muscle, Mysticality, and Moxie character, 2 per type, as you have in Kingdom of Loathing with the Turtle Tamer, Seal Clubber, Disco Bandit, Accordian Thief, Pastamancer, etc.
2) Expand a tad bit on the included features: make completing sidequests relevent for all the right reasons! Include monster books for monster identification, hidden collectibles, and a journal system.

Those are just a few suggestions! I don't want to make this long winded, because honestly, the team has done such a fantastic job on the game already, and I look forward to the many more hours I plan on putting in to play this.

I personally like FC3 more than 2, and I haven't tried 4 yet.  Most folks will say that FC2 is the best.  It is a great game.  It has a huge open world and a lot of stuff to do.  The guard posts along your routes respawn very quickly, which can be a pain when you're trying to do one of the main missions.  I'm currently 54% done with the main quest and I have over 30 hours in.
FC2 is set in a war-torn unnamed African country and it is up to your choices to see who comes out on top.  You can recruit "companions" that will assist you in the main missions (they don't follow you around, but will meet you at mission locations and provide you with alternate tasks in quests).  There are a handful of ground vehicles that you can use to get around the country as well as a few hang gliders and boats.  Gun stores throughout the country will allow the player to upgrade weapons, vehicles, and the player.  There are also a bunch of campsites all over where you can rest and save the game safely.
FC3 has more of a story and FC2 can be repetitive, but it is a great game and very much recommended (especially when it’s on sale for $2.50!!)

I originally played this on the 360 and as I've yet to beat the game again on PC, story related review stuff will mostly be from what I remember from my 360 playthrough. That's okay since I'm pretty sure the story wasn't really meant for human comprehension anyway. So let's get started:
This game has very unique art style. If you'll like it or not is up to personal opinion. It's mostly cel shaded, but everything is dark. It's not bright like Borderlands is. I personally like it, but I've heard others say they really didn't. Combat is hack and slash and I really enjoy it. It's very stylish and fun to be slashing one robot and then time a block to counter another. Performance was pretty good in the hour that I played, but the game is capped at 31fps and requires a .ini cofig to go higher. That results in the menu moving faster and possibly some other side effects I've yet to see.
Story is that you play as fellow named Mondo Zappa who gets a piece of paper offering him a job to murder people thrown at his boathouse a decides to take as he already has a katana (which I'm pretty sure isn't real hanzo steel) and an arm that looks like an abomination and shoots people. People you murder tend to be larger than life people who live in the strangest places and are also evil(?) or something. Mondo is also a ladies man and these ladies will often call him on missions asking him if he wants to lay some pipe or whatever. A reason to actually care about doing that is they give you new subweapons.
Overall, I remember liking this game a bit, but I quickly forgot about it after I stopped playing it. I'd say it's worth a run through if you like hack and slash games, just don't be looking for a story that even remotely makes sense.

I always enjoyed the old Pac Man game, games actually, the different versions and forms Pac Man has had through the years. This game is something I have always looked for, old school Pac Man in a brand new jacket. The 10 dollar price tag is more than worth it but you can just wait for the next best sale, the game is always on sale basically going down to 3 dollars every other month.
Don't expect giant story modes or thousands of hours of gameplay but if you love the old school arcade style Pac Man then this is the game for you. There are tons of levels, a bunch of different skins for the levels and even for Pac Man and the ghosts. You can nicely customize the look of the level and characters and even then there are enough different level lay-outs to keep you busy for a long time, that is, if you accept the game for what it is, old school 'trying to break the high scores' Pac Man. Great visuals, addictive gameplay and MASSIVE pellet munching ghost chewing combo streaks. Even then, the game still has a lot of different modes to offer, standard score attack, time trials, ghost combo mode and a few more, it IS jam packed with content for those that understand the way Pac Man games have always worked. It's great to see how high you rank among ALL of the game's players world wide.
The DLC pack is about a dollar when on sale, it gets you a few more game modes based off other Namco franchises and adds some more game modes and skins, more than worth it, even at full price.
Best pacman to date. Buy it.
