Disclaimer: I got this from the Yogscast Jingle Jam so I haven't technically bought this game.
Anyhow, it was a fun game. The plot is pretty simple: you are a convicted felon, but you are free to go if you can manage to get through the puzzles laid out before you.
Pros:
It is a beautiful game.
It has a portal-vibe but its puzzles are completly different so you don't feel like it's a copy.
Utilizes different kinds of puzzles which is refreshing.
The puzzles are not hard, I think the game focuses on being relaxing. Took me about 5 hours to complete the game.
Cons:
Jumping puzzles. This was a sad implementation in my opinion. I can't speak for others, maybe it's my computer that is not at its greatest, but I experienced the controls to be a little janky. Which lead to some frustrations since the jumping puzzles could be really precise at times.
They didnt provide any kind of thinking stimulus either since you easily could see where you needed to jump and the only challenge was to hope that the controls would not bug out and your character did a mysterious second jump the moment he/she landed. Some puzzles required you to use a 3rd kind of puzzle solving mechanic, block placing, but since you only can place these at desgineded positions on the walls it was not hard to figure out where to place them.
I would have been happier if they just skipped the jumping puzzles and released a game with fewer puzzles in it. It would be worth it.
All in all a really fun game to play if you feel like spending some hours in a really well made tribute to the Portal games

Really good game, despite a few annoying flaw, for both gamers and Shadowrun fans.
The game holds very well both to the lore and the basic vibe that the Shadowrun pen and paper games had, and does a decent job replicating the gameplay of it. It does a pretty good job of keeping with the open ended nature of the pen and paper games, considering it is still a video game and doesn't have the flexibility of a GM. There is, unfortunately, a pretty major problem with how the game handles combat. Instead of doing a virtual dice roll, like what Baldur's Gate and NWN did, it decides hits and misses based on percentages, which sometimes don't even seem to work correctly. There will be times when you are trying to shoot someone two feet from you with an autmatic rifle and only have a 60% chance of hitting altogether. Other times you'll have a 90% chance of hiting someone, yet will still consistently miss. It isn't game breaking, just something to look out for when playing
The story is well written, and fits in perfectly with the established universe. Having the setting away from the usual Seattle was a good choice, as it allowed more open story telling without stepping on the toes of the RPG fans. The characters are interesting with plenty of development for those who care about such things.
It  also has the support of Steam Workshop, meaning that there is plenty of user content to be accessed as well, making it well worth the price.

One of the best stories I have ever played in an RPG. Not too much choice, but the story (with great, amazing twists) and characters here are what you're paying for. Don't miss out on this game; it's one of my favourite RPGs.
As for cons, it's the music and jankiness of combat. The music is great, don't get me wrong, but there are so few tracks that playing for long amounts of time can feel repetative because of the music on a loop. Also, in combat, sometimes when I click on something it doesn't respond. These are only two minor quips in an otherwise great game that is worth every single penny.
***One more thing to note is that this game has no voice acting whatsoever and lots of text. If you hate reading, you will not like this game, although, compared to other text-based RPGs, the dialogue is actually pretty simple and far from lengthy (looking at you, Pillars of Eternity).
DO NOT MISS OUT. BUY THIS NOW!!!

The second installment in Harebrained Schemes' new Shadowrun franchise.  Classic CRPG gameplay with a cyberpunk/fantasy setting.  Overall I found this game to be much better than the first (Shadowrun Returns) - and the first was not disappointing either.  This time you're running in Berlin, which adds a hint of foreign flavour to the game too (unless you live in Germany, I suppose. =P)
This game provides you with a lot more opportunities to make choices while talking to NPCs or investigating things.  Choices that actually have noticeable consequences.  The main plot is still mostly linear, but you can influence how a given mission unfolds, at least.  Whether you kill someone or let them live, whether you complete the objective you were hired to do or not, when new revelations make it morally ambiguous.  That sort of thing.  There are also a lot more side-quests and unrelated "paydata" dumps to find, which makes you feel like you're actually running an operation here, choosing what missions to do and when, choosing whether or not to sell the data you hacked online, etc.  The unique Shadowrun atmosphere and setting is as strong as it was in the first game, too.
Also, there's an NPC with my name (first and last) in there!  (Spelled wrong, but I'll take it =P)
The most annoying thing to me - and I freely admit this is a minor complaint - is that I rarely saw any point in hiring shadowrunners other than my own crew for missions.  When you start most missions, you're presented with a screen to choose your team.  The people available to be hired here can be broadly divided into "Your Team" (the primary NPCs you work with) and "the Other Guys" (a short list of other shadowrunners in the area.)
Members of "Your Team" are free to bring along (0 nuyen), they have their own side-quest story missions and personalities revealed through conversation, and they occasionally gain new abilities or equipment after you run with them.  The "Other Guys" cost money to hire (not a lot, but not 0), they have no story missions or personality (except one, whom you can talk to between runs), and they don't ever upgrade their gear or abilities AFAICT.  Also, using "Your Team" keeps your bases covered fairly well, so it's not like you need the "Other Guys" to fill any tactical holes for a given mission.  I like that this screen is present - I like the idea of hiring runners off a roster of available people - there's just no reason to choose people other than your own crew every time, and that fell a little flat with me.  It would be nice if the list of available "Other Guys" rotated once in a while, too.
If you liked Shadowrun Returns, you will like this one too.  There's no plot connection, so it's not a sequel except in the sense that they're two games in the same universe, but it's still good times in a similar vein.
You like Shadowrun and cyberpunk in general.  If you're on the fence about this one or Returns, you can play them in either order, so get whichever you like best.  (I still recommend playing them in order of release, if only so that the UI / RP experience is
over time.)

Far Cry 2 is game that I would call a "victim of the bandwagon". It was generally hated by the community upon release because it had nothing to do with the first game. (Which frankly isn't a bad thing.)
Rather, FC2 tried to take the series in a new direction. No mutants or cliche action seqences. Just gritty violent dark chaos   unfolding in the African jungles around you. The stripped down approach is quite appealing because the game seems to take itself more seriously. Putting more emphasis on tactics than just going in guns blazing.
Story: You play as a hired gun that was sent by an unknown party to kill an infamous arms dealer named the Jackal. According to information provided, he is largely responsible for increasing instability inside Africa by stirring up civil wars in the country by providing weapons to both sides. Sounds easy, right? Go to Africa, find the Jackal, kill him. As you soon find out, it's not the simple. You soon start to play a part in the fate of the country and that perhaps, there's bigger problems than a person selling guns.
It's an interesting story if you're willing to invest into it. The Jackal is an interesting character to listen to as he describes his life in the country. How the increased violence and warfare is slowly tearing the country apart.
Gameplay: FC2 is a sandbox shooter at it's core. You're dropped into a beautiful lush world with various objectives to complete at your leisure. How you approach the goals is also up to you. Go guns blazing, go stealth, snipe, etc. As long as you got the tools, you got a plan. It's very satisfying to go in stealth and pick off guys from the darkness of the jungles. Watching them panic as their numbers get reduced one by one.
Overall, I can't complain about FC2. It's a well made shooter that will keep gamers entertained for while. If you like planning attacks out and you're all about think first, shoot later. This game is up your alley.

There are some amazing things about Far Cry 2, but anyone who doesn't admit it's a flawed game isn't confronting reality.. You will probably either feel unable to play it or addicted to it like I was.
ON THE GOOD SIDE...
The number one thing this game does right is atmosphere. The environment is beautiful but also suspenseful and slightly terrifying. The music and sound help to achieve this atmosphere. The graphics are great. I didn't play until 2015 but they look awesome to me. The game starts out feeling almost impossible, or at least very challenging, but as you get used to the non-stop survival you start to feel like you are a force to be reckoned with. Although the fights are quite formulaic, you are totally on your own and so you feel a sense of achievement when you lay waste to hordes of enemies. The game is like a sandbox shooter: At first you feel like a child abandoned in a war zone with a pistol, but over time you realize that you can choose how to fight (balls out or stealthy) and do things your way.
I also appreciate that I didn't have any technical problems or major bugs as I played; it was quite a smooth experience.
ON THE BAD SIDE...
I have to admit I enjoyed the game quite a lot in the end (I certainly got addicted until I finished it) but there are some problems with the game. No matter how much you get used to the non-stop "survival mode" feel - and some people absolutely love it - it always seems silly that the whole game is basically you vs a never ending rain of thugs. Everywhere you go you have to wipe down an outpost full of enemies to get anywhere, even if you just cleared it a few minutes ago. It's supposed to feel harshly realistic, but it almost feels cartoonish how much crap is thrown at you all the time. And then you get the opposite problem: You realize everything is just a formula and as soon as you get used to it, everything is too simple (almost too easy). I did say that it feels good to be the unstoppable predator and that you earned that position yourself, but it makes the game quite one-dimensional.
To sum up the gameplay problem, the game crosses the line between being difficult and being tedious. Yes you can still enjoy it, but always asking yourself why you are playing this game that is basically a map full of enemy camps you have to ravage time and time again. Also, guns you pick up from enemies jam quite often, and even your own guns can jam over and over again during certain fights. Personally I didn't see that as any kind of addition to the challenge, it was just irritating.
The only time you don't feel alone is with your buddies, which brings us to another problem. The buddy system, wherein you meet people who provide missions or can save your hide when you get knocked out, feels incomplete. After playing the game to the end, I still have no idea what "reputation" or doing extra side missions did for me. I'm pretty sure the answer is nothing.. The main interaction you have with buddies is that your best friend at any given time will call you after you receive each story mission and offer you a bizarre, convoluted way to do the mission. Sometimes it makes the mission more interesting, but given the brutal nature of the game I would usually just groan that I was given an extra set of tasks.
A quick note about the ending, which is SORT OF A SPOILER but not really. Actually, I might be doing you a favor if you play the game. Once you beat the final mission, you cannot go back and wrap up side stuff that you didn't finish. Considering there are 221 diamonds to find in the game (ugh) it's a bit funny. I guess this is just a choice developers make when ending the story of a sandbox game, but I personally never like when this happens. I wanted to wrap up the last side missions and diamond hunting, but now that I finished the story I don't feel compelled to load an old save and do all that again.
Also, the credits are like 10 minutes long and you can't skip them... I don't understand.
ALTOGETHER
This game is worth playing for the good parts, but for some the flaws can't be forgiven and I can honestly totally understand that. I actually almost put the game down the first time I realized that everywhere you go you will be attacked PLUS patrol cars make the roads unsafe as well.
A word of advice if you plan to play this game: Take it SLOW. Although it's kind a repetitive game, you'll still find it more enjoyable if you take it in and play wisely. If you try to rush all the time, you will probably just get frustrated (although I did choose to fly in with a truck and blow everything up half the time, instead of going stealthy). Also, buying the camo suit upgrade is a must, and I personally could not play without the silenced weapons.

I've got less than an hour in this game but I feel that is enough time to tell you why you should, or shouldn't, spend some time looking at this game. Let's face it, the CCG genre is filling up with games like Runescape's, Fairea, Gwent and of course... Hearthstone. All of these games require time to get to the point of being competitive, to get big decks with cool synergies and in some cases money for more cards. So why should you use some of your time to play TES: Legends?
Because it does enough things the same as the other giants of the genre, while still being fresh.
First off, TES: Legends has a pretty good story complete with cutscenes and voice acting. It's all picture stills but it still convey's a story that feels at home in the Elder Scrolls world.
Which is another bonus of this game, TES lore isn't too hard for people to understand and this game gives enough lore to keep it interesting but is grounded in what we already know. Each card is instantly relatable to people who may have only played Oblivion and Skyrim. Cards like Riften Watch, or Scuttler, people will recognize these and it just feels nice to feel at home in a world.
Speaking of cards, there's a feature here that I don't think I've seen else were; leveling up cards. You start with a card that's pretty plain jane, no special, medicore attack and deffence but you can level it up to give it a special attribute and more attack/deffence. I believe it also raises the mana cost and I don't believe you get too chose the card to level, but it's cool to see that some of your early on junk cards can be useful.
Again, I've put 17 minutse into this game so far and I'm in love. If you prefer the world of TES over Witcher or Blizzard, I'd recommend this game, it's interesting, it's stylish, the story is pretty decent and it's fun.

Played many hours on the Bethesda launcher so my hours played is inaccurate. Big fan of ESL and in my opinion is currently the best CCG at this time. It's very similar to Hearthstone as many point out, but personally feel like it improves on a lot of aspects over HS, certainlly more tactical and is less RNG-based card-wise.
- A free story mode with custom decks and choices which reward you with different cards. One of the strongest points in the game, and one that I prefer over the solo adventures from Hearthstone. New story modes are paid for, unfortunately, but from what I've seen, these modes are a lot more interactive compared to HS' quirky straightforward adventures.
- 50 cards and up to 3 copies of non-unique cards mean more dust/soulgems needed, but only 1200 for legendaries. The game is quite generous with it's packs however, and rewards come quicker and more frequently ie 3 win rewards
- The Solo arena along with the multiplayer arena. The Solo arena is great, and feels like an extension of the story mode where you face AI, but they tend to have an advantage in various ways and have themed decks
- The lane system is a welcome addition. Usually there's a standard lane which is a normal lane and a shadow lane where creatures basically have stealth against attacks (except spells) and you can't attack across lanes. This feature means a lot more strategy is required on creature placement.
- The rune system is something I have mixed feelings about. On one hand it makes the game a lot more tactical and calculated instead of going all-face all the time, but card draw isn't too rewarding - which is where prophecies come in. For those unaware, each player has 5 runes and breaks for every 5 health increment, and each time one is broken, you get a random card draw; prophecy cards can be played for free if drawn this way. It's extremely satisfying getting a prophecy, but with 50 card minimum decks, it's super RNG-based and is just inconsistent.
- The class system and flexibility with cards is a welcome addition. A lot of freedom when it comes to deck building.
- Beautiful and consistent art and design, a lot more intricate and mature - very similar to MTG artstyle.

OK let me start off by saying I enjoy this game and it was well worth the sale price however I'm going to be reviewing this game as if it was at it's full price.
First off it's simply not worth it. There's not really enough content (new content) to justify a whole new game. Honestly the best way I can explain it is that if the hub world and features were released as DLC for Xenoverse 1 there would be little  to no difference between the two titles.
Graphically it's the same, the progression system is the same, the customisation is the same, the quest structure is the same, most of the movesets are the same, 80% of the game just looks and feels like a copy/paste of Xenoverse 1.
Online play is the same right down to the unbearable lag for those of us in the EU. Also if you are in the EU and wish to try out the co-op multiplayer then you better have some friends because when you try and search for teams matches and missions all you'll get is "No group found" seems it's pretty dead in the EU. the shoddy servers likely have something to do with that. PvP is also horrid in execution and full of cheaters, don't bother.
This makes "Expert Quest" a chore sometimes. When the expert enemy has the "Mind Control" ability And you get mind controlled the friendly AI doesn't bother to free you or anybody else that's trapped. They simply fly around you or keep attacking the boss meaning if you're the only player controlled character you have to try and free EVERYONE that is captured or you'll find yourself 6v1 and screwed.
The combat system has changed slightly, there are more move sets, transformations are a plenty (With each race getting one) and now have a dedicated keybind rather than having to take out an attack to use it. You can now pull off more complex combo's (If you have super human relfexes and can work out the massively strict timing)
And just like Xenoverse 1, fighting AI feels unfair in the later stages. They can interupt your ultimate attack with a mere punch, kick or basic weak ki ball while you feel like you have to unload a full 20 hit combo before you can stop theirs. They can block mid combo while you just have to put your controller down and wait until they stop knocking you around like a pin ball when they trap you in one etc.. etc..
At later levels it really feels like the AI is just borderline cheating. They never seem to use much ki not matter what attacks they do, they ALWAYS seems to have loads of stamina no matter how many times they teleport dodge (Which drains stamina fast) They always predict which direction you are attacking from even when you teleport dodge, they dodge EVERYTHING with ease.
Your ultimate attacks will often miss because they dodged it (even when you're right up in their face) They can just basically hold the block button and block an ultimate attack fully with taking no damage and having no stamina drained where as if you attempt that your block breaks, you take damage and your stamina is basically put to zero.
The devs of this series seem pretty lazy. Not only have they just copy/pasted 80% of Xenoverse one in to a new "Full game" but their idea of dificulty is having the AI break the rules of their own game where as the player has no choice but to follow those rules. It's ridiculous.
Companion AI is also horrible. They can fight well but boy do they screw things up for you. They will knock enemies out of your combo, they will knock enemies out of the path of your ultimate, they will basically just stop you from getting any kind of good combat flow going.
And don't even get me started on the 3v1 time patroller gank fights where every single enemy attacks you at once and you can't do anything because you're stuck being juggled from one stun locking combo to another.
The star rating for the missions do not seem to mean much here. In XV1 you could get to max level, go in to a low star mission (1-5) And just start wrecking everything. Really felt like your character had become powerful but here even 3 star missions can utterly destroy a high level character. No matter how far you level it just doesn't feel like your character has any impact or does much damage unless you are spamming ults which is a boring way to play.
It has all the gameplay of Xenoverse 1 with all the issues of Xenoverse 1 and really is NOT worth a full price purchase. I'd get it on sale though for sure.

Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light is a great couch coop game.  It has puzzles to figure out together.  It has tons of enemies to overwhelm the both of you.  The visuals are nice, and the story, while absurdly unrealistic and unbelievable, isn't in-your-face too much.  You can't easily tell the depth of objects a lot of the time, but the gameplay is pretty straight-forward: shoot things, dodge things, and climb things.  The special aspect of this game is how it caters to the couch coop crowd with clever same-screen coop mechanics.  It also supports online play, though I never had much luck sticking with a single coop partner for the entire game that way, and I frequently experienced disconnections and glitches that way. In local coop mode, I enjoyed every minute of the game.
The only problem I see is that players can respawn right after dying and don't have to figure out how to stay alive through life-or-death puzzle elements.  There's a platforming puzzle early in the game that requires both players to take turns helping each other up a moving wall before they're pushed into an endless pit.  The only reason I ever managed to beat that level was the respawn system was too forgiving.
I do not recommend playing this game online, but it makes a great local coop game.

I've played some other puzzle games with a "cut the rope" mechanic, enjoyed them a lot, but compared to them, this one is annoying.
The first annoyance is the highlight-left-click-right-click mechanic: why do I need a double click to execute a single, defined action? I can see how that might be an necessity so thick-fingered users on a small phone don't tap the wrong chain by accident, but on a tablet this is already unnecessary, and on a PC, where the mouse cursor highlights the chain to be cut, this is unforgivable.
The second annoyance is that these are not so much physical puzzles as timing puzzles: you can usually figure out the mechanics quickly, but the timing is so unforgiving that it usually takes several tries to implement a solution that you have already figured out.
Add to this the observation that ball behaviour seems to depend on the color of the balls -- I put a small grey ball in a resting spot and hit it and I can hit it to a place 4 times out of 5, and I put a small colored ball in the same spot and never get it there.
My impression is that this game simply tries to prevent me from doing what I want to do. Few things are more annoying than that, and I'm certainly not going to annoy myself voluntarily. I'll stay away from this one.

Obulis is a pleasant, casual puzzle game, based upon little spheres transferring kinetic energy to one another, until each end up exactly where they're supposed to be: the pot (or sometimes, flower) of the same colour. There's something very calming about this premise, and the graphical design as well as sound direction really bolster this effect. The game opts to create a soft wall of sound out of sound effects appropriate to the setting, rather than plaster the levels with repetitive music. The result is a game that is a pleasure to play, for short bursts or long stretches.
Many of the puzzles do require precise timing, to varying degrees of difficulty, and some of the puzzles are difficult enough to become frustrating. However, when the solution is finally completed, it is often very elegant, and there is a great sense of satisfaction putting the complex little machinery into action, observing it working in perfect synchronicity, and watching the balls fall one by one into their respective pots, with a satisfying 'clink'.
It doesn't sound like much, but this atmosphere that the game fostered, has drawn me back to finish it three times. It's definitely worth a try.

Completely different in tone than the first Far Cry & the later games. Far Cry 2 takes place in an unstable African nation divided between 2 (or 4?) warbands and you are a government agent sent to find the arms dealer that's arming both sides.
The game has a lot of cool ideas that were abandoned in the later games, the coolest of which (imo) is that all maps & information that would normally be put in menus are handled as in game objects. The maps are objects that your character holds & weapons are bought on a computer & stored in an actual physical armory the you go inside & pickup what you want.
But the game isn't all good. Enemies will constantly re-spawn after you clear out their checkpoints & bases. And silly things like fighters in the faction you are working for attacking you because "they don't know you're on their side". The story also doesn't get good til the end & most of your time will be spent doing side missions & story missions for the previously mentioned fighter groups don't really have any depth or personality.
Though I didn't mind it's problems I would recommend Far Cry 3 or 4 to the average gamer over this one because they are simply more approachable. But if you're looking for a more "realistic" Far Cry game than you should pick this up.

"The game itself can be charge like 39.99 however it should be continuing updated throughout the years with new card sets consistently introduced to the game.
It contains all of the most common play mode both causal and hardcore including 1vs1 standard, 2-head-giant, free for all, free for all EDH, planechase, archenemy, as well as good singleplayer campaign. Each new expansion card set should bring most of the codable cards into the main game cardpool, and add additional cards(say 5 cards) to each of the prebuild decks sideboard from this new card set. Card pool:
Players are allow to gain access to core game card pool to create their custom decks to play after they have finish the storyline campaign by using the prebuild decks. They can also buy booster packs(coins or pay $) from variable sets to add more cards to their usable card pool.

First, I've played the first game (Xenoverse). And despite some of its...rather gamebreaking flaws, I did still like it enough. That being said, my opinion will be a little biased.
First of all this game stylized itself like previous titles such as Raging Blast 2, in the fact that is is a fighting game on a 3d plane. Unlike your mortal combat, marvel vs capcoms, and street fighters, this game allows a high freedom of movement, attack patterns, dodging ability, and overally diversity in combat. You start out more often that not, far away from your opponents, and have several options to close in on them, or wait for them to come to you, depending on your objectives. Close up Fighting does involve the X and Y (or square and triangle if you use a PS controller) for light and heavy attacks, though calling them that is a bit of a misnomer, as both have reasonable speed and damage, but are just different attack patterns. The B or Circle button controls your light ki-blasts, which are mostly useless, but sometimes fun to play around with. The A or X (on PS controllers) controls your 'dashing' ability which can allow you to move around the arena quickly, or rapidly close in on an enemy position. Of course dashing can be combined with both light, and heavy attack, and has a few unique patterns to utilize on it's own. You also have 'super' attacks, which can be ki-waves such as Kamehameha, or powerful combination moves. The game has a high variety of these, as well as extremely powerful 'ultimate' attacks. Button mashing will not work out for you.
Your character is created when you start the game and each character has a reasonable amount of customization options. You can either be a human, saiyan, friezas race, namekian, or a majin. Each race has their own stat balances and growth, meaning different strengths and weaknesses. Saiyans for example are glass cannons. They can deal high damage, but are poor at taking damage. Namekians and majins have high defense and unique moves, but low overall attack power. Humans are a jack of all trades and get bonuses to ki-regen. Friezas race have speed boosting abilities, which is far more useful than you may think if you chain together combos. They also have voice options, but these voices are mostly 'combat voices' meaning no real spoken dialogue. That being said, there are at least 11 voice options for each gender.
Fixes from the first Xenoverse_
- Your partner AI is now somewhat competent, now the equivalent to a mid-level enemy AI.
- Enemy AI that is not time patroller AI avoids ganking tactics. This was a problem in the first game where multiple opponents would gank the player, who had no way of defending or countering multiple attackers at once. Now the enemy AI will circle you if you are engaged with another enemy AI. If you switch the lockon, the AI will also switch out who is fighting you.
- There are almost no poise barriers on enemies (the thing where an enemy could take damage, but would not stagger, making fighting them ridicoulously tedious), however against higher level opponents such as broly, this makes thing somewhat trivial depending on your skill level.
- The area map for the hub world is much bigger and more interesting.
Pros_
- Incorporates fighting multiple opponents, often with your own allies, on a 3d plane, something I have never seen done except in the first game.
- More extended and diverse combos from the first game, many of which are race-specific, so playing a majin would feel very different from playing a saiyan or a namekian.
- Gameplay is very fun and diverse. It does not get as repetitive as most fighting games would.
- Wide range of super attacks to use.
- In game mechanics such as dashing, dodging, blocking, and just guard, allow the player to adapt to nearly any situation that isn't ganking (and some skilled player can overcome that if they are cautious).
- Lots of parallel quests to do and play around with so you don't get bored after the main storyline is over, which, lets be honest, the main story is basically a side mission.
- Full character customization, including supers, ultimates, costumes, z-souls, and ingame single use items.
- Parallel quests often feature supers, costumes, z-souls and more, giving you a reason to play them.
- Lots of side missions within the city itself to play around with.
- You can play as nearly an character from the game's roster once they are unlocked, if you want. This means you are not restricted to your created characters. Yes, you can play as goku, or frieza.
Cons_
- Ganking is possible, and while the AI tries to avoid it, nothing is stopping other player from doing so in pvp, which is entirely optional.
- Servers are rather poor, often resulting in lag in game with other players. I suppose this is now the standard for modern gaming -_-
- Super dashing is OP borderline broken, as it makes you invincible while using it, seeks in on enemy opponents automatically and attacks, interrupts enemy attacks, and will break their guard/stamina bars instantly, and it is extremely difficult to avoid, with very few specific super attacks to counter it (time skip/backbreaker).
- The main story goes through most of the same motions as the first game, only really deviating in any significant way towards the end.
Overall rating: I like this game, and that comes from someone who isn't terribly fond of traditional fighting games. But that is probably because this game is anything but traditional. Really, dbz games made today should have their own catagory. If you like fighting games, or even if you have a likeness for hack-n-slash style of gameplay, you will probably like this game, especially if you are a fan of the Dragon Ball series.

For some time now I had a thirst for a hack 'n slash game - one like Metal Gear Rising: Revengences in which you can just slice and slice and slice. I was scrolling through my Steam library when I saw Killer Is Dead. I remembered that purchased the game on some sale but didn't really play it. After a brief consideration I decided it was worth my time to play it; Boy, was I right.
Killer Is Dead is an action hack 'n slash game with a rather unique art style.
I'll start with the gameplay: in my opinion, the game has very smooth combat mechanics and great controller layout. As with many other hack 'n slash game, I strongly reccomend playing the game with a controller for the best experience possible. Another plus it that the game is not just a button mashing game, unlike certain series which have failed at this point and are only about pressing the attack button.
Outside of the missions, the game has a few activities that give the player a break from the usual fighting; including impressing ladies for gameplay benefits (New weapons, boosters, etc.) and motorcycle riding activity seemingly inspired by arcade games.
I wouldn't call this game's upgrade system 'impressive' as it is pretty small, in my opinion, but it's good to have it there in order to give the player something to look forward to.
The art in this game, regardless of the graphics (which I'll get to in a moment), is interesting and original, the envivorment is polished and the level design is very clever. The graphics remind me somewhat of various anime video games I played; the bold outline of the characters and diffrenet than most games shading techniques. Allthough I'm quite fond of the graphic style of the game, I did find the shading a bit too dark at some points, which made it quite hard to see at times.
What I found the most interesting in this game is the story. When I began playing, I thought the story was pretty shallow - just the usual go there and kill that. Fortunatley, as you progress through the game you find yourself more and more curious about the plot, as the game constantly makes more questions pop up.
On another aspect, the characters are very colurful. While some look silly but turn out to be very important, others look very important but turn out to be a very minor part of the plot.
Killer Is Dead is a very not sad of a game; by that I mean that you can find a lot of humor in it, whether it is the fourth wall casual breaks or just bizzare characters or missions.
Lastly, I feel that it's quite important to say that the game includes activities and endgame content even after the story ends.
All in all, I can strongly recommend this game if you are into hack 'n slash and/or looking for an interesting story with some light humor. An honest 9.5/10.

Damn, what a strange experience this was. The game got my attention because of its graphics and as I have played in the past other hack'n'slash games like DmC and Shadow Warrior I decided to give it a shot.
At first I didn't like it at all. Okei, the graphics and overall style was cool and different yes, but the game mechanics was hard to get used to. It's ported from consoles, so go figure. But after the tutorial missions (more or less Episodes 1 - 3) it got more enjoyable as the controls made more sense.
One thing you should notice though - if you are looking for games with extremely good stories that make sense then KiD may not be for you. Actually I prefer also games that contain good story, twists and character development but for a change KiD was not so bad. So if you're looking for something different, then definitely try.
Also the map was confusing as hell in the beginning because you will find a lot of different stuff and missions there that you just don't expect from a game. Like Gigolo-missions. These are the missions that give "Mature" label to this game. Basically you just date with beautiful girls, see them half-naked, give them presents and then after some dates (if they're satisfied with your presents) you will finish in the bed. Quite random. But still fun.
Now, the main missions are pretty straightforward, just go there and slash the f*****s. The boss fights are also quite similar (with some exceptions) but as the game offers you many difficulty levels to choose from you can spice things up with some hardcore level.
If you're interested in achievements or collecting a lot of stuff in the game, then sadly you will face totally senseless grinding marathon. First you have to complete episodes and challenges on good enough rank (A or AAA), like this you'll unlock gifts and costumes for the girls. Doesn't sound so bad, buut, then you notice the cost of this s**t. So go back and repeat the same missions again and again to earn more money. If you want to play honest of course. If you google, you can find tutorials that help you avoid this grind-fest.
So, what conclusion we make? I personally was pretty satisfied with the final result. It's like some cult game. It's not meant for masses. If you're looking for this kind of specific style or you happen to be tired of more regular games then why not to try.

If you like the Shadowrun universe, this is for you. If not, the Neuromancer/Tolkien crossover might not appeal to you.

I bought the original version new back in 1999 (big cardboard box version from my local Software Etc.).  It's been my favorite video game ever since.  I was thrilled to hear Tim Schafer and the folks at Double Fine would be releasing a remastered version.
I'm very happy to say this version is every bit as good as the original.  The graphics have been updated rather than overhauled, with higher resolution textures and improved shadows, so it still has the same look and feel as before, just less pixelated.  You can switch between the updated and original graphics at the push of a button to see the difference.
The controls have been updated to be more palatable to a modern gaming audience but the original "tank controls" are still an option.  There's even an achievement you can get for playing through the entire game using only the original control scheme, which is a nice nod to fans of the original version.
To top it all off, Grim Fandango's soundtrack is one of the best in all of videogames and has been re-orchestrated for the remastered version.  The soundtrack holds up on its own and is well worth buying separately in addition to the game.
Final note to new players:  If you just follow a walkthrough and march straight through all the correct choices, you'll miss out on much of the game's great dialogue.  Half the fun of these older-style adventure games was trying out as many conversation options as possible to find all of the jokes or backstory details hidden in the various characters' responses.  Also, trying to use inventory items on everything, even when it doesn't make sense, will frequently result in more, otherwise hidden, funny moments ("Run you pigeons, it's Robert Frost!").
I highly recommend Grim Fandango Remastered.  Definitely 10 out of 10, or 9.5 if you like getting every single achievement but hate using the "tank controls".
2017 update:
Double Fine has now released remastered editions of 2 more of Tim Schafer's other classic adventure games:  Day of the Tentacle and Full Throttle!  All 3 (including Grim Fandango) are labors of love, brining back some of the best representations of the genre.  If you like classic adventure games or think you'd like to try some, these are 3 of the best.

IonFX makes a fun little puzzle game that produces a special world that combines Newtons three laws with gravity pushing your puzzle solving to the test. With sweet music and pleasant level design Obulis offers a deceivingly peaceful play through.
After nine fearless hours I have completed Obulis. Obulis is an interesting game, but surely isn’t for everyone. In the category of puzzle games Obulis tests you by using a version of physics without friction to propel, roll, jump, shoot, catapult, and bounce spheres into containers. The levels vary and there are about 152 levels. The level difficulties go from Simple to Master with everything in-between. There is no difficulty setting for the campaign so in a single play-through you will play through a various difficulty settings, which pushes you through a rather smooth difficulty curve. Each section of Obulis has an ULTRA level which unlock after completing challenges throughout the “entire” campaign. These levels push you to the test and completing them unlocks achievements.
One of my favorite aspects of Obulis is that there is no rating for the puzzles. You either solve a puzzle or fail a puzzle, there is no score. I like this concept, but it essentially means there is no replay value to Obulis as there is nothing to do after you complete the game.  The puzzles keep you on your toes, and the slowly getting more difficult challenges keep pushing you to new levels. As you progress through the chapters of the game the not only are the levels changing, but they introduce new concepts: cannons, catapults, ballista, trebuchet, gears, horizontal moving floors, vertical moving floors, and more. These concepts differentiate the puzzles and make each of the levels seem unique rather than repetitive.
I write a lot about this, but if you love puzzles and like precise timing you will probably get past this quiet easily. My major gripe about this game is that the puzzles are really more based on precise timing rather than finding a solution. You may find the solution on your first attempt, but because you have to time each click perfectly you’ll be sitting there for hours. When I was playing Obulis there were actually times where I went online to look at guides to see if I was solving the puzzle correct only to find out I was, but my clicks were not timed exactly perfect. On some puzzles it gets to the point where it stops being a puzzle game and it becomes more like “Sports Arena” the arcade game made by Sammy USA Corporation where there are lights circling the border and to win prizes you must push a button right as the light next to the prize goes on. If you have never heard of this Arcade Machine you may be able to assume that it’s essentially impossible to win because of how difficult it is to time when to push the button. Obulis presents similar annoyances as “Sports Arena”. Essentially you are just sitting there clicking a button at slightly different times to solve a puzzle you figured out the answer too quite some time ago. One of the other annoyances was that Obulis didn’t always give the same result to the same physical interaction. Sometimes the ball would move slightly differently even though the same exact event was occurring. This “glitch” sometimes resulted in me having to restart even when all the clicks were correct. Luckily if you are worrying during gameplay about whether you solved a puzzle correct and are just timing the clicks wrong there is a way to ease the pain. Go on YouTube and all the puzzles have been solved and made into videos, this can allow you to view if you’re making the mistake or not.
The tedious timing issues and the minor glitches in the physics engine didn’t take away from Obulis; Obulis is actually a good play through. It offers about seven hours of puzzle solving (about two of the hours I played was with the game on pause while I was out doing other things). I recommend this game if you can get it in the Indie Puzzle Pack for a discount. I would not recommend paying full price for this game as it is essentially something you’d be able to find free elsewhere.
Pros:
+Over 152 different puzzles
+Fun simple puzzles with nice serene music
+Comes in the Indie Puzzle Pack with a few other games
+Puzzles of varying difficulty, not all puzzles have to be solved to complete the game (some of the hardest puzzles can be skipped)
+Very easy controls, only requires a mouse
+Puzzles vary, add new challenges, and increase in variation as you get further in the game.
Cons:
-All the achievements are for completing the Ultra Puzzles
-The game has some flaws in the physics engine
-Most of the puzzles have obvious solutions but require tedious work to correctly time to collisions

It's like Cut the Rope, but taken in a completely different direction. Whereas Cut the Rope had dozens of different ways to interact with the puzzles, in Obulis all you can do is drop marbles by cutting chains. But you need to cut them in the right order and with a strict sense of timing.
The physics of Obulis have no friction whatsoever. When looking at a level, you need to gain a sense of where momentum can come from and how to transfer that momentum from moving marbles to stationary ones. Sometimes it's easy to screw up the timing of a marble drop and need to repeatedly restart, which can get frustrating, but it's a skill you get better at if you play for long enough. There are also multiple solutions to most puzzles, so if you find yourself retrying a level for the 75th time, it means you're probably going for one of the harder solutions and you're missing an easier one.
If you're a puzzle enthusiast or an achievement hunter searching for a reasonably straightforward game to add to your 100% list, I recommend it. Just be warned that, also unlike Cut the Rope, this game is not afraid to pull out some difficult puzzles. There are a good 20 levels, especially near the end of the game, that will really give your mind a workout and make you earn that completion.

The game is a one-man project; naturally, that means the game has a few imperfections:

- The storyline has potential but is rather poorly executed. There are 'messages' from other inmates but they are well-hidden and don't serve much of a purpose. The ending comes as a bit of a surprise; there's no build-up of any sorts.
Despite all this, I'd still really recommend it. I wouldn't expect much from the storyline, but the puzzles are fun and challenging. And it's not clear at all when to walk jump and when to run jump.  So I hit room/level 20 and when I miss a jump it resets the puzzle completely. Looks to me like I'd have to repeat this level ad nauseam due to missed jumps to complete the level.  Not fun and doesn't forebode well for the rest of the game. This game is a joke.
What makes Magic a great game is taking your luck into your own hands and trying to overcome the random aspects of the game by building a deck that avoids the reliance on luck and replaces it with a well-thought-out strategy.
Having the decks be limited to 90 cards (and I don't mean deck-size, there are literally only 90 cards per deck) and not having the player even decide what kind of mana or what quantity of mana he wants in his deck removes the best aspect of this card game:
Building something and seeing it succeed, not because of luck, but because of wit.
Adding the new mode of Planechase where you are literally dependant on a good dice-roll to win, this version of Magic: The Gathering is nothing more than glorified Poker, and if you want to play Poker there are cheaper and more entertaining options available.
The first game was excuseable, this one is not.
As it stands this is nothing but a mere update to keep the collect-a-thon going.

When I first played this with my friend we really didn't know what to expect. A Lara Croft game from a birds eye view and puzzles? It seemed like it would be weird and at first it was a little but. The story is a bit far fetched, but oh well it has to be in a Lara Croft game I suppose. The story isn't the games strong suit, but where it does excel is in the game-play. There are two main characters, Lara and her new partner Totec, an ancient Mayan warrior who was awoken when Lara accidentally awoke an evil spirit that was imprisoned in a mirror, yeah it's weird. Anyway on to the best part about the game, the mechanics. So starting off the two players are distinct in that Lara uses guns and Totec has a shield and can throw spears. Now the best part about the game is the interactivity that happens between the two characters. All the levels are designed with two players in mind. When Totec throws a spear it sticks into a wall for a brief period of time, and while it's on there Lara is able to use that spear as a platform... pretty cool right? Lara can also stand on Totec's shield when he raises it above his head and the two can preform a double jump. As the game progresses new challenges arise that asks the player to call upon certain co-op moves that they already know or just made available to them. It's an awesome game and it's definitely worth the time.

Damn, what a strange experience this was. The game got my attention because of its graphics and as I have played in the past other hack'n'slash games like DmC and Shadow Warrior I decided to give it a shot.
At first I didn't like it at all. Okei, the graphics and overall style was cool and different yes, but the game mechanics was hard to get used to. It's ported from consoles, so go figure. But after the tutorial missions (more or less Episodes 1 - 3) it got more enjoyable as the controls made more sense.
One thing you should notice though - if you are looking for games with extremely good stories that make sense then KiD may not be for you. Actually I prefer also games that contain good story, twists and character development but for a change KiD was not so bad. So if you're looking for something different, then definitely try.
Also the map was confusing as hell in the beginning because you will find a lot of different stuff and missions there that you just don't expect from a game. Like Gigolo-missions. These are the missions that give "Mature" label to this game. Basically you just date with beautiful girls, see them half-naked, give them presents and then after some dates (if they're satisfied with your presents) you will finish in the bed. Quite random. But still fun.
Now, the main missions are pretty straightforward, just go there and slash the f*****s. The boss fights are also quite similar (with some exceptions) but as the game offers you many difficulty levels to choose from you can spice things up with some hardcore level.
If you're interested in achievements or collecting a lot of stuff in the game, then sadly you will face totally senseless grinding marathon. First you have to complete episodes and challenges on good enough rank (A or AAA), like this you'll unlock gifts and costumes for the girls. Doesn't sound so bad, buut, then you notice the cost of this s**t. So go back and repeat the same missions again and again to earn more money. If you want to play honest of course. If you google, you can find tutorials that help you avoid this grind-fest.
So, what conclusion we make? I personally was pretty satisfied with the final result. It's like some cult game. It's not meant for masses. If you're looking for this kind of specific style or you happen to be tired of more regular games then why not to try.

Obulis is your standard physics puzzle game. You try to get the balls in their containers by hitting off of walls and other balls, rolling on platforms, and swinging off of chains. It's a pretty known concept, but the different environments created for the game definitely make the game a relaxing one. There are about 150 different puzzles to solve, and they range from simple to master difficulty, with 6 difficulties in between.
I read the other reviews written so far, and I gotta say I disagree completely with them; If you repeat a level, and do exactly the same moves every time, you will always yield the same result. By definition, that means there isn't any luck involved. Some levels do take a bit of precise timing, but they tend to have large margins for error, and the levels reset very quickly, so it's not like messing up takes too much time. All you need to solve the puzzles is a bit of patience (only necessary for the hard ones) and a brain (also really only necessary for the hard ones).
It took me about 6 hours to get through all of the levels and unlock all of the achievements. For a puzzle game with a fairly simple premise, I think that's more than good enough. I was fortunate enough to be gifted a copy of this game, but I feel like  it's worth the $5 normal price, given that for me, that's like $0.80/hr of gameplay. And if you don't think it's worth it, pretty much all steam games go on sale 4 times a year, usually for more than half-off.
If you like Casual games, if you like puzzle games, if you care about atmosphere as much as gameplay, then I would recommend this game to you.

I will give it a positive review because it is fun and feels rewarding when you win and level up. Leveling up is very cool, usually (if not all the time) results in a card leveling up. Some cards have branching paths and can become different types of cards. Cards are split into a few groups, some of them are:
- Characters - Can vary in Races ie: Orcs, Nords, Kajhiit
- Items - Boosts stats of a character Attack Power/Defense(Health)
- Actions - Some sort of effect applied to a card(s)
- Guards - A type of character/creature that must be attacked first before you or your other cards.
- Prophecy - Given every 5 health lost, can be played immediatly
Cards are split into two lanes, sometimes with different effects in the lanes like shadow lanes and shifting lanes.
Creatures in the lane can only attack creatures in the same lane unless if theres a summon ability to damage other cards (or boost).
You can build your own decks or modify preset decks (given as awards) so you can set your own playstyle. Decks are limited to 2 types of cards, with the exception of neutral cards and actions. Preset Decks tend to be harder to use (in my experience) so its probably better to build your own.
You win by defeating the other player and lowering their health to zero. One player is decided to go first, the other is given a magicka ring which gives a bonus magicka point for the current turn.
Cool things:
- Card Duplicates are incredibly useful and are even rare especially if you like using that card in that deck.
- Opening packs is lucrative and results in new cards almost everytime (besides having duplicates being very useful)
- Freemium Currency is priced fairly and standardly (Even if Freemium currency is the root of all evil.
My only problems with the game:
- Novice difficulty for practice seems very challenging especially when cards given are random each turn.
- Card packs are difficult to get without putting money into the game.
- Freemium Currency (Gold Coins)
- Online is fairly hard to intergrate into for newer players.

ReThink is a first person puzzle game, similar to Portal, Talos Principle, Qube and Qbeh. If you enjoy this type of game and you’re looking for something new, ReThink is quite enjoyable, so you might want to check it out.
The main puzzle mechanic involves placing blocks in the correct positions to redirect coloured laser beams, to activate switches of the same colour, which then deactivates forcefields blocking your path to the next puzzle chamber. Later, more complex versions of these puzzles will require you to combine two different colour lasers to make a third colour, and use special blocks to split a single beam and send it in multiple directions simultaneously.
Some puzzles involve placing blocks to create platforms, allowing you to cross gaps and reach high ledges, while manipulating coloured barriers that can be either solid or incorporeal. Others require you to stand on a series of floor tiles, but if you touch any of them twice, the sequence is reset and you have to start again.
I finished the game in 5.5 hours, which is a little short, but the purchase price is already very cheap, so its worth it. The difficulty is a good balance of making you think and try different ideas, but never feeling impossible.
I found a bug when rebinding keys, but the developer patched it in less than 24 hours after I reported it on the forum, which was impressive. Otherwise I had no technical problems.

I'm used to FPP games (First Person Puzzle if you need a translation). Completed the Talos Principle, the Portal series and its main mods (Tag, Mel before the story mode patch), Q.U.B.E., Antichamber, the Witness, some others I forgot the name of (Magnetic Cage Closed? something like that)...
So when I saw that game in the store, I was: "oh, seems nice, I should try it". Then I did.
And honestly? I don't regret it.
When I first played the game, I noticed one downside: no rebindable keys. Asked about it in the forum, it got patched in (and fixed) in the following days. So now, I don't see any problem.
(And if you're wondering, that's why the dev is in my friend list now. It was easier to talk about fixing the problem with a direct conversation. I don't know him/her/carrot personnally, at all.)
I completed the game in
(according to Steam), but again, I'm used to those games.
For a 10€ indie puzzle game made by one person, it seems fair to me.
You might argue some game mechanics are in other more popular games, that they are "stolen"... Well, if you think that, it means puzzle games aren't the best thing for you. Have fun playing other things, and good luck finding a game which doesn't take anything from others. ;-)
What you can expect (spoilers about game mechanics, don't read if you want to keep the surprise):
- About 60 puzzles in 40 rooms (you guessed it, some rooms are divided into smaller puzzles, and some puzzles are optional).
- Beautiful graphics.
- No real plot or story. "You have to do puzzles because there's a reason". Not a problem to be honest, this isn't a philosophical game, just puzzles.
- Lasers and prisms for optic color-based puzzles.
- Tiles to walk on, but not too many times.
- Tiles to not walk on.
- Colored cubes to build your path, but they may not exist at all times.
- Just a bit of jumping, but not unfairly hard. Really, it isn't a big part of the game.
Everything else is logic and planning your actions.
If you enjoy puzzle games, I definitely recommend it. Looking forward to the next game. :P

This game is great!  I love the puzzles of all kinds (redirecting light, combining/splitting colors, "the floor is lava", movable blocks).  One of the best things that I love that this game did was teach you through experimentation.  This game doesn't hold your hand and tell you exactly what to do all the time.  It teaches you how to control the game and what the different mechanics are and how they are used through experimentation.  You might find yourself stuck in a room and staring at the puzzle for a few minutes before you're able to figure out what you're supposed to do but that's the mark of a great puzzle game, in my opinion.
Almost exactly when I would get used to a puzzle feature and think to myself, "Man, this could be taken up a notch if they did this..." that feature would be introduced in the next puzzle or two.  The slow progression of difficulty feels perfectly natural.  If you're really into puzzle games like Portal, QUBE, or Dream, this game is right up your alley.  Just keep in mind that it's a thinker so don't go into it expecting to have your hand-held.  But again, that's another bonus for this as well!  :D

Overall I'd say I enjoyed this.  Some of the puzzles feel a bit clunky (Like the block puzzles), and I feel like the character's default speed is just slightly too fast for some of the maneuvering this game needs at points.
Either way it's structured very similarly to puzzle games like Portal, Magrunner, or Q.U.B.E. so if you like those kinds of games you'll probably enjoy this.

Disclaimer: This Review is kinda biased because i'm a friend of the developer (but i still bought the game). I try to keep it as neutral as i can.
ReThink is a neat little puzzle game that will last about 2-6 hours. It does a great job of introducing new gameplay elements and change old ones to create a good difficulty curve and provide variety as well as a nice sense of progression. Some of the puzzles are really hard. But while there is a very good amount of variety in the main puzzles, some of the bonus puzzles are a bit repetitive (you have to solve the exact kind of puzzle three or four times over the course of the game for some "bonus cubes", just with different scales and placement).
The story is just for the mood. It is basically irrelevant. That wasn't a problem for me, as the focus of the game is on the gameplay which i enjoyed, but you should be aware of it and not expect a narrative like in Portal or The Talos Principle.
The visual presentation is really good for a project done by only one developer. Both the actual ingame graphics as well as the UI are clean and readable, supporting the gameplay nicely. There is even a color blind option, which is neat.
Sound and music aren't something special, but they fit. There are some sounds missing (at the elevators for example), but that doesn't take away from the game.
In my opinion, the price tag is justified for this game. It's definitely something you should try - you can always refund the game if you don't like it (as long as you have played it for less than 2 hours and within a 14 days period after buying it).
This is a game I replay every few years or so. And it's always entertaining. I find something new each time. Still holds up. Beautiful.

HOW TO FIX THE FREEZING ISSUE:
I can't get past the APEX fight without the game freezing. Here's the solution.
1) Access the developer console by pressing "Alt" + "~". It's Alt plus the tilde key, which is left of the 1 key.
2) On the right side, click where it says Cheats.
3) Click the cheat called Kill. This will kill all of your enemies, and this somehow unfreezes the game. I don't know why it works, but it does.

Something I can only describe as absolutely amazing.
I've been playing this game quite a bit. At times it was the only thing I played. Free to Play games are somewhat looked down upon but those bad games quickly dissapear from sight once Vindictus comes onto the screen. Vindictus is a Korean MMORPG brought by the people who made Mabinogi, another game with I believe the same lore. Nexon did a terrific job at making this game absolutely fantastic! It's combat is dungeon based, as well as addicting and flashy. The play style depends on the base character you choose. I chose Arisha because I like to balance between ranged and CQC. There are about 9 characters, each with their own particular set of skills and weaponry. Some even have armours in the game exclusively for them (ex. Arisha's Silver Fox armour). As well as combat, it's story is amazing. Something I never thought I'd EVER say about any MMO. The characters are brilliantly made and so much personality is put into them. I literally was shivering when I thought a certain favorite character was going to perish in the next part of the quest. I absolutely loved the characters in this game.
Speaking of characters, the Boss battles are EASILY one of the best parts about this game. Every single boss is different in some ways. They are all very unique. And while there are the occasional recycle of bosses, it is still surprisingly fun to fight them once again in a stronger state. And the enemy art styles are also amazing. Vampires got red eyes and bite your neck? F*CK THAT. Skeleton Vampires with big collar robes with devil horns! Pretty unique form of Vampire, I will say. There are quite a bit of enemy types in this game. And I bet some I havent even seen. I'm still in season 1 of the story and so far it is fantastic!
And now the Free to Play part of the game. Let me say this right now... This is a clear definition of Free to Play game. The very definition of a beautiful one. Vindictus does have microtransactions, of course. Yet if you compare the prices of them to other MMO games, this game's price on those transactions to me are a blessing! In other games where it takes 60 bucks just to get a full cosmetic set. I was able to get a full cosmetic set for 25 bucks! Yet sometimes, I don't even use my cosmetics sometimes due to the fact that this in game armour is beautiful on it's own. So in all honesty, it is completely up to you if you want to spend the extra few bucks on cosmetics if you don't like the look of what you got in game. They even have passes for hair styles and under armour (essentially under garments) so you don't have to pay. Though you may end up spending your skill points that you use for your skills (self-explanatory) for it so be aware of that.
There are other things to talk about for the game such as the in-game Marketplace (In game currency, thank the Goddess) and the crafting system that may need a bit of tweaking. There are also occasional crashes of the game but it hasn't been as bad for me lately. Nonetheless, I think I've made my point.
9/10 Even if you're not a fan of MMOs, I still think it is worth a try. Give it a go!

Revolve was showcased @ Indigo 2017 by Dutch Game Garden. Bought the game the same day to play it with my son. Nominated the game for the Steam 'Defies Description' award.

First impressions:
The game looked really great from the trailer and screenshots, so I figured why the heck not? It was also interesting to me that apparently you don't control the robot directly and it has "triggeractive" controls!
Revolve looks incredibly visually appealing, combined with potentially interesting controls... so let's give it a go!
It's not *too* bad, certainly fun for killing time when you have a few minutes to spare!

Revolve plays like it states on the tin, a minimalist inertia based platformer. You control a space bike traversing ever more challenging levels from left to right (essentially only in that direction) by providing input to it's primary/jump thrusters, brake, and some sort of gravity inverter.
It's designed to be played in self contained stages that realistically take only 2 minutes to clock each. The physics behave intuitively enough to effectively time leaps over deadly red glowing exposed power conduits (that make up the only hazard I've discovered so far), and yet it's compact layout, lack of time limit and gentle vangelis-esque soundtrack keep this simple premise from being either too frustrating or straight boring.
It's not a title to immerse yourself in, and here-in lies my only complaint. The soundtrack stops jarringly after each death returns you to the begining of the stage; and I personally think it'd add something to the gameplay flow if the  low key track just strummed away regardless of your untimely demise and immediate ressurection. That's a pure stylistic observation on my part though.
Pros - relaxing title that tests your hand eye co-ordination in a lushly drawn 2d space world. Perfect for someone looking for down time from more grueling games, Revolve requires minimal time investment to become accomplished at and the bite sized levels mean you can put it down and pick it up whenever.
Cons - lack of enough time in each stage to enjoy the soundtrack, and after an hour or sos playtime im yet to discover any change in aesthetic/stage backdrop.

Where to begin with this game?! Pac Man has always been one of my absolute favorite arcade style game. My friend bought me this game as my first actual game on Steam, and I was ecstatic to play all the different levels in order to earn the achievements.
Pac Man Champion Edition DX+ gives you even more than what you will remember about the classic version of this game. Over the years of playing Pac Man, the graphics on this Championship Edition really impressed me! There are so many bright and vibrant colors, with number different skin styles of boards you can play. There are also 8 different mazes that you can choose from to play on. These mazes include Championship II, Highway (introducing warp zones), Junction (more intersections and double the warp zones), Spiral (use of loop paths), Manhattan, Dungeon (use of tight small paths), Championship I (original map), Half (maze cut in half),  and Free (allowing custom rules).
Something else that is newly introduced to this game is the idea of “sleeping ghosts” that will idle inside of the maze.  When Pac-Man passes one of these idling ghosts, they will awake and begin to chase Pac-Man around the board.  Once Pac-Man eats one of the larger pellets, you will be able to turn around and eat these ghosts. With each ghost your Pac-Man consumes, he will increase the speed in which he travels around the board, sometimes making tight or sudden turns difficult. (This is where the ability to change the difficulty level for newer players comes in handy) Another useful tool to use, especially when Pac-Man is sprinting across the board with little to no control on your part, is the use of bombs. When you are starting to get overwhelmed with the number of ghosts following you, or the speed Pac-Man is traveling, you can just drop a bomb and it sends all of the ghosts that were following you back to their holding pen for a few extra seconds, before they return to your tail. It is important to also keep in mind that the use of these bombs will decrease your traveling speed as well as your score multiplier.
One last feature that I really enjoyed is that the game gives you the ability to compare your leaderboard scores with the scores of your friends that also own the game. You can compare scores, achievements, and play time with anyone in your friends list that also owns the game.

If you've played Returns, you really should play this. It's better in every way.
The combat is more hectic. There are larger battles and some fights throw enemy reinforcements into the mix. You need better skill at leading your runners but you also have you more options, especially in choosing how your core team develops. Every so often, they level up. They gain stats and you can choose one of two new abilities for each character. You can't totally respec your team, but you can tailor them to work the way you need them to work.
The story is more branching. You always do the same major plot missions, but you have plenty of choice in how to complete them. The first act sees you getting as much money as you can for ~reasons~, and you're given a choice of jobs to take or ignore. The last few missions allow you to choose how to finish them, with actual consequences attached to your choices, affecting the ending you get.
The missions are very fun to play as well. My favorite mission has you sneaking into a corporate lab. If you have the right skills, you can sneak through the whole building. Or you can just gun down everyone you see. Or your cover can be blown partway through and you have to fight through the rest of the facility. No matter what happens, it's exciting.
You've also got plenty of opportunities to talk with the residents of your neighboorhood, get to know them and help them with their problems.

I will allow myself to elaborate on some of the things that bothered me with a concrete example of FC:2:s gameplay: Say I want to travel to a safehouse and enjoy the facilities of it.
There is no fast way to travel to safehouses, in fact, contrary to what it's name suggests, the road to your safehouse is often very perilous, which defeats the purpose of getting there in the first place.
Now, there is a way to fast-travel in this game: it takes the form of a bus. The bus can take you to a different region on the map, but almost none of the bus stations are located close to a safehouse, to which you can travel, without hitting an OUTPOST. The outposts are always populated by enemies that shoot you on sight. You can either slowly sneak past the outpost, try to dash through it with a vehicle and hope they won't pursue you in one of their own, or you can, of course, wipe them out. Shooting things is fun, but one would think that killing everyone in an outpost might secure passage through later on. This is not the case though since enemies respawn every time you revisit the outpost.
You make it past anyway and carry on all the way to the safehouse. Here you can sleep and save the game! Yay! Saving the game in a safehouse is completely meaningless, since you can save the game anytime anywhere conditionless of your situation. Sleeping makes time pass by, so you can choose to play at morning, day, evening and night. This seems to be little more than esthetic. I can also choose to store a weapon here. I can take one of the weapons I have on my person and store it in one of the weapon boxes, provided I've bought one of those boxes. Now I have an empty weapon slot, but, should I int he future have wrong weapon for the occasion, I might travel here and pick up whatever weapon I stored here instead! Since I visit the weapon store frequently, buying improved weapons constantly AND since all my previous purchased weapons spawn here infinitly, this safehouse-weapon-storage feels like a self-defeating purpose. Wouldn't it be better to just have a caché or a safe in your safehouse with all the weapons you have acquired so far?
It might be fair to say that this game doesn't go easy on you and it doesn't give you anything (ANYTHING) without effort from the gamer. Maybe it's not particularily bad, just detrimentally cruel.

While the prospect of getting more Elder Scrolls lore while waiting on the next mainline game to come out may seem attractive, Legends is not worth the hassle. It's a Hearthstone clone, more or less. Pleagued by the same RNG and money-grabbing issues thatp lague ALL CCGs. Every element of the game is rigged to extort money from you. If you want a remotely competitive deck, as with all CCGs, be prepared to blow $100 on card packs so you can RNG the cards you need or get the dust you need to craft them. The non-paid content will last you a few hours at most, and then the game will begin demanding money for a few more hours, which will be depleted after you chew through it because they only have a few content packs out now.
All of which are hideously overpriced because the people who DO spend money on CCGs buy the packs 40 at a time. Because as psychological research has shown us, CCGs and other microtransaction schemes are tailored to prey on "whales". People with compulsive personality disorders or poor impulse control who cannot resist the urge to see what comes out of that next pack, or what card comes off the top of their deck next. They're biologically predisposed to take risks, minimize losses, overstate their gains, and keep pulling any lever or pushing any button that makes pleasant noises or flashes pretty lights at them. Game devs know this, so they make their games to milk these "whales" for their money. Legends is no different.
Beyond the hideously exploitative pricing model, the game itself is the usual RNG garbage that all CCGs are. You can be mopping the floor with someone and be up 20hp one turn, then the next they luck into a card combo that wins them the game. Likewise, you can be struggling all game against someone and then RNG hands you the perfect cards to turn the game around while stiffing your opponent. There's very little personal skill or tactical thinking involved. The personal skill element boils down to making a balanced deck and making wise trades in the games.
That's maybe 30% of what determines who wins and who loses.
Another 10% is probably the rock-paper-scissors game design philosophy that plays out like: Decks that spawn lots of small enemies lose to decks that spawn big enemies lose to decks with a lot removal/lethality lose to decks with lots of small enemies.
The other 60% is all luck. Plain, boring, dumb luck.
I can't recommend this or any other CCG. Ever. If you love these games, seek help instead. There are treatments for gambling addiction.
