+ Not a copy of Hearthstone
+ Tries to fix 'bad hand' and 'no comeback' problems by letting you redraw starting cards once and For every five of your starting health you lose, you draw a crad (with a machanic where some cards can be automatically played from this draw)
+ lots of cards that are interesting because of effects other than their stats.
~ Magicka Ring. Let's the player that goes second tap it once a turn to get +1 magicka (your resource to cast stuff). 3 uses. I personally think this is overpowered and should be reduced to 2 charges as it makes me want to go second so I have a field advantage for 3 turns, but that's me and would need more input and testing to make sure.
~ Unique two lane system. Some say it helps agro decks, some say it helps get around defnsive, wear-down decks. If anything it is new and the lanes are actually different. One lane makes creatures unable to be targeted for one turn by enemy creatures, so the situations you get into are intersting.
- A 50 card deck minimum, but only gives you a 3 card starting hand (+1 on draw). Means that the vast majority of the time you won't get the card you need to effectively counter the enemies' opening strategy unless you have alot of that counter. Really makes you fell like half the cards in your deck are useless because you will never get to them even with the draw on lost life. Yet, the arena/draft mode only let's you pick 30 cards, so, I don't even know.
- Cards that help you if you're winning and don't do♥♥♥♥♥♥if you're losing. These cards mostly involve the "if you have more health than your opponent, do some crazy thing." For some factions, their effects are fine, but for others the effect basically keeps you ahaed for a good few turns on it's own as your opponent tries to do something about it while he is already at a defecit.
- A card upgrade system. For some reason, few people talk about this but it is prevalent enough. A small number of core cards can come to you at a base level through the story. More cards to new players is good, but these cards are mostly worse than their upgraded version. The cards can only be upgraded when you reach a prespecified level and don't think it's like every level for the first ten or something, one took until level 75 when I looked at it. You can get the upgraded cards through packs so you can wait for rng or fork some cash. The big problem with these is how some upgraded are straight better than the unupgraded, the upgrade just straight gains a new ability with no increase in cost or any downside. This leaves players with the terrible choice of play a card that is worse than your opponents or have it sit there for however many levels.
- No reward for losing. The game gives you a daily mission each day and you can hold up to three. There is a counter for every three wins you get some gold and a single random card. However, if you lose, you get nothing except progress towards a daily mission. I'm really tired of this♥♥♥♥♥♥ All it does is try to get you to fork over cash so that you can get some better cards or new strategies. This hurts the people trying to learn, the people who lost a very close match, the people who lost from a bad starting hand, etc.
Pretty easy to get the cards and awesome 3 win rewards. Would recommend this over hearthstone if you haven't played either.

I've played this extensively before it came to Steam and on my iPad, and I have to say it's one of the most fun virtual card games out there.
My first thought when hearing about Legends at E3 2016 was "if this wasn't Elder Scrolls would it still be fun?" and the answer to that question is yes. It's a unique take on card games with fun mechanics and many ways to build a deck, the progression and earning of cards though free methods is well paced and doesn't make me feel required to spend money, the various modes are fun and playing with other people is enjoyable, and the story mode is equally enjoyable.
The fact that this is Elder Scrolls just adds to the already solid base by providing long-times fans with a lot of familiarity, and the immense customization of decks allows players with a specific favorite concept in Elder Scrolls games to build their playstyle around that.
For a free game that follows Hearthstone's footsteps, Legends is an amazing time waster and I highly reccomend it to anybody who's a fan of card games and Elder Scrolls, and encourage people with mobile devices to get the app, as all progress is shared accross the different versions.

Single handedly the most Free-To-Play friendly GAME I've played in a very long time, let alone cards games. This game, which uses the rich narrative of the Elder Scrolls world as a strong leverage, rapidly rewards players for their work / playtime and will constantly encourage players to continue playing and try new things. Elder Scrolls: Legends leaves out most elements of randomness (besides opening packs, arena, and a few card effects) to offer a card game experience that is mostly based on player skill. The two lane system is a uniqye gameplay system that offers tons of different strategies and deck archetypes. The story mode is very fun and helpful for new players, I almost wish there was more singleplayer content. However this IS a competitive card game, and for what it is, it's incredible.

Picked up this one in a bundle a while back, and I figured it would be a good time-waster hack n’ slash. Time-waster? Yes. Hack n’ slash? Yes. Good? Not even close. I guess it could be appealing to those who like Japanese arcade-style button-mashers, but it was just not my cup of tea.  My frustrations started right from the opening level. Mind-numbingly dumb narrative (I actually thought it was intentional at first, but hours into the game I realized that it was simply poor scripting & voice acting), terrible linear level design with invisible walls & glitches galore, long and boring cut scenes, atrocious camera locking, and non-customizable controls (all in-game overlays are for a controller! Stop telling me to execute the boss by button-smashing the right toggle… I’m using a keyboard so I have no idea what to push!). I read some other reviews that have stated that the game is literally unplayable due to glitches in certain levels. It seemed to work for me in those particular areas without any major issues. I certainly gave it a good try... I made it to the final boss at the end of Level 7 (out of 12 levels), took a quick break to have dinner, came back and it restarted me back from the beginning of the level! That was the final straw. 4 hrs of gameplay to reach this point, so the main campaign could probably be done in about 8 hrs - 10 hrs (more with the side missions). Give it a go if you want to, but there are so many other (better) options out there for time-wasting hack n’ slash games.

I first played this over at itch.io, and I really enjoyed it. It does a pretty good job of capturing the experience of emptiness and monotany that accompanies the lead-up to a suicide attempt in a way that was incredibly haunting. I also appreciated how it managed to pace the revelation of the player character's obsession with the painting so well, despite the game's incredibly short length.
My one main issue with the game though, is that this is all more or less ruined by the inclusion of the "man in the cage". Exploring themes like suicidal impulses and obsession through the medium of first-person gameplay has a lot of potential, but connecting it to some cartoonish concept of a "psycho killer" trope really dampens the aspects which make this game otherwise shine.
The ending seems to indicate that there is a chance this may be expanded upon one day, with the ability to experience many different suicidal scenarios, and if it does, I just really hope the creator relies more on the pathos of taking on the role of a suicidal person, rather than trying to make these people out to be wickedly deranged caricatures.

An excellent and fun introduction to sub-atomic particle physics (albeit in two dimensions) in a video game format.
Beginning as a lowly down quark in a tiny universe with only the electromagnetic forces in effect, you gradually work your way up through increasingly complex spatial puzzles.  Put this particle here, annihiliate N particles, don't be annihilated yourself.  The four fundamental forces of the universe are gradually flicked on, one at a time, then in combinations, culminating in all four.  Quantum physics seems quite arcane and complicated, but this game provides an excellent introduction to how it all fits together.  There's even a comprehensive "Particlepedia" in the game's escape menu that details the nature of many real-world particles (including how their physics differ in-game for gameplay purposes), in case you're a curious sort who wants to learn more.
The stages of the game are loosely bound together by disjointed quotations about a young scientist's life and the difficulties she has faced, as well as still-shot cinematics of her recent experiences.  There is a story, and though it is small and simple it is well-told.
In spite of the occasional frustration (Wait, it wants me to do WHAT? In THIS mess??) I think this is a very well put-together and interesting game that deserves more attention than it has received.  Both fun and educational, as well as unique in its approach to such an odd subject matter, it comes with my strong recommendation.

I'm a little bit surprised about the negative reviews that complain about the difficulty of the game (lack of hand-holding) and required knowledge of particle physics (false) because you don't see those same criticisms of a game like... dark souls...or ... super meat boy. Punishingly tricky this game can be, but it's elegant and almost educational.

I went into this game after the Director's Cut has been out for a while, so I never struggled with the numerous bugs and inconsistencies present in the original version. I can definitely recommend it as one of the better RPG experiences I've had. Dragonfall gets a lot of things right, including the story, the characters, the atmosphere, and the gameplay, and the things that it gets wrong seem minor in comparison. Most of the complaints I have about Dragonfall are actually resolved in the sequel, Hong Kong, including the undercooked matrix mechanics, poor party management, and a few others.
What I like about Dragonfall is that it's ultimately a story about family, so to speak, of stepping in to the boots of someone else and fulfilling their role as a mediator, leader, caretaker. It doesn't hurt that the companions in Dragonfall are varied and interesting, though only one particularly stood out to me, and the visceral combat mechanics play up the dangers of running in the shadows. If you like the world of Shadowrun, or you like the cyberpunk genre, you'll find your niche here. If you also want to play Shadowrun: Hong Kong, I don't recommend skipping Dragonfall. While Dragonfall isn't directly related to Hong Kong, I think the story is ultimatley better and more rewarding.

Missions are dull and repetitive - same mission for meds or gun runner every single time!  You also have to appear in person to start every story mission which just drags it out.  Your stealth options are a little limited as well.
This game was probably okay in 2008, but really doesn't hold to current standards of a run and gun game.

Killer is Dead is a game fall into infamous term of "bi-polar kind of game". You will either love it or hate it, And I can assure you it is within a really good reason.
Killer is Dead at its core was a standard hack and slash game you all should be familar by now. Mondo, our suave protagonist  got a sword to get his job done which you can easily attack with X button (on Xbox controller) which the game chose quite a strange approach since in Killer is Dead the only proper melee attack was all about mashing X button until your enemies lie dead.
Ofcourse the game also add a couple of mechanic such as a normal distance evasive, A timing dodge (where in result you get to mash even more X button), A "gun" on his left arm (where it use another important assest in game "blood") in overall Kller is dead got every components of any good hack and slash game right. Well, Most of them anyway.
Very first thing you would notice right away is a tank control, Your movement feel SLOW, You can't JUMP, You can't Cancle  mid comboes and worst of the worst which ruined should be good experience in hack and slash game is your enemies Boldness.
In most hack and slash games, Enemies attack can be easily cancel if they got HIT while in a movement of attack, which in result. Player can over power enemy with his/her attack and feel very overpower and satisfied when you unleashed killing blow on group of enemies. But in Killer is Dead, The enemies will not CANCELD their attack even they got hit by YOU, Instead they will press on attacking you and resulting in breaking your precious combo meter right away.
As for the game aesthetic.....Well.... Its a Grasshopper's game, same breed from Suda 51, You can expect every weird S..hit in every scene (which done incredibly beautiful and stylized to the black bone) and this is a part where it really hurt me the most, Since I'm always a sucker for a games that consider itself as art and doesn't give a crap on them AAA modern games model on how to present itself to please everyone. And I can assure you, Killer is Dead gave quite a middle finger to every players very much.
So.....Should I recommended Killer is Dead or not? Yes, Only when it was on a discount and only when you feel boredom of any generic story telling boring games out there and want to try something new and strange and weird. Ok so here I am reviewing this beatiful.. and jiggly.. game. It really is great fun until you run out of story quests and then either can make a new character and learn him/her or start grinding and practicing those reaction times in the raids. Anyways the main reason why im writing this review is specifically the "pay2win" aspect of the game. Previous writers stating this isn't a pay2win have not been lying to you BUT from what I have read they have left out a few key cash shop items. 1 would be an item, cant remember the name atm, that allows you to to rank up your item to make it more powerful. Did pacman need to be revamped? No, not at all!
Was it made to get a quick buck out of the franchise? I'd say yes.
Is it fun? Damn right it is!
Pacman championship edition DX plus (holy crap, what a name! will the sequel be called Super Pacman Championship Edition DX+ 64 HD?) is not like pacman at all. The goal is not just collecting all dots on a screen and avoiding the ghosts, this is instead a fast-paced, and I mean really fast-paced, to the point of adrenalyne rushing. The goal of this game is anything you can imagine. There's a surprising amount of variety in maps, gamemodes, objectives... To keep it simple, run like hell and collect everything. To keep it not-as-simple, kill ghosts, make epic combos, explore a dark map instead of the normal one, compare yourself to friends, share your scores on facebook... wait, no, don't actually do that, no one wants to know if you're a nerd! And all of this while listening to the stellar soundtrack!
The game doesn't fall short on the customization either, with many different graphics to choose from: Ms. Pacman, that lego arcade game, something full of neons... yeah, I can't really explain these well. You can even "port" the sprites from other arcade classics, such as Dig Dug or X-Rally, although I'm not sure how to unlock these, heheh.
So, is this game worth playing? You bet! This is a great little timewaster here!

So we have here 3 things togather:
1. a nice magnetic arcade of colliding discs
2. a laconical introspective melodrama
3. a comprehansive visual encyclopedia of contemporary subatomic theory

Grim Fandango appears to be an amazing game, with an excellent story and hilarious dialogue. I wasn't able to play it when it originally came out, and was naturally thrilled when (after years of unavailability) it was re-released.
However, this remaster is packed with problems, including one frustrating glitch which completely prevented me from solving one of the puzzles - essentially making the game unbeatable. As googling the solution resulted in info at least three different bugs connected to the same puzzle, it seems pretty clear that there are some significant technical issues here. I have to wonder if the positive reviews here are actually based on the version on sale, or on memories of the classic release - by all accounts, that isn't the only puzzle people have run into trouble with, and the lack of autosave almost ensures that major bugs will force a player to start over.
It's also a bit disappointing to hear "re-recorded soundtrack" used as a selling point. I'd much rather hear the original synthesized soundtrack than a later orchestral rendition, especially when the money required for an orchestra would clearly have been better spent on bugfixing and fine-tuning some of the more erratic puzzles. It's hard to tell which textures have been "remastered in high-res" and which haven't - but I can say that the lines on the back of Manny's head look surprisingly pixelated for a remaster.
I'd love to recommend this. Or even be able to play it fully. But there's really no excuse for a game this beloved to be released with so many major issues.

1999-2016: a Grim Fandango Odissey
Today, November 22 2016 I finally finished a game I started playing 17 years ago. No, gentle reader, I haven`t been playing GF for the whole time. This is the story of a game I originally purchased back in `99 when it was launched, while shuffling between NY and London. Those days GF was a feast for the eyes for the underpowered PCs of the time. The sight of the square with the circus made gamers` eyes pop back in the day. In my first attempt at finishing the game I only was able to get as far as year 2 before gremlins made the CD disappear/I got lost in work and trans-continental moves.
Forward thirteen years, gentle reader, and truly yours now well established in Asia, of all places, managed to get hold of a used CD of the game, well intentioned to finish what I started in another phas of my life. Alas, such attempt failed as new PCs could not run the game CD due to a killer bug (the infamous elevator scene). GF went once again back into that little folder of our existence where failed attempts rest. But fear not, gentle reader, as Steam came to the rescue four years later with a remastered version, which brings us to today`s fateful achievement. So, you may ask, how is the game? Well leaving behind the sentimental baggage of finishing something started in my salad days, esconced first in a tiny apartment on the upper west side and then continued in vain somewhere in Fulham Road, London, I must say the game is full of flaws despite the charming story and design. GF`s puzzles are amongst the most illogical and counterintuitive this gamer has ever run into (with a career spanning back as far as the Sinclair ZX81). Hence, play the game for the atmosphere but do keep a walkthrough by your side to avoid tearing out too much hair, fellow adventurer. Meliora!

Honestly, the series thrives on great storytelling, at least semi-interesting characters with some more or less shining examples and some good character development which can't be drowned by the amount of sloppiness that went into the technical execution, even though at times you'll rage at missing four times in a row >80% hit or combat design that's just atrocious, levels where you have to move as if in combat despite no opponents being anywhere near you or even having seen encountered them.
The game also has some bugs in regards to saving and loading, like NPCs moving differently or team members getting lost.
It could have been even more, but the game shines in places so often not even considered in today's gaming that I can give it a pass in that. They're still rather well-rounded and with, in this case, twenty hours of gameplay for a single playthrough (don't forget different ways of going about missions, some missions being rather hidden, different character builds and different endings because decisions, here, have consequences, unlike Mass Effect or wherever Deus Ex boyband edition is heading lately) you're absolutely getting what you're paying for.

This game is fantastic.
The writing is the main draw. There's so much charm and humor hidden away in the little corners of world, and there are a lot of options that are only available if you have certain items, information, or abilities. There is a lot to explore. The combat is actually pretty interesting, too. It's pleasant that the different classes have different combat abilities and actually change how you play the game.

If this game was a car, it would be a Mazda Miata NB. When you show up in your Miata, other people look weird at you because the car looks funny, and they laugh at you for driving it - but when they actually sit in the driver's seat, the laughs stop. Even though it doesn't look special and has a pretty mediocre engine, they look past it - and see pure, unhindered fun.
. There's an incredible number of perks, skills, abilities, items, all allowing you to play any way you want - or even all the ways at the same time. There's a ton of unique locations, each interesting enough to make you want to explore every single inch of the map. There's so many impactful choices and branching storylines that it feels like a Bethesda game at times, and every single one of them feels rewarding and thought out. There's no one-sided choices, and most challenges can be beaten multiple ways. There's so many sidequests it puts Skyrim to shame.
Most importantly, all of this is laced with amazing humor, cheekyness, irony, puns, absurdity and silliness that somehow manages to never feel like it hinders the experience you get. Even the settings menu isn't exempt from the jokes, with an option to turn on colorblind mode (in a black-and-white game) "just in case".
It took me eleven hours to "beat" the game once. I probably haven't seen even a third of what the game has to offer - with so many choices, you can't have your cake and eat it too. I've enjoyed every single second of the eleven hours, though. There hasn't been a single thing I disliked about the game - even though it doesn't shy away from making fun of the player, even though the graphics are not amazing (to put it very lightly), in my eyes it's a straight 10/10 game.
Definitely my GOTY 2017.

Welcome to the world of Nexon, where every aspect of a game is pay2win.
Before I get into the negative points, I wanna say a couple words about the good stuff:
-Extremely dynamic and responsive hack and slash combat system : This is not a tab-targetting/single unit combat system. It's very unique and it's very skill-based. A fraction of a second can be the deciding factor between life and death.
-Awesome physics/graphics/particles/effects/etc. : Visually appealing. That's pretty much all I have to say.
- Great free2play from lvl 1 to 70. Then from 70-90 its another story.
Now the bad part....
-Pay2win. Did I mention pay2win? Yea pay2win by the way: Anything ranging from EXP boosts to AP boosts (This is required to lvl up Skills) to increasing enchantment success.
- Bad servers : Unstable at most times but still manageable
- A lot of unfixed bugs/crashes : It gets frustrating. Most of these are reported but it seems Nexon doesn't fel like fixing them.
It's a great game. Great potential.... but Nexon. I feel invested in my character and the combat system is just too great for me not to play. I just get tempted a bit too much by the p2win aspect.
All in all, it's worth to play for the first 70ish levels, then it becomes a grindfest for rare loot and the p2win aspect comes into play. Play at your own risk. Very addicting if you're the type of guy with some spare change.

After beating this game, I have to say the effort of beating it, totally not worth that ending. The story itself is given in snippets after each level, and after a set you get a short cutscene. At first I thought this was a brilliant way of cluing people in on the story without being heavy-fisted about it, but some of the cutscenes repeat with tiny little details changed, and it gets a little confusing as to whether or not your game is broken at that point.
As for gameplay, you start out only having to deal with positive and negative fields. This is a simple mechanic, and it continues for a few sets before you learn something new about the game. By the end you'll have come across several different mechanics over time, which are interesting in their own right but some of the level layouts or rather...bad. You have to either clear out particles by making them smash into each other, or move a certain type of particle to a location. The problem comes when you start doubling up on forces you have to deal with. When massive particles are flying towards you constantly, and you have to precisely hit them to send them flying off to an exact place without yourself getting pulled in...the cluster of different forces makes it nigh impossible to effectively move, and by the end of the game it feels like random chance.
You shouldn't have to fight against the controls of a game to beat it. In the last few levels it took probably thirty-fourtyfive minutes each. Fine, some games that's normal. But this game puts you in a little arena against set entities to interact with. It probably takes five-ten minutes to figure out the puzzle, and after that it's just a frustrating journey of fighting against the game's forces to try and accomplish the goal you KNOW how to do but can't because of apparent randomness of the particles.
That said, this game isn't randomized. Like, at all. It's just the gravity-like attractions mean that if you're two pixels over from how you were last time, the ENTIRE board can suddenly shift around and end up moving in a completely different way than how it did before. So you have to be picture-perfect to get some of the levels completed, and even then it still feels like you just have to plain get lucky.
The story is fairly simple, but delivered in a delightful way. But the difficulty of some of the later levels in each set is pretty damn stupid, it feels like you're trying to break through a wall with a wooden spoon, while you're on fire. The beginning of the game? Very simple, a child could probably do the first set of levels or two and get a fair grasp at the science behind it. It's actually really relaxing towards the beginning, and mashing particles together in a sandbox is actually really fun. But when you have a specific goal to do, and that goal requires super precise timing in a game where you have to fight just to keep from moving, it's super frustrating.
It's a beautifully crafted game. The visuals are sleek, the science behind it is rock solid, and the transitions are really beautiful. In fact, if it wasn't for the difficulty being absolute trash at some points I would highly recommend this game. As is, the repeating cutscenes and frustrating gameplay are so bad I simply can't recommend it. Unless you just REALLY want a hardcore physics-based particle game, you probably shouldn't get this.

Ahh yes one of those cult classic games, remastered and made more convenient for players of the modern era. For which I am thankful, I'd wanted to play this one for a while but probably would've never gotten around to it if not for the remaster.
I do wish that they had at least fixed up a number of game-breaking bugs; more than once I got caught in an infinite animation loop that forced me to reload a save, and there was one spot where the game crashed a few times while I was trying to work out a puzzle, which was quite irritating. The game still looks pretty old but with the blocky design of the characters working aesthetic I suppose it doesn't really matter much.
Gameplay-wise the puzzles... vary. There's a bit of moon logic here and there and the area map for year 2 is a bit big and daunting and kind of hard to figure out everything you need to do in it, but it vaguely makes sense overall, I supppose. I wouldn't say it's better or worse than the average in terms of gameplay, but it's alright enough.
The real draw here is the characters and the writing, both of which are quite good. The game has a noir-tinged mexican aesthetic and a lot of the characters play to that, making for a pretty diverse and unique cast with a lot of personality. Glottis in particular is especially loveable, and a lot of the villains are the best kind of hateable. And there's a number of other characters thta leave an impact, and a few noteworthy death scenes as well, the story isn't tame by any means. And there's a good sense of humor running through everything too. It's just a pleasant game world that keeps me invested in the game when the puzzles do not.
The game's a decent length, too; over 10 hours on my first playthrough and that was with resorting to a guide a few times when I got really stuck (because at the point where things stop being fun I don't want to ruin the game by allowing it to let me suffer). The third and fourth chapters do feel a bit rushed compared to the rest though, things happen really fast but everything feels like it gets tied up in a satisfying enough way by the end so it's not a huge problem.
There's not really a lot negative to say about this, and the remaster even includes some nice developer commentary (implemented in the most infuriating way though, seriously now...) But yeah, it's a good game, though I wouldn't personally call it a great one, but still.

Killer is Dead is a game fall into infamous term of "bi-polar kind of game". You will either love it or hate it, And I can assure you it is within a really good reason.
Killer is Dead at its core was a standard hack and slash game you all should be familar by now. Mondo, our suave protagonist  got a sword to get his job done which you can easily attack with X button (on Xbox controller) which the game chose quite a strange approach since in Killer is Dead the only proper melee attack was all about mashing X button until your enemies lie dead.
Ofcourse the game also add a couple of mechanic such as a normal distance evasive, A timing dodge (where in result you get to mash even more X button), A "gun" on his left arm (where it use another important assest in game "blood") in overall Kller is dead got every components of any good hack and slash game right. Well, Most of them anyway.
Very first thing you would notice right away is a tank control, Your movement feel SLOW, You can't JUMP, You can't Cancle  mid comboes and worst of the worst which ruined should be good experience in hack and slash game is your enemies Boldness.
In most hack and slash games, Enemies attack can be easily cancel if they got HIT while in a movement of attack, which in result. Player can over power enemy with his/her attack and feel very overpower and satisfied when you unleashed killing blow on group of enemies. But in Killer is Dead, The enemies will not CANCELD their attack even they got hit by YOU, Instead they will press on attacking you and resulting in breaking your precious combo meter right away.
As for the game aesthetic.....Well.... Its a Grasshopper's game, same breed from Suda 51, You can expect every weird S..hit in every scene (which done incredibly beautiful and stylized to the black bone) and this is a part where it really hurt me the most, Since I'm always a sucker for a games that consider itself as art and doesn't give a crap on them AAA modern games model on how to present itself to please everyone. And I can assure you, Killer is Dead gave quite a middle finger to every players very much.
So.....Should I recommended Killer is Dead or not? Yes, Only when it was on a discount and only when you feel boredom of any generic story telling boring games out there and want to try something new and strange and weird. Killer is Dead will very much make you frown, sometime laugh and sometime inspired by its artistic approached.

And it doesnt matter if it is the main story, fascinating side-quests, or the background of your party mates - it is all superb and the world of cyberpunk and running through the shadows just springs to life from the first mission on. Also: quite some nice humour in there, I certainly had a good laugh or two, like in the good old Fallout-titles.
Oh and you have choices, lots of, and you better think twice, even about seemingly trivial ones. Because unlike other contemporary games your choices really matter and can either reward you, ♥♥♥♥ you up, or just surprise you way back later in the game.
Heavily recommended to anyone who wants to run the shadows and is not too lazy to read some real good texts. ;)
Another pro: this game runs fine on weak hardware, like a standard laptop. So help yourself to this nice little cRPG treasure, and enjoy it also on the train, in the hotel or at work (show those Corps!), you wont regret it.

The game is everything I expected from a "turn-based isometric cyberpunk RPG" and more. Though I really hate the music. I'm no fan of 'good music' tags and can usually appreciate whatever any game has in store as part of its gameplay design. But here it's just off-putting and I do mind that because I'm having a blast taking my time to appreciate the level design, scenery, dialogues, lore, etc.
The skill mechanics and menus are quite complex and deep (I'm not through with the first level and), while the gameplay manages to stay casual on the surface. I was sceptical about this being an RPG, but that's exactly what it is and that's exactly who I recommend this to - people looking for a solid RPG with some cyberpunk instead of Middle Age. As an added bonus, the visuals and the music will remind strongly of isometric futuristic anything from the late ninetees - only the gameplay is much much deeper.
The character writing isn't excellent. Take that as you will - a contribution to the casual surface? Or lacking in something you are very strict about? To me the character depth is on par with the old Ninja Turtles. I find it charming as the gameplay focuses enough on the pew-pew and strategy that you don't feel like you're owed a classic novel anyway.

Shadowrun: Dragonfall is, oh shock horror, set in the Shadowrun universe, which is a tabletop RPG setting. It's Cyberpunk meets magic, and it's actually a very compelling setting, if a bit dreary and hopeless. Dragonfall conveys the setting very well and has a very nice story, but gets marred by its gameplay.
Storywise, you're a young shadowrunner (basically a criminal for hire) who recently rejoined with an old friend named Monika. Monika is the leader of a small team of runners, and also apparently the mother figure to an entire quarter of Berlin. (Berlin is run by organized anarchists now. The irony in that needn't be pointed out, I hope.) You're on what they refer to as a "milk run" (basically a contract that proclaims itself to be very simple; it never is) and Monika gets killed by the haunted machinery. And turns out there seems to be a long-dead dragon behind it. (Dragons are the corporate overlords of this future. But, like, they are also literal dragons, with wings and firebreath n♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's a long story.) So now you're trying to figure out what is going on, avenge Monika, befriend the troll girl who hates you and get some really cool cybernetic implants.
So that's the story. It does a good job of conveying the setting, even to a newcomer, and it takes some very interesting turns throughout. It's also not above having a few quirky episodes, as any RPG worth its harddrive space should. The characters are likable and with defined personalities, your hub is atmospheric, and it's all very downtrodden and horrible, so they got the atmosphere of Berlin down correctly. Now the only thing it needs to do is be fun to play!
... Oh.
Well, to be fair, it starts out being fun to play. For the first half of the game, the turnbased combat is engaging, entertaining and pretty reasonably paced. But somewhere around the halfway point, it reaches critical mass and becomes an utter chore. There's three reasons for that.
1. It's sooooo ♥♥♥♥ing slow. When there's more than four enemies on screen, all doing their little actions and taking for-♥♥♥♥ing-ever to get anything done, it's already annoying. And when you then die and have to go through the whole bloody thing again and again, it becomes utterly nervewracking. A little "Skip to your turn" button wouldn't have gone amiss.
2. It's formulaic. Seemingly every mission, no matter what it's about and how interesting it may have been, ends up having a shootout with the police in the end. It's predictable, and really not all too much in the SR spirit. What I would've given for a mission where instead of killing anyone, you have to get in and out without shedding blood and without a singular combat instance. And true, there are some encounters you can talk your way around, like for instance having a friendly chat with a janitor so she wouldn't punch the alarm, and some more minor instances. But inevitably, there's always a shootout with some gangers, or the Lone Stars (future police) or some giant scorpions. Your character's killcount ends up being in the hundreds, even if you try your hardest to avoid bloodshed.
And lastly, especially in the last few stages, they REALLY go overboard with it. Fight your way through an entire office block full of police. Gun down hordes and hordes of drugged up communists and drones. Fight off tanky-as-♥♥♥♥ gargoyle statues, an entire cellar full of fire lizards and massive scorpions, and guess what, even MORE gangers. PACING is a nice word. This is the same problem I had with Planescape Torment's second half - too much samey combat with little to no breathing room inbetween and no way to avoid it. And again, SR isn't the kind of setting where you play a gun-totin' untouchable hero. Avoiding conflict is almost always preferrable. So making it a ♥♥♥♥ing horde shooter really misses the mark. It wouldn't be so bad if there were some more interesting unique boss encounters sprinkled in with everything else, but while there are certainly bosses and they are very good, there's just too much chorey combat inbetween it all. And you can't even overlevel yourself to the point of absurdity, because there's no avenues for grinding.
So I'm torn on this. Story is excellend and definitely makes it a worthwhile product, but the combat just bugs me to no end. I'll get around to playing the other Shadowrun games too based on my enjoyment of this one, but I'm not looking forward to the combat in those either. Mabye I'll just cheat in a bunch of karma, overlevel myself to the point of absurdity and name my character Old Man Henderson.

Obulis is a wonderful physics-based puzzle game that will really put your brain to work. Through 150 levels, colored marbles found on platforms and hanging from chains must be knocked into their respective colored pots while the grey marbles, which are only used as tools to move colored ones, must not.
Chains are highlighted and cut with the mouse and you'll have to make use of order, timing of cuts and shots, and momentum from swinging, rolling and bouncing marbles to make it all work.  There are also cannons, catapults, crossbows and moving platforms you'll have to work with.  Difficulty varies wildly and there can be multiple solutions for a level, with some making you feel like a genius and some feeling like pure dumb luck.
The mobile game Cut the Rope has some similarities if you've ever played it, but Obulis is more serious and challenging.

Legends is the new free-to-play collectible card game in the Fantasy universe of The Elder Scrolls by Zenimax/Bethesda, produced by the experienced strategy card game developer Dire Wolf Digital.
Instead of explaining the rules systematically in their entirety, which you can read about elsewhere, I will point out some differences to the model archetype of the genre, Magic: The Gathering, which I used to play both with real cards and online in the past.
In general, deck building and duels are the major aspects of the game in both cases. Also, both ESL and MTG Online offer the alternatives of casual and tournament battles against real players or a competent AI. However, ESL adds stories that form the framework of series of AI battles, one of which comes with the base game and one („Dark Brotherhood“) can be obtained with real or ingame currency. I did not find the stories incredibly interesting, they give you good bonus cards though. Additionally, you can choose a profile picture from a lore-friendly selection, connected with a certain voice and way to express yourself during a battle. You receive rewards and card upgrades from „levelling up“ by collecting game experience, and your chosen race determines what kinds of creatures you are likely to receive this way - a nice touch for all those RPG fans who flock to ESL coming from Skyrim or The Elder Scrolls Online. So far, ESL offers slightly more than the genre dinosaur.
With regard to deck building, I have to mention that in ESL, there is no free card market like in MTGO, where I spent quite some time and real money to get the rare cards I needed for a competitive deck, and that was full of ugly bots as well. Instead, you can break down cards to receive gems, that can be used to buy cards, a simple and clean process and the reason why it is to be labelled as a collectible card game rather than a trading card game.
The developers of ESL also prevented abuse and spam by replacing the formerly common free ingame chat (as you can use in MTGO) with a selection of eight verbal expressions, like „Hello“ or „Good game“, which are voice acted according to your chosen profile character (see above). Even though this is somehow restrictive, I think it is an intelligent solution to a common problem in all multiplayer games. I found these „verbal emoticons“ to be quite sufficient to have basic and polite human interaction. You can still invite your friends from real life or from Steam if they tell you their Bethesda account name in order to play with them, which of course means you can use other chat channels for a nice conversation while you play ESL in a small window.
The most welcome feature in ESL that makes it impossible for me to enjoy MTGO ever again is the rune mechanic: As you lose health, „runes“ are broken one after the other, which lets you draw additional cards and in some cases („prophecies“) even play them instantly and without spending magicka. This creates a balancing effect to the benefit of a losing player and makes the game dynamic more interesting. It also makes the attacker think twice before dealing minor damage to his opponent that just might give him a tactical option that could turn the game in his favour.
In ESL, the „battlefield“ is limited in space, usually to eight creatures in total. In MTG, there is no such restriction, and more than once, I have been beaten by insane combos giving the opponent opportunity to summon infinite numbers of weak creatures who then overwhelmed my forces, which I did not enjoy. In fact, I quit MTG because of such auto-win combo decks, which made the whole game kind of pointless: Either they got it and won instantly, or they did not and lost, my own efforts did not really matter; not so here.
The magical resource that lets you summon troops and perform other actions is obtained in completely different ways. In MTG, you have to play land cards that give you mana every turn. This necessity means that approximately half your deck consists of land cards, most of which are quite bland and boring. In ESL, magicka is gained every turn without such lands, and your magicka pool is increased automatically. This has two effects: One, deck building is more interesting without such bland basic cards. Two, the battle escalates more dynamically, you cannot get stuck with good cards, but no resource to use them because you had bad luck with the distribution of land cards.
You have almost complete freedom in how to build your deck, however, focussing on a certain race of Tamriel has advantages, as you can gain buffs specific cards can give each other. Each race implicates its own playstyle: Imperials rely on collective buffs and numbers, Redguards mostly benefit from weapon and armor item cards, Argonians increase their magicka pool more quickly... Those playstyles and the free combinations of tactical choices guarantee a good variety of gameplay.
Until now, I have not become bored with regard to the outcome of the duels either. Even after making a lot of efforts to optimize my deck, I win three out of five games in average. Either the different common deck builds are that well balanced, or the player matchmaking process has been improved since the early reviews that complained about this aspect.
The graphics and the voice acting are of the same high quality as TES V. They even reused some of the voice actors (e.g. General Tullius' voice for the card „Scouting Patrol“; the voice for the card „General Tullius“ proper is female, which slightly confused me until I remembered Legate Rikke who might give orders in the general's name – just one example of how true this game is to the Elder Scrolls lore).
As you would expect, graphical and sound effects are designed to make you become addicted to the game. That's OK with me, as I am a gaming addict anyway, and it is done competently.
The stories are told in largely static images, which is not what I would wish for, but I understand that a free-to-play product can only use a limited budget for such a secondary part of the game.
The game is completely free. You can use real money to buy card packs and a storyline expansion, but even that is not necessary. You get random cards from winning duels, which you can exchange for those you need at a rate between 10:1 (common cards) and 4:1 (legendary cards), and the Dark Brotherhood story can be bought with ingame gold – which I achieved within three weeks of casual activity. I have not spent a dime on ESL, and I got a lot of fun out of it.
This game is a very nice addition to this legendary franchise. Building my Imperial deck inspired me to play Skyrim's Civil War questline once again. Apart from that, it can hold its head high among competitors of the same genre. According to my bias in favour of the Elder Scrolls universe, I call it an 8/10.
With "Heroes of Skyrim" out, rumours have spread that ESL would be pay-to-win now, which is complete nonsense:
1. Those cards were distributed for free on expansion release, a 50 cards pack for everyone and then, for a whole week, you could get HoS cards for free via daily quests, 18 per day. You didn't have to pay, you didn't even have to win, just attack opponents 30 times over an unlimited number of duels. Basically, HoS was given away.
2. If you got into the game later, you can still buy HoS packs with ingame gold, and single cards with regular gems, without any money involved. If you want to use dragons and shouts, just - get them and play.
3. HoS is not as overpowered as some sore losers want to make it seem. You can beat those decks with pre-expansion builds if your synergies are optimized. I do not see a p2w situation at this point.
The game continues to be fun for a completely free account such as mine, therefore the update does not change my rating.

Never mind the "hours played" field, I'd played Grim Fandango when it first came out, and the core game is much the same.
I grew up on LucasArts, on their slapstick Monkey Island games and the absurdist Day of the Tentacle. But Grim Fandango caught me completely off-guard.
Grim Fandango is an adventure game, set in the Land of the Dead. The music and visuals are reminiscent of film noir, but also incorporate Mesoamerican styles to the art. This was, as I recall, the first 3D adventure offering from LucasArts. It was wonderful to play through, like playing through Casablanca and The Maltese Falcon in video-game format.
What struck me was how grown-up the story was. It was funny, it could be silly, but it was a serious story. There's death, corruption, sorrow, but also triumph and joy. Many of the characters fall into familiar archetypes, but they are interesting, they have presence. Most importantly, our protagonist, Manny Calavera is such a joy to be around. He has something to say about everything, and the world comes to life as he moves through it, commenting about this thing or that.
"My scythe. I like to keep it next to where my heart used to be."
The music lends to that melancholy tone, with Mexican strings playing in the quieter points of the game, while jazz and big band plays in the nightclubs. It sets the tone, and then shifts it. But it never tries to upstage the actors, never drowns out their voices.
I'm just surprised that the debate about "video-games as art" didn't come up when this game came out.
They've done quite a bit of work on the Remaster, never deny that. All of the models are crisp, and the sound is clear. I'd advise you to play it in 4:3 with borders (that's the default), and turn on developer commentary. It doesn't play over everything, you can have it run with a button press (and stop it by pressing the same button again in case you've heard it before). And play it with the classic controls.
And remember how the story started. The four year journey of the soul across the Land of the Dead will come around, and when it does, it will be a special moment. Watch for it.

The first time I ever played Grim Fandango, I was still new to the very concept of PC gaming. I had a home computer for only a few months prior but looking back now, I can safely say that I became a PC gamer during its Golden Age. The last few years belonging to the ‘90s saw the inception of classic franchises nowadays such as Age of Empires, Grand Theft Auto, Baldur’s Gate, Thief, Half-Life and Starcraft among many others. And I was in all seriousness, an enthusiastic newbie  when it came to adventure games in general. Even my English skills were rusty, to put it mildly. Video games helped a lot. Especially dialogue rich ones featuring satire and complex sentences. Fandango had them both in ample supply. LucasArts concocted a perfect formula which contained social commentary, pop culture references and a noir-like atmosphere within a game that at fist glance, seems little more than just talking skeletons with Art Deco elements in the background. I struggled back then to finish it, especially since even the strategy guides were at their humble beginnings.
From a gameplay point of view, it’s pure point & click, with dialogue trees and an interesting inventory system. It’s worth playing Grim Fandango for its plot twists alone. The remastered graphics are clearly showing their age, but I would play such a video game any day of the week over eye candy ridden but shallow on content, modern 3D shooters. I guess it’s an acquired taste or I’m just getting old. But adventure games in the vein of Grim or the Monkey Island series are an extinct genre in our contemporary gaming environment. Double Fine Productions brought Fandango back to life (and on modern computers) and they are still carrying the torch of creative freedom and ingenuity which was once reflected in a gaming era that was more about the customer experience and less about trying to squeeze every last penny from gamers through irrational marketing choices.

Particulars is a game with a unique combination of arcade-action and puzzle gameplay, set in the mysterious world of subatomic particles.

So let us take Particulars apart and thus delve into the subatomic world of quarks, bosons and the like. As always, I’ll talk about the
first, which are particularly brilliant. Especially noteworthy is the minimalistic interface. Every particle has its own icon and shading, the goal and timing of a level are indicated in the central area with a circular bar and while all of this might need a couple of minutes of getting used to, it looks amazing. I cannot say the same for the art of the cutscenes however, as I feel this drawn comic style is out of place in an environment of minimalistic vector aesthetics.
The overall
is very good as well. There is a crackling indicator when you are getting too close to a particle than would annihilate you and in general every sound effect is unique and very recognisable in terms of its effect. Overall, the creative choices blend very well to create a surreal subatomic world, excluding the cutscenes.
As for the
, I feel I need to fragment this review into two parts, just as I felt game significantly alters in its gameplay after the fifth chapter. The
of the game is mostly about carrying particles from A to B, destroying other particles or plainly surviving for a set period of time. This feels a lot like an action arcade game with barely any puzzling involved. In the majority of the levels, speed is of the essence, which led to a bunch of frustration for me. Controlling fast paced particles into their target area, with other anti-particles flying about the place, which obviously are also attracted to their counterpart and kill it instantly on contact, felt like I had little chance of actually impacting the outcome. Thus many levels, even after completion, seemed as if I relied heavily on random chance instead of personal skill and overall Particulars feels rather unrewarding. This critique almost ended up being a pure ranting on fast paced twitch-heavy gameplay with a sluggish player particle. Luckily most of the game’s levels are skippable, however for some reason excluding the last level of each chapter.
Once you completed chapter five, you’ll delve into what feels like a completely different game with the same skin on top.
, essentially switching the family and spewing out a W with the respective charge of the originating particle. Sounds complicated? Well, I do consider my physics knowledge to be as weak as a biochemist’s knowledge about physics can be, which is essentially non-existent and suffice to say, I have a really hard time understanding what is going on. Particulars tries to remedy the complication a bit by providing a pause menu, which gives you all details about subatomic particle transformation. After working through this encyclopaedia for a couple of times, you can get at least a slight grasp of what is going on. Nonetheless, compared to the action oriented gameplay beforehand, the game now plays essentially like a puzzle game, that requires you to think something through first and afterwards additionally asks you to execute the presumed solution in a rather complicated environment, meaning that even if you understand what you are supposed to be doing, it is not given that you will succeed in the first, second or even third try. Therein lies my main gripe with Particulars. As mentioned previously, I either like playing fast-paced platformers with a very tight control scheme along the lines of Super Meat Boy or Spelunky or very deep, mechanical puzzle games like SpaceChem. Particulars tries to mix the action, twitch-paced gameplay with a bunch of thinking and while the subatomic puzzling is difficult and satisfying when understood, working towards the solution can be frustrating, especially if you know exactly what to do, but fail to execute it properly. In terms of controls, I found the keyboard controls to be okay, however due to the only eight directional digital movement, some levels are harder than they need to be. Therefore I recommend a controller for playing, which however also has the downside that when inspecting particles in the pause menu, using the right analog stick to move around is painfully slow.
My conclusion of Particulars is, that this game is just not for me, even as a scientist. While the physics in Particulars seem solid and you can surely learn more than a thing or two during the gaming experience, I personally do not like the combination of fast-paced, sluggish movements with puzzling as I get frustrated when I figured out the solution but fail to execute it. Similarly to my earlier critique of Luna’s Wandering Stars, games like these are just not for me. If you are amongst the people to enjoy these kinds of games however, you should definitely check Particulars out, as it is a very insightful exploratory experience into the world of subatomic particles.

A truly innovative take on games as a medium for telling stories, particulars is the story of a particle physicist looking inwards.
The main gameplay is an arcade style particle physics simulation - essentially marbles with magnets, explosions and puzzles. You don't need to know any science to play though, because the game teaches you everything experientially as you go.
Between levels, we see glimpses into the life of Allison, our deeply flawed but nonetheless inspiring protagonist. It seems that she's very good at particle physics, and would rather run simulations than deal with the strife and hardship that has beset her personal life.
You follow her emotional journey. Step by step unravelling clues of her life and psyche... all the while you play as her, running the simulation. In this way the game is a metaphor, as you look deeper into the soul of allison she looks deeper into the quantum world. As I said, this is a game about a particle physicist looking inwards.
Allison is an inspiring role model. She teaches us that it's ok to not have all your♥♥♥♥♥♥together, and that scientists are allowed to be human. Together with her friends and colleagues, this game also normalises the idea of successful women in science (Alison's mentor is female, and gives her career advice. That's right an indie arcade game passes the bechdel test) and shows us that you don't need a barbarian saving a princess to tell a compelling story. Like seriously, this game normalises both the idea of a female protagonist, and the idea of a scientist protagonist - these characters are just compellingly HUMAN, and a refreshing change from the testosterone charged male-jock protagonists most games present.
This game is a must have for science geeks, for anyone who cares about portrayal of women in media, and for anyone who wants to see games used as a medium for telling stories. Or for anyone who wants their kids to have positive attitudes towards any of those things.

I had heard Particulars compared favourably to Spacechem, which I regard as hands-down the best puzzle game ever made, so I was interested to see what it had in store. A big difference between the two titles (aside from their fundamental gameplay being completely dissimilar) is that Spacechem requires absolutely no pre-existing knowledge of chemistry, and what little knowledge it does require is clearly explained as the game progresses. Particulars assumes a basic level of familiarity with particle physics, which I do not have, as its efforts to explain the concepts it introduces are half-hearted at best.
The first few levels work on the basis of opposite particles attracting one another and colliding. Anybody can follow along with this. However as the game progresses and you need to absorb, mutate, eject particles into both other particles and yourself to be re-absorbed, broken apart, annihilated, so on and so forth, there is almost no effort taken to explain how this works. Consequently I had absolutely no idea what I was doing. None. I simply pressed buttons and flew my particle around the screen performing these actions until I eventually stumbled upon the winning combination. This was not trial and error so much as pure luck. Trial and error would actually be somewhat acceptable, however as the game operates on a chaotic plane, with particles quickly flying into one another and exploding or mutating, trial and error is not really possible. To succeed on any level beyond luck, you need to know exactly what you're doing so you can perform the task quickly enough.
There is a very original, compelling game to be found here, however until and unless a tutorial which assumes complete scientific ignorance on the player's behalf is implemented, I cannot possibly recommend this to a layperson.

If you played Xenoverse 1, then you'll love this. It has everything you wanted from the first game. Now while lots of people might complain about the game being broken or unfun or bad servers, but thats only if you live for the PvP. While I enjoy the PvP, I enjoy the PvE part of the game a lot more, and that's what really excells with this game. You have so much more to do than in the first one. You have boss raids, and plenty of PQ's again. You even have a little battle simulator mode that you use figures as of the new update. Here are some pros and cons:
Pros:
-Great character customization
-Fun combat and combos
-You can now make QQ Bangs which allow you to wear any clothing you like without worrying about the stats
-Plenty new skills
-Lots of instructors
-Just has a good feel to it
-Story mode is great
-Lots of transformations for each and every playstyle
Cons:
-There are little strike supers compared to ki blast supers
-PvP can be laggy
-Saiyans still don't have a tail option :(
-Still RNG but not as bad as the first game
-Game has less people playing it and online might take a while unless you have friends
All in all I rate this game 9/10. It's a fun game to play some PvE with some friends or just farm PQs for abilities/clothes for the best experience.

I found it annoying that conversation options didn't go away after you used them. Like, you can ask the same NPC the same question multiple times. I know that this isn't uncommon, but it made it hard to know if that character was important to the game world.
Cover. It is an important part of gameplay, but it shouldn't effect more than chance to hit. Like, the enemy is in full cover, but I still have a 99% chance to hit? This game single handedly reignited my love for cyberpunk, got me into Shadowrun as a whole, and is a superb RPG in it's own right. If you're the kind of guy who makes their character with a whole backstory in your mind, you may be somewhat pigeonholed, but not too noticeable. If you want to play a character who avoids fighting as much as you can, that's not impossible here. Don't be a♥♥♥♥♥♥and pirate this game, buy it. These developers need it for their Battletech.
A definite improvement of the gameplay of the original. I love seeing a Shadowrun game set outside of Seattle, too. It's always nice to see how things have panned out elsewhere.

First off, one of the best plots/stories I've experienced in a long time. Secondly, my hat's off to Harebrained Studios for releasing the Director's Cut free of charge, to the people that paid for the Dragonfall DLC that was originally for Shadowrun Returns. The added plot and character development in this edition was fantastic.
Aside from that, I'll start with the cons.
Point and click with average graphics.
No voiceovers.
Sometimes the game would hang for 20-30 seconds (mostly in the matrix), but the times when it happened were few and far between.
No real need to hire any runners other than your main party. You still have to pay your squad whether or not you use them.
That's basically it for the cons. Considering its price, it's priced fairly. Which is something a lot of the big studios don't do anymore.
Now for the pros.
Like I said, an absolutely fantastic story. From start to finish, I kept my eyes glued to the text on the screen the entire time.
Fantasy meets cyberpunk. Humans, elves, trolls, magic, attack drones, matrix hacking, what's not to love about that?
Plenty of additional user content in the steam workshop. You'll get at least another campaign or two out of it.
Free reign over character development via karma (aka ability points).
Classless system. Want to be an ork decker that casts fireballs, has cybernetic legs, and wields a sniper rifle? Lol, go for it!
All in all, it's worth its current price. It's also a steal of a deal when you pick it up on sale.

Surprisingly mediocre, what with all the praise it's gotten.
Takes itself way, way too seriously—it's needlessly angsty and overdramatic, even when the story is all but an average attempt at cyberpunk fantasy. All of the characters have the *exact same* edgy teenage personality, the lack of variety in which makes it useless as a RPG to begin with, and your choices don't matter in the grand scheme of things. Sure, you get to see exactly what you say, but they all lead to the same path. What's the point in giving dialogue choices to begin with if it does ♥♥♥♥-all to change how it's going? I mean, half of my issues with the game in this regard are because whoever wrote the horrible dialogue throughout should stick to wannabe-bestseller YA fiction. Hell, it might even be below that.
Not to mention how it looks exactly like a Facebook flash game... I mean, I get that it's an indie game, but they could make sure it's a little less apparent. Nothing bad looking, but the cheapness of it all is a little immersion-breaking. Even though there's no 'Made in Unity' splash, you can practically feel its limitations while playing. The cover system is horrible, difficulty is outstandingly inconsistent, and the overall gameplay is presented rather poorly.
If this were still the late 80s, it might be a game worth considering, but by today's standards? A subpar story, almost painfully bland characters, and weak gameplay makes the game a 1-2 'no thank you' punch. Wouldn't call it bad, only stress that it's below average in all respects.

There are a few really cool features Far Cry 2 has. There is an open world, freedom of mission choice and with a few tweaks the graphics are ok. Open world games like this one are actually surprisingly few in number if you are a fan of such game and have played through them all. The background into which your character is introduced is promising: dirty war-torn Africa full of mercenaries and white interference.
However the magic quickly wears off. The story structure is virtually non-existent. There is little to no introduction to missions and the characters are as bland as they get. Also many missions are just copy-paste repeats, only moved to a different location. Also the game is very easy even on hardcore difficuly modes because you can sneak around quite effectively at a distance and the sniper rifle has no bullet drop or any windage to worry about. All of this makes the game feel boring and lifeless (wild zebras notwithstanding).
Every now and then I come back to it and play it for a little but then I my interest starts wilting down like an electric appliance that's running out of battery juice. And like in an old cell phone where with time the battery becomes worse and worse at keeping its charge, so does this game get boring quicker and quicker everytime I play it.
Having said that, if you can wait until it is on sale and buy it for something like 2 buks then you get an open world game that is at least fun to explore for a little while.
If you are wondering how it compares to later Far Cry games, although I have not played either the 3rd or 4th installment, I have seen quite a bit of coverage of them and Far Cry 2 seems to have a more relaxed and more serious tone. Of course the content is far worse in this one.

Grim Fandango
Double Fine Productions
Double Fine Productions
3D (with 2D backdrops) adventure
The first time I ever played Grim Fandango, I was still new to the very concept of PC gaming. I had a home computer for only a few months prior but looking back now, I can safely say that I became a PC gamer during its Golden Age. The last few years belonging to the ‘90s saw the inception of classic franchises nowadays such as Age of Empires, Grand Theft Auto, Baldur’s Gate, Thief, Half-Life and Starcraft among many others. And I was in all seriousness, an enthusiastic newbie  when it came to adventure games in general. Even my English skills were rusty, to put it mildly. Video games helped a lot. Especially dialogue rich ones featuring satire and complex sentences. Fandango had them both in ample supply. LucasArts concocted a perfect formula which contained social commentary, pop culture references and a noir-like atmosphere within a game that at fist glance, seems little more than just talking skeletons with Art Deco elements in the background. I struggled back then to finish it, especially since even the strategy guides were at their humble beginnings.
From a gameplay point of view, it’s pure point & click, with dialogue trees and an interesting inventory system. It’s worth playing Grim Fandango for its plot twists alone. The remastered graphics are clearly showing their age, but I would play such a video game any day of the week over eye candy ridden but shallow on content, modern 3D shooters. I guess it’s an acquired taste or I’m just getting old. But adventure games in the vein of Grim or the Monkey Island series are an extinct genre in our contemporary gaming environment. Double Fine Productions brought Fandango back to life (and on modern computers) and they are still carrying the torch of creative freedom and ingenuity which was once reflected in a gaming era that was more about the customer experience and less about trying to squeeze every last penny from gamers through irrational marketing choices.

If I had to describe this game in one word, it would be "weird".

Overall, if you're looking for a game that is both weird and creative, I would recommend getting it when it's on sale. If you're just looking for a good hack-and-slash/spectacle fighter/character action/who even cares/ game, I suggest looking somewhere else.

If you...
...you really should just buy this game.
It may look simple initially, but there's plenty of depth here. The writing is great, the quests are fulfilling, the puzzles are enjoyable without being frustrating, and the plot is well-developed (though, yes, rather weird). The art and animation style is also of higher quality than I expected from the screenshots. The lighting in caves, for example, is particularly cool and adds a bit of clever realism. There are plenty of non-obvious things to interact with and enjoy. I found that I never tire of finding another little clever addition to the game.
One thing: You have to enjoy (or at least feel comfortable with) reading a lot of text. So much of the richness of the game comes down to if the player is paying attention to the dialog and descriptions. If you don't actively read or if you just skim, you can miss important hints for quests and jokes that might be built upon later.
There are a few significant references here and there to jokes you find in KoL (for example, certain numbers are often used) which made me feel connected to this game in a way I may not otherwise have been had I not been such a devout KoL player from 2004-2010. I'd expect that someone unfamiliar with KoL would not notice nor be any worse off, however.
The only complaint I have is that I really really want to be able to change how the keyboard controls are set up. I do not find it possible (or comfortable) to use only the keyboard, which I would much prefer.
Overall, this game is entertaining as hell and I find myself literally laughing aloud. I think it does a great job of capturing and keeping the interest of the player. The price is quite reasonable and it surpassed all my expectations. A+.

This is one of the most mechanically frustrating games of all time.
Everyone wants to kill you all the time unless you are in a safe area.  They will bum rush you in a straight line spraying bullets nonstop.  Some guy just driving his car down the road?  He'll swerve to intercept you immediately.  The pacing in this game is awful.
Getting anywhere is a chore.  There are bus stations you can use to fast travel, but they are only slightly faster than just driving to the location.  Cars can get stuck on rocks and oter terrain.  When you encounter enemies (all the time) they will damage your vehicle and make it slower.  There is a repair mechanic, but it's made useless by your ability to just use the car that somehow remained unscathed when it rammed you.
Gun play is somewhat satisfactory.  Enemies seem to line up to their deaths, but buildings are not safe.  Enemies have X-Ray vision (They managed to keep the worst part of Far Cry in this game) and will shoot you through walls.  There are silenced weapons, but being stealthy is essentially impossible.
Can't forget the malaria.  Oh no, my screen is blurry...Gotta take my pills!  What an interesting mechanic.
The lack of an automatic save function intensifies the frustrating mechanics tenfold.  Learn to love the F5 button because the other option is to go out of your way to a save point.  The bus stations prove to be a little more useful as they will prompt you to save after using them.
The voice acting is pathetic, which is appropriate for the paltry story of people wanting to kill each other almost as much as they want to kill you.  I've made it about half-way through and there's nothing to make me think it will get any better.
Honestly, it feels like the developers set out to make everything extremely tedious and unrewarding.  Far Cry 3 is what this game should have been.
I plan to complete this game so I can hit rock bottom and maybe motivate myself to reevaluate my life choices.

I like this game. I genuinely do. But, sadly, if you have an OS that was develpoed AFTER this game's release (or the day they stopped patching it, which I think are quite close together) then you cannot play this game standalone. This game depends on the system it asks to be ran on, which is XP (no longer supported) and Vista. Unless you run either of those two OS's, (If you do, buy this game, I SERIOUSLY recommend it) this game will not run on any OS higher than Vista. So that includes 7, 8 and soon 10. At least, without the help of third-party fixes and patches. I do not trust third-party files that claim to be able to fix things, unless I have entrusted them for a long time and they work. If you are the sort of person who would spend a long (or short time, depending how good you are with computers) time fixing the game then good for you. But, if you're not that sort of person, then bad news, because you have to fix it, or else it won't run.
Now, on to the actual review:
This game is amazing. If this game came out with today's specifications, I would rate it GOTY 2015. There is no doubt. This had a gritty, harsh survival scenario where everything starts to spiral out of control and you lose everything. Like beginning at the end of the game, unlocking everything then losing it and having to work your way back up the chain to reclaim what you lost. The psychics in this game are STILL better than that of some games companies make today. If you happen to max the graphics on this game out, it looks like it came from 2014. And even then on low quality, it still manages to look fairly recent. With the amount of problems that modern Ubisoft games face today, this one beats them by far. Don't let my 0.5 record fool you, I spent 100+ hours on this game on the 360 version. It was great, and I have completed this game twice over.
Final Review:
Taking into consideration the fact that this game looks like a 2015 game but was made a fair few years ago, and the sad factor that the base game unfortunatly does not run on modern OS's without third-party support, I give Far Cry 2 a rating of...
7/10.
P.S. Ubisoft, take note from your past expericences, and put them into modern games! Also, please for the love of god don't make your games unbearable to play. Thank you.

Harkening back to old-school video game RPGs is a thing lately, most notably with popular titles like
, and this is a really great exploration of the Shadowrun game universe. I only ever bought the rulebook for the game when it first came out (am I dating myself?!?), but I never managed to get enough friends interested to play it. It did help inspire me to create a similar campaign using the HERO System that allowed combining multiple RPG genres.
But back to Shadowrun. The story was excellent. There were plot twists I didn’t see coming. There was also a variety of endings,
. The characters were also well written with detailed histories and gave a much deeper sense of personal interaction than is normal for most games today. By the end I loved my team (well, except one of them – guess who?) and wanted to go on more runs with them. I wish I could take them with me to Hong Kong. :D
My character was a Dwarven Mage. My backup skill set was Decking.
The game is not perfect, however. Several glitches posted to the forums when the devs were still pushing out patches never got fixed. None of them are show-stoppers. Additionally it’s a good idea to save-quit and exit the game every few hours because the memory footprint keeps growing. I have 32GB RAM on my machine and there were times after several long sessions when re-loading from a save point or transitioning to a new location took 4-5 minutes.
My biggest complaint is that other team members can’t pick up loot items except during combat. Outside of combat only the player is allowed to do so, and if you didn’t have room you could only send items to your stash (your storage locker back at your HQ that can only be accessed by team members prior to the start of a mission). This setup meant team members would have space free up in their inventory as they used items but no means to replace them with items found during a mission.
But these issues shouldn’t discourage playing if this kind of game appeals to you. It’s definitely worth the time if you like this genre! :)
