We're in 5th edition territory for the tabletop game. I decided to invest time in playing this game as I like the universe but am left cold by the flagship tabletop game's current direction.
I've played Shadowrun Returns. To me that game was a good start but wasn't particularly memorable in terms of its plot, but the core gameplay was there.
I feel this game was better thought out. The setting of Berlin was great given that fans and the series are often fixated on Seattle as a starting point.
The supporting characters are decent; there's nothing that you're going to be writing home about if you're a seasoned sci-fi/cyberpunk dabbler. There's some nice personal touches with certain missions and how some characters approach them, very much styled like Dragon Age in that regard.
The plot is, as above, nothing that you won't have seen before if you're into this kind of fiction. There's a lot of mildly obvious plot threads taken as cues from other fiction; Neuromancer and parts of Deus Ex come to mind. The fantasy elements are underplayed which is very much for the best; there's one particularly memorable encounter just before the credits which, for fans of the lore, was a nice insert without it beating you over the head with it.
By far, the best part is the game system itself. With some good character customisation, the game does well to provide you with that chance to play as a particular archetype. I played a Rigger and transitioned into decking late game, which made for a fun experience.
My only criticism is that there's pretty much 3 other supporting cast members as part of your team. I didn't use any of the mercs and I've seen some people complain about them. To me, I don't think it is incentivising me into replaying for a while.
Your three cast members have default abilities and equipment, with a two columned advancement system for extra linearity. While I appreciate you don't want to spend years tinkering around with each character's individual stats, it is disappointing to see that you're denied of more extensive options that you have with your player character. I managed to equip them with the occassional items I've picked up but their progression is strictly linear in terms of their abilities.
This I'd imagine could present as an issue; I feel that the mage cast member in particularly strikes me as very situational,  mainly statted with many buffing abilities and not much in the way of legitimate nuking, aside from the conjured spirits he can get and his rather paltry AOEs.
The Street Samurai suffers from a similar issue; she's meant to be a combat medic with melee but I ended up using her as a suicide unit on speed steroids who can incap a NPC each round, purely because she has a ton of extremely disrupting and beneficial melee attacks.
The weapons specialist for one was the only one that felt particularly balanced for me, which I felt, due to the linearity of leveling up your companions, was what the devs were aiming for. The weapons specialist had a nice long range weapon, a close range weapon and a variety of grenades, functionally speaking she was general enough to get more mileage out of her. Compare this to the other two, which I felt synergistically were very dependant on each other.
People who are used to isometric RPGs will find that this won't last them for a particularly long time. Other than that, it's a very good game and worth its price, as well as being much more polished than its predecessor.

Ok, one of the only things I really hate about steam is you can't leave a neutral review. Either you love it or you hate it in the way this stupid review system is set up. Now with that out of the way, let's get to my poinst:
Positive:
This game has great atmosphere, pays great homage to the RPG Shadowrun, really captures that dark distopia vibe. The Soundtrack is quite good, but it does get annoying after awhile.
The characters are interesting, the story is engaging with great writing and lots of choice. Your skills sometimes allow you different diologue options which is a great mechanic
A good mix of XCOM and Balder's gate
Lots of choice with your character build
Negative:
The Story NPC's are TERRIBLE UNITS. They SUCK and I mean SUCK. You really need to use them to support yourself, who can actually deal more than five damage
The RNG screws you over, it is not fair. You'll find yourself missing 80%'s, 90%'s, and even 99% chances to hit, sometimes many times in a row, while enemies consecutively snipe you with shotguns.
The end mission is AWEFUL. It's a monotonous slog where they constantly pit you against hordes of enmeies with excessive amounts of HP, which the RNG will rarely allow you to hit
The last fight is disgustingly easy, and disapointing.
The enemies do't do enough damage to actually cause you to loose because of RNG, however it becomes frustrating when you know that you will win but it takes forever
Conclusion: I like this game, I like the series, It's just the developers seem to think that the combat is the best part, and it's not. The best part of this game is the story and the choice you have to play the main character the way you want to.

Pros:
+Good variety of very different weapons, and they are all fun to use.
+Beautiful graphics
+Great deal of freedom when doing missions and freedom to do things when you want to do them.
+Gun degradding, wound healing, and no pausing to look at a map add to the immersion.
+Always plenty of guys to shoot and generally good AI
Cons:
- GENERALLY good AI. On harder difficulties, they can see through vegetation unusally well, but not consistently. They're also bullet sponges if you don't use explosives, shotguns, and sniper rifles. Sometimes they are smart and try to flank you, other times they bum rush you like it's their first time playing a shooter.
- Voice acting is very odd; it feels rushed. Considering what kind of game this is trying to be though, this isn't a big deal because...
- ... the plot is more of an excuse to be shooting people in Africa than an actual story.
- Driving to objectives is a 'female dog' (thanks for the PG censorship on an M rated game, Valve) and a half with all the patrols and guard posts that respawn if you walk more than 100m away. I opt to go on foot most of the time becuase, aside from discovering more that way anyway, it's safer.
Objective score: 8/10
It's a tremendous amount of fun to feel like a hunter and methodically approach every conflict, but you don't have to always be stealthy. Constatnly changing up your play style is what makes this game so much fun. It's my go-to game if I just want to relax after a hard day. I like to take my time, slowly pick guys off one by one with the dart rifle, then finish off any remaining bad dudes with a shotgun. But again, I switch it up often.
Silly ways to have fun:
+ The flare gun is a one hit kill and magically kills everyone in a car, even though it doesn't set the car on fire nor directly hit anyone inside.
+The AS50 can shoot through more than one person.
+ Sneak up behind an enemy, place an ied, back up, *boom*.
+ I never get tired of sniping guys in boats. They fly out sideways about 5-7 feet in a perfectly straight line.
Subjective score: 10/10 - Would bless the rains down in Africa again... but fire spreads more easily when it's dry.

1. There are tons of new abilities on top of the old ones, the animations for varius were also improved on.
2. The transformation system has been completely re-worked. Instead of a tranformation skill taking up an ultimate slot, it takes up it's own special "awoken" slot which is seperate from your two ultimate slots. You can also transform into multiple stages (SS1, SS2, SS3) using the same ability, as the stage you transform to is directly proportional to the amount of ki you have charged up. Until you upgrade your character to have a certain amount of ki avalible, you won't be able to access SS2 / SS3 respectively.
3. The lobby area has also been completely reworked, instead of being this pretty small circular shaped city like in the first game, it's a huge floating island with an insane amount of detail put into it, and the best part? You can fly anywhere you want! It's completely open for exploration and it's really big and not small and enclosed like the first one.
4. The instructors system has been reworked too. You can take someone on as your instructor like in the first game. In Xenoverse 2 you have a ranking system where after a certain amount of training with your instructor(s) you'll be qualified for a rank advancement test. If you pass the test, your rank increases and more instructors for that rank appear, and more lessons become avalible from the already existing instructors. So for example, if you pass the god level advancement test, you'll be able to do god level classes with your instructor.
5. You can now befriend your instructor. To make things more personal between you and your instructor, you can actually become friends with them. The way this works is simple, once you select someone as your instructor, the more of their classes you complete, the more you get to know them, and the more you bring them with you as a secondary character on parallel quests, the closer you get to them. You can talk to them whenever you want on the lobby, and some instructors are hilarious to befriend (e.g. Broly as he calls you his "slave").
6. Inter-character dialogue has been improved, which means whoever you bring with you on a parallel quest, they will interact with other characters, either on your own team, or on the oppenents team. So for example, if you bring Vegeta along with you and you're fighting against Broly, Vegeta will proceed to mock Broly. Or if you bring Android 18 and Android 16 together on the same team, 18 will start asking 16 how strong he actually is and 16 will reply annoyed as he's a relatively peaceful Android.
7. There's more stuff to do! The main storyline is definitely longer than the first game's storyline, there are even more parallel quests than before, and you get to do side-activities too, where in the lobby there are rifts in time that open around and you can go through them and fight extremly hard versions of enemies. You can also visit several different houses (Capsule Corp, Buu's House, Hurcule's House etc) which you can undertake secondary missions from. Like for example, if you visit Capsule Corp, you can train and spar with Vegeta. If you're a saiyan, at that point he and Goku will teach you how to go super saiyan. There are also small side-quests that you can take from the people around the city, and there are special events or "special classes" which you can take from instructors every now and then which has you do something different.
8.  For modders out there this is the easiest to mod, most mod-rich Xenoverse game yet. Quite easily I managed to find CAC mods that add tons of new transformations, that support both male, and female (finally) models. As transformations now work relative to the amount of ki you have rather than being seperated into different abilities altogether, you can now using mods, transform from SS1-SS2-SS3-SS4-SS5 or SS1-SS2-SS3-SS4-SSG-SSGSS all within the same ability, with changing hair support and easily replacable hair models for each transformation, and with support for female models. That's essentially a dream for Xenoverse 1 modders. There also isn't a need for the old unpack/repack method of modding anymore! The way you mod with Xenoverse 2 now is by patching it to load loose files, which means essentially all you have to do is drop your files in a folder and you're done!
9. There is an anti-cheat system a lot of people are complaining about, but really it's not a big deal, it didn't "kill" mods, it's just people can't bother looking up how to turn it off. All you have to do is go into the "Easy Anti Cheat" folder inside of your Xenoverse 2 install directory and drag the 64-Bit DLL out, or just delete it, whatever works. You won't be able to play online, nor will you get banned for doing this. You'll receive your sweet modding capabilities back though!
10. You can select your character from your Xenoverse 1 save as a hero in Xenoverse 2, which means your own character from the previous Xenoverse will appeae throughout the story and will fight with you and go on missions with you, there's also a giant statue at the center of the lobby in the image of your Xenoverse 1 character. Spoilers:
11. The story takes a lot from the Xenoverse 1 story and feels a little copy-pastey at first, except once you start to look past that, it does have a lot of original content of it's own mixed in, but I guess it depends on the person and your tolerance for seeing similarities.

I have spent over 10 hours on the Xbox Arcade version of this title, as well as the additional time you see here on steam. Pac-Man CE DX+ is fabulous. This isn't the original pac-man at all. This is a much faster paced, more intense score attack. The "just one more round" syndrome applies here, although after 3-4 rounds I have to stop to give my eyes a rest. Things move at such a breakneck speed at the higher difficulties that you won't want to blink. This game tests your reflexes and your ability to change a plan on the fly. The music is okay, but could have benefitted from more variety. Turn up the subwoofer and enjoy the womps.
The biggest flaws in this game are inherent of most console ports. While the game supports a 1080p display, the graphics and assets were designed with only 720p in mind, making most edges blurry and a bit messy. Not a big deal in most cases, but certainly not sharp and pristine like what you'd want to see.
The menus and UI are designed with a console-first approach, requiring you to click on the [ (A) Next ] to move on even if you're only using a keyboard and mouse. ESC doesn't provide any menu movement (typically "back" in most cases), instead you're limited to the backspace key to go backwards within menus. Not gamebreaking by any means but certainly an annoyance. The options menus are extremely limited and don't provide much flexiblity in settings, but with such a straightforward arcade experience I'm not totally sure what all options could be provided.
Graphics - 6/10
Sound - 6/10
Gameplay - 9/10
Controls - 8/10
Replay Value - 5/10
Get this if you can find it on sale for 10 USD or less. It's a no brainer if you like quick, consumable gameplay that could also be fun in a home arcade setting with friends.

Do you love eating dots, dodging ghosts and completing challenges in x time whilst listening to crazy music and looking at flashy visuals? Then this game is for you! However, even though it still has it’s problems I can still recommend this to you and here is why:
Pros:
♦ Awesome Highscores that just work (This is one of the best Highscores I’ve seen as you can easily scroll through the different levels, modes, friends, see where your score and even watch anyone in the scores replay if the mode allows it)
♦ Decent Music (Fits the game and isn’t annoying)
♦ Nice Visuals/Graphics (Courses, Skins etc look really well made)
♦ Awesome amount of replayable content (Even though the game is easy to 100% all Steam Achievements, it still has a nice number of Game Modes and Courses to play through. Also even if you finish all modes on every course, you can still try and beat your own scores, your friends scores or even try to become number one in the world... Which adds a hell of a lot of game play to the game)
♦ Easy to get 100% of Achievements (If you just focus on the achievements you can probably get 100% in 2 hours)
♦ Right Price (Reasonable price, especially when this game goes on sale more often than any other game on Steam, so if it’s too much atm, pick it up on sale)
♦ Keyboard Controls just work (I don’t own a controller)
♦ Very Relaxing (This game is really easy to pick up and put down. Therefore if you need to relax, have a few spare minutes and want to play a game or even are waiting for something this game is really good to pass the time or relax as you can just start and stop whenever)
Cons:
♦ The Course titled “Free” isn’t entirely a free play mode (It does give you 99 lives and bombs, but the mode is still timed, which in my opinion it shouldn’t be).
♦ The Course titled “Free” doesn’t show your highscore anywhere (This is annoying if you want to beat your old Free Course scores).
♦ No Classic Mode (This is annoying as every mode is timed, there is no way to play the courses like the classic style Pac-Man with lives, no bombs and no time. There should be at least one classic Pac-Man mode).
♦ Comparison with friends (Should only list and show friends who own and have played the game, not everyone on my friends list)
♦ Too much DLC (This is a personal preference but having to buy skins and music for a Steam Game ruins the whole PC gaming experience and makes it more of a mobile game for me. DLC should be playable content that adds content to increase gameplay time to the game which is why I think the level DLC is reasonable. However, having to pay for skins/music does not add content to increase gameplay time and shouldn’t be an unlockable and not a purchasable in my opinion)
♦ Has ingame Medals which seems pointless as they should be Achievements (In-game Medals seem redundant and should just be converted to Steam Achievements)
♦ Game doesn’t give you classic Pac-Man Skin by default and tries to make you share things on Facebook to unlock it (Apparently you can just cancel the share screen once it comes up, but still the fact that the Devs try to make you Facebook Share in a Steam Game shouldn’t be a thing)
♦ Ghosts seem the same difficulty in Beginner, Medium and Expert (This is annoying as the only difference in difficulty is the speed. In each difficulty the ghosts should increase in hardness, however it seems as though in each difficulty all the ghosts do is follow you. Even when you are in eat ghost mode, the ghosts still follow you. This shouldn’t be case as in eat mode, the ghosts should indeed run away from you which isn’t the case making it way too easy. Also in harder difficulty modes such as Expert, the ghosts should take the quickest path to try to reach Pac-Man and kill him, not just follow him)
Side-Note:
This is not original Pac-Man and don’t buy it expecting it to be. It’s more an easy do x in x time game to unlock the next do x in x time etc. No way does it let you play Classic Pac-Man which sucks as I think personally they could’ve easily added a Classic Pac-Man Mode.
Overall, even though there are lots of cons with the game, I still recommend if you like Pac-Man in any form to pick up a copy when it’s on sale as you will get decent hours out of it if you are into highscore competitiveness and are a person who strives to be better than their friends and must be number one. Also, even though the game isn’t very challenging, it 100% works and there are no major errors. Likewise, I’d also recommend picking this up if you want another game to easily 100%.

Do you remember when MTV used to play cool new wave and 80's metal bands instead of lame reality tv shows and miss those days?  DId you spend most of your quarters and trade in your cash for tokens because you were obsessed with Pac-Man, Dig Dug, Centipede, and other 80's greats?  If so, you're a child of the 80's and you most likely also had a Rubik's Cube that you may or may not have figured out, and may have been a Pac-Aholic.  If so, Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ is for you.  No, it doesn't look or play exactly like the original classic but it still maintains the same magic as the original, this could be due to the developer of the original supposedly having a role in making the game.  Pac-Man Championship Edition DX, which I'll refer to as PMCE from here on out, has Pac-Man gobling pellets, running from or chasing after Inky and the other ghosts, and trying to score big (no, not with Ms. Pac-Man, this is a game for all ages).
If one gets all of the DLC content for the game there's even more 80's nostalgic fun to be had since they added Dig Dug and Rally X skins to the game so you can play as Dig Dug or a little racing car.  And all the sound effects and background music, its also a lovely flashback to the 80's, a highly entertaining decade (sure, the PMRC tried to poop on the party but Twisted Sister and others pooped on them instead).    In short, PCME is a lovely flashback to the 80's and highly recommended to children of the 80's who loved the original, or younger people who are obsessed with all things 80's.
For you keyboard and mouse junkies, the keyboard and mouse control in the game seem to work fine but I find it far more pleasing to play it using a gamepad.  But well, different strokes for different folks.

Very basic and sort of enjoyable old school arcade game, but given the price I can not recommend it at all, it reminds me a lot of "Snood", which is basically just another game like "Bubble Bobble", but Snood did the whole "blocks have faces" type of thing. In essence if you've played your typical mobile phone game or any "PopCap Games" games before, you get the gist of it.
But as opposed to those games, this is not about placing a similar block in the right place, instead it's a puzzle where you have to match 3 blocks to get rid of them, but you can only do so with the blocks at the front. In essence you have to reverse-engineer how the puzzle was made in the first place, remove the wrong blocks and you no longer have 3 set of the same blocks in the top row for you to match.
It's the kind of game I play a short session of and then never again. Seems well enoug made, but when I came in here to write a quick review and noticed the price tag, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ DO NOT PAY FULL PRICE FOR THIS, jesus it's like 10 times the cost it should be. This is a throwaway puzzle game, it has no right to be priced over critically acclaimed indie games.

Grim Fandango is a classic and that can mean a few things. The puzzles can be very frustrating for modern gamers. They don't often make sense and they require a person to be very observant as well as familiar with the tools the game provides such as viewing items and people, conversating with people, and trying everything out on everyone. You will need a notebook to keep track of all the possibilities and most people will likely take a peek at a walkthrough. That is okay because the story is fun and the world is really fun. The voice acting is top of the line. A lot of games wish they had the design elements of Grim Fandango. The game is a beast but if you are patient and observant it can be very rewarding.

To start with, I highly recommend this game - it is both classic and epic in scale.
Grim Fandango is an excellent adventure game that manages to look better in this remaster.  Full disclosure: I am a big fan of classic adventure games like Space Quest and this was one of those 1998 releases I missed at the time.  When I found this game on Steam, I was thrilled.
Some of the puzzles are pretty difficult on a first playthrough, but many are very straightforward and provide you with more context about the game world.  I also enjoyed the art style and cutscenes throughout the game.  There were a few graphical glitches on Linux, but really I am happy if Linux is supported at all.

Listen, I don’t have long. I've got to stay ahead of this thing. The powers that be just beneath the surface of the makings of reality as we know it have sent me a signal. I burned a bowl to chill out and watch mumblecore Keanu Reeves psycho-noir thriller A Scanner Darkly, you know, like you do to test your cognitive fortitude against a super trippy movie that’s obviously trying to make someone who’s surely on drugs in the room freak the ♥♥♥♥ out, feel the hot red eye of something staring in from the outer dark. Somehow I ended up I sitting down afterward to cut the buzz with a video game, but I was intercepted by a free title called the static speaks my name. I had to tune in.
The thing says that it’s a ten minute game. And you’ll see that my play time is some 2 hours. That is because I experienced, while entrenched in this whackadoo walking simulator fattened up for an epistemological feeding frenzy, what they call on the X-Files “lost time.” First off, my high self kept hitting the Escape key to try to pause the game, which makes you have to start the whole thing over. Moreover, my girlfriend, who herself has seen her friends die at the hands of drug culture in Southern California, was understandably feeling pretty bad about the somber end to a movie featuring Robert Downey Jr. circa 2006 (e.g., A Scanner Darkly, stay with me here), and was all the more enraged that I would freely admit (albeit in a facetious manner) to being okay to continue using marijuana, which is a narcotic that bears, if we're really generous and kind of bad at abstract thought, a passing resemblance to the fictional drug at the center of A Scanner Darkly, which is itself likened to “death growing from the earth.” She stormed to the bedroom and stormed back as I ponderously poked around in the imaginary apartment of a guy living a life that he’s on the verge of departing from that very same minute (this is the part where I review the game, here). She announced that she at some point had flushed all the weed down a toilet, soon thereafter taking the stance that I obviously cared more about the drug than I could ever care for her, given that I didn’t try to stop her from storming away.
I doubted that was the case. I was just high. We made up in no time after our little screaming fit, in which I accused her of trying to script her own life, which is kind of hard and unfair thing to do around someone who’s not exactly, could we say, stomping around in the same cognitive mudpuddles as you.
As I said, we made up. She admitted that she hadn’t drowned the rest of the weed. That was a nice twist. I sat back down and took another large taste from my glasspiece, and went about settling the affairs in this video game I’d supposedly randomly found. Was its interactive experience, which can best be likened to privately performing a Hitchcockian stage play you conceived while you thought you were reduced to your most threadbare cognitive functions in a chemically-induced daydream where you discovered an ancient wisdom that to the outside observer appeared as nothing more than an impressionistic understanding of human psychology playing out in juicy, primary colors, influenced by the past hour’s experience? You bet. A Scanner Darkly? That too. But I think it was also influenced by a piece of performance art I found on Youtube a few hours prior, in which someone wearing a polyester suit designed to make their head the shape of a human’s♥♥♥♥♥flailed around on a stage, whooping and coughing up something that we are supposed to think is metaphorically feces.
I have tricked my brainstem into thinking I’ve seen the edge of a world that often looks very flat in the two-dimensional lives we are able to accept as comfortable, and how we are all only the vicitims of a series of accidents, that we are each the casualty of something, and that the world does not follow the scripts we intend for it. Nor does love, nor discovery, whatever else you can think of. But yet we beat on, don’t we, beating off into the burning horizon. Interactive media can change your way of life, my man.
So, just use your life to make art as best you can. That’s it. You can’t make everyone, and possibly anyone, happy, but you can damn well design a video game that can at least imagine what it would be like to change the first line of Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥from “Call me Ishmael” to “Hey, gang, this is George Bailey in a technicolor dream coat, and I’m here to do a little rewiring of your emotional centers with a game about the end of a life that embarked somewhere it never felt it ever belonged.”

starts asking you for money upon completion of the tutorial.
Not only that, but at that time you are given one pack of cards to open and, once you do, you find yourself in a screen that seems deliberately designed to trick you into buying more packs.
It takes a whole for you to locate a "back" button (which is golden, on a golden backround, and static, on the top left corner), while the only other option on screen seems to be the "Get More Packs" button (which is red on a golden background, presented on the right of the screen - usually the "next" button position - and has a "pulsating" effect to it, which quickly catches the eye).
I would have been willing to give the game another hour, make sure I wasn't underestimating it, but that sort of tricky, sneaky design is a clear sign that the game is not interested in establishing a playerbase and providing an entertaining experience - it is merely trying to use the Elder Scrolls franchise name to capitalize on the success achieved by Hearthstone, Ascension, or even Gwent.

This game becomes pay-to-win after level 50 or 60. There aren't enough people playing to put together a party of 2 let alone a party of 6 to 8 required for many of the raid bosses (which are required to beat in order to progress). This pushes players to go solo* which isn't realistically possible unless you spend real money on Goddess Graces (revive your self when you die) and Merc healing pots. I didn't mind spending money on things like inner armor (under wear), more storage, extra character slots etc. But I refuse to pay to progress.
The developers have come up with some of the laziest boss designs I've seen in a while. Far too many bosses in this game have adds. Remember how cheap Capra Demon felt in Dark Souls - not really challenging once the dogs were gone? This developer decided to take that cheapness to a whole new level with dozens of bosses that have a dozen adds or more, some of them continually respawn through out the boss fights. The developer also decided to toss in a few bosses (like Thor) that can one shot kill any character. Lazy!
The servers are ridiculously slow, and the game is buggy. Wait an hour to get a small team together for a raid just to have the server eject everyone from the party and toss all the characters back in town.
It's a shame because the first 3 or 4 locations in the game are pretty good. They're realistically solo-able, even on harder difficulty settings, if you learn the boss move sets and timing. There are enough new people playing these early levels (that haven't quit yet) that getting a team together for a raid doesn't take an eternity.  Then the game turns to crap around Hoarfrost Depths so most new players just quit, leaving anyone with a desire to continue faced with waiting hours or paying to solo.
*The developer is falsely claiming that this game is single-player on the Steam store page.

The game is difficult, you will lose your expeditions, you will lose your cities.  You will get better, and then sometimes you lose anyway; life is not fair.
If you want to always be able to win, maybe play on super easy, or go play basketball with midgets.  Part of the charm of the game is accepting that sometimes circumstances dictate that you will lose no matter what.  This adds to the satisfaction you get when you finally have a mobile force 20-30 strong, with even the old ladies armed with 1-H crystal swords that would make the average muscle-bound adventurer weep with inadequacy.  The distribution of resources means that playing well means you'll have to adapt to your spawn and circumstances, and take agvantage of the bonuses afforded by your god.
If you like strategy games, slavic mythology, and being able to control many aspects of your party I think you'll like this.  If lots of details and micromanagement irk you, or if you can't handle the tyranny of fate, maybe this is not for you.

Far Cry 2 is the Far cry 3 i always wanted. I know many people dislike this game; "It is too hard", "there are no clear quest markers", "Its not obvious when enemies can see you". But this game has certain realisms which, for a rising storm/RO2 fan, makes it more appealing.
Certain features in this game make it just that bit better than the alternatives out there:
+Your gun jamming when you have used it too many times. (With a nice rust effect to warn you prior)
+Enemies don't just drop money, meaning that sometimes it is better NOT to kill all the lifeforms in a 30 mile radius.
+There is a certain variety in the vehicle selection which i really like (The big white 'Tank' is truly a beast!)
+Guns overheating, knife bouncing off hard targets; small features like this, and more, make the game beleivable.
+You look at REAL maps instead of just  pausing and going to the menue, meaning you can look on the drive!
All these features, at least for me, make this game probably the best in the trilogy, and i have played all excessivly (bar 4), and despite the malaria being a bit of a bummer, it is pleasant to have a character who isn't just super amazingly tough and perfect in every way.
Would definitely reccomend buying, as long as you are more into 'realism' (as obviosly you can still soak up bullets like nobody else can).

Do you remember when MTV used to play cool new wave and 80's metal bands instead of lame reality tv shows and miss those days?  DId you spend most of your quarters and trade in your cash for tokens because you were obsessed with Pac-Man, Dig Dug, Centipede, and other 80's greats?  If so, you're a child of the 80's and you most likely also had a Rubik's Cube that you may or may not have figured out, and may have been a Pac-Aholic.  If so, Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ is for you.  No, it doesn't look or play exactly like the original classic but it still maintains the same magic as the original, this could be due to the developer of the original supposedly having a role in making the game.  Pac-Man Championship Edition DX, which I'll refer to as PMCE from here on out, has Pac-Man gobling pellets, running from or chasing after Inky and the other ghosts, and trying to score big (no, not with Ms. Pac-Man, this is a game for all ages).
If one gets all of the DLC content for the game there's even more 80's nostalgic fun to be had since they added Dig Dug and Rally X skins to the game so you can play as Dig Dug or a little racing car.  And all the sound effects and background music, its also a lovely flashback to the 80's, a highly entertaining decade (sure, the PMRC tried to poop on the party but Twisted Sister and others pooped on them instead).    In short, PCME is a lovely flashback to the 80's and highly recommended to children of the 80's who loved the original, or younger people who are obsessed with all things 80's.
For you keyboard and mouse junkies, the keyboard and mouse control in the game seem to work fine but I find it far more pleasing to play it using a gamepad.  But well, different strokes for different folks.

Y'know what? I didn't think I was going to like this. I got it in the Namco Humble Bundle, and installed it because I felt like I was going to need something simple to play between rage sessions in Dark Souls. I was fully ready for the same stale Pac-Man experience they've been rehashing to 80's kids since the 90's. I was ready for the same stages, with the same music, and the exact same gameplay.
Well I was just wrong. I'm sorry, Namco.
This game is what Pac-Man would be like if Pac-Man did coke. Following lines of dots wakes up nearby sleeping ghosts, causing them to chase you in a massive line, adding the classic "Snake" gameplay of "don't run into your own tail" to the difficulty. As the stage goes on, it gets faster and faster, and it's honestly just out-of-control fun. Picking up a Power Pellet with a train of ghosts behind me for the first time was completely insane. I never thought a Pac-Man game (of all the games I've played) would make me happily exclaim "HAHA, WHAT" out loud.
Also, online leaderboards will keep you playing in order to be the best.  "Just one more time" is something I probably said about 20 times to hit S-Rank on more than a few courses.

PAC-MAN Championship Edition DX+ [XBLA/PSN/Steam/iOS/Android]
Developer: Mine Loader Software
Publisher: Namco Bandai Games
Overview: 9
A twist on the Pac-Man formula, this time with 20% less stupid platformers! Instead of ghosts chasing you, Pac-Man now chases the ghosts to get them to follow him, so he can eat entire lines to rack up massive points. Watch out, as when you hit score boundaries however, roaming ghosts will spawn.
Gameplay: 9.5
It's hectic, it's fast-paced, it's Pac-Man. This game is the epitome of an arcade game. It goes crazy fast and even so fast on the Expert difficulty that it becomes hard to control a bit, but this is the one genre where I will allow that as an exception, because it's supposed to challenge every bit of skill you have (and it's not a fault of the game having bad controls, just being *very* hard). And when you do finally get the hang and nail those corners at 50 speed, it just feels magical. The addition of the slowdown feature I feel like was their greatest fix for any problem that one might have with the speed (other than a difficulty select), but that can actually be abused very much, unless you want to go fast.
Graphics: 8
Holy crap this game is pretty looking. It has that feeling like when you are really little and you go to an arcade for the first time, and you see all those flashing lights and it just leaves you in awe. It is honestly gorgeous looking, but only with the right Visual setting, sadly. Most of the other ones just look plain awful and make you question why you're not playing with the pretty one, although Dig Dug and Rally X are really interesting concepts.
Sound: 8.8
Holy crap this game has good music. The sound effects are not intrusive but are still informative, telling you about score boundaries and when roaming ghosts have spawned. I found myself mini-dancing along to the music while I was playing, which probably means that it is really good.
Creativity: 9
It's a... creative Pac-Man game? Yes indeed! It changes up the formula drastically, in my opinion, for the better. It feels refreshing to play, and the addition of time attack is also a really interesting twist. However, it still ties in aspects of the old series very nicely (like the 4 classic ghosts, who still endlessly chase you) to where it feels like a reinvention, rather than a reboot.
Fun!: 10
This game is an absolute blast to play, and like any arcade game should be, it leaves you wanting more. I have about 15 hours logged on Steam (keep in mind that this is only while online), but each game is about 5 minutes. This game is unsurprisingly endlessly replayable, because it is primarily about score attack, but also the addition of time attack really opens up replayability and adds an entire new way to think about the game. When you do manage to gain control at the top speeds, it has this indescribible feeling to it where you just start to move without thinking flawlessly, and that is what this game lives for.
Level Design: 8
Every level, even though they don't look like they are very different, have extremely different routes, strategies, and feeling to them: Highway II has really sharp and blazing fast rapid turn sections, Championship II involves quick turn-arounds, and Big Eater is honestly just strange. Nevertheless, the level design adds to the replayability ten-fold: instead of being able to grind score and time attacks on one map, you can do it on like 12 now! Hooray!
Final Thoughts:
This game is well worth the buy to anyone, I'd say, unless you're not into fast-paced games. This is the game that got me into speedrunning. I honestly can't say enough good things about this game. Go get it.
Fantastic score attack evolution on the original. Great visuals and fast paced gameplay.

about a decade ago or so, in elementary school, my brother's friend went on a website randomizer and up popped the Kingdom Of Loathing website.
I played off and on for a few years after that, I loved the charming humor and the text adventure game mechanics.
Fastforward to now and theres a fully animated single player RPG? Hell yes.
The game is charming and always has an answer to whatever decision you make. Almost every object has a description when you walk up to it, and there are thousands of things to interact with.
Its somewhat easy at some points, but at other point you'll get one shot by something and you'll just decide to revisit that later.
I'm nearly 20 hours in at the moment and i'm not finished with my first character and partner yet, so its not just some small scale, app store kind of deal here.
Buy it. Its hilarious, strategic at some points, and a great story.

As far as indie RPGs go, it checks all the right boxes if you are interested in a standard RPG romp. The whole thing is fun. Even the menus.
Now some games hide this grind exceptionally well, and others, well, don't. How well the layers of complexity cover this basic element generally define the fun, help with immersion, and keep you coming back for more.
This is really the only fault I find with this title, although you must understand that it is a big one. When I play in anything less than short bursts, it totally gets real spam clicky because I'm just rushing around from point A to B. Yes, all RPGs are like this, but it is a fundamental weakness in the genre.
+Great humor
+Major props for getting around having to hire some big expensive artist; the art here is quirky, charming, and works well and could be done by someone who has a little bit of skill
+Music is really fitting
+Good amount of content
+Everything is fun; even the menus
-The fetch quest is strong in this one
-Could use a 'dark' mode (yes I use Nostalgia option); the bright white on a large television is too much
Worth full price.

A great successor to 2013's Shadowrun Returns with more content, a brand new cast of characters, and much more replayablity as it supports a TON of custom campaigns. This is a game designed with community expansion in mind and it shows, coming with it's own campaign editor.
This is quite a RNG heavy game when it comes to combat. You will miss a 70% shot three times in a row and it will feel rage enducing. You will also mess up grenade throws and cast spells wrong and have your summoned creature turn on you on the third turn after you summoned it even though it only has a 8% escape chance. And you will love it all because in the end the combat is deeply satisfying and the story is rich with this one.
Dialog and interaction options based on skill investment is much richer then in SR and the varity of enviroments, dispite almost all taking place in the urban landscape of Berlin, is much greater. Your compainons also have their own side quests now and get a lot more fleshed out, with unique dialog after each completed run.
All in all, this is a better game then SR. So if you liked SR, buy it. If you like CRPGs with great stories, get it. It's a little heavy on the nonsense jargon sometimes and the Matrix sections are kinda boring (shout out to Blitz's side-quest for having the one interesting Matrix sequence) but hey, it's a cyberpunk world where people summon demons for fun and dragons are trying to rule the world via corperate concilidation. Give it a go. It's a unique setting and a great game.

When compared to combat in games like DmC and Metal Gear Rising, Killer is Dead comes out feeling uninspired and underwhelming. The past few years have supplied us with more competent action games, more fully realized and stylish worlds, and much more interesting forays into marrying video games with mature sexual themes. Killer is Dead contains a handful of good ideas that are sadly marred by a wealth of technical flaws, tonal inconsistencies, and an offensively juvenile attitude toward sexuality.

It's DMC meets Gungrave meets Cowboy Bebop.
A silly, sometimes serious experience, with an interesting tone and a blazing-fast pace.
Gameplay is fun and exciting, though a little repetitive. While the main campaign may feel a little short, there's plenty of side-quests and challenges, as well as the leaderboards, for those who want replayability.
Sadly suffers from classic Bad Port Syndrome. The way this game comes out of the box is absolutely atrocious, and some modifications are required to get the full experience.
Every player should ramp up the FPS to 60 through the configs, and use their driver settings to force max anti-aliasing and texture filtering. Seriously, out of the box this game looks severely dated and very trashy, but with these simple, easy changes, Killer is Dead looks deliciously slick and stylish, with some absolutely stunning set pieces.
The camera can be a ♥♥♥♥♥ at times, and the shading, while pretty, can cause some stages to melt into amorphous brown blobs that are difficult to navigate.
Be warned, the story is EXTREMELY esoteric and very little is explained; you'll have to read between the lines a great deal, and likely go and research the lore online if you want to grasp even half of what is going on. Nevertheless, the plot is dramatic, fun and engaging.
Absolutely worth picking up, though I'd reccomend waiting for a sale. Thoroughly enjoyed the experience and WILL be replaying it at harder difficulties.

While I personally appreciated the game as a whole, the intended audience is a bit confusing (much like the plot to a lesser extent), so I place a conditional recommendation on Killer is Dead. Veteran character action fans will want to think twice, as the movesets and overall difficulty are simpler than a Devil May Cry or Platinum game. This rivals STALKER as my favorite game of all time. As far as immersion goes, FC2 is unsurpassed. The game feels exactly like my real life experience in overthrowing an unstable African nation. It's hard, especially on the higher difficulty levels. YOu have to think about how to approach each mission, which works well because you have a variety of options. While most of the missions can feel repetitive after a while, it's fine because the actual combat is intense. You can never let yourself be distracted or opting for the mindless approach, as each (infuriatingly respawning) checkpoint can kill you, no matter how many similar checkpoints you've cleared. Even the respawning checkpoints work out to a greater point, nothing you do is improving the country, no matter how many nameless enemies you kill. It's not perfect, as I mentioned many of the missions are repetitive, but the gameplay feels as intense and dark as the narrative, and every aspect of the game seems to blend together into a cohesive whole.
Gunplay is absolutely amazing, with each shot deadly for both you and the enemy. Flare guns in particular deserve a special mention, as the fire physics are devastating in this game. Apparently during early stages of testing, the fires would rage out of control, spreading across the entire map and killing every single character. The developers restricted fire to spread to a perfect circle, but to be completely honest I never noticed that as I usually used fire as a temporary distraction to flush enemies out of cover or to cover my escape.
It can be frustrating to escape enemies in vehicles, as they'll chase you to hell and beyond, but now I'm just nitpicking. Nothing in the game breaks the immersion or flow, the map is an item you can pull out and look at while driving, and the entirety of the game reinforces the brutality of the setting and the fact that you're not a golden hero, magically fixing everything for the natives. Even the ending goes for the same, I won't spoil it but suffice to say, The Jackal (FC2's antagonist) is probably my favorite character in video game history.
Graphics are good for the date, depth is good, story is good, just a good game all around.

This is not as good as farcry 3, but it still is better, kind of, eh...
Want to travel to Africa and experience a gritty story with no heroes, tuly immersive gameplay, and beautiful vistas? This game nailed that, perhaps too well. Because the realistic approach in this game made you feel like a hard working ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, not a happy super hero with no regrets as in Farcry 3.
This game is probably one of the most dynamic and realistic game I have ever tried. There is no handholding and It is incredibly immersive, and difficult. Yet, I have not finished it, and I don't know if I have the time and effort to do so. Because this game is serious work. This is a game to come back to and play over time.
What is good?
No UPLAY
It looks fantastic, it really does. And runs well without the most amazing graphics-card. In some ways I think it looks better than farcry 3, because is feels more real. There are really beautiful vistas in this game that makes you stop and just look around for a while, over and over.
It is very immersive. You are "always" in the game. No menus to constantly interrupt you as in farcry 3. The map is held in your hand for example. I really enjoy this interface-idea, way better than farcry 3. You are no super hero that can take on everybody and thousands of bullets. You have to plan ahead and you have to be smart. You are vulnerable and everything can go wrong. You guns suddenly might jam, the fire you (accidentally) started might burn you alive if you are not careful. Perhaps your car suddenly needs repair?
AI is smart and will flank you, hide, and attack you even when wounded and lying down. Foliage is beautiful and will move and react to your running and shooting.
You do have some help (well, time will tell). You have friends who offer you help, and can even revive you if you get shot down. How you interact with these friends are totally up to you, and creates varied gameplay and events. You can work for arms dealers and upgrade your weapons and gears. You can find vehicles with mounted guns and a lot of firepower.
The game has few and short cutscenes that don't constantly interrupt and tell you what to do all the time. It is up to you, and if you have your wits about you, you can do it. It feels less like a game this way. Farcry 3 is a "Disney roller coaster entertainmnet island". Farcry 2 is serious work where you feel and smell the dirt, the burned oil and grass, the dust and the misery of the place.
There is wildlife, but no all over the place. They hide like real animals do. And you don't have to mass slaughter every animal to get a belt, in fact not at all.
Guns behave realistically; whatch that recoil, you can't snipe with a handgun from 200 metres away. And the weapons break. I know many hate all these problems with the guns. But for me it makes the game tense, and you always have to be on your toes, comming up with a quick alternative if something goes wrong. - You cannot always rely on your super weapon.
What is bad?
Well, all these great things, are also the problem. As said before, the game is hard, sometimes too hard, and I found that I enjoyed shorter times with the game, rather than sitting for hours playing it. Every time I came back to the game, I marveled at the greatness of the game, and everytime I finished a session I was a little tired of it. It can be quite repetitive. Traveling around the map takes time and you constantly have to deal with angry people shooting at you, every time you pass a guardzone, even if you took the place out a moment ago - yes the guards respawn. Missions are not very varied either. If you compare to Farcry 3, there is not much to the game in terms of activities. The AI is tough, and sometimes it feels like they never give up. And they see you from far away with fantastic accuracy. It is not easy to sneak.
Conclusion:
If you play this game like farcry 3, you will be disappointed. The game does not constantly feed you content, and happy colors. Far cry 3 is truly fantastic in its own way and improved many flaws that far cry 2 had, but far cry 2 feels so much more dynamic. The game creates content for you by interacting with the world, not by feeding constantly what to do, say and think. It the dynamic moments that are special, where anything can happen, and how you react to it. The world is more realistic and beautiful than farcry 3. In a way it feels more like roleplay, because the protagonist is silent, and the game really shines when you put effort into it, and you get immersed. But that is also the problem, do you have time to get that involved without being entertained all the time by the game?
I wish Farcry 3 (and 4) would be more a mix of far cry 2 and 3. Where you are more free to do what you want, and you are not constantly spoonfed every minute, and less collecting stuff and upgrading this and that. It felt like filler in farcry 3 that stopped you from getting on with the game. Far cry 3 is a better game. But Far cry 2 is unique, special and amazing, and it has created a deeper effect on me than far cry 3.

Vindictus is a game that can be both enjoyable and challenging, but can also be tedious and long. The first couple of levels are a cake walk. You start out with the basic skills and equipment and as you further move along the game, you gain more points for skills, random weapon/equipment drops fit for your current level, and in-game money for future spending. This stage of the game is easy and can be finished, solo with little effort. However, as the levels get harder and the bosses get bigger (polar bears to trolls to wolves to dragons to demons), more effort is needed to continue further. Solo is pretty much gone unless you're a high enough level and have high tier equipment. But at this stage, team work and the in-game market come into play. You will need other people to play with to complete the oncoming barrage of difficult levels and the Market in-game is needed to get more powerful and resilient equipment (in-game money used). So if communication and grinding aren't your thing, Vindictus' mid-late and late game will not be for you. However, with enough hard work and dedication, you can be a hulking image in Vindictus with no real life money spent whatsoever. Vindictus trully is a game for the dedicated and skilled.

Epigenesis presents a promising take on the next few hundred years: no grim future centered entirely on war, no post-apocalyptic earth where Darwinian human instinct has taken over; instead, humanity created the most popular sport in history, some strange hybrid of Basketball, Soccer, and Unreal Tournament. It's also an interesting case for why "e-sports" doesn't necessarily have to conjure up images of multiplayer battle arenas and first-person shooters, but that more traditional (albeit fictional) sports can exist in that space alongside the likes of Dota 2 and Counter-Strike. I really like what Epigenesis represents: it's an innovative take on traditional sports that still provides the adrenaline rush of something like Quake or Unreal Tournament, in a well-produced package that you rarely see in games fresh out of Steam's Early Access.
"In Epigenesis, two teams face off in an attempt to plant a ball inside an enemy's goal more times in ten minutes than the opposition across a platformed ravine. The arenas aesthetically resemble something out of Tron but play like something out of Quake. Each player is given a non-lethal laser with two modes: rail (an instant, focused beam which pushes enemies back a small amount) and shot (a mode which fires a missile-like projectile which travels slowly but produces an explosion that pushes back enemies a lot). The gun is a key part of both offense and defense -- pushing an enemy back and causing them to fall off a ledge or preventing them from landing on one in the first place spells instant death, producing a 5-second respawn timer. In addition, hitting an enemy who's in the air with your melee attack sends them straight downward, and if they fail to land on a platform? Splat.
In order to score a goal, a player has to pick up the ball from the middle of the arena, take it to the enemy goal, and toss it in. It's simple, but when presented with power-ups like "smokescreen" (which creates a cloud of smoke over a large area for a few seconds), along with arena-based hazards (like the desert maps' Twister, which pulls players it catches high up into the air), it gets complex and interesting. Upon scoring, a player is given a seed, which they can plant on one of the unoccupied platforms, which in turn spawns a plant, a kind of "turret" which produces effects ranging from firing projectiles which slow enemies, to creating a shield in which players can hide. In addition, each plant provides the entire team with a buff to either jump height or speed. Each player also has a gauntlet called a "meth-glove," whose use is two-fold: the first, called "methylation," allows a player to power up a plant; the other, called "demethylation," allows them to cause an enemy's plant to wither and eventually become inactive. It's here where the strategy of Epigenesis starts to shine: its rules are deceptively easy to learn, but when other humans are thrown into the mix, their collective strategies coalesce into something truly spectacular." ~~Tamriilin

Update:
I've had a change of heart. Yes, it does seem like the computer cheats. But I've been having fun playing casual matches. I recently sold my entire collection of MTG cards because I just don't use them anymore. So I wanted to get back into a digital card game. Over the past month, I dumped some time (and money) into Hearthstone and I wish it had all gone towards this instead. This game has more content, gives you more ways to earn gold, and both the soul gem payouts and crafting costs are MUCH better than Hearthstone. I like being able to combine two classes, I like having a 50 card deck instead of 30, and I like the fact that I can go over 50 if I want. Bethesda and Blizzard are like polar opposites at this point. Pun intended.

Original Review:
It seems like every company is trying to cash in on the recent digital card game craze, and while this one is a huge improvement over others I've played, it still needs some work. Whoever beta tested this clearly doesn't know much about game design, particularly how to balance the various abilities. I think the game should still be in beta and I can't believe they are already releasing paid expansions. The microtransactions introduce the potential for pay-to-win, as players with more disposable income can just keep buying card packs until they get the best cards in the game.

My main gripes with the overall design are as follows:
1) They seriously need to reevaluate the magicka costs of these cards. The cost seems to be more dependent on rarity than on strength. Two cards with the same stats can have different costs, while two cards with different stats can have the same cost. A 2/1, 3/1, 2/2, 3/2, and 2/3 could all have similar costs, and abilities like lethal, guard, and drain don't seem to affect the cost very much. A 0/2 guard and a 1/2 guard  both cost 0. A 1/1 with charge costs 0, while a 1/1 without charge costs 1. A 1/1 with no abilities, a 1/1 with lethal, and a 1/1 that summons a 1/1 upon death all cost 1.
2) Going second gives an unfair advantage as the special ring that gives 1 extra magicka per turn can be used 3 times.
3) I think the CPU cheats. Not only do CPU opponents tend to have better cards in their decks, including rare cards that players typically won't get in card packs, but they seem to also get the exact cards they need. You can't have more than 3 of a particular card in your deck, yet with a 50 card deck and only 1 new card per turn, the CPU still gets all 3 within 4-5 turns. It is not unusual for the CPU to have 2-3 creatures on turn 1 and for you to be half dead by turn 3. You think you're safe because you have creatures with guard in both lanes and you still have 20 health and your opponent only has 7 magicka. Think again! It is not unusual to lose your entire army and the match with no warning. The opponent has 6 health left. You have a 1/1 and a 5/2. You attack with the 1/1. It destroys a rune. They get a prophecy card that kills the 5/2. You end up losing the game.
It feels like the game either lets you win or makes you lose. Yes, all card games have an element of luck, but this is ridiculous. Luck and randomness are the bane of fair game design. Video games are supposed to be skill based, and while the dual lane setup and various lane effects add a layer of strategy that is non existent in MTG or Hearthstone, there is only so much you can do with the hand you are dealt. The deck is stacked against you.
This game feels like hearthstone with more lane interactions and more versatility because of the deck sizes.

+ Good rewards, you can build a sizeble core collection easily by playing Arena or simply playing ladder where the rewards are 50-500% better compared to Hearthstone (15-50g per 3 wins AND 1 common-to-legendary card)

Cons:

Thea: The Awakening is a game in which you control a village with its inhabitants. You guide them in their struggle to survive in a hostile environment. Will be an immediate 'click' for anyone who's spent time in Kingdom of Loathing. The same
stick figures, the same sense of humour, the same mix of fun and a sense of casual accomplishment. All of that, taken to the next level with a decent inventory system, slightly more fleshed out combat (yet still quite simple), and the ability to walk around side scrolling maps.
Perhaps the only very, very slightly negative difference is that it doesn't have the same sense of reward that KoL did. Because KoL had a limited resource in the number of turns available in a day, when you got lucky with a good drop you genuinely
lucky. Whereas in West of Loathing you simply don't have the same limits. You're able to keep wandering about, having random encounters and gaining more and more loot and gaining more XP, as long as you want. And since your health bar resets at the end of every encounter, there's really no cost or risk at play.
But likely that's missing the point - just as in KoL, the enjoyment is ultimately
in gaining wealth or loot, it's in the enjoyment of the small details. From unlocking the ability for your character to 'silly walk' everywhere (has yet to get old for me), to the enourmous amount of puns and absurd mixtures of gaming tropes, the real meat of the game is in the casual, laid back atmoshpere and the ability to turn nearly everything into something that will make you smile.

The game has a paper-thin overarching plot that is pretty much second to the main activity of the game: completing side quests. When you play this game, you will essentially be on a never ending chain of side quests. You get one side quests that requires you to go to a new place, and the person there sends you on another side quest that you have to do in order to complete the original side quest. Don't get me wrong, it's a fun game, and it's a funny game. For the first few hours. It just lacks any staying power.

They boosted some weapons, like the Sniper Rifle, which now is a complete monster at long range.

The last great adventure game of all time, and one of the best examples of its genre. Grim is a wonderful mix of classic adventure game tropes, with personality and style lifted from the Mexican holiday, Dia de Muertos. The art it top-notch and memorable, and I still listen to the soundtrack almost 20 years later. Manny and Glottis will always remain in my mind as great friends.

Grim Fandango is one of those old games, that even when it wasn't available anymore there were still many people asking for it. Sadly people were forced to play the modded pirated version thanks to that. Last year Double Fine finally brought the game back to life with Grim Fandango Remastered so that all fans can finally get it and that new people can play it. I myself never played the original, so this was the first time I ever played Grim Fandango.
Grim Fandango itself is an adventure game which can be played through with tank controls and point and click. I would myself recommend to play with a mix of those two, because they both have their advantages and disadvantages. Before playing the game I would recommend changing and looking at the controls, because that makes it possible to run in the game and manually switch objects.
The story takes place on the land of the dead, where recently departed souls aim to make their way to the Land of Eternal Rest. (Which is based on Mexican folklore) You play as Manny, who is a travel agent, that follows his client, Meche. This happens in multiple years’ time, during which he encounters many different problems, relationships and characters. The game is at no part scary, even though you would expect that with a subject like that. Instead everything is really in a cartoon noir style told. What is also nice about the story is that it is pretty well executed with the gameplay.
Because of the story being connected with the gameplay the gameplay makes more logic which makes it easier to figure things out. However, there were still moments, especially in year 2, where I was walking around not knowing anymore what to do. Mostly that has to do with the fact that year 2 has a pretty big open world unlike the other parts which are smaller. This makes the other years easier and shorter, because it is easier to figure out what to do. In the game the items you collect don't keep stacking up, because they disappear after leaving the area. This can be considered a good thing since it would be easy to get confused otherwise.
The soundtrack in the game is really catchy and atmospheric and really suits the film noir style in the game. In the Remaster they also re-recorded the soundtrack with a real orchestra to make it sound even better. The sound design is overall really well executed. Both the voice acting and the sound effects suit the characters and the tone of the game.
Let's talk more about the Remaster itself. In addition to letting the original game work with modern computer systems, They also added new things. The first thing they added is a graphics upgrade. Better textures and lighting of the characters and the interactive objects. The backgrounds still look the same but they aren't that compressed as the original game though. The backgrounds still look good for a late 90s pre-rendered static background. The only problem with the Remastered graphics I have is that they sometimes are actually worse, because they more obviously show mistakes were hidden away with tricks (for example a rope that isn't fully connected in the Remaster). Here is an example of the differences between the Remastered and the original versions, thanks to the in-game option that lets you switch between them:
As you can see the original is more pixelly.
The game also includes an option to have in-game commentary from the developers of the game. If you are interested in that stuff I would recommend you to watch:
Grim Fandango might not be a perfect Remaster, because I still experienced some buggy animations. Still it's good enough to be played. The take on the day of the dead as game is really well executed. With the story, characters an gameplay being very well mixed together. This results in making that it still is holding up after all those years.

This game has a LOT of (usually) increasingly difficult puzzles, as new block types are added. If you're a completionist, this will give you a lot of time.  There are, however, some problems, too.
It appears that no one is ever online for multiplayer - so if you want to go head-to-head, bring a friend.
It calls it a "story" and also award "xp" for completing levels. This is dumb, and shoe-horned on.  It's a giant collection of puzzles, and that's it. Instead of XP, just count the # of puzzles solved and the # solved on the first try. Can you imagine if someone tried to tack a story onto a book of Sudoku puzzles? No, right? It's a preposterous idea.
The puzzles are fun, and it's nice to sit down and knock out a few until one challenges and requires that fun level of frustration to solve. To call it an action-puzzle game - eh. Original? Eh. Completely reinventing - WHAT? No.
IMO, it's thinly skinned with other aspects to justify the price. It is pretty fun - but not revolutionary.

In this age of amazingly looking indie games everywhere, often made by one-man bands, Tumblestone makes an impression for the lack of flair in its presentation; the writing, sound design and graphics all seem bland, sub-par, uninspired.
All of this rapidly fades in the background, though: you'll hammer your way through dialog bubbles, and just focus on solving the damn puzzles, without paying too much attention to anything else.
From a distance, it quacks and walks like a Match-3; in actual play, it reminds me more of Mahjongg Solitaires: to solve each puzzle, the player is expected to figure out the correct sequence of moves in advance (mostly), so that there are always 3 tiles (tumblestones) of the same type that can be removed, until the board is left empty. Unlike Mahjongg Solitaires though, where a number of tiles are partially or totally hidden, in Tumblestone the player can see the board in its entirety.
In most Match-3 games I've played, there was a certain level of randomness in each level, conversely allowing for a degree of imperfection, or fuzziness, in clearing it. Each level in Tumblestone is instead a puzzle through and through, that must be solved in its entirety, in order to advance.
This also introduces my only true complaint so far; it's not an irrelevant one, though: whenever stuck, it was because a critical point comes up, where the two alternatives are either mind-calculating the winning sequence entirely in advance, or brute forcing the puzzle by trial and error.
With so many tiles on screen, mind-calculating may be quite challenging, and trial and error just isn't fun. Actually, some will consider its being an option a deal-breaker, however I would consider it unavoidable in this design.
This annoyance is also compounded by the fact that, sometimes, the critical point will also turn out to be unsolvable, because it is caused by a previous move that, however, I suspect most players won't be able to readily detect as decisive, if not in hindsight, after running into walls, trying to solve the critical point itself, and having to reassess the entire sequence of moves, which led them there in the first place.
Ultimately whether this is a good or bad thing depends on what kind of puzzle games you like. So the final recommendation could go the two different ways: am I only liking the game for the fleeting sense of accomplishment sparked by nailing down a bunch of solutions first try?
To be fair though, I've only scratched the surface there, so for the time being I'm going with a tentative positive.

I've only really got the Gwent beta to compare this to having never got into the Magic games, but it's kept my attention since I tried it out.
From the online matches I've played it seems like you can build some decent competitive decks without paying money.
EDIT: I'm now 130 hours into the game, thought I'd write a quick update. Thanks to doing the dailies in the game, streaming a bit of twitch and buying one $9 card pack, I've managed to unlock the Brotherhood campaign (& obviously 100% of the cards associated with it), 73% of the core cards & 80% of the Skyrim cards. Which all includes unique 49 legendary cards.

Despite not besting Hearthstone in terms of playerbase, The Elder Scrolls Legends has most certainly outdone Blizzard's RNG-fest in terms of gameplay.  Set in the rich universe of TES series, Legends is an excellently balanced card game that offers a rewarding experience, regardless of whether you win or lose.  Not once have I felt like I lost because the game's RNG cheated me out of a win (except against the A.I., which does tend to be gamey, but at least it offers a challenge).
There's a variety of modes in the game, including a Story Mode which mainly serves to introduce you to the game mechanices and offers rewards such as starter packs and beggining resources, a practice mode where you can grind for Soul Gems (this game's version of Hearthstone's Dust) or try out your new decks, a solo arena and vs. arena, for single player or multiplayer, and finally play mode, which is the standard multiplayer experience of the game, with ranked and unranked options available.
Throughout each mode, you can acquire resources to earn card packs or individual cards in a manner similiar to Hearthstone, which is by purchasing a pack for 100 gold, or summoning cards with Soul Gems individually.  F2P players should feel fully capable of gathering the base cards without any need of spending money, though the game is of high enough quality to where it deserves a few card packs to be paid for here and there.  You can also unlock the first expansion for the game, that being the Dark Brotherhood, with gold, though each chapter is priced at 1,000 gold.  A bit excessive, but the expansion is only $20.  Even so, you don't need the cards that the expansion comes with to be competitive.  I was able to reach Rank 9 in ranked play with base cards, which is where you earn the rewards for the month.  You also can't de-rank back to square one in this game, which is incredibly fair and much appreciated by myself.  Instead, what happens is that you'll need to win two extra games to go back to climbing up the ladder that you are currently on.  Much better than getting squashed all the way to the bottom rung like in HS, if you ask me.
The cards in the game fall under six different categories;  Strength, Intelligence, Agility, Endurance, Willpower, and Basic.  You are able to combine two of the categories when making a deck, or focus solely on one category, with the Basic cards being available no matter which of the other 5 you choose.  This system is excellent, as it allows for a plethora of strategies, synergies, and combo plays that do a tremendous job of keeping any over-bearing meta in the game at bay.  I could have probably looked up some guides to show me how to make a stronger deck for any of these combinations, but I've thouroughly enjoyed experimenting with the cards at my disposal myself, and while I've taken plenty of losses, I've also earned plenty of wins.
Finally, the game's board adds on another layer of depth that helps to make the game even more balanced.  Unlike HS, the board is divided into two lanes, each capable of holding 4 creatures.  One lane is a shadow lane, which gives your creatures cover so that your oppenent can not attack them with a creature until your next turn (although they are still vulnerable to spells and abilities).  The other lane offers no bonuses, and is a normal playing space.  Next are the runes around your character's health bar.  Each time you lose 5 points of health, you can randomly draw a card from your deck. You may be able to draw a card with the 'Prophecy' label, which allows you to play that card on the spot for free, which can quickly swing the tide of the game in your favor if you play them correctly.  Lastly is the mana ring, which unlike HS, has 3 charges.  Some have claimed that this item is over powered, and causes the game to favor the player going second.  This is not the case.  The health runes and the lanes more than make up for the slight advatage that the second player gains with the ring.  A second player can easily burn through their charges in an ineffecient way, leaving them to the mercy of the player who used their normal mana curve properly and took advantage of the lane system.  Additionally, it has been reported that the win rate with the ring is roughly 50/50.  That is, the player going first generally wins as many times as the player going second.
Overall, my complaints are few and far between with TES:L.  The game is excellently balanced, and the art style, while perhaps a bit drab when compared to Hearthstone, is still excellent (especially if you're looking for something far less cartoony than HS).  The main problems with the game are the slow loading menu screens, which favor style over responiveness, and the perhaps the very design of the game itself.  It is modelled incredibly similiarly to HS, and though it is not the first game to do this (Duelyst comes to mind) it still might be a bit grating for some CCG verterans.  While it succeeds at offering an accessible CCG experience that still has great amounts of depth and skill, I do find myself wondering what the game would have been like if it had been made in a more original and complex manner, rather than being designed as a way to combat HS's many flaws.  I'd like to see that card game one day, but until then, Legends does what it sets out to do very well, and that is to offer an accessible experience that mechanically surpasses HS in nearly every respect.  Now it would just be nice if more people traded the RNG-fest of HS for a game with some amount of skill.  Maybe you'll be one of those people.

This game gave me cancer so instead I'll tell you the 10 easy steps you can take to making a traditional tiramisu at home!
Ingredients
3 large eggs
500 grams [~12.3 oz.] Mascarpone cheese
Espresso or Strong Coffee
Boudoir biscuits/ Lady fingers/ thin cakes
(optional) 1 cup of cognac
Powdered cocoa [or instant chocolate drink mix]
Sugar (to taste)
STEP 1 : Crack and make 3 large eggs into two different bowls (use a large bowl for the egg white and a smaller bowl for the yolk). Make sure that none of the yolk gets mixed with the egg white, otherwise the egg whites won't whisk properly.
STEP 2 : Whisk the egg yolks with an electronic whisk and gradually add sugar until the egg yolk becomes thick, creamy, and light yellow.
STEP 3 : Add about 5oo grams [~12.3 oz.] of Mascarpone in another bowl and give it a quick stir to loosen it up. Then, with the electronic whisk, mix the egg yolks and Mascarpone together.
STEP 4 : Wash and dry your whisk and then whisk the egg whites until they form firm peaks. Continue to fold the egg whites into the Mascarpone and mix until there are no lumps.
STEP 5 : Put that to the side. Make some strong espresso and let it cool.
STEP 6 : Line a large and fairly deep dish with lady fingers (boudoir biscuits) and pour over two thirds of the coffee mixture.
STEP 7 : Put half of your egg mixture over the top of that, followed by a thick dusting of cocoa. Use an instant drinking chocolate, as it's a little sweeter.
STEP 8 : Dip more lady fingers into the rest of your coffee mix (don't worry if you run out; you can just knock up some more) and carefully place them over the the top of the cocoa.
STEP 9 : Empty the rest of your egg mixture over that and dust with cocoa again.
STEP 10 : Leave it in your refrigerator for two hours and serve.
Now take the tiramisu out of the fridge and stuff it all into your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, wait 3-4 days for results.
