Unique game.
I have never played a game that blends a card based combat system with other types of genres and liked it.
This will be my first.
The game is not easy to pick up, which for me is brilliant. It takes time to learn, learn how certain events effect you, and game mechanics, even though they are pretty simple.
I would recommend that you play the game on Normal or Easy first, playing on harder difficultly when you first start the game will be painful. But if you like pain go for it :)
The combat is simple, yet effective.
The base management is simple but again effective.
The management of resources and equipment on your units is not so basic. It takes time to learn what to spend your tech points on first, how to manage a base efficiently, and what power spikes the monsters have when you fight them. You need to be really careful, mistakes early game can really hurt you, as the game progresses from early to mid and late the consequences for bad decisions are not as impactful.
Playing on hard settings, early game is VERY important, you cant make mistakes, and any mistakes will lead to a downhill spiral. Best to start over.
This game has a lot of potential to expand on. I have played the game through more than once now, replay value is there.
All events that occur are voice acted, and the voice actor does a brilliant job at reading the events out, and changing his voice for characters when they speak, its very engaging, and a brilliant decision on the behalf of the developers, I  for one am over reading mountains of text in a game, if I wanted to spend hours reading, I would pick up one of my fantasy novels. Also once you know the events as well its easy to speed through them.
AAA developers need to really lift their game, I haven't enjoyed a AAA title like this in a long time. The new Civilization games are just downright pathetic, so its nice to get that fix from a different sort of game that offers a unique experience, with good mechanics.
There are a few downsides:
I would love to see more focus on Base building and resource management. I believe the game will really excel if they had some really good expansion in this area. As it is, its far too simplistic.
I find that sometimes you are put into battle far too often, especially when playing on harder difficulty. I get that its harder, but its not really harder if I can win, but I just need to win 4x more than usual. That just gets tedious, and the challenge is not a challenge but a grind.
Graphical improvements.
Not being able to adjust combat speed (card speed) while in combat is a real downside. I would love to be able to slow down the speed when I am in a really tough fight.

What is Thea? (
I've been pondering that question. And after 13 hours, and 2 plays, i can't answer that. but i get the same fun and enjoyment from Thea as i did from the old Master of Magic.
don't get me wrong, it has more things different than similar, and yet.
Gameplay:
* you are a deity, who is incharge of their last followers. (similar to MoM)
* the game is on an overhead map, turn based. (similar to MoM)
* you only have ONE city. and you can
expand the city's border. this is important... (NOT LIKE MoM)
Improvements:
* you need to farm resources, since you cannot expand your city, you need to make expeditions. These expeditions are made with your villagers, where you need to supply them with food and fuel (wood). (Not MoM).
* These resources can be used to craft. a lot. buildings in the city, tools, weapons, food (get a bonus the more food variety you use), etc. (I consider this to be like Create Artifact in MoM. loved that :) )
* you CANNOT raise your population as in other games. meaning, there is no growth mechanics. instead, you have children, which can, randomly, mature. when a child matures, you can choose a class for it.
* you can attract people to join your city. i use people but it can be animals, magical beasts, other races, etc. for example, i had a werewolf, a shade, a witch and a sage (male witch), medics, inventor etc. the list is huge.
Combat:
* the combat is encounter based. in most encounters you can either "fight", or use a special skill. either way, the resulting fight is done with cards. in a very nice way. however, don't get me wrong, the fights/encounter are brutal, and good planning and understanding of the mechanics is needed. the tutorial is great on this, DO NOT skip it. (not even close to MoM... yet fun in it's own way).
* every encounter, be it a fight or something else, rewards you with loot. it can be a weapon/shield/armor etc, or a raw resource. furthermore, every item can be broken down for it's raw materials if you don't want/need it.
* the enoucnters gets harder and harder as the game progress. as far as i can tell, it depends on the number of turns passed.
I believe this covers the basic of the game. i enjoyed it a lot.

This is a great game for those who want an immersive experience in a little-explored mythos. The gameplay is fun and unique, while still reminding me of a graphic version of playing a D20 game. With the team who made this game taking all of the feedback of the players - such as multiple towns, etc - and making Thea 2, I am personally excited to see where they take the next game!

Thea is a fantastic and unique 4x game that focuses on narrative, survival, and the single player experience over the traditional elements you see in strategy games in this genre.
You take control of a single small city in a fantasy world based on Scandavian mythos.  With a small group of villagers you must scavenge the land, complete quests, and fight to keep enough food and wood in your invetory and in your city to keep the game going.  It's difficult and punishing with a uniquely customizable difficulty to fit any level of play.
The story based, quest system is amazing and the games strong suit.  There are a large ammount of unique events that you can stumble upon making the game experience feel unique and exciting as you find new things around every corner.  There are choices to be made, and sometimes those choices present a real dellima, others have "right" answers that you learn to respond with.
The combat is card based and extremely fun.  Don't get turned off if you heard the word "card" and want to peace out.  It's well implemented and makes a ton of sense.  It's a series of turns back and forth placing cards based on your units stats and eqipment they get from leveling up.  It's almost a hybrid blend of card game and turn based combat to oversimply.  It's one of the few games that has an autoresolve function that I don't rely on merely for the enjoyment.
The game isn't as massive or in depth as other 4x games such as Civilization.  The tech trees are horrizontal not vertical.  You only have one city.  Development is based on combat, looting, and leveling up more than it is about research and buildilng.  For the price however, this is fine.  Especially when you consider that this is a unique game in the genre that exists as a breath of fresh air.
My only critic is that there isn't more too it.  A more fleshed out game with more than two victory paths would be more than welcome, or even different ways to approach the ways to play and win.  Lik I said before, there is a "best" way to play and altough it takes some time to feel that out, once you get there it loses some luster.
I don't consider Thea to be a must buy, but if fans of the strategy/ 4x genre need a breath of fresh air and want somethign new, this should be your #1 go-to.

I just did a rage un-install.
So, I've been on the fence for a long time -- it's been on my wishlist.  I couldn't remember the exact reasons I held off  when I bought it on sale.  I definitely liked it enough to not return it at the 2-hour mark.  I was hooked for about a week.
It has alot going for it.  I like 4x, but this is a little different.  You only ever have one city.  It's after a low-magic apocalypse with slavic mythology (familiar from the Witches and Quest for Glory), so ever settler in your village really counts and the story seemed interesting - I wanted to find out more.  You can rename everything except your character (not being able to rename is a pet peeve of mine in 4x games).  The interface could be better, but is acceptable -- it's a game with alot of micromanagement on what to craft and gather.  There is a narrator but it's a little odd, it's a guy who will try to do a princess impression if there's a princess talking for example.
My first game everybody in my expeditionary force and my village got wiped out by random events and fights I should've avoided pretty quick.  (I then read some guides to increase my survivability).  There are alot of random events, rarely do they repeat so far, and they are interesting and have big effects.  I traded a party member to an orc tribe after succeeding in a few challenges, and then fought other orcs in a challenge and another joined me.  And then I was attacked by shadows and after a tough fight one joined me.  You can disassemble items and scavenge resources.  I read some guides online, and decided to go for mithril asap.  So I'm playing with two expeditions, 1 is a warrior heavy with a couple gatherers and the others the opposite.  I got a few craftsmen and warriors left in the main village.
Here's the problem, there's a day and night cycle -- you can't see anything really at night, and the monsters are more aggressive.  But you can camp out.  So Expedition 2 is mining mithril, they are getting attacked pretty much non-stop.  The combat is a strategic cardgame (this was probably my big holdout on buying the game, I'm not big on card games) and you may or may not get your warriors in the more useful part of the stack.  Anyway, I have a few tough fights the last against the shadows (at dawn, now in "Day")  I win, but 7 characters have "wounds."  Being in a camp and  having a medic are supposed to lower your chances of dying from wounds.  So I save, as I have learned there is a random chance to die when wounded.... and I load about 5 times.  Every single time between 2 and 4 of the 7 wounded die.  So even with a healer and a camp, the odds are bad.  (They also had pretty good gear by my estimation).  And it's a massive loss to lose that much of my party -- I've have about 20 people total in all 3 groups.    I've put up with losing characters here and there before (and this camp had already lost 2 I think, and gained one), but this is ridiculous.   There's only one save game on normal and one autosave, so my mithril mining plan is pretty much over.
So I reflected on this design for a moment, and then rage-quit.  There's no way to stop getting attacked, you can't see them coming and "the night is dark and full of terrors."   I apparently cannot keep up with the tech race even though I thought I mapped it out making light gold items and then going for mithril (monsters get tougher over time) despite playing on normal difficulty.  And there's alot of time invested in the game already.  It's too hard to recover from the fickle card/random event system.
I'll keep an eye out for part 2, maybe they'll fix some of the issues.

Let me clear this up, I love puzzle games, I really do. Among some of my favorites is the Portal Series and Tetris (An old favorite).

The trailer does a great job of making you think the gameplay has tons and tons of hours of gameplay. (Claims 40+ hours of campaign) But, the campaign is worthless. I don't mind games that don't take themselves seriously, but this, is just so bad you cringe every five seconds. Oh, and if you're only playing it to kill time, well expect puzzles that are way too easy or are way too difficult, right next to eachother. It isn't like Overwatch or Guns of Icarus Online, where every match feels different, it's repetitive. The moment the fun shines off, it get frustraiting and it becomes boring.
If this game was 2.5 bucks, I would recomend it. But, with 25 bucks you can buy a way better game. The game is worth 10 times less than it is, do not buy this game. I can emphasize it enough. (I got this from humble bundle, so it was really more of a bonus becasue I payed 12 bucks for 6 great games and 1 bad one, so I am fine. But, just heed my warning)

I selfishly want to recommend this game just to try to get more people to play to actually experience what it could be because I really liked the idea and feel. But, I cannot.
I became enamored with the game over a free weekend. The sparsely populated servers with people as new and clueless as me made the game seem fun and the three-something dollar price tag appealing. I bit.
Over the course of the next week or two the population disappeared. But I was able to learn the nuances of the game and navigate the not-steep, but completely unexplained, learning curve thanks to spotty appearances of other players. This made the game seem fun all over again. Over the following weeks I became comfortable with the game and really enjoyed the few times another human was actually on a server. Some players were better, a lot were as lost as I previously was.
But in the end, I never witnessed a game larger than 2v3. Morning, noon or night. Any day of the week. Any server from West to East to Europe to Asia. There just isn't people playing this game. Perhaps some games just shouldn't be open betas or 'Early Access'? People were done and bored before it had legs.
Or perhaps other issues are really holding it back.
The learning curve isn't hard but requires other players to actually learn. There's documentation of what items do or how to prime your two jumps. But nothing about the useful ways to use the items, tactics to employ, using momentum from items/jumps/enemy fire, etc. All things you can only learn with a live enemy. And I still feel like I only really learned how to play 1v1 and what tactics to use in that situation because that's all I ever got to regularly.
The devs have an idea of what they believe gameplay *should* be like if you read around the web some. In the perfect world all the servers would be 5v5 and somebody would be playing "goalie" and people would pass the ball. Combine those Ideas with the game that really does feel smooth and man that sounds great!
But the dead community means you'll rarely see 5v5 or in my case; never. I tried to play "goalie" in a 2v2 after I had read about the concept on a forum. But it's just not a logical choice to do when you aren't realistically going to stop many chances.
And passing? That would make the game that much more interesting but the speed of the players (especially once powerups are planted) makes that a colossal undertaking to time correctly. And because of this, nobody ever expects a pass. I never witnessed anybody else even attempt one.
I could go on and on. Its a great concept that is fairly polished and fun in theory. But has a dead community and suffers from a multitude of other problems. I could never recommend it even at the price I paid much less it's regular price. My twenty-plus hours of play consists of maybe five with other players and maybe three of those five hours was "competitive" play rather than goofing around. The vast majority of my play time was spent alone achievement hunting. The bots are awful.
If it gets lots of people suddenly, better maps (another issue I didn't delve into), and one or two other things I forgot to whine about... And it's like $0.99USD. Consider it.

Not really enjoying my experience with this game. The main-gameplay is a bit unforgiving in that: the dodge intervals for unblockable attacks can be tight,  some enemies don't seem to telegraph their attacks, and all enemies are capable of attacking from out of frame. Additionally, the sub-missions/mini-games aren't particularly fun.
The game has some amateurish design issues. The challenge maps (aka Scarlet Challenges) do not have a restart option once you've begun. More than once, I had a bug where the game wouldn't register that I wasn't holding the Right-Trigger. There are some unskippable sceness. And, the difficulty achievements are not cummulative. (Beating all main missions on Very Hard doesn't unlock the achievements for beating it on Normal and Hard).
The money/difficultly system in the game also seems a little broken. It's possibly to farm money rather quickly by repeating short missions on the hardest difficulty. (The hardest difficulty is immediately available without you having to complete the game on normal, hard, or very hard). The money allows you to take shortcuts in upgrading your character.
As for the story and voice-acting, the story isn't bad, but it's presented in a disjointed style. You start the game with practically no context for your actions, and the story fills in blanks here and there. The voice-acting is a bit too close to anime; no one sounds ordinary in the game, and one character in particular has a very high voice.
Graphically, the game has lots of style, but the enemy designs and special effects can sometimes make it hard to see. On that note, the game lacks a lock-on feature, and the camera and auto-target systems in the game aren't particularly good. Another graphics issue is that the game runs at 30fps by default, and you can't change that while the game is running.
Overall, the game feels clunky.

This game had an amazing atmosphere that the sequels didn't manage to do.

It's not the violent slapstick and chain-splodes of the hysterically volatile camps, filled to the brim with ammo dumps and fuel tanks. It's not the moments of pure adrenalised catharsis, where, rifle in hand, you power through smoke and machinegun fire, enemies to the left and right. It's not even when you stride through the ruins, calmly putting down survivors by plunging a machete into their chests.
No. Its appeal is in the moments beforehand - when, from some lofty perch, you think of what's to come. You check your ammo. You reload your weapons. You heal up. You anticipate. It is the calm before the storm. You are the match before the flame. In the most player-centric world yet created, in a game that you know is about to surprise, delight and enthral you, standing still, waiting to strike, is one of the finest pleasures you can experience.
After playing Far Cry 2, I'm simply unable to go back to straight and simple first-person shooters. This game has executed my expectations. Would you, could you, go back to games with similar gunfights as this, but along a more rigid axis? I think your own expectations are going to rise dramatically. And I think you really should play this game.

I personally cannot recommend this game, but I don't think it's bad for someone who wants to go around shooting people/things and exploring terrain.

West of Loathing uses a unique blend of comedy and trope pointing to create a fantasy western, a genre not probed often but that has just seen a formidable contender for top of the field.

My previous review was negative and it remains negative for anyone having the annoying "BlackCipher" glitch while using Windows 10. For people like me, I had to revert my Windows back to 8.1 to play, and I know that this sounds insane just to play 1 game. The only reason I did this was I had very high hopes for this game. Was it worth it? Well you probably know the answer to that just by the rating of this review. This game has a lot to offer and I am barely so far scratching the surface for this game. This game feels like a game I would be willing to pay retail price for, but of course it is free. The number one question people always ask though is "Is it P2W?" My answer to this is no. The only thing I would recommend paying for is the .99 starter pack for it is one hell of a deal and makes low level leveling easier if you are by yourself. Other then that you can pay for cosmetics and let me just say the cosemetics range from really scimpy or cute to full blown f*cking awesome! So unless you want to pay for some of the costumes this game is fair and balanced in combat. Combat is awesome because I have never met a game where you can just grab a enemy and use the enviroment to kill him. These kills range from Sparta kicking some one of a cliff to body slamming them on a pile of rubble. Think of this game as a beat them up with very hard but rewarding boss fights. The only thing I could say that has been annoying so far is the random bots who stand in town and advertise their account stealing websites. Do not trust these sights because they just hijack your account. These bots are always being activley banned, but not quick enough. Other then that this game is a blast and there is NO reason you shouldn't give it a try! Also last thing is this game is optimized REALLY well. I don't have the best computer but I still get 60FPS on medium graphics, Have fun!
Edit: Radi boss waiting times are stupid long. I know this isn't the games fault, but it still sucks.

Some background: This will be my first time reviewing an electronic card game. I've played MTG (Magic: The Gathering) online and IRL, but only at casual levels. I enjoyed Elder Scrolls' games as well.
I'd like to begin my review by saying that this game is easy to understand. Like many games, you can learn it in hours, but take weeks to start really excelling and mastering. With all card games as well, you have to learn what every card does and be prepared to do a lot of learning from mistakes.
After about 30 hours of rummaging through the main story, some play modes, practice modes and AI arena modes, I decided to drop $20 into the game to download the Dark Brotherhood expansion. The expansion is punishing, challenging, but FUN. You have to tailor a new deck to face off with the new chapters with cards you've earned from arenas, leveling up, play modes, and the initial story mode. There is an option to buy packs if you're impatient with earning them with the in-game mechanics.
I've almost beaten the normal Dark Brotherhood story mode. After the normal story mode, there is a master Dark Brotherhood story mode, which is supposedly like the Dark Souls of card games. You'll lose a lot, learn a lot, and eventually defeat your AI opponent. A lot of the time, you are at some disadvantage which you must figure out how to overcome. I like games like this because if a game doesn't challenge you, it doesn't change you at all.
I recommend this game over MTG games due to its MUCH faster pace, challenge, and rewards. You don't have to enjoy Elder Scrolls first-person games to get into this card game. You'll learn everything as it goes. I also like how there's AT LEAST over 100 strategies with the current card sets available in the game, which adds to the challenge and mixes up the meta substantially.
It's free to play, so just give it a shot and see if you'll like it.
UPDATE: After 120 hours played, I can fully recommend this game to anybody who has appreciated Hearthstone, MTG, and even Pokemon TCG. The new expansion Heroes of Skyrim just came out and now the meta is changing again. I would say now is a great time to get into the game because when there is new expansions, there is also new players. This game is simple, but addicting.

Not too happy with this game, after playing the included campaign basically everything costs gold or cash. Farming gold is kinda slow (you need 3-4 daily missions for 1 event ticket), and to unlock another campaign or state-of-the-art decks, you'll need about 20-40 dailies.
There are resources to improve cards that are quite grindy to get.
In addition, even if you have all the stuff to improve cards, you might notice that your level is too low for that and you'll have to grind some more.
The AI decks look pretty rigged to me, and the campaign often gives advantages to the opponents.
It suffers from all TCG probs like getting wrong cards at the wrong time, while opponents seems to get just what they need. To compensate, the AI seems to play worse when you retry a campaign mission, so even the dumbest will make it at some point so he can purchase the next campaign.
Card packs (6 cards) cost 2 bucks, and more often than not contain crap cards or cards for different schools you can't use with your main deck.
Event tickets are 2 bucks each, and you can fight up to 9 AI opponents for rewards, but without some special cards, you'll start to loose after 3-5 enemies, making this a bit cheaper than buying packs, but still expensive.
Not a bad game if you want to spend some bucks or invest serious time to unlock things, but for casual play, it's just to grindy and boring. Did not dare to start PVP fights, and bailed out after I finished the included campaign and reaching level 9.

Dark Quest is a turn-based board game-esque fantasy strategy game, loosely based off of the old Hero Quest board game. In it, you play as three characters (Warrior, Dwarf, and Wizard) seeking to make your way through a series of dungeons to complete a set of quests which are posed to you. Along the way, you need to deal with traps, secret doors, and collecting gold to upgrade your equipment/spells back in town.
The game is quite short, taking roughly 3 hours to 100%. Combat is largely random, and there are other random events which can lead to damage to your characters, which can occasionally feel a little imbalanced because some runs you won't be touched, while others you end up getting into dire straits rather quickly.
It's moderately fun, but in my case it's likely at least partially due to nostalgia from enjoying Hero Quest itself. Consider the gameplay, and the length of the game, and choose a price point which seems appropriate to you.

Did you ever sit there and think.
"Man, I wish someone would take Hero's Quest and turn it into a single player digital board game experience, avoiding all potential law suits by changing the the character and set design just enough as to undermine copyright and intellectual property laws"
If you answered "Yes" your and Dark Quest's developers think alike!

Tumblestone is an action puzzle racing game.
-Gameplay-
Tumblestone puts you in the role of a KING, from different varieties. Anywhere from Mermaid to Goblin to Sausage kings are all feartured, with the objective of one thing, to finish the puzzle at hand as fast as possible. You take puzzle pieces out in variables of 3 and race to be the first one to rid your screen of stones.
-Graphics, Sound & Artstyle-
Nothing particularly stands out in this game with regards to graphics, sound or artwork. To be perfectly frank, it has the look of a F2P game.
-Price-
The retail price is 24.99 USD
-How many hours estimated?-
It is estimated to have a single player campaign lasting 40+ hours.
But for this review, I will put down the estimated hours for multiplayer only. To which I say is a good 15-20 hours because of the daily challenges and variations of powerups that make the game feel different to its core.
-Buy it Now? Wait for Sale? Don't Buy?-
As stated before, the game looks like a f2p game, but its forte is it's gameplay. Puzzle racing game sounds lame in theory but The Quantum Astrophysicists Guild (name of the devs) really made a great multiplayer game. However the price for this game despite it having TONS of content is too much in my opinion. It's a great game with great ambitions and I love the feature to let your friends have a key to the game as well, but for 24.99 USD I just cannot recommend it. I'd be willing to shell out 9.99 USD and have no problem doing 7.49 USD. An awesome game with lots of fun.

Not really enjoying my experience with this game. The main-gameplay is a bit unforgiving in that: the dodge intervals for unblockable attacks can be tight,  some enemies don't seem to telegraph their attacks, and all enemies are capable of attacking from out of frame. Additionally, the sub-missions/mini-games aren't particularly fun.
The game has some amateurish design issues. The challenge maps (aka Scarlet Challenges) do not have a restart option once you've begun. More than once, I had a bug where the game wouldn't register that I wasn't holding the Right-Trigger. There are some unskippable sceness. And, the difficulty achievements are not cummulative. (Beating all main missions on Very Hard doesn't unlock the achievements for beating it on Normal and Hard).
The money/difficultly system in the game also seems a little broken. It's possibly to farm money rather quickly by repeating short missions on the hardest difficulty. (The hardest difficulty is immediately available without you having to complete the game on normal, hard, or very hard). The money allows you to take shortcuts in upgrading your character.
As for the story and voice-acting, the story isn't bad, but it's presented in a disjointed style. You start the game with practically no context for your actions, and the story fills in blanks here and there. The voice-acting is a bit too close to anime; no one sounds ordinary in the game, and one character in particular has a very high voice.
Graphically, the game has lots of style, but the enemy designs and special effects can sometimes make it hard to see. On that note, the game lacks a lock-on feature, and the camera and auto-target systems in the game aren't particularly good. Another graphics issue is that the game runs at 30fps by default, and you can't change that while the game is running.
Overall, the game feels clunky.

When it comes to classic shoot'em-up games, I'm not excactly an expert-in-field. But when it comes to a puzzle games, you can pretty much call me and amateur-proffesional-ish player, who simply has to prove himself that he's not as stupid as everybody's telling him. And then comes Galacide. Game that made me feel as a man with not so bright future in action puzzle games.
Now, let's scrap all of that and focus on the game itself, which made very interesting enterance by its combination of both said genres, being classic shoot'em-up and puzzle games.
You, as the commander of the greatest ship in the known universe*, have to move yourself trough great number of enemies and vast network of... colorful... nice... blocks... that will make your life a living hell.
Choosing from several ships offering different abilities, your main goal will be to get from left side, to the right side. Pretty simple, ey?
If this game would offer the same sort of repetitive gameplay as most of other shoot'em-up games, I wouldn't honestly like it. But this game does offer something twisting to the known mechanics - a "quick-thinking tactics of puzzlers". And that, ladies and gentlemen, is what makes Galacide so very unique game using so very known genres and gameplay.
During your missions, you, along with different types of enemies, will encounter a lot of colorful blocks... "block-ing" in open space and especially in (and) your way. In order to destroy them, you must line up at least four block of the same color. AKA Bejeweldy Tetris (tm). So not only that, you must also awake your mad matrix skills and don't get shot by enemies. You have to literally think about your next move in miliseconds. Otherwise your career will go to the bottom on the unkwnown faster than that one of Hayden Christensen after Star Wars Episode II and his compaining about sand. From the left side, only death awaits. Around you, only block. On the right side, only enemies and "scraps" which can be used to create new block and ultimately destroy them.
Navigating yourself through very narrow and tight spaces around blocks, picking up those scraps you need, shooting them, destroying them and also shooting enemies and evading their shots. THAT is what makes Galacide a Galacide. THAT is what makes Galacide a unique games. THAT is what makes Galacide a game you will either love or hate. Or both.
This game offers not only a campaing, made up from 7 missions (each lasting around 10-20 or more minutes), but also Endless Play and Puzzle Play. Which, as you might've guessed, is puzzle-only mode. And here, you find 25 levels divided into 5 categories, each aimed to test your brain in different manners. But nonetheless, in every level, you'll have to shoot scraps and destroy blocks (bits, as they are called in game). This game also offers something extra, which you'll have to discover yourselves.
When it comes to an audiovisual of the game, there's pretty much nothing bad you can say. Sounds are nice, music is thrilling, graphic itself is very colorful and pretty and animations along with effects are superb.
The game also has minimum of bugs, but it may get repetitive over time. Especially when the levels are so long, it just gets "not-so-exciting" after a while.
If you are fan of both shoot'em-up games and puzzle games, this is sort of must have game. For that price, it's a deal of the year. But if you don't like shoot'em-up games or match-four types of game that much, you should probably wait for either a sale or just skip this game. Galacide is really for only few "chosen" people. But it doesn't make this game any bad. It's fun. It's challanging. It's interesting and nice. What else to say? Galacide awaits you.
Pros:
+ Fun and challanging gameplay combining classic shoot'em-up with logic match-4 elements
+ Very nice audiovisuals
+ Minimum bugs
+ Up to 4-player coop
+ Puzzle mode and Endless mode
+ Price
Cons:
- It may get repetitive after a while, especially "thanks" to long levels
- More diversity in gameplay mechanics could be nice too
- It may be hard for some players
Rating: 7/10 -- moderately above average

My review of Galacide:
Galacide is a sidescrolling shoot-em-up that also adds in puzzle elements from games such as Bejeweled. You fly through each stage from left to right while avoiding enemy spacecraft. In addition to enemy craft and bullets, there are also colored fields that block your path through the stage. Your only way of clearing a path through these fields is by picking up colored scraps and launching them at the fields; upon impact, they turn into another square of whatever color the scrap originally was. When they connect and form a group of 4 or more, the group vanishes, clearing a path further into the stage.
The game is an absolute blast to play! The controls are extremely tight and I never felt like I didn't have solid control of my spacecraft. The puzzle elements, while they may sound odd at first, become second nature after a little bit of play, and add a really satisfying twist to the shoot-em-up formula. Up to three friends can also join you for the stages, leading to all sorts of chaos! Sadly, I haven't gotten to try this myself yet.
I do have a couple of complaints, though. There isn't a whole lot of content at the moment, though that'll likely get better as development proceeds, to that's not really a problem at the moment. My only other complaint is that one of the bosses is extremely difficult to predict. His tell isn't very long, and as far as I could tell he uses the same tell for every attack he does, making it hard to react to his attacks. Also, the only way to damage him is by shooting scrap of the same color into him until he gets damaged, and a brief window of vulnerability thereafter, dragging the fight out and making it last far too long.
In the end, though, those are pretty minor complaints in light of how great the rest of the game is.
VERDICT:
Would I recommend Galacide? Definitely, at least so long as the core gameplay doesn't immediately turn you off. It's a ton of fun to play, and will only continue to improve as development gets further.
CAVEAT: As with all Early Access games, make sure you buy any Early Access game for how it is in its current state, NOT FOR WHAT IT MAY BECOME IN THE FUTURE. Be smart, people.

Our video about Galacide:
Galacide is a match 4, side-scrolling bullethell shooter in which you have to take down enemy fighters while dodging their bullets. There are three colours of scrap that can be used to match scraps of the same colour together; doing so will clear blocks in the level and allow you to move forwards. You have 3 lives which get reduced by either dying or by leaving the (slowly scrolling) screen.
You are given the option to take 1 out of 4 ships, each ship has its own abilities and stats ranging from a tractor beam to the ability to store scrap for later use, leveling up will enhance these abilities. In addition there are multiple bonus items including weapons upgrades, heals and even bombs to clear the path.
After making your way through a certain amount of scrap, you will dash forward while fighting enemies or bosses with pattern shots and special abilities. After beating these enemies you will either progress to the next level or proceed into another match-4 stage of the same level. In addition to enemies and bosses there also are turret defence systems, these can be cleared out by either matching up the scrap of the colour they are on or just by shooting them.
Apart from the basic levels you also have endless mode or puzzle play. Endless mode lets you play as far as you can get without running out of your 3 lives. In puzzle play, you have to beat a preset level with limited scrap, testing your scrap placement to the limit.
Pro’s
+ Easy to get into, hard to master
+ Interesting mix between A match-4 and shoot ‘m up
+ Variety of power ups (heal/weapon upgrade/rapid fire/bomb)
+ Enemy variety (laserbeams/turrets/bosses/pattern shots)
Cons
- Unclear when ships are unlocked (early access; unlocked by completing levels?)
- Some controllers don’t work with the game yet (early acces)
- Same button for shooting and shooting block/scrap

The Shadowrun games are perhaps the best example of a game telling a story I've played since Chrono Trigger on the SNES. They go perfectly back and forth from story to gameplay. You're given meaningful choices to make, even if it isn't always reflected gamewise, you really feel that the people around are real and reacting to your decisions. Being able to choose nearly every line of dialog, even relatively minor ones, keep the feel of investment in the story up. And you can really screw things up in the game, although I don't think you can lose the game just through story choices.
Combat is good, you can do a number of different styles and still have a decent challenge. It's tactical turn-based combat, deep but not too deep.
Story and art are both really good. I really like a lot of the NPCs I meet, and your section of Berlin feels really alive. I liked Shadowrun Returns as well, but I thought the story flagged a bit toward the end. Not the case here. I enjoyed my time from start to finish.
If you're even a little interested in good storytelling in gaming, you need to check out the Shadowrun series. And if you're only going to play one, make it Dragonfall.

I feel obligated to give this a thumbs up, because Grim Fandango is legitimately one of the best adventure games out there, and I fully endorse having everyone play it.
However, let it be known that this remaster is a fairly shoddy job. During my play though of the game, I saw instances of:
* Models bugging out (speaking with one character constantly had them bouncing all over the place, and one memorable time Manny managed to draw his scythe upside down.)
* Audio errors (music and/or audio getting all choppy – normally right after a cut scene.)

* Video errors (one area ended up with an item whose shadow was totally unanimated, and all the sections that should have been white instead being transparent.)
* Script/interface errors (there were several times when I had the correct solution, but the game wouldn’t let me use the object/talk to the NPC I needed to. I found that the best way around this was to swap to mouse control, which let me work around the issues I ran into.)
* And one instance of the game hanging – I could move the mouse, but no other input was accepted – couldn’t even exit to the menu, had to force-quit the program. Ended up losing all my progress since my previous save.
From a brief glance at the official forums, it appears that the developers are no longer patching the game, so assume that these issues are still there.
Again, however, I will note that I was able to play all the way through the game, with the only major problems of losing some time to the crash, and having to hit up a walk through website to confirm that I had the correct answer when the game initially refused to accept my answer to a problem.
If you’re willing to put up with those problems, I’d rate this as well worth picking up on sale.

Some of the puzzles are quite tricky and, for me at least, caused me to end up running back and forth to try different items in my inventory on each character and anywhere else you could try them resulting in a lot of these quotes from our hero Manny:
"I don't think that would shed any light on things"
"I don't really want to do that"
"I don't want to mess up my blade" (But you'll drag it through
?)
"That soul has already been reaped" (No, I don't want to reap their soul. I want to hit them with the scythe!)
I know this wasn't present in the original and this is only a re-release but having not played this before, I missed that you couldn't combine items in your inventory together like in Broken Sword or Kaptain Brawe (both really good adventure point and click games too). Obviously I understand this isn't something that they would add just for a remastered version but is something I like in adventure games when they merge two seemingly unrelated items together often resulting in comedic one liners from the character. Although you do end up doing this in the last year but it's not like you can select one item and try adding it to another in your pockets as that feature isn't available.
The Inventory did get quite tiresome to navigate. Rather than having a list of your items pictured, you instead have to open Manny's coat and then select right or left to see the next item which he removes from his inside pocket. Here you can then either select the item to use it in some way on someone/something or you can examine the item, in which Manny will talk about the item to give you clues. Because of the way this is set out its quite slow if you want to try a few items on something as you first have to select the item so he removes this from his inside pocket, and then before you can try another item you have to put it away. This was especially slow when taking out and putting away the scythe and got quite annoying as you cannot do anything while he is putting the item away and also cannot interact with anything else if you still have an item out that doesn't fit with what you are interacting with. Another annoyance was that he would have to walk to a certain point until he would interact with an item or talk to a person. Even if I just pressed the look option and was right next to the item he would walk half way across the screen, or several paces, stop and then comment.
Apart from the downsides of the game the story still keeps you playing and there are lots of funny comments from Manny and this makes up for the downsides in the game. Although the "remastered" version, for me, isn't much more than a 1080p resolution upgrade with shadows, the game is still enjoyable to play and at the end, I wanted more :(

I don't even know where to begin with this game, so here's the TL;DR: if you want to play an addicting, fun, and balanced CCG with nuanced mechanics and innovative gameplay not dependent on RNG, download this game now.
---------------
So here is the long review. I started playing this game less than a week ago and have over 40 hours already. It's intoxicatingly addicting in a few respects:
* STORY MODE: It's great; there's a ton of content, and great rewards: card packs, Soul Gems (aka Dust), cards themselves. As far as the Dark Brotherhood storyline goes, you can pay for them ($7.99 for each Act, or $19.99 for all three if you want a discount), or you can grind ladder/casual/arena for gold to purchase each Act one at a time. Speaking of grinding...
* REASONABLE F2P: It is achievable to grind gold, soul gems, and card packs. Every 3 wins in casual or ranked will get you some gold (between 15g-50g) and either a card or a card pack. Though rare, you can sometimes even get a Legendary card from this. Packs are 100g, Arena 150g.
* ALWAYS A CHANCE: win or lose, you never feel like the game was out of your control. I've had countless games where my opponent has had a 15+ HP advantage, and I was able to come back. That might sound like the game is broken, but the comeback mechanics (Runes, which I'll get to in a bit) in this game force players to think before they consider face-rolling their opponent instead of taking a more measured approach. Aggro decks are viable, but are much more punishable than in a game like Hearthstone. The feeling of "you're never out of it" is really great in a CCG.
Now, here are some of the mechanical nuances of the game that make it so amazing and unique:
* RUNES: This is one of the most intriguing features. Both players start with 30 HP; it can be raised higher with certain healing items/drain abilities from creatures (aka minions), etc. As far as I know, there is no cap on health. Every 5 HP you lose (25, 20, 15, etc.), it will break a Rune. When a Rune procs, you automatically draw a card. Some cards have an attribute called Prophecy, which allows them to be played instantly and free of charge if it's drawn by a Rune proc. So if your opponent buffs his creatures and goes full aggro on your face carelessly, he will proc one or two Runes, maybe more... you might draw the beloved Piercing Javelin—a 5 magika (aka mana) card that kills any creature... but since it's got a Prophecy attribute, you can play it for free in the middle of your opponent's turn and destroy a high-cost creature on the board. Or maybe you draw a Loyal Housecarl, a 2/2 Creature for 5 magika (again, free if proc'd by a Rune break) that is able to give another creature (or itself) +2/2 and Guard (aka Taunt) to prevent further damage to your hero. Runes are what make players think twice before going full faceroll mode. I can't tell you the amount of times I've had full board control but both of us have empty hands, so I don't even attack for 2 (or even more) turns in a row just to build up more card advantage. You have to be very careful about when you want to break Rune thresholds, because it can backfire badly.
* LANES: The board is separated into two halves that creatures can be played in. You have the Field Lane on the left (regular lane), and the Shadow Lane on the right which gives any creature summoned to that lane Cover (aka Stealth) for one turn (i.e. the turn you play the creature). This prevents your opponent from insta-trading the card if he has creatures already established in that lane; however, Covered creatures can still be targeted by removal spells, so it balances out. This is a great mechanic that allows more versatility with creature play and forces you to think where you want to throw down your Guard creatures (which don't gain Cover in the Shadow Lane since they're Guards) and also makes you think whether you want to spread your defense/offense more thinly, or just dominate one lane hard early on. Periodically, they will enable Chaos Arena, which is like Versus Arena, except it has gimmicky lane(s). For example, a lane that might buff creatures with +2/0 when they take damage, etc. The campaign mode against AI also has quite a few of these gimmick lanes, but in constructed/ranked play, it will always only be the Field Lane and the Shadow Lane.
* DECK BUILDING: It's actually FUN in this game. I don't know about anyone else, but I absolutely HATED deck building in Hearthstone. I just wanted to get it over with. In ES:L, I love it. It's not like deck building itself is fundamentally different, but for whatever reason, in Legends, I really look forward to building decks. There are 5 Attributes in this game: STRENGTH (aggro with a lot of charge and weapons/buffs), INTELLIGENCE (lots of wards [aka Divine Shield], summons, and spells), WILLPOWER (lots of creatures that buff other creatures, e.g. "All friendly creatures in lane have +0/1," or Buff-on-Summon spells), AGILITY (lots of lethal and Pilfer mechanics, which I'll get to later), and finally ENDURANCE (decent amount of lethal as well, a lot of defensive buffs... very strong late-game). Your deck is comprised of any combination of two of these Attributes, plus cards from the Normal Attribute. There are also Dual Attribute cards that can be extremely powerful. Essentially, your imagination is the only limit when it comes to deck building. Also, there are 6 cards to a card pack, one more than the 5 you get in HS. You also get a Legendary roughly every 10-15 packs, and the pity-timer is nearly confirmed by multiple people to be at 20 where you're guaranteed one Legendary (as opposed to HS which is supposedly at a whopping 40).
PILFER: This is a creature attribute/ability that procs whenever that creature attacks the opponent. So for example, Daring Cutpurse is a 2/2 for 2 magika that has Prophecy (can be played instantly on Rune break) and has Pilfer: +1/1. So every time he hits face, he will gain +1/1.
SLAY: This is a mechanic that's associated with Pilfer because of its synergy with Agility decks (which has a lot of Pilfer), but there are also a lot of Slay attributes in Endurance decks. Slay is a attribute that activates whenever a creature kills another creature. So for example, Stalking Shadowscale is a 3/4 for 3 Magika that has the attribute "Slay: +1/1." So every time he kills another creature, he will gain +1/1.
SUPPORT: Supports are cards that you play that either have limited uses, or are Ongoing (aka Infinite). For example: Elixir of Deflection is a 5 magika support that has 3 uses, and allows you to give any creature Ward; it can also be used the turn the card is played (any active Support can) which makes for some very clutch moments in trading out creatures in the mid to late game. Imperial Might is a 5 magika support that is Ongoing and summons a 1/1 Imperial Grunt in a random lane at the end of every turn you have. There are only handful of creatures that can destroy supports with their Summon (aka Battlecry) ability, so supports can be very influential on the outcome of a game.
---------------
In the end, Elder Scrolls: Legends is a fantastic game with tons of depth, managable RNG, a great story/campaign, and a lot of replay value. It is also very affordable: any money you put into this game is simply if you want to get good decks faster—I strongly hesitate to say this game is "P2W" at all because I have spent only $20 on it for the Dark Brotherhood campaign, and none of it on card packs or anything like that. And yet I still can destroy players who have tons of Epics and Legendaries just from smart play and good card synergy. It's very reasonable to play ES:L and have fun and even win without forking over a single dollar.
Closing thoughts: Just try the game out. Get addicted. It's free. Don't like it? It's still free. But you will like it. And you will inevitably find yourself wanting to explore more... and that's a sign that a game is great.

I absolutely adore Dragon Ball, I watched the anime, read the manga and played a bunch of the video games.
So I was rather happy when Xenoverse 1 came out and basically did most of the things I wanted in a new Dragon Ball game.
Me making my own OC, an "Original" Story and Budokai Tenkaichi like Combat. But the game featured many problems that I am happy to say were fixed mostly with the second game. The combat flows more nicely, combos actually have a point now, more super moves, alot of missing battles (Vs. Dodoriy, The Androids and Fat Buu along with Vegeta) were included, a traversable and sizeable overworld that didn't feel too empty, a teacher system that does not take 100 hours to 100%, transformations for all races and the game looks nice. What I am sad about is all of the other flaws that felt like were coming from this being sequel.
This game is unbalanced, Saiyans are much stronger because of their huge buffs on SS and Strike moves feel much weaker compared to all other moves and are a pain to combo with. Some transformations are just boring and uninspired (Every Buu turning into a different colored Kid Buu is lame and Golden Freeza is meh to look at). The story often falls short of just saying "This guy is stronger than he is supposed to be in this battle!" or literally just throwing a movie villain in like "I bet Broly fits in here somewhere", rarely does it go beyond the time travel ideas beyond those like with Hercule in Xenoverse 1 and lastly the Netcode and glitches in the expert missions are awful, even if those bosses are really cool.
If you are a Dragon Ball fan and enjoy more grindy kinds of games where you work hard for what you want, even if that means you'll have to do the same mission like 5 times, I do recommend it. If you liked XV1, you'll like XV2.

I swear by the name of Svarog that this is a very good game.
Actually the genre itself is nothing I enjoy much. There are hardly any similar games in my library. I gave Thea: The Awakening a chance and I didn't regret it.
Pros:
- The story. While it's semi-linear it offers you to make choices that matter. You're entitled to make the right choices for Thea and decide the fate of that world. And there is no turning back once you've made a decission because the game only offers one save at a time and not everything you do shows its consequences immediatly. It offers a solid motivation to replay this title.
- I do like the fact that the uncountable little sidestories are based on an actual mythology, that - chances are high - you've never heard of. Depending on were you were born and raised, but I was surprised by and excited about the rich cultural aspects of slavic mythology. Not that I care too much but it was really interesting and is presented in this game in a catchy way. Like, for example: Who'd have thought that you could fight off demons by rubbing garlic all over you and urinate on your hands? Yea! Now you've learned something. Play the game to learn more!
- Still it's not a game that is immature. It's not some generic colorful-magic-awkwardness-hack'n'slash-rescuetheprincessoreternaldarknesscomesohandbtwthereareatonofdragonssoyourprotagonistneedstofindthemeaningoflovetofightthosenastydragons kind of game. It's mature. I'd even say that it touches realism to a certain degree. Not that you don't have to fight dragons in this game, it's just, the way the developers present it, that is actually really good.
- The graphics are fine. Not sure whatelse I can say about the graphics. They met my requirements? They created enough immersion to not ruin the game for not having good enough graphics? I liked some of the artwork presented in the game. Whoever made them has got talent. I'm just not that kind of person and shouldn't judge things I don't understand.
- I loved the complexity of this game and I loved the micromanagement. I strongly disagree with other reviews I've read before buying this title that the micromanagement is a pain and I strongly disagree that the game should be simplified. There are enough games on the market that are easy and simple. Allthough I do agree that the developers could have made changes to decrease the number of clicks needed to, for example, transfer the loot of an expedition to your town's inventory, the plain complexity is a good thing .... for people who are bored by simple games too quickly.
- The way RNG is used in Thea: The Awakening is performed well, which is important because the game is full of it. First of all because some events, characters and items are so rare, they don't show up untill you're playing your 10th village allready so you always get to discover something new every playthrough. Secondly because even when something familiar happens that you have mastered before you don't always know the outcome of it and get surprised by either something good happening or something bad. I liked that!
- It is not grindy! You can grind and level your people up but you don't have to in order to progress. You're free.
- The DLC policy of the developers is pretty cool. They offer every DLC with actual game content for free but you can buy the coffee DLC which is basically you giving them money so they can buy a coffee. That's rare in the gaming industry and I respect that and I'll consider buying the coffee DLC.
- Speaking of the developers, I think you can feel when playing the game that they tried to make a great game because they wanted to make a great game and not because they wanted to make money. Someone put his heart and his sweat in this title with a lot of love for details. I respect that, too.
Cons:
- Not enough to explore in the open world. There should be something special to find every now and then. You shouldn't depend on random encounters to find something special to happen but you should also be able to find something special on the map while uncovering it. Otherwise you'll find yourself thinking: "Why should I even go to the east, it'll be the same as going west, north or south.". I hope you get my point.
- Lack of endgame content in general. I know the game is not supposed to give you an endless experience of adventurous exploration and rather wants you to start a new game once you're finished an old one but .... just in case you want to continue with your beloved village full of witches, goblins, orks and spiders because you somehow bonded to them, there should be something more you are able to do with them.
It's a good game which has the potential to keep you entertained for long nights and days. I'd fully recommend it. It's one of those indie titles you want to get to know.

Dark Quest, for better or for worse, is an indie clone of HeroQuest, both in aesthetics and gameplay. Unfortunately, it's hampered by incredibly poor writing, a clumsy UI, a painful bug that made the game significantly harder and more awkward, and a failure to measure up to the 1989 boardgame in almost every way.
Since it's the core of the gameplay, there's no real getting around it - Dark Quest is HeroQuest in many ways. However, many of the relevant numbers are hidden from the player, you are only given control of three heroes instead of four, the fairly wide variety of magic spells for the Wizard (and Elf, who isn't in this game) from the board game is mostly missing, items are all purchased or looted consumables instead of HeroQuest's variety of purchasable equipment, mostly-found consumables, and found artifacts, and there's only eight (or nine? I'm honestly unsure, because the game is bad at communicating things and I wasn't writing it down...) quests instead of the original HeroQuest's twelve. Also there's a turn limit on each quest, but it's so generous that I never felt I was in risk of hitting it, so that's kind of a non-point.
Several of these differences I mentioned are related to the clumsy UI, which makes selecting heroes who aren't on the same screen as each other awkward (unless there's a hotkey for it that I'm missing), as you need to scroll over to and click on them, and frequently gives little information - item/spell descriptions are there and useful, but knowing any stats other than BP for heroes and monsters is impossible except by guesswork. Similarly, how traps are detected was never entirely clear to me even by the end of the game - moving the dwarf "near" them seemed to detect them after his move, but it wasn't always clear what determined whether or not he was "near" enough for it to work. When buying things in town, you are also not told what your inventory looks like slot-wise, in terms of whether you have any empty slots, just whether or not you have any of those items and, after attempting to purchase an item, perhaps that you didn't have any item slots and your purchase was cancelled.
Moving to the square you want and taking the action you want are also frequently mutually exclusive - for instance, you can't very easily retreat while casting spells, because while you get to move and act in the same turn, they have to be done in a single order. This also sometimes makes picking up loot / smashing barrels / otherwise checking for treasure awkward, because you have to click on the square beyond the one you want to end up in.  Doing things like sorting your inventory and transferring items between heroes is also not possible, nor does the game have real configuration options for doing things like changing the volume, just turning it on or off. Also, while you can quickly click through most windows to speed up game play, you're stuck at the "roll the skull of fate" screen for a good few seconds before it becomes enabled to click on, slowing down the game notably whenever it randomly happens. Ultimately, you'll spend almost as much time fighting the UI as having fun fighting Azkallor's minions.
The bug I mentioned was simple, but rather terrible - you couldn't use any items that came after a blank slot in your inventory. Given that you couldn't move items around in your inventory, nor trade items between heroes, this put you in the awkward position of using the last item in an inventory slot disabling your access to any items in later slots for the rest of the quest. There seemed to be a related bug where the description of items in your inventory would also be wrong, with the description of the item your mouse was over belonging to a different item in your inventory. If you knew what your items did, of course, this wasn't a problem, just awkward.
As far as the poor writing goes, the story in this game is obviously not the draw, much as it wasn't for HeroQuest, but the in-game English script was incredibly badly written, featuring many typographical errors, grammatical errors, wrong capitalizations, et cetera. It was fairly distracting, and the game really could have used an editing pass.
In the end, I actually had some fun with Dark Quest because it was a take on a good game design, and it reminded me of the fun times I had playing the original HeroQuest board game as a kid. However, it just didn't compare, and not because I was blinded by nostalgia - a straight adaptation of the board game would have been a better game, and almost none of the changes were, in my opinion, for the better. It's also rather short and without much replay value, as I completed all of the quests included in the game in around two and a half hours of play. So, unfortunately, I can't really recommend purchasing it - but I can say that I'm at least tentatively interested in Dark Quest II, because I can see a lot of ways for the designers to get to a good game from here, and hope the designers manage it.

As a child, I played a ton of a little board game called Hero Quest. While many have attested that this game is very similar, I can tell you that a lot of the tiles used in this game as well as the monsters are EXACT copies. However, there are some differences.
In this game, you play as 3 characters, all of whom have different strengths and weaknesses. They move along a set of tiles like a board game in a turn-based strategy RPG style. The story in this game is very light with no real purpose.
Having said that, I absolutely recommend this game to any board game fanatics or Dungeons and Dragons fans out there that wish they could play solo. The levels are fast-paced, fun, and the abilities and attacks are very chance-based, similar to rolling dice.
I absolutely loved my playthrough of this game and I hope a sequel comes out at some point!

This game makes me want to rip the skin off my face and eat it.... Pretty sure that would be more fun and better use of my time than it is.
Now that we've got that out of the way.....
I played this game a lot before it was on steam, I had no money at the time and a friend that loved it to death.
He got me playing it to pass the time, as I had nothing better to do and and my aforementioned activity had not yet occurred to me, I went for it.
At first glance the game seems alright, a nice cast of characters, a mediocre customization menu, the game doesn't look too shabby graphically, and it was free.
Then I started walking.... The animation was smooth, so smooth in fact that I seemed to be sliding my feet along the ground, only moving about half as fast as my animation suggested I should be.. So I turned and ran to the left and I glided along in a way that could almost be compared to a cat trying to gain traction on a recently waxed floor, I mean I did turn, just not in the way one might expect a human to move across dirt and grass.
I got to a combat section and because thought to myself "This is where the game will redeem itself!!" but I was Let down by this as well! It's by no means awful, but in my eyes it was typical, it didn't do anything I hadn't seen before and the execution of the system didn't wow me either, It lacked polish.
That's when things started getting weird, suddenly I noticed that my character's physics would randomly spaz out while I was standing still, parts of her armor and/or body would jolt around like a kid who's had too much sugar. And I would randomly become stuck at odd angles against terrain during combat
Lets move on from all of that though.
I feel like I should mention a few more things that struck me as odd...
There are more loading screens in this game than you can shake a stick at. You wanna go to the docks where you access the missions? Loading screen! You wanna start a mission? Loading screen, which then leaves you on a tiny dock with a boat on it. You wanna start the mission for real this time? Loading screen!!!!! Just when you think that's all of 'em done, you kill a few baddies and walk a little ways... LOADING SCREEN!!!! I think you get the picture...
The camera controls are shockingly sluggish for an ARPG.
They call it an MMO, it's not an MMO it's a Co-Op multiplayer ARPG with a giant chat room where you can find up to 4 players to run missions with you.
You need to use real money for most of the cool looking stuff.
TLDR: The game claims to be things it isn't. It's not an awful game it's just a huge let down.
If you like the concept of this game play Warframe, or nearly any other ARPG instead. (I mention Warframe only because it's similar to this game)
If you think this review is unfair, feel free to dislike it. We're all entitled to our own opinions.
P.S. Shortly before writing this I redownloaded the game on steam and nothing has changed.

is a turn based RPG/Strategy game. It's pretty strait forward if you are not new to the genre. Shadowrun is based on a table top game and furthermore the SNES original. Shadowrun is a strange ol' bird. The specifics of the lore are more suggested rather than have it be derived from any over arching canonicity. The lore is so large that none of these games can appropriately do it justice, each instance is something usually very character specific and only touches on small areas of the universe.
Shadowrun is also unique in that it combines traditional fantasy roles and races with futuristic cyberpunk cities, robotics and it's own version of cyberspace. Mixing hacking, drone control and the ability to summon spirits within your party is what makes Shadowrun stand out despite its relatively ubiquitous mechanics and traditional roleplaying.
Now, I have some complaints that I'd like to talk about because I feel that'd be a better way to get my points across rather than reiterate what is traditional about it.

An awesome story, many subplots in it, beautifuly crafted atmosphere which gives you the real immersive ambience of the era you find yourself in.
Battles are good, sometimes hardcore tough, but generally you won't have any major problems with them, since it all scales pretty good. Different classes and some story-forks make the replayability of the game quite possible.
The dialogs are awesome and the characters are amazingly crafted.
I am sure you will thoroughly enjoy this awesome game as I did.

Shadowrun Dragonfall is a standalone expansion to Shadowrun Returns. Shadowrun is a turn based strategy game filled with RPG elements such as choice-based dialogue as well as character creation and customization.
The thing that allows Dragonfall to stand out from Returns is that its campaign is almost twice as long as the original, features open quest hubs and removes the linearity of getting a quest, being teleported to the location, and then being teleported back without any choice or say in the matter. This time around you get to actually get a permanent team together instead of having to hire generic NPCs that you never get to talk to like in Returns.
The gameplay here is one and the same with Returns though. Your typical turn and cover based strategy game with abilities and characters inspired by the world of shadowrun. The intensity of the fights for a turn based strategy game is actually surprising. You can have a decker hacked into the matrix and fighting off hordes of defense programs while the rest of your team is trying to protect his actual body from hordes all the same. It’s a lot of fun, but this time around with the extended campaign length? It’s VERY repetitive. Shadowrun Dragonfall features far less choices of how to go about things than Returns did. While you can avoid certain confrontations, most jobs and situations you get into will end in a fight no matter what. This game LOVES to force you into combat and spam groups of a dozen enemies per room at your four man squad. The entire last mission was four levels of unit spam. Because of this the gameplay, while fun, does become tedious very quickly and even disappointing if you were hoping for more options for diplomacy or tricks that could help you avoid combat. One good thing I did love now though is that your permanent companions CAN be used to fulfill skill checks that you yourself cannot make. For example, need something decked or need a wall broken down, but you’re just a weak not tech-savvy shaman? Your teammates can fulfill these skill checks for you! Sounds great right? Well, there’s a catch. The catch is that while they did implement this desired feature...they only did it for about 2/3rds of the skill checks in the game. There are plenty that just lack the option for no apparent reason. Find a wall you can knock over with your troll? Great! Well two levels from now you’re gonna find a wall that she won’t be able to help you with. No explanation given. Ok. Movement outside of combat is still turn based unfortunately so be careful about running around because you may enter a fight and find none of your team has AP because they lost it all running up to the fight.
The story really stood out to me for most of the game. I’ve never seen a game’s story do quite what this one does. From the very first level you are given an antagonist, but that antagonist changes like three different times and the one that you finally find out to be the main antagonist of the game? It’s also the most boring character you meet in the entire game! And what’s worse is that everything this antagonist does is so generic and so easily predictable that you know how it’s gonna end an hour in advance. The addition of so many interesting side quests (on top of generic boring ones) was definitely a treat though. I do LOVE the amount of story choices you do get to make. Especially with the addition of permanent companions and quests for those companions, but what sucks is that every choice you make up til the end of the game carries absolutely no impact on your ending. There’s only three choices that affect your ending in any notable manner. They’re all made in the last three hours of the game and the one with the biggest effect is a decision made through one line of dialogue in the last two minutes of it with zero explanation, zero chance to look for explanation, just a choice and a GIANT paragraph of text in what is honestly the most disappointing ending to a videogame I have ever seen. It was not an ending worth fighting for and it was certainly not satisfying. The dialogue wasn’t much better either. Whoever wrote the dialogue for a lot of the side characters didn’t care to give them distinct personality and had them say very obscure things that you could never imagine anyone saying and using a lot of real-life words that aren’t common at all in the Shadowrun setting OR in real life.
And the biggest issue that plagued Shadowrun Returns is back but this time in a dozen more ways! Bugs! Since we’re on the topic of dialogue, let’s start with dialogue bugs. For one, there’s a VERY boring side character that hangs out in a bar who repeats her intro twice. Why? I don’t know. She intros when you meet her, and then a few hours later if you go back to her she’ll intro again. After that we have BROKEN dialogue! Everyone’s favorite type of dialogue bug! There are several accounts I experienced of dialogue that was completely missing. I had an optional objective to complete late into the game where I had to retrieve something for somebody, but after getting it for them the person only looked at me and said “Well?” with no option for me to hand her anything. After looking it up I found she was supposed to tell me about it first, so I reloaded to try to see if talking to her before getting it would help, but nothing. It’s a broken side objective and there’s more than one in Dragonfall. There’s the occasional graphical bug. Most of it revolves around how characters stand in this game. Maybe it’s just the 2D art, but there’s a lot of examples of characters just looking like their legs are broken or spun around for some reason. Clicking on npcs doesn’t always work correctly. Sometimes it moves you to them instead of starting dialogue or attacking. Sometimes you need to click twice to do what you want to do. It’s a stupid bug from Returns but is far more prominent in Dragonfall. Shamans and Riggers are also bugged in this expansion/sequel thing. Shamans will occasionally randomly gain an AP that they shouldn’t have while maintaining a summoned creature for a few rounds before it disappears again. Riggers will occasionally LOSE an AP as if they were maintaining a second drone even if they only have one. Mission items get broken less than halfway into the game which cause certain items to get stuck there for the rest of the game even if you already completed the relevant quest. It’s most likely to happen with a penthouse code you receive on a sidequest. And lastly towards the end of the game your main computer terminal where you take on jobs and check your messages gets bugged and reads “one new message” for the last four hours of the game even though you have no new mail. Oh yeah, and when you start the game there’s a chance it may break on you. When I first started it I hit new game and was greeted by a black screen!
Do I think it was a better game than Returns? Yes. Do I think it deserves a higher score? No. I gave Returns an 8/10 because it was a fun game with barely any bugs or issues. Dragonfall may be better at its core, but it’s so much buggier and has so many more issues and bad design choices that I can’t justify giving it a higher score, not even the same score. Shadowrun Dragonfall gets a 6/10 from me. With all of its issues it was enjoyable, but by the end of the game you’ll find yourself so tired of all its crap you won’t even want to try any mods whereas playing the user generated content was one the pros I gave to Returns for extending the life of the game. Do I recommend Dragonfall? Sure. If you can put up with all of these problems, go ahead and buy it. I know I still had fun despite them. But since none of these issues will ever get fixed, it is entirely up to you to decide whether or not you can put up with them as I did.

I won't recommend this game. Don't look at my time count from this Steam account, I played the game entirely on my flatmate's PC.
The game doesn't lacks interesting concepts. It could eventually be appreciated as a mostly okay game, if your standards about gaming are those from early 2000's. Simply, things have changed a lot during ten years, and an average, generic beat'em all with an archaic game-design (the upgrade system, the combat, the game objectives and progression, they all terribly lack luster and originality). The level-design is on the verge of simple laziness, with its linearity, lack of explanation for many mechanics, and bad implementation of new (or not) enemies, making the learning of the game very tedious. All these mechanics were interesting back in the days because they were experimentations, the beginnings of certain styles of games and how to design a game well, but in 2014 (the game's release date), it's mostly disappointing. Which is why I'm saying, the game design as a whole is very lazy.
I'd almost like to compliment the game on its risky decision of visual style, with strong contrasts and metallic ink effects, but that plus the strange camera movements make the game very hard to read sometimes, without mentioning the showers of disparate loots that come out of your dead foes for no good game-design reasons.
The game could maybe find its salvation in its very anime-ish story, which is kind of interesting in its own rights, but the writing is very ordinary (you couldn't ever compare that to anything like Psychopass, GitS, Steins;Gate, which aren't masterpieces but are still quite good - KiD is far, far below that). You're often in complete confusion about what's going on, and why you're doing what you're doing (fetching cupcakes and flowers in a small - yet gigantic and inconsistent Escher-esque - suburban house to a woman in servant costume asking you to kill her sister since she's a monster... wait, why am I even fetching her that stuff?). Women are also terribly represented, they're sexualized about as much as one can expect from a japanese author, and are generally either pathetic and childishly portrayed, or a perfect cliché of the evil femme fatale.
All in all, it was... fun-ish, but I'd recommend to someone who likes beat'em all to go back to a nice game of Bayonetta or God of War, and for manga/anime fans... well, There's still Re:Zero, Yuri!!! On Ice, and Your Lie in April. Which are masterpieces. And worth your time. But maybe you should pass on Killer is Dead.
