It's a character action game, much like Bayonetta in a lot of ways, and nothing like Bayonetta in many others.
As far as any combat system goes, it's not even nearly as deep as Bayo or DMC, in that it has one normal attack button, one guard break button that doesn't find itself part of many combos, a dodge/guard button and then a subweapon you can use. The subweapons are fairly boring, in that you have a gun that slows, a gun that stuns, a gun that just shoots and a drill that breaks armor. Really, combat comes down to mashing your attack button, guarding/dodging at the right time (and as per usual, you get a big bonus for timing guards/dodges perfectly), and shooting things that need shot.
In terms of polish, it looks good, it plays really nicely (even if not all that deep) and it sounds good. English VA is mostly about as good as you can expect from a title like this. That is, intentionally cheesy but not really *bad*.
The most interesting part of this game is probably the Gigolo missions, in which you hang out with a lovely lady and, while she isn't looking, look at her, uh, nicest areas, until you build up the 'Guts' to give her a present. Give her enough presents that she likes, and you have successfully completed the mission, and you get a nice cutscene. Then you get an item, be that one of the subweapons or a temporary boost item.
A very fun but relatively small game. If you like fast, skill-based combat and like to replay missions for ranks or on higher difficulties, this game will have a lot for you. If you like playing through cheesy, funny and outright weird Japanese games, this game will have a lot for you too.
I'd recommend it for a few days of fun.

I've gone back-and-forth about whether to give this game a thumbs-up or thumbs-down.  Ultimately, I decided to give it a thumbs-up because I *did* enjoy playing it.  However, in my opinion this is a game with some serious flaws.  I picked this up as part of the Far Cry franchise pack, so I don't regret buying it.
POSITIVES:
- It's a hardcore open-world sandbox FPS.  If you're into that, you will almost certainly enjoy much of the game.  "Hardcore" here refers to variety of things.  For example, there is very limited fast-travel.  Expect to spend a lot of your time driving back and forth between the same places.  This game doesn't hold your hand or give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about you and your time.
- Continuing the hardcore theme, you don't carry much ammo and your guns often jam, especially when you don't routinely replace them with brand new ones.  I enjoyed this part, but some might see it as a nuisance.
- There is a very good variety of guns.
- The graphics hold up quite well.
NEGATIVES:
- RESPAWNING ENEMIES.  This is by far the worst, IMHO.  When you clear an area of enemies, they will respawn as soon as the area is unloaded.  This creates some really awkward situations where your missions expect you to drive back-and-forth over the same area repeatedly, and you have to re-clear it (or painstakingly avoid it) each time.  It's entertaining for the first few times, but it gets really repetitive.  Early on, I died to these guys a lot.  Later, I was just trying to avoid boredom by finding creative ways to kill them.  I don't *mind* enemies respawning, but these ones are way too fast.
- The AI is inconsistent.  Sometimes they spot you when you're hiding in the brush.  Other times , they miss you when you are in the open right in front of them.  I can partially forgive this, since it is an older game.
- Gun damage is very inconsistent.  Five pistol shots to a bare chest at point-blank won't kill.  But a sniper rifle is always a one-shot kill.  I would be more forgiving of this from a normal FPS, but FC2 is obviously a game that takes itself seriously and I feel like this detracts from the "hardcore" feeling for me.
- The two sides in the civil war are completely interchangeable.  This is at least partially intentional, since the game is creating a bleak, mercenary-driven civil war where everyone is bad.  However, the player hardly ever sees the two factions fighting, and both sides seem to always want to kill the main character on sight.  While it's partly justifiable, it also seems a bit lazy to me.  I feel like the game loses it's appeal a lot faster because of this.
- The main plot feels somewhat railroaded.  For example, you *must* work for both sides of the ongoing civil war to advance the plot (i.e. one side just stops giving you missions and you need to start going to the other side).  The ending was completely railroaded, as well.  Some have argued that this is because the player doesn't have complete control over the main character.  This is supported somewhat by the journal entries he writes during the game.  However, it strikes me as a bit lazy.
Bottom Line: My enjoyment of this game was like a bell curve.  Early on, I was very frustrated by some of the questionable mechanics.  By the middle of the game, I had adapted, gotten a good loadout, and was having a pretty good time.  But by the end of the game, the repetitiveness and plot-railroading got to me and I just wanted it to end.  There's a really good game somewhere in there, though.
If it sounds appealing to you, get it while on sale or as part of the franchise pack.

Well, what can be said about Far Cry 2 ? The follow-up to FC 1 - not developed by Crytek which should focus on the to-be-released first Crysis that would set new standards in graphics and enactment in FPS in the day, but Ubisoft Montreal instead  - which was a great sandbox/openworld shooter promised many things and many hands-on by Game magazines made me long for this game back in the day.
It should became some years later until I finally managed to get my hands on it during a steam sale and I was pretty disappointed after the credits rolled.
Strange thing is, the
the developers had for this game sounded really great: A breathing, living, open world, choosing a side between different factions, a buddy-system, choices and consequences, degrading weapons (first FPS-game since System Shock 2 that had this mechanic at least from the games I know of), gorgeous visuals... I mean, what's not to love ? Well, Practice turned out different than Theory.
Well, first let's focus on the things the Game got right.
now the bad and the ugly:

It builds itself on being somewhat realistic, instead of hyperstimulating like its sequels. Hindering mechanics allow you to live out your mercenary power fantasy while still feeling vulnerable,and most of the mechanics are handled in game rather than in menus, so there's very little pausing. At the same time, it remains far simpler in formula compared to similar titles, like Stalker. Much of the game's open world has you doing side missions which, while sticking to very repeated formulas, are still very enjoyable. The faction and story missions, which offer choices within them, are sadly often served to the player in a fashion that gives the player very little choice at first, for example, forcing the player to work for a faction he may not want to. Other than that, it is very open-ended, allowing the player to make any decision about loadout, and almost any story choice. This can lead to permanent consequences if the player is not careful. The end of the game, while linear, neatly ties up the depressing (for all the right reasons) story, which is memorable because it is told through a combination of dialogue and the unique faction missions. Most notable is the deuteragonist, the Jackal, and how you learn most about him through the tapes and the dialogue of other characters.
The stealth mechanic is something that is often brought up concerning this game. Many people say that stealth is pointless here, but I must disagree. It's not that stealth is futile; It's that stealth sometimes works in a very realistic manner, and sometimes the enemy can't tell when you accidentally almost step on his heel. Variable, yes, but I have not encounted the supposed clairvoyant AI this game has.
Cons:
-First, the AI. Having AI that relentlessly pursues in vehicles and takes cover when needed is one thing I wish more games of this style did, to make it feel dangerous, like there's really a group of lunatics chasing me. Then I saw a car full of baddies plunge off a cliff into a river, while I was safely standing several hundred feet away. Why they did this, I have no idea.
-The graphics. It's not the brown and bloom I have a problem with. In fact, I'd say it sets a very good scene for the atmosphere of the game, and even if you don't want it, you can turn it off in the options. My problem is the pop-in. Maybe it's my toaster of a computer, maybe it's just the game, but it kills my immersion to see everything from billboards to distant hills jump in and out of existence, while enemies and vehicles stay in perfect focus, when I move all of a hundred feet. Also, some of the textures seem stretched, but at least they covered it up with foliage.
-The sound. The music is too loud, while the talking is too quiet. This can be fixed in the options menu, but when I'm trying to have a talk with someone in a building while there's a firefight raging outside, and the voice of those outdoors are muffled, the voice of the guy talking indoors gets muffled in an identical way. Like, this dude standing two feet in front of me sounds like we're speaking through a wall.
-Invisible walls. I'm not talking about the edges of the map. The game world needs to end somewhere, and it rarely encourages you to go out that far. The invisible walls on hills, ledges, and fences where it looks like I should be able to jump over simply do not allow it. Why these could not have been covered by actual objects, I do not know.
-Ubisoft account requirement for a lot of the features. Multiplayer requires a Ubisoft account, as does the promotional content and mapshare (which is sad, because this mapmaker is one of the easiest to use and gives very fine results).
-Programming errors. Sometimes music tracks loop endlessly if a game is loaded under certain circumstances, requiring a trip back to the main menu, and then another load to the game.
The Jackal Tapes are also a bit bugged. Every tape I picked up after the one about the boy with the boots has been about the boy with the boots. Thank heavens for YouTube.
When I take a bus into some of the ceasefire zones, especially later in the game, sometimes a soldier on patrol in the town will just spontaneously die for no reason. It even happened to the APR doorman at Mosate Selao, and the game claimed I broke the ceasefire, so I had to leave and come back to make everyone once again nonhostile.
Other than that, the game is an experience like few others. If you want an open world game that gives you something to do, that makes you actually feel in danger, that punishes you for not taking it seriously, this is for you.

Here's my Quick Look at Galacide:
Galacide is a mashup of a horizontal Shmup + Columns. If you are unfamiliar with Columns, it was a simple match-3 game to be a competitor for Tetris.  Sega bought the game from Jay Geertsen and bundled the game with the Game Gear to have their own must-have puzzle game on a handheld.
If you rotate the Columns into Rows, you have the same idea but in a Shmup.  Enemies drop different colored pieces that you then have to append to other structures creating 3 or more of the same color in a pattern to remove those obstacles.
You start off with three ships that have varying degrees of Health, Power, Speed and each have their own unique ability.  The starting ship has a tractor beam for pulling in colored gems faster, but cannot store any colored gems.  The second ship allows you to store colored gems for later use and the third ship allows you to create a clone of your ship that attracts enemies while you are now freely allowed to go through any of the blocks.
The third ship is really interesting in that it plays more like a traditional bullet hell shmup because you don't need to worry yourself about the puzzle element of the game.
Right now, the game is still in early access and the first two ships play against the meat of puzzle aspects of the game.  I think it needs to be tweaked a bit.  Right now, the game can slow down tremendously with very long sequences of bricks to break. I tend to prefer the third ship at higher difficulties to get a more traditional sense of the shmup genre.
Still, I look forward to seeing this game progress as it's an interesting mash-up.

Full Release Review:
So it's been five months since Galacide entered Early Access and damn, is this game a blast. This is coming from a guy who typically doesn't like Puzzle games or side scrolling shooters (because I suck) yet this game makes for an interesting and challenging experience. Basically, you choose from 1 of 4 ships (there is local multiplayer and it's controller compatible) and attempt to blast your way through literally HUNDREDS of enemies while at the same time matching colored blocks that literally BLOCK your path (I have fun). It's more indepth than your regular bullet hell game because of the varying blocks that get harder and harder to match up as levels drag on. Plus there are bosses at the end of each mission which require different strategies to eliminate. The music is great, the controls are smooth and the gameplay is fluid, what more could you ask for? Did I mention the developers are actually super cool and communicate with the community? Definitely a recommended title!
Early Access Review:
Impressions and Summary:
Fun and challenging as hell. A mix of side scrolling shoot em ups of yesteryear but with a mix of quick puzzle madness. The best way I describe it is mix Galaga or Ikaruga with Puzzle Quest or Tetris. It's difficult, even on the lower settings and one false move can cost you a life. Add in a cheap price, a good musical score and developers who actually keep in contact with their fans, you're left with a game that is worth every single penny.

Update! 7/28 - Launch Day!
First Let me congratulate Puny Human on a successful Early Access and the Wonderful game Galacide!
I've gotten a chance to play some more of Galacide since the initial review and wanted to update my review.
This game is still great and now with the polish through-out early access it has gotten even better.
Now with an overarching single player mode where you select your levels from the 'starmap' (there's even a little story to go along with your puzzle solving).
I also wanted to point out the tutorial/introduction level, it walks you through the mechanics of the game very well, even introducing what I think is a new mechanic that allows you to morph bits and change their color (this is great especially if you get trapped in a wall of puzzle pieces).
So now in the finished version of Galacide you have 6 worlds of the campaign mode, an endless mode, and the newly introduced Puzzle Mode, which is premade puzzles where you must clear all the blocks from to complete the stage.
With all this added content I still highly recommend checking out Galacide as a unique, fun, and challenging Puzzle Shooter.
**************************************************************************************************************
Galacide is a side-scrolling shooter puzzle game, full of action and challenge.
The goal here in Galacide, is to blast through enemies and collect the bits they drop, which are different colored squares. As your ship moves to the right of the screen you must shoot these bits at a moving wall of other bits to make matches of 4 or more to clear your path.
So not only are you dodging enemies and bullets, you must also try to clear the puzzle to fly onto the next zone.
The game keeps the pace with some great music, and design. Meshing the shooter and puzzle genres together in a fun and challenging way.
There are three of four ships available in the Early Access, each with it's own unique blaster and tiers. As you progress your weapon tiers up. So, for instance, the start ships tiers are. Single laser, tri-laser and a giant death beam of death murder (totally not what it's called) which shoots a giant laser across the screen. It destroys just about everything.
Currently, all that's available is the training map and an endless mode, however, those are enough for me to recommend this game. With the promise of a campaign mode and additional ships, this game will be a fun challenge for puzzle seekers out there.

One look at Thea's World Map view and one might think, "Ah, a Civilization knockoff."  It turns out this couldn't be further from the truth!  Thea isn't even in the 4X genre.  I would say Thea is mainly a turn-based RPG in which you scavenge and plunder resources from the surrounding world to strengthen your team by crafting more powerful gear for them.  You can use this power to complete the main quest chain which will lead you to fulfilling one of the three Victory conditions of Thea, and then a second if you choose to keep playing after the first is complete.  Of course you can also just ignore the main quest and do what you please, sandbox style.
There is no expansion through the building of additional settlements.  Instead, your one settlement serves as a home base where you can bring the resources you earn during your travels.  It is also important to ensure your home is adequately defended, for you will lose the game if it falls!
Each patron god in Thea's Pantheon earns EXP when you complete a game with them, unlocking new bonuses in future games and adding replay value.  Additional replay value is added by the randomized world of Thea.  Aside from the randomization of the map itself, random events will trigger as you go, each of which can be solved (or failed) in multiple ways.
Yes, combat is not the only way to deal with the problems Thea will throw at you.  Apart from Warriors, various classes in the game specialize in different non-combat skills, such as stealth and magic.  There are social skills to talk your way out of troubles, and also healing skills to combat sickness and death by injury.
One thing Thea does have in common with Civilization is the insidous "one more turn" mentality that can keep you playing for hours longer than you realized.  It is an exceptional and unique RPG, and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys turn-based games.

A good turn based mix of RPG and Builder/Explorer.
Developing your village at the start takes some time, but as you gather more people, you will eventually be able to put multiple exploration groups out.
Combat is an interesting stylized card match. Half your squad is randomly in the front line (round up), and can thus attack twice in the first round.  The other half can only join confused, getting one attack in the first round, but can instead use their skills to modify the battlefield. I prefer to knock out my opponents cards when possible, and confuse powerful enemies, if done right, you can set up precise kills without wasting damage.
Do watch out, taking even a little damage can have negative effects, so save frequently. Iron man mode game, one save file, although there is an autosave.
Crafting in village is also an interesting part, since once you get mutliple resources, you can craft your particular item crafting to make exactly what you want. I recommend turning OFF use new items automatically, and manually turn on things you DON'T want to craft with, which is just about nothing. Let your people eat nothing but base food and burn cheap wood, save the good stuff for crafting.
I'll leave the story line to you, so as not to spoil it.
Overall if you like party management, resource gatherer, or explorer games, there will probably something in this one you will like, if you like all those, this is a definate get. If full price still scares you, get it on sale, I think you will be pleased.

TLDR: Good story and good game mechanics all things considered, but lots of small (and one huge) issues just bothered me too much. I bought it when it was on sale and despite the issues I would recommend anyone to do the same if interested in tactical RPGs.
The good things:
- I liked the selection of dialogue choices and the fact that what you see on screen is what your character will actually say. This is opposed to Bioware games (Mass Effect, Dragon Age) where the actual response may not even have the attitude the selection seemed to give.
- Target hit chance is given per bullet and not per ability. Meaning if you burst fire, you may miss with first bullet, but may still hit with the second one. Seems like obvious game design, but considering it's not the case with the popular X-Com reboot, thought I'd mention it.
- More than one way to approach missions, depending on your skillset.
- If you care about them, then all the achivements can be acquired with 1 playthrough with minimal backtracking, that's including the game endings. Make sure to read through an achievement guide, because there's one thing that can force you to replay almost half the game (the 2 Dante achievements). Also you can create a character that will have access to majority of "optimal" paths while still being good in combat (Tip: Get security etiquette, then probably gang and corporate).
The annoying things:
- While overall the story and setting were good, there were many things that just irked me. We are in this future high-tech cyber society where secrecy and flow of information is important, and I completely understand that they had to make "hacking" something playable and the way it was done doesn't bother me, but these passwords are just nonsense. Important company terminals have one short dictionary word as passwords (and no username), private apartments are locked just behind a 4 digit PIN that doesn't even lock after inputing it wrong numerous times. There are other small things like that which break the suspension of disbelief for me, though that's probably a personal problem.
- UI and team/item management. Why can't I see the stats or equipment of my team members while in the hub area? Why can't I see the upgrades I've chosen for my team members during missions? Why can't I give items I find during a mission to a team member? Why can't I equip a (newly acquired) weapon during a mission? Why can't I look at mission items while having the keypad menu open (mission items contain also passwords so you want to see them for input)? Why don't the abilities have keybinds?
- Difficulty. Game recommended hard for players who are at home with tactical team based combat, so I chose hard. While the first mission felt challenging (mostly cause it was the first time I played it), the game got easy quite fast and the last 4 or more missions were a cakewalk and that's even without relying on loading a save. I am fairly certain it's because at later stages of the game I invested a lot of points into Quickness, Ranged weapons and Rifles while using an automated rifle, and it definitely felt like the strongest weapon in the game. I had 90%+ chance to hit and most hits were criticals.
- Two smaller bugs I remember, that annoyed me enough to mention them. When equipping a new weapon at character loadout screen and when you already have the maximum weapon slots used (I had a deck and 2 grenade launchers), the new weapon just disappears. It's as if you don't have it anymore, though it seems to be only a visual bug since I had it equipped in the mission, but regardless I had to waste a bit of time in reloading my game a few times. For Eiger's final upgrade I chose the ability Speed Loader, which reloads all of your weapons for free (no AP usage), I used it 3 times and it didn't reload either of my weapons. Didn't bother to try more than that.
All of the bad things I mentioned so far wouldn't have been enough to actually give a thumbs down, but there's this one bug, that unless you know what the issue is, can make you waste a lot of time or outright make you quit the game. In the second to last mission, APEX Rising, there is an issue with saving the game. You save the game and then the game stops responding, you can move the camera around and even go to the menu, but nothing else really works. Now this happened 2 or 3 times before while playing, but in that particular mission there's a difference - it also removes your saves from certain point. Granted it kept the saves from a certain point in that mission, so you don't need to restart it, but after 3 reloads, I was done. I googled and there was a developer response to it in 2015, they are aware of the issue and it's caused by saving the game when you have started the decking and need to hold out for a number of turns and the workaround is simply to NOT save your game during that time. To this day the developers have not fixed this bug, they explained it to be very complex and most likely did not want to dedicate that much time for it. That's the main reason for not giving this game a thumbs up, for wasting a lot of my time on lost progress. When doing APEX Rising mission, just make sure you save after arriving in the basement and never again during this run. The mission itself was very easy.

It's been a long time since a game has come out that really makes me want to play through a second time.
The storytelling in Dragonfall is something one rarely sees in a video game. Simple narration most of the time, but sublimely detailed, and loaded full of complex and subtle characters that all feel real and deep. When you act nice for no reason, they tell you to screw off, and when you pry into their backstory, they resist. Dragonfall brings the world of Shadowrun alive like no game in the franchise ever has before.
The actual gameplay has a narrow focus, and consists of equal parts roleplaying and simple-tactics, cover-based combat. The various classes, spells, equipment, and level system give you enough to get creative with your strategy but keep the fights moving along. Combat WILL seem too slow or simple for some players, so keep that in mind if you think this may apply to you.
Another fantastic selling point is the way Dragonfall consistently hammers the player with legitimate, difficult moral choices. As a tool to the people with real power, the player has to be willing to accept a job on very little information, and compromising one's morals is nigh-inevitable in the face of daunting odds and the never-ending pressure to acquire more money for a greater purpose.
I can't recommend this game enough. Dragonfall does what the Shadowrun Returns sought to do, better.

Grim Fandango is a LucasArts classic adventure game, and hoo boy, is it a classic.
It's hard to go wrong when you've got this many skeletons in one game as it is, but Grim Fandango excels beyond expectations even then.
The characters are all memorable, the dialogue is hilarious and witty, the design of the world is gorgeous, the story is intriguing and complex, the visuals are striking (if you're a fan of 90's CGI you're in for a treat), and it ticks every box for me when it comes to what I want out of an adventure game.
For those curious between the differences between the original and the Remastering, the Remastering mostly offers a visual facelift (for the most part anyway), developer commentary, concept art, a point and click system, and not much else. The cutscenes and some backgrounds are noticably dated still, the cutscenes just being scaled up to widescreen and not actually having any visual upgrades. However, I'm willing to forgive it as the actual creation process behind the remaster was a nightmare, as none of the original source material had been preserved and it had to be hacked together through all sorts of crazy means.
Overall, the biggest benefit to the remastering is the fact that it is uploaded digitally, keeping this game, ironically enough, from death, easily accessible for the forseeable future. You can even switch to the original visuals any time you want if you want that classic 90's goodness.
The game's biggest weak point is probably the puzzles. Many adventure games feature puzzles less about logic and more about figuring out what kind of drugs the devs were doing, and Grim Fandango frequently is no different. I was not able to make it through the game without hints, and I imagine you won't be able to either. It's certainly a flaw, but it's one that people who like adventure games are used to dealing with.
If you like spooky skeletons, calacas, and stuff with heavy Spanish themes, you'll love this. If you're looking for a game for Halloween, this is right up your alley. If you like good games, you'll love this. Play this. I can't recommend it enough. THIS GAME. IS GOOD. BUY IT.

Let me start by saying that this open-world FPS isn't for everyone. I started playing this game years ago, and i finally finished it only a couple weeks ago. This is partly because of the massiveness of the game, and partly because of the repetitive nature of it. One review i read of this game said it's the game that "doesn't give you what you want, and slaps you for asking". This is very true, the game presents many obstacles (guns that deteriorate and jam, malaria that makes you have to take medicine at any given point in the game, lack of ammo & resources, etc.) and doesn't have a single auto save. Every save is manual. Every. One. Fast travel is hardly any faster than driving across the giant map, because you can only travel to and from one of 5 fast travel stations on the map. And let me tell you, vehicles in this game do NOT go fast.
This giant stew of inconveniences is what gives this game it's value. The setting is Africa, a wasteland containing only violence, disease, and scarcity. By making the player endure these frustrations, Far Cry 2 gives every convenience you recieve a kind of personal importance. The regular attacks from enemies beat you down until you become a proud killing machine. The slow and dangerous nature of transportation in this open world gives you a familiarity with the map, and maybe (what happened in my case) an unprecedented respect for the design. The story plays a passive role in this game (kill things, get payed, get closer to completing your main mission), but it fits into the violent & depressing theme. The ending, however, is fantastic.
This game is slow. The combat is relentless and routine. You have to struggle to complete each mission, and the characters are all shallow. By stripping away all the usual comforts you would expect to find, Far Cry 2 does something extraordinary. It puts you outside of your comfort zone. You're alone in this troublesome world, and you have to discover for yourself how to make it out alive.
Was fun for a little bit, but went to play Far Cry 3 instead since it is a vast improvement over Far Cry 2.

It only allows you to make a mistake if there are no valid moves... Not allowing your players to make a mistake and fail removes the challenge from the game.
The graphics are good, it has a nice art style and runs smooth, as it should from a 2d puzzler.
The settings screen however is extremely bugged, options have arrows to set the setting, now for anyone that would mean that one of the arrows increases the value (for example sound level) and the other decreases it. This is not the case with this game, the arrows are only for show, clicking them simply increases the value until it reaches max and then it will reset to 0. This is one of the more daunting problems with the game, the lack of finish.
Apart from the art style I would say this is a simple semester project from someone studying game design and not paying attention in class.
Gameplay is horribly repetitive and lacks any originality, movement is not as smooth as you expect, there is a noticable and annoying delay after going to the side before you can do anything again, and the game lacks action, which is not good for a game that advertises itself as an action-puzzle gamer.....

This was a fun ride.
It's nonsensical Suda51 goodness. I finished it and I'm pretty sure about 90% of what the story was trying to say was entirely lost on me. Something about the moon?
It's a character action game, much like Bayonetta in a lot of ways, and nothing like Bayonetta in many others.
As far as any combat system goes, it's not even nearly as deep as Bayo or DMC, in that it has one normal attack button, one guard break button that doesn't find itself part of many combos, a dodge/guard button and then a subweapon you can use. The subweapons are fairly boring, in that you have a gun that slows, a gun that stuns, a gun that just shoots and a drill that breaks armor. Really, combat comes down to mashing your attack button, guarding/dodging at the right time (and as per usual, you get a big bonus for timing guards/dodges perfectly), and shooting things that need shot.
In terms of polish, it looks good, it plays really nicely (even if not all that deep) and it sounds good. English VA is mostly about as good as you can expect from a title like this. That is, intentionally cheesy but not really *bad*.
The most interesting part of this game is probably the Gigolo missions, in which you hang out with a lovely lady and, while she isn't looking, look at her, uh, nicest areas, until you build up the 'Guts' to give her a present. Give her enough presents that she likes, and you have successfully completed the mission, and you get a nice cutscene. Then you get an item, be that one of the subweapons or a temporary boost item.
A very fun but relatively small game. If you like fast, skill-based combat and like to replay missions for ranks or on higher difficulties, this game will have a lot for you. If you like playing through cheesy, funny and outright weird Japanese games, this game will have a lot for you too.
I'd recommend it for a few days of fun.

Not even Dungeons and Dragons Online which was pretty bad inventory management and incredibly time-wasting.
The devs could have created a way to optimize gear with one button, but chose not to. So instead you'll spend most of your time trying to optimize gear so your people don't die permanently faster than they otherwise would.
The game - beyond that major complaint - is fun and innovative, with definitely interesting twists on the 4X tropes. But because of the inventory problems, I can't reccomend the game. There are other, better 4X games out there to "one more turn" in.

My introduction to the Shadowrun series (yeah, I know playing a game that was originally DLC for another game, Shadowrun Returns) and I gotta say I'm pretty impressed.
I really dig the setting first of, it's like if the characters and creatures of Dragon Age lived in the world of Blade Runner. The story is very good, it doesn't feel like it's over stating it's welcome and does a good job and keeping you on your toes as to what the big mystery is and it's a good pay off. The characters overall are very interesting though I wish there was more development with them, you look at older RPGs like Planescape Torment and the first two KOTOR games, I really felt like I got to know my party and they interacted with each other in interesting ways. Here, we get to know some of their backstories and what their personalities are but the game doesn't go much beyond that, there are no personal missions for the characters like in Mass Effect for example but they do a good enough job with them.
The combat is good. It requires very good strategy and patience especially on the harder difficulties. The role playing is also very good, you can definitely play this game your own way and portray yourself the way you want, although all of the classes have their own limitations so don't expect a street samurai to be a hacking expert which is good, it makes the player have to work around their limitations for a solution instead of looking for the easy way out all the time. I don't like that you can't control your party members outside of combat. What if I'm approaching a room and I want my party members positioned in a certain way? Well, tough luck, You can't (still not as bad as the PS2 version of Persona 3 where you can't control your party members at all)
The graphics are average especially with the character models, it's an indie game so I won't be too hard on it but artistically, it gets the job done. It's suppose to make you feel like you're in a dystopian city and it succeeds at that although I find the environments kinda samey. I'm not saying make it like Zelda with fire, water, forest environments or whatever but they could've definitely done more with it than gray hallways, sewers, and more gray hallways. Games like Deus Ex and System Shock I feel did a better job with freshening up the environments and levels while still being consistent with their world
The music I also think is okay. There are some good tracks here and there but overall it's not a soundtrack I see myself desperating wanting to listening to
Overall, It's very good game for fans of cyberpunk. It's not perfect, it's no Deus Ex, System Shock 2, or Snatcher but if you're looking for another cyberpunk game to hold you over until Cyberpunk 2077 finally comes out. This is a solid one to check out and I give it an 8/10

It's hard to judge Shadowrun games. If you own just Dragonfall - DC, you'll get it over with a couple of lines like "amazing! Very cool story, engaging combat!" but if you played Returns, Dragonfall and Hong Kong, it becomes a little harder.
I think in this case it's about "Quality over quantity", in comparison to Hong Kong, Dragonfall really takes the cake for quality. Even so, even quantity overflows in comparison of what Dead Man's Switch in Returns has to offer. The main campaign of Dragonfall is one of the best out there, imho, even though I still need to dig in the mods (got a couple of titles that look promising) and to be completely honest, if I had played Hong Kong before Dragonfall... dunno, I think the spark wouldn't... spark. I fell in love with Dragonfall: The Flux State, Berlin, your party and the world around are SO passionate.
Options for resolving the missions are WIDE. With wide I mean that I was not prepared for it: there are a ton. Having played Returns AFTER Dragonfall I can totally see the sheer amount of dialogue options they added.
Combat is better than in Returns, and bugs are non-existant. Atleast, my run was glitch-free. I enjoyed it every minute and I would recommend this over anything.
To notice that I did not know anything about the Shadowrun world before this game, and I've read a lot on the wiki just to get a shape of what those various events/tidbits you find about the world are supposed to really be (Hong Kong does this a bit more than Dragonfall, but still you'll find a lot of sidequests pointing you at things happening at other cities in the world, Chicago or Seattle included).
The price is a bit hefty, but it's Returns all over again: a very good official campaign, and the campaign editor. Totally recommended.

This is an early access game (atleast I think it is), so I'll give it a bit slack. Plus I got only got this game for a dollar, so I can't expect too much.
As of right now, this game looks like the older NFS games (Between Underground and Carbon) but just drifting, with the controls being noticibly more refined for simulated racing, rather than an arcadey one. This isn't that bad, the graphics are surprisingly decent for an indie game and you can tell a lot of effort went to the cars and drifting mechanics. Plus there's also a legitimately decent driver camera and there's a good selection of popular modern and classic tuner cars to choose from.
One bad part is that the game is just badly optimized. I can run most modern racing titles just fine, but this thing struggles badly with framerate issues, even when I've restorted to almost minimal settings. Another problem is that the game's UI is too minimalistic and lacks crucial information (a pretty glaring problem for a simulator). Nothing there doesn't explain what you're suppose to do, how your tuning settings affect vehicle performance, or how races work. Sure, there's online explanations elsewhere, but the thing is; players aren't suppose to look elsewhere to explain how the game works. The game itself should be explaining the core game mechanics.
You're just suppose to go in there and either sink or swim and overall the game kinda just feels dead. Not the "no players" dead, there's some multiplayer activity, but you have little to no interaction with everything else that the entire game feels souless.
Overall, its nice to look at and there is a lot of potential for this game, but the actual game just isn't fun right now. If you want a better low-performance racing game that has better drifting mechanics; I'd really just recommend playing NFSU2 or GRID 1 (granted GRID 1 doesn't have the tuning aspect but its' still leagues better, especially for a game that came out almost a decade ago).

The issue with Far Cry 2 is that it's marketed incorrectly. They sell it as a shooter and so people think they should run around and engage enemies whenever they see them. If you try to do that in Far Cry 2, you'll die - first in the game, then of boredom.
It's a realistic, stealth based shooter and that's how it should be treated. Imagine that you're actually running around in Africa trying to survive and you'll do better. You avoid combat unless you need not to or have a great advantage, if you are discovered by a multitude of enemies, you wreak havoc and run for your life. You infiltrate during the night, not the daytime. You don't drive around on the road near checkpoints in a country at war. You kill without mercy and you get better at it as the game goes on. Not through XP and levels, but just by improving. That's an amazing experience in itself.
If you think carefully, stealth around a bit and plan your approach, there's literally no game ever made that'll reward you like this one will. You can choose to go in hard with granades and LMGs, or snipe from a hill top or sneak up close and take them down one at a time (or not take them down and just do what you came for). You'll pull off amazing infiltrations and assassinations, you'll experience an enemy truly scared of you and you play a story that transcends any attempted in a shooter before. Based on Conrad's great novel "The Heart of Darkness" (like Apocalypse Now is), you'll get an interesting and raw approach to Africa and the wars that ravage the continent. This game actually has something to say and it knows how to say it. It is, however, not a sandbox, casual fun shooter and it was a mistake to market it as such.
A word of advice, put the game on top difficulty. The AI seems broken on the lower ones and the game doesn't become too hard on the hardest one. Just as long as you remember that if you're outnumbered five to one and they know where you are, you're not going to win. At least not always. Collapse

OK, and now for the review i have been waiting to do......
What can i say about this game, aside that i believe it's about as close to perfection as a game can get...???  From the AI, the weapons, the amount of immersion, graphics, story, sound, everything in this game just oozes awesomeness.
This was a game that managed to draw a fine line between what people enjoyed and didnt.  Either you absolutely hated it, or you loved it dearly, with no middleground.  Most of the complaints revolved around the respawning checkpoints, which didnt bother me because, well, IT IS a shooter afterall.  If you're playing a shooter and you're not shooting something, then it can get a little boring sometimes.
First on the discussion list is the story.  Loosely based on the short book titled "Heart of Darkness," the story has the player hunting an arms dealer named The Jackal who supplies two rival factions with an armory to start, and continue waging war against each other.  On your journey you aid both factions in search of information of the Jackal's whereabouts.  Now, this isnt a story that unfolds like you initially think it will.  Far Cry 3's story is very similar in context, but told in a more dude-bro lingo, while Far Cry 2 does so in a rich, yet immensly dark tone that will test what kind of man (or woman) you would become in this situation.  Considering that you're thrown into a real-world senario in a fictional African country, the story is constantly unfolding without the player even knowing.  Many games these days have taught us that the story is only told through dialogue or cutscenes, but this game has a story that unfolds with every bullet you fire, and every death you cause.  It's a morailty tale that might give each player the insight as to who or what kind of person he or she is, or will become.
The gunplay is some of the best i've personally encountered in any game.  From the sniper rifles, to the assault rifles, to my personal favorite, the 6P9 silenced Makarov, every gun feels rather unique in its own right.  Each sniper rifle has a different characteristic, the 2 rocket launchers each perform differently, even (most of) the pistols perform differently.  And, of course, everyone's favorite is unlockable very early in the game:  the flare gun.  Spreading fire was the key innovative feature in this game, and when done correctly is a very strategic tactic when taking on the numerous guardposts.
The AI is unscripted and acts accordingly to you.  If you haven't engaged the targets, they talk amongst themselves.  If they think someone is nearby, they will slowly approach the location of the disturbance.  Also, your reputation determines how aggressively the AI will combat you.  The lower your reputation is means the AI will hunt you down because they dont fear you.  The higher the reputation is the more cautious they are, meaning they may find cover or try to flank you.
The graphics and sound seem very dated in 2015, but for it's time it was top notch.  Some might argue that the graphics in Far Cry 2 are better overall than Far Cry 3.  When you factor in small details like shadow resolution, texture quality, and Ambient Occlusion, Far Cry 2 does have the upper hand over 3.
Lastly, the immersion plays a pivotal role in this game.  There is next to no regenerating health and health is restored using syringes or water bottles.  Malaria can attack you at any given point, although as your symptoms improve the time between attacks increases.  When very low on health your character performs a "surgical technique," in what is basically described as one of the coolest animations in a video game.  Gruesome, sure.  Cool???  You bet!
I've logged over 600 hours in this game on steam, and another 200+ on disk, and almost all invested in single player.  I can't even describe why i keep coming back to this game so much.  Maybe it has to do with the fact that this game allows my imagination to run wild in the combat senarios.  Maybe because the story is that engaging.  I don't know.  What i do know is that since this game came out 6+ years ago, i've only found 1 other game like it, and it still doesn't hold a candle to this sheer brilliance.
Advice for new players reading this???  Give the game some time.  Allow yourself to sink into the story and REALLY think about your every action and what it's doing to you.  Study how every decision you make affects YOU, not your character, but YOU.  And for the love of god, play with all the guns.  There's only 31 guns (with DLC).

The Static Speaks My Name is a very interesting game that has a good deal of potential. My take on it was that you are somehow able to live through someone right before they died and see their thought process and a window into their madness. You get to see what really drove them to the edge. In this particular scene you play as a man named Jacob who has some serious problems. He has boarded off all of the doors leading to the outside of his house, his alarm is set to wake him at 3:22 in the morning. His house has no food, just a shrimp tank that he eats from as they are still alive. Probably the most interesting aspect is his obsession that is way past insane over a painting. I do not want to spoil to much but it is a fun little game. Its free so it is definitely worth playing, just be warned, it has some depressing undertones that one can relate if bad enough.
However I do believe it is a game that we can all relate to on some personal level. This man has no friends, he talks to people that obviously are not there. And he has an obsession that drives him to madness. I can see this game definitely picking up some momentum and really going somewhere but I suppose only time will tell. There are also a lot of interesting theories floating around about this game, so kudos on sparking that. Its one of those games that stands out, my only nit pick is the design of the game, but hey better graphics don't make a better game.
Overall, its a good little waste of time and definitely worth a damn. 6/10

I want to preface this review by saying i first started playing this series around halfway through 2K13, i fell in love with it despite not knowing very much about basketball, i grew more and more familiar with it and i was hooked, playing the game most days which led to my interest in real basketball, which has now become my favorite sport to watch.
I want to start the review by addressing the micro transactions you've probably heard about by now - i'm not going to beat a dead horse, it's extremely prevalent here, 2K takes every opportunity they can to advertise VC, you can buy it from most menus within the game and its extremely encouraged by the developers. You're at an extreme disadvantage in every single facet of the MyCareer mode by not opening your wallet for those attributes.
MyCareer.
The fan favorite mode returns here worse than it's ever been, riddled with cliches, cringe and cutscenes. The scenes are all unskippable so if you enjoy having multiple players good luck to you. The cliches within said cutscenes ruins any immersion and realism of having a player career, if you dont care for immersion within your unskippable story then this wont hinder your experience at all, you have the zen master guy who sells made-up fruit smoothies, the stat guy who spews nothing but numbers among many others, your friend who you start the game with "bee" is arguably the worst character ever made within a sports title, little to no thought put into this character, will make you either wince with sheer cringe or burst out laughing at how laughably shocking some of her lines and actions are. All in all, it's a pay to win mess that doesn't incentivise actually playing it and instead opening your wallet to fast track to the point where you can actually become competitive within each mode.
MyTeam
I usually dont play this mode but found myself goofing off within the normal domination single player mode which has you pit your team against each of the current teams to collect stars, once you have beaten each team with the max rating you unlock exclusive rewards, which is a choice of a nice Amethyst card with a high overall, however - this turns to garbage nearing the end as the devs confuse difficulty with cheating. The CPU often making ridiculous shots on too frequent an occasion to be luck, your players missing wide open shots even with a good release and high rating and odd cheese like the ball clipping through your players yet the CPU is able to keep possession of the ball, the CPU "bumping" into your players, causing legendary players who are some of the greats of the game to just magically drop the ball for...reasons?
The online play is no different to what has become the norm, people abusing the system to win, playing sim basketball how you see it on TV isn't incentivised and instead it turns into a cheese-off, with players "zig-zagging" side to side to abuse the defense, blow by animations which gift the offensive player a straight run to the hoop by simply holding down the turbo button, regardless of which player is on offence or defense, not to mention 5 out and pick and roll/pop spam. In short, it's an absolute mess. Yes you can stop these cheesy tactics and part of this is also me being bad, but for me there's just a point when fighting against this cheese is just too much and quickly becomes not fun.
In conclusion
This game is a total cash grab as stated by everyone and their pet goldfish, this game is a far cry from what it used to be and because of that i can't recommend this game to anyone, if you're a basketball fan and have a console too, then NBA Live is much improved this year, if you don't then the older games are much better than whatever this is.

The game is hard to get the hand of but it provides many ways to run your country and taking a country like Botswana and turning it into a nuclear power is one of most rewarding things in a game. Relations between countries are realistic and change with even the smallest action that you take, making gaining influence over other countries a challenge. One of the best features of the game is the large choice of map types that you can use to display all kinds of information on. These maps turn the globe into a detailed infographic for things from millitary strength to something as minor as car production.
The millitary side of the game is quite disapointing, as it is very simple, and the crude cutscenes that show your troops and vehicles fighting are quite ugly. The game rewards patience and one who strives to achieve global dominance through gaining allies and economic manipulation is more likely to achieve their goal than someone who musters up the biggest army possible and starts invading their neighbours.
This game is very detailed and hard to master, and will provide many hours of entertainment, however it can become repetative and boring at times and is probably best suited to someone who is very patient.

Several reviews here have touched upon price as a primary consideration in the purchase, but for what is on offer - if you play and take advantage - there is great depth  and longevity to the game.  It is, at its heart, a match jewel game akin to those from Popcap, but much deeper.  Instead of just reactionary matching, here you MUST plan ahead to make sure that your matches line up properly and allow completion of the puzzle.  As such, it is a neat inversion of that easy click addiction; on the surface it is simple, but to advance requires forethought, planning, and keen attention to detail.  In short, it is a puzzle game with all the trappings of matching but with all the puzzling you can handle.
At full price I think it is still well worth the purchase for the single-player content alone.  And if you desire to go into competitive puzzling, there is a whole repaste of multiplayer modes.  Included in your full price purchase is a regenerating Steam key for you to distribute among friends so you can always have a multiplayer faceoff.  Quite recommended if you have some patience and enough gray matter to know you'd like to test it.
EDIT: I've not come nearly close enough to finish the game (there are 300 puzzles!) but a few wearisome issues have popped up.  It may be a puzzle game, but some puzzles are extremely unforgiving: unless you wish to work the solution out before even shooting pieces, some puzzles are unsolvable with 1 bad start.  As there is no in-puzzle "save" option, you must re-work the puzzle completely.  Granted, few take a long time to complete (or mess up, it may be!) but it becomes irritating to replay a level over and over.  It isn't that the puzzles are too hard so much as that there is only 1 way to solve them, which after time means you feel it is less a "puzzle" and more an exercise in rigid logic that must be done in just the right way ... or you do it over.  With more eventual diversity in the game mechanics this is more acceptable, but with 30 levels in each stage they tend to drag on, which discourages most from completing them (to wit, the Steam-wide sub 3% completion percentage for just the 2nd level!).  With no in puzzle save option, a small error in selecting which color at the proper time can cause you to replay the level several times.  There is zero room for creative approach for most puzzles.  That is not a complaint about the game design, just a word of warning to interested buyers.  There is still much here to recommend, but be aware that the bright colors, silly animations & story mask a game that requires much commitment, focus, and patience.

You can't play FC2 the way you play FC3 or a CoD. The harder you try to win the game, the harder it fights back.
To play FC2 , to love FC2, you have to break your mind. Players have this idea that they can fight with dignity, that there's a proper way to kill someone. It's absurd. It's anaesthetic; players need it to endure the bloody horror of murder. FC2 destroys that idea, it shows them what a messy, terrible thing it is to kill a man, and then makes players relish in it. Shoot AI to wound, then execute the wounded. Burn AI. Take AI in close combat. Destroy AI's preconceptions of what a player is and  become it's personal monster. When AI fears player, player becomes stronger. Player becomes better. But let's never forget: it's a display, it's a posture, like a lion's roar or a gorilla thumping at its chest. If player loses himself in the display, if player succumbs to the horror, then player becomes the monster. Player becomes reduced; not more than a player, but less—and it can be fatal.

Let me preface this by saying, I've only played 5 hours as of writing so this is more of a first impressions rather than a full review.
Going into the game, I didn't know quite what to expect. When it had first come out I had seen videos of it on youtube but I had never played it because up until recently I did not have access to a decent PC. I remember when I first had contact with the game through youtube I thought it looked fun and wished I could buy it, but I could not. Now I have.
This is my first proper Far Cry game, I own and play Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon but we can probably agree that's not a proper far cry game, though it is fun. And I'm going to be completely honest, Far Cry 2 is amazing. It is by far my favorite singleplayer FPS game. The world while not very large, is large enough to give the illusion of freedom and is definitely what makes this game a lot more fun than say Call of Duty or Battlefield.  The game takes place in an unnamed African country that is torn by war. Two factions, the APR and the UFLL vie for power. You are a mercenary, getting paid to run errands for the factions.
The gameplay can get very repetitive, as it's mostly driving to one location, getting a mission, driving to another location, shooting people, completing objective, driving back to the first location and get paid. However the landscape breaks up the monotony of driving with beautiful and distinct regions. As you travel, you'll notice smooth changes from jungle to desert to plains to swamp. It keeps the game fresh and unique, even the combat is different in different areas as cover options/vantage points change.
The graphics are lacking, but what can you expect from an old game? It runs beautifully on my Dell Inspiron 660s (with an upgraded GPU, nVidia GT 730). I'm running the game at 900p at high settings at a stable 60 FPS. I tried playing at 1080p, but my rig simply could not handle it without dipping down to 30. Any modern gaming pc should easily tackle this game at 1080p. The graphical options are a bit lacking in diversity, mainly boiling down to a few generic sliders but decent enough.
I can't rate the multiplayer, as I have not played it. But if you want a good multiplayer FPS, go buy CS:GO.
There are some things in this game though that are quite annoying, the lack of an autosave feature means that if you forget to save, you may have to backtrack large portions of the game (which can be annoying, however if you remember to save often you should have no problems). Combat can also get repetitive and enemies tend to be extremely bullet spongy (it takes several headshots to take down an enemy). But overall, a solid fun game that will give you many hours of enjoyment.
The story is the last thing I want to touch on. The story is what really makes this game. The characters are well developed and make this game memorable, due to the buddy mechanic you can make friends with characters by completing missions for them and they'll help you out. These buddies really make the game interesting and keep the game fresh even after a while. Often times you'll start a mission and they'll call you up and give you a slightly backstabby but good mission to do instead.
Gameplay - 8/10. The open world and original missions make this game feel fresh and fun, but the repetitiveness of combat and the lack of an autosave features knock it down a couple points.
Story/Characters - 9/10. This is what really makes this game good. The memorable and admirable characters are what makes this game worth playing.
Fidelity - 6/10. It's an older game, but it by no means looks bad. Don't let the older graphics turn you off from playing, this game is really, really good.
Overall - 9/10. The setting/story/characters all come together to make this an extremely fun to play game and a wonderful experience.

So besides "Day of the Tentacle" another LucasArts adventure game classic got its Remastered edition: "Grim Fandango" (1998).
In it you are Manny Calavera, one of the employees working for a travel agency for dead people. Yes, you are in fact dead, too and in the land of the dead. However, Calavera doesn't seem to have good luck on his side when it comes to this businesses. He notices traces of a conspiracy and corruption going on in his company...
Back then in 1998 this was LucasArts' attempt to step into the 3D world with their adventures. The result is great, however, not without small flaws.
First, let's look at the good things the game in general offers (I will come back to the "remastered" element later): It's quite a sophisticated point & click adventure that should keep you occoupied for good chunks of time. The style and humor of "Grim Fandango" are legendary. The world you walk through in "Grim Fandango" is quite fascinating: obviously inspired by the Mexican tradition "Dia de los muertos" (Day of the Dead) but also by 1940's/1950's crime stories. Even if you are not into these topics you might dig this other kind of underworld.
It also might be LucasArts' finest 3D adventure. Even though the graphics might look dated (also now in the remastered edition) it still works. It still looks cool, the animations are fine, it's dark or colourful where it needs to be and the game contains a row of very good cutscenes, including one of the better ending sequences in LucasArts history (at least in my opinion). And it is also fascinating to see how life and personality was put into skeleton characters without eyes.
Speaking of characters: There is a range of great characters, including the main character Manny Calavera.
When it comes to sound: The soundtrack is highly enjoyable to listen to (very jazzy here and there), very well composed! And the voice actors do a great job. Here I also like the German version which includes mostly great voice actors and good wordplays.
The only flaws I can make out in "Grim Fandango" are some frustratingly hard puzzles that are hard to figure out or don't seem to be logical (let alone what you are basically suppoused to do). It is LucasArts tradition to think laterally but sometimes it takes much time and trial & error to come one step further, especially in the "Year 2" chapter. Also in general I wished for a map system like in the "Monkey Island" games so you are forced to run across entire large areas multiple times just to get an item or to talk to somebody.
You can't really die or lose in that game but I have discovered one spot in "Year 2" where you can get stuck just because you forgot to pick up one item somewhere else.
But with that said: The flaws never make the game bad, just a little harder than you are maybe used to. So if you are not at all experienced in point & click adventures you might have a couple of frustrating moments. That's not an advice to avoid the game, just a friendly warning.
Now about the "remastered" in Remastered Edition: This includes polished graphics (characters look less pixelated and were added dynamic light and shade), a fully orchestrated soundtrack (I heard via gaming website ScrewAttack that this had to be done since the original recording couldn't be used anymore), a different game menue (including game-related artwork), Steam achievements (which are not hard to get) and trading cards, an in-game commentary by the makers and - VERY important - the ability to control the game via mouse which was impossible in the original 1998 version (you were forced to use the keyboard which was so annoying back then).
So the "remastered" elements are very fine and might help bring this great adventure classic to a new audience. But don't expect voice recordings or new puzzles and such.
My verdict: Experience this game if you haven't but have some affection for adventure games.
And if you already know "Grim Fandango": just relive this classic one more time and let your love for it revive (as this happened to me).

This game took me a while to "get it", but once I understood the mechanics, I realized the depth of it.  Definitely recommended.
(Note: I dunno why the time counter shows I played 0.2 hours, it was definitely far more).
It is a blend between games like Civilization, Rebuild, Rimworld, and adventure games. It plays in a slavic/eastern european post-apocaliptic fantasy world. Instead of general "units", you have people with various strengths, like one might be great at gathering stuff, the other is very clever and can open up new solution paths, the third is a great warrior, etc. The game is a roguelike, so if a character dies, it stays dead.
You can make small parties that gather stuff away from your village,  hunting parties that can hunt monsters without actually getting into battle, or a general big party that can solve a lot of adventures. Crafting is also great, where different materials used will result in different items (if you make a mace out of gold, it will increase the wearer's willpower, if you make it from part bone, part metal, it will deal more damage, if it is mostly wood, it will be lighter, etc). Even buildings created from different materials won't be the same.
The game is not without flaws, like the UI is hard to use, it is hard to see how much movement points you have left, movement rules are a bit blurry, and requires a lot of micromanagement if you want to play optimally, but the overall strength of the mood and the refreshing nature of the game still makes it worth to play.

Great addition to the Shadowrun series. A well designed squad-based TBS with a solid narrative throughout.
Branching choices and story arcs really make you feel your decisions matter and the multitude of ways to tailor your character and your team mean you can play whatever way you want (don't stick everything into decking though, you need guns, lots of guns).
Highly reccomend this and the previous and subsequent releases from HBS.

Shadowrun universe offers something for everyone - you can use magic, summon elementals, hack into matrix and get through code or send everyone to hell with drones and rifles. This combined with our world, twisted by awakening of magic creates really interesting setting for the Players.
Dragonfall story is really solid and focuses on your team, which creates great pace of progressing, without losing sixth world vibe. Character development is really easy to understand and straightforward, allowing you to focus more on what you would like to do than worrying about numbers and mechanics. You forge your own path - and only yours. This mean that while you have company, they level up and get stronger with less of your influence which gives a nice feeling of being leader, but not playing out their characters - it's more like playing with them.
Mechanically, it's really easy to get into the fight - you have a pool of action points which you can spend on movement, attack, skills, reloading, healing. Cover system is similar to what you probably know from X-Com, however here it actually makes sense and works. All rolls and chances are taken down to minimum, so it's easy to work your way out throught the battlefield. Which does not mean that it's easy to survive - even on normal difficulty, wrong move or bravado can cost you a lose.
Overall, it's one of the best isometric RPGs you can get. It takes about ~24 hours to get through story, so it's a decent lenght to pay a good dime for it and not feel robbed. Also old timers with 9-5 work can easily chill with it after getting home and still play it in some decent manner of time.

Buy this.
Like Shadowrun Returns, a simple turn based RPG, got it in a bundle and therefore, so worth it.

I didn't play Dragonfall until well after it came out where I played Shadowrun Returns almost entirely within the first week it came out; something about the advertising and the art just didn't catch me.  And then, on a whim, I dove in - and it's one of the best RPG stories in recent memory, while addressing many of the issues with Shadowrun Returns.
To give context within the series of games, Shadowrun Returns felt like a nostalgia trip while Hong Kong felt like an excellent role playing session with friends - fun, a little impractical, with a lot of loose ends that don't get quite tired up satisfactorily and have to be explained by the GM.
Dragonfall feels like Shadowrun if Joss Whedon decided he wanted to blow your mind with a complex mystery that makes you think you know where it's going - until you realize you didn't, because the Big Bad wasn't even who you were looking at.  It's phenomenally written, with characters you learn to love with backstories that make them relatable and interesting.  Better yet, it's morally ambiguous and some of the biggest choices are the ones that leave you uneasy in the end - one of the final scenes of the game has been stuck in the back of my head for weeks as one of the most genuinely creepy, threatening things I can think of.
With no caveats at all, Dragonfall is a blast and a story more people should get to experience - one of my favorite RPG experiences in years.

The combat starts off quite challenging. Enemies take multiple hits and do significant damage, but I never felt that an encounter was unbeatable.
One fairly major negative, however. While combat starts out very difficult, as you gain in level the enemies don't really keep up. The power creep is fairly severe. Definitely gets two thumbs up, well worth the buy.

Good game. One of the very few RPGs I really got into in the last decade or so.
None of the hassle:
-Almost no unnecessary inventory management. Still, some choices and upgrades when it comes to weapons/armor/spells.
-An objective-based XP system (you don't have to worry about getting XP from killing baddies, and there are many interesting ways to get around combat that yield the same reward.
-Many missions that are concise, interesting, and never feel too long.
All of the substance:
-A thematically interesting hub connecting all other missions, loaded with NPCs with backstories that reveal over the course of the game, and sometimes reflect the choices you've made.
-Backstory and missions for all the guys in your team
-Some branching over decisions that have an interesting impact in the world, but at the same time don't feel forced, don't make you overthink things or feel that you've ruined the timeline. There aren't obvious 'right' or 'wrong' choices.
-Lots of ways to solve each problem. For example, there's a room full of baddies, you can tamper with the vent system and fill it with poison gas, hack a door that opens a path around them, or walk in and kill everyone.
All in all, it feels deep, but not overwhelming; it has complexity in the right places, but tries to keep it simple everywhere else. Many, relatively short missions which all feel different. Good game.

As you might have guessed, this is a Japanese game.
It's the creation of Goichi Suda, better known as Suda 51, whose previous projects include Killer7 and No More Heroes—excellent console action games that, sadly, never made their way to PC. As you might expect from a man with a number in his name, he's not your typical developer. His games are famous for their surreal visuals, slick action, bizarre stories, and musical influences.
Killer Is Dead has all of these things, but it feels like Suda is on autopilot. It's like he randomly flipped through his ideas notebook, indiscriminately tossing whatever caught his eye into the game. A woman turning into a lobster? Sure. Staring at boobs with X-ray specs to unlock weapons? Oh yeah. A level set on the Moon? Why the hell not. It's so self-consciously weird and tonally inconsistent that it actually becomes tiresome—especially since they're trying to tell an emotional story in the middle of it all.
The visual design in Killer Is Dead is brilliantly imaginative, but it's never more than window dressing. One level is like Hansel and Gretel's candy house crossed with an M.C. Escher drawing. Another sees you fighting in an ornate palace on the dark side of the Moon. Interesting settings in theory, but wasted on boxy, uninspiring levels made up of empty corridors and chambers.I really wanted to love Killer Is Dead, but it didn't take me long to realise just how superficial it is. There's such a sharp contrast between the wildly imaginative art and the tepid game underneath. The dull, ponderous cutscenes and indulgent interactive dream sequences—which are almost as bad as the ones in the first Max Payne—only make matters worse. The combat, as limited as it is, is the best thing about it. There's an enjoyable rhythm to the battles, and I love the feeling of evading an attack at the last second and responding with a tornado of slashes. But that's about as much praise as I can muster.

I finished it the other day. I would not recommend it. The entire time I was playing, I was praying for it to be over so I could move on to trying Far Cry 3 (which I finished a little over an hour ago).
Lemme list some grievances with FC2.
1. It's an open world game and there's no fast travel or quick means of travelling except for bus stations in opposite corners of the map. You have to drive miles upon miles, having to stop every half mile because there's enemies every half mile that you have to stop to kill. Even if you drive past them, you'll still have to stop to fix your car and they'll probably get in an armed jeep and chase you anyway. You have no idea how tedious that got. I swear half my play time (28 hours as opposed to FC3's 18 hours) came from driving to mission locations.
2. The enemies every half mile respawn, so you have no hope of ever escaping having to constantly stop - nor is there any motivation to engage them (save for the ones that chase you in vehicles that you HAVE to get out and kill).
3. Weapons wear down. While this was an interesting concept, the weapons wear down way too quickly. They go from brand new to exploding in your hand in like a day.

"Far Cry 2," at a basic level, has respectable production values and is reasonably fun. The combat is challenging without being crushingly hard, and you can eventually get ahold of the weapon combination that fits your style.
At the same time, the game suffers from a few issues. The driving can get really tedious, ironically because of how often you get into combat. (You want to get somewhere to do a mission, but every 30 seconds you have to deal with someone shooting at you.) The game world seems strangely disconnected from your actions, especially because you're always "fair game" for everybody - even the faction you're temporarily allied with. It all ends up feeling very contrived after a short while.
...and only a few of the missions are really interesting, with the rest just feeling like a lot of "samey" padding. The game basically feels like a long series of not-actually-important fetch quests for people you either don't care about or flat-out dislike.
Also, the characterization of the main antagonist seemed cartoony. It seems like the developers wanted to make an expy of Kurtz from "Apocalypse Now," but only succeeded in creating a parody. The voice acting for the character is rather hammy, especially in the few audio logs I found. In the end, I'm not sure if the people involved were trying too hard, nor not trying hard enough.
I definitely stuck with the game because I wanted to get my money's worth, and also because various aspects of the title are "pretty okay." At the same time, I wasn't overly impressed by how it all came together.
