Pac-Man was the first game I EVER played. My parents used to tell me I was only three years old. Of course, I have no idea how true that really is.. but I do have one very old memory of playing the game on the Commodore64.
That being said, it's a true classic. I still love that old game to this very day... but this isn't a review of the original game, is it?
I had to give that brief history lesson, because the sheer amounts of nostalgia I feel while playing this version is almost overwhelming.. yet, at the same time, it also feels amazingly fresh. The first time you gobble down a long string of ghosts, you'll have the biggest grin and probably not even realize it. Why? Because that huge speed increase caught you off guard.. so you'll remember that instead.
The goal is still to get as many points as possible, only now it's done with a time limit. Mazes are divided in two, and clearing one half of dots will place a fruit on the other half. Eating the fruit will cause more dots to appear on the empty half while also altering the maze layout on that half as well.
The dot patterns also often contain green sleeping ghosts. Getting close will wake them and they'll immidiately give chase, becoming rainbow colored in the process (their color constantly shifts and changes). Gathering large strings of these ghosts is a primary method of scoring points when you come across a power pellet.
Blinky, Pinky, Inky, and Clyde are also present and act much like they used to before. Getting too close will also make these guys angry and they can join the train. If so, their eyes will pop back into ghost house to reappear. As such.. Blinky will add quite a bit to the train just because he's the chaser, and the angry ghost train is that on crack anyway. Clyde ends up being a bit dangerous thanks to his somewhat random nature when combined with the train following you and the overall speed of the game. Pinky and Inky are also dangerous in their own regards, just not as much.
<3 Inky
The music also must be stated. Whoever it is who made these tracks deserves more credit than they probably got. There is absolutely no way you'd be able to take your eyes off the action to glance up at a timer at the higher speeds. The closer the timer is to running out, the more intrusive the music gets compared to the sound effects of the game itself.. and it builds up to a climax as the timer runs out. The brilliance behind that cannot go without being mentioned.
This game, man. It's an updated take on a legend, and it's done perfectly. A 'classic' mode would have been icing on the cake.. but whatever. If you're a fan of Pac-Man, you're doing yourself a huge disservice by not AT LEAST trying out the demo.
EDIT Sept. 16, 2015: So having unlocked the 'classic' skin and giving it a go... I feel let down by it, honestly. Keep in mind that Pac-Man is a game I loved since a VERY young age.
But anyway... to nitpick the 'classic' skin if I may, and I certainly may...
..The colors on the sleeping/angry ghosts are horribly muted. I know they didn't exist in the old game, but still. They just look bad. All of the other 'characters' are bright and colorful, but these look drab and boring.
..Inky isn't cyan. For the non-classic skins this is fine. But for the 'classic' skin, why isn't he cyan?
..The ghosts have black eyes. I'm fine with this in regards to the angry ghost chain, but why do the four main ghosts not have blue eyes?
..The normal 'pac-dots' are round. In the original game, circles weren't invented yet. The dots were small squares. In this regard, and for the eye color of the ghosts, the Type A skin does a better job than the classic skin does!
I dunno. The classic skin does some things right, but I just can't get over the nitpicks. It completely fails at being 'classic'. But I can't change my recommendation on that alone.. nobody can. It's still a fantastic game. ...I just won't be using the classic skin all that much. :)

The time it takes for “anything” to become a classic depends largely on the the nature of this “anything”. A literary classic is rarely younger than 50 years and in architecture maybe 500 years is typical. The time perspective is a bit different for computer games. Grim Fandango is certainly a classic game, and has been for some time, although it is not yet even twenty years since it was originally released. More recently the game has been remastered, receiving the new title Grim Fandango Remastered in the process, to reach both a new audience and, naturally, the old and nostalgic audience that is firm in their belief that “games were better in the 1990s”.
Grim Fandango is an adventure game set in the Land of the Dead. Manuel (Manny) Calavera is a travel agent at the Department of Death whose work involve selling transportation to recently departed souls so that they can reach the gates of the Land of Eternal Rest. If the newly dead has lived a good life he/she/it can get access to better travel packages, which also would give Manny a better provision. However, for some reason Manny’s clients are always on the bad end of the goodness scale while his colleague Domino Hurley consistently gets the good clients, which leads to Manny stealing a promising client, Mercedes (Meche) Colomar, from Domino. Something strange is going on, though, since even if her heart should be pure enough for the best possible travel package, only the worst one is actually available. This realisation starts the epic adventure which takes place over four years (four acts in the game) and where Manny navigates through crime and corruption among the dead.
The whole game is soaked in a film noir atmosphere, complete with an adapting excellent soundtrack that follows the different settings in which the adventure takes place. The style of the characters, on the other hand, is based on Mexican calaca-figures. This contrast between the atmosphere and the styling makes the visual appearance of the game very distinct. And I like it. I also like the story, which manages to be original while still keeping the traditional elements in the film noir genre. I believe I am not the only one who enjoys this experience. It is clear though that the success of the game builds mainly on its atmosphere, its soundtrack and its story. On the other hand, the games suffers somewhat from the typical problem of all point-and-click style of puzzle based adventure games I have played: it seems to be extremely difficult to construct puzzles that are neither far too simple nor far too unintuitive. I found that I solved many puzzles in the game more or less by mistake, and only afterwards understood the logic behind them. There were also a small number of situations where I had to seek online help to be able to get further, but these situations were all of the type that I had missed an object I could interact with somewhere, or that there were an area I had not realised I could access. At least I am proud to be able to truthfully say that I solved at least the fourth act in the proper manner.
What is most noticable for the player from the remastering process in Grim Fandango Remastered is that the graphical representation of the characters has been modernised as well as the controls. For me, the most important remastering effort is that the whole soundtrack has been fully orchestrated (using Melbourne Symphonic Orchestra). There were some minor glitches in the game which are not expected to be found in a game that has had almost twenty years to mature, but I only encountered one that forced me to restart from an earlier save. That is a minor issue in a game that I truly enjoyed.

There's a lot of nostalgia at work behind the ratings here. Grim Fandango starts brilliantly but loses sight of what makes an adventure fun. The story and characters are wonderful, the voice acting on the re-master is fun and expressive, and the theme is engrossing. It's a great start to an adventure game.
What the remaster didn't fix is an obnoxious inventory system and a set of puzzles that explodes outward until the game becomes unmanageably sprawling. Chapter 2 in particular is absolutely nuts in map size and puzzle density. You have some straightforward end goals but an absurd Rube Goldberg Device chain of causation to get there that can't possibly be understood. So instead of working to achieve your goals, you're working to do weird unrelated things just so your inventory will grow or something about the game state will change. It becomes less about intuition and more about "how many things do I have to fiddle with until the story finally advances?" Why am I stealing from a lawyer? Why am I borrowing a metal detector? Why am I helping an alcoholic relapse? None of it has a clear purpose when you do it. The purpose becomes clear when a hundred other things have been set in motion. It makes for intricate puzzles but really rips apart the idea that you're a character with goals and a story.
In total it feels unnecessarily padded out, which is really unusual for LucasArts. It feels more in line with the old Sierra games that were designed to get you buying the game guide. If you're looking for a kick of nostalgia, wait for a sale. Modern game design wouldn't tolerate such an unsatisfying slog. You've been taught to demand better than this by now.

I wasn't old enough to really be into adventure games, or really play many PC games at all when Grim Fandango came out. As I got older though, I kept hearing about how good it was from people, and as I got into adventure games I kept wanting to see it firsthand for myself. The Remastered version seemed like a good opportunity, but as I started playing I had very mixed feelings.
First of all, the dialogue and charm people talk about with the game is certainly there. The voice acting has some real effort put into it considering this was before that became a big thing in games, and the characters feel three dimensional. The setting is very unique, and it has a good mystery plot. I have no real complaints about the story.
My problem was with the game part. Again, I didn't play this growing up, and maybe I would have liked it better then, but with so many modern adventure games on Steam Grim Fandango seems archaic in a lot of places, and it hasn't been updated beyond the point and click mode (which is admittedly a very good addition, since I can't imagine navigating these areas with tank controls the whole game). And even that isn't implemented entirely well, as while you can double click to make Manny run where you want him to go, selecting any object will make him take his sweet time walking there, meaning you have to get as close as possible to whatever you want to interact with first. It's a minor nuisance, but one that didn't need to be there.
And speaking of interacting, the puzzles you face...well, they just aren't very good. A lot of them seem to be reliant on either you checking absolutely everywhere it's possible to go (assuming you don't miss a screen transition or a camera change, which it is possible to), picking up everything (and again, hopefully you don't miss an object), or doing things a player would have no reason to try. I can think of a couple reasons why - wanting to boost playtime on a game that sold for a lot more back then, or to help sell guides and LucasArts' hintline - but none of them are really relevant today, so that just leaves you with a lot of nuisances in your way. There hasn't been any hint system implemented in the game either, so it's looking up a guide or trying everything.
I don't really feel like I'm bad at adventure games, either. I've beaten a lot of them that felt like they had more reasonable puzzles: Anna's Quest, the two Journey Down games, the Blackwell series, Technobabylon, Harvey's New Eyes...it's probably unfair to compare an older game with newer ones, but this remaster came out just last year for around what those cost. I can't really recommend this game over them; if you want to experience it, buying it on sale and watching the story on youtube might be the better way.

After one year (a bit more) of collecting plants, watering, organizing, and being patient, I've decided to write this review. This is not a thing i do very often, but I felt the need to share what this game may bring to all that play it. First of all, and probably one of the most important aspects I would like to refer, is that what you see above, is what you are going to get. If you dont think this game is for you, it probably isn't. If you think you are going to be pleased and you enjoy this kind of experience, thats what you gonna get. Nonetheless, its free, so everyone should at least give it a try. Afterall, its doesn't take that long to download, and you are going to spend just a couple of minutes a day with it... so there's nothing to lose here.
Ok, now about the game itself. Viridi is a game with a simple concept: you are given a pot to plant all kinds of succulents (or fat plants, often generalized and called cacti), and your only "job" is to take care of them. Watering, plucking weeds, naming them and... singing, are probably the only ways you have to interact with your plants, aside from moving them from place to place when needed. If you are wondering or thinking this might be kinda boring, well... if you were hoping to spend an afternoon playing this game, it will get boring for sure...
The main "selling point" of this game ends up being its ambience and general vibe and atmosphere, which match perfectly with everything in it, from the music, to the visuals, to the gameplay itself. You always get this relaxed feeling whenever you come home from work or school, and you go check your plants (especially when you find them in bloom), and doing this not everyday, but at least regularly, ends up being almost like a ritual, a part of your everyday life, and probably that was the main aspect Ice Water Games tryed to convey with this game.
By the way, I really recomend checking the work from the guys at Ice Water Games. Their games kinda have the same vibe, and the artstyle is very unique and pleasing.
Now, what does the game offer besides a relaxing experience? For starters, I really like the visuals and artstyle. Its simple, but it does its job very well. The one thing that stands out the most though, its probably its music. Its just so relaxing and calm, but at the same time it gets sort of catchy, and you can immediately hum the rest of a tune just by hearing the first notes. Its really well composed, but to be honest, 7 euros for the soundtrack is a bit too much... One more reason to at least check the game out.
The controls are pretty simple and straight foward, and if you dont know how to do something, just click on the various menus and icons until you find out what you want to do. The layout is simplistic and blends quite nicely, in an organic way, with the game itself, preserving the zen aspect of it.
Your plants grow in real time, and everything is actually very scientifically accurate. There's a ton of information about the species, and its a great way to know more about the subject, either if you are into succulents or not. Its also great for people who dont have space, or time, or maybe patience to raise all kinds of plants at home, but always found the concept apealing. As one last final note, the game is free, and it obviously has its ways of proffiting... You start with a set of plants, and recieve one extra random succulent every week. If you dont mind recieving one extra plant every week, and have the patience to wait until you get the one you want, there's no need to spend any money, in my opinion, it even adds to the experience and its totally possible to get every plant week by week (you can always trade), but if you either want to support Ice Water Games, or you just want to get your hands on some specific plant, you can always spend a couple of cents!
In conclusion, this is a really nice and enjoyable game, and "free" is the perfect price for it! They could have implemented some extra features and mechanics, like a store to sell your fully grown plants (or the extra ones), a more deeper system in terms of taking care of your succulents, more plants and from arround the world, more customization, etc... There are also a couple of "DLC's", but you only get more pots, and to be honest its also a bit overpriced.
I wont give this game any kind of rating, mainly because this ends up being more of a personal experience, but one last time, at least check it out, and it's totally understandable if there are a lot of people that end up not liking it, but that's just how it is...

Firstly, it's in fair shape for an early access, and it's had a good update history, so don't be scared away by that. It does start with some wonky graphics settings, but after adjusting them it looks and plays pretty well, and many of the astetics (like the hideous alpha-style menus) will likely be fixed as more polish is added to the game.
Now, onto the game itself. It remindes me a lot of a ball game mode from Unreal Tournament concept wise. It essentially uses shoot mechanics in a hoop and ball game similar to soccer (football), however it leans more heavely on the sports side of the shooter-sports hybrid. It is a high flying, high speed, and it does suffer a bit from a lack of feedback on landings and jump hieghts, but that forces you to pay attention to both the game and the platforms (I'd recomend using the highest FOV settings to help), as falling to your death is a constant threat. There are a lot of deep mechanics and power ups that make this game very strategic and competetive; It probably has the potental to compete with CS:GO's competitive scene.
Over all, I would recomend this to someone who dislikes CoD style shooters but enjoyed the interesting gamemodes from old competitive games like Unreal Tournament, Counter Strike, and Quake Arena.

A game with a lot of grit. That grit is present in the game's mechanics, where staving off malaria, contending with weapon jams, and extracting bullets from your flesh to permit healing are all common issues. It's also more difficult than its successors. Enemies respawn at every guard post and have ungodly marksmanship, vehicles threaten to ram you off the road every few moments, ammo is scarce, and the lack of autosaves will leave you angry at yourself when you falter and lose 45 minutes of progress. These factors make every completed mission more rewarding, and every confict an interesting challenge with multiple ways to tackle it, even if there's little variety in the actual mission objectives. The landscapes are also gorgeous by 2008 standards, and flare guns, flamethrowers, and molotovs are all viable methods of incineration that the game embraces.
Gritty, Challenging, Pretty, and Flammable/69

After about a day of playing this, I went to Google and entered "how to have fun in Far Cry 2".  And then I reflected on what a bizarre thing I had just done.  But for such a good-looking game, the fun seems to be hard to find.  I even considered that that might be the point; actually contracting malaria in a war-torn hellhole where you must kill or be killed wouldn't actually be much fun.
The game felt repetitive far too quickly for my tastes; you accept a quest from somebody, then drive from point A to point B (walking is far too slow.)  Along the way you'll likely pass two checkpoints on the road; no you can't avoid them by travelling off-road.   Each checkpoint has a few goons who would like to kill you, so you kill them.  Then you arrive at point B, where there are a few goons that would like to kill you, so you kill them.  Killing everyone at Point B usually accomplishes the quest goal, so now you must just return to point A, except that those damned checkpoints have already repopulated, so you need to murderdeathkill their residents over again just to get back.   The majority of the game, as I found it, was shooting my way through the same checkpoints over and over again.
Part of the misery of the situation is that you will spend a certain amount of time trying to fight with crappy, unreliable firearms.  You will be able to purchase reliable guns that perform well at your safehouses, but for some reason you are unwilling to bring enough ammo for all the butchery that a typical quest demands, so at some point you will end up dropping your well-maintained and functional firearm in favour of a fallen foe's rusted-out jam-prone piece of scrap metal.  You will then have the joy of finishing the quest with this vaguely gun-like object, because continual weapon jams in difficult situations are an essential part of the experience.
That's my Far Cry 2 experience: repetitive, unrewarding shootouts, weapon jams, and malaria.  Subjectively, the experience is cohesive and thematic -- it feels as though the creators successfully realized their vision -- it just wasn't enjoyable to play.

Farcry 2 is an FPS ,with slight RPG qualities, game set in a fictional African country currently engaged in a civil war. You play as one of the few preset characters that you can choose from. As a mecenary and gun for hire, tasked to kill the infamous arms dealer " The Jackal ", you'll be traversing and fighting your way through the grim of civil war, waged by the APR and UFLL factions, and the natural beauty of the African savanah and jungle. However, upon your arrival to the nearest hotel, you discover you have a severe case of malaria and are hindered by it occasionally through out your game experience. It impedes your mission, but you will have to overcome it and the civil war to get your target, and possibly find a way out of the country.
Gameplay:
The game is an FPS and as such you'll be seeing the world through the characters POV. From this perspective you'll be able to see your characters health, ammo, healing syringes and throwable weapons (grenades and molotoves) count. You can also bring up your handheld map to see your current location, objectives and available missions. However, you are unarmed while you have your map in hand.
The gameworld is divided into two main zones: The Northern district ( Leboa-Sako ) and the Southern District ( Bowa-Seko ), the latter only being accesible during the later half of the game. Each zone is sub-divided into 9-grid squares, namely NW,N,NE,E,SE,S,SW,W and Central, with the exception of the one grid connecting the two main zones. Each zone is free for you to explore at your own pace and leisure. The game also features a day and night cycle that will affect your visibility and that of the AI.
The main missions follow the story and will have you doing unique missions for which ever faction gave it to you. You'll also meet and aquire buddies, othere mecenaries and foreigners, that will help give optional missions to do as well as affect how you finish a main mission. They will also rescue you should you get knocked out.
Currency:
As this is a civil war, paper and any official money is trash, as one man puts it: "I wound't wrap a fish with it." Diamonds are used as the only currency worth anything and you aquire them through either doing main missions or finding diamond cases ( which give from 1-3 diamonds ). Diamond cases are scattered around the map and you'll need your tracker, which is equiped with your map or when driving, to identify their presence and locate them. In the top left corner of each grind is a number indicating the amount of diamonds in that area. There are 221 diamond cases in total, 1 is given to you in the tutorial part of the game and shows how to work the tracker at the same time.
Traveling:
As this is a quite a large map to explore you'll often more than not be taking a vehicle to get to your destination or simply to drive in. the game has a small selection of vehicles ( including jeeps, a car, trucks, a quadbike, a buggy and boats ) that you can use to traverse around and get about to where you need to go. Each vehicle is unique in its properties as some are more practical, having mounted weapons but being slightly more bulky, while others are more simple and smoother to drive. There are also fixed bus stations located in the NW,NE,SW,SE and central grids of the map that will allow a form of fast-travel between them. In anycase, it's up to you on how you want to go about getting to places. Driving is solid with a firm handling on steering, but the speed of your vehicle can only go to a certain limit.
Combat:
The AI in this game are quite aggresive and perceptive. They will fight and chase you ( if you drive away and they have a vehicle nearby ) "till death, no matter which faction your working for at the moment. They will flank you if you stay too long in one spot and thier snipars have a sharp eye for things moving a good distance away from them ( thankfully they are poor shots ). The AI will also respawn, whether it be at key outpost that you have already cleared or just a patrol vehicle on the road, and very quickly I will add. You can move a good half km from an outpost only to return to it and find it filled with enemies again. This can both a nuisance and problem at times, depending on your difficulty, playstyle and general mood. This is why I stated that vehicles with mounted weapons are more practical as you can easily use them to clear out outpost or patrols and move on. Alternatively you can avoid outposts by giving them a good distance and at night their perception is much lower.
Weapons:
You have 4 weapons in the game that you can carry on you at a once: Your melee weapon ( a Machette ), your primary weapon ( Assualt rifles, SMG, shotguns and snipar rifles ), your secondary weapon ( pistols, IED's, semi-automatics and a grenade luancher ) and your special weapons ( flamerthrower, mortar, RPG's, LMG's ect ). You'll start out with the basics, but you'll be able to aquire and purchase more weapons and upgrades as you do special missions given at the weapon stores/storages. Weapons handle well in the game and feel as powerful as they should, accordingly.
Upgrades:
You can upgrade your weapons ( after you purchase them ) as well as purchase some general upgrades to your equipment and gear. Weapon upgrades include accuracy, reliability and total ammunition count. General upgrades include increased syringe count, camo suit, vehicle repair speed and degradation reduction.
Degradation:
Weapons and vehicles will deteriorate over time and use. As weapons become more broken they will jam more often and miss fire occasionally, while vehicles will tend to break down more quickly and appear "rekt" after constant assualt. ( Literally, your vehicle will look as if it was vandalised and striped of any useful parts and then driven through a mound of♥♥♥♥♥♥) Weapons can easily be replaced for new ones at your weapon stores/storages. As for vehicles, simply steal a new one.
DLC content:
This simply adds two new vehicles , the quadbike and the armored assualt truck, as well as 3 new unique, free weapons to your storage ( a sawn-off shotgun, a silenced, pump-action shotgun and an explosive bolt crossbow ). Not very game changing, but nice to have non the less.
Bugs:
There are a few bugs i've noticed, but non break the game or how you play it. Oddly enough, I don't recall these bugs on my retail version of the game that I bought back when this came out. Sometimes a NPC will "slide" up a wall or vertical surface, often when leaning agaisnt it, other times they will seem to randomly burst around the room if they are performing an animation ( such as giving malaria pills ) and their model colides with a fixed asset. It happens occasionaly, but I just find these bugs funny.
Tips and Hints
>If you have to drive a good distance that is on the path of a few outposts, simply move along the edge of the outer grids, in that way you can avoid them until you reach your point.
>If you want to find all the diamonds in the game, you can find the maps on the Farcry 2 wiki with all the locations listed.
>Note that even with all the diamonds found and main missions done, you won't be able to purchase every weapon and upgrade, so spend wisely.
>Purchasing the primary,secondary and special storage crates is very situational. It simply allows you to universally store that weapon type in a specific crate that can be accessed at any of your safe houses that you have unlocked. However, you will have to replace the weapon once it has been taken out.
>If a buddy has rescued you recently, he/she will be on a cooldown of sorts. You can reset this cooldown by finding them at any one of your unlocked safe houses and talking to them.
>Beware of veldt fires.
>Golden AK-47's do not rust, and do not respawn.
>The Machette will insta-kill any enemy.

You could say that this game is PAC-MAN on drugs, and that's a very good thing. You need to note that this doesn't play like the classical games, but a whole new arcade PAC-MAN game. While in the classic style you go through a maze collecting points, getting power-ups and killing ghosts, here is mostly about tracing a path and perfecting it. I'll explain. The maze can be divided in half, each independent from the other. When you clear all points in a half, you must collect a fruit to refresh that half with new points. Most of the time, the points are layered out in a path, so you almost always follow a certain route, clearing the maze and collecting the fruits to refresh it. It sounds and it is easier to play, because you mostly always know where to go, instead of collecting points randomly. The challenge in classic PAC-MAN is to survive as long as possible, getting as much points as possible. Here the challenge is to perfect each run, trying to fix the mistakes you did in the last one. There's also a lot of ghosts, where you wake them, they follow you until you got a power up and then mow them all. Doing that is awesome. You can also customize the maze, choosing it's style (also for pac-man and the ghosts), the color and changing the background music. There's plenty of options, from neon to bricks. And the music is awesome. There's plenty of mazes and modes, all of them with global leaderboards. For each course and mode, you can see where you are standing, and the ranking is based on your position. To get S rank, you need to be at the top 5%. And you can even access a replay for each player, so you can compare strategies and try to score higher. The game doesn't have a story or progression, it's all about climbing the leaderboards and comparing with your friends. There's even a global rank, which considers all the modes and courses. One thing that i didn't like to see was cheaters in the leaderboards, because they screw the real positions of everyone else. This is also the developers fault for not fixing this, because a clean leaderboard would mean that the legit number one was really number one. But that doesn't ruin the overall experience. It's an awesome game, with great graphics and music, fun to play casually, but hard to master. PAC-MAN on drugs, oh yeah!

Okay, look, I know I've only just starting playing it, but I must let this out.
Dragonfall is so much better than Shadowrun Returns in every way. It is so good that I want to go back and play the original again, because I've gotten so many ideas on what sort of character I want to play.
The gameplay and the graphics are essentially the same. The mechanics are still the same, though I think they've expanded on a few things, and they've balanced a few options (in an already very tightly-balanced game). So, they've kept what was good, and they've tightened things up, and improved, which is how things should be.
First of all, they've improved the UI. Spells and inventory items can be seen on-screen along with weapon (or spell) talents at the same time. Drone controls have been split off from weapon controls, so your rigger always has access to his active weapons. The UI also shows when a character is "In the Open" or flanked or under cover, so that you can take actions accordingly.
From a gameplay perspective, the Dragonfall campaign is leaps and bounds ahead of Dead Man's Switch. The Dead Man's Switch campaign wasn't bad, but it was very linear, felt very much like a film noire mixed in with "The Thing", with the ending feeling like a shaggy dog story; or maybe like the Chinatown movie. It wasn't bad, but Dragonfall is already so much better.
For one thing, there is now a hub from which you can get multiple missions, and you have a team. The team don't feel like cookie-cutters either, but like other player characters. There's one who's gone the cyberized route, there's one who's decided to go all out on magic, there's one who's decided to go badass combat (with the background to boot), and there's the guy whose character buys it in the first session, and decides to make a l33t hacker to get revenge on the GM.
And your teammates are pretty good. What I really like is that it feels as though it is perfectly valid to create any character you want, and even if you make a bad character, your teammates can pick up the slack. So, you could make a jack-of-all-trades, and your team could carry your useless♥♥♥♥♥through the campaign, no problem.
My main problem though, is that I'm having to deprogram myself from leaping into combat all the time (or betraying other people). I'm so used to getting XP for fighting that it's refreshing to play a game where talking your way out of trouble is as valid as fighting. You don't get karma for defeating enemies (so yes, your main character could be a coward who runs and hides at the back of the formation), but for completing objectives. Yes, there will be times when you have to fight, but if you have a choice, you won't be losing out on any karma by not killing everyone.
I suspect that close-combat/adept is still underpowered compared to the other options, but looking at some of the arguments online, I can see that there's no such thing as a bad decision (so far as character concepts are concerned; you can still screw up execution). Don't create a character with the express objective of trying to milk every karma point available in the game, because being a points-♥♥♥♥♥ is a pointless activity.
So yeah, big fan. I suspect that trying to get all of the achievements will be a pain ("Down Boy" or "It Was a Massacre"), but that's what re-playing is for.
I can't wait to get through this so that I can do Dead Man's Switch again, and then move on to Hong Kong.

The story in Shadowrun: Dragonfall. is excellent. The story in Shadowrun Returns was decent to me, as a newcomer to the Shadowrun universe, but this definitely felt like a step up - you have your own party this time instead of a bunch of rentals for every mission, there is a larger central hub, and the characters are easier to care about. There are also lore tidbits that spice up the game, in particularly the very excellent Shadowlands BBS, that make the world just feel so much more *alive*.
There are more optional missions in Dragonfall than Returns, yet they are less "missable" than Shadowrun, and some of the missions can be done in any order so as to break up the linearity a little. The plot was very satisfying and engaging as well, escalating at a nice pace and instilling a suitable sense of danger to the player without randomly introducing something outlandish like Returns did. Some quests have more than one possible ending as well.
Overall there is also more content in Dragonfall than Returns - both in that there are more missions (About 19 or so in Dragonfall vs 13 or so in Returns), and that the maps tend to be a bit bigger, or involve more than just blowing everything to bits with Eiger. They do stretch the engine to make more creative objectives. There is also a "mass effect" feel to the way they did things, with a central hub and companion loyalty arcs and a changeable companion roster, plus the unfortunate side effect of having to talk to every single person between each mission to see if you missed anything. Gear and karma progressions felt good without being overpowering.
Why then does this game get a downthumb? Because of bugs. Several of these are decker/rigger specific, so you may not feel it as much if you used another character, however this engine is such a piece of drek and the issue with having a longer and more complex game than Returns is that it also magnifies all the issues with the engine.
General:
- There is some sort of an internal memory leak that drags the game's response time down, either over time, or as you make more saves per session (which is also sort of the same as over time, I guess). It usually isn't an issue until a couple hours in, but save games and loads start to take longer and longer, from about 20 seconds when the game first boots, to well over a minute to load a savefile several hours in. The game itself will eventually begin to respond a little more sluggishly than usual to commands or NPC conversations, until eventually at some point you try to save the game and the game freezes up and dies.
- But if you're lucky, you'll never get that far, because you will just run into another game-ending bug instead. Rarely, your controlled character will just stop responding to anything out of the blue. You can click on the ground and they won't move there. You can select skills and get a highlighted border around it, but you cannot select a target. You can hit escape, and navigate that menu, and that is about it. Everything else in the game doesn't respond to your commands. This can happen regardless if you are controlling your own character, controlling another character, or in free move mode nowhere near a battle. Thankfully, you can usually save/load out of this bug, but sometimes you have to close out and restart anyway.

This only happened once to me in the penultimate Apex Rising, and seems to happen to other people in that same mission more than any other mission, but it was infuriating. Workaround: DO NOT SAVE AFTER DEFENDING THE TERMINAL AND BEFORE ZONING BACK TO KREUSBAZAR. That won't fix it all, but that was a 100% crash situation for me over 4 or 5 science attempts. Your loadout screen at the start of a mission then becomes hilariously wrong, with it showing the weapon and two other items, but the item that it overwrote will not be an option to equip or unequip. It is possible to end a combat with one or both drones in a ventilation system used for drone passage between one room and another. Before I begin I would like to say I have many more hours on an actual vindictus account and have played since beta. I would not recommend this game as there is a huge grind to get anything once you hit level 50 and the community is extremely elitist. Nexon as a company also does a terrible job maintaining the NA servers and responding to any and all tickets. Despite what it says for my gametime on my steam record, I've been playing this game long before steam had vindictus on their store page. In fact, I've been playing ever since the closed beta. With that being said, I've seen this game change and grow for the better and also take a couple steps back, let me explain.
The Pros:
-Good graphics considering that this game is aging.
-A hack and slash combat system which is still really unique in the MMORPG market.
-An AMAZING soundtrack when you reach the bosses and fight in raids. Also has nice background music that plays in the towns as well.
-AWESOME bosses, these range from giant hammer wielding chieftains to huge 24 man raids where you fight these epic dragons.
-Cool level designs (in the earlier levels, they're a little linear, but in season 2 and season 3 dungeons, they're a lot more open and have really impressive looking environments).
-The source engine still works pretty well with this game and the physics all respond nicely when you destroy objects around in the levels and make enemies crash into objects as well.
-REALLY COOL looking weapons and armor.
-A robust cast of characters which all offer unique experiences and ways to play the game.
-The game has been a lot more streamlined over the years so that it's easier to level up and get through some of the more tedious quests.
The Cons:
-The free to play model isn't the best. While it's definitely not as difficult for a free to play player to actually have a decent character, players who pay have an advantage over those who don't.
-The servers have gotten better over the years, but at big events or at random intervals, there'll just be lag and it'll take longer to join parties or to get loot at the end of a dungeon.
-High level raids are STACKED. If you do not meet the attack requirements of the boat, you will be kicked. This is counter balanced however by these same raids having slightly lower level intervals for those players who don't have enough attack or defense to take on the hardest difficulty.
-The marketplace charges you way too much for certain items and materials.
-After a while, the game can be kind of grindy.
Conclusion: After playing this game for five years, I could recommend it back then and despite the issues, I can still recommend it now! If you're willing to invest a little bit of time with this game, you can have an amazing character and it's worth sticking around, if not for the combat system, then for the amazing raid bosses.

This game is delightful. In terms of basic structure it's similar to most RPGs where you have a main quest and sidequests that you're going on and along the way you're collecting stats, new equiptment, meeting NPCs, visiting towns, etc.
The best part of the game is definitely the creativity, humor and sense of discovery -- because of the simplicity of the graphics and just the style of the game, it allows for a lot more varied combinations of stuff and situations. Unlike most RPGs, it doesn't really have a part where you're just grinding away mindlessly; the story's constantly moving forward and there's constantly new locations to be discovered (that's the beauty of simple graphics!).
Also, don't let the stick figures fool you -- this is a very thought out and carefully made game. It's well-balanced in terms of item drops, difficulty progression, fun plotlines and stories, variations to enhance replayability, etc. Each aspect of it feels very intentional. For item drops, for example, I find that in a lot of RPGs it's either too flukey in terms of getting good items (to the point where there's too muck luck involved) or more frequently most of the junk you collect doesn't matter except after a boss battle. This game is not like that at all, you're constantly getting different stuff in the way thay makes sense. There's no part of it that feels like an afterthought.
Plus, people familiar with the genre will notice that they've taken the time to consider the little things to take annoyances out of the game -- there's no inventory management (unlimited inventory) and you don't spend time trudging around (you can always go straight back the main map and there's no long stretches of walking -- I personally hate watching my character walk around in games so I love when developers have taken that into consideration). I love, love, love that you can speed up the combat animation to 300% under the options. I love games that don't waste my time.
This game looks casual, but there's so many decisions in the design of it that were clearly very intentional and thoughtful.
The only downside I could find was that there's so much going on especially once you get further into the game - locations, quests, things to go back to - that it's a little hard to keep track of. I hardly think that's a big knock against this. Beyond that, it's up to you to decide if you're OK with the graphics -- I loved Kingdom of Loathing back in the day so I knew what I was getting into.
For most seasoned RPG players, this game won't be too difficult. As long as you're careful, you can avoid a lot of the stuff that'll kill you outright, plus there's no permadeath (you just wake up and it's a new day) so you might get slowed down but it's not going to feel like you can't progress. It's heavy on puzzles which, depending on what you're into, may be a plus or minus for you.
That said, there's also a hidden Hardcore Mode (
) where the game gets significantly more difficult in terms of combat. As far as I could tell, the puzzles stay the same. So, if you're not into the puzzles and want a harder game, you can always find a walkthrough to get the answers to the puzzles and do it that way.
My recommendation would be to play through normally the first time and once you've figured out the puzzles, then try it again on hardcore.
You will definitely want to replay the game at least once. There's multiple ways to solve a bulk of the interactions (largely depending on what type of character you are), plus there's different mounts you can ride with different attributes (standard, sneaky, spooky and crazy), and three different companions -- so you'll be rewarded by playing through it again with a pretty varied experience.
Honestly, this is one of the better games I've played in a while, It's very well balanced and fun. If you like RPGS and puzzles and stories and humor, you'll love this.

I had my skepticism coming into this. I was going to buy it either way, but given the state of Kingdom of Loathing in recent years I can't help but feel that Asymmetric have started to lose their touch with that game; from disbanding one of their lead writers (for a game that rides almost entirely on its writing) to revamping a quest that used to parody "collect all two dozen manual pages" into a quest where you ACTUALLY collect all two dozen manual pages... it's not the breath of fresh air it once was.
I'm happy to say that, in spite of or perhaps because of this, West of Loathing has been a pleasant surprise. I now wonder if part of the reason KoL has been on the wane is because they were pouring their best efforts into this instead. I've laughed more at the first half hour of this than I have at KoL in
now, and the RPG-lite mechanics and combat system are done in a novel and compelling way (although the writing is still what you'll be playing for).
My primary gripes are that playing a completely black-and-white game for an extended period is slightly murderous on the eyes, and that it only seems to support a single save file... which is ludicrous given there's a fair number of things that you can permanently miss on one playthrough, and there are 3 character classes to play as. I'm also not convinced that there's actually enough depth to the game to give it much replayability, but at any rate I'm having fun so far.

I'm a fan of KoL for a long time, despite having kept up with the game. Having a fresh experience, new story and setting, and completely revamped gameplay is such a great shot in the arm of the company, it's reminded me within the first few minutes of gameplay why I fell in love with it in the first place. It's sharp writing, unique humor that hits multiple angles, and strong RPG and exploration gameplay make it a fun solo experience that makes it a fun RPG. Its RPG challenge and wide selection of pop culture targets make it so expansive that it may not welcome newcomers to the RPG genre itself, and don't expect to catch every reference on the first reading as some of them are so subtly written as such to avoid overselling a joke.
If you aren't familiar with the MMO, basically KoL game is a text-based MMO with stick figure graphics. This game removes the MMO aspect, adding complete animations and character control to the experience, which makes exploration so much fun. Just like the original, each area is themed, and if you think you know what the joke is at the end, you are generally thrown off by a complete change of direction. How advant-garde! Seriously, where else are you going to find a game that references the Foo Fighters AND X-files in a single room, keeps it thematically appropriate, maintains the suspension of disbelief by keeping it within the realm of possibility of the world, tells a completely original joke that's only amplified by the understanding of the reference, AND continues to build its world and challengingly strategic RPG gameplay all in one? They never hesitate to waste a reference: the tooltips for the graphics options are Good, Bad, and Ugly. There's a ton of hidden gags that are too numerous to be called "easter eggs" that reward any and all exploration.
The game is challenging yet approachable. In accordance to old school RPG rules, you never really know the difficulty of an enemy until you engage it. This makes the beginning area extremely annoying once you open the map up, as you don't know whether an area can net you some good experience or have you face off enemies that can one shot you down. There's plenty of opportunity for leveling given that your stats are based on the XP earned rather than an arbitrary level threshold, and there's a lot of depth to gain from the choices you make. Fans of stat-building, and hardcore buff enthusiasts will feel right at home trying to min-max their stats for the most benefit using the spleen/liver effect system to potion or drink yourself to perfection. This game may seem simple, but it demands your attention in order to be effective and not waste all your money on health kits and free-use damage items.

With this remaster of Grim Fandango, you'll find an amazing snapshot of 90s adventure games. With this comes the esoteric puzzles, but that's just part of the charm, there's no shame in using a walkthrough at some point or another. If you can ignore the few bugs that occur while rendering cutscenes, it should run smooth as butter on modern computers for the first time in over a decade.
Highly recommend checking this out at some point in your gaming career.

I loved this game. I didn't think I would, but I knew it was popular back in the day.
I've always had trouble with adventure games. They're either not interesting or entertaining enough. Usually the puzzles take forever or are just plain time wasters or requires you to run errands back and forth. This had had just the right amount of stuff I wanted in an adventure game.
This game didn't have any dumb time waster puzzles. I did have trouble with some parts because I've never been good at adventure games, but I thoroughly enjoyed this game. The story was entertaining and kept moving along at a nice pace.
This was the first time I've played through this game and I also listened to the commentary along the way, which was entertaining as well. I highly recommend this game. It brings back memories of games during this time period such as Final Fantasy VII and the like. It makes me want to make an adventure game myself.
Once I started playing 'Grim Fandango', I could not stop!

The theme of the game is a little bit of film noir detective fiction, a little bit of the Mexican Day of the Dead. In the land of the living, the graphics change to a kind of twisted photo cut-and-paste look.
The best thing about Grim Fandango, as with all other classic LucasArts point-and-click adventures is the sassy humour. It works extra well in the context of a noir crime thriller like this. The story has all the basic hallmarks of a Raymond Chandler private-eye novel, with layers of absurdist jokes and puzzles on top.
My only issue with the game is how long it takes to get around on foot. I discovered after a couple of hours that double clicking equals running. The game might be a bit slow for someone without a lot of patience or who gets easily frustrated by puzzle solutions that are deliberately abstract. I wish I had the patience to wait for Manny Calavera to casually walk to each location because it suits his character. Grim Fandango is a game that has a leisurely pace and doesn't really deserve to be rushed.

I have over 2000+ hours on Chronicle:Runescape Legends so I think I have some say in this, I can't recommend this game. The game does not follow the rich lore of Runescape and the lands of Gielinore, just for some context I will summarise the history of the game here:
The Past
The First Age - Creation
The world of Gielinor was shaped by the Elder Gods at the start of the First Age. It was their perfect creation, and it was their last in a long line of worlds. Theologians and priests state that for much of this time the gods were still in the process of forming the world. Much of this time must have been spent making the various lands, seas, plants and animals. The First Age is said to have lasted four thousand years.
The Second Age - The Age of Gods
Scholars have deduced that the Second Age was roughly two thousand years long. Having laid silent and undisturbed for thousands of years, Gielinor was discovered by a young Guthix whose desire to share the world with others meant that he opened portals to bring other peaceful beings to the world.
Many of the intelligent mortal races began to form the beginnings of their great civilisations in this age though not all of the races that rose at this time have survived into the modern ages, so we know very little of them.
At this time the Guthix interacted much more directly with the mortals than the gods do in current times, but it was never his intention to stay. Believing that no god should have such influence over a world, when he felt Gielinor was ready, Guthix went to sleep, and left the inhabitants of Gielinor to live their lives without the influence of a god.
This peace was all to end in the Third Age.
The Third Age - The God Wars
The Third Age lasted for around four thousand years long and is also known as the time of the God Wars. Stories tell of when the gods found the peaceful world of Gielinor and wanted to claim it for themselves. This desire saw new portals to the world created, with new races who desired power, not balance and harmony.
Violence swiftly followed, with great and powerful entities, and agents of the gods, fighting cataclysmic wars during which time humanity could only just cling to survival.
The wars raged for centuries, but they came to an end when Guthix woke from his deep slumber when a large area of Gielinor was destroyed by Zamorak.
He cast them out, blocking their return with his edicts, so their wars would not further damage the fragile lands. But the damage had already been done, not just to the land now known as the Wilderness, but to Guthix's desire that the inhabitants would not worship the gods. Having been ruled for so long by these powerful beings, many of the mortal races stayed with their chosen deity, and continued to worship them despite them no longer being able to come to Gielinor.
The Fourth Age - The Age of Mortals
The Fourth Age, sometimes known as the Age of Mortals, lasted for roughly two thousand years. With the God Wars over, the mortal races were at last able to multiply and prosper. There were many races competing to make their mark in the world, though. Humans, dwarves, goblins, ogres, gnomes and many more all competed for land and resources. There was much fighting between the different races, so cultural and scientific advances were slow.
To make things even harder there were tales of strange undead necromancers who arose from time to time, summoning armies of undead skeletons and zombies which swept across the land destroying all in their path.
During the early parts of the Fourth Age most of the humans lived in nomadic tribes, battling to stay alive against each other and against the tribes of other races. Over time they started to make more permanent settlements throughout the world, but they continued to have to war with their neighbours.
Many legends, tales and poems exist from this time and tell of the exploits of many heroes such as Robert the Strong and Arrav of Avarrocka.
No race had supremacy in these wars for many centuries until human mages on the north-west continent stumbled across ancient runic magics!
The human mages learnt how to create powerful magical stones known as runestones. They began to create them in large numbers. How they made the runestones was kept a closely guarded secret between just a few of the mages so as not to let the information fall into enemy hands.
These stones meant that many people - not just accomplished mages - could use powerful magic. Virtually anybody with even a small amount of magical ability was able to do something with the runestones and so the humans started to become dominant throughout the world. These events mark the start of the Fifth Age - the Age of Humans.
The Fifth Age - The Age of Humans
The human settlements became big cities. They expanded their territories and the human tribes combined to form larger kingdoms. The kingdoms of Misthalin and Asgarnia quickly grew to become the kingdoms of RuneScape they still are today. The mages who discovered rune magic set up a great tower of wizardry in southern Misthalin.
Soon these rune stones were spread to neighbouring human tribes and the Kingdom of Kandarin came into existence. Smaller human strongholds were also established in places such as Al Kharid, Karamja, and Entrana.
For a period of time, things appeared to being going extremely well for the human kingdoms. Some people tried to stand in the way of their expansion, most notably a wave of invading barbarians who objected to the use of rune stones and rampaged through northern Kandarin and Asgarnia, but the rune stones were powerful enough that the kingdoms could deal with all that came their way.
Then disaster struck! At this point in time, the wizards allowed followers of Zamorak to join their ranks, which proved to be a fatal mistake. At a summit in the Wizards' Tower with most of the powerful mages gathered, the Zamorakian mages betrayed the others, igniting a great fire which razed the tower to the ground. Most of the great wizards were killed, and their great library which stored the key to much of their power was also destroyed.
Still, there were plenty of runes left in the world. Enough that the existing kingdoms were able to adequately defend themselves from invaders, though they no longer wished to expend runes to expand their borders any further.
Following the burning of the tower there was a massive backlash against Zamorak's followers, who had previously been tolerated, if not exactly welcomed. In many areas the Zamorakians quickly became outcasts who had to hide away from the rest of the world, though the Black Knights of the Kingdom of Asgarnia still held much political sway in that land.
Thus a relative equilibrium was found for the next hundred years, as the three great kingdoms held off all invaders. Although the wizards remained worried that the stocks of the powerful runes they had used to protect the kingdoms were running low. The enemies of Misthalin, Asgarnia and Kandarin were beginning to find footholds in their lands again in dark corners everywhere, and new heroes arose to maintain order and prevent the collapse of civilisation under the forces of evil!
As with most of Gielinor's history, all was not peaceful for long. The gods had been searching for ways back into Gielinor for some time and the path was paved with the events that took place not long after an archaeological dig unearthed an ancient home believed to belong to Guthix.
As the dig was explored further an alarm was set off, triggering a number of powerful beings to head towards the source. These generals and followers of the gods knew very well what had been discovered - the resting place of Guthix. There were many reasons that these characters sought out Guthix, though most were seeking the return of the gods; how this would happen varied between the groups. Introduction
Thea is some kind of mix between 'civilization' and 'king of dragon pass'. i also got a strong 'kingdom death monster' vibe from it. the game should be fun for anyone, who likes cardgamestrategy and simultations. but let me explain in detail:
Setup:
you are a god awakening from your slumber and lording over a small settlement of people. you decide what those people do, which means, some you send to explore, while others gather wood and food in the village.
The Game:
you gather wood and food by dragging the villager to the corresponding field, he then does this automatically wach turn, similar with the construction of buildings or items.
The fights are basically a cardgame you play each of your fighters, in each round and when both people do not have cards anymore the fightingphase plays out automatically. the cards you play are your settlers, whos strengths you customized with their class and items.
Those items you find, or make yourself, to make them yourself, your expedition usually needs to go out and loot them or gather resources to make them, since you can only have one town and this town is usually not at a good resource-rich spot.
While exploring, you will frequently find a lot of !voiceacted! events in which you decide what to do. (even after 44 hours, i most likely have not seen all events, though i have seen a couple of events twice or thrice)
All in all the gameplay does certainly not have a lot of action, i would even say, it has less action, than 'civilization V', however if you like to think and plan it is a lot of fun.
The Good:
-Lots of events and no real 'wrong' answer.
-great art
-Harvest moon effect (Once you start, you are reluctant to stop)
-decent tactical challenge during card battles(if the difficulty is done right)
The Bad
-You can not choose your city-starting spot. (i swear i would pay money for such a DLC, not being able to choose makes you unable to choose in big parts how hard your game will be, i for one would like to try a start, where my city does not have a food source.)
-Somewhat repetitive, if you know all the events.
-modifier during difficulty are unbalanced. (though i assume this is not a very important point for most people reading this review, just know you can make it very easy and rewarding for you at the same time, with the right costumdifficulty.)
Conclusion
I picked the game up in a (this) summer sale and can warmly recommend it, it certainly delivered for me.
But please devs, make a 'choose your city starting spot addon'!

And plus getting a high score really makes you feel great for some odd reason. If your in mood for a game that's great to tell everyone your high score about than play this game NOW!

First, you may look at this like it's stupid. Then you see a video of it, and instantly it's cool.
Well, apart from the social media, the lack of options, the lack of vanilla Pac-Man, and the social media, this is quite a good game. Oh, did I mention social media? Yes, you can see your friends' scores. Even if they don't even play the game.
Alright, this game is quite good, apart from the social media. It's Pac-Man, but the ghosts will chase you, build up super long lines, then you can eat them for delicious, delicious points. Hold on, another con. After a certain point, the ghost chain stops growing, which is super disappointing. And the point of an arcade game, such as this, is to get points. The more ghosts, the more points. Another con: the game has specific points where you're supposed to, and really have to, get the power-up that makes the ghosts eatable. Sometimes, it's unaviodable. Why can't we get a chain of ghosts that contains over 9000 ghosts, then eat them all? That would be really fun! With a gamemode where you're supposed to eat as many ghosts as possible, these two mechanics make the game less fun.
This game has a few mediocre things, but I think I'll not mention them.
Now for actual pros: It's hyper-speed Pac-Man. That should cover it. That's the only thing that's good, and that is an extremely broad thing, with all the levels. There's many hours of fun, though social media and the "Championship Edition" part of the game's name is just more social media.
But I got this for a dollar in the Humble Bundle. With all the DLC. If you can get this for a dollar, get it. As for full price, no. As for half price, maybe. 75% off is the pretty good, because this is a Pac-Man spinoff, not the full Pac-Man experience. I will recommend this to those who can accept Pac-Man spinoffs, and are okay with no vanilla.
If you wanted to play the actual old-school pac-man like i did don't get this game.

I spent the first twelve minutes of this game shooting clouds and tumbleweeds and getting a meat bounty of 9011.  I'm serious, it's not even funny.
As a long-time fan of Asymmetic Publications's...well, publications, I am well-aquainted with the weird, wonderful and wacky hijinks one can have with their wares. PSA: For those familiar with Kingdom of Loathing, skip the next few paragraphs, these are going to be for the newcomers.
To those that have never played Kingdom of Loathing (KoL), this game could can your laughter and sell it off on the open market for premium rates. Premium Canned Laughs. It is a thing. Asymmetic believes "If it isn't funny or story-building, it doesn't belong."  and that motto is proved through the dense liana of jokes, quips, minor cattle-prodding at grammar and spelling, bizzare, surreal and otherwise humorous interactions that spice the game in liberal quanitities.
If Fallout 4's ideology is "It's not the destination (or the dialogue), but the journey that's important", WoL gives Bethesda a Double-Fisted Skull Smashing pound to the noggin and proclaims in proud fashion, "You're an idiot." and proceeds to strip the padding out of boring searching for the next waypoint.  Travel is point-to-point with random encounters happing about once every travel, but they are quick interludes (that half-way decent Outfoxin' stats can resolve in most cases) in between the points of interest.
Every location has numerous interesting points to inspect; if it looks interesting, it's got something worth your time. Characters have depth to them, even if the dialogue can be linear at least it's not faking you out.  It's been a while that I've played a game where I want to talk to every NPC.
Combat is fluid and deeper than your usual fare with satisfying results.  Statistics are limited to three main stats and a few damage+ stats, so the initial difficulty curve is lower as you're getting into it.  The automatic leveling suggestions are well-thought out and give you the option to spend your exp elsewhere for a bit if you wish (or all the time, the game only slightly judges you for this.)
The game deserves the praise it gets and it's a solid investment of your money and time.  Why are you still reading this?  I mean, thanks for doing that, but buy the game already!  Go on, I'll only judge you if you take more than a minute to hit that "Add to Cart" button.  I mean it, I'll judge you. *stares in judgement*
To those that have played KoL and know the score, this is up to Jick's usual stratospheric standards.  Best ten bucks I've spent for any Loathing-related purchase.  I do have a Dancing Frog, but that's 2 Mr. A's so that doesn't count.
But you KNOW this already, so why are you reading this? You probably want the skinny on what's different, right?  You played the WoL path...buuuuut...something's gotta be different, right?
You bet your bottom meat there is:
Stats defend against themselves - Mustle to Mustle, Myst to Myst, and Moxie to Mojo; maybe it's them hellcows been chewin' on the fabric of reality.  This is the biggest change aside from...
Semi-grid-based combat - Positioning is important, but mostly for protecting yourself against ranged attacks.  Duck behind that barrel of beans, or beans in the shape of a barrel to keep stuff from shooting you in the <kneecap>.
Action Points are your MP - And you get your AP back at the end of every combat.
HP recovers at the end of combat - And it's a good thing it does...
Death comes on swift hooves - Did I mention the hellcows?  I'm sure I mentioned the hellcows.
Exp is a single resource - Instead of being split up into the substats you're used to, you just buy your stats with your accmulated exp.
No character levels - As there are no character levels in the West (guess they had a meeting and shot the guy that suggested it), you directly upgrate your levels in everything which includes...
Skills have individual levels - No more one-size-fits-all skills, if you want them to be good, you have to put your exp into it.
Food/Booze/Spleen gives buff effects last for a day - As such, your consumption is no longer about turn-gen, but what stats you want to buff that "day".  You can sleep, but that incriments...
The Day counter - guess there's a thing for speedrunners.  Wonder how that will work out in the future. I dunno, I just got this today!
Much Dialogue - Great speeching! Very talk! Must pat devs! Devs good bois.
Speak to Goblins! - No word on FARQUAR yet though...
There's enough the same that you'll feel comfortable slotting yourself into the world.  It breathes the same air as KoL does, but the Wild West has it's own flavor to it.
It's worth it.  Take that Mr. A money you were going to use and shove it in here. Asymmetric made this for you, after all.  They made it for others to get a glimpse of what KoL offers, but between the ghost pickles, Ellsbury (poor guy) and all the other subtle nods to KoLore, it was made for us first of all.  That Asymmetric made the game enjoyable for others to be able to play and feel included in is just Knob frosting on the Knob cake.
tl;dr: Buy it.  Yes, buy it now.

Probably the best thing this game has going for it is the story and setting.  The writing is above average for a computer RPG.  I'm mostly hooked into this world, its characters, and a bizarre plot about a German homicidal dragon. There are some interesting plot choices to make but it doesn't escape the feeling of being a fairly linear game with a single planned outcome.
Having said that, there's a lot in here that I find frustrating. I know this is classic 2D stuff, but not being able to rotate the camera view is infuriating.  Similarly, the environment is often so dark and bland that I struggle to find enemies against the background and properly identify cover.
The combat is terribly mediocre.  Shooting, melee, magic - none of it feels exciting, in part because the animations/spell effects/etc. are so drab and bland.  Because of this, the character classes feel empty and meaningless.  You start up the game and start drooling over the idea of a Street Samurai, or a Technomage, or whatever - but the reality is that each of them has a few different melee/ranged attacks that do damage - or they can buff/heal.  There's nothing exciting here, and the depth to each class is quite shallow.
I gave up before finishing the main plot-line.  There are far too many better games out there to waste your time on.  4/10

I bought this game on sale and enjoyed playing it very much to this point. I have finally finished the game, and am now editing my review. See below for the Original Review.
=========
New Review
=========
While I finally did finish the game, it doesn't wholly change my opinion of it. I realize this game has some age to it, but I will still review it based on my experience of it, regardless of the time period I played it in. If it hasn't aged well...then that is unfortunate.
Story 7.5/10 - The story is actually pretty decent. Not great, but decent. I've said this before and I'll say it again, this game still tops FF15's story tenfold for one major thing...characters. I did actually like the characters, and the little twist near the end was pleasant as well. Overall it survives but still lacks something...like a soda with no sugar.
Music 10/10 - I LOVE the music in this game, all from the ambient music while wandering the Kreuz to the remixed/whole title screen battle music near the end. Well done.
Sound effects 6/10 - Barely passable. Not great, not horrible. I felt like I heard the same sound effect for guns and magic over and over just at a slightly different pitch.
Gameplay and Polish 3.5/10 - This is what gets me the most. The battle system, as stated in the old review, feels like the isometric RPG version of a generic cover shooter. What I mean is...the Isometric RPG is there, but it lacks any real depth and contains very little strategy. Imagine Gears of War but theres no quick running, or jumping from one set of cover to another, no bonuses for proper reloading, etc.
You cannot setup most "normal battles" in any way, shape, or form besides maybe entering a different door to the same location to start the battle itself. The animations for magic all look almost identical and have no weight to them. The way the characters run looks like a running animation I did when I first started my college animation classes, or something I threw together in Flash back when Newgrounds was more popular. The environments you explore are almost entirely linear and 95% of the quests and locations can easily be found or solved by holding the Alt button, which reveals objects you can interact with. This would be fine if there wasn't only 2-4 interactable objects in each area. It's bland.
There's also a very tedious bug while jacked in that prevents the character you're controlling from finishing his/her turn. You have to end the turn, even if you have 3 remaining turn points, in order to continue (or reload a previous save). This annoyed the hell out of me.
Overall 5/10 - In my whole hearted opinion, I believe story and characters are the most important aspect of any story, whether that be told in a book, or a game, or a movie. The story in this game does hold up, but this story is told in a videogame, so gameplay must be mentioned. The gameplay and polish of Shadowrun Dragonfall just doesn't hold up in its current state, however, I will say it now, this game is better than FF15. Tabata (director of FF15), if you ever somehow read this, get a better ♥♥♥♥ing writer. In fact, just take the writer from this game (as he/she are arguably good), slap him on your team, and make a better FF.

I want to like this series so badly, but so far, I'm just not impressed. Open world Shooters are few and far between and it's a concept that should be awesome. But for me, Far Cry 2 falls short, and while it's technically a better game than the first one, it fails in many new areas which I just can't get past. I think what's the most frustrating is that because I had such high hopes for this series, its appearant flaws are making it crash and burn all that much harder for me.
I'd talk about the story, but it just didn't interest me. You're a gun for hire in some part of Africa who catches malaria and you have to do a bunch of stuff for two waring factions. That's really about it.
The game is quite a large open world. The map is big, and there's lots of areas to explore and do missions in. But not long into the game, this is where I discovered the first huge irritation. To travel around in this open world, you should probably have a vehicle. Jeeps are plentiful and fairly fast. The problem is the trigger happy twitchy enemy AI who will shoot at literally anything that moves. They will also follow you to the ends of the earth. It's so damn frustrating to have your vehicle be shot at, and once it starts smoking it slows to a grinding halt, and you have to fight off these dumb f***ing AI who hunt you down just so you can repair your damn vehicle and move on. Travelling on foot would take so long it's not even worth trying. At least you don't walk or sprint as slow as the first game.
There's enemy outposts you can clear out, but there's absolutely no point though. The game tells you how many of them you've "scouted", AKA killed every last idiot there, but if you ever come across the outpost again, which you will, all the enemies will have respawned like nothing ever happened. Going around the outposts isn't always an option because it guards a bridge you might have to cross to continue on the road to whatever your goal is.
One bit of realism that is in the game for some reason is gun jamming. Why? This is a damn game. On several occasions I go into a fire fight, only to have my primary killing tool jam within the first ten seconds. Then the seconds tick by as I am getting slowly riddled with bullets as I attempt to fix the gun. Ten, fifteen seconds go by. Twenty seconds, oh, I'm dead. Or I would be if I hadn't rage quit. Seriously, why is this a thing? It's such a stupid gimmick that detracts from the overall experience and adds exponential frustration to the game.
Now, credit where credit is due, this is an open world game. While I said that was one of my main problems with the game, you can approachs situations however you like. Stealth, guns blazing, whatever. And this game isn't nearly as difficult as its predecessor. I just find that the unrealistically stupid AI just ruins it for me. I tried really hard to get through this game. I have probably 8 hours of playtime with the off Steam play I did, but I just couldn't take the AI anymore, having to constantly fight off goons just to repair my Jeep and move on with what I actually want to do.
Now you may be confused as to why I am actually recommending this game with how negative I've been. This isn't a bad game. Far from it. It's just that my experience with the game has been less than stellar and it frustrates me to no end. I think I can summarize the game, at least in my opinion, as a dissapointment. Should you play this game? Yes. Will you like it more than I did? Most likely.

While SmashBall is about having nerves of steel and fulfilling your chosen role, Epigenesis is more of a thinking man's game. It's strategic action, it's truly a sport with original (as far as I've seen) game mechanics, and it avoids feeling like a team deathmatch that has Those-Objectives-That-Mean-Nothing. Pick up the ball from the center and throw it through the enemy's gate, and you earn a seed to customize. Bring it safely to an uncaptured node, and you will earn a team bonus and a structure of your choosing.
Personally, I prefer ramps with an air control team bonus (Option 2 of Loadout 1) so that my teammates and I have vantage points, can advance across the field faster, can dodge and pursue enemies better, and avoid falling as often. And I really want extreme air control with ramps everywhere, so I focus on the objective and work with people. That way I can separate myself from multiple pursuers if I run back to my side of the field, take a ramp, and change direction to fool the remainder who anticipate the ramp getting used. Oh, best part yet? Take a seed to the enemy's gate with a neighboring node under your control, and you will instantly win the game for your team.
Fun? Yes. Recommended? Yes. I'd join the official Epigenesis group if you're looking to buy it; a little community effort and a few new friends should help keep your games full and interesting.
