Pretty good game! It's refreshingly intuitive compared to other F2P CCGs on steam like faeria or infinity wars, and it plays more like hearthstone than those games. To be frank, it plays a LOT like hearthstone, but that's OK. It's fun, intuitive, it's well put-together, and it's got a decent little stroyline on top of that. I do have a few criticisms tho.
1) Lack of real turn-around cards. The game doesn't have enough swing. An early advantage and staying on curve will almost always garuntee you the game. I haven't seen any boardwipes so far, and removal is more minimalistic overall than huge swingy effects, so that reduces a lot of the player choice, and it can sometimes feel like the result is going to be inevitable after even very early advantages or disadvantages. There is a system set up to try and mitigate this, the prophecy system, whereby when you reach certain life thresholds, you draw a card, which you can play for free if they have the prophecy keyword, but generally prophecy seems underwhelming, and the cards seem significantly under-curved when played normally, and are very rarely game-changers; however, there are many cards that give you advantage for being ahead in life, and honestly, they seem to me to be a bigger advantage than prophecy.
2) going 2nd is a HUGE advantage. You get an item (ring of magicka) that's essenetially the coin from hearthstone, but can be used 3 times, once per turn. You'd be very hard pressed to find anyone familiar with CCGs at all who could argue that going 2nd isn't a blatant overall advantage. Curve being so vital in this game only compound the problem, as the ring will almost gauruntee you stay on perfect curve for a long series of turns.
Overall though, it's a solid enough game, and for free, it's definately worth trying. It's a nice change of pace from some other steam CCGs, and i could see the game improving with future updates.

Absolutely fantastic game. Anyone who is a fan of turn based games, card based games, stat management, settlement management, or a host of other features should definitely get this.
I have hundreds of hours in the GoG version so I have no hours on Steam.
The only negatives I can state are:
If you get a bad start it can make the early game very hard/slow - and the game is unforgiving as it is. However, you can save your settings so starting a new game takes 30 seconds if you want to game the map generation.
The end game is really fun, and punishing - but after you go through levelling up all the gods and optimising your playstyle there isn't much beyond it since the story is quite linear - you're trying to decide the fate of Thea. You have lots of choices don't get me wrong, but you'll end up at the same point in the story whether it takes you 100 days or 500. That aside, if you are a completionist there are hundreds of hours worth of content here, and if you're not then maybe you'll get 30-60 hours which for the price is not bad at all.

I would say this game is worth playing, but, only until the final completion of all three quests, lines, which can all be done on the same playthrough. I was irked by the fact that I could 'quit' after completing one, thinking I had to restart or I couldn't complete the other victory requirements until the end credits told me otherwise.
I like Thea in a, I have a gambling problem, sort of way. In many ways, it's a really easy game to lose early on and it requires losing consistently in order to come to understand how the game mechanics work. On normal difficulty, I think I had about 10 play throughs before I finally figured out a strategy to win the initial quest. Losing is a part of the game's progression and the gods that are suppose to serve as the player's avatar will level up and give you cheap bonuses. That part of the game I absolutely hate and I found myself resetting the playthrough in order to avoid getting freebies in order to avoid rewarding myself for failure. I suppose in the grand scale of Thea, if the player is suppose to be a diety then your followers really don't matter, you just keep picking up one tribe, one after another until you finally find a successful one, and that's incredibly meta.
The game does a lot stuff like that, where you're the God(dess) guiding your civilization, but, at the same time, you encounter yourself or avatars of yourself and you're basically talking through your worshippers but at the same time getting critized / praised by yourself for the actions you take in accordance with other guidance you have recieved from another aspect of yourself. The game's tutorial mentions this, but, it can be a slightly jarring experience if you forget that warning.
Personally, I think the game probably is at it's best when it's ramped up to the highest difficulty setting and it's also a lot easier on it's highest difficulty setting. Choices really matter then and the risk of losing your village members helps cement the feeling of caution against going against an opponent that on a lower difficulty, may not appear to be such a big threat. There's no deadline in Thea, no  countdown timer, so it's a game in which the patient will truly be the victor. In fact, it can become quite boring in time because it's a game in which micromanagement is a key factor to victory.
Advancement of your civilization is based on research, which is done by going on quests, fighting or crafting objects and buildings. Fighting and quests are straightforward, so really in order to advance, you may need to have your craftsmen build 50 objects, but at the same time, you can recycle those objects, so the player has to manually go in, drop the shields into the recycling icon, and let the workers keep building objects. It's tedious.
Even though I'm selecting a yes recommendation, I could go either way on this particular game. It's basically advanced solitaire and a way to suck up time, but, I don't feel like it'll ever be a cult classic or anything more than just a game.
Not bad, better than the first version of the game (though it's the same exact game). Let's hope the next title will be a bit more immersive (and add vegeta wig pretty please).

This was a HUGE improvement from the first Xenoverse game! I played the first one on PS3 and was super frustrated with the controls and missions, but this game was enjoyable the entire way through.
I was enjoying this game so much to the point where I would actively do all of the side missions that came up all the time (and that's something I usually don't do in games). I didn't end up having trouble at any point either. It was comfortably challenging (unlike the first game).
I played through the whole game as a Saiyan, so leveling up to Super Saiyan was quite straight-forward. On the other hand, I know someone who played as a Majin and did not do the side missions, so when they got to the point where Majin Buu had to have 6 kids before they could progress, it was a painful and dumb process.
So in short - if you play this game, I highly recommend you play as a Saiyan first or do every side mission as they come up, or the end game part will take a looong time to get caught up.
Overall it was fun gameplay, and I enjoyed the custom story with actual DB story elements in it. It's also a really cool combination to mix a fighting game with an MMO; and this one was much more well-done than the first one.
Although there is one complaint I have with the MMO aspect. If you are playing in the online server, but not using the online functions, you will be kicked out of the game if your internet goes down. Also it will kick you off if you have not used online functions after a certain time limit.
I also really enjoyed the character customization in this game. I wish there was a way to have certain costumes that affected the stats and others that did not, because since I enjoy playing a balanced game style, I would only choose clothing with balanced stats, and I would not get to customize my character how I wanted them to look because I would be too focused on the stats. I wish you could have different characters in the same save file as well though, because I feel that would be easier to max out the special skills for your characters without having to repeat a whole lot of story elements. Another aspect I wish you could customize is the Hero from the first game. I played my save file on PS3, so I was unable to link the game to this version. Instead I had to choose one of the default characters they provided. I wish you could have created a new character in Xenoverse 2 to be the Hero character, instead of just choosing from a list of maybe 10 options.
I would recommend this game for all DBZ fans!

If you enjoy Runescape or board-game-ish CCGS, or both, you'll likely enjoy Chronicle.
Not only are there a lot of references to various quests and characters from the MMO Runescape, the gameplay in Chronicle is pretty unique too. Rather than standard CCG gameplay, you set up a set of obstacles and rewards for your character, trying to keep your health and gold up while minimizing your opponent's hero's gains.
Your hero generally defeats monsters you place, in order to gain gold or other rewards(armor, which acts like bonus health, or weapons, which temporarily boost your damage are the most common) and then spends them in a variety of ways.
Getting a powerful(but fragile) sword, dueling the opponent to reduce their health, or buying a pie to restore your health being some examples.
There are also a few combination cards or cards with effects beyond those simple ones, but the best way to learn about that stuff is to try it out(also because this review would get overly long if I tried to list every quirky effect or neat reference.). It's free to play after all.

I
didn't buy this game. But I'm so glad that I did. I was looking for something of a certain kind of niche genre, and it sounded like SuperPower 2 was exactly what I was looking for. But then I started reading the reviews, and read through the first few pages, which at the time were filled with mostly negative ones, speaking of a game that was mortally wounded by utterly game-breaking bugs and frequent crashes.
Disappointed, I continued my search for other games. I came across a few that sounded promising; RealPolitik, GPS etc, but once again, reading the reviews, it seemed that desite their grand intentions -- all of these great sounding titles were fatally flawed with varying degrees of gameplay issues.
A few days later, I still felt the pull towards SP2, and came back for another read. I don't know if it was (unintentionally) my settings, but this time the first few pages were full of mostly positive reviews, which led me to the discovery of the Realism2016 mod, and that the vast majority of all those bugs I'd read about had actually long since been fixed by a dedicated modding community. So I took the plunge, and gave it a try.
I'm in the year 2147 currently, playing as Palestine -- and I'm delighted to report that my game has not crashed at all at any point. Not one single crash, or any game-breaking bugs in sight. The
thing that I've seen occur so far, is when moving units around on the map, maybe they don't always end up
where I wanted them, but seriously, it's a minimal margin of error on most occasions, and certainly not something that cannot be easily lived with, when considering all that this game gives back for the investment of your time. And it will certainly guzzle up large portions of that, if you let it. ;)  It is extremely immersive, and an engaging musical score really adds to the feeling of playing.
This game's depth and complexity is majestic. If you enjoy a game that asks for a lot of investment from you in your attention to the finest of details in order to be truly successful - but rewards you in great measure for your efforts - then I'd imagine you'll derive a lot of enjoyment from SuperPower 2. I have found it to be thoroughly absorbing, and you can become so deeply involved within it, that hours of (real) time have slipped by almost unnoticed.
Due to its vast intricacies, this is primarily a game for intelligent, patient and thoughtful people if you really want to get the most out of it; but then if all you want to do is just jump straight into inflaming a global thermonuclear war, to hell with the economy and all your people who empower it -- and everything else is simply extraneous collateral damage -- well, I guess there's even something in it for you too. ;)  But why you would wish to destroy such a beautifully rendered interactive world, I cannot fathom. :)
TLDR: Don't be put off by the many negative reviews that write this game off as broken and unplayable. With the dedicated modding community working to keep this great classic game up to date, all major game-breaking bugs have been fixed, and from the time of writing in the (gametime) year 2147 - not had a single crash so far. The game works almost perfectly (show me one that is
100% bug-free?), at least on this windows 7 machine anyway.
A very deep and complex game which can offer you endless hours of enjoyment if you're prepared to invest in learning the underlying mechanisms of effectively operating the State Machinery; or -- if you just want to blow sh*t up -- there is plenty of fun to be had there for you too. ;)

mod. Enjoy.

I feel this is a difficult game to review in 2015, it's a  game that I feel wouldn't be loved if it was released in todays industry.
The original game  FarCry was quite a difficult game to complete, there's very little in terms of aids to help the player in  FarCry and FarCry2 takes a similar stance.
There's no indicators to tell the player where they're taking damage from, if they're in stealth or not and there's no ability to tag enemies. For me these things only adds to the immersion, it's more brutal that way but for a lot of players not having those indicators would leave them feeling frustrated or that the game is broken.
There's no minimap, you need to get the map out from your pocket to have a look, once again for some people this only adds to immersion but to others it's just awkward, I guess it just depends on the type of player you are.
The biggest flaws with FarCry2 are the fact it's an open World 1st person shooting game that fails to deliver a decent open World to explore and at the same time having sloppy weapon mechanics and for those 2 reasons I wouldn't recommend FarCry2.
I've spent over 30 hours with FarCry2 on the PC and there's aspects of the game I really liked.
Visually I find it very pleasing, the setting and atmosphere are rather nice.
The fire mechanics I feel are the best in the series and creating mass scale fires to clear out check points never got old.
Plant physics, so they move when you touch or drive over them and branches will drop down if you shoot though them.
The vehicles although extremely bland to drive with awful sound effects have had some nice little touches added, they get dirty when driven in the jungle and the level of destruction is greater than that in FarCry3 in terms of your car falling apart, lights being smashed, bumpers or bonnets flying off.
But in the end FarCry2 feels empty, the map is lifeless and barren. There's no civilians who live there, it's pretty much you and everyone else is your enemy. The check points you clear and even other locations will have guards re-spawning, so it's this never ending army and it's not even that they  re-spawn hours later, they do it with in a couple of minutes and it feels cheap and breaks the immersion.
The auto-save system doesn't work very well, you often have to go back an hour in to game after you die. There is the option to press F5 and do a quick save, which is great if you remember to do it every 10 minutes but you're meant to be immersed in the game, not thinking about saving.
An open World game should entice you to explore and FarCry2 doesn't. A 1st person shooting game should have solid gun mechanics and FarCry2 doesn't.
FarCry2 has a nice physics engine, it's an enjoyable African grassland fire simulator but that's sadly all it has to offer.

This game was quite a slog to me, and the only reason I finished was because I am a bit of a completist. It is quite a long game, especially if you finish all side missions. I think my main issue was that every mission was the exact same. Blow this up or kill that person. I do enjoy 'splosions and assassination missions, but nothing changes in the world as you go through the campaign, so playing them gets mundane quickly.
The world itself is large. I loved the day/night cycle and weather. The thing that aggravated me the most about traveling in this world was the rapidly respawning guard shacks. You wipe out everyone in the area, drive down the road for a bit, turn back around, and voila, everyone is back. It feels like an annoying tactic to make the game last longer than it should. I'd understand guards being there after 6 in-game hours or something, but just getting out of sight of the area shouldn't prompt automatic respawns.
Far Cry 2 was quite a change from the original. While I appreciated some changes, the lack of an engaging narrative and repetitive missions/opponents made this game more of a bore the longer it lasted.

Wow, not entirely sure what to say about this one. For those looking to try it, it's a very short and disturbing experience.
I think there's a lot of ways you could interpret the games content, but analyzing it makes me feel a little bit like the character in the game, trying to apply meaning to something that may or may not be meaningful. Perhaps what got to me the most was how much I related to the character who seems to be experiencing a substantial amount of pain and paranoia.
SPOILERS
I found the ending a bit disappointing, but maybe that says something about me as a person. At first I wandered all around the apartment after being given the last objective, looking for something else to do. Personally I feel that the game would have more impact if the player were able to repeat the few given objectives almost endlessly with only one real option for "progression". To me that would further cement the feeling of having only one way out in the players mind.
As is though, being forced to hang myself I found both disturbing and oddly cathartic, to the point where I found myself strangely eager to proceed into the other lives (I had the woman who jumps from her condo to be my next potential experience) and really disappointed to see credits rolling. Please don't take this as me seeing the game encouraging the idea of suicide, however. I see it more as demystifying it. Often I take out aggression, sadness, and other negative emotions by playing games that allow the player to do something you aren't able to really would never want to do in real life, so I think that having a game that allows you to flush out your own depression through the eyes of someone else could actually be kind of theraputic.

Once I started playing 'Grim Fandango', I could not stop!

The theme of the game is a little bit of film noir detective fiction, a little bit of the Mexican Day of the Dead. In the land of the living, the graphics change to a kind of twisted photo cut-and-paste look.
The best thing about Grim Fandango, as with all other classic LucasArts point-and-click adventures is the sassy humour. It works extra well in the context of a noir crime thriller like this. The story has all the basic hallmarks of a Raymond Chandler private-eye novel, with layers of absurdist jokes and puzzles on top.
My only issue with the game is how long it takes to get around on foot. I discovered after a couple of hours that double clicking equals running. The game might be a bit slow for someone without a lot of patience or who gets easily frustrated by puzzle solutions that are deliberately abstract. I wish I had the patience to wait for Manny Calavera to casually walk to each location because it suits his character. Grim Fandango is a game that has a leisurely pace and doesn't really deserve to be rushed.

I was first introduced to this game by my brother (CrispyMarshmellows) back in... 2012 I think. I liked what I saw, it was the first FPS I ever really played and you know, I had fun. But one day I stopped playing (probably the day I discovered TF2) and didn't return to it ever again. But then one parculiar day in 2015, three years later, I see the game has had a Steam release. I decided this was the time to give it a second chance.
Now before I continue, I'd like to point out that I've played Team Fortress 2 A LOT. 2,072 hours and continuing to climb. I am fully aware that this is not a class-based shooter and therefore won't compare Brick Force's structure to TF2's Structure because class based gameplay is not what this game is going for. It's going for something comparable to CoD (oh lord...) thrown in a rusty blender with Minecraft.
Story:
What's that? There isn't one?   ...ok then... Allow me to make up some bullsh*t for you:
Brick Mannly stole Sir Brickenstein's lawnmower one day so Brickenstein gathered some friends to go to kick Mannly's♥♥♥♥♥and take back the lawnmower. In retaliation, Mannly gathered his friends to go kick Brickenstein's♥♥♥♥♥even harder and keep his prized lawnmower. This developed into a global war because this world's population is are a bunch of overzealous dunces.
Gameplay:
Oh sweet lord the gameplay, Back on track with my story.
I started up the game to be greeted by a message to make a Brick-Force profile... "Hmm" I asked myself. "Why can't I just use my Steam profile?" I asked again. I did as told and proceeded to a mandatory tutorial. It was here I started noticing somewhat problematic issues. My feild of view (FOV) was set to what, 30? I wanted to change it. I was shocked to find that I couldn't. In a first person shooter, that's a huge red flag. I continued without many issues regarding control. The game didn't crash at all either, something I see others mention alot. I must just be lucky.
Anyway, Once done, I jumped into a game on a map featuring floating islands. The blue base situated on a lonely floating island where as red base was a castle turret. You see the issue right? Map balance seems non existant here. In team deathmatch, this gives red a huge defense advantage over blue. So much is wrong with that kind of map design, Any TF2 player will tell you that map designers. Onwards with the story, I left blue spawn to find red mercilessly camping our one and only tiny exit door. I facepalm hard enough to leave a mark on my forehead and leave the game. I join another, on a bridge map of some description. The map balance was much better here though. Both sides looked roughly the same. Delighted, I carried on towards horrendous death. I foundmyself blindsighted one too many times however. Oh boy, isn't this FOV just WONDERFUL?
I spent a bit of time before remembering one thing about this game. The ♥♥♥♥ing pay-to-win model. The stock weapons you have are a horrendous AK-47 and a crappy little peashooter that looks like a pistol. At this point the game says: "Oh do you not like my very balanced stock weapons? You want better things? Well why not buy them from the store with real money!" The realisation came fast and I was appauled. This game was pay-to-win. Various clothing you can buy exists as well in a manor something like TF2. But unlike that certain good game, These things gave you advantages over the competition. I simply shook my head, closed the game and uninstalled it.
Graphics:
The game looks alright enough but one key issue was that some pinhead on the dev team cranked the gamma level up way too high. The game is a visual eyesore with no actual lighting. Like Minecraft Indev except... ♥♥♥♥♥ier.
Sound:
As far as I'm aware the game has no music. If it does it didn't work for me. As for actual sound direction the weapons make good enough sounds when using them. But there's no hitsound. That is a standard thing for this genre. To know when you've hit someone and how much damage you did is crucial to planning your moves. Even CoD has a hitsound. And for the record, TF2 might not START with a hitsound but you can head into the advanced options and turn it on at least.
One last thing. Whenever you get a kill, you hear the most obnoxious little sounds these guys call voice acting.
The Verdict:
Stay far away from this game. There are so many other, better games both in the FPS genre and  in the sandbox genre. I'd say only poke this game with your ten foot pole when you require a dead horse to beat. Even then, Internet Explorer is better for dead-horse beating.

there's a lot to do in thea. from micro managing your village, your expeditions, making sure they're armed, and with enough food, and wood to set camp, all while roaming the vast expanse of the land. in the meantime, gathering resources, and building up your village, crafting tons of items ... and you keep going and going.
but one of the best feature i suppose, is the almost endless amount of random encounters you'll get each and every time you take a turn. it doesnt matter how long you've clocked, chances are, you still havent seen it all. and even within the same encounters, how it plays out could differ each time, based on so many various factors such as the god you worship, the skills of the characters in your party, the type of characters in your party, etc. all these things gives it a lot of replayability in itself.
the combat is also unique, presenting itself as cards to the players, and that too, requires some learning before you start developing strategies to beat those battles. while there are basic properties to them, and they're obviously not as large a variety like a proper TCG, it still makes it interesting enough.
all in all, thea is a unique experience to say the least. of course, there are some things i personally wished were in the game, such as the ability to build more villages, or a bit more depth to the battles, but those are minor gripes. and with some luck, we might get to see them in thea2.
also, for the price you're paying, the devs are giving out ALL dlcs for free! in this day and age, not many would do a thing like that. it's always nice to have devs that put the customers first. definitely well worth the support, especially if you're a fan of the genre.

You might wonder why I’m still giving this game a thumbs up eh?
Aight so let’s clear some things up.
I started this game up and expected nothing besides a weird♥♥♥♥♥japanese hack ‘n slash.
What I got was a horrible, horrible, HORRIBLE, first experience.
The game ran like a dead hamster without legs under water. It was unplayable.
I had to force the game to run at 120FPS in order for it to work as I’d like it to work.
I mean I really don’t care about the whole 30FPS stuff but dude … at least fix your darn game.
Anyway after I fiddled with the .ini files it worked and I actually enjoyed it for what it is.
Now I first started the game on Very Hard because I always try to play my games at the hardest difficulty. The thing with Killer is Dead or KiD is that it’s not meant to be played just once for several reasons.
If you care ‘bout achievements then get ready to play through the game three times since difficulty doesn’t stack.
Since you can just jump from mission to (sub)mission once you’ve beaten or unlocked it it’s clear that this game’s going to be rather grindy like, well, most if not all JRPGs.
After I’ve then changed the difficulty to normal and actually dealt damage to enemies it wasn’t all that bad. In fact it was quite enjoyable.
So what’s KiD all ‘bout you might ask.
You’re slippin’ into the role of Mondo Zappa, an executioner, working for Bryan Execution Firm.
From said firm you’re getting paid to go ‘round the world and to kill dangerous killers and assassins.

Mondo’s wielding, of course, a Katana with his right hand and his left arm’s basically cyberkinetic and you’re able to transform it into several sub weapons like a drill for example which you can use in order to break down walls to find secret areas and to break through enemy shields.
Besides that the arm’s also sucking blood which you’ll need for several things.
After you’ve chosen your desired mission you’re job’s to kill everything on sight as fast and as cool as possible in order to get as many heal, rose and moon crystals.
Health and rose crystal increase your max health and blood level while the moon crystals are used in order to upgrade Mondo.
The combat heavily relies on you having a decent reaction since you deal the most damage after dodging an enemy attack. If you successfully dodge an attack you’re able to mash the X button as fast as you can in order to deal maximum damage.
Some enemies, including bosses, might be immune to normal attacks so you have to stun’em in order to use your blood burst.
Once you’ve stunned an enemy you’ll see an icon and RT over their head which tells you to hold RT and press X in order to either cut something off or to kill.
That’s pretty much the whole combat I mean hey it’s a hack ‘n slash.
There’s a combo system as well and it’s actually somewhat important. Well it’ll make things a lot easier if you’re able to maintain a good combo.
If you reach a combo of 35 you’re able to execute your enemies by pressing X for moon, Y for health, B for roses and A for nothing.
Basically if you execute an enemy you can press the desired button in order to get more of said material.
To make it simple: The better the combo, the more upgrade materials, the easier the game.
That’s pretty much it.
The thing’s just that every mission is relatively short and there’s no challenge when you’re playing on normal and every boss fight’s exactly the same.
A boss fight has between two or three phases and you get into the next phase by successfully performing the blood burst attack.
There’re quite some neat mini games and references though like the motorcycle battle in FF VII.
The game features 12 main missions and several sub missions that you can do if you fancy those.
Then there’s the Mondo’s Girls mission.

Basically you’re trying to get laid. In order to get laid you have to use your … sigh … Gigolo Vision … to accumulate guts. You gain guts by checking out the body of the beauty in front of your with said vision in order to see her underwear. Once you’ve gained enough guts you can gift her a present in order to woo her and to achieve your goal: TO GET LAID!
So that’s fun.
I mean I wouldn’t recommend the game for its full price but it’s usually always on a discount somewhere around four bucks and it’s alright to pick it up for that price.
There’re some issues you’ll have to deal like screen tearing and so on but overall it’s worth playing through at least once. Especially if you’re looking through a rather weird game and hey ...did I mention it’s made by Suda 51?

You know, I loved the works of Suda51. They always have this bizarre and surreal storylines as well as exciting gameplay plus some unusual yet unique visuals. However, what about his another stylistic opus, Killer is Dead? Is it a hack n slash fan’s wet dream or just another irritating action experience?
Killer is Dead is another artistic effort made by the visionaire himself Suda51, along with his guys at Grasshopper Manufacture. It has some familiar elements from Suda’s previous titles, such as the gameplay of Lollipop Chainsaw mixed with the visual style of No More Heroes.
First, let’s talk about the story a bit, shall we? You enter the shoes of Mondo Zappa, an assassin-for-hire who works for an assassination firm who tasks Mondo to kill dangerous bad guys around the world. Along with him in missions are his beloved katana and his mechanical arm “Musselback”, who helps him when fighting enemies as well as his friends the cyborg Bryan, the hot chick Vivienne, and his sidekick
Mika. The game lets you go through the missions of Mondo’s assassinations as well as his personal struggles and his childhood later on.
Out of all the stories that Suda51 has written for his games, KID has the most bizarre and nonsensical of them all. Not David Lynch’s Eraserhead type of bizarre, but really bizarre♥♥♥♥♥♥that makes people go “What the hell is going on?”.  Most of the time the plot doesn’t make any sense and doesn’t correlate well with each episode. There are some characters that were introduced to the story with little to no explanation at all and certain events in the game just.........sorta happened for the sake of the story. Also (ehem, spoilers),

The gameplay is what you might expect from a Suda51 title. It’s the usual “You hack this, you slash that, you dodge this, you block that, plus press this to parry” style of gameplay. However, it doesn’t really add anything new to the table and just revising the old stuff that has been the thing in the hack n slash games over the years. Well, there’s a cool counter-attack system when you dodge an attack successfully and an easy-to-understand character upgrade system, but besides those things, gameplay is “meh” at best. There’s nothing wrong with it, but it could’ve been done much better.
Another thing that I kinda have mixed feelings with is the game’s soundtrack. I appreciate that the composer was trying to be diverse with its style of music in each episode, but cmon man, try harder than that. Most of the tracks are generic and forgettable. They don’t really get you in the mood of fighting the biggest, baddest villains of the game. Probably the only good thing about the whole soundtrack is that the jazz-themed loading screens are nice, so kudos to that.
The English voice acting in the game is okay (I guess???). Well, it kinda falls into the “generic anime English dub” territory a bit, but it wasn’t exactly the worst English voice acting I’ve heard from a Japanese-made video game. Just wished the whole cast could put more effort into it. However, if you really want the true KID experience, try playing with the Japanese dub on. It’s much more fitting and just fun to hear characters banter with each other in Japanese.
What the game really truly shines on is in its art direction. The cel-shaded visual style of KID does fit with its weird story and the settings, with each of them having a distinct tone and atmosphere. Characters are pretty diverse in the game, with each of them having a unique appearance and personality. Although I can say Mondo himself is one of those protags who is pretty much OP with little character development whatsoever.
At the end of the day, Killer is Dead is just your another ordinary hack n slash title. The story makes little sense whatsoever and the gameplay doesn’t really add anything new to the hack n slash formula. However, its striking visuals, diverse cast of characters and settings, and its overall creativity does made the game sort of different from other hack n slash titles. Still, I can’t really say that the game would be a killer among other well-known HnS games such as DmC or Bayonetta. However, its worth a try, so buy it if you ever have a chance.

So I really liked this game when it first came out. One of my friends got a 4-pack during the free weekend and we all played a few hours. 3 days later the community was dead and there was nobody on any of the servers. I've been thinking about why this happened.
First of all,  the player has only 3 weapons- the projectile weapon (rocket launcher), the railgun (sniper weapon), and melee. Out of the 6 plants that players can plant on captured platforms, only the turret and the ramp are useful in most situations. This severely limits the player's playstyle and makes the overall game less interesting.
Secondly, because the three combat options are hitting a fast moving enemy with your fist while moving very fast, shooting a fast moving enemy with a projectile weapon with a tiny area of effect, or sniping a fast moving enemy without any sort of scope there will be a huge skill gap. New players will have a very hard time actually doing anything, so they won't want to stick around. The only way to get better is to practice.
This brings me to my third point; you can't practice because there is nobody to practice against. Most of the time, there are zero players on. The only time anyone is on is for the weekly dev game and the occasional password-protected tournament match.
Also, a lot of the maps aren't much fun to play. The only good maps are the ones with ball spawn areas that are much lower than the goals. Putting the ball spawn lower down makes it easily accessible from multiple routes, making it harder to camp the ball. It also makes it easier to defend because the ball carrier has to climb all the way up to the goal. On a flat map, one team gets to the ball first, camps there, and can easily hold off the other team while they send one player to zip across the map with a powerup and score instantly over and over again.
To the devs- I still think this game is very promising. If you can update it to make it more diverse and suitable for multiple playstyles and narrow the skill gap, then get it featured on the store frontpage with a sale you might be able to build a lasting player base.

Far Cry 2 is one of the best open world games out there. Set in a war-torn African country, there's a wide variety of places to see: from deserts, to deep jungles, small towns...
The story is pretty good. You arrive at this country in order to kill the Jackal, the guy who armed both sides of the conflict. Things go wrong, and you end up taking jobs from the different factions in order to gain their trust, and, in exchange, getting information about your target. Luckily, you're not alone in this mission; although the troops will shoot you on sight even if you're working for them, you'll still come across several buddies (foreigners, just like you) who will help you out during missions.
There's plenty of stuff to do in this game. Besides the main missions, there are different missions you can take, including taking convoys transporting weapons, assassinating certain targets, and helping your buddies out. Also, you'll encounter enemy outposts, and, although taking them out is fun, they respawn quickly, which gets tiring after some time, and you'll end up trying to use fast travel (which, by the way, is only available at certain locations, in the form of bus stops) as much as you can to avoid the outposts.
The environment, as mentioned, is quite varied, and the map is huge. You can move around it using different vehicles, including jeeps, trucks, quads, boats, to name a few. You can unlock safehouses on the different areas, and there's hidden stuff to look for.
Another interesting mechanic is the sickness level: your character is infected with malaria, and there's nothing you can do to cure it, you can only take pills in order to control it. While it's an annoyance most of the time (especially if you have a malaria attack right in the middle of a firefight), it's still an interesting mechanic. There's also weapon degradation, meaning that you'll need to get new weapons from time to time, or run the risk of a weapon jamming at the wrong time. Luckily, weapons bought at stores are always available at armouries next to them.
Well, in conclusion, this is a really good game, one you should really play.

Modern shooters have become little more than corridor crawls. You enter a mission and are funneled through the map with almost no deviation available. As far as the possibility of "next-gen" world building goes, shooters are stuck in a rut. Interestingly enough, Ubisoft made a valiant effort to push the FPS genre forward back in 2008.
Far Cry 2 is one of the most invigorating ideas for a shooter that I've ever played. It doesn't always succeed in it's ambition, but the sense of freedom and the massive size of the world lend themselves to some fantastic moments. Those moments are spread a bit thin, though.
While the very first thing you do in the game has an objective, the next 16 hours are pretty much you exploring. There are light story elements driving some of your actions, but you would be forgiven for not knowing that a plotline even exists. Your starting goal is simply "Kill the Jackal" and that is about as far as the narrative goes.
This is the biggiest flaw with the game. There is no urgency in anything you are doing. You could easily spend years combing over every inch of the game world and never feel obligated or inclined to tackle any missions. While that is very intriguing as a launching point, it makes for a game that feels lackadaisical and pointless.
When you do take up a mission, that is when the game starts to breathe. The fast travel spots are rarely convenient, so you are (almost always) forced to find your own path. The in-game map can help you from getting lost, but it doesn't point out any direction to you. You simply need to chart your own course.
During your travel to the objective spot, you often run into bandits. This emergent style of gameplay leads to some fantastic shoot outs that have you scrambling for your life. These moments do happen a bit too often to stay truly enveloping, but barely dodging a missile and sniping guys across a chasm never cease to be quick fixes of joy.
When you finish a mission, you simply are left with nothing. The currency system in this game is almost entirely worthless. Since your weapons can break down or jam at random intervals, it makes some sense to want to buy fresh ones that you can replenish. Seeing as how you run out of ammo fairly quick, there doesn't seem to be a need to buy those weapons; just grab them off the endless amounts of bodies you pile up.
There is also the threat of malaria consuming you, which can make for some tense shootouts where a question of your mortality comes into play. Honestly, though, apart from some flashy effects on the screen, the whole malaria side of the game seems like an excuse to extend the length. You have to undertake missions devoid of originality to get more medication and it just ends up feeling like wasted time.
I find it hard to remain angry at this game. It took me several months to muster up the desire to even see the conclusion, but the moments of bliss I encountered cannot be understated. I can't think of any game on current generation systems that even comes close to capturing the amount of freedom you are given.
Developers love to throw around the claim that their game will allow you to "go anywhere and see anything." Ubisoft is pretty much the only one that let you do this. Traveling through most of Far Cry 2, though, you begin to wonder if you really want to see every facet of the map.
All in all, I won't say the game is bad. I don't even think it's bad. While there are some crashes here and there, everything works as it should. Enemies are sometimes smart and I never fell through the gameworld. I just wished I could travel around faster. I would also have loved to have a sense that my actions were doing something.
For the average gamer, though....I would take a pass. A game like Far Cry 2 takes a lot of maturity to conquer. It's joys are not quick and easy to obtain. A lot of effort needs to happen on the player's part to make anything of this game. If you're willing to sit through some rough terrain, you'll eventually find the diamond in the rough that lies at the core of Far Cry 2.

One of the best RPGs in resent years. I had very little expectations after Shadowrun Returns, and was simply blown away by Dragonfall. Allow me to share some of my thoughts on the matter.
1. Story and characters.
Probably the most important part of any RPG in my opinion. And I am happy to say, that Dragonfall' s characters stayed with me long after I finished the game. And then came back a year after. And then came back again next year.
I understand, that the richness and the impact of the story are highly subjective variables based on the cultural level of the player. So, basically, what I find deep and engaging you might find boring and formulaic, because you might have seen it before a thousand times. So let me just tell you, that Dragonfall's story managed to surprise me not on one, but on two occasions. I can't recall the last time that happened in video game. Seriously, probably not since Planescape Torment....
What you must understand, that it is not my first dance. I am well accuanted with cyberpunk genre both in literature and in games, and usually begin new journey with “been there, done that” attitude. So, you can imagine my surprise, when the story managed to not only engage me, but also surprise me.
2. Atmosphere.
Another Dragonfall's strong suit. I haven't felt this tense being hunted by nebulous foe since KOTOR 2, which is hight praise for me, since KOTOR 2 is my favorite game. Take it as you will. The atmosphere in Dragonfall does something magical: it sucks you in, it encourages you to read into context, to learn who the major players in this world are and what is your place in the grand scheme of things.
Let me put it this way: when you find yourself reading 3d and 4th editions of Shadowrun rolebook and the “Sixth World Almanac”, while analyzing discussions about the nature of elf immortality, after replaying Dragonfall, then you know the game does something right.
3. Gameplay and UI
There are things that Dragonfall does right. And then there are Gameplay and UI. First of all the UI. I don't know who had the brilliant idea of putting all the text in a small window on the right side of the screen in a game MOSTLY CONSISTED OF TEXT. All I can say is get accustomed to eye strain. The text itself is very well written, but sometimes feels redundant.
The combat is basically the same that it was in Shadowrun Returns, which is to say: not very good. It's slow, it's boring, it's not very tactical, and it's repetitive as hell. And since roughly 60% of the game consists of combat, I can practically guarantee that you ll be grinding you teeth by the end of the story.
The structure of the gameplay is basic enough: hub-mission-hub, but it works well, and allows for a lot of quite time, which is essential for creating complex and interesting story. The game has a very “cheap” feeling overall: assets are used, then reused, and then used again for good measure, which is not a problem per se, but considering the astronomical sum that Shadowrun Returns was able to acquire on Kickstarter, I can't help but wonder, where did it all go.
In conclusion: take it, not as a review, but as a love letter to a game, which came out of nowhere, took my hearth by storm, and permanently occupied part of my brain for itself. Both Dragonfall and Hong Kong are worth your time, if you re not afraid of reading, but hey, if you made it here, all the way until the end (for some mysterious reason) then I know, that you re the right metahuman for the job. Until then, I ll see you all in shadows. Oh, and never, EVER cut a deal with a dragon.

A "thinking man's" match-three puzzler with charming graphics and very forgettable background music. Every choice is critical, every move requires careful consideration, often forcing you to calculate two or three moves ahead. If you do something dumb, you will pay for it. I got it in a bundle. I enjoy that the animated faces on the blocks reflect their color (green is sickly, blue is sad, yellow is afraid, red is angry). It has a lot of game modes, and "modifiers" for even more variety. There is quite a bit packed into this initially simple seeming game.
THIRTY BUCKS!? My eyes popped out of my head when I saw the regular retail price. This game is not a total revelation or reinvention of the match-3 genre, it is simply good - possibly the best in the field, in fact. The single player is more like the "puzzle" mode in most puzzle games, where you have to remove blocks in a specific order to solve the puzzle. I don't generally enjoy this kind of gameplay very much, but I enjoy it in Tumblestone. It's fast, it controls tightly, and it seems that there's more than one way to skin a cat with these puzzles.
When, on the "Mario 3" style overworld map, you get to castles, it mixes the gameplay up. I will not spoil anything. The castle puzzles are random (I think), possibly procedural. Throughout the campaign, various gameplay modifications are introduced that really twist things up. In the multiplayer and arcade mode, it punishes you by lowering the ceiling if you match incorrectly, or if you paint yourself into a corner and are forced to pick a block from above the ceiling.
The colorblind option is appreciated, but does not help my type of colorblindness. Telling the yellow bricks from the green bricks is difficult when they're behind the 'glass' ceiling, and this colorblind mode does not seem to affect the yellow/green blocks at all. And, once you've chosen a block, there is no way to cancel your selection. Blocks are shot out of the puzzle immediately to unlock what is beneath - so be careful (I said it was fast).
I would recommend this game at $15 for puzzle enthusiasts only. $30 is a mind-bending price for what this is.
Tumblestone gets a soft thumbs up from me, because it achieves what it sets out to achieve, feels fast, controls well, and is cute, but not distastefully so. I thought I would be in and out in 5 minutes, and almost was. Give it 15 or 20 minutes and you'll begin to understand. This developer also made "The Bridge", a brilliant puzzle platformer. So give them the benefit of the doubt, and a bit of your time, and I believe you will enjoy Tumblestone, as long as you pick it up on sale.

Let me start off by saying this is deceptively addictive. The controls are tight and by default you control the player with just the keyboard's arrow keys and the 'a' and 'd' buttons (QWERTY, of course). This may strike you as a bit bizarre. I can understand to a degree why the devs would choose to seperate the keys to prevent accidental frustration in later levels, but why not simply use the w, a, s, d, q, e setup gamers are familiar with?
Regardless, the concept is very basic- match three, create a situation where you can clear the board. Some levels randomize, some do not. Every 10 levels you'll have a sort of 'boss puzzle' where you will get three or more puzzles on the same board with an invisible timer that will start moving the board downward (you clear from the bottom up) after a time. These can get super frustrating very quick, and all of them seem to be randomized each time you restart.
The selling point of this game is that it has quite a lot of polish oft absent from these sorts of titles. Until I complete the game the jury's out on the price, but it does seem there's an awful lot of content to play through here. Would I buy it for full price? Probably not. That being said, it far surpasses its peers on the market, near as I can tell, and feels quite satisfying to play. From what I can tell the 'story' is just some cheesy humor, and I've noted a number of spelling errors.
That's it for now.

The land of the dead is where Manuel Calavera, fallen from grace agent, sells travel packages for the land of the of eternal rest to freshly deceased. All is about to change as Manny meets his latest client, Dolores and embarks on wild ride of mystery, conspiracy, betrayal, love and discovery across the strage world of the dead.
A fine example of how remasters of old adventure games should be done.Grim Fandango Remastered stays true to the original material, focusing on polishing the rough spots of original release. Probably one of the most criminally underrated Lucas Arts games and easily one of the best in genre. A must buy for all adventure game fans.
GOOD:
Excellent humor and noir-eske art deco stylization mixed up with the day of the dead theme.
Excellent voice acting and music
Cleaned up and upscaled 3D models
Fixed and improved interface with much better pathfinding and overhauled mouse control. Moving Manny around is now a breeze and frustration with pigeons or fire-beavers in original release is nothing but a distant memory.
BAD:
Slightly more difficult than what younger adventure game players might expect (but could be considered postive to veteran players).
Still requires controlling manny with a keyboard in forklift puzzle, which is easier to figure out than execute. I could have easily been redesigned out, as use of the mechanic of driving a vehicle isn't used anywhere else in game.

“You must come with me, young ones, for I am the Grim Reaper.”
Grim Fandango can be considered as Tim Schafer’s swan song for his work on adventure games at LucasArts. Although the game was highly praised and given considerably good scores in reviews, the game’s sales were relatively unsuccessful, which indicated that other computer game genres might have been starting to generate more popularity than the traditional adventure game genre.
Despite this, Grim Fandango is nothing short of a masterpiece that excellently captures the spirit of the 90s adventure games combined with the film noir vibe of crime and corruption through amazing dialogues and stunning visual art in the form of pre-rendered three-dimensional backgrounds, not to mention the incredibly creative rendition of the Aztec concepts of the afterlife.
With the remastered edition new players are able to be introduced to this amazingly composed game as well as allowing old player to re-experience the Land of the Dead and rememberable characters such as the reaper Manny Calavera and the crazily car-fixated demon Glottis on their journey to find the saint-like woman Mercedes Colomar and help to escort her safely through purgatory into the next life. If that wasn’t enough, the remastered version also come with in-game developer commentaries with people such as the project leader Tim Schafer and visual artist Peter Chan that will give you an insight in the process of creating computer games in the late 90s.
Although Grim Fandango might not be a game fit for everyone, it gives you a good insight in the late period of classic adventure games and offers you a rich story in terms of characters, visuals and dialogue, which could be a change of pace from today’s games, where you don’t try to figure out- and solve puzzles for hours on end in a charming world where dead men still tell their tale.

This game really surprised me with its simultaneous balance of simplicity and complexity. The only real downside of the game is its low playerbase, which is due to lack of continued support from Jagex.
What the game does best: It almost entirely eliminates the worst part of card games in that top decking is almost never the key to success. This is because you draw a minimum of three cards each turn and have the option to play from 0-4. There are five turns total and that means that if you didn't draw what you need yet, you can just keep the cards in your hand until you do. Max of 10 cards in your hand (30-35 in deck) though so if you want to discard cards you have to play them.
The order that you and your opponent play cards matters a lot. Therefore, the potential for personal skill improvement is sky high because there's an element of bluffing and mindgames involved. To win at higher elos, you have to not only thouroughly understand your deck's strengths and weaknesses, but also your foe's. You're never playing solitaire. Every turn is interactive in that you have to carefully consider what your opponent might do.
New players have somewhat of a learning curve, but back when this game actually had a playerbase that wasn't an issue because the ranking system is great at matching people of similar skill levels. This is true for both normal play and dungeoneering (arena in hearthstone).
Aesthetics: The game has just enough of a cartoony feel to appeal to younger audiences, while not being off-putting to older audiences. Graphics are about what you'd expect out of a card game.
FREE SINGLE PLAYER CAMPAIGN
- requires careful deck-building, execution, and has great rewards
10/10 for the campaign - Since it's free, this game is worth downloading just to try to beat the campaign.
LOTS OF FREE STUFF
Free packs/cards/currency just for logging in daily
Free pack/cards at the end of ranked seasons
Cons: Low playerbase

- You can't seem to increase animation speed of all actions. It's fun to watch the figues do their thing for like 2 hours -  then it gets old.

- Low population. The game's multiplayer oriented. Waiting for 5-39 minutes for a match (you'll probably loose (described next)) is a bad deal. Getting matches outside primetime is TOUGH.

- Menu seems to be a bit clanky. To get from campaign selection to the deck builder you need to do about 10 clicks. Haven't noticed any shortcuts.
- Opening chests (or w/e they are called) - 1 chest takes 5-10 clicks. You have to open hundreds in this game in the long run...
To be honest I am not sure what this game has in common with runescape apart from the name. But I've only dabbled in Runescape 10+ years ago, so who am I to judge.

Killer is Dead is a 3rd person hack and Slash spectacle fighter game in the same vein as DMC, Ninja Gaiden, and God of War. The story revolves around a hired assassin named Mondo Zappa, who wields a katana and has a robot arm. The story starts off simple enought, but later escalates and the story introduces fake memories, amnesia, betrayals, and even a unicorn that comes out of nowhere. As you can probably guess by now the story gets really confusing near the end. The episodic nature of all the missions will make it so that you can play the game in short bursts if you please. It has a "Monster of the week" feel since almost every mission has nothing to do with the rest and the assassination targets can be anything from a simple samurai to an evil Thomas the tank engine.
Now for the bread and butter of the game. The gameplay in this game will primarily consist of slicing enemies with your katana and occasionally using your arm's subweapons, such as the blood cannon or drill. I found myself only using one of the four available subweapons though, but maybe you'll find more use of the other ones. You attain these subweapons by seducing women in so called "Gigolo" missions. Basically all you have to do during these missions is stare at a womans breast when shes not looking to fill up your "guts" meter, and when the "guts" meter is full you push a button to give them a present. Repeat until sex. Tasteless? perhaps. Now your only weapon in this game is the katana and there is no combos since there is only one attack button so you'll be mashing the left click a lot. The collest feature of the combat however is the "dodge burst" where if you dodge an opponents attack perfectly at the last second time will freeze for a few seconds and you get to slice up your opponent. It is very satisfying to pull off and takes a while to truly master. If you are a fan of hack and slash games I would highly recommend that you give this one a try. It's very button mash based, but it is a great deal of fun and it should not be overlooked.

In my opinion Far Cry 2 is the best game in the series. If you liked Far Cry 3/4 but found it too easy or dumbed down, you will love Far Cry 2. Lacking features such as crafting and such from the more recent games (crafting is too overrated), it gives you a gritty experience of guerrilla warfare in an African state.
I'd recommend playing with Dylans Realism Modification (gives the game an extra tweak to make you plan your attacks)
I'd also recommend installing Far Cry 2 Graphical Enhancement Suite (to make sunsets and the overall atmosphere look even more beautiful)
The game engine is solid, the only occasional physics bugs you will encounter will be when one vehicle crashes into another, or when you walk around the safe zones and the AI  occasionally gets killed by the physics objects. This can be hillariously funny, especially when the wildlife gets involved. (It doesnt happen often enough to be something to worry about, it's only happend to me about 3 times in my entire playtime).
I have never had the game crash, ever. Even with the use of Dylans mod and the Graphical ES.
The gunplay is satisfying, people complain that jamming weapons are annoying, however if you purchase your own you will rarely or even never encounter this. I rather enjoy the weapon jamming as it makes the combat more exciting and unpredictable.
There is also a multiplayer feature for the game which you could make use of if you want to fight some friends.
With a reasonably cheap price, and occasional sales, i'd definatly recommend picking this game up.

FarCry 2 is a first person shooter you probably either love or hate. Some people have called it a central African truck driving simulator rather than a first person shooter, and it all depends on how you look at the gameplay mechanics. It has a lot going for it with the open world, letting you tackle the missions as you prefer. The graphics and the African setting looks great. The game has a lot of features that really immerse you in the game, as the lack of minimap, instead utilizing a map you actually have to equip as an item and look at.
The game puts you in a central African nation, where different factions are waging war at each other, and your mission is to stop the arms dealer supplying both sides. You have "buddies" helping you with missions (giving you optional ways to tackle the main missions) as well as giving you side missions of their own. They will also help you out of trouble if you get shot down.
It's up to you to choose how to tackle each mission: get to the mission in an open world, utilizing buses for instant fast travel to a few set locations, otherwise the other vehicles available or going on foot, then finishing the mission objective in the way that best suits your playing style. Stealth, guns blazing, a tactical approach with grenades/molotovs to smoke the enemies out, or any other way? Your choice. Getting to the point of interest for each mission can take 1-4 minutes per mission, and sometimes involve shootouts as you get discovered by enemy patrols or checkpoints.
The story sets out ambitious but doesn't hold together all that well. Most of the game is standard missions that are somewhat similar. One odd thing is that the DVD release of the game required the developers to speed up all recorded dialogue to make it take up less space. This is also in the steam version of the game. The fast talking NPC:s sound really odd!
There are four things I got tired of while playing the game:
1) Guards at guard posts always shoot at you, if you clear them out while passing they respawn until next time you pass.
2) Enemies locate you way to easy, and fire at you with expert aiming, even almost dead enemies seem to have no problem hitting you with handguns at 300m range.
3) Some enemies (this gets more frequent later in the game) can take almost a whole clip of ammunition before going down.
4) If you do the buddy quests for the main missions, it can get quite tiresome to get to 3-4 different locations (some times at different sides of the map) to prepare everything needed for completing the main mission in an alternate way.
I found out the perfect solution for problems 1-3:
. It fixes the stealth, the enemy health and the checkpoints (you can pass checkpoints without being fired upon most of the time). The game also gets a lot harder since your health is reduced as well (remember to save a lot), but much more satisfying. You're best off planning your assault, and it's really satisfying approaching an objective, taking out a few guards from afar with a sniper rifle, staying hidden to not draw enemy fire, then moving in closer and finishing the last guards off at close range with a silenced sub machine gun. You also come to appreciate strategic advantages as an elevated position. One of my best experiences with the game was behind cover with an assault rifle at an elevated position, moving from cover to cover, mowing down the enemies below. All the time the action being really tense since you know that getting hit by one or two bullets can end it all, so all firefights are really tense. At moments like these the game is glorious.
I would really recommend the realism mod, and the game requires a bit of patience. For the right player, driving to each mission, sometimes avoiding (or taking out) enemy patrols along the way just builds up the tension, but will be tedious for other players, so you have to ask yourself if the way the game plays suits your taste.
Except for running the realism mod, my recommendation would be to skip most of the buddy quests. It gets far to tedious to do them all, and the rewards aren't that great. The pacing is much better if you just stick to the main mission most of the time (ignoring the complaint calls you get from the buddy).
Far Cry 2 is one of the best FPS games I've played, and also one of the most immersive games of all genres. It has a few drawbacks, mostly solved by the realism mod, and it requires the right player for the game, it isn't for everyone. If you want all action all the time, it isn't the game for you, but the realistic and short but immersive and tense firefights this game can offer are hard to beat if you're in to that kind of action.

Too many overpowered cards with ridiculous effects that instantly turn an entire game around just by getting lucky. Luck plays too much of a factor for me to properly enjoy this game still. Strategy and deckbuilding helps, no doubt. It's not *all* luck, but it is too prevalent for me to keep enjoying the experience.
When a person randomly gets a prophecy card that instantly gives lethal, drain, guard, and other assorted unit passives to ALL their cards on the field, just by a pure luck draw, and then goes from slightly losing to having instant lane dominance, or blows away your entire advantage by wiping an entire lane without you being able to do anything about it whatsoever, that's when I say: enough is enough.
Other TCG's have game changing effects too, but then you are usually in a position to do something about it. Trap cards in Yu-gi-oh for instance can cancel magical effects that can turn a game around by having them on the field. ES:L has no such thing. There is no protection against large scale effects with dramatic consequences, and thus it turns into "who has the most OP card in their draw/prophecy this time?"
You can't prevent someone from dropping a unit on the field that wipes something out. You can't stop someone from playing a spell that deals massive damage. You can't prevent someone from playing a luck prophecy by health loss via protective means. That last one also means that there is generally no reason NOT to play a prophecy for free because you're safe anyway.
You can't place a card in anticipation of an event. You can't prepare yourself for what you expect the opponent to do. You can't play a card solely for the purpose of negating an enemy's potential comeback. You are playing your own game while praying to the nine that they don't draw or play something that wipes out your entire board or gives them some kind of advantage you couldn't prevent and it starts all over again.
A comeback in this game will rarely ever come from planning and will mostly consist of luck because you as a player have such very limited means to respond to something.
There need to be more measures that you can take to protect yourself from the large-scale effects of certain cards. Without it, strategy will take a backseat to frustration as many powerful cards as possible are spammed because there is little danger in doing so. This is a sad consequence of the fact that there are absolutely NO preventative cards in the whole game, besides "guard" units that can only stop direct attacks, which is not enough when the majority of the cards in the game are good because of their EFFECTS and not their attack strength.

An aged, but well-preserved adventure with a story that's brimming with charm, a uniquely realized world, and some good old-fashioned dev logic.
I never played Grim Fandango at it's original release; my PC gaming days were too far off yet, and frankly the lo-fi paper skulls aesthetic would have put me off at at age when I was pretty sure better graphics made better games. I entered into Tim Schafer's vision of the Land of the Dead with virgin eyes, unburdened by the heavy lenses of nostalgia, unchained by any sense of loyalty to the characters and stories and with a keen ability to criticize Mr. Schafer, despite liking much of his work.
Which is why I'm glad to say that Grim Fandango is absolutely fantastic. Super duper. The♥♥♥♥♥♥ Not without reservation, but it's a game that easily landed on my "must replay" list; almost without even trying. Let's break down why.
Graphically, it's impressive how little was remastered for this version--better shading on the character models, a bit of uprezzing for HD, but not much else--and even more impressive how well everything still holds up. It's rare for pre-rendered backgrounds to age as immaculately as these have, but here they are, twelve years old and still looking good. On a technical aesthetic level, Grim Fandango is a stellar example of a game that traded fidelity for style and traded well. That's not to say it doesn't show its age, a wonky animation here, that weird stutter any time something pre-rendered has to move, the slight jar for whenver it has to go from in-engine static images to fully animated cutscenes, but those were infrequent and unobtrusive. Everyone is paper maché paper skulls and it works. It just works.
What works slightly less is gameplay. the oft-bemoaned tank controls have been removed (though can be turned back on for you purists) and while that's great, it also means that Mr. Calavera can fall prey to the "walking, walking, scene change, camera flip, TURN AROUND! walking, walking, repeat" problem. Left between that and tank controls, I decided tank controls were worse, but I still did occasionally suffer from a break in the action to stop and reorient myself, when I could have been moving on. This, compounded by things like that the inventory menu, while clever, made it difficult to consistently locate items in a timely manner or that the second major area, Rubacava, is uncomfortably huge, and it takes a not-insignificant amount of time to traverse it, even once you've figured out where everything is. All of that, on top of a healthy serving of Dev logic sprinkled throughout. Oh yes, we're going there.
Grim Fandango, despite how well it's aged, is still a game of its time. Grim Fandango's time, as it happens, share a lineage with Secret of "Attach rubber chicken to pulley"Monkey Island. I wont spoil any of the puzzles in this game, but I encourage you to spoil them for yourselves. Maybe don't look everything up right away, sure, I didn't. Explore, learn, try to puzzle it out for yourself, but keep a guide on hand for when you can't, because there's a pretty good chance you'll hit that point more than once. I'm not just talking like hard puzzles, mind you, I'm talking things that are just unintuitive, going to places you have no reason to be, looking at things you would otherwise pass up, that sort of thing.
So why do I still reccommend Grim Fandango, a puzzle adventure game, so strongly despite its flaws being so harshly concentrated around puzzling and adventuring?
It's ♥♥♥♥ing great, that's why. The land of the dead is colorful, varied, and fascinating, the characters are all well-drawn, with special attention to the extra dimensions of the main cast, and the writing is surprisingly mature for Tim Schafer, and not just in the "They kill people sometimes" sort of way. Manny Calavera is palpably not a good guy, but neither is he especially bad, just unscrupulous and a little desperate. Meche Colomar starts as a very good guy, girl, person, but later develops a very real (and thankfully not overdone) edge to her. The world itself has that great quality of showing you lots, while still hinting that there's so much more just beyond your horizon and it's all. Just. So. Fantastic.
Look, do you like adventure games? Do you like funny things? Do you like Mexicana, even Americanized, kinda whitebread Mexicana? Do you Like Tim Schafer? Lucasarts? Do you like Skulls? If you answered yes to any of the above, get this game, download a guide, and give it a go. You won't regret it.

So, at first glance, this looks like a stick figure side scrolling RPG in a weird western setting.  That's what it looks like at second glance as well.  That's what it is.  But there's a little more going on.
West of Loathing is a new game from the fantastic and brilliant creators of Kingdom of Loathing, a long running browser based RPG.  If you've played and enjoyed, then I don't know why you're still reading this.  Go play WoL.
If you have no idea what's going on, that's fine.  West of Loathing is an Western Themed RPG where you set out west to seek your fortune.  Along the way you'll encounter miners, minors, goblins, skeletons, dynamite hoarders, and pale (ghost) horses.  And that's just what I ran into today.  It's smart, it's simple, it's hilarious, and I'll probably go back to playing it after I finish this review.  I highly recommend this game to fans of humor, westerns, and stick figures.

Watch_Dogs is quite an impressive game. Far better than I expected.
+ wonderful graphics, detailed damage models
+ realistic behavior. Even stuff you wouldn't expect like the driver getting off the car from the door that isn't blocked. If both doors are blocked, he climbs out through the window. Nice!
+ partially destructable environment. Even things that you wouldn't want to break like the ATMs, cash terminals that also serve as saving points.
+ good main story, has some strong moments. I sometimes felt like Liam Neeson in "Taken".
+ huge, lively town to explore. You see and hear the people's stories. Funny, sad, silly, tragic... they got it all covered. Interesting enough: You can even learn about the motives of the criminals sometimes, which puts you in a moral dilemma.
+ various ways to achieve your goals. Sneak, stealth kill, use traps or run in guns blazing. Or heck, even drive in. Open the gate and just run every enemy over with your car! Works too - sometimes.
++ mini games: I only tried a couple of them, but each and every one is very unique and feels like a new world. Want to go for a killing spree with your car in "Madness"? Feel like the last human left on earth, facing killer robots in "Alone"? Or play a deadly hacker version of hide and seek against online players which will have your heart racing while you hunt or are being hunted. As well as some other games that I didn't have the time to explore yet.
~ rather arcade-like driving. Significantly easier to keep control of the vehicles than in other games. You can drift like a pro and turn 180° with your car as if you were born with a wheel in the hands. Some may criticize this aspect for a lack of realism.
~ AI drivers tend to do some strange things like driving off bridges, into pedestrian zones and shopping malls or face-hugging stairs and walls and working that horn for ages. I don't know if that's a lack of AI or if they are supposed to do random stuff to make the world feel more alive, but it sure looks funny.
- Unlike the story missions, side missions don't use checkpoint saving. If you mess up even one step before reaching your goal, you have to repeat the whole process again from zero. Some of the missions are hard and long enough to make this annoying.
- last story mission is ridiculously hard.
The DLC "Bad Blood" is not a must-have. It doesn't add much to the story. But I guess it was nice to use the R/C car, the laser puzzles were a good change of pace and the rotating hacker puzzles got more complex.
