WATCH_DOGS
I'm gonna write a simple pro-con review this time 'cause i'm tired as a spotted hyena that has just ran 10 kilometers through Africa's rainforests without taking breaks to drink redbull every once in a while.
- Takedowns are cool as hell, especially the firearm ones which were sadly omitted from the sequel, most likely due to the protagonist's more lighthearted personality. The baton takedowns seem to have issues with audio syncing and volume, but the gun executions are brutally awesome each and every single time!
- Graphics, despite the controversial downgrade, are very gorgerous when certain conditions are met such as the weather, time of the day and obviously high graphical settings. WIth the help of restoring mods, Watch_Dogs has some SERIOUS potential to look photo-realistic and heck, almost like real life in some instances.
The occassional rainfall is where the game really shines and many have come accustomed to associated dark rainy city with W_D1 and for a good reason, the graphics are at their utmost best during such occasions.
- Performance is great even though Ubisoft ♥♥♥♥ed up by making the mouse movement just emulate a controller instead of utilizing actual raw mouse input which results in somewhat sluggish mouse controls at time, but nothing too bad to get work up about. The general performance is very good when the high visual quality of W_D is taken into account.
I personally average around 60-70 fps with mostly high settings on my current build.
I also often like to use the photo-realistic graphic mods which drop my fps by around 10 frames or more, but it's not terribly much for degree of improvement on the quality.
- The story is something that surprised me with how intense and interesting it gets along the way. Maybe it's just 'cause i like revenge stories and anti-heroes, but either way, i definitely regard the story of W_D as a strong point.
Shortly put: It's about an ex-criminal called Aiden Pearce who loses his beloved niece in a hit gone wrong for angering mobsters for the things he did in his shady years which resulted in a hitman being hired after Pearce. This incident caused Aiden to go in a deep depression which prompted him to become the vigilante of chicago and avenge the death of his niece.
- Characters, ahh yes, Ubisoft really nailed on this one! The now iconic Aiden Pearce has always been one of my favorite video game char... heck, scrap that, fictional characters of all time since W_D was first announced. The rough badass attitude and voice, coupled with his cool trenchcoat flapping in the wind, can result in only one thing and THAT is the definition of a badass.
W_D cast is full of fashinating and well written characters such as Jordi the comical and psychopathic hitman, Damien the ex-partner of Aiden from their criminal days, and not forgetting Aiden's own family which includes his sister and nephew, both of whom Aiden protects with his whole heart.
- The lack of customisation is very apparent, though it's not that much of a big deal if it didn't extend to vehicles too. You can only buy different skins for your trenchcoat WHICH would be fine if the majority of them weren't so unappealing. There are some cool ones, but about 80% of the skins are either too hipster-like or have that horrible ballcap or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ those rounded caps that the modern kids wear, are called. This is obviously a personal gripe of mine, keep that in mind.
- The lack of playable aircraft, this is a very interesting point of critique i have since it has just recently come to my knowledge that airfacts in FACT, are coded in the game to be flyable by Aiden, and with a tricky glitch you CAN hijack a helicopter which is very much functional, so either Ubisoft cut the playable airfact in a very late stage of development or the game's engine requires them to be controllable by both NPCs and the player character.
Anyway, fast travelling IS an option after unlocking certain objects around the city so travelling quickly around Chicago is not a problem.
- No talk radio, this is something that only the more mature and sophisticated, such as myself, enjoy. R* is known for recording hundreds of interesting and comedic talk radio for their GTA series and i myself always loved to cruise around the cities listening to the funny adverts and chat shows.
Nothing similar exists in W_D and the radios work more like MP3 players instead of actual radios, because entering a vehicle always starts a new song right from the beginning instead of dynamically playing whatever would be on. I get it that it's more requiring for a game engine to always play long recordings in the background, only to become audible when the player does something requiring to do so, but nonetheless, i'd have enjoyed some talk shows in W_D.

FarCry 2 is a first person shooter you probably either love or hate. Some people have called it a central African truck driving simulator rather than a first person shooter, and it all depends on how you look at the gameplay mechanics. It has a lot going for it with the open world, letting you tackle the missions as you prefer. The graphics and the African setting looks great. The game has a lot of features that really immerse you in the game, as the lack of minimap, instead utilizing a map you actually have to equip as an item and look at.
The game puts you in a central African nation, where different factions are waging war at each other, and your mission is to stop the arms dealer supplying both sides. You have "buddies" helping you with missions (giving you optional ways to tackle the main missions) as well as giving you side missions of their own. They will also help you out of trouble if you get shot down.
It's up to you to choose how to tackle each mission: get to the mission in an open world, utilizing buses for instant fast travel to a few set locations, otherwise the other vehicles available or going on foot, then finishing the mission objective in the way that best suits your playing style. Stealth, guns blazing, a tactical approach with grenades/molotovs to smoke the enemies out, or any other way? Your choice. Getting to the point of interest for each mission can take 1-4 minutes per mission, and sometimes involve shootouts as you get discovered by enemy patrols or checkpoints.
The story sets out ambitious but doesn't hold together all that well. Most of the game is standard missions that are somewhat similar. One odd thing is that the DVD release of the game required the developers to speed up all recorded dialogue to make it take up less space. This is also in the steam version of the game. The fast talking NPC:s sound really odd!
There are four things I got tired of while playing the game:
1) Guards at guard posts always shoot at you, if you clear them out while passing they respawn until next time you pass.
2) Enemies locate you way to easy, and fire at you with expert aiming, even almost dead enemies seem to have no problem hitting you with handguns at 300m range.
3) Some enemies (this gets more frequent later in the game) can take almost a whole clip of ammunition before going down.
4) If you do the buddy quests for the main missions, it can get quite tiresome to get to 3-4 different locations (some times at different sides of the map) to prepare everything needed for completing the main mission in an alternate way.
I found out the perfect solution for problems 1-3:
. It fixes the stealth, the enemy health and the checkpoints (you can pass checkpoints without being fired upon most of the time). The game also gets a lot harder since your health is reduced as well (remember to save a lot), but much more satisfying. You're best off planning your assault, and it's really satisfying approaching an objective, taking out a few guards from afar with a sniper rifle, staying hidden to not draw enemy fire, then moving in closer and finishing the last guards off at close range with a silenced sub machine gun. You also come to appreciate strategic advantages as an elevated position. One of my best experiences with the game was behind cover with an assault rifle at an elevated position, moving from cover to cover, mowing down the enemies below. All the time the action being really tense since you know that getting hit by one or two bullets can end it all, so all firefights are really tense. At moments like these the game is glorious.
I would really recommend the realism mod, and the game requires a bit of patience. For the right player, driving to each mission, sometimes avoiding (or taking out) enemy patrols along the way just builds up the tension, but will be tedious for other players, so you have to ask yourself if the way the game plays suits your taste.
Except for running the realism mod, my recommendation would be to skip most of the buddy quests. It gets far to tedious to do them all, and the rewards aren't that great. The pacing is much better if you just stick to the main mission most of the time (ignoring the complaint calls you get from the buddy).
Far Cry 2 is one of the best FPS games I've played, and also one of the most immersive games of all genres. It has a few drawbacks, mostly solved by the realism mod, and it requires the right player for the game, it isn't for everyone. If you want all action all the time, it isn't the game for you, but the realistic and short but immersive and tense firefights this game can offer are hard to beat if you're in to that kind of action.

No tuve la oportunidad de jugar a este título cuando salió, y ni siquiera había jugado antes a las típicas aventuras gráficas de LucasArts.  No obstante, este juego me ha parecido fantástico.
El estilo artístico me encanta, los personajes son memorables, las historias y conversaciones divertidísimas. Este es, básicamente, un juego de puzzles; pero en mi opinión no son los puzzles los que te atraparán, sino la música, los personajes y los escenarios.
Los puzzles... pues son una locura. No tienen sentido. Eso no significa que no sean divertidos, todo lo contrario, pero muchas veces son tan locos que al resolverlos no sentirás que has resuelto un enigma, sino que pensarás que los desarrolladores estaban locos. No todos los puzzles son así, obviamente, pero pasarás tanto rato con ellos que serán los que te marquen.
El juego no es perfecto: el ritmo del juego es muy variable, ya que tiene un formato prácticamente episódico y algunas partes del juego se me antojan poco trabajadas; sobre todo si las comparamos con la joya de este juego: la ciudad de Rubacava.
En definitiva, un juego muy divertido,  limitado por las mecánicas de su época (donde los puzzles tenían que hacerte arrancar los pelos de la cabeza para ser considerados buenos)  y de ritmo y calidad variable, con unos personajes memorables, una música increíble y una dirección artística sobresaliente.

One sentence review: The game combines a very enjoyable combat system with an engaging plot + RPG elements.
You spend most of your time on 'runs', which are the 21st century, post 'magical awakenening' equivalents of classic RPG dungeons. It is clear that all of these missions are very well thought out, with an excellent balance of combat and non-combat puzzle solving (think: exploration, using dialogue to achieve non-combat ends, hacking computers, etc.). This makes each run memorable and unique. The developers are at their best with unique missions formats: for example in one mission your 'decker' (computer hacker) needs to hack a computer system (with its own unique turn-based combat system) of a compound you are infiltrating while you are in it, challenging you to balance the combat in the digital and real worlds (for example the decker needs to bring the turret security system onto your side while fighting anti-infiltration computer programs).
The combat system is excellent turn based, tactical combat. Different characters bring different strengths to the battlefield, and its up to you to figure out how to maximize your team's effectiveness. There is a major strategy component in terms of rationing your resources: during any one run you do not get to restock on items, and so you have to tactically use them based on how hard any one fight is. Because all of your companions enter each run with their own items there is no feeling of 'saving the items until the ultimate boss' (they restock after each run) - you want to spend them on each run and its fun to figure out when its worth to use a re-usable magic ability vs lobbing a one-time use grenade. Combat probably provides the most replayability, with radically different strategies coming from using magic vs. melee/ranged weapons vs. drones to defeat your enemies.
The RPG elements are also great. All of the major chracters have fantastic backstories, and I have spent considerable time learning and reading all of them. This is my first introduction to the Shadowrun universe, and the game delivers a fantastic intorduction in terms of allowing different character backstories/the main plot to paint the picture of how this world came to be. The RPG element also provides some replayability, with different dialogue options available based on what sort of skills you bring to the table (for example a medic can talk about surgeries better) - but note it is not limiting in terms of learning about the universe so it does not force a replay (otherwise I would consider this sort of replayability cheating!).
Overall a fantastic game.
The cons worth mentioning:
- The difficulty settings are off. I'm playing on the highest difficulty and am breezing through most of the game (compare this to Throne of Baahl difficulty on Bauldar's Gate where I am re-loading every 10 minutes). Note: even 'breezing through it' I find some of the combat challenging so a veteran strategy player will not be dissapointed, though the real sadists among you might be.
- I've noticed a pattern where many of the dialogues boil down to "tell me more" or "stop talking". Additionally while many of the diologues give you options on what to say, they all lead to the same response (for example you can either chastise or forgive a rogue character, but they will simply give you the same apology dialogue in response). Though a con, the pro of the overall engaging dialogue mentioned above still dominates here. Basically I think of this as an out for people who already know the backstories and just want to move the game forward.

This game is an excellent old-school CRPG set in the Shadowrun universe.
Shadowrun is a world where magic returned to the world that is technologically advanced. You can meet hackers and drone manipulators as well as mages and spirit conjurers in this world. Also there are other than human races such as elves or orcs. All these races and techno/magic skills you can use make very variable character creation. For your character you pick race and gender and then you can either pick one of the standard preset classes such as street samurai or shaman or you can create your own class from the ground choosing your own unique set of skills.
After Shadowrun Returns, which was a good start,  Dragonfall has more of everything.
The story is great and rich. The dialogues are very well written and there is really a lot of reading. But all the text being so good it doesn't really matter you spend a lot of time reading. And if you don't like it, you can click throught it, which I don't recommned, as you will miss a lot of interesting details, story branches and even some good jokes.
Apart from the main story there are also a lot of side missions you can take on to earn some extra cash and experience some more cyberpunk adventure goodness. These are also very engaging and varied, it's just a waste to leave them untouched.
The main characters in the game, the people (well, people and various "metahumans") who are part of your shadowrunning team, are greatly detailed, each of them has their distinct personality and their own backstory, which you can explore by talking to them and doing side missions for them.
The combat is turn-based and very tactical. It is very varied with all the weapons, magic spells, cyberware and drugs you can use. You fight in a small group of max 5 characters against often overwhelming numbers and figuring out the right tactics and annihilitaing your opponents can be very rewarding in this game.
The graphics are colorful yet they capture the dark Shadowrun universe well.
For sci-fi CRPG fans 10/10

I have fond memories of playing the Shadowrun game on the Super Nintendo back in the 90s, but I've never delved into the tabletop game or novels. When I saw there were a series of Shadowrun games available for PC I was interested, and going on what I'd read in forums, I decided to jump in with Dragonfall - Director's Cut which is an enhanced stand-alone expansion for the previous title, Shadowrun Returns.
The game has you create a character with a great deal of customization options including gender, race, combat class, appearance, and even an advanced mode that lets you create a custom build from scratch. Once that's done, you're thrown into a heist with a crew of Shadowrunners - the term used for mercenaries in this dystopia/fantasy world hybrid - and things soon turn ugly as your team leader is mysteriously killed on what should have been a routine mission. This sets the tone for most of the well written, and well balanced campaign. You're running in the shadows doing questionable acts for often unscrupulous clients in order to uncover a greater plot and seek revenge for your fallen teammate.
The gameplay is segmented into two parts: You'll hang around the Kreuzbasar in Berlin which functions as a hub complete with story to investigate, team members to form relationships with, and merchants to buy weapons and upgrades from. Once you've got everything together, you head out on jobs to earn money, gain Karma
and advance character and story elements. This is the meat of the game and it plays out in turn based battles in the vein of
or
. You and your team will use guns, swords, magic, fists, remote controlled drones, performance enhancing drugs, and explosives to dispatch enemies and reach objectives.
Overall, I found the experience pleasant and addictive. I have a habit of not finishing RPGs, but this one kept me playing to the end with
a pretty satisfying conclusion. As I mentioned before, the characters and plot are well written, and the world is a nice departure from generic swords and sorcery and heavy handed dystopia by instead combining the two genres pretty seamlessly. You really have to experience it to fully appreciate a world where Adam Jensen could hang out with a gun toting Legolas the elf. You'll often be presented with difficult moral and leadership choices as you muddle and force your way through the campaign.
I would recommend this game for fans of tactics games and role playing games. The unique setting is intriguing, and the campaign is well-written.

Shadowrun Dragonfall, while not a direct sequel to Shadowrun Returns, is set in the same universe with the same mechanics. And yet, Dragonfall has some vast improvements over its predecessor.
Unlike the predecessor, in which you hired mercenaries for each mission, Dragonfall sets you up with a dedicated team of story-related companions. Each companion has their own quest (think loyalty quests from Mass Effect, but if they weren’t garbage), which you access via dialogue between missions.
Additionally, each party member has special skills you can unlock as they level up. Unlike your own character, who still levels up with Karma, your companions level up as you progress through the story and complete specific missions.
The combat system seems a little more streamlined than in Shadowrun Returns. While the UI received some minor changes, everything just felt smoother and more fluid.
I think the most notable change was the fact that combat would end when I had eliminated all of the enemies that I was currently engaging. This was a huge improvement over Shadowrun Returns, as it left me free to explore the map without having to move my entire party each round.
The story is definitely of a much higher quality in this game. There were no notable writing errors, at least none that were so extreme as to break my immersion. Furthermore, the plot made sense. The twist at the end was indeed unexpected, but was completely believable. And the ending felt epic - I did not walk away going “What just happened?”, like I did with Shadowrun Returns.
Perhaps this comes from playing the games back to back, but it really felt like more of the same. Sure, things were improved upon, but not so much as for it to feel like a new game.
Also, I hate decking. Like, REALLY hate decking.
Worth playing. Take a break between the predecessor and this game, and it might feel more refreshing than it did to me.

Dragonfall is without a doubt much better than Shadowrun Returns (Dead Man's Switch aka DMS). The game feels longer, with a more intriguing story and overall more meaningful choices. If you enjoy isometric, story-rich, turn-based, post-apocalyptic, team-building combat this is a good one.
Story - *Some spoilers ahead*
The comparisons to DMS is inevitable. Dragonfall's story to me was much better than DMS - there was more at stake and certainly much deeper connection to each of the team's characters. In DMS, you start the story based on a friend's dead man's switch triggering you to find his killer and collect the money held in escrow. Along they way you collect team members through the storyline. Dragonfall throws you into an existing team, with your old friend as the leader. Immediately the team members each have unique personalities. The motivations are much stronger for you to resolve the story and the grand conspiracy at the end of Dragonfall is much more interesting than DMS' cultist bug spirits. You also get to see each character grow, as you support and work through their problems with them (and maybe go through a few missions to help each of resolve something from the past). Overall, fantastic writing and I actually felt like choices mattered. I actually wanted to replay stuff and try different dialogue options.
Gameplay
The gameplay in Dragonfall is largely similar to DMS on the surface level. It's isometric turn-based combat, with a lot of different dialogue options that can open up depending on what skills/etiquette your character has. I roleplayed as vegeance incarnate as a decking rigger that dabbled in magic. In DMS, it really seemed that it doesn't matter if you were a jack of all trades, and whilst Dragonfall didn't punish you too harshly for it, it's highly recommended that you become a master. I also felt that Dragonfall allowed for more varied non-combat approaches which were nice.
Graphics
Similar graphics to DMS - again the character portraits are a bit ugly.
Sound
The music was actually quite good this time around
Overall
Would definitely recommend buying, especially as a pack together with DMS and Hong Kong.

Although I haven't finished this, I am far enough into it (16 hours) to be quite comfortable giving this an easy thumbs up.
I really haven't played an isometric RPG since Fallout 2, well, not that there's a wide range of them out there. But that's a rather difficult act to follow. On the whole the combat is actually quite similar, though this does not have Fallout's body targeting system. That's honestly not a particularly big loss. I do think the combat could use a slightly better tutorial for newcomers, but in a few fights one gets the hang of it all the same. The AI is not overly punishing to you on normal. The game does have combat difficulty levels that allow you to twek your experience as you see fit.
Overall the story is quite good, and very well written for a video game, and I think is the biggest draw here. A RPG without a good story is just an immense slog. It's unusual to play a RPG that is neither a Japanese or American game and as such brings in a few different influences and ideas. I have to say, combining high fantasy stuff like elves and orcs and dragons with cyberpunk dystopia, it really doesn't add anything to the game world for me at all. At first I found it very hard to get my head around putting them together, or why one would do this. But it's also not enough to detract from what is an excellent story full of characters that have that video game just-enough-depth to be interesting. I enjoy how this is a game full of grey choices, where things are very rarely black and white. You will often not really be sure if you're helping the good guys or not, and really have to rely on your own feelings (or, if you like, your own persuit of money) to guide you.
The game has mod support through Steam Workshop including some fully functioning custom campaigns, and the game comes with an editor. I have not played any of these yet nor have I fiddled with the editor itself, but this is a clear bonus for those that really enjoy the game and want more.
On the whole I'm very comfortable calling this an excellent, and somewhat underplayed RPG title, that is far superior to certain larger franchises' offerings.

Brick force lets you build, publish and play your own maps and everyone ells maps, these are mostly setup with square blocks and some decorations, you can build everything that comes to mind and publish it for everyone ells to play and rate, once you do that you can make your map free or set up a price for others to download you're stage, then you join or create a waiting room and start shooting at each other for exp, cash and so on in different game modes.
The building aspect lets you build anything that comes to mind into a map with limits such as the block and decoration theme packs being sold for real money and the limit on each block or decoration type placed on the map, people can then rate and report your published map.
This is where your finished map ends up and where most people feel cheated, to publish your map you must pay a one time fee, this would be perfectly fine if that fee wasn't so expensive and required many hours of play time to earn for non paying players, In basic: the larger and more detailed your map is the more you will have to pay.

A few of these cash shop items can be brought for in-game cash but here is the trick, every item being pay to win or earned is timed, so if you wish to stay as non paying player you will find you're self in a constant race against time, because you will "not" use the free permanent weapons that comes with every created account cause they will literally make your enemies feel like sponges as they slowly turn around and kill you with a couple of bullets.
PS: You can buy permanent weapons and cosmetics cheap if you pay money,
if you wish to stay as a non-paying player you will need huge amounts of in game cash.
Fun semi addictive game that tries to appeal to a younger audience who want's to shot and have fun.

It's been almost a year since I've originally written this review and since then the game has been improved greatly. There are still issues that exist in the game that have yet to be fixed, but overall it can be a more satisfying experience than before. Before I really go into the review, I must admit I had a lot of fun playing this game. It's very unique and I've yet to see another MMO come close to the smooth combat system that Vindictus has. The game, much like any other popular MMO's, is a drug and you have this tendency to keep playing (which still happens to me sadly). However, with that said, the other aspects of this game are atrocious. The easiest way to get into things would be a pro-neutral-con chart.
Vindictus overall isn't necessarily a bad game by any definition. What makes the game great is the awesome combat system combined with doing full party raids to take down these heavy hitting bosses. The problem isn't that, it's everything else surrounding the combat system. The game is very poorly optimized, and strictly relies on Peer to Peer connections; this in combination with a heavily timing based combat system is a recipe for disaster. Not only this, but at higher levels, raids (at least most raid parties) require a minimum damage requirement, which ends up being an obsurd number that is difficult to reach without heavy amounts of grinding. The game isn't necessarily a "wallet warrior" type of Free to Play, and is definitely playable without the use of your money; the game just makes it harder to do so, especially with the current enhancing system in place. And don't even get started on expertise, as I've spent countless hours farming pre-pre-requisite materials to spend countless hours crafting pre-requisite materials to finally craft all that into materials I need to craft armor pieces, and it only yields a few armor pieces and a few points to level up my expertise. If I have to idle craft stuff in any game, that normally isn't a good sign.
The game is good; some of the stuff inside, not so much. If you feel inclined to play; I'd recommend that you reach level 60 and really decide if you want to continue playing, as the daily raids are available to you at that level.

As a person who frantically searched for a good hack and slash MMO I thought I had finally found a slice of heaven in Vindictus. It's very interactive and requires you to be attentive and think on your feet in fights, lest your enemies best you. Additionally, the character design and physics engine are quite unique for a free-to-play game.
Unfortunately, there are several things keeping Vindictus from being a good MMO; the pay-to-win feature being in first place. To elaborate a bit, the first thing that comes to my mind is the 'inner armor' feature, where your character can be fitted with customizable undergarments that is worn under the armor. Your character is fitted with defult inner armor, but the nicest way to move on with this review, is to state that if you don't want to look like an idiot, you must purchase nexon points to buy new armor to look less foolish in the armors you pick up in the game. Inner armor is only the beginning, players can purchase 'temporary armor' which allows for any level player to rent a set of high-level armor for about 7 days, for nearly a real dollar each day, as well as items that can selected in a random lottery (purchaseable of course!) that are not necessarily usable by your character, but that also can not be sold in the in-game trading post. Finally for this topic, there are also 'bound' items; which are items that get locked to your character and make them unsellable in the marketplace or trading post. To unbind these, you must then purchase from the game store, potion stacks that may or may not have enough per stack, to unbind your item and make it sellable.  Which brings me to my next problem with Vindictus: ingame money system.
The ingame money system in this game is absolutely in shambles. There does not seem to be any rhyme, reason or hierarchy for items which may be put up for sale. I have, on more than one occassion, found something as simple as cloth for sale for around 1k gold, and something that's difficult to pick up or find, on sale for 400 gold. If I check the market the next day, the cloth may have gone down to 200 gold, and the rarer item could inflate up to 3k in gold. It doesn't seem Nexon is setting any rules for these items to be sold at a minimum or maximum price, resulting in player prices that are unheard of, be they high or low. This means when you get to higher levels, paying for armor past level 54 is nearly impossible as armor inflates from around 24k per piece to 1-2 million quite quickly and weapons are even higher in price. The burden becomes real when you realize you're exchanging around 70k in gold for repairs and health potions. Not to mention that the pay rate between NPC sale rates and user marketplace rates have a very significant gap.
Making money is out of the question for your first 15-20 levels; and that is no exaggeration. Nexon actually released a patch that prevented players below a certain level from gaining monetary rewards in dungeons, and to impress upon this, I would like to add that Vindictus is completely instanced; there are no open world opportunities. Now you may pick items up in a dungeon that could sell for money, but nothing noteable enough to allow you to upgrade things such as armor or weapons. Making money in later dungeons is a bit easier, but often requires quite a bit of trickery or repeat trips, which can ocassionally be fun I admit, but becomes cumbersome after the first few times you attempt it. Be that as it may, it's still very difficult to save enough money for crafting or purchasing new armor or weapons as you get higher in level, which makes doing dungeons, and more importantly raids, where the majority of your money comes from at higher levels, very difficult. In some cases, after completing a raid a certain amount of times, you completely stop gaining money from it.
Speaking to dungeons, or more specifically, speaking to raids requires quite a good internet connection as you carry anywhere from 4-8 players on your back. It's often hard to find raids to join that do not require you to be well-equipped, well-backed by your internet and beginner friendly for those unfamiliar with the way they work. Additionally, Nexon does not seem to have stable enough servers for large party raids requiring 16-24 people, which can halt a player's progression completely. Rather than being stable, the player-to-server ratio is very ill-managed.
Now I could go into the many other and much smaller issues that Vindictus has, such as the abismal drop rate for rare items, which is comparable to squeezing a diamond from a squirrel's behind, the stat fluxuation between armor and weapons from one level to the next, the chance meter for enhancements which fails about 70% of the time, the lack of character updates and gender locking, or even the fact that Nexon tries to make up for these issues by running events which can leave the user with a lot of useless and unsellable items to take up precious inventory space, but I think I've said enough.
All of these problems, which are serious drawbacks for players who really want to enjoy the game, can be put aside to a certain degree and the game, especially when played with a good team, can be distracting and immersive in the level of fun it creates. That being said, these problems together whether they're big or small seem to be the result of a mis-managed product that eventually becomes more of an expensive toy that repeatedly breaks and requires money to fix, than a free-to-play immersive fantasy game for people to enjoy together.

I got this from Humble Monthly and thought to myself "Why not?" so I installed the game and played for a solid 10 minutes before I realised that the trailer for the game has 10 times the production value of the game itself. I mean, seriously guys? I think that the reviews from Destructoid, The Escapist and Ars Technica really show how low those reviewers have sunk (were they ever any good?) if they're saying anything positive about a game that you're selling for £18.99 with such little gameplay value or originality.
Let's look at how you play the game, you use the arrow keys to move your avatar left and right and then A & D to "move quickly" to either side of the screen, then you can press space to fire at the Tumblestones, match three to take them off of the board and that's that. They don't move, they make stupid "Bleh" noises everytime you hit them and if you make one mistake? You start the puzzle again. It honestly couldn't be more mundane, I think the reason there hasn't been an "original action puzzle game" in 15 years is because those games had it all covered, this is essentially a worse, reversed, version of Bubble Bobble and I'd much rather play that because it's far more interesting and engaging. It's not an "action puzzle game" if you have to restart the level everytime you shoot one block out of order, it's a normal friggin' puzzle game, it discourages you from playing fast because you don't have any room for error.
Whether the money from the bundle went towards this complete rip off or not, this game is unpolished, quickly thrown together and quite honestly, not fun! I like puzzle games too but there is so much more on the market for a fraction of the price. Small team or not, it's no excuse to push a terrible game and overcharge for them, that's just adding to the reason that people are scared to buy indie games.

I'm going to say "not recommended with caveats".
Tumblestone is simple. It's not ultra groundbreaking, but it's interesting. It's easy to pick up and, as far as I've played, easy enough to play without getting stumped.
Basically, it's kind of like Bust-A-Move, a bit, without the trajectory calculations, and then mixed with a crazy simplified Mahjong. You match three of the same color by shooting from the bottom until the board is empty. That's it, pretty much.
What I take issue with, personally, is the price. This isn't god's gift to puzzle games, it's ultra simple and it'd honestly work better as a mobile puzzle game for a buck or two in the Play Store rather than a full-blown puzzle game on desktop. It's clever and kind of fun, actually, but absolutely not worth $25.
When and if the price comes down, I may change my recommendation, but at its current price, I simply can't say I'd suggest anyone buy it. There are other puzzle alternatives on Steam that are just as good for far, far less money.

This is just a first impression.
Far Cry 2 is an interesting piece of work. It is an Ubisoft open world game, you know what I'm talking about. Go here do this, go there do something similar. And sure there's a story. But the world is not introduced well to you. The characters in the game are not very interesting. I've heard of some big bugs, but I haven't played enough to see any. And I don't intend to play any more.
The reason is not because of the graphic; the graphics are great considering the game was made in 2008. The reason is not because of the controls, which are tight and responsive. The reason is not because of the gunplay, which is fun. No, dear reader. The reason is because of one thing: respawning enemies. When you kill enemies in one area, and you come back to that area later, the enemies come back. Every. Single. Time. And the enemies are strong; just a few can bring you to your knees. Perhaps you get upgrades later that makes this less of a problem, but I spent most of my 2 hours with the game at the reloading screen. This breaks the game for me. FarCry turned into Rambro but once, it was Full Metal Jacket. A game about violence that isn't a power fantasy but rather a rare acknowledgement in gaming that violence is unpredictable, screwed up and frightening. Your gun is breaking, you have malaria, plans A-G have fallen apart and everything is on fire. The AI is still game AI, yes, never perfect, but these NPCs hunt, flank and stay under cover when you're shredding up an area with a mounted MG. And I hesitate to even call them "enemies" because the narrative makes it very clear that there are very few "Good Guys" in this horrible war, least of all the player character and his friends. Even if you stealth through everything and hit all your targets clean, you're still baseline playing as an opportunistic mercenary who uses blood diamonds as currency. If you enjoy games like Spec Ops: The Line, Kane & Lynch or Hotline Miami, games that use the language of game violence to unpack and interrogate the corroding effects of real world violence, then FarCry 2 is for you.
One simple difference between this FarCry and the later two entries in the series ups the tension level significantly and that's how you interact with the map. Instead of your standard issue Game Character Omniscience minimap in the corner, in FarCry 2 you must select your map like a weapon and take your eyes off the battlefield to look at it. No enemy icons either; you'd best be watching the brushline closely if you want to avoid an ambush. As a result, even though these graphics aren't as lush as those of FC3 or 4, I'm way, way more immersed in this game world, watching it closely for patrols and attacks. It's a game world that Does Not Like You and will spoil your plans, making it thoroughly satisfying and compelling to push back against. To my mind, the object of FC2 isn't to blast as many dudes as possible and wreck everything up but rather to make it through the narrative w/o your player character becoming a total monster in the process.
A complaint and an acknowledgement: FC2 definitely suffers from the "Africa as a single nation" problem that western media always struggles with. It's not as weird and icky as FC3's "Best Spring Break Evar" approach to a war story, but it still comes off somewhat tone deaf. And as for the infamous respawning checkpoints that you've read so much about, yes, the reports are accurate - the militias seem to get reinforcements in place awfully quick. That said, as I read complaints about them, part of me is always wondering "why aren't you sneaking past those by now? Save that ammo for the mission!" To me, FarCry 2 is a winner because it's an FPS about trying to stay out of gun battles.

The Elder Scrolls: Legends is the first of many (imo) CCGs from big publishers looking to cash in on the success of Hearthstone. This is Bethesda’s effort and it’s a good one. TES: L is similar to Hearthstone in many ways, with almost identical game modes. There are also card similarities with abilities such as guard, ward, last gasp and summon being identical to Hearthstones, albeit with different names (see my first impressions video for a more detailed analysis).
Cards in TES: L also cost mana (magicka here) and this goes up every turn, although there is no cap of 10 in this game. Where the game really differs from Hearthstone is the higher deck limit (50-70), attributes (card types), lanes and prophecy cards. Most matches feature two lanes and sometimes a lane gives a special effect to units. Prophecy cards can be played automatically for free when you lose runes. Your character has a certain number of runes that disappear as you lose health. Ongoing effects cards also add an extra dynamic. The higher deck number and card attributes mean there appears to be a great deal of customisation in terms of deck building. I’ve got a lot of experimenting to do in that area.
I’d definitely recommend trying it out, especially if you fancy a change from Hearthstone. There is some rng and luck involved as it’s hard to get away from that in these games, but this is the best free to play Hearthstone-ish CCG I’ve played since Blizzards monster.
One thing I’d like to see now this is on PC proper, is an improvement in the presentation. Blizzard is streets ahead in this department with numerous game boards that are all interactive. The soundtrack is also disappointing for an elder scrolls game and the card animations for spells are lacklustre. Improve these and you’d have a decent contender for the PC CCG throne.

I don't know about Hearthstone as I never played it, but I can't help but notice it's comparison with Magic the Gathering which I played for many years. Let me start off by saying I think this game is really good, if you've played MtG than you'll notice it's very similar yet with a slightly streamlined style which works very well. For a start you don't have to tap cards, and instead of declaring attackers and choosing defenders, this game has implemented a sytem where you directly choose who you want your creatures to attack. This makes the game play very smoothly and it's much quicker too. The drawback this game has in comparison however is that it does lack the same level of depth as MtG as there's less phases to the game, such as you can't case instant spells or react to enemy moves. However, what this game does so well is implement a few other mechanics which retain a level of depth which keeps the game challenging and engaging. One of these is the prophesy/rune system which allows you to draw a particular card in reaction to being attacked at certain stages of the game, this system actually allows for a bit of reaction play such as tapping down an attacker if they're making a critical attack in the last moment. Another great thing about the prophesy system is that it allows the losing player to draw extra cards which forces the later stages of the game to remain challenging for both players. Another interesting system is the lanes mechanic which means you have to plan ahead which side of the board you want to play cards, this works very well and adds yet more depth to the game.
As a MtG player I've found it very easy to translate my skills directly across to Elder Scrolls Legends, the colours mostly play the same rolls with a few aspects mixed around, there's also a lot of the same creature skills but with different names such as; breakthrough-trample, lethal-deathtouch, drain-lifelink, charge-haste, etc... although there's no flying. ESL although has it's own guard system which works well with the way it lets you choose attackers giving the defending player a sufficient way of protecting themselves.
I've played through the story mode which is really fun and the rewards are satisfying and allows for great fully customised decks. The soulstone system is great allowing you to gain extra cards of choice to further improve your decks strategy. The arena mode is also great allowing you to use tickets which can be bought with real money or earned in game coins and enter as sort tournament fighting against other real players where you draft a deck on the spot from card choices. The card art is wonderful, and although there's some aspect of pay to win I've found no problem with playing my decks against other players and not getting overpowered.

Although I haven't finished this, I am far enough into it (16 hours) to be quite comfortable giving this an easy thumbs up.
I really haven't played an isometric RPG since Fallout 2, well, not that there's a wide range of them out there. But that's a rather difficult act to follow. On the whole the combat is actually quite similar, though this does not have Fallout's body targeting system. That's honestly not a particularly big loss. I do think the combat could use a slightly better tutorial for newcomers, but in a few fights one gets the hang of it all the same. The AI is not overly punishing to you on normal. The game does have combat difficulty levels that allow you to twek your experience as you see fit.
Overall the story is quite good, and very well written for a video game, and I think is the biggest draw here. A RPG without a good story is just an immense slog. It's unusual to play a RPG that is neither a Japanese or American game and as such brings in a few different influences and ideas. I have to say, combining high fantasy stuff like elves and orcs and dragons with cyberpunk dystopia, it really doesn't add anything to the game world for me at all. At first I found it very hard to get my head around putting them together, or why one would do this. But it's also not enough to detract from what is an excellent story full of characters that have that video game just-enough-depth to be interesting. I enjoy how this is a game full of grey choices, where things are very rarely black and white. You will often not really be sure if you're helping the good guys or not, and really have to rely on your own feelings (or, if you like, your own persuit of money) to guide you.
The game has mod support through Steam Workshop including some fully functioning custom campaigns, and the game comes with an editor. I have not played any of these yet nor have I fiddled with the editor itself, but this is a clear bonus for those that really enjoy the game and want more.
On the whole I'm very comfortable calling this an excellent, and somewhat underplayed RPG title, that is far superior to certain larger franchises' offerings.

Great game overall.  If you like Shadowrun, or cyberpunk in general this might be right up your alley.  The game is much improved over Shadowrun Returns in terms of its mechanics, structure, and pacing.  I personally found the writing, story and character development to also be much more enjoyable and fleshed out than Returns managed.  The only thing I would suggest you consider is if you're okay with a somewhat darker tone, since this one leans more towards the black trenchcoat side of the spectrum than the pink mohawk.
Pros:
+The writing (The dialogue in particular is great and the story sets a fairly consitent tone)
+Never takes itself *too* seriously (Yes this is a somewhat dark story but it never forgets that it is a Shadowrun game and as such has some silly stuff as well)
+Mechanically the game is fun and most possible builds seem pretty viable, even on Hard difficulty
+Replay value (Both mechanically rolling different characters and narratively making different choices)
+Your core team of runners is almost always available and you don't have to hire on mercs or be a jack of all trades
+The soundtrack sets the mood well
Cons:
-Too many unavoidable ambushes (Open a door, enemies get free shots on you and you cannot position your team manually, often leaving them clumped and prime targets for AoEs)
-Over-reliance on a few of the etiquettes, others are fairly useless
I think that this game is a gem and probably the best computer RPG I've played since Baldur's Gate II.  At several points the game allows you to make your own connections to what is going on (What is your relationship to Monika? What sort of Shadowrunner ARE you?)  I love that it allows you to have teammates do things if your character can't deal with certain skillchecks (Have a low strength decker? Get Eiger or Glory to force a door for you!)  At its best it feels a bit like an actual tabletop RPG with all the dice-rolling abstracted out.  Even at its worst it's a pretty fun tactical RPG.  I'd absolutely recommend it to anyone who wants a good RPG or digs Shadowrun's aesthetic.

Fended off blood wizards and megacorporate security while scouring the matrix to free vat-grown sacrificial humans from their fate, this game achieves the juxtaposition of meat-/cyber-space that often epitomises cyberpunk action. I really, really enjoyed that. When it worked.
Some of the gameplay systems are a bit questionable (ambiguous extremes in dialogue, insufficient information to form the ideal team, not being able to simply outfit your entire crew - despite the wide array of weaponry, spells and decker gear on offer), but it's an enjoyable enough narrative experience for fans of cyberpunk that it stands in spite of those flaws. The game is prone to softlock in the matrix, arbitrarily being able to fix itself after a variable amount of time: at least a few occurances in my twenty hours played, it's been alt-f4 worthy.
There are a number of missable flags in this game, which in the context of playing with the sideaim of achievement acquisition is a bit disappointing. You even stand to miss out on missions outright if you're not consistently talking to everyone, or if you do things in a slightly incorrect order. That bothers me: it should at least be flagged that characters have unique dialogue. Saving early and often works to get around this, but my experience of the game featured some pretty lengthy save and load times (even playing on an SSD).
Cool game. Happy to have experienced it.

The goal being to come out of your adventure strong enough to defeat your opponent in the final showdown. Although highly, highly subjective to random chance it is still fun to experience so long as you do not mind losing because of something you have no control over. It also does not feel much like it requires real money to make any meaningful progress in.
The main problem is that the default system of building your own adventure is essentially the only one the game really has, and so if you get tired of it then that is pretty much the end. The system also does not feel as satisfying as playing cards against an opponent directly, which also leads to a more gradual feeling of dissatisfaction.
Best played with a person you know.

No tuve la oportunidad de jugar a este título cuando salió, y ni siquiera había jugado antes a las típicas aventuras gráficas de LucasArts.  No obstante, este juego me ha parecido fantástico.
El estilo artístico me encanta, los personajes son memorables, las historias y conversaciones divertidísimas. Este es, básicamente, un juego de puzzles; pero en mi opinión no son los puzzles los que te atraparán, sino la música, los personajes y los escenarios.
Los puzzles... pues son una locura. No tienen sentido. Eso no significa que no sean divertidos, todo lo contrario, pero muchas veces son tan locos que al resolverlos no sentirás que has resuelto un enigma, sino que pensarás que los desarrolladores estaban locos. No todos los puzzles son así, obviamente, pero pasarás tanto rato con ellos que serán los que te marquen.
El juego no es perfecto: el ritmo del juego es muy variable, ya que tiene un formato prácticamente episódico y algunas partes del juego se me antojan poco trabajadas; sobre todo si las comparamos con la joya de este juego: la ciudad de Rubacava.
En definitiva, un juego muy divertido,  limitado por las mecánicas de su época (donde los puzzles tenían que hacerte arrancar los pelos de la cabeza para ser considerados buenos)  y de ritmo y calidad variable, con unos personajes memorables, una música increíble y una dirección artística sobresaliente.

This is an example of a game that belongs in a museum. Witty humor, clever puzzles, and an amazing atmosphere ties everything together in this fantastic remaster. Buy it to support more LucasArt classics on Steam for the future.

Despite that, the characters are fantastic, the story is fantastic, the humor was spot on, and its because of that I could get past a few minor graphical hitches here and there or any weird controller issues/puzzle solutions. This is an exceptionally great game that I had a wonderful time with, and would definitely reccomend to anybody.

There's not much I can say here that hasn't already been covered well by release day reviews in The Escapist, Polygon, PC Gamer, Venture Beat, Pixel Related or Recombu, all of them absolutely glowing.  What I can tell you is that this made my face hurt.  Why?  I was laughing out loud so much my cheeks were sore the next day.  What I can tell you is that my wife banned me from playing the game after she went to bed, because the roaring laughter at a new spittoon gag or crazy dialog about a cow would wake her.  And what I can tell you is that I had hours and hours of fun (about 50 so far) solving all the puzzles and crazy, quirky side quests.
I don't 100% a lot of games but you can bet the farm I'm going to get every cheevo on this one.  Every piece of writing is the highly polished, subtle, droll humor you expect if you have played Kingdom of Loathing.  Chock full of references not just to American pop culture and nerd-friendly media, but also deep cuts in literature and tons of gaming tropes.  Everything from undergraduate D&D games to Skeleton fort is represented in hilarious fashion.
Polygon says that it's "a genuinely deep and hilarious game" and I can't overstate my agreement.  It's a huge game, bigger than you think before you buy it, bigger than you think when you start playing it, and bigger than you think when you finish your first playthrough.  Don't be deceived by the low price point, this is hours and hours of face-hurting levels of belly laughs and incredible fun.  The systems are fun, the puzzles have a great range of difficulty, and combat is satisfying and offers a diverse selection of available approaches.
If you like Kingdom of Loathing, if you like things that are funny, if you like nerdy or pop culture references, or if you just like silly walks or horrifically disgusting descriptions of spittoons, you'll love the game.   If you only like games that are in all purple colors and Japanese, you probably will not.
